Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 1 (part 1 of 2):

Surat al-An'am has one hundred and seventy-six verses. It is Meccan, or it is Medinan.

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿All praise is due to God, who created the heavens and the earth and made the darknesses and the light. Yet those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord.﴾ ﴿It is He who created you from clay, then decreed a term, and a term specified with Him. Yet you still doubt.﴾ [Al-An'am: 2] ﴿And He is God in the heavens and on the earth. He knows your secret and your open, and He knows what you earn.﴾ [Al-An'am: 3] ﴿And no sign from the signs of their Lord comes to them but they turn away from it.﴾ [Al-An'am: 4] ﴿So they have denied the truth when it came to them, and there will come to them the news of what they used to mock.﴾ [Al-An'am: 5] ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them, whom We had established on the earth in ways We have not established you, and We sent the sky upon them with abundant rain, and made the rivers flow beneath them? Then We destroyed them for their sins, and We produced after them another generation.﴾ [Al-An'am: 6] ﴿And if We had sent down to you a Book on paper, and they had touched it with their hands, those who disbelieve would have said, "This is nothing but manifest magic."﴾ [Al-An'am: 7] ﴿And they say, "Why was an angel not sent down to him?" If We had sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided, and they would not then be reprieved.﴾ [Al-An'am: 8] ﴿And if We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man, and We would have confused them as they confuse themselves.﴾ [Al-An'am: 9] ﴿Messengers before you were mocked, but those who scoffed at them were encompassed by what they used to mock.﴾ [Al-An'am: 10] ﴿Say, "Travel through the earth and then observe how was the end of the deniers."﴾ [Al-An'am: 11]

Al-tin (clay): a known substance. From it one says: "Tana al-kattan yatinuhu" (he plastered the flax with clay) and "Tinuhu ya hadha" (O you, plaster it with clay).

Al-qarn (generation): a community united within a period of time. From it comes the saying "The best generations are my generation" (khayr al-qurun qarni). Its root meaning is elevation above a thing, and from it comes "qarn al-jabal" (the peak of the mountain). They were named thus because of the elevation of age. It has also been said that it derives from "qaranta al-shay'a bi al-shay'" (I joined one thing to another): I placed it beside it or facing it. They were named thus because some of them are joined to others. It has also been said that they were named thus because a period of time gathered them, a period whose extent is the one in which the people of that time are most commonly joined together. This is the view preferred by al-Zajjaj.

The duration of a qarn is one hundred and twenty years, said by Zurara ibn Awfa and Iyas ibn Mu'awiya. Or it is one hundred years, said by the majority. They argued for this with the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Abdullah ibn Bishr: "You will live a qarn," and he lived a hundred years. He also said: "Do you see this night of yours? At the end of a hundred years, none of those who are upon the earth today will remain." Ibn Umar supported that it is the passing of that generation. Or it is eighty years, related by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. Or it is seventy years, related by al-Farra'. Or it is sixty years, based on his (peace be upon him) saying: "The arena of deaths is between sixty and seventy," or "forty." This was said by Ibn Sirin, who traced it to the Prophet (ﷺ), and al-Zahrawi related it in the same way from the Prophet (ﷺ). Or it is thirty years. It is related from Abu Ubayda that he said: "They consider that the distance between two qarns is thirty." This was related by al-Naqqash. Or it is twenty years, related by al-Hasan al-Basri. Or it is eighteen years. Or it is the average lifespan of the people of that time. This is good, because earlier nations had people who lived four hundred years and three hundred, and some lived a common lifespan, and some lived more or less than that. Likewise is the difference among Muslims, and God knows best. It appears that he looked to the furthest extreme and the nearest extreme. Whoever looked to the furthest limit said: from sixty and above, up to one hundred and twenty. [p-66] Whoever looked to the nearest said: twenty, thirty, forty.

Ibn Atiyya said: the qarn is when the elders die and then children are born, and this appears from His saying: ﴿and We produced after them another generation﴾ [Al-An'am: 6]. Ibn Atiyya is referring to those who limited it to forty or less, which are layers (tabaqat) and not qurun.

It has been said: the qarn is a people gathered together. I say: [this applies] whether they are many or few years, based on his saying: "The best generations are my generation," meaning his companions. Qus said:

"Among those who passed away, the first generations, there are insights for us."

Another said:

"When the people in whom you lived have gone, and you are left among a people, you are a stranger."

It has also been said: the qarn is time itself, so his saying "min qarnin" is to be read as "min ahli qarnin" (from the people of a generation).

Al-tamakkun (establishment) is the opposite of inability. Tamkin from a thing is what makes the action possible by means of the instruments and powers. It is more complete than qadar (bestowing capacity), because qadar is merely granting power, and one who has power over a thing may still be unable to act for lack of an instrument. It has been said: tamkin from a thing is the removal of the barrier between the one who is established and that which he is established over. Al-Zamakhshari said: "makkana lahu fi al-ard" means he made a place for him; similar is "ardun lahu" (land for him). His establishment of him in the earth means his firm placement in it.

Al-midrar: the one that is continuous. One says "matarun midrar" (abundant rain) and "ata'un midrar" (abundant gift). It is more often used for rain. Midrar is on the pattern mif'al from al-darr (flow), for emphasis, like "midhkar" (one who produces many males), "mi'nath" (one who produces many females), and "mihdhar" (one who talks much).

Al-insha' (creation): creating and bringing into being without a prior cause. Whoever initiates something has produced it (ansha'ahu). Al-nasha' means the newly created, its singular is nashi', like the pattern "khadim" and "khadam" (servant and servants).

Al-qirtas: the name of what is written upon, whether parchment, paper, or other things. The poet, who is Zuhayr, said:

"Upon it are grooves from the traces of its dwellers, as the pen moves back and forth on its qirtas."

It is not called qirtas unless it is written upon. If it is not written upon, it is tirs, or kaghad, or waraq. The kasra of the qaf is more common in usage and more famous than its damma. It is non-Arabic, and its plural is qarati.

Haqa yahiqu haqan, huyuqan, and hayaqan: meaning "ahata" (surrounded). This was said by al-Dahhak. It is not used except for evil. The poet said:

"He trampled the chargers of horses onto the ruin of their homes, and there encompassed them, from the might of his lord, an encompassing evil."

Al-Farra' said: haqa bihi means the evil consequence of his scheming returned upon him. Al-Nadr said: it became obligatory upon him. Muqatil said: it turned around (dara). It was also said: it descended and alighted. Whoever derived it from al-hawq, which is what surrounds a thing, his statement is not correct, because the two roots differ. Likewise whoever said its origin is haqqa, and one of the two qafs was changed to a ya', as they said in "tazannantu" becoming "taznayatu," because that is a claim without evidence for its soundness.

Sakhira minhu: he mocked him. Al-sukhriyya (ridicule), al-istihza' (mockery), and al-tahakkum (scorn) have closely related meanings.

Aqibat al-shay': its end and what it returns to.

﴿All praise is due to God, who created the heavens and the earth and made the darknesses and the light, yet those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord.﴾ This surah is entirely Meccan. Al-Kisa'i said: except two verses that were revealed in Medina, and they are ﴿Say, "Who revealed the Book"﴾ [Al-An'am: 91] and what is connected to it.

Ibn Abbas said: it was revealed at night in Mecca, with seventy thousand angels around it, crying out in glorification, except six verses: ﴿Say, "Come, I will recite"﴾ [Al-An'am: 151]; ﴿They did not measure God with true measure﴾ [Al-An'am: 91]; ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against God﴾ [Al-An'am: 93]; ﴿If you could see when the wrongdoers﴾ [Al-An'am: 93]; ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book know it﴾ [Al-An'am: 114]; ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recognize it as they recognize their sons﴾ [Al-An'am: 20]. End of quote. It is also related from him, and from Mujahid and al-Kalbi, that three verses of it were revealed in Medina: ﴿Say, "Come, I will recite"﴾ [Al-An'am: 151] up to His saying ﴿that you may be mindful﴾ [Al-An'am: 153].

Qatada said: except ﴿They did not measure God with true measure﴾ [Al-An'am: 91] and ﴿It is He who produced gardens﴾ [Al-An'am: 141].

Ibn al-Arabi mentioned that His saying ﴿Say, "I do not find"﴾ [Al-An'am: 145] was revealed in Mecca on the Day of Arafa.

The connection between the opening of this surah and the end of al-Ma'ida: when He (exalted is He) mentioned what the Christians said about Jesus and his mother, that they were two gods besides God, and that exchange took place, and He mentioned the reward of the truthful, He followed that with the fact that to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is in them, and that He is capable of everything. He then mentioned that all praise is due to Him, encompassing all praises, so it is impossible that a partner in divinity could exist with Him who could be praised. Then He drew attention to the cause that necessitates all praises, and that necessitates that the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is in them belongs to Him, by the attribute ﴿who created the heavens and the earth﴾, because the one who brings a thing into being and alone invents it has authority and sovereignty over it. Since the Christians' statement about Jesus and their disbelief in that had preceded, and the mention of the truthful and their reward, He followed with ﴿created the heavens and the earth﴾ with "and made the darknesses and the light", and this was suitable to both the disbeliever and the truthful.

The explanation of ﴿All praise is due to God﴾ was given at the beginning of al-Fatiha. The explanation of the creation of the heavens and the earth is in His saying ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Al-Baqara: 164] in al-Baqara.

As for "ja'ala" (made) here, Ibn Atiyya said: no meaning other than this is permissible. Consider why the heavens and the earth were specified with "khalaqa" (created), while the darknesses and the light with "ja'ala" (made).

Al-Zamakhshari said: "ja'ala" takes one object when it means "ahdatha" (brought into existence) and "ansha'a" (produced), as in His saying "ja'ala al-zulumat wa al-nur" (He made the darknesses and the light), and it takes two objects when it means "sayyara" (turned something into something), as in His saying ﴿and they made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾ [Al-Zukhruf: 19]. The difference between khalq (creation) and ja'l (making) is that khalq contains the meaning of measuring and determining, while ja'l contains the meaning of transforming, like bringing something into being from something, or changing one thing into another, or moving it from one place to another. Among this is ﴿and made from it its mate﴾ [Al-A'raf: 189] and ﴿and made the darknesses and the light﴾, because the darknesses are of dense bodies, and the light is from fire.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 1 (part 2 of 2):

﴿He made you pairs﴾ [Fatir: 11], ﴿Has he made the gods one God?﴾ [Sad: 5]. End of quote. As for his claim that (ja'ala, "to make") in His words ﴿and they made the angels﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 19] means (sayyara, "to turn into"), this is not correct, because they did not turn the angels into females. Some grammarians said only that it means (sammā, "to name"). As for al-Tabari's statement that (ja'ala) here is the one that operates on the beginning of a sentence (taṣarrafu fi ṭaraf al-kalam), as when you say, "I began to do such-and-such" (ja'altu af'alu kadhā), it is as though he said: "The making of its darkening and its illumination is confusion." This is because those [verbs] are verbs of approximation (af'al al-muqarabah, verbs that enter upon the mubtada' and khabar), while the one in the verse takes a single object (maf'ul wahid). So the two are different in meaning and usage. It was fitting to coordinate the second relative clause (silah), with its complement, of the plural "darknesses" and the singular "light," with the first relative clause, which concerns the plural "heavens" and the singular "earth." The discussion of the plural of "heavens," the singular of "earth," the plural of "darknesses," and the singular of "light" has already been presented in al-Baqarah. There is disagreement about what is meant here by ﴿the darknesses and the light﴾. Qatadah, al-Suddi and the majority said: the night and the day. Ibn Abbas said: polytheism (shirk), hypocrisy (nifaq) and disbelief (kufr), while the light is Islam, faith (iman), prophethood and certainty (yaqin). Al-Hasan said: disbelief and faith, which is a summary of Ibn Abbas's view, and he cited the verse of al-Baqarah as evidence for this. Qatadah also said: Paradise and Hellfire. God created Paradise and the spirits of the believers from light, and Hellfire and the spirits of the disbelievers from darkness. So on the Day of Resurrection the spirits of the believers are judged to Paradise, because they were created from light, and the disbelievers to Hellfire, because they were created from darkness. It was also said: the bodies and the spirits. It was said: the desires of the souls and the secrets of the hearts. It was said: ignorance and knowledge. Mujahid said: what is meant is the literal darkness and light, because the zanadiqa (heretics) used to say: God creates the light and everything good, and Iblis creates the darkness and everything ugly, so it was revealed as a refutation of them. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: in this there are two views. One is that they are the two perceptible matters, and this is the literal meaning. The second is what was reported earlier from Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan, and it is figurative. Al-Wahidi said: it is to be taken as both literal and figurative together; it is not possible to take it as one of the two alone. End of summary. Abu Abdullah al-Razi also said: darkness is not an expression for an existential quality (kayfiyya wujudiyya) opposed to light. The evidence for this is that if two people sit near a lamp and another sits far from it, the distant one sees the near one and sees that air as clear and bright, while the near one does not see the distant one and sees that air as dark. If darkness were an existential quality, it would be present in relation to these two persons, and since this is not the case, we know that darkness is not an existential quality. Once this is established, we say: the non-existence of created things precedes their existence, so darkness precedes light in reality, and so it is necessary to place it before light in wording. What strengthens this is what is reported in the divine reports (al-akhbar al-ilahiyya): that He, exalted is He, created creation in darkness, then sprinkled upon them of His light.

Ibn Umar reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Indeed God created His creation in darkness, then cast upon them His light. Whoever is struck by that light on that day is guided, and whoever misses it goes astray." End of quote. Abu Abdullah ibn Abi al-Fadl said: his statement about darkness is an error; rather, it is an expression for an existential quality opposed to light. The evidence for this is His words: ﴿and made the darknesses and the light﴾, and non-existence is not said to be "made." Then (thumma, "then") as is established in the Arabic language, its origin is for sequence in time. Ibn Atiyya said: (thumma) indicates the ugliness of the act of ﴿those who disbelieved﴾, because the meaning is: His creation of the heavens and the earth and other things has been established, His signs have shone forth, and His favor in that has become clear. Then after all this they have made equals to their Lord. So this is like when you say: "O so-and-so, I gave you, I honored you, and I did good to you, then you insult me," meaning: after the clarity of all this. If the conjunction in this and similar cases were with (wa, "and"), reproach would not follow, as it does with (thumma). End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "What is the meaning of (thumma)?" I say: it expresses astonishment (istib'ad) that they would make equals to Him after the clarity of the signs of His power. Likewise ﴿Then you still doubt﴾ [Al-An'am: 2] expresses astonishment that you would doubt Him after it has been established that He gives you life, causes you to die, and resurrects you. End of quote.

What Ibn Atiyya held, that (thumma) is for reproach, and what al-Zamakhshari held, that (thumma) is for astonishment, is not correct, because (thumma) was not laid down for that. Rather, reproach or astonishment is understood from the context of the speech, not from the denotation of (thumma). I know of no grammarian who mentioned this. Here (thumma) is for sequence in time, and it conjoins a nominal sentence to a nominal sentence. God, exalted is He, informed that praise is due to Him, and drew attention to the reason that calls for praise from all people, which is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the darknesses and the light. Then He informed that those who disbelieve in Him make equals, so they do not praise Him.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: If you ask, "To what is the statement ﴿then those who disbelieved﴾ conjoined?" I say: either it is conjoined to His words ﴿Praise be to God﴾, in the sense that God deserves praise for what He created, since He created it only as a blessing, ﴿then those who disbelieved in their Lord make equals﴾, so they deny His blessings. Or it is conjoined to His words ﴿who created the heavens and the earth﴾, in the sense that He created what He created, which none other than Him is able to create, and then they make equal to Him what has no power over any of it. End of quote. This second possibility which he allowed is not permissible, because in that case it would be conjoined to the relative clause (silah), and what is conjoined to a relative clause is itself a relative clause. If you made the sentence ﴿then those who disbelieved﴾ a relative clause, this construction would not be valid, because there is no connecting pronoun (rabit) in it linking the relative clause to the relative pronoun, except if it is explained as in the saying of the Arabs, "Abu Sa'id, whom I related from al-Khudri," meaning: "whom I related from him." Then the apparent noun would stand in the place of the pronoun, so it would be as though it said: "then those who disbelieved in Him make equals." This is so rare that it cannot be used as a rule, and the Book of God should not be made to bear it, especially when there is a preference for reading it as the correct and eloquent construction.

As for (those who disbelieved, alladhina kafaru), its apparent meaning is generality, so it includes idol-worshippers and the People of the Book: the Christians worshipped the Messiah, the Jews worshipped Uzair, and they took their rabbis as lords besides God, and the Magians worshipped fire, and the Manichaeans worshipped light. As for whoever restricts "those who disbelieved" to the Manichaeans, as Qatadah did, or to idol-worshippers, or to the Magians, since they said, "Death is from Ahriman, and life is from God," or to the People of the Book, as Ibn Abi Abza did, no evidence for such restriction appears. The preposition (bi, "with/by") in (bi-rabbihim, "with their Lord") may be connected to (ya'dilun, "they make equal"), and the (bi) would then have the sense of (an, "away from"), meaning: they turn away from Him to another, something that creates nothing and has no power. Or the meaning may be: they make equal to Him another, meaning they place another on par with Him in taking it as lord and god, and in creating and bringing into existence. To make one thing equal to another (adl al-shay' bi-al-shay') is to place it on par with it. In the verse there is a refutation of the Qadariyya in their saying: "Good is from God, and evil is from man," so they made equal to Him another in creating and bringing into existence.

﴿He is the One who created you from clay﴾ [Al-An'am: 2]. Its apparent meaning is that we are created from clay. Al-Mahdawi, Makki and al-Zahrawi mentioned this from a group. So the sperm (nutfah) from which a human is created originally comes ﴿from clay﴾ [Al-An'am: 2], then God turns it into sperm. Ibn Atiyya said: This follows from the view of those who say that after generation and numerous transformations it returns to sperm, and that is rejected by the usuliyyun (scholars of the principles of jurisprudence). Al-Nahhas said: It is possible that God created the sperm ﴿from clay﴾ [Al-An'am: 2] literally, then transformed it until a human came from it. End of quote. Abu Nu'aym al-Hafiz reported from Buraydah ibn Mas'ud a hadith about creation, at its end: "and He takes the dust that will be buried in his grave, and kneads his sperm with it," and that is His words, exalted is He: ﴿From it We created you, and into it We return you﴾ [Ta-Ha: 55], and so on. It was also transmitted from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "No child is born except that some of the dust of its grave has been scattered upon it." Abu Abdullah al-Razi said, in summary: I have another view on this, which is that the human is created from the seed (mani) and the menstrual blood, which are generated from foods, and foods are either animal or plant. The account of how they are generated is like the account of the human, or they are plant-based, and so the generation of the human from plant-based food is established, and that food is generated from clay. So every human is generated from clay. This view is closer to the truth. End of quote. This which he mentioned as his own additional view, which he says is closer to the truth, is an elaboration of what the exegetes related from a group. Ibn Atiyya said regarding it that it is rejected by the usuliyyun, meaning the view about generation and transformations. What is well-known among the exegetes is that the one created ﴿from clay﴾ [Al-An'am: 2] here is Adam. Qatadah, Mujahid, al-Suddi and others said: the meaning is that Adam was created ﴿from clay﴾, and mankind is from Adam, and therefore He said: ﴿He created you from clay﴾ [Al-An'am: 2]. Ibn Sa'd mentioned in al-Tabaqat from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "People are the children of Adam, and Adam is from dust." One of the poets of the Jahiliyya said:

"And to the root of the earth my veins have been drawn, and this death strips me of my youth."

The commentators explained that "the root of the earth" (irq al-tharā) is Adam. Accordingly, the interpretation here involves an omitted noun (hadhf mudaf). Either in (khalaqakum, "He created you") meaning "He created your origin," or in (min tin, "from clay") meaning "from a root of clay and its branch."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 2–5 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Then He decreed a term, and a specified term is with Him; then you doubt.﴾ (*Qada*, "decreed," as in the Arabic *qada*): if it here means "measured and wrote," then *thumma* ("then") indicates sequence in mention, not in time, because that is prior to our creation, since it is an attribute of essence (*sifat dhat*). If it means "manifested" (*azhara*), then *thumma* indicates temporal sequence according to its original usage, because that is subsequent to our creation, so it is an attribute of act (*sifat fi'l*). The apparent sense of the indefiniteness of the two terms (*ajalayn*) is that God has left their matter undetermined.

Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ikrimah, Khasif and Qatadah said: the first term is the term of the worldly life, from the time of creation until death, and the second is the term of the Hereafter, because life in the Hereafter has no end, and no one knows the condition of this term except God the Exalted.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the first is his death through sleep, and the second is his death through dying. He also said: the first is the term of this world, and the second is the Hereafter. Mujahid also said: the first is the Hereafter, and the second is this world.

Ibn Zayd said: the first is the time of taking the covenant from the children of Adam when He brought them out from the loins of Adam, and the specified term is in this worldly life.

Abu Muslim said: the first is the term of those who have passed away, and the second is the term of those who remain. He described it as "specified with Him" because God alone is characterized by knowledge of it, unlike those who passed away, for when they died their terms became known.

It was said: the first is what lies between one's creation and one's death, and the second is what lies between death and resurrection, which is the *barzakh* (the intermediate realm).

It was said: the first is the measure of what has elapsed of each person's life, and the second is the measure of what remains.

It was said: the first is the term of the earlier nations, and the second is the term of this community.

It was said: the first is what we know, that there is no prophet after Muhammad (ﷺ), (p-71) and the second is from the Hereafter.

It was said: the first is what people know of the terms of the crescent moons, the years and the created beings, and the second is the establishment of the Hour.

It was said: the first is among the times of the crescent moons and what resembles them, and the second is a person's death.

Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid also said: ﴿decreed a term﴾ refers to the ending of the world, and the second refers to the beginning of the Hereafter.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: every person has two terms. If he is pious and keeps the ties of kinship, something is added to his term of life from the term of resurrection; and if it is the reverse, something is reduced from his term of life and added to the term of resurrection.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: every person has two terms, the natural (*tabi'i*) and the premature (*ikhtirami*). The natural is that which, if that temperament remained preserved from external accidents, its duration would end at the astronomical times. The premature is that which occurs through external causes, such as burning, drowning, the stings of insects and other separate matters. End of quote. This is the view of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school), which he attributed to them, saying: this is the view of the philosophers of Islam. End of quote.

The meaning of ﴿specified with Him﴾ is known to Him, or it is recorded in the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfuz*). "With Him" is a metaphor for His knowledge, not a reference to a place.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: an indefinite subject whose predicate is an adverbial phrase must have the predicate placed first, why then was it permissible to place it first in His saying ﴿and a specified term is with Him﴾?

I say: because it is specified by a qualifier, so it approaches a definite noun, like His saying: ﴿a believing slave is better than a polytheist﴾ (2:221). End of quote.

What he mentioned as the justification for beginning with an indefinite noun, namely that it is qualified, is not necessarily the only justification here, since the justification may be the detailed explanation (*tafsil*). Among the justifications for beginning with an indefinite noun is that the context is one of detailed explanation, as in the verse:

*When she weeps behind her, she turns toward him with one side, and the other side is not turned by us.*

We have previously discussed this line, and we explained that it is not permissible for *indana* ("by us") to be in the position of a qualifier here, but rather it must be in the position of a predicate.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: the common usage is to say "I have a good garment" (*indi thawbun jayyid*) and "I have a clever slave" (*li 'abdun kayyis*) and similar expressions. I say: what required it is that the meaning is "and whichever (*ayyu*) term is specified with Him," magnifying the matter of the Hour. Since this meaning is intended, the fronting became necessary. End of quote.

This is not permissible, because if the meaning is "and whichever term is specified with Him," then *ayyu* is a qualifier of an omitted noun, its full form being "and a term, whichever term is specified with Him." It is not permissible to omit a qualifier when it is *ayyu*, nor to omit its modified noun while retaining it. So if you say "I passed by whichever man" meaning "by a man, whichever man," it would not be permissible.

*Tamtarun* ("you doubt") means "you suspect" or "you dispute with the disputing of skeptics." *Tamari* (disputation) is argument on the basis of doubt, as some commentators have said.

The discussion of *thumma* here is like its discussion in His saying: ﴿Yet those who disbelieve﴾ (6:1). What appears to me is that His saying, ﴿It is He who created you﴾, in the form of address, is an *iltifat* (shift) from the third person, which is His saying ﴿Yet those who disbelieve﴾ (6:1). Although creation and the decreeing of the term are not specific to the disbelievers, since believers and disbelievers share in it, it is directed at the disbeliever in order to alert him to the origin of his creation, to God's decree over him, and to His power. I only said that it is a case of *iltifat* because His saying ﴿then you doubt﴾ cannot include in this address the one whom God has chosen with prophethood and faith.

[p. 72] ﴿And He is God in the heavens and on the earth; He knows your secret and your open deeds, and He knows what you earn﴾. When the preceding verses established complete power and free choice, this verse mentions what establishes complete knowledge. Drawing attention to these attributes indicates that He, exalted is He, is capable, choosing, and knowing of universals and particulars, and it refutes the doubts of those who deny the Return (al-ma'ad). The apparent reading is that (huwa) is a pronoun referring back to what the pronouns before it referred to, namely ﴿wa-Huwa Allah﴾ ("and He is God"). This is the view of the majority, as reported by al-Kirmani.

Abu Ali [al-Farisi] said: (huwa) is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n, the pronoun of the situation, which refers forward to what follows), (Allah) is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is what follows; the clause explains the pronoun of the matter. He resorted to this because, if it were not the pronoun of the matter, it would refer back to God, exalted is He, and the sense would become "God is God," forming a subject and predicate from two nouns identical in wording and meaning with no predicative relation between them, which is impermissible. For this reason, and God knows best, he interpreted the verse this way. Abu Ali said: the pronoun is the pronoun of the matter, (Allah) is the subject, and its predicate is (ya'lamu) ("He knows") in ﴿in the heavens and on the earth﴾, which is linked to (ya'lamu). The sense is: God knows ﴿in the heavens and on the earth﴾, ﴿your secret and your open deeds﴾.

Al-Zajjaj held that the phrase ﴿in the heavens﴾ is linked to what the name of God contains of meanings, just as one says: "the Commander of the Faithful is the caliph in the east and the west." Ibn Atiyya said: "In my view this is the best of the opinions, and the most comprehensive in preserving the eloquence of the wording and the solemnity of the meaning, and its clarification is that He intended to indicate His creation, the traces of His power, His encompassing and dominion, and similar attributes. So He gathered all of these in His saying ﴿wa-Huwa Allah﴾, i.e. the One to whom all these belong, ﴿in the heavens and on the earth﴾, as if He said: He is the Creator, the Provider, the Giver of life, the All-Encompassing, in the heavens and on the earth. As you say: Zayd is the sultan in al-Sham and Iraq. If you intended Zayd's essence, you would be speaking absurdly; but if the intent of your saying 'Zayd is the sultan' is the one who commands and forbids, who annuls and decrees, who dismisses and appoints in al-Sham and Iraq, and you put 'the sultan' in place of all these, it is eloquent and correct. Likewise, in the verse, the word ﴿Allah﴾ is placed in the position of those mentioned attributes." End of quotation.

What al-Zajjaj said, and what Ibn Atiyya explained, is correct in meaning, but the science of grammar (sina'at al-nahw) does not support it. They claimed that ﴿in the heavens﴾ is linked to the word ﴿Allah﴾ because of the meanings it contains. But not all of those meanings operate on the word; if they were all explicitly stated, they would not govern it. Rather, the governing in terms of the wording belongs to one of them, even though ﴿in the heavens﴾ is linked to all of them in terms of meaning. The better view is that the prepositional phrase is governed by what the word ﴿Allah﴾ contains of the meaning of divinity (al-uluhiyya), even though ﴿Allah﴾ is a proper name, because a adverbial phrase or prepositional phrase may be governed by a proper name through what it contains of meaning. As the poet said: "I am Abu al-Minhal, sometimes (ba'ḍa al-aḥyān)," where (ba'ḍa) is in the accusative by what Abu al-Minhal contains, as if he said: "I am the well-known one at certain times."

Al-Zamakhshari said something similar. He said: ﴿in the heavens﴾ is linked to the meaning of the name of God, as if it was said: He is the One worshipped in both of them. Compare His saying: ﴿wa-Huwa al-ladhi fi al-sama' Ilah wa-fi al-ard Ilah﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:84] ("And He is the one who is God in heaven and God on earth"), meaning: He is the one known for divinity, or the one singled out for divinity in them, or the one who is called God in them, with no partner in this name. End of quotation. Observe all his estimates: how he took the governing element as one of the meanings rather than all of them.

A group said (huwa) stands for an omitted attribute which is intended in meaning, as if it was said: He is the God who is worshipped ﴿in the heavens and on the earth﴾. Some estimated it as: He is God, the Manager ﴿in the heavens and on the earth﴾.

Another group said: ﴿wa-Huwa Allah﴾ is a complete sentence here, then the next part begins anew, and the prepositional phrase is linked to (ya'lamu).

Another group said: ﴿wa-Huwa Allah﴾ is complete, and ﴿in the heavens and on the earth﴾ is linked to the object of (ya'lamu), which is ﴿your secret and your open deeds﴾, and the sense is: He knows your secret and your open deeds in the heavens and on the earth. This is weak, because it involves placing the object of the verbal noun (the relative clause's object) before it. It is strange that al-Nahhas said: "This is among the best that has been said about it."

Another group said: it is the pronoun of the matter, Allah is nominative as subject, and its predicate is ﴿in the heavens﴾; the clause is a predicate of the pronoun of the matter, and the sentence is complete. Then he begins anew, saying: ﴿and on the earth He knows your secret and your open deeds﴾, i.e. He knows on the earth.

Ibn Jarir said something similar, except that (huwa) refers back to what the pronouns referred to before, and is not the pronoun of the matter.

It was also said: ﴿in the heavens﴾ is linked to His saying (taksibun) ("you earn"). This is an error, because (ma) is a relative pronoun linked to (taksibun), and whether it is a verbal particle (ḥarf maṣdarī, a particle forming a verbal noun) or a noun meaning (alladhi, "that which"), it is impermissible to place the complement of the relative clause before the relative word.

It was also said: ﴿in the heavens﴾ is a circumstantial element (ḥal) of the verbal noun which is ﴿your secret and your open deeds﴾, placed before the element it describes and before the governing word. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that ﴿Allah in the heavens﴾ be a predicate following a predicate, meaning that He is God, and that He is in the heavens and the earth, in the sense that He knows what is in them, nothing of it being hidden from Him, as if His essence were in them. But this is weak, because the prepositional phrase introduced by (fi, "in") does not indicate a specific attribute; it indicates only a general state of being. Upon these views the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of this verse is built.

The people of knowledge went to these interpretations, and departed from the apparent meaning of ﴿in the heavens and on the earth﴾, because of what rational proof establishes: that God, exalted is He, cannot dwell in places, cannot touch bodies, cannot be opposite them, and cannot be confined to a direction. Ibn Atiyya stated its meaning and part of its wording.

In His saying ﴿He knows your secret﴾ to the end, there is a statement which implicitly contains a warning and a rebuke. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: By "secret" is meant the qualities of the hearts, which are motives and restraints, and by "open" are meant the actions of the limbs. The secret is mentioned first because mentioning the agent of an act is the combination of power with motive; the motive, which belongs to the category of the secret, is what influences the deeds of the limbs called "open." It is established that knowledge of the cause is the cause of knowledge of the effect, and the cause precedes the effect, and what is prior in essence must be placed first in wording. End of quotation.

Al-Tabrizi said: its meaning is: He knows what you conceal of your deeds and intentions, and what you reveal of your deeds. ﴿What you earn﴾ is general to all beliefs, sayings, and actions. The earning (kasb) of each person is his deed which leads to bringing about benefit or warding off harm, and for this reason it is not predicated of God, exalted is He.

Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: In the beginning of his statement there is something of the meaning of al-Zamakhshari's statement. His saying ﴿what you earn﴾ must be understood as what a person deserves for his deed of reward or punishment. It is thus taken to mean what is acquired (al-mukatasab), as one says: "this wealth is the earnings (kasb) of so-and-so," i.e. what he acquired. It is impermissible to take it to mean the earning itself, for that would necessitate joining a thing to itself. This verse is a refutation of the Mu'attilah (those who deny God's attributes), the Thanawiyya (dualists), the Hashwiyya (literalists who fill the text with crude meanings), and the philosophers. End of quotation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "What is the position of His saying ﴿He knows your secret and your open deeds﴾?" I answer: if the meaning is "the One singled out for divinity," then it is a confirmation of this, because the one whose knowledge equally encompasses secret and public is God alone. Likewise if you make ﴿in the heavens﴾ a predicate following a predicate; otherwise, it is an independent statement, or a third predicate. End of quotation. This follows the view of those who permit the subject to have multiple predicates.

[p. 73] ﴿And no sign comes to them from among the signs of their Lord except that they turn away from it﴾. The first (min) ("from") is redundant (za'ida), for the purpose of encompassing the whole category; the meaning of its redundancy is that what follows it is the object governed by what precedes it, the agent of (ta'tihim, "comes to them"). When the indefinite noun after it is one that is used only in general negation, (min) serves to emphasize the encompassing, as in: "There is no one (min ahad) in the house." When it is one that may be used for encompassing, or for negating unity, or for negating completeness, then (min) indicates encompassing, as in: "No man (min rajul) stood." The second (min) is partitive (lil-tab'id). Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is: no proof ever appears to them from among the proofs whose consideration, reflection and inference are required, except that they turn away from it, leaving consideration, not turning to it, not raising their heads to it, through the scarcity of their fear and their contemplation of consequences. End of quotation.

Al-Zamakhshari's use of (qaṭṭ, "ever") with the present tense in his statement "no proof ever appears to them" is not good, because (qaṭṭ) is an adverb specific to the past tense, unless he meant by his saying "appears" the sense of "has appeared." There is no need to use that.

It was said: (the sign, al-ayah) here means the indicator of God's oneness and His singular divinity. It was also said: the message. It was also said: the miracle that breaks habit. It was also said: the Qur'an. The meaning of ﴿from it﴾ is: from accepting it or hearing it. Turning away (i'rad) is the opposite of turning toward, and it is a metaphor, since its literal meaning applies to bodies. The clause containing (kanu, "they were") and its complement is in the position of a circumstantial element (ḥal). Thus (ta'tihim, "comes to them") may have past meaning, by virtue of (kanu), or (kanu) may have present meaning, by virtue of (ta'tihim). The element described (dhu al-ḥal) is the pronoun in (ta'tihim). A verb in the past tense does not occur as a circumstantial clause except under one of two conditions: first, that it be preceded by a verb, as in this verse; second, that the past verb be preceded by (qad, "indeed"), as in: "Zayd has indeed struck Amr." This is a shift (iltifat) from address to third-person reference, and the pronoun refers back to ﴿those who disbelieved﴾. This verse includes a condemnation of those who disbelieved, in that they turn away from every sign that comes to them. Since the discourse earlier dealt first with monotheism, second with the Return, and third with establishing these two matters, it then mentioned what relates to establishing prophethood, and explained that they turned away from reflecting on the proofs. This indicates that blind imitation (taqlid) is invalid, and that reflection on the proofs is obligatory, and for this reason they are censured for their turning away from the proofs.

﴿So they have indeed denied the truth when it came to them﴾. (The truth, al-haqq) is the Qur'an, or Islam, or Muhammad, or the splitting of the moon, or the promise, or the threat; these are the views. What appears to be the case is that it is the sign that comes to them, and it is as if it was said: "they have denied the sign that comes to them," which is "the truth." Thus the apparent noun is used in place of the pronoun, because of the description of it as true, and its reality is that it is from the signs of God, exalted is He. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿So they have denied﴾ is that the (fa, "so") indicates sequence, and that their turning away from the sign was followed by denial. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿So they have denied﴾ is a response to an omitted statement, as if it was said: "If they are turning away from the signs, then they have denied something greater than any sign and more magnificent, namely the truth when it came to them, meaning the Qur'an, by which they were challenged despite their extreme eloquence, and they were unable to match it." End of quotation. There is no need for an omitted condition, since the speech is coherent without this assumption.

﴿So there will come to them the news of that at which they used to mock.﴾ This indicates that mockery had actually occurred from them. So the speech contains an elided conjoined element (ma'tuf mahdhuf), which the end of the verse indicates, and its implied meaning is: "and they mocked it, ﴿so there will come to them﴾." These are three stages that proceeded from these disbelievers: first, turning away from reflecting on the proofs; then turning away was followed by denial, which is more than turning away, since one who turns away may be heedless of a thing; then denial was followed by mockery, which is more than denial, since one who denies may not reach the point of mockery. This is the exaggeration in rejection. Al-naba' (the news; a report whose impact is great) is news whose impact is great. In the speech there is an elided modifier (hadhf mudaf): that is, ﴿there will come to them﴾ [the] news (anba') is implied. Some said: what is meant is what they were punished with in this world, of killing, captivity, plunder, expulsion and other things, and some restricted that to the Day of Badr. It was said: it is the punishment of the Hereafter. This sentence includes threat, rebuke and warning, as you say: "Do what you wish, the news will come to you." He attached the threat to mockery rather than to turning away and denial, because it encompasses both, since it is the utmost extreme in rejecting the truth.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is the Qur'an, that is, its reports and its circumstances, meaning: they will know at what they were mocking, and it will become clear to them that it was not a matter for mockery. That is at the sending down of punishment upon them in this world, or on the Day of Resurrection, or at the manifestation of Islam and the elevation of its word. End of quotation.

He, in his habit, is verbose and explains wording and meaning in ways that these two words do not indicate.

Here the restriction of denial to the truth (bi'l-haqq) occurs, and the softening through (sawfa). In al-Shu'ara' it says ﴿they have denied, so there will come to them﴾, because al-An'am was revealed before al-Shu'ara'; so the wording was complete in it, and it was omitted in al-Shu'ara', while it is intended in the first state. The omission matched the brevity in the particle of futurity, so he came with the letter sin (السين).

The apparent reading is that (ma) in His saying (ma kanu) is a relative pronoun (ism mawsul), meaning "that which," and the pronoun in (bihi) refers back to it. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it may be a verbal-noun particle (masdariyya), with the estimate "the news of their being mockers." In that case the pronoun in (bihi) refers back to the truth (al-haqq), not according to the view of al-Akhfash (the grammarian), who claimed that masdariyya (ma) is a noun, not a particle. There is no necessity compelling it to be masdariyya.

(p-75)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 2–5 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Then He decreed a term, and a specified term is with Him; then you doubt.﴾ (*Qada*, "decreed," as in the Arabic *qada*): if it here means "measured and wrote," then *thumma* ("then") indicates sequence in mention, not in time, because that is prior to our creation, since it is an attribute of essence (*sifat dhat*). If it means "manifested" (*azhara*), then *thumma* indicates temporal sequence according to its original usage, because that is subsequent to our creation, so it is an attribute of act (*sifat fi'l*). The apparent sense of the indefiniteness of the two terms (*ajalayn*) is that God has left their matter undetermined.

Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ikrimah, Khasif and Qatadah said: the first term is the term of the worldly life, from the time of creation until death, and the second is the term of the Hereafter, because life in the Hereafter has no end, and no one knows the condition of this term except God the Exalted.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the first is his death through sleep, and the second is his death through dying. He also said: the first is the term of this world, and the second is the Hereafter. Mujahid also said: the first is the Hereafter, and the second is this world.

Ibn Zayd said: the first is the time of taking the covenant from the children of Adam when He brought them out from the loins of Adam, and the specified term is in this worldly life.

Abu Muslim said: the first is the term of those who have passed away, and the second is the term of those who remain. He described it as "specified with Him" because God alone is characterized by knowledge of it, unlike those who passed away, for when they died their terms became known.

It was said: the first is what lies between one's creation and one's death, and the second is what lies between death and resurrection, which is the *barzakh* (the intermediate realm).

It was said: the first is the measure of what has elapsed of each person's life, and the second is the measure of what remains.

It was said: the first is the term of the earlier nations, and the second is the term of this community.

It was said: the first is what we know, that there is no prophet after Muhammad (ﷺ), (p-71) and the second is from the Hereafter.

It was said: the first is what people know of the terms of the crescent moons, the years and the created beings, and the second is the establishment of the Hour.

It was said: the first is among the times of the crescent moons and what resembles them, and the second is a person's death.

Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid also said: ﴿decreed a term﴾ refers to the ending of the world, and the second refers to the beginning of the Hereafter.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: every person has two terms. If he is pious and keeps the ties of kinship, something is added to his term of life from the term of resurrection; and if it is the reverse, something is reduced from his term of life and added to the term of resurrection.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: every person has two terms, the natural (*tabi'i*) and the premature (*ikhtirami*). The natural is that which, if that temperament remained preserved from external accidents, its duration would end at the astronomical times. The premature is that which occurs through external causes, such as burning, drowning, the stings of insects and other separate matters. End of quote. This is the view of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school), which he attributed to them, saying: this is the view of the philosophers of Islam. End of quote.

The meaning of ﴿specified with Him﴾ is known to Him, or it is recorded in the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfuz*). "With Him" is a metaphor for His knowledge, not a reference to a place.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: an indefinite subject whose predicate is an adverbial phrase must have the predicate placed first, why then was it permissible to place it first in His saying ﴿and a specified term is with Him﴾?

I say: because it is specified by a qualifier, so it approaches a definite noun, like His saying: ﴿a believing slave is better than a polytheist﴾ (2:221). End of quote.

What he mentioned as the justification for beginning with an indefinite noun, namely that it is qualified, is not necessarily the only justification here, since the justification may be the detailed explanation (*tafsil*). Among the justifications for beginning with an indefinite noun is that the context is one of detailed explanation, as in the verse:

*When she weeps behind her, she turns toward him with one side, and the other side is not turned by us.*

We have previously discussed this line, and we explained that it is not permissible for *indana* ("by us") to be in the position of a qualifier here, but rather it must be in the position of a predicate.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: the common usage is to say "I have a good garment" (*indi thawbun jayyid*) and "I have a clever slave" (*li 'abdun kayyis*) and similar expressions. I say: what required it is that the meaning is "and whichever (*ayyu*) term is specified with Him," magnifying the matter of the Hour. Since this meaning is intended, the fronting became necessary. End of quote.

This is not permissible, because if the meaning is "and whichever term is specified with Him," then *ayyu* is a qualifier of an omitted noun, its full form being "and a term, whichever term is specified with Him." It is not permissible to omit a qualifier when it is *ayyu*, nor to omit its modified noun while retaining it. So if you say "I passed by whichever man" meaning "by a man, whichever man," it would not be permissible.

*Tamtarun* ("you doubt") means "you suspect" or "you dispute with the disputing of skeptics." *Tamari* (disputation) is argument on the basis of doubt, as some commentators have said.

The discussion of *thumma* here is like its discussion in His saying: ﴿Yet those who disbelieve﴾ (6:1). What appears to me is that His saying, ﴿It is He who created you﴾, in the form of address, is an *iltifat* (shift) from the third person, which is His saying ﴿Yet those who disbelieve﴾ (6:1). Although creation and the decreeing of the term are not specific to the disbelievers, since believers and disbelievers share in it, it is directed at the disbeliever in order to alert him to the origin of his creation, to God's decree over him, and to His power. I only said that it is a case of *iltifat* because His saying ﴿then you doubt﴾ cannot include in this address the one whom God has chosen with prophethood and faith.

It is strange that al-Nahhas said: "This is among the best that has been said about it."

Another group said: it is the pronoun of the matter, Allah is nominative as subject, and its predicate is ﴿in the heavens﴾; the clause is a predicate of the pronoun of the matter, and the sentence is complete. Then he begins anew, saying: ﴿and on the earth He knows your secret and your open deeds﴾, i.e. He knows on the earth.

Ibn Jarir said something similar, except that (huwa) refers back to what the pronouns referred to before, and is not the pronoun of the matter.

It was also said: ﴿in the heavens﴾ is linked to His saying (taksibun) ("you earn"). This is an error, because (ma) is a relative pronoun linked to (taksibun), and whether it is a verbal particle (ḥarf maṣdarī, a particle forming a verbal noun) or a noun meaning (alladhi, "that which"), it is impermissible to place the complement of the relative clause before the relative word.

It was also said: ﴿in the heavens﴾ is a circumstantial element (ḥal) of the verbal noun which is ﴿your secret and your open deeds﴾, placed before the element it describes and before the governing word. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that ﴿Allah in the heavens﴾ be a predicate following a predicate, meaning that He is God, and that He is in the heavens and the earth, in the sense that He knows what is in them, nothing of it being hidden from Him, as if His essence were in them. But this is weak, because the prepositional phrase introduced by (fi, "in") does not indicate a specific attribute; it indicates only a general state of being. Upon these views the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of this verse is built.

The people of knowledge went to these interpretations, and departed from the apparent meaning of ﴿in the heavens and on the earth﴾, because of what rational proof establishes: that God, exalted is He, cannot dwell in places, cannot touch bodies, cannot be opposite them, and cannot be confined to a direction. Ibn Atiyya stated its meaning and part of its wording.

In His saying ﴿He knows your secret﴾ to the end, there is a statement which implicitly contains a warning and a rebuke. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: By "secret" is meant the qualities of the hearts, which are motives and restraints, and by "open" are meant the actions of the limbs. The secret is mentioned first because mentioning the agent of an act is the combination of power with motive; the motive, which belongs to the category of the secret, is what influences the deeds of the limbs called "open." It is established that knowledge of the cause is the cause of knowledge of the effect, and the cause precedes the effect, and what is prior in essence must be placed first in wording. End of quotation.

Al-Tabrizi said: its meaning is: He knows what you conceal of your deeds and intentions, and what you reveal of your deeds. ﴿What you earn﴾ is general to all beliefs, sayings, and actions. The earning (kasb) of each person is his deed which leads to bringing about benefit or warding off harm, and for this reason it is not predicated of God, exalted is He.

Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: In the beginning of his statement there is something of the meaning of al-Zamakhshari's statement. His saying ﴿what you earn﴾ must be understood as what a person deserves for his deed of reward or punishment. It is thus taken to mean what is acquired (al-mukatasab), as one says: "this wealth is the earnings (kasb) of so-and-so," i.e. what he acquired. It is impermissible to take it to mean the earning itself, for that would necessitate joining a thing to itself. This verse is a refutation of the Mu'attilah (those who deny God's attributes), the Thanawiyya (dualists), the Hashwiyya (literalists who fill the text with crude meanings), and the philosophers. End of quotation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "What is the position of His saying ﴿He knows your secret and your open deeds﴾?" I answer: if the meaning is "the One singled out for divinity," then it is a confirmation of this, because the one whose knowledge equally encompasses secret and public is God alone. Likewise if you make ﴿in the heavens﴾ a predicate following a predicate; otherwise, it is an independent statement, or a third predicate. End of quotation. This follows the view of those who permit the subject to have multiple predicates.

[p. 73] ﴿And no sign comes to them from among the signs of their Lord except that they turn away from it﴾. The first (min) ("from") is redundant (za'ida), for the purpose of encompassing the whole category; the meaning of its redundancy is that what follows it is the object governed by what precedes it, the agent of (ta'tihim, "comes to them"). When the indefinite noun after it is one that is used only in general negation, (min) serves to emphasize the encompassing, as in: "There is no one (min ahad) in the house." When it is one that may be used for encompassing, or for negating unity, or for negating completeness, then (min) indicates encompassing, as in: "No man (min rajul) stood." The second (min) is partitive (lil-tab'id). Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is: no proof ever appears to them from among the proofs whose consideration, reflection and inference are required, except that they turn away from it, leaving consideration, not turning to it, not raising their heads to it, through the scarcity of their fear and their contemplation of consequences. End of quotation.

Al-Zamakhshari's use of (qaṭṭ, "ever") with the present tense in his statement "no proof ever appears to them" is not good, because (qaṭṭ) is an adverb specific to the past tense, unless he meant by his saying "appears" the sense of "has appeared." There is no need to use that.

It was said: (the sign, al-ayah) here means the indicator of God's oneness and His singular divinity. It was also said: the message. It was also said: the miracle that breaks habit. It was also said: the Qur'an. The meaning of ﴿from it﴾ is: from accepting it or hearing it. Turning away (i'rad) is the opposite of turning toward, and it is a metaphor, since its literal meaning applies to bodies. The clause containing (kanu, "they were") and its complement is in the position of a circumstantial element (ḥal). Thus (ta'tihim, "comes to them") may have past meaning, by virtue of (kanu), or (kanu) may have present meaning, by virtue of (ta'tihim). The element described (dhu al-ḥal) is the pronoun in (ta'tihim). A verb in the past tense does not occur as a circumstantial clause except under one of two conditions: first, that it be preceded by a verb, as in this verse; second, that the past verb be preceded by (qad, "indeed"), as in: "Zayd has indeed struck Amr." This is a shift (iltifat) from address to third-person reference, and the pronoun refers back to ﴿those who disbelieved﴾. This verse includes a condemnation of those who disbelieved, in that they turn away from every sign that comes to them. Since the discourse earlier dealt first with monotheism, second with the Return, and third with establishing these two matters, it then mentioned what relates to establishing prophethood, and explained that they turned away from reflecting on the proofs. This indicates that blind imitation (taqlid) is invalid, and that reflection on the proofs is obligatory, and for this reason they are censured for their turning away from the proofs.

﴿So they have indeed denied the truth when it came to them﴾. (The truth, al-haqq) is the Qur'an, or Islam, or Muhammad, or the splitting of the moon, or the promise, or the threat; these are the views. What appears to be the case is that it is the sign that comes to them, and it is as if it was said: "they have denied the sign that comes to them," which is "the truth." Thus the apparent noun is used in place of the pronoun, because of the description of it as true, and its reality is that it is from the signs of God, exalted is He. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿So they have denied﴾ is that the (fa, "so") indicates sequence, and that their turning away from the sign was followed by denial. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿So they have denied﴾ is a response to an omitted statement, as if it was said: "If they are turning away from the signs, then they have denied something greater than any sign and more magnificent, namely the truth when it came to them, meaning the Qur'an, by which they were challenged despite their extreme eloquence, and they were unable to match it." End of quotation. There is no need for an omitted condition, since the speech is coherent without this assumption.

﴿So there will come to them the news of that at which they used to mock.﴾ This indicates that mockery had actually occurred from them. So the speech contains an elided conjoined element (ma'tuf mahdhuf), which the end of the verse indicates, and its implied meaning is: "and they mocked it, ﴿so there will come to them﴾." These are three stages that proceeded from these disbelievers: first, turning away from reflecting on the proofs; then turning away was followed by denial, which is more than turning away, since one who turns away may be heedless of a thing; then denial was followed by mockery, which is more than denial, since one who denies may not reach the point of mockery. This is the exaggeration in rejection. Al-naba' (the news; a report whose impact is great) is news whose impact is great. In the speech there is an elided modifier (hadhf mudaf): that is, ﴿there will come to them﴾ [the] news (anba') is implied. Some said: what is meant is what they were punished with in this world, of killing, captivity, plunder, expulsion and other things, and some restricted that to the Day of Badr. It was said: it is the punishment of the Hereafter. This sentence includes threat, rebuke and warning, as you say: "Do what you wish, the news will come to you." He attached the threat to mockery rather than to turning away and denial, because it encompasses both, since it is the utmost extreme in rejecting the truth.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is the Qur'an, that is, its reports and its circumstances, meaning: they will know at what they were mocking, and it will become clear to them that it was not a matter for mockery. That is at the sending down of punishment upon them in this world, or on the Day of Resurrection, or at the manifestation of Islam and the elevation of its word. End of quotation.

He, in his habit, is verbose and explains wording and meaning in ways that these two words do not indicate.

Here the restriction of denial to the truth (bi'l-haqq) occurs, and the softening through (sawfa). In al-Shu'ara' it says ﴿they have denied, so there will come to them﴾, because al-An'am was revealed before al-Shu'ara'; so the wording was complete in it, and it was omitted in al-Shu'ara', while it is intended in the first state. The omission matched the brevity in the particle of futurity, so he came with the letter sin (السين).

The apparent reading is that (ma) in His saying (ma kanu) is a relative pronoun (ism mawsul), meaning "that which," and the pronoun in (bihi) refers back to it. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it may be a verbal-noun particle (masdariyya), with the estimate "the news of their being mockers." In that case the pronoun in (bihi) refers back to the truth (al-haqq), not according to the view of al-Akhfash (the grammarian), who claimed that masdariyya (ma) is a noun, not a particle. There is no necessity compelling it to be masdariyya.

(p-75)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 2–5 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Then He decreed a term, and a specified term is with Him; then you doubt.﴾ (*Qada*, "decreed," as in the Arabic *qada*): if it here means "measured and wrote," then *thumma* ("then") indicates sequence in mention, not in time, because that is prior to our creation, since it is an attribute of essence (*sifat dhat*). If it means "manifested" (*azhara*), then *thumma* indicates temporal sequence according to its original usage, because that is subsequent to our creation, so it is an attribute of act (*sifat fi'l*). The apparent sense of the indefiniteness of the two terms (*ajalayn*) is that God has left their matter undetermined.

Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ikrimah, Khasif and Qatadah said: the first term is the term of the worldly life, from the time of creation until death, and the second is the term of the Hereafter, because life in the Hereafter has no end, and no one knows the condition of this term except God the Exalted.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the first is his death through sleep, and the second is his death through dying. He also said: the first is the term of this world, and the second is the Hereafter. Mujahid also said: the first is the Hereafter, and the second is this world.

Ibn Zayd said: the first is the time of taking the covenant from the children of Adam when He brought them out from the loins of Adam, and the specified term is in this worldly life.

Abu Muslim said: the first is the term of those who have passed away, and the second is the term of those who remain. He described it as "specified with Him" because God alone is characterized by knowledge of it, unlike those who passed away, for when they died their terms became known.

It was said: the first is what lies between one's creation and one's death, and the second is what lies between death and resurrection, which is the *barzakh* (the intermediate realm).

It was said: the first is the measure of what has elapsed of each person's life, and the second is the measure of what remains.

It was said: the first is the term of the earlier nations, and the second is the term of this community.

It was said: the first is what we know, that there is no prophet after Muhammad (ﷺ), (p-71) and the second is from the Hereafter.

It was said: the first is what people know of the terms of the crescent moons, the years and the created beings, and the second is the establishment of the Hour.

It was said: the first is among the times of the crescent moons and what resembles them, and the second is a person's death.

Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid also said: ﴿decreed a term﴾ refers to the ending of the world, and the second refers to the beginning of the Hereafter.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: every person has two terms. If he is pious and keeps the ties of kinship, something is added to his term of life from the term of resurrection; and if it is the reverse, something is reduced from his term of life and added to the term of resurrection.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: every person has two terms, the natural (*tabi'i*) and the premature (*ikhtirami*). The natural is that which, if that temperament remained preserved from external accidents, its duration would end at the astronomical times. The premature is that which occurs through external causes, such as burning, drowning, the stings of insects and other separate matters. End of quote. This is the view of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school), which he attributed to them, saying: this is the view of the philosophers of Islam. End of quote.

The meaning of ﴿specified with Him﴾ is known to Him, or it is recorded in the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfuz*). "With Him" is a metaphor for His knowledge, not a reference to a place.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: an indefinite subject whose predicate is an adverbial phrase must have the predicate placed first, why then was it permissible to place it first in His saying ﴿and a specified term is with Him﴾?

I say: because it is specified by a qualifier, so it approaches a definite noun, like His saying: ﴿a believing slave is better than a polytheist﴾ (2:221). End of quote.

What he mentioned as the justification for beginning with an indefinite noun, namely that it is qualified, is not necessarily the only justification here, since the justification may be the detailed explanation (*tafsil*). Among the justifications for beginning with an indefinite noun is that the context is one of detailed explanation, as in the verse:

*When she weeps behind her, she turns toward him with one side, and the other side is not turned by us.*

We have previously discussed this line, and we explained that it is not permissible for *indana* ("by us") to be in the position of a qualifier here, but rather it must be in the position of a predicate.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: the common usage is to say "I have a good garment" (*indi thawbun jayyid*) and "I have a clever slave" (*li 'abdun kayyis*) and similar expressions. I say: what required it is that the meaning is "and whichever (*ayyu*) term is specified with Him," magnifying the matter of the Hour. Since this meaning is intended, the fronting became necessary. End of quote.

This is not permissible, because if the meaning is "and whichever term is specified with Him," then *ayyu* is a qualifier of an omitted noun, its full form being "and a term, whichever term is specified with Him." It is not permissible to omit a qualifier when it is *ayyu*, nor to omit its modified noun while retaining it. So if you say "I passed by whichever man" meaning "by a man, whichever man," it would not be permissible.

*Tamtarun* ("you doubt") means "you suspect" or "you dispute with the disputing of skeptics." *Tamari* (disputation) is argument on the basis of doubt, as some commentators have said.

The discussion of *thumma* here is like its discussion in His saying: ﴿Yet those who disbelieve﴾ (6:1). What appears to me is that His saying, ﴿It is He who created you﴾, in the form of address, is an *iltifat* (shift) from the third person, which is His saying ﴿Yet those who disbelieve﴾ (6:1). Although creation and the decreeing of the term are not specific to the disbelievers, since believers and disbelievers share in it, it is directed at the disbeliever in order to alert him to the origin of his creation, to God's decree over him, and to His power. I only said that it is a case of *iltifat* because His saying ﴿then you doubt﴾ cannot include in this address the one whom God has chosen with prophethood and faith.

[p. 72] ﴿And He is God in the heavens and on the earth; He knows your secret and your open deeds, and He knows what you earn﴾. When the preceding verses established complete power and free choice, this verse mentions what establishes complete knowledge. Drawing attention to these attributes indicates that He, exalted is He, is capable, choosing, and knowing of universals and particulars, and it refutes the doubts of those who deny the Return (al-ma'ad). The apparent reading is that (huwa) is a pronoun referring back to what the pronouns before it referred to, namely ﴿wa-Huwa Allah﴾ ("and He is God"). This is the view of the majority, as reported by al-Kirmani.

Abu Ali [al-Farisi] said: (huwa) is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n, the pronoun of the situation, which refers forward to what follows), (Allah) is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is what follows; the clause explains the pronoun of the matter. He resorted to this because, if it were not the pronoun of the matter, it would refer back to God, exalted is He, and the sense would become "God is God," forming a subject and predicate from two nouns identical in wording and meaning with no predicative relation between them, which is impermissible. For this reason, and God knows best, he interpreted the verse this way. Abu Ali said: the pronoun is the pronoun of the matter, (Allah) is the subject, and its predicate is (ya'lamu) ("He knows") in ﴿in the heavens and on the earth﴾, which is linked to (ya'lamu). The sense is: God knows ﴿in the heavens and on the earth﴾, ﴿your secret and your open deeds﴾.

Al-Zajjaj held that the phrase ﴿in the heavens﴾ is linked to what the name of God contains of meanings, just as one says: "the Commander of the Faithful is the caliph in the east and the west." Ibn Atiyya said: "In my view this is the best of the opinions, and the most comprehensive in preserving the eloquence of the wording and the solemnity of the meaning, and its clarification is that He intended to indicate His creation, the traces of His power, His encompassing and dominion, and similar attributes. So He gathered all of these in His saying ﴿wa-Huwa Allah﴾, i.e. the One to whom all these belong, ﴿in the heavens and on the earth﴾, as if He said: He is the Creator, the Provider, the Giver of life, the All-Encompassing, in the heavens and on the earth. As you say: Zayd is the sultan in al-Sham and Iraq. If you intended Zayd's essence, you would be speaking absurdly; but if the intent of your saying 'Zayd is the sultan' is the one who commands and forbids, who annuls and decrees, who dismisses and appoints in al-Sham and Iraq, and you put 'the sultan' in place of all these, it is eloquent and correct. Likewise, in the verse, the word ﴿Allah﴾ is placed in the position of those mentioned attributes." End of quotation.

What al-Zajjaj said, and what Ibn Atiyya explained, is correct in meaning, but the science of grammar (sina'at al-nahw) does not support it. They claimed that ﴿in the heavens﴾ is linked to the word ﴿Allah﴾ because of the meanings it contains. But not all of those meanings operate on the word; if they were all explicitly stated, they would not govern it. Rather, the governing in terms of the wording belongs to one of them, even though ﴿in the heavens﴾ is linked to all of them in terms of meaning. The better view is that the prepositional phrase is governed by what the word ﴿Allah﴾ contains of the meaning of divinity (al-uluhiyya), even though ﴿Allah﴾ is a proper name, because a adverbial phrase or prepositional phrase may be governed by a proper name through what it contains of meaning. As the poet said: "I am Abu al-Minhal, sometimes (ba'ḍa al-aḥyān)," where (ba'ḍa) is in the accusative by what Abu al-Minhal contains, as if he said: "I am the well-known one at certain times."

Al-Zamakhshari said something similar. He said: ﴿in the heavens﴾ is linked to the meaning of the name of God, as if it was said: He is the One worshipped in both of them. Compare His saying: ﴿wa-Huwa al-ladhi fi al-sama' Ilah wa-fi al-ard Ilah﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:84] ("And He is the one who is God in heaven and God on earth"), meaning: He is the one known for divinity, or the one singled out for divinity in them, or the one who is called God in them, with no partner in this name. End of quotation. Observe all his estimates: how he took the governing element as one of the meanings rather than all of them.

A group said (huwa) stands for an omitted attribute which is intended in meaning, as if it was said: He is the God who is worshipped ﴿in the heavens and on the earth﴾. Some estimated it as: He is God, the Manager ﴿in the heavens and on the earth﴾.

Another group said: ﴿wa-Huwa Allah﴾ is a complete sentence here, then the next part begins anew, and the prepositional phrase is linked to (ya'lamu).

Another group said: ﴿wa-Huwa Allah﴾ is complete, and ﴿in the heavens and on the earth﴾ is linked to the object of (ya'lamu), which is ﴿your secret and your open deeds﴾, and the sense is: He knows your secret and your open deeds in the heavens and on the earth. This is weak, because it involves placing the object of the verbal noun (the relative clause's object) before it. It is strange that al-Nahhas said: "This is among the best that has been said about it."

Another group said: it is the pronoun of the matter, Allah is nominative as subject, and its predicate is ﴿in the heavens﴾; the clause is a predicate of the pronoun of the matter, and the sentence is complete. Then he begins anew, saying: ﴿and on the earth He knows your secret and your open deeds﴾, i.e. He knows on the earth.
