This indicates that blind imitation (taqlid) is invalid, and that reflection on the proofs is obligatory, and for this reason they are censured for their turning away from the proofs.

﴿So they have indeed denied the truth when it came to them﴾. (The truth, al-haqq) is the Qur'an, or Islam, or Muhammad, or the splitting of the moon, or the promise, or the threat; these are the views. What appears to be the case is that it is the sign that comes to them, and it is as if it was said: "they have denied the sign that comes to them," which is "the truth." Thus the apparent noun is used in place of the pronoun, because of the description of it as true, and its reality is that it is from the signs of God, exalted is He. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿So they have denied﴾ is that the (fa, "so") indicates sequence, and that their turning away from the sign was followed by denial. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿So they have denied﴾ is a response to an omitted statement, as if it was said: "If they are turning away from the signs, then they have denied something greater than any sign and more magnificent, namely the truth when it came to them, meaning the Qur'an, by which they were challenged despite their extreme eloquence, and they were unable to match it." End of quotation. There is no need for an omitted condition, since the speech is coherent without this assumption.

﴿So there will come to them the news of that at which they used to mock.﴾ This indicates that mockery had actually occurred from them. So the speech contains an elided conjoined element (ma'tuf mahdhuf), which the end of the verse indicates, and its implied meaning is: "and they mocked it, ﴿so there will come to them﴾." These are three stages that proceeded from these disbelievers: first, turning away from reflecting on the proofs; then turning away was followed by denial, which is more than turning away, since one who turns away may be heedless of a thing; then denial was followed by mockery, which is more than denial, since one who denies may not reach the point of mockery. This is the exaggeration in rejection. Al-naba' (the news; a report whose impact is great) is news whose impact is great. In the speech there is an elided modifier (hadhf mudaf): that is, ﴿there will come to them﴾ [the] news (anba') is implied. Some said: what is meant is what they were punished with in this world, of killing, captivity, plunder, expulsion and other things, and some restricted that to the Day of Badr. It was said: it is the punishment of the Hereafter. This sentence includes threat, rebuke and warning, as you say: "Do what you wish, the news will come to you." He attached the threat to mockery rather than to turning away and denial, because it encompasses both, since it is the utmost extreme in rejecting the truth.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is the Qur'an, that is, its reports and its circumstances, meaning: they will know at what they were mocking, and it will become clear to them that it was not a matter for mockery. That is at the sending down of punishment upon them in this world, or on the Day of Resurrection, or at the manifestation of Islam and the elevation of its word. End of quotation.

He, in his habit, is verbose and explains wording and meaning in ways that these two words do not indicate.

Here the restriction of denial to the truth (bi'l-haqq) occurs, and the softening through (sawfa). In al-Shu'ara' it says ﴿they have denied, so there will come to them﴾, because al-An'am was revealed before al-Shu'ara'; so the wording was complete in it, and it was omitted in al-Shu'ara', while it is intended in the first state. The omission matched the brevity in the particle of futurity, so he came with the letter sin (السين).

The apparent reading is that (ma) in His saying (ma kanu) is a relative pronoun (ism mawsul), meaning "that which," and the pronoun in (bihi) refers back to it. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it may be a verbal-noun particle (masdariyya), with the estimate "the news of their being mockers." In that case the pronoun in (bihi) refers back to the truth (al-haqq), not according to the view of al-Akhfash (the grammarian), who claimed that masdariyya (ma) is a noun, not a particle. There is no necessity compelling it to be masdariyya.

(p-75)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 2–5 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Then He decreed a term, and a specified term is with Him; then you doubt.﴾ (*Qada*, "decreed," as in the Arabic *qada*): if it here means "measured and wrote," then *thumma* ("then") indicates sequence in mention, not in time, because that is prior to our creation, since it is an attribute of essence (*sifat dhat*). If it means "manifested" (*azhara*), then *thumma* indicates temporal sequence according to its original usage, because that is subsequent to our creation, so it is an attribute of act (*sifat fi'l*). The apparent sense of the indefiniteness of the two terms (*ajalayn*) is that God has left their matter undetermined.

Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ikrimah, Khasif and Qatadah said: the first term is the term of the worldly life, from the time of creation until death, and the second is the term of the Hereafter, because life in the Hereafter has no end, and no one knows the condition of this term except God the Exalted.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the first is his death through sleep, and the second is his death through dying. He also said: the first is the term of this world, and the second is the Hereafter. Mujahid also said: the first is the Hereafter, and the second is this world.

Ibn Zayd said: the first is the time of taking the covenant from the children of Adam when He brought them out from the loins of Adam, and the specified term is in this worldly life.

Abu Muslim said: the first is the term of those who have passed away, and the second is the term of those who remain. He described it as "specified with Him" because God alone is characterized by knowledge of it, unlike those who passed away, for when they died their terms became known.

It was said: the first is what lies between one's creation and one's death, and the second is what lies between death and resurrection, which is the *barzakh* (the intermediate realm).

It was said: the first is the measure of what has elapsed of each person's life, and the second is the measure of what remains.

It was said: the first is the term of the earlier nations, and the second is the term of this community.

It was said: the first is what we know, that there is no prophet after Muhammad (ﷺ), (p-71) and the second is from the Hereafter.

It was said: the first is what people know of the terms of the crescent moons, the years and the created beings, and the second is the establishment of the Hour.

It was said: the first is among the times of the crescent moons and what resembles them, and the second is a person's death.

Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid also said: ﴿decreed a term﴾ refers to the ending of the world, and the second refers to the beginning of the Hereafter.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: every person has two terms. If he is pious and keeps the ties of kinship, something is added to his term of life from the term of resurrection; and if it is the reverse, something is reduced from his term of life and added to the term of resurrection.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: every person has two terms, the natural (*tabi'i*) and the premature (*ikhtirami*). The natural is that which, if that temperament remained preserved from external accidents, its duration would end at the astronomical times. The premature is that which occurs through external causes, such as burning, drowning, the stings of insects and other separate matters. End of quote. This is the view of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school), which he attributed to them, saying: this is the view of the philosophers of Islam. End of quote.

The meaning of ﴿specified with Him﴾ is known to Him, or it is recorded in the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfuz*). "With Him" is a metaphor for His knowledge, not a reference to a place.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: an indefinite subject whose predicate is an adverbial phrase must have the predicate placed first, why then was it permissible to place it first in His saying ﴿and a specified term is with Him﴾?

I say: because it is specified by a qualifier, so it approaches a definite noun, like His saying: ﴿a believing slave is better than a polytheist﴾ (2:221). End of quote.

What he mentioned as the justification for beginning with an indefinite noun, namely that it is qualified, is not necessarily the only justification here, since the justification may be the detailed explanation (*tafsil*). Among the justifications for beginning with an indefinite noun is that the context is one of detailed explanation, as in the verse:

*When she weeps behind her, she turns toward him with one side, and the other side is not turned by us.*

We have previously discussed this line, and we explained that it is not permissible for *indana* ("by us") to be in the position of a qualifier here, but rather it must be in the position of a predicate.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: the common usage is to say "I have a good garment" (*indi thawbun jayyid*) and "I have a clever slave" (*li 'abdun kayyis*) and similar expressions. I say: what required it is that the meaning is "and whichever (*ayyu*) term is specified with Him," magnifying the matter of the Hour. Since this meaning is intended, the fronting became necessary. End of quote.

This is not permissible, because if the meaning is "and whichever term is specified with Him," then *ayyu* is a qualifier of an omitted noun, its full form being "and a term, whichever term is specified with Him." It is not permissible to omit a qualifier when it is *ayyu*, nor to omit its modified noun while retaining it. So if you say "I passed by whichever man" meaning "by a man, whichever man," it would not be permissible.

*Tamtarun* ("you doubt") means "you suspect" or "you dispute with the disputing of skeptics." *Tamari* (disputation) is argument on the basis of doubt, as some commentators have said.

The discussion of *thumma* here is like its discussion in His saying: ﴿Yet those who disbelieve﴾ (6:1). What appears to me is that His saying, ﴿It is He who created you﴾, in the form of address, is an *iltifat* (shift) from the third person, which is His saying ﴿Yet those who disbelieve﴾ (6:1). Although creation and the decreeing of the term are not specific to the disbelievers, since believers and disbelievers share in it, it is directed at the disbeliever in order to alert him to the origin of his creation, to God's decree over him, and to His power. I only said that it is a case of *iltifat* because His saying ﴿then you doubt﴾ cannot include in this address the one whom God has chosen with prophethood and faith.

[p. 72] ﴿And He is God in the heavens and on the earth; He knows your secret and your open deeds, and He knows what you earn﴾. When the preceding verses established complete power and free choice, this verse mentions what establishes complete knowledge. Drawing attention to these attributes indicates that He, exalted is He, is capable, choosing, and knowing of universals and particulars, and it refutes the doubts of those who deny the Return (al-ma'ad). The apparent reading is that (huwa) is a pronoun referring back to what the pronouns before it referred to, namely ﴿wa-Huwa Allah﴾ ("and He is God"). This is the view of the majority, as reported by al-Kirmani.

Abu Ali [al-Farisi] said: (huwa) is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n, the pronoun of the situation, which refers forward to what follows), (Allah) is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is what follows; the clause explains the pronoun of the matter. He resorted to this because, if it were not the pronoun of the matter, it would refer back to God, exalted is He, and the sense would become "God is God," forming a subject and predicate from two nouns identical in wording and meaning with no predicative relation between them, which is impermissible. For this reason, and God knows best, he interpreted the verse this way. Abu Ali said: the pronoun is the pronoun of the matter, (Allah) is the subject, and its predicate is (ya'lamu) ("He knows") in ﴿in the heavens and on the earth﴾, which is linked to (ya'lamu). The sense is: God knows ﴿in the heavens and on the earth﴾, ﴿your secret and your open deeds﴾.

Al-Zajjaj held that the phrase ﴿in the heavens﴾ is linked to what the name of God contains of meanings, just as one says: "the Commander of the Faithful is the caliph in the east and the west." Ibn Atiyya said: "In my view this is the best of the opinions, and the most comprehensive in preserving the eloquence of the wording and the solemnity of the meaning, and its clarification is that He intended to indicate His creation, the traces of His power, His encompassing and dominion, and similar attributes. So He gathered all of these in His saying ﴿wa-Huwa Allah﴾, i.e. the One to whom all these belong, ﴿in the heavens and on the earth﴾, as if He said: He is the Creator, the Provider, the Giver of life, the All-Encompassing, in the heavens and on the earth. As you say: Zayd is the sultan in al-Sham and Iraq. If you intended Zayd's essence, you would be speaking absurdly; but if the intent of your saying 'Zayd is the sultan' is the one who commands and forbids, who annuls and decrees, who dismisses and appoints in al-Sham and Iraq, and you put 'the sultan' in place of all these, it is eloquent and correct. Likewise, in the verse, the word ﴿Allah﴾ is placed in the position of those mentioned attributes." End of quotation.

What al-Zajjaj said, and what Ibn Atiyya explained, is correct in meaning, but the science of grammar (sina'at al-nahw) does not support it. They claimed that ﴿in the heavens﴾ is linked to the word ﴿Allah﴾ because of the meanings it contains. But not all of those meanings operate on the word; if they were all explicitly stated, they would not govern it. Rather, the governing in terms of the wording belongs to one of them, even though ﴿in the heavens﴾ is linked to all of them in terms of meaning. The better view is that the prepositional phrase is governed by what the word ﴿Allah﴾ contains of the meaning of divinity (al-uluhiyya), even though ﴿Allah﴾ is a proper name, because a adverbial phrase or prepositional phrase may be governed by a proper name through what it contains of meaning. As the poet said: "I am Abu al-Minhal, sometimes (ba'ḍa al-aḥyān)," where (ba'ḍa) is in the accusative by what Abu al-Minhal contains, as if he said: "I am the well-known one at certain times."

Al-Zamakhshari said something similar. He said: ﴿in the heavens﴾ is linked to the meaning of the name of God, as if it was said: He is the One worshipped in both of them. Compare His saying: ﴿wa-Huwa al-ladhi fi al-sama' Ilah wa-fi al-ard Ilah﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:84] ("And He is the one who is God in heaven and God on earth"), meaning: He is the one known for divinity, or the one singled out for divinity in them, or the one who is called God in them, with no partner in this name. End of quotation. Observe all his estimates: how he took the governing element as one of the meanings rather than all of them.

A group said (huwa) stands for an omitted attribute which is intended in meaning, as if it was said: He is the God who is worshipped ﴿in the heavens and on the earth﴾. Some estimated it as: He is God, the Manager ﴿in the heavens and on the earth﴾.

Another group said: ﴿wa-Huwa Allah﴾ is a complete sentence here, then the next part begins anew, and the prepositional phrase is linked to (ya'lamu).

Another group said: ﴿wa-Huwa Allah﴾ is complete, and ﴿in the heavens and on the earth﴾ is linked to the object of (ya'lamu), which is ﴿your secret and your open deeds﴾, and the sense is: He knows your secret and your open deeds in the heavens and on the earth. This is weak, because it involves placing the object of the verbal noun (the relative clause's object) before it. It is strange that al-Nahhas said: "This is among the best that has been said about it."

Another group said: it is the pronoun of the matter, Allah is nominative as subject, and its predicate is ﴿in the heavens﴾; the clause is a predicate of the pronoun of the matter, and the sentence is complete. Then he begins anew, saying: ﴿and on the earth He knows your secret and your open deeds﴾, i.e. He knows on the earth.

Ibn Jarir said something similar, except that (huwa) refers back to what the pronouns referred to before, and is not the pronoun of the matter.

It was also said: ﴿in the heavens﴾ is linked to His saying (taksibun) ("you earn"). This is an error, because (ma) is a relative pronoun linked to (taksibun), and whether it is a verbal particle (ḥarf maṣdarī, a particle forming a verbal noun) or a noun meaning (alladhi, "that which"), it is impermissible to place the complement of the relative clause before the relative word.

It was also said: ﴿in the heavens﴾ is a circumstantial element (ḥal) of the verbal noun which is ﴿your secret and your open deeds﴾, placed before the element it describes and before the governing word. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that ﴿Allah in the heavens﴾ be a predicate following a predicate, meaning that He is God, and that He is in the heavens and the earth, in the sense that He knows what is in them, nothing of it being hidden from Him, as if His essence were in them. But this is weak, because the prepositional phrase introduced by (fi, "in") does not indicate a specific attribute; it indicates only a general state of being. Upon these views the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of this verse is built.

The people of knowledge went to these interpretations, and departed from the apparent meaning of ﴿in the heavens and on the earth﴾, because of what rational proof establishes: that God, exalted is He, cannot dwell in places, cannot touch bodies, cannot be opposite them, and cannot be confined to a direction. Ibn Atiyya stated its meaning and part of its wording.

In His saying ﴿He knows your secret﴾ to the end, there is a statement which implicitly contains a warning and a rebuke. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: By "secret" is meant the qualities of the hearts, which are motives and restraints, and by "open" are meant the actions of the limbs. The secret is mentioned first because mentioning the agent of an act is the combination of power with motive; the motive, which belongs to the category of the secret, is what influences the deeds of the limbs called "open." It is established that knowledge of the cause is the cause of knowledge of the effect, and the cause precedes the effect, and what is prior in essence must be placed first in wording. End of quotation.

Al-Tabrizi said: its meaning is: He knows what you conceal of your deeds and intentions, and what you reveal of your deeds. ﴿What you earn﴾ is general to all beliefs, sayings, and actions. The earning (kasb) of each person is his deed which leads to bringing about benefit or warding off harm, and for this reason it is not predicated of God, exalted is He.

Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: In the beginning of his statement there is something of the meaning of al-Zamakhshari's statement. His saying ﴿what you earn﴾ must be understood as what a person deserves for his deed of reward or punishment. It is thus taken to mean what is acquired (al-mukatasab), as one says: "this wealth is the earnings (kasb) of so-and-so," i.e. what he acquired. It is impermissible to take it to mean the earning itself, for that would necessitate joining a thing to itself. This verse is a refutation of the Mu'attilah (those who deny God's attributes), the Thanawiyya (dualists), the Hashwiyya (literalists who fill the text with crude meanings), and the philosophers. End of quotation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "What is the position of His saying ﴿He knows your secret and your open deeds﴾?" I answer: if the meaning is "the One singled out for divinity," then it is a confirmation of this, because the one whose knowledge equally encompasses secret and public is God alone. Likewise if you make ﴿in the heavens﴾ a predicate following a predicate; otherwise, it is an independent statement, or a third predicate. End of quotation. This follows the view of those who permit the subject to have multiple predicates.

[p. 73] ﴿And no sign comes to them from among the signs of their Lord except that they turn away from it﴾. The first (min) ("from") is redundant (za'ida), for the purpose of encompassing the whole category; the meaning of its redundancy is that what follows it is the object governed by what precedes it, the agent of (ta'tihim, "comes to them"). When the indefinite noun after it is one that is used only in general negation, (min) serves to emphasize the encompassing, as in: "There is no one (min ahad) in the house." When it is one that may be used for encompassing, or for negating unity, or for negating completeness, then (min) indicates encompassing, as in: "No man (min rajul) stood." The second (min) is partitive (lil-tab'id). Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is: no proof ever appears to them from among the proofs whose consideration, reflection and inference are required, except that they turn away from it, leaving consideration, not turning to it, not raising their heads to it, through the scarcity of their fear and their contemplation of consequences. End of quotation.

Al-Zamakhshari's use of (qaṭṭ, "ever") with the present tense in his statement "no proof ever appears to them" is not good, because (qaṭṭ) is an adverb specific to the past tense, unless he meant by his saying "appears" the sense of "has appeared." There is no need to use that.

It was said: (the sign, al-ayah) here means the indicator of God's oneness and His singular divinity. It was also said: the message. It was also said: the miracle that breaks habit. It was also said: the Qur'an. The meaning of ﴿from it﴾ is: from accepting it or hearing it. Turning away (i'rad) is the opposite of turning toward, and it is a metaphor, since its literal meaning applies to bodies. The clause containing (kanu, "they were") and its complement is in the position of a circumstantial element (ḥal). Thus (ta'tihim, "comes to them") may have past meaning, by virtue of (kanu), or (kanu) may have present meaning, by virtue of (ta'tihim). The element described (dhu al-ḥal) is the pronoun in (ta'tihim). A verb in the past tense does not occur as a circumstantial clause except under one of two conditions: first, that it be preceded by a verb, as in this verse; second, that the past verb be preceded by (qad, "indeed"), as in: "Zayd has indeed struck Amr." This is a shift (iltifat) from address to third-person reference, and the pronoun refers back to ﴿those who disbelieved﴾. This verse includes a condemnation of those who disbelieved, in that they turn away from every sign that comes to them. Since the discourse earlier dealt first with monotheism, second with the Return, and third with establishing these two matters, it then mentioned what relates to establishing prophethood, and explained that they turned away from reflecting on the proofs. This indicates that blind imitation (taqlid) is invalid, and that reflection on the proofs is obligatory, and for this reason they are censured for their turning away from the proofs.

﴿So they have indeed denied the truth when it came to them﴾. (The truth, al-haqq) is the Qur'an, or Islam, or Muhammad, or the splitting of the moon, or the promise, or the threat; these are the views. What appears to be the case is that it is the sign that comes to them, and it is as if it was said: "they have denied the sign that comes to them," which is "the truth." Thus the apparent noun is used in place of the pronoun, because of the description of it as true, and its reality is that it is from the signs of God, exalted is He. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿So they have denied﴾ is that the (fa, "so") indicates sequence, and that their turning away from the sign was followed by denial. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿So they have denied﴾ is a response to an omitted statement, as if it was said: "If they are turning away from the signs, then they have denied something greater than any sign and more magnificent, namely the truth when it came to them, meaning the Qur'an, by which they were challenged despite their extreme eloquence, and they were unable to match it." End of quotation. There is no need for an omitted condition, since the speech is coherent without this assumption.

﴿So there will come to them the news of that at which they used to mock.﴾ This indicates that mockery had actually occurred from them. So the speech contains an elided conjoined element (ma'tuf mahdhuf), which the end of the verse indicates, and its implied meaning is: "and they mocked it, ﴿so there will come to them﴾." These are three stages that proceeded from these disbelievers: first, turning away from reflecting on the proofs; then turning away was followed by denial, which is more than turning away, since one who turns away may be heedless of a thing; then denial was followed by mockery, which is more than denial, since one who denies may not reach the point of mockery. This is the exaggeration in rejection. Al-naba' (the news; a report whose impact is great) is news whose impact is great. In the speech there is an elided modifier (hadhf mudaf): that is, ﴿there will come to them﴾ [the] news (anba') is implied. Some said: what is meant is what they were punished with in this world, of killing, captivity, plunder, expulsion and other things, and some restricted that to the Day of Badr. It was said: it is the punishment of the Hereafter. This sentence includes threat, rebuke and warning, as you say: "Do what you wish, the news will come to you." He attached the threat to mockery rather than to turning away and denial, because it encompasses both, since it is the utmost extreme in rejecting the truth.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is the Qur'an, that is, its reports and its circumstances, meaning: they will know at what they were mocking, and it will become clear to them that it was not a matter for mockery. That is at the sending down of punishment upon them in this world, or on the Day of Resurrection, or at the manifestation of Islam and the elevation of its word. End of quotation.

He, in his habit, is verbose and explains wording and meaning in ways that these two words do not indicate.

Here the restriction of denial to the truth (bi'l-haqq) occurs, and the softening through (sawfa). In al-Shu'ara' it says ﴿they have denied, so there will come to them﴾, because al-An'am was revealed before al-Shu'ara'; so the wording was complete in it, and it was omitted in al-Shu'ara', while it is intended in the first state. The omission matched the brevity in the particle of futurity, so he came with the letter sin (السين).

The apparent reading is that (ma) in His saying (ma kanu) is a relative pronoun (ism mawsul), meaning "that which," and the pronoun in (bihi) refers back to it. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it may be a verbal-noun particle (masdariyya), with the estimate "the news of their being mockers." In that case the pronoun in (bihi) refers back to the truth (al-haqq), not according to the view of al-Akhfash (the grammarian), who claimed that masdariyya (ma) is a noun, not a particle. There is no necessity compelling it to be masdariyya.

(p-75)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 6–9 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them, whom We had established on the earth as We have not established you, and We sent the sky upon them in abundant rain, and We made the rivers flow beneath them? Then We destroyed them for their sins and produced after them another generation.﴾ When He had threatened them and warned them for their turning away, their denial and their mockery, He followed that with what serves as admonition and advice, and urged reflection upon the past generations. Here "yaraw" (they see) means "ya'lamu" (they know), because they did not witness the destruction of the earlier generations. "Kam" (how many) is in the position of the object of "ahlakna" (We destroyed). "Yaraw" is suspended (mu'allaqah), and the clause is in the position of its object. The first "min" (from) is for the beginning of the limit (li-ibtida' al-ghayah), and the second "min" is for partitive meaning (li-al-tab'id), and the singular noun after it stands in the position of the plural. Al-Hawfi erred in making the second "min" a substitute (badal) for the first. The apparent sense of destruction is literal, as He destroyed the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud and others; it is possible that it is figurative, by transformation into apes and swine. The pronoun in "yaraw" refers to those among the deniers and mockers who came before. "Lakum" (for you) is an address to them, so it is a shift (iltifat), and the meaning is that the destroyed generations were given of ease in the world and abundance of wealth which were not given to these people who were urged to take warning from the past nations and what happened to them. In this shift there is an implicit reproach for the small extent of these people's establishment and their deficiency compared with the conditions of those who came before; and despite those others being established on the earth, destruction befell them, so how would it not befall you, given your smallness and the narrowness of your plans? Thus destruction is closer to you than it was to them. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The address in "lakum" is to the believers, and to all contemporaries of theirs, and to all people in general, as if he said: "ma lam numakkin" (what We did not establish), O people of this age, for you. It is possible to assume the sense of speech directed at these disbelievers, as if he said: O Muhammad, say to them: "Have they not seen how many We destroyed" to the end of the verse. When you report that you said, or that it was said to him, or that you ordered that it be said to him, you have in eloquent Arabic the option of relating the spoken words exactly as they were, so you bring the address form, and you have the option of rendering the meaning in other words, such as mentioning the absent party without direct address, and that ends. So you say: "I said to Zayd: 'How generous you are!'" and "I said to Zayd: 'How generous he is!'" The pronoun in "makkannahum" refers to "kam" in consideration of its meaning, because its meaning is plural, and what is meant by it is the nations. Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it refers to "qarn" (generation), but that is weak, because "min qarn" is a specification (tamyiz) of "lakum"; so "kam" is what is spoken of with destruction, and so it is what is spoken of with establishment and what follows it, since "min qarn" functions as clarification and is not spoken of. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "kam" here be an adverb of time, and that it be a verbal noun (masdar), i.e.: How many times did We destroy? Or how many destructions did We bring about? The object of "ahlakna min qarn" is by the addition of "min", and what he permitted is not permissible; because in that case the singular does not stand in the position of the plural, rather it indicates the singular. If you say: "Kam azmanan darabtu rajulan?" (How many times did I strike a man?) or "Kam marratan darabtu rajulan?" its meaning would not be the meaning of "rijal" (men), because the question is only about the number of times or occasions in which a man was struck; and also because this position is not one of the positions for the addition of "min", since it is not added except in a pure interrogative or in an interrogative intended as negation, and the interrogative here is neither pure nor intended as negation. The apparent view is that His saying "makkannahum" is an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: What was their condition? So it was said: "makkannahum fi al-ard" (We established them on the earth). Abu al-Baqa' said: "makkannahum" is in the position of a predicate, an attribute (sifah) of "qarn", and it is put in the plural according to its meaning, and what Abu al-Baqa' said is possible. As for "ma" in His saying "ma lam numakkin lakum", they allowed in its parsing that it be in the sense of "alladhi" (which), and the estimate would be: the establishment which "lam numakkin lakum" (We did not establish for you), so the modified noun is deleted and the attribute takes its place, and the relative pronoun returning to "ma" is deleted, i.e., "ma lam numakkinhu lakum" (what We did not establish for you). This is not permissible, because "ma" in the sense of "alladhi" does not occur as an attribute of definites, even if its signified meaning is that of "alladhi"; rather it is the word "alladhi" that occurs as an attribute of definites. If you say: "darabtu al-darb ma darab Zayd" (I struck the striking which Zayd struck), intending "alladhi darabahu Zayd", it is not permitted; but if you say: "al-darb alladhi darabahu Zayd", it is permitted. They also allowed that it be an indefinite attribute of a deleted verbal noun, its estimate being: an establishment which We did not establish for you; and this too is not permissible, because indefinite "ma" as an attribute does not allow the deletion of its modified noun. If you say: "qumtu ma" or "darabtu ma", intending "qumtu qiyaman ma" and "darabtu darban ma", it is not permitted; and these two aspects were permitted by al-Hawfi. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "ma" be a direct object of "makkana" according to meaning, because the meaning is: We gave them what We did not give you; and this which he permitted is a transference (tadmin), and transference is not systematic. He also permitted that "ma" be a verbal (masdariyyah) particle, with the time deleted, i.e., a period "ma lam numakkin lakum", meaning the duration of the absence of establishment for you. He also permitted that it be an indefinite noun described by the negated clause after it, i.e., a thing which We did not establish for you, and the returning pronoun of the attribute on the described noun is deleted; and this is closer to correctness. "Makkana" here is transitive to persons directly and by means of a preposition, and its more common transitivity is by "li-" (for): "makkanna li-Yusuf fi al-ard" (Yusuf 12:21), "inna makkanna lahu fi al-ard" (18:84), "awa lam numakkin lahum" (28:57). Abu 'Ubayd said: "makkannahum" and "makkana lahum" are two eloquent dialects, like "nasahtuhu" and "nasahtu lahu". "Al-irsal" (sending) and "al-inzal" (sending down) are close in meaning, because its derivation is from "risl al-laban", which is what descends from the udder in succession. "Al-sama'" (the sky), the canopying sky; they said: because rain descends from it to the clouds; and it would be with an elided genitive, i.e., the rain of the sky, and "midrar" would be a circumstantial (hal) of that elided genitive. It was also said: "al-sama'" means the rain. In a hadith: "fi athar sama' kanat min al-layl" (in the aftermath of a rain that fell during the night). The Arabs say: "ma zilna nata' al-sama' hatta ataynakum" (we have not ceased treading the rain until we came to you), meaning the rain; and the poet said:

When the rain falls upon the land of a people, we pasture upon it, even if they are angry.

("Midraran" here is then a circumstantial from the very "sama'".) It was said: "al-sama'" here means the cloud, and it is described as "midrar", so "midraran" is a circumstantial from it. "Midrar" is applied to the masculine and the feminine, and it is for intensification of the continuity and persistence of the rain at the time of need, except that it is raised by night and by day so it spoils; so said Ibn al-Anbari. And because these attributes were mentioned only to enumerate the blessings bestowed upon them and to set them against disobedience. "Wa ja'alna al-anhar tajri min tahtihim" (And We made the rivers flow beneath them): the manner of the flowing of rivers from beneath was already mentioned at the beginning of al-Baqarah. Some who interpreted "al-anhar" here as horses have gone far astray, as was said regarding His saying: "Wa hadhihi al-anhar tajri min tahti" (43:51). When a horse is swift in running and wide in stride, it is described as a sea and as a river. The meaning is that He, exalted, established them with complete establishment, and widened their provision; He mentioned its cause, which is the successive rains in measure to their needs, and the earth retaining that water until the rivers flowed beneath them, so fertility increased, and they committed sins, so they were destroyed for their sins. The apparent view is that "al-dhunub" (sins) here are their disbelief and their denial of God's messengers and signs; and destruction here is not meant as mere annihilation and causing death, but the destruction resulting from sins and being seized for them, like His saying: "Fa-kullan akhadhna bi-dhanbihi, fa-minhum man arsalna 'alayhi hasiban..." (29:40), because destruction in the sense of causing death is shared by the righteous and the wicked. The benefit of mentioning the producing of another generation after them is to display complete power over the annihilation of one people and the production of another; He, exalted, is not overwhelmed by destroying a generation, devastating its lands, and producing in its place another that populates its lands. It also contains an implicit reproach to the addressees with their own destruction if they disobey, just as He destroyed those before them. He described "qarnan" with "akharin" (another, plural), taking it according to the meaning of "qarn", and the taking according to meaning is more eloquent, because it is the end-rhyme of the verse.

﴿And if We had sent down to you a writing on paper, and they had touched it with their hands, those who disbelieved would have said: "This is nothing but manifest magic."﴾ The occasion of its revelation was the proposal and obstinacy of 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah, when he said to the Prophet ﷺ: "I will not believe in you until you ascend to the sky, then descend with a book from the Lord of Might to 'Abd Allah ibn Umayyah, commanding me to believe in you." And I do not think that even with this I would have believed you. Then he became Muslim after that, and was killed as a martyr at al-Ta'if. When He, exalted, mentioned their denial of the truth when it came to them, then admonished them and reminded them of the destruction of the earlier generations for their sins, He reminded them of their extreme exaggeration in denial: that even if they saw a written speech "in paper", and with their seeing they touched it with their hands, the seeing and touching would not increase them except in denial, and they would claim that this is of the kind of magic, not of the kind of miracle, out of obstinacy and stubbornness, though whoever has the least portion of intellect would not dispute what he perceived by sight just now, nor what his hand has touched. He mentioned touching because they would not restrict themselves to seeing, lest they say: "Our eyes have been intoxicated." And since miracles are things seen and heard, He mentioned things touched, in exaggeration that they do not hesitate in denying all these kinds, to the extent that what is touched by the hand is for them like what is seen by the eye and heard by the ear. The mention of the hand here: it was said for emphasis of confirmation, and because the hand is stronger in touching than other limbs. It was said: people are divided into those who see and those who are blind, so He mentioned the way by which knowledge is attained for both groups. It was said: He attached it to touching with the hand, because it is further from magic. It was said: touching with the hand is the preface to seeing, and does not occur with forgery. It was said: "al-lams" (touching) is used and is meant as investigating a thing and uncovering it, as He said: "Wa anna lamasna al-sama'" (72:8); so the hand is mentioned so that it is known that touching of that kind is not what is meant. "Laqala alladhina kafaru" (those who disbelieved would have said) came because such a purpose requires the division of people into believer and disbeliever: the believer sees it as one of the greatest miracles, and the disbeliever makes it a matter of magic. Describing magic as "mubin" (manifest) is either because it is clear in itself, or because it is more manifest than others.

﴿And they said: "Why has an angel not been sent down to him?"﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah and Nawfal ibn Khalid said: "O Muhammad, we will never believe in you until you bring us a book from Allah, and with it four angels who testify that it is from Allah, and that you are His messenger." It ends. The apparent view is that His saying "wa qalu" (and they said) is a resumptive report from God, relating that they said this; and it is possible that it is conjoined to the answer of "law" (if), i.e.: "laqala alladhina kafaru" and "laqalu: lawla unzila 'alayhi malak", so then these two statements, arranged upon the supposition of the sending down of the book "fi qirtas", would not be occurring, because the descent did not happen, and the second statement would be an extreme of obstinacy. Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Abi al-Fadl has pointed to this possibility, saying: there is an elision in the speech; its estimate is: even if We had responded to them in what they asked, they would not have believed; "wa qalu: lawla unzila 'alayhi malak" (and they said: why has an angel not been sent down to him?). The apparent sense of the verse requires that it concerns the disbelievers of the Arabs, and some have mentioned that it concerns the People of the Book; the pronoun in "alayhi" refers to Muhammad ﷺ, and the meaning is: an angel whom we see, and who informs us from God, exalted, of his prophethood and truthfulness. "Lawla" here means "halla" for urging (tahdid), and this is the saying of one who is obstinate and denies prophethood.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 6–9 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided﴾, meaning: ﴿Had We sent down﴾ upon him (an angel) whom they could see, the Resurrection would have come to pass. This is the view of Mujahid. Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: there is an ellipsis in the speech, and its sense is: ﴿Had We sent down an angel﴾, and they denied him, ﴿the matter would have been decided﴾ by their punishment, and they would not have been reprieved, as was the practice with every nation before them. Another group said: the meaning of ﴿the matter would have been decided﴾ is that they would have died from the terror of seeing the angel in his true form. This interpretation (ta'wil) is supported by the words ﴿Had We made him an angel﴾ and so on, for the people of ta'wil (interpretation) agree that they would not have been able to endure seeing the angel in his own form. Ibn Atiyyah said: the preferable reading of ﴿the matter would have been decided﴾ is that they would have died from the awe of seeing him. Al-Zamakhshari said: the matter of their destruction would have been decided.

﴿Then they would not be reprieved﴾: after his descent, not even for the blink of an eye. This may be because, when they witnessed the angel descended upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in his own form, nothing is clearer or more certain than that, and yet they would not believe, as He said. And had We sent angels down to them, it would have been necessary to destroy them, as the people of the table (al-ma'idah) were destroyed. Or it may be because the free choice, which is the basis of moral responsibility, is removed upon the descent of the angels, and so their destruction becomes necessary. Or it may be because, when they behold an angel in his own form, their souls depart from the terror of what they witness. The first option ("because") is the view of Ibn Abbas, and the third is the view of that group. His saying "as He destroyed the people of the table" is because, in his view, they were disbelievers; the discussion of them has already passed at the end of Surah al-Ma'idah. Abu Abdullah al-Razi mentioned the three aspects that al-Zamakhshari mentioned, explaining them at length. Al-Tabrizi said that there are two views regarding the meaning of ﴿the matter would have been decided﴾: first, the Resurrection would have come, because the unseen would become witnessed by sight; second, the fear of their destruction, because the divine custom in sending down angels operates in one of two ways: revelation or destruction. Since the first has been ruled out, the second is necessarily the one. Accordingly, on this view, the meaning of His saying ﴿They say: "Why has an angel not been sent down upon him?"﴾ is: "by our destruction." Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning of "then" (thumma), after clarifying the two matters, the decision of the affair and the absence of respite, is that he made the absence of respite more severe than the decision of the affair, because the sudden onset of hardship is more severe than hardship itself.

﴿Had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾: that is, had We made the Messenger an angel as they proposed, We would have made him a man. This is because they used to say: "Why has not an angel been sent down upon Muhammad?" and at other times they said: "This is none but a human like you, and had our Lord willed, He would have sent down angels." The meaning of ﴿We would have made him a man﴾ is that We would have fashioned him in the form of a man, just as Jibril (Gabriel) used to descend upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in most circumstances in the form of Dihyah, and at other times he appeared to him and to the Companions in the form of a man of very white garments and very black hair, on whom no trace of travel was seen, and whom none of the Companions recognised. In a hadith: "Sometimes the angel appears to me as a man." Just as Jibril appeared to Maryam (Mary) as a well-formed human, and the angels were the guests of Ibrahim (Abraham) and the guests of Lut (Lot), and the ones who scaled the prayer niche (al-mihrab), for they appeared in the form of humans. The reason he would appear in the form of a man is that people have no capacity to see the angel in his own form. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd, and it is supported by the death of the one who heard the voice of an angel in the clouds saying: "Go forward, Hayzum," and he died upon hearing its voice. So how would it be if he saw him in his true form? Ibn Atiyyah said: this is not contradicted by the Prophet's (ﷺ) seeing Jibril and others in their forms, because he (peace be upon him) was given a strength, meaning a strength other than the powers of human beings. The word "man" was used in reply to those addressed, since they claimed that the angels were females. Al-Qurtubi said: if God had made the Messenger to mankind an angel, they would have fled from being close to him, and would not have felt at ease with him; the awe would have entered them from his speech so much that it would have silenced them from his speech and prevented them from questioning him, so the benefit would not be complete. And if He had transferred him from the form of the angels to a form like theirs, they would have said: "You are not an angel, you are only a human, so we will not believe in you," and they would have returned to the same state as before. This is the summation of what the earlier exegetes said. In this verse there is evidence against those who deny the descent of angels to the earth, and who say that they are subtle bodies with nothing in them requiring them to descend to the earth. This has been answered: He, exalted is He, is able to place in their bodies a heaviness that causes them to descend to the earth, and then remove it so that they return to their former subtlety and lightness, and this would be the cause of their ascent. That is the end of this reply. What we say is that divine power brings down the light and lifts up the heavy without placing heaviness in the light or lightness in the heavy, and this is not impossible, so there is no need to burden oneself with placing heaviness in the light and lightness in the heavy. In this verse there is also evidence for the possibility of angels taking the form of humans, and this is a true matter established by continuous transmission (mutawatir).

﴿And We would have confused them in what they confuse﴾: that is, We would have mixed up for them what they mix up for themselves at that time. For when they saw the angel in the form of a human, they would say: "This is a human and not an angel." I base this on my having brought the inimitable Qur'an, which states that I am an angel and not a human. They would have denied him as they denied the messengers, and so they would have been forsaken as they are forsaken. It is also possible that the meaning is: ﴿And We would have confused them﴾ at that time, similar to ﴿what they confuse﴾ for themselves now in their disbelief in the signs of Allah. This was said by al-Zamakhshari, with some condensation. Ibn Atiyyah said: And We would have mixed up for them what they mix up for themselves and their weak ones, meaning We would have done to them a confusion through which they would be confused, and that is not fitting. The speech may bear another intention: that We Ourselves would have confused them, as they confuse their weak ones, so We would have forbidden them from confusing, and We would have done it ourselves. Some said: confusion would occur because they believed the angels were females, so if they saw him in the form of a man, confusion would arise for them, just as they confused others. Some, including al-Dahhak, said: the verse was revealed concerning the Jews and Christians regarding their religion and their books, which they distorted, and they denied their messengers; so the meaning of the confusion is: We increased them in error upon their error. Ibn Abbas said: Allah confused them with what they confused for themselves by distorting speech from its proper places. The particle "ma" (what) is a verbal noun (masdariyyah), and He attributed the confusion to Himself from the standpoint of creation, and to them from the standpoint of acquisition. Ibn Muhaysin read (ولبسنا) with a single lam, and al-Zuhri read (ولَلَبَّسْنا) with the ba' shaddah (doubled).

﴿And if We had sent down to you a writing on paper, and they had touched it with their hands, those who disbelieved would have said: "This is nothing but manifest magic."﴾ The occasion of its revelation was the proposal and obstinacy of 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah, when he said to the Prophet ﷺ: "I will not believe in you until you ascend to the sky, then descend with a book from the Lord of Might to 'Abd Allah ibn Umayyah, commanding me to believe in you." And I do not think that even with this I would have believed you. Then he became Muslim after that, and was killed as a martyr at al-Ta'if. When He, exalted, mentioned their denial of the truth when it came to them, then admonished them and reminded them of the destruction of the earlier generations for their sins, He reminded them of their extreme exaggeration in denial: that even if they saw a written speech "in paper", and with their seeing they touched it with their hands, the seeing and touching would not increase them except in denial, and they would claim that this is of the kind of magic, not of the kind of miracle, out of obstinacy and stubbornness, though whoever has the least portion of intellect would not dispute what he perceived by sight just now, nor what his hand has touched. He mentioned touching because they would not restrict themselves to seeing, lest they say: "Our eyes have been intoxicated." And since miracles are things seen and heard, He mentioned things touched, in exaggeration that they do not hesitate in denying all these kinds, to the extent that what is touched by the hand is for them like what is seen by the eye and heard by the ear. The mention of the hand here: it was said for emphasis of confirmation, and because the hand is stronger in touching than other limbs. It was said: people are divided into those who see and those who are blind, so He mentioned the way by which knowledge is attained for both groups. It was said: He attached it to touching with the hand, because it is further from magic. It was said: touching with the hand is the preface to seeing, and does not occur with forgery. It was said: "al-lams" (touching) is used and is meant as investigating a thing and uncovering it, as He said: "Wa anna lamasna al-sama'" (72:8); so the hand is mentioned so that it is known that touching of that kind is not what is meant. "Laqala alladhina kafaru" (those who disbelieved would have said) came because such a purpose requires the division of people into believer and disbeliever: the believer sees it as one of the greatest miracles, and the disbeliever makes it a matter of magic. Describing magic as "mubin" (manifest) is either because it is clear in itself, or because it is more manifest than others.

﴿And they said: "Why has an angel not been sent down to him?"﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah and Nawfal ibn Khalid said: "O Muhammad, we will never believe in you until you bring us a book from Allah, and with it four angels who testify that it is from Allah, and that you are His messenger." It ends. The apparent view is that His saying "wa qalu" (and they said) is a resumptive report from God, relating that they said this; and it is possible that it is conjoined to the answer of "law" (if), i.e.: "laqala alladhina kafaru" and "laqalu: lawla unzila 'alayhi malak", so then these two statements, arranged upon the supposition of the sending down of the book "fi qirtas", would not be occurring, because the descent did not happen, and the second statement would be an extreme of obstinacy. Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Abi al-Fadl has pointed to this possibility, saying: there is an elision in the speech; its estimate is: even if We had responded to them in what they asked, they would not have believed; "wa qalu: lawla unzila 'alayhi malak" (and they said: why has an angel not been sent down to him?). The apparent sense of the verse requires that it concerns the disbelievers of the Arabs, and some have mentioned that it concerns the People of the Book; the pronoun in "alayhi" refers to Muhammad ﷺ, and the meaning is: an angel whom we see, and who informs us from God, exalted, of his prophethood and truthfulness. "Lawla" here means "halla" for urging (tahdid), and this is the saying of one who is obstinate and denies prophethood.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 6–9 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided﴾, meaning: ﴿Had We sent down﴾ upon him (an angel) whom they could see, the Resurrection would have come to pass. This is the view of Mujahid. Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: there is an ellipsis in the speech, and its sense is: ﴿Had We sent down an angel﴾, and they denied him, ﴿the matter would have been decided﴾ by their punishment, and they would not have been reprieved, as was the practice with every nation before them. Another group said: the meaning of ﴿the matter would have been decided﴾ is that they would have died from the terror of seeing the angel in his true form. This interpretation (ta'wil) is supported by the words ﴿Had We made him an angel﴾ and so on, for the people of ta'wil (interpretation) agree that they would not have been able to endure seeing the angel in his own form. Ibn Atiyyah said: the preferable reading of ﴿the matter would have been decided﴾ is that they would have died from the awe of seeing him. Al-Zamakhshari said: the matter of their destruction would have been decided.

﴿Then they would not be reprieved﴾: after his descent, not even for the blink of an eye. This may be because, when they witnessed the angel descended upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in his own form, nothing is clearer or more certain than that, and yet they would not believe, as He said. And had We sent angels down to them, it would have been necessary to destroy them, as the people of the table (al-ma'idah) were destroyed. Or it may be because the free choice, which is the basis of moral responsibility, is removed upon the descent of the angels, and so their destruction becomes necessary. Or it may be because, when they behold an angel in his own form, their souls depart from the terror of what they witness. The first option ("because") is the view of Ibn Abbas, and the third is the view of that group. His saying "as He destroyed the people of the table" is because, in his view, they were disbelievers; the discussion of them has already passed at the end of Surah al-Ma'idah. Abu Abdullah al-Razi mentioned the three aspects that al-Zamakhshari mentioned, explaining them at length. Al-Tabrizi said that there are two views regarding the meaning of ﴿the matter would have been decided﴾: first, the Resurrection would have come, because the unseen would become witnessed by sight; second, the fear of their destruction, because the divine custom in sending down angels operates in one of two ways: revelation or destruction. Since the first has been ruled out, the second is necessarily the one. Accordingly, on this view, the meaning of His saying ﴿They say: "Why has an angel not been sent down upon him?"﴾ is: "by our destruction." Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning of "then" (thumma), after clarifying the two matters, the decision of the affair and the absence of respite, is that he made the absence of respite more severe than the decision of the affair, because the sudden onset of hardship is more severe than hardship itself.

﴿Had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾: that is, had We made the Messenger an angel as they proposed, We would have made him a man. This is because they used to say: "Why has not an angel been sent down upon Muhammad?" and at other times they said: "This is none but a human like you, and had our Lord willed, He would have sent down angels." The meaning of ﴿We would have made him a man﴾ is that We would have fashioned him in the form of a man, just as Jibril (Gabriel) used to descend upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in most circumstances in the form of Dihyah, and at other times he appeared to him and to the Companions in the form of a man of very white garments and very black hair, on whom no trace of travel was seen, and whom none of the Companions recognised. In a hadith: "Sometimes the angel appears to me as a man." Just as Jibril appeared to Maryam (Mary) as a well-formed human, and the angels were the guests of Ibrahim (Abraham) and the guests of Lut (Lot), and the ones who scaled the prayer niche (al-mihrab), for they appeared in the form of humans. The reason he would appear in the form of a man is that people have no capacity to see the angel in his own form. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd, and it is supported by the death of the one who heard the voice of an angel in the clouds saying: "Go forward, Hayzum," and he died upon hearing its voice. So how would it be if he saw him in his true form? Ibn Atiyyah said: this is not contradicted by the Prophet's (ﷺ) seeing Jibril and others in their forms, because he (peace be upon him) was given a strength, meaning a strength other than the powers of human beings. The word "man" was used in reply to those addressed, since they claimed that the angels were females. Al-Qurtubi said: if God had made the Messenger to mankind an angel, they would have fled from being close to him, and would not have felt at ease with him; the awe would have entered them from his speech so much that it would have silenced them from his speech and prevented them from questioning him, so the benefit would not be complete. And if He had transferred him from the form of the angels to a form like theirs, they would have said: "You are not an angel, you are only a human, so we will not believe in you," and they would have returned to the same state as before. This is the summation of what the earlier exegetes said. In this verse there is evidence against those who deny the descent of angels to the earth, and who say that they are subtle bodies with nothing in them requiring them to descend to the earth. This has been answered: He, exalted is He, is able to place in their bodies a heaviness that causes them to descend to the earth, and then remove it so that they return to their former subtlety and lightness, and this would be the cause of their ascent. That is the end of this reply. What we say is that divine power brings down the light and lifts up the heavy without placing heaviness in the light or lightness in the heavy, and this is not impossible, so there is no need to burden oneself with placing heaviness in the light and lightness in the heavy. In this verse there is also evidence for the possibility of angels taking the form of humans, and this is a true matter established by continuous transmission (mutawatir).

﴿And We would have confused them in what they confuse﴾: that is, We would have mixed up for them what they mix up for themselves at that time. For when they saw the angel in the form of a human, they would say: "This is a human and not an angel." I base this on my having brought the inimitable Qur'an, which states that I am an angel and not a human. They would have denied him as they denied the messengers, and so they would have been forsaken as they are forsaken. It is also possible that the meaning is: ﴿And We would have confused them﴾ at that time, similar to ﴿what they confuse﴾ for themselves now in their disbelief in the signs of Allah. This was said by al-Zamakhshari, with some condensation. Ibn Atiyyah said: And We would have mixed up for them what they mix up for themselves and their weak ones, meaning We would have done to them a confusion through which they would be confused, and that is not fitting. The speech may bear another intention: that We Ourselves would have confused them, as they confuse their weak ones, so We would have forbidden them from confusing, and We would have done it ourselves. Some said: confusion would occur because they believed the angels were females, so if they saw him in the form of a man, confusion would arise for them, just as they confused others. Some, including al-Dahhak, said: the verse was revealed concerning the Jews and Christians regarding their religion and their books, which they distorted, and they denied their messengers; so the meaning of the confusion is: We increased them in error upon their error. Ibn Abbas said: Allah confused them with what they confused for themselves by distorting speech from its proper places. The particle "ma" (what) is a verbal noun (masdariyyah), and He attributed the confusion to Himself from the standpoint of creation, and to them from the standpoint of acquisition. Ibn Muhaysin read (ولبسنا) with a single lam, and al-Zuhri read (ولَلَبَّسْنا) with the ba' shaddah (doubled).

(p-79)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 6–9 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them, whom We had established on the earth as We have not established you, and We sent the sky upon them in abundant rain, and We made the rivers flow beneath them? Then We destroyed them for their sins and produced after them another generation.﴾ When He had threatened them and warned them for their turning away, their denial and their mockery, He followed that with what serves as admonition and advice, and urged reflection upon the past generations. Here "yaraw" (they see) means "ya'lamu" (they know), because they did not witness the destruction of the earlier generations. "Kam" (how many) is in the position of the object of "ahlakna" (We destroyed). "Yaraw" is suspended (mu'allaqah), and the clause is in the position of its object. The first "min" (from) is for the beginning of the limit (li-ibtida' al-ghayah), and the second "min" is for partitive meaning (li-al-tab'id), and the singular noun after it stands in the position of the plural. Al-Hawfi erred in making the second "min" a substitute (badal) for the first. The apparent sense of destruction is literal, as He destroyed the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud and others; it is possible that it is figurative, by transformation into apes and swine. The pronoun in "yaraw" refers to those among the deniers and mockers who came before. "Lakum" (for you) is an address to them, so it is a shift (iltifat), and the meaning is that the destroyed generations were given of ease in the world and abundance of wealth which were not given to these people who were urged to take warning from the past nations and what happened to them. In this shift there is an implicit reproach for the small extent of these people's establishment and their deficiency compared with the conditions of those who came before; and despite those others being established on the earth, destruction befell them, so how would it not befall you, given your smallness and the narrowness of your plans? Thus destruction is closer to you than it was to them. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The address in "lakum" is to the believers, and to all contemporaries of theirs, and to all people in general, as if he said: "ma lam numakkin" (what We did not establish), O people of this age, for you. It is possible to assume the sense of speech directed at these disbelievers, as if he said: O Muhammad, say to them: "Have they not seen how many We destroyed" to the end of the verse. When you report that you said, or that it was said to him, or that you ordered that it be said to him, you have in eloquent Arabic the option of relating the spoken words exactly as they were, so you bring the address form, and you have the option of rendering the meaning in other words, such as mentioning the absent party without direct address, and that ends. So you say: "I said to Zayd: 'How generous you are!'" and "I said to Zayd: 'How generous he is!'" The pronoun in "makkannahum" refers to "kam" in consideration of its meaning, because its meaning is plural, and what is meant by it is the nations. Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it refers to "qarn" (generation), but that is weak, because "min qarn" is a specification (tamyiz) of "lakum"; so "kam" is what is spoken of with destruction, and so it is what is spoken of with establishment and what follows it, since "min qarn" functions as clarification and is not spoken of. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "kam" here be an adverb of time, and that it be a verbal noun (masdar), i.e.: How many times did We destroy? Or how many destructions did We bring about? The object of "ahlakna min qarn" is by the addition of "min", and what he permitted is not permissible; because in that case the singular does not stand in the position of the plural, rather it indicates the singular. If you say: "Kam azmanan darabtu rajulan?" (How many times did I strike a man?) or "Kam marratan darabtu rajulan?" its meaning would not be the meaning of "rijal" (men), because the question is only about the number of times or occasions in which a man was struck; and also because this position is not one of the positions for the addition of "min", since it is not added except in a pure interrogative or in an interrogative intended as negation, and the interrogative here is neither pure nor intended as negation. The apparent view is that His saying "makkannahum" is an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: What was their condition? So it was said: "makkannahum fi al-ard" (We established them on the earth). Abu al-Baqa' said: "makkannahum" is in the position of a predicate, an attribute (sifah) of "qarn", and it is put in the plural according to its meaning, and what Abu al-Baqa' said is possible. As for "ma" in His saying "ma lam numakkin lakum", they allowed in its parsing that it be in the sense of "alladhi" (which), and the estimate would be: the establishment which "lam numakkin lakum" (We did not establish for you), so the modified noun is deleted and the attribute takes its place, and the relative pronoun returning to "ma" is deleted, i.e., "ma lam numakkinhu lakum" (what We did not establish for you). This is not permissible, because "ma" in the sense of "alladhi" does not occur as an attribute of definites, even if its signified meaning is that of "alladhi"; rather it is the word "alladhi" that occurs as an attribute of definites. If you say: "darabtu al-darb ma darab Zayd" (I struck the striking which Zayd struck), intending "alladhi darabahu Zayd", it is not permitted; but if you say: "al-darb alladhi darabahu Zayd", it is permitted. They also allowed that it be an indefinite attribute of a deleted verbal noun, its estimate being: an establishment which We did not establish for you; and this too is not permissible, because indefinite "ma" as an attribute does not allow the deletion of its modified noun. If you say: "qumtu ma" or "darabtu ma", intending "qumtu qiyaman ma" and "darabtu darban ma", it is not permitted; and these two aspects were permitted by al-Hawfi. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "ma" be a direct object of "makkana" according to meaning, because the meaning is: We gave them what We did not give you; and this which he permitted is a transference (tadmin), and transference is not systematic. He also permitted that "ma" be a verbal (masdariyyah) particle, with the time deleted, i.e., a period "ma lam numakkin lakum", meaning the duration of the absence of establishment for you. He also permitted that it be an indefinite noun described by the negated clause after it, i.e., a thing which We did not establish for you, and the returning pronoun of the attribute on the described noun is deleted; and this is closer to correctness. "Makkana" here is transitive to persons directly and by means of a preposition, and its more common transitivity is by "li-" (for): "makkanna li-Yusuf fi al-ard" (Yusuf 12:21), "inna makkanna lahu fi al-ard" (18:84), "awa lam numakkin lahum" (28:57). Abu 'Ubayd said: "makkannahum" and "makkana lahum" are two eloquent dialects, like "nasahtuhu" and "nasahtu lahu". "Al-irsal" (sending) and "al-inzal" (sending down) are close in meaning, because its derivation is from "risl al-laban", which is what descends from the udder in succession. "Al-sama'" (the sky), the canopying sky; they said: because rain descends from it to the clouds; and it would be with an elided genitive, i.e., the rain of the sky, and "midrar" would be a circumstantial (hal) of that elided genitive. It was also said: "al-sama'" means the rain. In a hadith: "fi athar sama' kanat min al-layl" (in the aftermath of a rain that fell during the night). The Arabs say: "ma zilna nata' al-sama' hatta ataynakum" (we have not ceased treading the rain until we came to you), meaning the rain; and the poet said:

When the rain falls upon the land of a people, we pasture upon it, even if they are angry.

("Midraran" here is then a circumstantial from the very "sama'".) It was said: "al-sama'" here means the cloud, and it is described as "midrar", so "midraran" is a circumstantial from it. "Midrar" is applied to the masculine and the feminine, and it is for intensification of the continuity and persistence of the rain at the time of need, except that it is raised by night and by day so it spoils; so said Ibn al-Anbari. And because these attributes were mentioned only to enumerate the blessings bestowed upon them and to set them against disobedience. "Wa ja'alna al-anhar tajri min tahtihim" (And We made the rivers flow beneath them): the manner of the flowing of rivers from beneath was already mentioned at the beginning of al-Baqarah. Some who interpreted "al-anhar" here as horses have gone far astray, as was said regarding His saying: "Wa hadhihi al-anhar tajri min tahti" (43:51). When a horse is swift in running and wide in stride, it is described as a sea and as a river. The meaning is that He, exalted, established them with complete establishment, and widened their provision; He mentioned its cause, which is the successive rains in measure to their needs, and the earth retaining that water until the rivers flowed beneath them, so fertility increased, and they committed sins, so they were destroyed for their sins. The apparent view is that "al-dhunub" (sins) here are their disbelief and their denial of God's messengers and signs; and destruction here is not meant as mere annihilation and causing death, but the destruction resulting from sins and being seized for them, like His saying: "Fa-kullan akhadhna bi-dhanbihi, fa-minhum man arsalna 'alayhi hasiban..." (29:40), because destruction in the sense of causing death is shared by the righteous and the wicked. The benefit of mentioning the producing of another generation after them is to display complete power over the annihilation of one people and the production of another; He, exalted, is not overwhelmed by destroying a generation, devastating its lands, and producing in its place another that populates its lands. It also contains an implicit reproach to the addressees with their own destruction if they disobey, just as He destroyed those before them. He described "qarnan" with "akharin" (another, plural), taking it according to the meaning of "qarn", and the taking according to meaning is more eloquent, because it is the end-rhyme of the verse.

﴿And if We had sent down to you a writing on paper, and they had touched it with their hands, those who disbelieved would have said: "This is nothing but manifest magic."﴾ The occasion of its revelation was the proposal and obstinacy of 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah, when he said to the Prophet ﷺ: "I will not believe in you until you ascend to the sky, then descend with a book from the Lord of Might to 'Abd Allah ibn Umayyah, commanding me to believe in you." And I do not think that even with this I would have believed you. Then he became Muslim after that, and was killed as a martyr at al-Ta'if. When He, exalted, mentioned their denial of the truth when it came to them, then admonished them and reminded them of the destruction of the earlier generations for their sins, He reminded them of their extreme exaggeration in denial: that even if they saw a written speech "in paper", and with their seeing they touched it with their hands, the seeing and touching would not increase them except in denial, and they would claim that this is of the kind of magic, not of the kind of miracle, out of obstinacy and stubbornness, though whoever has the least portion of intellect would not dispute what he perceived by sight just now, nor what his hand has touched. He mentioned touching because they would not restrict themselves to seeing, lest they say: "Our eyes have been intoxicated." And since miracles are things seen and heard, He mentioned things touched, in exaggeration that they do not hesitate in denying all these kinds, to the extent that what is touched by the hand is for them like what is seen by the eye and heard by the ear. The mention of the hand here: it was said for emphasis of confirmation, and because the hand is stronger in touching than other limbs. It was said: people are divided into those who see and those who are blind, so He mentioned the way by which knowledge is attained for both groups. It was said: He attached it to touching with the hand, because it is further from magic. It was said: touching with the hand is the preface to seeing, and does not occur with forgery. It was said: "al-lams" (touching) is used and is meant as investigating a thing and uncovering it, as He said: "Wa anna lamasna al-sama'" (72:8); so the hand is mentioned so that it is known that touching of that kind is not what is meant.
