﴿Had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾: that is, had We made the Messenger an angel as they proposed, We would have made him a man. This is because they used to say: "Why has not an angel been sent down upon Muhammad?" and at other times they said: "This is none but a human like you, and had our Lord willed, He would have sent down angels." The meaning of ﴿We would have made him a man﴾ is that We would have fashioned him in the form of a man, just as Jibril (Gabriel) used to descend upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in most circumstances in the form of Dihyah, and at other times he appeared to him and to the Companions in the form of a man of very white garments and very black hair, on whom no trace of travel was seen, and whom none of the Companions recognised. In a hadith: "Sometimes the angel appears to me as a man." Just as Jibril appeared to Maryam (Mary) as a well-formed human, and the angels were the guests of Ibrahim (Abraham) and the guests of Lut (Lot), and the ones who scaled the prayer niche (al-mihrab), for they appeared in the form of humans. The reason he would appear in the form of a man is that people have no capacity to see the angel in his own form. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd, and it is supported by the death of the one who heard the voice of an angel in the clouds saying: "Go forward, Hayzum," and he died upon hearing its voice. So how would it be if he saw him in his true form? Ibn Atiyyah said: this is not contradicted by the Prophet's (ﷺ) seeing Jibril and others in their forms, because he (peace be upon him) was given a strength, meaning a strength other than the powers of human beings. The word "man" was used in reply to those addressed, since they claimed that the angels were females. Al-Qurtubi said: if God had made the Messenger to mankind an angel, they would have fled from being close to him, and would not have felt at ease with him; the awe would have entered them from his speech so much that it would have silenced them from his speech and prevented them from questioning him, so the benefit would not be complete. And if He had transferred him from the form of the angels to a form like theirs, they would have said: "You are not an angel, you are only a human, so we will not believe in you," and they would have returned to the same state as before. This is the summation of what the earlier exegetes said. In this verse there is evidence against those who deny the descent of angels to the earth, and who say that they are subtle bodies with nothing in them requiring them to descend to the earth. This has been answered: He, exalted is He, is able to place in their bodies a heaviness that causes them to descend to the earth, and then remove it so that they return to their former subtlety and lightness, and this would be the cause of their ascent. That is the end of this reply. What we say is that divine power brings down the light and lifts up the heavy without placing heaviness in the light or lightness in the heavy, and this is not impossible, so there is no need to burden oneself with placing heaviness in the light and lightness in the heavy. In this verse there is also evidence for the possibility of angels taking the form of humans, and this is a true matter established by continuous transmission (mutawatir).

﴿And We would have confused them in what they confuse﴾: that is, We would have mixed up for them what they mix up for themselves at that time. For when they saw the angel in the form of a human, they would say: "This is a human and not an angel." I base this on my having brought the inimitable Qur'an, which states that I am an angel and not a human. They would have denied him as they denied the messengers, and so they would have been forsaken as they are forsaken. It is also possible that the meaning is: ﴿And We would have confused them﴾ at that time, similar to ﴿what they confuse﴾ for themselves now in their disbelief in the signs of Allah. This was said by al-Zamakhshari, with some condensation. Ibn Atiyyah said: And We would have mixed up for them what they mix up for themselves and their weak ones, meaning We would have done to them a confusion through which they would be confused, and that is not fitting. The speech may bear another intention: that We Ourselves would have confused them, as they confuse their weak ones, so We would have forbidden them from confusing, and We would have done it ourselves. Some said: confusion would occur because they believed the angels were females, so if they saw him in the form of a man, confusion would arise for them, just as they confused others. Some, including al-Dahhak, said: the verse was revealed concerning the Jews and Christians regarding their religion and their books, which they distorted, and they denied their messengers; so the meaning of the confusion is: We increased them in error upon their error. Ibn Abbas said: Allah confused them with what they confused for themselves by distorting speech from its proper places. The particle "ma" (what) is a verbal noun (masdariyyah), and He attributed the confusion to Himself from the standpoint of creation, and to them from the standpoint of acquisition. Ibn Muhaysin read (ولبسنا) with a single lam, and al-Zuhri read (ولَلَبَّسْنا) with the ba' shaddah (doubled).

(p-79)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 6–9 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them, whom We had established on the earth as We have not established you, and We sent the sky upon them in abundant rain, and We made the rivers flow beneath them? Then We destroyed them for their sins and produced after them another generation.﴾ When He had threatened them and warned them for their turning away, their denial and their mockery, He followed that with what serves as admonition and advice, and urged reflection upon the past generations. Here "yaraw" (they see) means "ya'lamu" (they know), because they did not witness the destruction of the earlier generations. "Kam" (how many) is in the position of the object of "ahlakna" (We destroyed). "Yaraw" is suspended (mu'allaqah), and the clause is in the position of its object. The first "min" (from) is for the beginning of the limit (li-ibtida' al-ghayah), and the second "min" is for partitive meaning (li-al-tab'id), and the singular noun after it stands in the position of the plural. Al-Hawfi erred in making the second "min" a substitute (badal) for the first. The apparent sense of destruction is literal, as He destroyed the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud and others; it is possible that it is figurative, by transformation into apes and swine. The pronoun in "yaraw" refers to those among the deniers and mockers who came before. "Lakum" (for you) is an address to them, so it is a shift (iltifat), and the meaning is that the destroyed generations were given of ease in the world and abundance of wealth which were not given to these people who were urged to take warning from the past nations and what happened to them. In this shift there is an implicit reproach for the small extent of these people's establishment and their deficiency compared with the conditions of those who came before; and despite those others being established on the earth, destruction befell them, so how would it not befall you, given your smallness and the narrowness of your plans? Thus destruction is closer to you than it was to them. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The address in "lakum" is to the believers, and to all contemporaries of theirs, and to all people in general, as if he said: "ma lam numakkin" (what We did not establish), O people of this age, for you. It is possible to assume the sense of speech directed at these disbelievers, as if he said: O Muhammad, say to them: "Have they not seen how many We destroyed" to the end of the verse. When you report that you said, or that it was said to him, or that you ordered that it be said to him, you have in eloquent Arabic the option of relating the spoken words exactly as they were, so you bring the address form, and you have the option of rendering the meaning in other words, such as mentioning the absent party without direct address, and that ends. So you say: "I said to Zayd: 'How generous you are!'" and "I said to Zayd: 'How generous he is!'" The pronoun in "makkannahum" refers to "kam" in consideration of its meaning, because its meaning is plural, and what is meant by it is the nations. Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it refers to "qarn" (generation), but that is weak, because "min qarn" is a specification (tamyiz) of "lakum"; so "kam" is what is spoken of with destruction, and so it is what is spoken of with establishment and what follows it, since "min qarn" functions as clarification and is not spoken of. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "kam" here be an adverb of time, and that it be a verbal noun (masdar), i.e.: How many times did We destroy? Or how many destructions did We bring about? The object of "ahlakna min qarn" is by the addition of "min", and what he permitted is not permissible; because in that case the singular does not stand in the position of the plural, rather it indicates the singular. If you say: "Kam azmanan darabtu rajulan?" (How many times did I strike a man?) or "Kam marratan darabtu rajulan?" its meaning would not be the meaning of "rijal" (men), because the question is only about the number of times or occasions in which a man was struck; and also because this position is not one of the positions for the addition of "min", since it is not added except in a pure interrogative or in an interrogative intended as negation, and the interrogative here is neither pure nor intended as negation. The apparent view is that His saying "makkannahum" is an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: What was their condition? So it was said: "makkannahum fi al-ard" (We established them on the earth). Abu al-Baqa' said: "makkannahum" is in the position of a predicate, an attribute (sifah) of "qarn", and it is put in the plural according to its meaning, and what Abu al-Baqa' said is possible. As for "ma" in His saying "ma lam numakkin lakum", they allowed in its parsing that it be in the sense of "alladhi" (which), and the estimate would be: the establishment which "lam numakkin lakum" (We did not establish for you), so the modified noun is deleted and the attribute takes its place, and the relative pronoun returning to "ma" is deleted, i.e., "ma lam numakkinhu lakum" (what We did not establish for you). This is not permissible, because "ma" in the sense of "alladhi" does not occur as an attribute of definites, even if its signified meaning is that of "alladhi"; rather it is the word "alladhi" that occurs as an attribute of definites. If you say: "darabtu al-darb ma darab Zayd" (I struck the striking which Zayd struck), intending "alladhi darabahu Zayd", it is not permitted; but if you say: "al-darb alladhi darabahu Zayd", it is permitted. They also allowed that it be an indefinite attribute of a deleted verbal noun, its estimate being: an establishment which We did not establish for you; and this too is not permissible, because indefinite "ma" as an attribute does not allow the deletion of its modified noun. If you say: "qumtu ma" or "darabtu ma", intending "qumtu qiyaman ma" and "darabtu darban ma", it is not permitted; and these two aspects were permitted by al-Hawfi. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "ma" be a direct object of "makkana" according to meaning, because the meaning is: We gave them what We did not give you; and this which he permitted is a transference (tadmin), and transference is not systematic. He also permitted that "ma" be a verbal (masdariyyah) particle, with the time deleted, i.e., a period "ma lam numakkin lakum", meaning the duration of the absence of establishment for you. He also permitted that it be an indefinite noun described by the negated clause after it, i.e., a thing which We did not establish for you, and the returning pronoun of the attribute on the described noun is deleted; and this is closer to correctness. "Makkana" here is transitive to persons directly and by means of a preposition, and its more common transitivity is by "li-" (for): "makkanna li-Yusuf fi al-ard" (Yusuf 12:21), "inna makkanna lahu fi al-ard" (18:84), "awa lam numakkin lahum" (28:57). Abu 'Ubayd said: "makkannahum" and "makkana lahum" are two eloquent dialects, like "nasahtuhu" and "nasahtu lahu". "Al-irsal" (sending) and "al-inzal" (sending down) are close in meaning, because its derivation is from "risl al-laban", which is what descends from the udder in succession. "Al-sama'" (the sky), the canopying sky; they said: because rain descends from it to the clouds; and it would be with an elided genitive, i.e., the rain of the sky, and "midrar" would be a circumstantial (hal) of that elided genitive. It was also said: "al-sama'" means the rain. In a hadith: "fi athar sama' kanat min al-layl" (in the aftermath of a rain that fell during the night). The Arabs say: "ma zilna nata' al-sama' hatta ataynakum" (we have not ceased treading the rain until we came to you), meaning the rain; and the poet said:

When the rain falls upon the land of a people, we pasture upon it, even if they are angry.

("Midraran" here is then a circumstantial from the very "sama'".) It was said: "al-sama'" here means the cloud, and it is described as "midrar", so "midraran" is a circumstantial from it. "Midrar" is applied to the masculine and the feminine, and it is for intensification of the continuity and persistence of the rain at the time of need, except that it is raised by night and by day so it spoils; so said Ibn al-Anbari. And because these attributes were mentioned only to enumerate the blessings bestowed upon them and to set them against disobedience. "Wa ja'alna al-anhar tajri min tahtihim" (And We made the rivers flow beneath them): the manner of the flowing of rivers from beneath was already mentioned at the beginning of al-Baqarah. Some who interpreted "al-anhar" here as horses have gone far astray, as was said regarding His saying: "Wa hadhihi al-anhar tajri min tahti" (43:51). When a horse is swift in running and wide in stride, it is described as a sea and as a river. The meaning is that He, exalted, established them with complete establishment, and widened their provision; He mentioned its cause, which is the successive rains in measure to their needs, and the earth retaining that water until the rivers flowed beneath them, so fertility increased, and they committed sins, so they were destroyed for their sins. The apparent view is that "al-dhunub" (sins) here are their disbelief and their denial of God's messengers and signs; and destruction here is not meant as mere annihilation and causing death, but the destruction resulting from sins and being seized for them, like His saying: "Fa-kullan akhadhna bi-dhanbihi, fa-minhum man arsalna 'alayhi hasiban..." (29:40), because destruction in the sense of causing death is shared by the righteous and the wicked. The benefit of mentioning the producing of another generation after them is to display complete power over the annihilation of one people and the production of another; He, exalted, is not overwhelmed by destroying a generation, devastating its lands, and producing in its place another that populates its lands. It also contains an implicit reproach to the addressees with their own destruction if they disobey, just as He destroyed those before them. He described "qarnan" with "akharin" (another, plural), taking it according to the meaning of "qarn", and the taking according to meaning is more eloquent, because it is the end-rhyme of the verse.

﴿And if We had sent down to you a writing on paper, and they had touched it with their hands, those who disbelieved would have said: "This is nothing but manifest magic."﴾ The occasion of its revelation was the proposal and obstinacy of 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah, when he said to the Prophet ﷺ: "I will not believe in you until you ascend to the sky, then descend with a book from the Lord of Might to 'Abd Allah ibn Umayyah, commanding me to believe in you." And I do not think that even with this I would have believed you. Then he became Muslim after that, and was killed as a martyr at al-Ta'if. When He, exalted, mentioned their denial of the truth when it came to them, then admonished them and reminded them of the destruction of the earlier generations for their sins, He reminded them of their extreme exaggeration in denial: that even if they saw a written speech "in paper", and with their seeing they touched it with their hands, the seeing and touching would not increase them except in denial, and they would claim that this is of the kind of magic, not of the kind of miracle, out of obstinacy and stubbornness, though whoever has the least portion of intellect would not dispute what he perceived by sight just now, nor what his hand has touched. He mentioned touching because they would not restrict themselves to seeing, lest they say: "Our eyes have been intoxicated." And since miracles are things seen and heard, He mentioned things touched, in exaggeration that they do not hesitate in denying all these kinds, to the extent that what is touched by the hand is for them like what is seen by the eye and heard by the ear. The mention of the hand here: it was said for emphasis of confirmation, and because the hand is stronger in touching than other limbs. It was said: people are divided into those who see and those who are blind, so He mentioned the way by which knowledge is attained for both groups. It was said: He attached it to touching with the hand, because it is further from magic. It was said: touching with the hand is the preface to seeing, and does not occur with forgery. It was said: "al-lams" (touching) is used and is meant as investigating a thing and uncovering it, as He said: "Wa anna lamasna al-sama'" (72:8); so the hand is mentioned so that it is known that touching of that kind is not what is meant. "Laqala alladhina kafaru" (those who disbelieved would have said) came because such a purpose requires the division of people into believer and disbeliever: the believer sees it as one of the greatest miracles, and the disbeliever makes it a matter of magic. Describing magic as "mubin" (manifest) is either because it is clear in itself, or because it is more manifest than others.

﴿And they said: "Why has an angel not been sent down to him?"﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah and Nawfal ibn Khalid said: "O Muhammad, we will never believe in you until you bring us a book from Allah, and with it four angels who testify that it is from Allah, and that you are His messenger." It ends. The apparent view is that His saying "wa qalu" (and they said) is a resumptive report from God, relating that they said this; and it is possible that it is conjoined to the answer of "law" (if), i.e.: "laqala alladhina kafaru" and "laqalu: lawla unzila 'alayhi malak", so then these two statements, arranged upon the supposition of the sending down of the book "fi qirtas", would not be occurring, because the descent did not happen, and the second statement would be an extreme of obstinacy. Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Abi al-Fadl has pointed to this possibility, saying: there is an elision in the speech; its estimate is: even if We had responded to them in what they asked, they would not have believed; "wa qalu: lawla unzila 'alayhi malak" (and they said: why has an angel not been sent down to him?). The apparent sense of the verse requires that it concerns the disbelievers of the Arabs, and some have mentioned that it concerns the People of the Book; the pronoun in "alayhi" refers to Muhammad ﷺ, and the meaning is: an angel whom we see, and who informs us from God, exalted, of his prophethood and truthfulness. "Lawla" here means "halla" for urging (tahdid), and this is the saying of one who is obstinate and denies prophethood.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 6–9 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided﴾, meaning: ﴿Had We sent down﴾ upon him (an angel) whom they could see, the Resurrection would have come to pass. This is the view of Mujahid. Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: there is an ellipsis in the speech, and its sense is: ﴿Had We sent down an angel﴾, and they denied him, ﴿the matter would have been decided﴾ by their punishment, and they would not have been reprieved, as was the practice with every nation before them. Another group said: the meaning of ﴿the matter would have been decided﴾ is that they would have died from the terror of seeing the angel in his true form. This interpretation (ta'wil) is supported by the words ﴿Had We made him an angel﴾ and so on, for the people of ta'wil (interpretation) agree that they would not have been able to endure seeing the angel in his own form. Ibn Atiyyah said: the preferable reading of ﴿the matter would have been decided﴾ is that they would have died from the awe of seeing him. Al-Zamakhshari said: the matter of their destruction would have been decided.

﴿Then they would not be reprieved﴾: after his descent, not even for the blink of an eye. This may be because, when they witnessed the angel descended upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in his own form, nothing is clearer or more certain than that, and yet they would not believe, as He said. And had We sent angels down to them, it would have been necessary to destroy them, as the people of the table (al-ma'idah) were destroyed. Or it may be because the free choice, which is the basis of moral responsibility, is removed upon the descent of the angels, and so their destruction becomes necessary. Or it may be because, when they behold an angel in his own form, their souls depart from the terror of what they witness. The first option ("because") is the view of Ibn Abbas, and the third is the view of that group. His saying "as He destroyed the people of the table" is because, in his view, they were disbelievers; the discussion of them has already passed at the end of Surah al-Ma'idah. Abu Abdullah al-Razi mentioned the three aspects that al-Zamakhshari mentioned, explaining them at length. Al-Tabrizi said that there are two views regarding the meaning of ﴿the matter would have been decided﴾: first, the Resurrection would have come, because the unseen would become witnessed by sight; second, the fear of their destruction, because the divine custom in sending down angels operates in one of two ways: revelation or destruction. Since the first has been ruled out, the second is necessarily the one. Accordingly, on this view, the meaning of His saying ﴿They say: "Why has an angel not been sent down upon him?"﴾ is: "by our destruction." Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning of "then" (thumma), after clarifying the two matters, the decision of the affair and the absence of respite, is that he made the absence of respite more severe than the decision of the affair, because the sudden onset of hardship is more severe than hardship itself.

﴿Had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾: that is, had We made the Messenger an angel as they proposed, We would have made him a man. This is because they used to say: "Why has not an angel been sent down upon Muhammad?" and at other times they said: "This is none but a human like you, and had our Lord willed, He would have sent down angels." The meaning of ﴿We would have made him a man﴾ is that We would have fashioned him in the form of a man, just as Jibril (Gabriel) used to descend upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in most circumstances in the form of Dihyah, and at other times he appeared to him and to the Companions in the form of a man of very white garments and very black hair, on whom no trace of travel was seen, and whom none of the Companions recognised. In a hadith: "Sometimes the angel appears to me as a man." Just as Jibril appeared to Maryam (Mary) as a well-formed human, and the angels were the guests of Ibrahim (Abraham) and the guests of Lut (Lot), and the ones who scaled the prayer niche (al-mihrab), for they appeared in the form of humans. The reason he would appear in the form of a man is that people have no capacity to see the angel in his own form. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd, and it is supported by the death of the one who heard the voice of an angel in the clouds saying: "Go forward, Hayzum," and he died upon hearing its voice. So how would it be if he saw him in his true form? Ibn Atiyyah said: this is not contradicted by the Prophet's (ﷺ) seeing Jibril and others in their forms, because he (peace be upon him) was given a strength, meaning a strength other than the powers of human beings. The word "man" was used in reply to those addressed, since they claimed that the angels were females. Al-Qurtubi said: if God had made the Messenger to mankind an angel, they would have fled from being close to him, and would not have felt at ease with him; the awe would have entered them from his speech so much that it would have silenced them from his speech and prevented them from questioning him, so the benefit would not be complete. And if He had transferred him from the form of the angels to a form like theirs, they would have said: "You are not an angel, you are only a human, so we will not believe in you," and they would have returned to the same state as before. This is the summation of what the earlier exegetes said. In this verse there is evidence against those who deny the descent of angels to the earth, and who say that they are subtle bodies with nothing in them requiring them to descend to the earth. This has been answered: He, exalted is He, is able to place in their bodies a heaviness that causes them to descend to the earth, and then remove it so that they return to their former subtlety and lightness, and this would be the cause of their ascent. That is the end of this reply. What we say is that divine power brings down the light and lifts up the heavy without placing heaviness in the light or lightness in the heavy, and this is not impossible, so there is no need to burden oneself with placing heaviness in the light and lightness in the heavy. In this verse there is also evidence for the possibility of angels taking the form of humans, and this is a true matter established by continuous transmission (mutawatir).

﴿And We would have confused them in what they confuse﴾: that is, We would have mixed up for them what they mix up for themselves at that time. For when they saw the angel in the form of a human, they would say: "This is a human and not an angel." I base this on my having brought the inimitable Qur'an, which states that I am an angel and not a human. They would have denied him as they denied the messengers, and so they would have been forsaken as they are forsaken. It is also possible that the meaning is: ﴿And We would have confused them﴾ at that time, similar to ﴿what they confuse﴾ for themselves now in their disbelief in the signs of Allah. This was said by al-Zamakhshari, with some condensation. Ibn Atiyyah said: And We would have mixed up for them what they mix up for themselves and their weak ones, meaning We would have done to them a confusion through which they would be confused, and that is not fitting. The speech may bear another intention: that We Ourselves would have confused them, as they confuse their weak ones, so We would have forbidden them from confusing, and We would have done it ourselves. Some said: confusion would occur because they believed the angels were females, so if they saw him in the form of a man, confusion would arise for them, just as they confused others. Some, including al-Dahhak, said: the verse was revealed concerning the Jews and Christians regarding their religion and their books, which they distorted, and they denied their messengers; so the meaning of the confusion is: We increased them in error upon their error. Ibn Abbas said: Allah confused them with what they confused for themselves by distorting speech from its proper places. The particle "ma" (what) is a verbal noun (masdariyyah), and He attributed the confusion to Himself from the standpoint of creation, and to them from the standpoint of acquisition. Ibn Muhaysin read (ولبسنا) with a single lam, and al-Zuhri read (ولَلَبَّسْنا) with the ba' shaddah (doubled).

(p-79)

﴿And messengers were certainly mocked before you, but those who scoffed at them were overtaken by what they used to mock.﴾ This is a consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for what he suffered from his people, and an example set by the messengers who came before him. It is similar to ﴿And if they deny you, then messengers before you were denied﴾ [Fatir 35:4], because what is shared in an unpleasant matter is lighter on the soul than what one bears alone. The comfort and the example of others carry a relief that is obvious. Al-Khansa said:

*"Were it not for the great number of those weeping around me over their brothers, I would have killed myself.*
*They do not weep like my brother, but I console myself for him through the example of others."*

One of the later poets said:

*"There is no escape from complaining to one of noble character,*
*who will share your grief, console you, or feel your pain."*

Since the disbelievers gained no benefit from sharing in the punishment, and found no consolation in it, Allah, exalted is He, negated this for them, saying: ﴿And it will not benefit you today, since you wronged, that you are sharers in the punishment﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 43:39]. It is said: some people used to say, mockingly, "He ought to be an angel from among the angels." The Messenger's heart would tighten on hearing this, so Allah, exalted is He, consoled him by informing him that mockery by their peoples had already befallen the messengers before him, so that this would serve as a means of easing the heart. In His words, ﴿so what they mocked overtook them﴾ and onward, there is information about what happened to those who mocked the messengers before you, and a certain warning for whoever mocks the Messenger, peace be upon him. It is also a reassurance to the Messenger that he should not care about them, because their end is destruction and the severe punishment that follows mockery. Allah, exalted is He, is sufficient to protect him from their evil and harm, as He said: ﴿Indeed, We are sufficient for you against the mockers﴾ [Al-Hijr 15:95].

The meaning of (sakhiru) is "they mocked," except that (istahza'a) takes the particle "bi-" while (sakhira) takes "min," as He said: ﴿If you mock us, then we mock you as you mock﴾ [Hud 11:38]. With "bi-" one says "sakhirtu bihi." The verb is repeated here because the triliteral form is lighter, and it is not repeated in ﴿And messengers were certainly mocked (istuhzi'a)﴾, so the construction would have been ﴿so it overtook those who⁠ mocked them⁠⁠﴾ with (istahza'u bihim), because the form (istaf'ala) is heavy. The apparent reading of (ma) is that it means "that which" (alladhi), though some allowed that (ma) be a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah). Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' allowed that it refers to other than the messengers. Al-Hawfi said: "among the nations of the messengers." Abu al-Baqa' said: "among the mockers," and (minhum) would then be a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the subject of (sakhiru). What they both said and allowed is not sound. ﴿Say: Travel through the earth, then observe how was the end of the deniers.﴾ When He mentioned what befell the deniers who mocked, and since those addressed were an unlettered nation that had not studied the scriptures nor sat with scholars, they were commanded to travel the earth and to reflect on what befell the deniers, so that they would take lesson from it, and so that the report of the truthful information would be reinforced by what they could see. Sight has an extra degree of lesson that does not exist otherwise, as one of the modern poets said:

*"Subtle meanings exist in what is seen, which cannot be grasped except through visiting and meeting."*

The apparent reading is that the travel commanded is moving from one place to another, that the observation commanded is observation by the eye, and that "the earth" means the lands near their own, the abodes of those destroyed for their sins, such as the land of 'Ad, Madyan, the cities of the people of Lut, and Thamud. Some said that the travel and observation here are not sensory, but rather the roaming of thought and intellect over the conditions of past nations that denied their messengers. For this reason al-Hasan said: "Travel through the earth" means recite the Qur'an, that is, read the Qur'an and observe what became of the deniers. The metaphorical use of "travel in the earth" for reciting the Qur'an is far-fetched. Some said: "the earth" here is general, because in every region there are traces of the destroyed and lessons for those who observe. Al-Zamakhshari said regarding the difference: he made observation a consequence of travel, so travel was a cause of observation; then he said: "as if it were said: travel in order to observe, and do not travel the way of the heedless." As for examples such as "I struck Zayd, so he wept," and "Ma'iz committed adultery, so he was stoned," the causal link is understood from the content of the sentence, since the particle is not established for causation. It only indicates that the weeping followed the striking and the stoning followed the adultery. Even if we grant that (fa) indicates causation, why would travel here be travel of permission, while elsewhere it is travel of obligation? That would require a distinction between this place and those places.

﴿And messengers were certainly mocked before you, but those who scoffed at them were overtaken by what they used to mock.﴾ This is a consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for what he suffered from his people, and an example set by the messengers who came before him. The comfort and the example of others carry a relief that is obvious. Al-Khansa said:

*"Were it not for the great number of those weeping around me over their brothers, I would have killed myself.*
*They do not weep like my brother, but I console myself for him through the example of others."*

One of the later poets said:

*"There is no escape from complaining to one of noble character,*
*who will share your grief, console you, or feel your pain."*

Since the disbelievers gained no benefit from sharing in the punishment, and found no consolation in it, Allah, exalted is He, negated this for them, saying: ﴿And it will not benefit you today, since you wronged, that you are sharers in the punishment﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 43:39]. **Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 12–13:**

﴿Say: "To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?" Say: "To God."﴾ When the Exalted mentioned His disposing of those whom He destroyed for their sins, He commanded His Prophet ﷺ to ask them this, for they cannot answer except that it belongs to God the Exalted. Thereby it is established against them that He, the Exalted, is the Owner and the One who destroys them. This question is a question of rebuke (tabkit) and affirmation (taqrir). Then He commanded him to attribute this to God the Exalted, so that he would be the first to hasten to acknowledge it. It has been said: there is an ellipsis in the speech, its implied sense being: "If they do not answer, [say:] ﴿Say: To God.﴾" Some people said: the meaning is that he was commanded to ask, and it is as if, when they did not answer, they were asked, and so it was said to them: ﴿Say: To God.﴾ "Lillah" (to God) is the predicate of an omitted subject; the implied sense is: "Say, that is so," or: "It is to God."

﴿He has prescribed for Himself mercy.﴾ When the Exalted mentioned that He is the Originator of the world, Who disposes of its inhabitants as He wills, and that this indicates the executed power of His might, He followed it with the mention of His mercy and kindness to creation. The apparent meaning of "kataba" (prescribed/written) is "inscribed" and "wrote down." Some people held this view here, and that the literal sense of writing is intended, meaning: He commanded that it be written in the Preserved Tablet. It has been said: "kataba" here means He promised it as a favour and generosity. It has been said: it means He informed. It has been said: He made it obligatory by way of favour and generosity, not by way of compulsion. It has been said: He decreed it and enforced it. Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, He made it obligatory upon Himself, in guiding you to knowledge of Him, and set up for you the proofs of His oneness concerning what you yourselves affirm, namely the creation of the heavens and the earth, end quote. And "al-rahmah" (mercy) here: the apparent view is that it is general, encompassing both the good and the wicked in this world. It is an expression for His bestowing and His kindness upon them. He did not mention the object of the mercy, to whom it is directed, so it is general, as we have mentioned. It has been said: the alif and lam (the definite article) is for a known reference, so that what is meant is the single mercy which God the Exalted sent down out of the hundred mercies that He created, and He deferred ninety-nine, by which He will show mercy to His servants in the Hereafter. Al-Zajjaj said: "al-rahmah" is the reprieve of the disbelievers and granting them a lifespan so that they may repent, for He did not hasten punishment upon them for their disbelief. It has been said: "al-rahmah" is for whoever believes and affirms the messengers. In Sahih Muslim: "When God had finished creating, He wrote in a Book, which is with Him, concerning Himself: 'Indeed My mercy overcomes My wrath.'"

﴿He will surely gather you to the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt.﴾ When He mentioned that the Exalted had shown mercy to His servants, He mentioned the gathering (hashr), and that in it is recompense for good and evil. This sentence is the object of an oath, and it has no grammatical connection with what precedes it, although in terms of meaning it is connected to what precedes it, as we have mentioned. Al-Mahdawi related that a group of grammarians said: it is an explanation of the mercy, its implied sense being: "that He will gather you," so the sentence would be in the accusative position as an apposition (badal) to "al-rahmah." This is like His saying: ﴿Then it occurred to them, after they had seen the signs, that they should imprison him﴾ [Yusuf: 35], meaning: that they should imprison him. Ibn Atiyyah rejected this, saying: the heavy nun (nun al-tawkid) would then have entered an affirmative statement, and it only enters commands and prohibitions, and in the case of the obligatory in an oath. He said: that is what he mentioned. This does not limit the positions in which the nun of emphasis enters; do you not see its entering the conditional? And none of the cases he mentioned applies, like His saying: ﴿And if an evil suggestion from Satan should come to you﴾ [al-A'raf: 200]. Likewise His saying: and the specific case of the obligatory in an oath; this is not absolute, rather it has conditions mentioned in the science of grammar. They may say: the form of the sentence is the form of what is sworn to, which is why the nun attached, even though the meaning is contrary to an oath. Their claim is refuted, since the sentence sworn to has no position of its own in i'rab (grammatical analysis of case endings). So when you say: "By God, I will surely strike Zayd," then "la-adribanna" (I will surely strike) has no place in i'rab. But when you say: "Zayd, by God, I will surely strike him," the sentence of the oath and what is sworn to is in the nominative position. The verb "gather" here is said to be literal, i.e., ﴿He will surely gather you﴾ in the graves until the Day of Resurrection. The apparent sense is that "ila" (to) denotes the endpoint, and the meaning is: He will surely resurrect you, reaching ﴿the Day of Resurrection﴾. It has been said: the meaning is ﴿He will surely gather you﴾ in this world, creating you generation after generation until the Day of Resurrection. "Ila" may here have the sense of "li" (for), i.e., for the Day of Resurrection, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed You will gather the people for a Day about which there is no doubt﴾ [Al 'Imran: 9]. Further from the truth is the one who claimed that "ila" means "fi" (in), i.e., "in the Day of Resurrection," and even further from that is the one who held that it is superfluous, the implied sense being ﴿He will surely gather you﴾ on the Day of Resurrection. The apparent view is that the pronoun in "fihi" (about it) refers to the Day of Resurrection, and in it is a refutation of those who doubted the gathering. It may also refer to the gathering (jam'), which is the verbal noun understood from His saying: ﴿He will surely gather you﴾.

﴿Those who have lost themselves—they do not believe.﴾ There has been disagreement about the i'rab of "alladhina" (those who). Al-Akhfash said: it is an apposition (badal) to the pronoun of address in ﴿He will surely gather you﴾. Al-Mubarrad rejected this, saying that an apposition to a pronoun of address is not permitted, just as "marartu bika Zayd" (I passed by you, Zayd) is not permitted. Ibn Atiyyah rejected al-Mubarrad's rejection, saying: what is in the verse does not conform to the example, because the benefit of an apposition is contingent upon the second term; whereas when you say "marartu bika Zayd," there is no benefit in the second term. His saying ﴿He will surely gather you﴾ is suitable for addressing people in general, so the apposition of "alladhina" to the pronoun informs us that they are the ones specifically addressed, and they were singled out in the manner of a threat. This would be an apposition of part from whole. Ibn Atiyyah's words in this rejection are not good, because if we take ﴿He will surely gather you﴾ as suitable for addressing people in general, then "alladhina" would be an apposition of part from whole, and that would require a pronoun at that point; the implied sense would be ﴿Those who have lost themselves﴾ from among them. And his saying "so the apposition of alladhina to the pronoun informs us that they are the ones specifically addressed" implies that it should be an apposition of whole from whole, so the beginning of his speech contradicts its end: from the standpoint of suitability it would be an apposition of part from whole, and from the standpoint of the address being specific to them it would be an apposition of whole from whole. Whether an apposition to a first-person or second-person pronoun is permissible is disputed: the view of the Kufans and al-Akhfash is that it is permissible, and the view of the majority of the Basrans is that it is not permissible. This applies when the apposition does not convey the meaning of emphasis, for in that case it is permissible. All of this is established in the science of grammar. Al-Zajjaj said: "alladhina" is in the nominative case by way of the inceptive (mubtada'), and the predicate is His saying: ﴿then they do not believe﴾, and the fa' (then) entered because the subject contains the meaning of a conditional, as if it were said: "Whoever loses himself, then he does not believe." Whoever holds the view of apposition makes the fa' a conjunction joining one sentence to another. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that "alladhina" be in the accusative case by way of censure, i.e., "I intend those who have lost themselves." Ibn Abi Hayyan: His estimate "bi-urid" (I intend) is not good; grammarians only estimate the accusative of censure as "adhummu" (I censure). Further from the truth is the one who held that the position of "alladhina" is genitive as an adjective to "al-mukadhdhibin" (the deniers) or an apposition to them. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: how is their not believing made the consequence of their losing, when the matter is the reverse? I say: its meaning is "those who have lost themselves" in God's knowledge, because of their choosing disbelief, "then they do not believe," end quote. In this there is a trace of Mu'tazilite doctrine in his saying "because of their choosing disbelief."

﴿And His is whatever dwells in the night and the day.﴾ When the Exalted mentioned that the dominion of what place contains of the heavens and the earth belongs to Him, He mentioned what time contains of night and day. Although each of time and place entails the other, the explicit mention of both is more eloquent in establishing ownership. Place was mentioned first because it is closer to minds and thoughts than time. For this reason al-Zamakhshari and others said: it is coordinated (ma'tuf) on His saying "to God." The apparent view is that it is a resumptive statement of information, and it is not included under His saying: "Say." "Sakana" (dwells) here: al-Suddi and others said: it is from habitation (sukna), i.e., what is established and settled. Al-Zamakhshari did not mention anything else, and said: its transitivity with "fi" (in) is as in His saying: ﴿And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves﴾ [Ibrahim: 45]. A group said: it is from stillness (sukun), which is the opposite of motion (harakah). These differed: it was said there is an omitted conjunction, i.e., "and what moves," and it was omitted as in His saying: "that protects you from the heat and the cold." It was said: there is no omission here, and it restricted itself to the still, because everything that moves may become still, but not everything that is still moves. It was said: because stillness is more prevalent in existence than motion. As for His saying "and the day," it is because some of the created things rest by day and spread out by night; this was said by Muqatil. Ibn Atiyyah preferred the first view, saying: the aim of the verse is the generality of everything, and that is only ensured if "sakana" means settled and established; otherwise, moving things among created beings are more numerous than the still. Do you not see that ships, the sun, the moon, the wandering stars, the angels, and kinds of animals are moving, and night and day are containers of time? End quote. This is not good, because he said that generality is ensured only if "sakana" means settled and established, and this is not confined to what he mentioned. Do you not see that generality is ensured on the view of the one who made it from stillness and posited an omitted conjunction, i.e., "and what moves," and on the view of the one who claimed that everything that moves may become still, but not everything that is still moves? So each of these two views entails generality, and therefore generality is not confined to what Ibn Atiyyah mentioned.

﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ Since the disputations of the disbelieving deniers have been mentioned earlier, and the gathering in which recompense occurs has been mentioned, the attribute of hearing is fitting, because of the dispute that took place, and the attribute of knowledge is fitting, because it includes the meaning of recompense, since that indicates threat and warning.
