Al-Mubarrad rejected this, saying that an apposition to a pronoun of address is not permitted, just as "marartu bika Zayd" (I passed by you, Zayd) is not permitted. Ibn Atiyyah rejected al-Mubarrad's rejection, saying: what is in the verse does not conform to the example, because the benefit of an apposition is contingent upon the second term; whereas when you say "marartu bika Zayd," there is no benefit in the second term. His saying ﴿He will surely gather you﴾ is suitable for addressing people in general, so the apposition of "alladhina" to the pronoun informs us that they are the ones specifically addressed, and they were singled out in the manner of a threat. This would be an apposition of part from whole. Ibn Atiyyah's words in this rejection are not good, because if we take ﴿He will surely gather you﴾ as suitable for addressing people in general, then "alladhina" would be an apposition of part from whole, and that would require a pronoun at that point; the implied sense would be ﴿Those who have lost themselves﴾ from among them. And his saying "so the apposition of alladhina to the pronoun informs us that they are the ones specifically addressed" implies that it should be an apposition of whole from whole, so the beginning of his speech contradicts its end: from the standpoint of suitability it would be an apposition of part from whole, and from the standpoint of the address being specific to them it would be an apposition of whole from whole. Whether an apposition to a first-person or second-person pronoun is permissible is disputed: the view of the Kufans and al-Akhfash is that it is permissible, and the view of the majority of the Basrans is that it is not permissible. This applies when the apposition does not convey the meaning of emphasis, for in that case it is permissible. All of this is established in the science of grammar. Al-Zajjaj said: "alladhina" is in the nominative case by way of the inceptive (mubtada'), and the predicate is His saying: ﴿then they do not believe﴾, and the fa' (then) entered because the subject contains the meaning of a conditional, as if it were said: "Whoever loses himself, then he does not believe." Whoever holds the view of apposition makes the fa' a conjunction joining one sentence to another. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that "alladhina" be in the accusative case by way of censure, i.e., "I intend those who have lost themselves." Ibn Abi Hayyan: His estimate "bi-urid" (I intend) is not good; grammarians only estimate the accusative of censure as "adhummu" (I censure). Further from the truth is the one who held that the position of "alladhina" is genitive as an adjective to "al-mukadhdhibin" (the deniers) or an apposition to them. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: how is their not believing made the consequence of their losing, when the matter is the reverse? I say: its meaning is "those who have lost themselves" in God's knowledge, because of their choosing disbelief, "then they do not believe," end quote. In this there is a trace of Mu'tazilite doctrine in his saying "because of their choosing disbelief."

﴿And His is whatever dwells in the night and the day.﴾ When the Exalted mentioned that the dominion of what place contains of the heavens and the earth belongs to Him, He mentioned what time contains of night and day. Although each of time and place entails the other, the explicit mention of both is more eloquent in establishing ownership. Place was mentioned first because it is closer to minds and thoughts than time. For this reason al-Zamakhshari and others said: it is coordinated (ma'tuf) on His saying "to God." The apparent view is that it is a resumptive statement of information, and it is not included under His saying: "Say." "Sakana" (dwells) here: al-Suddi and others said: it is from habitation (sukna), i.e., what is established and settled. Al-Zamakhshari did not mention anything else, and said: its transitivity with "fi" (in) is as in His saying: ﴿And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves﴾ [Ibrahim: 45]. A group said: it is from stillness (sukun), which is the opposite of motion (harakah). These differed: it was said there is an omitted conjunction, i.e., "and what moves," and it was omitted as in His saying: "that protects you from the heat and the cold." It was said: there is no omission here, and it restricted itself to the still, because everything that moves may become still, but not everything that is still moves. It was said: because stillness is more prevalent in existence than motion. As for His saying "and the day," it is because some of the created things rest by day and spread out by night; this was said by Muqatil. Ibn Atiyyah preferred the first view, saying: the aim of the verse is the generality of everything, and that is only ensured if "sakana" means settled and established; otherwise, moving things among created beings are more numerous than the still. Do you not see that ships, the sun, the moon, the wandering stars, the angels, and kinds of animals are moving, and night and day are containers of time? End quote. This is not good, because he said that generality is ensured only if "sakana" means settled and established, and this is not confined to what he mentioned. Do you not see that generality is ensured on the view of the one who made it from stillness and posited an omitted conjunction, i.e., "and what moves," and on the view of the one who claimed that everything that moves may become still, but not everything that is still moves? So each of these two views entails generality, and therefore generality is not confined to what Ibn Atiyyah mentioned.

﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ Since the disputations of the disbelieving deniers have been mentioned earlier, and the gathering in which recompense occurs has been mentioned, the attribute of hearing is fitting, because of the dispute that took place, and the attribute of knowledge is fitting, because it includes the meaning of recompense, since that indicates threat and warning.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 14–16 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Say: "Shall I take as a protector other than Allah, the Originator of the heavens and the earth, who feeds and is not fed?" Say: "I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit, and do not be among the polytheists."﴾ ﴿Say: "Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous Day."﴾ ﴿Whoever is spared it on that Day, Allah has had mercy upon him, and that is the manifest triumph.﴾ ﴿And if Allah touches you with harm, there is none to remove it except Him; and if He touches you with good, then He is over all things competent.﴾ [Al-An'am: 17] ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants, and He is the Wise, the All-Aware.﴾ [Al-An'am: 18] ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest in testimony?" Say: "Allah is Witness between me and you. And this Qur'an has been revealed to me that I may warn you thereby, and whomever it reaches. Do you indeed testify that there are other gods with Allah?" Say: "I do not testify." Say: "He is only one God, and I am free of what you associate."﴾ [Al-An'am: 19] ﴿Those to whom We gave the Scripture recognize it as they recognize their own sons. Those who have lost themselves, they do not believe.﴾ [Al-An'am: 20] ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah or denies His verses? Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed.﴾ [Al-An'am: 21] ﴿And the Day We will gather them all, then We will say to those who associated others with Allah: "Where are your partners that you used to claim?"﴾ [Al-An'am: 22] ﴿Then their trial will be only that they will say: "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists."﴾ [Al-An'am: 23] ﴿Look how they lie against themselves, and what they used to invent has failed them.﴾ [Al-An'am: 24] ﴿And among them are those who listen to you, but We have placed over their hearts coverings lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness. And if they should see every sign, they will not believe in it. To the extent that when they come to you, disputing with you, those who disbelieve say: "This is not but the fables of the former peoples."﴾ [Al-An'am: 25] ﴿And they forbid it and keep away from it, but they destroy none except themselves, and they do not perceive.﴾ [Al-An'am: 26] ﴿If you could see when they are made to stand over the Fire and they say: "Oh, would that we were returned, and we would not deny the signs of our Lord, and we would be among the believers!"﴾ [Al-An'am: 27] ﴿Rather, what they used to conceal before has appeared to them. And even if they were returned, they would revert to what they were forbidden, and indeed they are liars.﴾ [Al-An'am: 28] ﴿And they say: "There is only our worldly life, and we will not be resurrected."﴾ [Al-An'am: 29] ﴿If you could see when they are made to stand before their Lord. He will say: "Is this not the truth?" They will say: "Yes, by our Lord." He will say: "Then taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve."﴾ [Al-An'am: 30] ﴿Those have lost who denied the meeting with Allah, until when the Hour comes upon them suddenly, they will say: "Oh, our regret over what we neglected concerning it!" while they carry their burdens upon their backs. Unquestionably, evil is what they carry.﴾ [Al-An'am: 31] ﴿And the worldly life is not but amusement and diversion, and the Hereafter is better for those who fear Allah. Then will you not reason?﴾ [Al-An'am: 32]

**Fa-ṭara** (فَطَرَ): created and originated without a model. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "I did not know the meaning of *fa-ṭara* until two Bedouins came to me disputing over a well, and one of them said: *anā faṭartuhā*," meaning, "I originated it and brought it into being." *Faṭara* also means to split, as in *faṭara nāb al-baʿīr* (the camel's tooth split), and from it is the Qur'anic phrase ﴿Do you see any flaw?﴾ and His saying ﴿about to be split apart from it﴾.

**Kashaf al-ḍurr** (كَشَفَ الضُّرَّ): he removed the harm. And *kashafat ʿan saqayhā* means she uncovered her shins, i.e., removed what covered them.

**Al-qahr** (الْقَهْر): overpowering, and compelling someone toward a thing without his choice.

**Al-waqr** (الوَقْر): heaviness in hearing. One says *waqarat udhunuhu*, with *fatḥ* and *kasr* of the *qāf*. It is also heard as *udhun mawqūrah*, so the verb on this basis is *waqarat*. *Al-waqr* with *fatḥ* and *kasr* of the *wāw* is also reported.

**Asāṭīr** (أساطِير): the plural of *isṭārah*, meaning trifles, as stated by Abū ʿUbayda. It is also said: the singular is *ussṭūrah*, like *uḍḥūkah* (a joke). It is also said: the singular is *ussṭūr*, or *isṭīr* and *isṭīrah*. It is also said: it is a plural with no singular, like *ʿabābīd*. It is also said: it is a plural of a plural, one says *saṭr* and *suṭur*. Whoever says *saṭr* forms its paucal plural as *asṭur* and its plural of multitude as *suṭūr*. Whoever says *suṭur* forms it as *asṭār*, and then forms *asṭār* into *asāṭīr*, as stated by Yaʿqūb. It is also said it is a plural of a plural of a plural: *saṭr*, *asṭur*, then *asṭār*, then *asāṭīr*, as reported from al-Zajjāj. *Asṭār* is not the plural of *asṭur*; rather both are paucal plurals of *saṭr*.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: It is also said that it is a collective noun (*ism jamʿ*, a noun with plural meaning but no singular form from its own root), like *ʿabābīd* and *shamāṭīṭ*, ending his statement (p. 85). The grammarians do not call this an *ism jamʿ*, because it follows the pattern of plurals; rather they call it a plural, even if no singular is pronounced for it.

**Nā'á** (نَأى): he went far away. Its transitive form takes an object in the accusative marked by the *hamzah* (i.e., *anʾā*), not by doubling, and likewise everything of similar form whose middle radical is a *hamzah*.

**Waqafa ʿalā kadhā** (وقَفَ عَلى كَذا): he detained (*ḥabasa*). The verbal noun of the transitive form is *waqf*, and the verbal noun of the intransitive is *wuqūf*; he distinguished between them by the verbal noun.

**Al-baghtu wa-al-baghtah** (البَغْتُ والبَغْتَةُ): suddenness. One says *baghatahu yabghatuhu*, meaning he came upon him suddenly. It is the arrival of a thing swiftly without your paying attention to it and without your knowing the time of its arrival.

**Farraṭa** (فَرَّطَ): he fell short while having the ability to avoid falling short. Abū ʿUbayd said: *farraṭa* means he neglected. Ibn Baḥr said: *faraṭa* means he preceded, and *al-fāriṭ* is the one who precedes; *faraṭa* also means he left the lead to another.

**Al-awzār** (الأوْزار): sins and transgressions. Its root meaning is heaviness from carrying. *Zartuhu* means I carried it. *Awzār al-ḥarb* means the weight of weapons. From it comes *al-wazīr* (the vizier), because he bears on behalf of the ruler the burdens of what is entrusted to him from managing his kingdom.

**Al-lahw** (اللَّهْو): turning the soul away from seriousness toward jest. One says from it *lahā yalhū*, and *luhiya ʿan kadhā*, meaning he turned his soul away from it. The root is one, and the *wāw* became *yāʾ* because of the *kasrah* before it, like *shaqiyy* and *raḍiyy*. Al-Mahdawī said: the one whose meaning is turning away has a *yāʾ* as its final radical, as evidenced by their saying *lahayān*, and the final radical of the first is a *wāw*. This is nothing, because the *wāw* in the dual became *yāʾ*, and its origin is not *yāʾ*. Do you not see the dual of *shajj* being *shajiyān*, and it is from the roots with *wāw*, from *al-shajw*?

﴿Say: "Shall I take as a protector other than Allah, the Originator of the heavens and the earth"﴾ Since it has preceded that He, the Exalted, originated the heavens and the earth, and that He owns what place and time contain, Allah commanded His Prophet to say this to them as a rebuke, meaning: the One who has these attributes is the One who is to be taken as protector, helper, and supporter, not the gods you have, since they neither benefit nor harm, for they are either inanimate objects or subjugated animals. The interrogative *hamzah* entered on the noun and not the verb, because the denial concerns taking other than Allah as a protector, not taking a protector in general. This is like your saying to one who struck Zayd, who does not deserve to be struck but deserves honor: "Did you strike Zayd?" You are denying that someone like him should be struck. Similar to this is ﴿Is it other than Allah that you order me to worship, you ignorant ones?﴾ [Az-Zumar: 64], and ﴿Has Allah given you permission?﴾ [Yunus: 59].

Al-Ṭabarī and others said: he was commanded to say this statement to the disbelievers who invited him to worship their idols, so the verse on this view is an answer to their speech. This needs a chain of transmission establishing that the occasion of revelation of this verse is what he mentioned.

*Ghayr* (غَيْر) is in the accusative as the first object of *ittakhadha* (he took).

The majority read *Fāṭiri* (فاطِرِ) [in the genitive]. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Zamakhsharī interpreted it as an adjective (*naʿt*, descriptive modifier) of Allah. Al-Ḥūfī transmitted it the same way. Abū al-Baqāʾ interpreted it as an appositive (*badal*, substitute noun in apposition), and it seems he considered that separating the appositive from what it is in apposition to is easier than separating the qualified noun from its adjective, since the appositive according to the well-known view is a restatement of the governing word.

Ibn Abī ʿAbla read it with *ḍamma* on the *rāʾ* (*Fāṭiru*), by supposing a pronoun *huwa* (he) is omitted. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: or it is in the nominative as the subject of a sentence (*al-ibtidāʾ*). It requires supposing an omitted predicate, and there is no evidence for its omission.

It was read irregularly with *fatḥa* on the *rāʾ* (*Fāṭira*). Abū al-Baqāʾ interpreted it as an adjective of *walī* (protector), with the intention of the nunation, or an appositive of it, or a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*, a word describing the state of the subject at the time of the action). The meaning on this reading is: Shall I take as a protector *Fāṭira al-samāwāti wa-al-arḍ* (the Originator of the heavens and the earth), other than Allah? The best is to read it in the accusative as a term of praise.

Al-Zuhrī read *faṭara* (فَطَرَ), making it a past-tense verb.

﴿And He feeds and is not fed﴾: that is, He provides sustenance and is not provided for, like His saying: ﴿I do not want any provision from them, nor do I want them to feed Me﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 57]. The meaning is that all benefits are from Allah. Feeding was singled out from among the types of benefit because of the great need for it, just as usury was singled out for "consumption," even though the intended purpose is benefiting from usury.

Mujāhid, Ibn Jubayr, al-Aʿmash, Abū Ḥaywa, ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd, Abū ʿAmr, and in one report from him, read *wa-lā yuṭʿamu* (and is not fed) with *fatḥa* on the *yāʾ*. The meaning is that He, the Exalted, is exempt from eating and is not similar to created beings.

Yamān al-ʿAmmānī and Ibn Abī ʿAbla read *wa-lā yuṭʿimu* (and does not feed), with *ḍamma* on the *yāʾ* and *kasra* on the ʿayn, like the first. So the pronoun in *wa-huwa yuṭʿimu* (and He feeds) refers to Allah, and the pronoun in *wa-lā yuṭʿimu* refers to the protector.

Ibn al-Maʾmūn transmitted from Yaʿqūb: *wa-huwa yuṭʿamu wa-lā yuṭʿimu* (and He is fed and does not feed), with the first verb in the passive and the second in the active, and the pronoun referring to other than Allah.

Al-Ashhab read *wa-huwa yuṭʿimu wa-lā yuṭʿimu* with both verbs in the active. It was interpreted to mean: and He feeds, and does not seek to be fed. Al-Azharī related that *aṭʿamtu* can mean *istaṭʿamtu* (I asked for food).

Al-Zamakhsharī said: It may also be that the meaning is: He feeds at one time and does not feed at another, according to what is in the interest, like your saying: "He gives, withholds, extends, restricts, enriches, and impoverishes."

In the reading of the one who reads with differing verbs, there is paronomasia by vowel marks (*tajnīs al-tashkīl*, a figure in which two words share the same consonants and differ only in their vowel marks), and this is when the vowel marking distinguishes between two words. Usāmah ibn Munqidh called it in his book *al-Badīʿah* *tajnīs al-taḥrīf* (paronomasia by alteration), but *tajnīs al-tashkīl* is more fitting for it.

﴿Say: "Indeed, I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit."﴾ Al-Zamakhsharī said: Because the Prophet is the foremost of his community in Islam, like His saying: ﴿And I have been commanded to that, and I am the first of the Muslims﴾ [Al-An'am: 163], and like the statement of Moses: ﴿Glory be to You; I have repented to You, and I am the first of the believers﴾ [Al-A'raf: 143].

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: The meaning is: the first to submit from this community and with this law. The speech does not include anything beyond that. What al-Zamakhsharī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya said is the view of al-Ḥasan. Al-Ḥasan said: its meaning is: the first to submit from my community.

It was said: there is a problem with this view, because the Prophet (ﷺ) never refrained from the truth or failed to submit to it. This is rather an indirect statement regarding Islam, like when a king commands his subjects to do something and then follows it with: "I am the first to do this," in order to move them to do it.

It was also said: he intended first in rank and virtue, as in the report: "We are the last and the first," and in another report: "the foremost."

It was said: *aslama* (submitted) means he sincerely devoted himself, and did not associate anything with Allah.

It was said: *istaslama* (surrendered).

It was said: he intended his entry into the religion of Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him), like His saying: ﴿The religion of your father Ibrahim. He named you Muslims before [in previous scriptures]﴾ [Al-Hajj: 78].

It was said: the first to submit was on the Day of the Covenant, so he would be prior to all creation, as He said: ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 7].

﴿And do not be among the polytheists.﴾ That is, and it was said: "to me," and the meaning is that he was commanded to submit to Islam and forbidden from associating others with Allah. This is how al-Zamakhsharī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya interpreted it, supposing an omitted *wa-qīla* (and it was said): "to me." This is because its conjunction cannot be coordinated with the wording of ﴿Indeed, I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit﴾, so that it would fall under the wording of *qul* (say), since if it were so, the construction would be: "and I will not be among the polytheists." It was also said: it is coordinated with the object of *qul* on the basis of meaning, and the meaning is: ﴿Say: "Indeed, I [am commanded]"—it was said to me: "Be the first of those who submit, and do not be among the polytheists"—so both are governed by the verb of saying, but the first came without the word of saying while carrying its meaning, so the second is governed by the meaning. It was also said: it is coordinated with *qul* (say), commanded to say such and such, and forbidden from such and such. It was also said: it is a prohibition against allying with polytheists. It was also said: the address is to him in wording, but what is meant is his community. This is the apparent meaning, because of His saying: ﴿If you should associate others with Allah, your deeds will surely be nullified﴾ [Az-Zumar: 65], and infallibility is incompatible with the possibility of association.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 14–16 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Say: Indeed I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous Day.﴾ The apparent meaning is that "fear" (al-khawf) here is in its proper sense, which is the anticipation of something disliked. Ibn 'Abbas said: the meaning of "akhaf" (I fear) is "a'lam" (I know). And "'asaytu" (I disobey) is general in regard to all kinds of sins, but here it refers only to shirk, which was forbidden, as stated by Ibn 'Atiyyah. The fear is not actually realized, due to his infallibility (ismah); rather it is conditional upon a condition that is impossible in his case, and its response (jawab) is omitted. For this reason it came in the past tense. It was said: it is an intervening conditional clause (shart mu'taridah), having no place in i'rab, like an intervening oath. It was also said: it is in a position of nasb as a circumstantial clause (hal), as if it were said: "Indeed I fear, disobeying my Lord." Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: the example of the verse is, if five were an even number, it would be divided into two equal parts; meaning that it is a conditional upon an impossibility. The tremendous Day is the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Whoever is turned away from it on that Day, He has indeed shown him mercy.﴾ Hamzah, Abu Bakr and al-Kisa'i read "man yasrif" in the active voice, so "man" is a fronted object (maf'ul muqaddam), and the pronoun in "yasrif" refers to Allah. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy: "man yasrifi Allah." The pronoun in "'anhu" refers to the punishment, and the hidden pronoun in "rahimahu" refers to the Lord. That is: whoever Allah turns the punishment away from, He has shown him the great mercy, which is salvation from punishment; and when he is saved from punishment, he enters Paradise. It is also permissible to parse "man" as a subject (mubtada'). The pronoun in "'anhu" refers to it, and the object of "yasrif" is omitted for brevity, since it was mentioned earlier in the verse before the estimation; that is: whoever Allah turns the punishment away from, He has shown him mercy. On this view it may also be a case of al-ishtighal, so "man" is in the accusative by an implied verb which is explained by the meaning of "yasrif." It is also permissible, on parsing "man" as a subject, for the object to be mentioned, namely "yawma'idhin," with an omission, meaning "the terror of that Day," so "yawma'idhin" is in the accusative as an object. The rest of the Seven read "man yusraf" in the passive voice, and it is known that the one who turns away is Allah the Exalted, so it was omitted for knowledge of Him, or for brevity, since the Lord was previously mentioned. In this case it is also permissible that the pronoun in "yusraf" refers to "man," and in "'anhu" refers to the punishment; that is: whoever is turned away from the punishment. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to "man," and the object of "yusraf" is "yawma'idhin," which is built (mabni) because it is annexed to "idh," so it is in a position of raf' by "yusraf." The tanwin in "yawma'idhin" is the tanwin of compensation (tanwin 'iwad) for a omitted clause implied by the preceding speech; the estimate is "the Day when the recompense occurs," since no explicit clause preceded it, the tanwin serves as a compensation for it. The grammarians discussed the preference between the two readings, as is their custom. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose... Abu 'Ali pointed to the goodness of reading "yasrif" in the active voice, to suit "fa-qad rahimahu," and he did not come with "fa-qad ruhima," and the reading of 'Abd Allah and Ubayy supports it: "man yasrifi Allah." Al-Tabari preferred the reading "yusraf" in the passive voice, saying: because it involves less implication. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: as for Makki ibn Abi Talib, he was confused in his book al-Hidayah in preferring the reading with the vowel fatha on the ya', and he gave corrupt examples in his argument. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is a verbal justification, whose connection to the preference is weak; as for the meaning, the two readings are one. We have mentioned on more than one occasion that we do not prefer one of the two mutawatir readings over the other. Abu 'Amr al-Zahid related in his book al-Yawaqit that Abu al-'Abbas Ahmad ibn Yahya Tha'lab did not see preference between the seven readings. He said: Tha'lab said from his own words: if the i'rab differs in the Qur'an among the Seven, I do not prefer one i'rab over another in the Qur'an; but when I turn to ordinary speech, the speech of people, I prefer the stronger. The best predecessor for us is Ahmad ibn Yahya, who was knowledgeable in grammar and lexicography, pious and trustworthy.

﴿That is the manifest triumph.﴾ The reference of "dhalika" (that) is to the verbal noun implied by "man yusraf," meaning: that turning away is the success and the salvation from destruction. "Al-mubin" means clear in itself, or making others clear.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 14–16 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Say: "Shall I take as a protector other than Allah, the Originator of the heavens and the earth, who feeds and is not fed?" Say: "I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit, and do not be among the polytheists."﴾ ﴿Say: "Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous Day."﴾ ﴿Whoever is spared it on that Day, Allah has had mercy upon him, and that is the manifest triumph.﴾ ﴿And if Allah touches you with harm, there is none to remove it except Him; and if He touches you with good, then He is over all things competent.﴾ [Al-An'am: 17] ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants, and He is the Wise, the All-Aware.﴾ [Al-An'am: 18] ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest in testimony?" Say: "Allah is Witness between me and you. And this Qur'an has been revealed to me that I may warn you thereby, and whomever it reaches. Do you indeed testify that there are other gods with Allah?" Say: "I do not testify." Say: "He is only one God, and I am free of what you associate."﴾ [Al-An'am: 19] ﴿Those to whom We gave the Scripture recognize it as they recognize their own sons. Those who have lost themselves, they do not believe.﴾ [Al-An'am: 20] ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah or denies His verses? Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed.﴾ [Al-An'am: 21] ﴿And the Day We will gather them all, then We will say to those who associated others with Allah: "Where are your partners that you used to claim?"﴾ [Al-An'am: 22] ﴿Then their trial will be only that they will say: "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists."﴾ [Al-An'am: 23] ﴿Look how they lie against themselves, and what they used to invent has failed them.﴾ [Al-An'am: 24] ﴿And among them are those who listen to you, but We have placed over their hearts coverings lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness. And if they should see every sign, they will not believe in it. To the extent that when they come to you, disputing with you, those who disbelieve say: "This is not but the fables of the former peoples."﴾ [Al-An'am: 25] ﴿And they forbid it and keep away from it, but they destroy none except themselves, and they do not perceive.﴾ [Al-An'am: 26] ﴿If you could see when they are made to stand over the Fire and they say: "Oh, would that we were returned, and we would not deny the signs of our Lord, and we would be among the believers!"﴾ [Al-An'am: 27] ﴿Rather, what they used to conceal before has appeared to them. And even if they were returned, they would revert to what they were forbidden, and indeed they are liars.﴾ [Al-An'am: 28] ﴿And they say: "There is only our worldly life, and we will not be resurrected."﴾ [Al-An'am: 29] ﴿If you could see when they are made to stand before their Lord. He will say: "Is this not the truth?" They will say: "Yes, by our Lord." He will say: "Then taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve."﴾ [Al-An'am: 30] ﴿Those have lost who denied the meeting with Allah, until when the Hour comes upon them suddenly, they will say: "Oh, our regret over what we neglected concerning it!" while they carry their burdens upon their backs. Unquestionably, evil is what they carry.﴾ [Al-An'am: 31] ﴿And the worldly life is not but amusement and diversion, and the Hereafter is better for those who fear Allah. Then will you not reason?﴾ [Al-An'am: 32]

**Fa-ṭara** (فَطَرَ): created and originated without a model. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "I did not know the meaning of *fa-ṭara* until two Bedouins came to me disputing over a well, and one of them said: *anā faṭartuhā*," meaning, "I originated it and brought it into being." *Faṭara* also means to split, as in *faṭara nāb al-baʿīr* (the camel's tooth split), and from it is the Qur'anic phrase ﴿Do you see any flaw?﴾ and His saying ﴿about to be split apart from it﴾.

**Kashaf al-ḍurr** (كَشَفَ الضُّرَّ): he removed the harm. And *kashafat ʿan saqayhā* means she uncovered her shins, i.e., removed what covered them.

**Al-qahr** (الْقَهْر): overpowering, and compelling someone toward a thing without his choice.

**Al-waqr** (الوَقْر): heaviness in hearing. One says *waqarat udhunuhu*, with *fatḥ* and *kasr* of the *qāf*. It is also heard as *udhun mawqūrah*, so the verb on this basis is *waqarat*. *Al-waqr* with *fatḥ* and *kasr* of the *wāw* is also reported.

**Asāṭīr** (أساطِير): the plural of *isṭārah*, meaning trifles, as stated by Abū ʿUbayda. It is also said: the singular is *ussṭūrah*, like *uḍḥūkah* (a joke). It is also said: the singular is *ussṭūr*, or *isṭīr* and *isṭīrah*. It is also said: it is a plural with no singular, like *ʿabābīd*. It is also said: it is a plural of a plural, one says *saṭr* and *suṭur*. Whoever says *saṭr* forms its paucal plural as *asṭur* and its plural of multitude as *suṭūr*. Whoever says *suṭur* forms it as *asṭār*, and then forms *asṭār* into *asāṭīr*, as stated by Yaʿqūb. It is also said it is a plural of a plural of a plural: *saṭr*, *asṭur*, then *asṭār*, then *asāṭīr*, as reported from al-Zajjāj. *Asṭār* is not the plural of *asṭur*; rather both are paucal plurals of *saṭr*.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: It is also said that it is a collective noun (*ism jamʿ*, a noun with plural meaning but no singular form from its own root), like *ʿabābīd* and *shamāṭīṭ*, ending his statement (p. 85). The grammarians do not call this an *ism jamʿ*, because it follows the pattern of plurals; rather they call it a plural, even if no singular is pronounced for it.

**Nā'á** (نَأى): he went far away. Its transitive form takes an object in the accusative marked by the *hamzah* (i.e., *anʾā*), not by doubling, and likewise everything of similar form whose middle radical is a *hamzah*.

**Waqafa ʿalā kadhā** (وقَفَ عَلى كَذا): he detained (*ḥabasa*). The verbal noun of the transitive form is *waqf*, and the verbal noun of the intransitive is *wuqūf*; he distinguished between them by the verbal noun.

**Al-baghtu wa-al-baghtah** (البَغْتُ والبَغْتَةُ): suddenness. One says *baghatahu yabghatuhu*, meaning he came upon him suddenly. It is the arrival of a thing swiftly without your paying attention to it and without your knowing the time of its arrival.

**Farraṭa** (فَرَّطَ): he fell short while having the ability to avoid falling short. Abū ʿUbayd said: *farraṭa* means he neglected. Ibn Baḥr said: *faraṭa* means he preceded, and *al-fāriṭ* is the one who precedes; *faraṭa* also means he left the lead to another.

**Al-awzār** (الأوْزار): sins and transgressions. Its root meaning is heaviness from carrying. *Zartuhu* means I carried it. *Awzār al-ḥarb* means the weight of weapons. From it comes *al-wazīr* (the vizier), because he bears on behalf of the ruler the burdens of what is entrusted to him from managing his kingdom.

**Al-lahw** (اللَّهْو): turning the soul away from seriousness toward jest. One says from it *lahā yalhū*, and *luhiya ʿan kadhā*, meaning he turned his soul away from it. The root is one, and the *wāw* became *yāʾ* because of the *kasrah* before it, like *shaqiyy* and *raḍiyy*. Al-Mahdawī said: the one whose meaning is turning away has a *yāʾ* as its final radical, as evidenced by their saying *lahayān*, and the final radical of the first is a *wāw*. This is nothing, because the *wāw* in the dual became *yāʾ*, and its origin is not *yāʾ*. Do you not see the dual of *shajj* being *shajiyān*, and it is from the roots with *wāw*, from *al-shajw*?

﴿Say: "Shall I take as a protector other than Allah, the Originator of the heavens and the earth"﴾ Since it has preceded that He, the Exalted, originated the heavens and the earth, and that He owns what place and time contain, Allah commanded His Prophet to say this to them as a rebuke, meaning: the One who has these attributes is the One who is to be taken as protector, helper, and supporter, not the gods you have, since they neither benefit nor harm, for they are either inanimate objects or subjugated animals. The interrogative *hamzah* entered on the noun and not the verb, because the denial concerns taking other than Allah as a protector, not taking a protector in general. This is like your saying to one who struck Zayd, who does not deserve to be struck but deserves honor: "Did you strike Zayd?" You are denying that someone like him should be struck. Similar to this is ﴿Is it other than Allah that you order me to worship, you ignorant ones?﴾ [Az-Zumar: 64], and ﴿Has Allah given you permission?﴾ [Yunus: 59].

Al-Ṭabarī and others said: he was commanded to say this statement to the disbelievers who invited him to worship their idols, so the verse on this view is an answer to their speech. This needs a chain of transmission establishing that the occasion of revelation of this verse is what he mentioned.

*Ghayr* (غَيْر) is in the accusative as the first object of *ittakhadha* (he took).

The majority read *Fāṭiri* (فاطِرِ) [in the genitive]. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Zamakhsharī interpreted it as an adjective (*naʿt*, descriptive modifier) of Allah. Al-Ḥūfī transmitted it the same way. Abū al-Baqāʾ interpreted it as an appositive (*badal*, substitute noun in apposition), and it seems he considered that separating the appositive from what it is in apposition to is easier than separating the qualified noun from its adjective, since the appositive according to the well-known view is a restatement of the governing word.

Ibn Abī ʿAbla read it with *ḍamma* on the *rāʾ* (*Fāṭiru*), by supposing a pronoun *huwa* (he) is omitted. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: or it is in the nominative as the subject of a sentence (*al-ibtidāʾ*). It requires supposing an omitted predicate, and there is no evidence for its omission.

It was read irregularly with *fatḥa* on the *rāʾ* (*Fāṭira*). Abū al-Baqāʾ interpreted it as an adjective of *walī* (protector), with the intention of the nunation, or an appositive of it, or a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*, a word describing the state of the subject at the time of the action). The meaning on this reading is: Shall I take as a protector *Fāṭira al-samāwāti wa-al-arḍ* (the Originator of the heavens and the earth), other than Allah? The best is to read it in the accusative as a term of praise.

Al-Zuhrī read *faṭara* (فَطَرَ), making it a past-tense verb.

﴿And He feeds and is not fed﴾: that is, He provides sustenance and is not provided for, like His saying: ﴿I do not want any provision from them, nor do I want them to feed Me﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 57]. The meaning is that all benefits are from Allah. Feeding was singled out from among the types of benefit because of the great need for it, just as usury was singled out for "consumption," even though the intended purpose is benefiting from usury.

Mujāhid, Ibn Jubayr, al-Aʿmash, Abū Ḥaywa, ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd, Abū ʿAmr, and in one report from him, read *wa-lā yuṭʿamu* (and is not fed) with *fatḥa* on the *yāʾ*. The meaning is that He, the Exalted, is exempt from eating and is not similar to created beings.

Yamān al-ʿAmmānī and Ibn Abī ʿAbla read *wa-lā yuṭʿimu* (and does not feed), with *ḍamma* on the *yāʾ* and *kasra* on the ʿayn, like the first. So the pronoun in *wa-huwa yuṭʿimu* (and He feeds) refers to Allah, and the pronoun in *wa-lā yuṭʿimu* refers to the protector.

Ibn al-Maʾmūn transmitted from Yaʿqūb: *wa-huwa yuṭʿamu wa-lā yuṭʿimu* (and He is fed and does not feed), with the first verb in the passive and the second in the active, and the pronoun referring to other than Allah.

Al-Ashhab read *wa-huwa yuṭʿimu wa-lā yuṭʿimu* with both verbs in the active. It was interpreted to mean: and He feeds, and does not seek to be fed. Al-Azharī related that *aṭʿamtu* can mean *istaṭʿamtu* (I asked for food).

Al-Zamakhsharī said: It may also be that the meaning is: He feeds at one time and does not feed at another, according to what is in the interest, like your saying: "He gives, withholds, extends, restricts, enriches, and impoverishes."

In the reading of the one who reads with differing verbs, there is paronomasia by vowel marks (*tajnīs al-tashkīl*, a figure in which two words share the same consonants and differ only in their vowel marks), and this is when the vowel marking distinguishes between two words. Usāmah ibn Munqidh called it in his book *al-Badīʿah* *tajnīs al-taḥrīf* (paronomasia by alteration), but *tajnīs al-tashkīl* is more fitting for it.

﴿Say: "Indeed, I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit."﴾ Al-Zamakhsharī said: Because the Prophet is the foremost of his community in Islam, like His saying: ﴿And I have been commanded to that, and I am the first of the Muslims﴾ [Al-An'am: 163], and like the statement of Moses: ﴿Glory be to You; I have repented to You, and I am the first of the believers﴾ [Al-A'raf: 143].

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: The meaning is: the first to submit from this community and with this law. The speech does not include anything beyond that. What al-Zamakhsharī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya said is the view of al-Ḥasan. Al-Ḥasan said: its meaning is: the first to submit from my community.

It was said: there is a problem with this view, because the Prophet (ﷺ) never refrained from the truth or failed to submit to it. This is rather an indirect statement regarding Islam, like when a king commands his subjects to do something and then follows it with: "I am the first to do this," in order to move them to do it.

It was also said: he intended first in rank and virtue, as in the report: "We are the last and the first," and in another report: "the foremost."

It was said: *aslama* (submitted) means he sincerely devoted himself, and did not associate anything with Allah.

It was said: *istaslama* (surrendered).

It was said: he intended his entry into the religion of Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him), like His saying: ﴿The religion of your father Ibrahim. He named you Muslims before [in previous scriptures]﴾ [Al-Hajj: 78].

It was said: the first to submit was on the Day of the Covenant, so he would be prior to all creation, as He said: ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 7].

﴿And do not be among the polytheists.﴾ That is, and it was said: "to me," and the meaning is that he was commanded to submit to Islam and forbidden from associating others with Allah. This is how al-Zamakhsharī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya interpreted it, supposing an omitted *wa-qīla* (and it was said): "to me." This is because its conjunction cannot be coordinated with the wording of ﴿Indeed, I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit﴾, so that it would fall under the wording of *qul* (say), since if it were so, the construction would be: "and I will not be among the polytheists." It was also said: it is coordinated with the object of *qul* on the basis of meaning, and the meaning is: ﴿Say: "Indeed, I [am commanded]"—it was said to me: "Be the first of those who submit, and do not be among the polytheists"—so both are governed by the verb of saying, but the first came without the word of saying while carrying its meaning, so the second is governed by the meaning. It was also said: it is coordinated with *qul* (say), commanded to say such and such, and forbidden from such and such. It was also said: it is a prohibition against allying with polytheists. It was also said: the address is to him in wording, but what is meant is his community. This is the apparent meaning, because of His saying: ﴿If you should associate others with Allah, your deeds will surely be nullified﴾ [Az-Zumar: 65], and infallibility is incompatible with the possibility of association.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 14–16 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Say: Indeed I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous Day.﴾ The apparent meaning is that "fear" (al-khawf) here is in its proper sense, which is the anticipation of something disliked. Ibn 'Abbas said: the meaning of "akhaf" (I fear) is "a'lam" (I know). And "'asaytu" (I disobey) is general in regard to all kinds of sins, but here it refers only to shirk, which was forbidden, as stated by Ibn 'Atiyyah. The fear is not actually realized, due to his infallibility (ismah); rather it is conditional upon a condition that is impossible in his case, and its response (jawab) is omitted. For this reason it came in the past tense. It was said: it is an intervening conditional clause (shart mu'taridah), having no place in i'rab, like an intervening oath. It was also said: it is in a position of nasb as a circumstantial clause (hal), as if it were said: "Indeed I fear, disobeying my Lord." Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: the example of the verse is, if five were an even number, it would be divided into two equal parts; meaning that it is a conditional upon an impossibility. The tremendous Day is the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Whoever is turned away from it on that Day, He has indeed shown him mercy.﴾ Hamzah, Abu Bakr and al-Kisa'i read "man yasrif" in the active voice, so "man" is a fronted object (maf'ul muqaddam), and the pronoun in "yasrif" refers to Allah. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy: "man yasrifi Allah." The pronoun in "'anhu" refers to the punishment, and the hidden pronoun in "rahimahu" refers to the Lord. That is: whoever Allah turns the punishment away from, He has shown him the great mercy, which is salvation from punishment; and when he is saved from punishment, he enters Paradise. It is also permissible to parse "man" as a subject (mubtada'). The pronoun in "'anhu" refers to it, and the object of "yasrif" is omitted for brevity, since it was mentioned earlier in the verse before the estimation; that is: whoever Allah turns the punishment away from, He has shown him mercy. On this view it may also be a case of al-ishtighal, so "man" is in the accusative by an implied verb which is explained by the meaning of "yasrif." It is also permissible, on parsing "man" as a subject, for the object to be mentioned, namely "yawma'idhin," with an omission, meaning "the terror of that Day," so "yawma'idhin" is in the accusative as an object. The rest of the Seven read "man yusraf" in the passive voice, and it is known that the one who turns away is Allah the Exalted, so it was omitted for knowledge of Him, or for brevity, since the Lord was previously mentioned. In this case it is also permissible that the pronoun in "yusraf" refers to "man," and in "'anhu" refers to the punishment; that is: whoever is turned away from the punishment. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to "man," and the object of "yusraf" is "yawma'idhin," which is built (mabni) because it is annexed to "idh," so it is in a position of raf' by "yusraf." The tanwin in "yawma'idhin" is the tanwin of compensation (tanwin 'iwad) for a omitted clause implied by the preceding speech; the estimate is "the Day when the recompense occurs," since no explicit clause preceded it, the tanwin serves as a compensation for it. The grammarians discussed the preference between the two readings, as is their custom. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose... Abu 'Ali pointed to the goodness of reading "yasrif" in the active voice, to suit "fa-qad rahimahu," and he did not come with "fa-qad ruhima," and the reading of 'Abd Allah and Ubayy supports it: "man yasrifi Allah." Al-Tabari preferred the reading "yusraf" in the passive voice, saying: because it involves less implication. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: as for Makki ibn Abi Talib, he was confused in his book al-Hidayah in preferring the reading with the vowel fatha on the ya', and he gave corrupt examples in his argument. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is a verbal justification, whose connection to the preference is weak; as for the meaning, the two readings are one. We have mentioned on more than one occasion that we do not prefer one of the two mutawatir readings over the other. Abu 'Amr al-Zahid related in his book al-Yawaqit that Abu al-'Abbas Ahmad ibn Yahya Tha'lab did not see preference between the seven readings. He said: Tha'lab said from his own words: if the i'rab differs in the Qur'an among the Seven, I do not prefer one i'rab over another in the Qur'an; but when I turn to ordinary speech, the speech of people, I prefer the stronger. The best predecessor for us is Ahmad ibn Yahya, who was knowledgeable in grammar and lexicography, pious and trustworthy.

﴿That is the manifest triumph.﴾ The reference of "dhalika" (that) is to the verbal noun implied by "man yusraf," meaning: that turning away is the success and the salvation from destruction. "Al-mubin" means clear in itself, or making others clear.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: "I did not know the meaning of *fa-ṭara* until two Bedouins came to me disputing over a well, and one of them said: *anā faṭartuhā*," meaning, "I originated it and brought it into being." *Faṭara* also means to split, as in *faṭara nāb al-baʿīr* (the camel's tooth split), and from it is the Qur'anic phrase ﴿Do you see any flaw?﴾ and His saying ﴿about to be split apart from it﴾.

It is also said: the singular is *ussṭūr*, or *isṭīr* and *isṭīrah*. It is also said: it is a plural with no singular, like *ʿabābīd*. Whoever says *suṭur* forms it as *asṭār*, and then forms *asṭār* into *asāṭīr*, as stated by Yaʿqūb. It is also said it is a plural of a plural of a plural: *saṭr*, *asṭur*, then *asṭār*, then *asāṭīr*, as reported from al-Zajjāj. *Asṭār* is not the plural of *asṭur*; rather both are paucal plurals of *saṭr*.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: It is also said that it is a collective noun (*ism jamʿ*, a noun with plural meaning but no singular form from its own root), like *ʿabābīd* and *shamāṭīṭ*, ending his statement (p. 85). The grammarians do not call this an *ism jamʿ*, because it follows the pattern of plurals; rather they call it a plural, even if no singular is pronounced for it.

**Nā'á** (نَأى): he went far away. Its transitive form takes an object in the accusative marked by the *hamzah* (i.e., *anʾā*), not by doubling, and likewise everything of similar form whose middle radical is a *hamzah*.

**Waqafa ʿalā kadhā** (وقَفَ عَلى كَذا): he detained (*ḥabasa*). The verbal noun of the transitive form is *waqf*, and the verbal noun of the intransitive is *wuqūf*; he distinguished between them by the verbal noun.

**Al-baghtu wa-al-baghtah** (البَغْتُ والبَغْتَةُ): suddenness. One says *baghatahu yabghatuhu*, meaning he came upon him suddenly. It is the arrival of a thing swiftly without your paying attention to it and without your knowing the time of its arrival.

**Farraṭa** (فَرَّطَ): he fell short while having the ability to avoid falling short. Abū ʿUbayd said: *farraṭa* means he neglected. Ibn Baḥr said: *faraṭa* means he preceded, and *al-fāriṭ* is the one who precedes; *faraṭa* also means he left the lead to another.

**Al-awzār** (الأوْزار): sins and transgressions. Its root meaning is heaviness from carrying. *Zartuhu* means I carried it. *Awzār al-ḥarb* means the weight of weapons. From it comes *al-wazīr* (the vizier), because he bears on behalf of the ruler the burdens of what is entrusted to him from managing his kingdom.

**Al-lahw** (اللَّهْو): turning the soul away from seriousness toward jest. One says from it *lahā yalhū*, and *luhiya ʿan kadhā*, meaning he turned his soul away from it. The root is one, and the *wāw* became *yāʾ* because of the *kasrah* before it, like *shaqiyy* and *raḍiyy*. Al-Mahdawī said: the one whose meaning is turning away has a *yāʾ* as its final radical, as evidenced by their saying *lahayān*, and the final radical of the first is a *wāw*. This is nothing, because the *wāw* in the dual became *yāʾ*, and its origin is not *yāʾ*. Do you not see the dual of *shajj* being *shajiyān*, and it is from the roots with *wāw*, from *al-shajw*?

﴿Say: "Shall I take as a protector other than Allah, the Originator of the heavens and the earth"﴾ Since it has preceded that He, the Exalted, originated the heavens and the earth, and that He owns what place and time contain, Allah commanded His Prophet to say this to them as a rebuke, meaning: the One who has these attributes is the One who is to be taken as protector, helper, and supporter, not the gods you have, since they neither benefit nor harm, for they are either inanimate objects or subjugated animals. The interrogative *hamzah* entered on the noun and not the verb, because the denial concerns taking other than Allah as a protector, not taking a protector in general. This is like your saying to one who struck Zayd, who does not deserve to be struck but deserves honor: "Did you strike Zayd?" You are denying that someone like him should be struck. Similar to this is ﴿Is it other than Allah that you order me to worship, you ignorant ones?﴾ [Az-Zumar: 64], and ﴿Has Allah given you permission?﴾ [Yunus: 59].

Al-Ṭabarī and others said: he was commanded to say this statement to the disbelievers who invited him to worship their idols, so the verse on this view is an answer to their speech. This needs a chain of transmission establishing that the occasion of revelation of this verse is what he mentioned.

*Ghayr* (غَيْر) is in the accusative as the first object of *ittakhadha* (he took).

The majority read *Fāṭiri* (فاطِرِ) [in the genitive]. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Zamakhsharī interpreted it as an adjective (*naʿt*, descriptive modifier) of Allah. Al-Ḥūfī transmitted it the same way. Abū al-Baqāʾ interpreted it as an appositive (*badal*, substitute noun in apposition), and it seems he considered that separating the appositive from what it is in apposition to is easier than separating the qualified noun from its adjective, since the appositive according to the well-known view is a restatement of the governing word.

Ibn Abī ʿAbla read it with *ḍamma* on the *rāʾ* (*Fāṭiru*), by supposing a pronoun *huwa* (he) is omitted. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: or it is in the nominative as the subject of a sentence (*al-ibtidāʾ*). It requires supposing an omitted predicate, and there is no evidence for its omission.

It was read irregularly with *fatḥa* on the *rāʾ* (*Fāṭira*). Abū al-Baqāʾ interpreted it as an adjective of *walī* (protector), with the intention of the nunation, or an appositive of it, or a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*, a word describing the state of the subject at the time of the action). The meaning on this reading is: Shall I take as a protector *Fāṭira al-samāwāti wa-al-arḍ* (the Originator of the heavens and the earth), other than Allah? The best is to read it in the accusative as a term of praise.

Al-Zuhrī read *faṭara* (فَطَرَ), making it a past-tense verb.

﴿And He feeds and is not fed﴾: that is, He provides sustenance and is not provided for, like His saying: ﴿I do not want any provision from them, nor do I want them to feed Me﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 57]. The meaning is that all benefits are from Allah. Feeding was singled out from among the types of benefit because of the great need for it, just as usury was singled out for "consumption," even though the intended purpose is benefiting from usury.

Mujāhid, Ibn Jubayr, al-Aʿmash, Abū Ḥaywa, ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd, Abū ʿAmr, and in one report from him, read *wa-lā yuṭʿamu* (and is not fed) with *fatḥa* on the *yāʾ*. The meaning is that He, the Exalted, is exempt from eating and is not similar to created beings.

Yamān al-ʿAmmānī and Ibn Abī ʿAbla read *wa-lā yuṭʿimu* (and does not feed), with *ḍamma* on the *yāʾ* and *kasra* on the ʿayn, like the first. So the pronoun in *wa-huwa yuṭʿimu* (and He feeds) refers to Allah, and the pronoun in *wa-lā yuṭʿimu* refers to the protector.

Ibn al-Maʾmūn transmitted from Yaʿqūb: *wa-huwa yuṭʿamu wa-lā yuṭʿimu* (and He is fed and does not feed), with the first verb in the passive and the second in the active, and the pronoun referring to other than Allah.

Al-Ashhab read *wa-huwa yuṭʿimu wa-lā yuṭʿimu* with both verbs in the active. It was interpreted to mean: and He feeds, and does not seek to be fed. Al-Azharī related that *aṭʿamtu* can mean *istaṭʿamtu* (I asked for food).

Al-Zamakhsharī said: It may also be that the meaning is: He feeds at one time and does not feed at another, according to what is in the interest, like your saying: "He gives, withholds, extends, restricts, enriches, and impoverishes."

In the reading of the one who reads with differing verbs, there is paronomasia by vowel marks (*tajnīs al-tashkīl*, a figure in which two words share the same consonants and differ only in their vowel marks), and this is when the vowel marking distinguishes between two words. Usāmah ibn Munqidh called it in his book *al-Badīʿah* *tajnīs al-taḥrīf* (paronomasia by alteration), but *tajnīs al-tashkīl* is more fitting for it.

﴿Say: "Indeed, I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit."﴾ Al-Zamakhsharī said: Because the Prophet is the foremost of his community in Islam, like His saying: ﴿And I have been commanded to that, and I am the first of the Muslims﴾ [Al-An'am: 163], and like the statement of Moses: ﴿Glory be to You; I have repented to You, and I am the first of the believers﴾ [Al-A'raf: 143].

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: The meaning is: the first to submit from this community and with this law. The speech does not include anything beyond that. What al-Zamakhsharī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya said is the view of al-Ḥasan. Al-Ḥasan said: its meaning is: the first to submit from my community.

It was said: there is a problem with this view, because the Prophet (ﷺ) never refrained from the truth or failed to submit to it. This is rather an indirect statement regarding Islam, like when a king commands his subjects to do something and then follows it with: "I am the first to do this," in order to move them to do it.

It was also said: he intended first in rank and virtue, as in the report: "We are the last and the first," and in another report: "the foremost."

It was said: *aslama* (submitted) means he sincerely devoted himself, and did not associate anything with Allah.

It was said: *istaslama* (surrendered).

It was said: he intended his entry into the religion of Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him), like His saying: ﴿The religion of your father Ibrahim. He named you Muslims before [in previous scriptures]﴾ [Al-Hajj: 78].

It was said: the first to submit was on the Day of the Covenant, so he would be prior to all creation, as He said: ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 7].

﴿And do not be among the polytheists.﴾ That is, and it was said: "to me," and the meaning is that he was commanded to submit to Islam and forbidden from associating others with Allah. This is how al-Zamakhsharī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya interpreted it, supposing an omitted *wa-qīla* (and it was said): "to me." This is because its conjunction cannot be coordinated with the wording of ﴿Indeed, I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit﴾, so that it would fall under the wording of *qul* (say), since if it were so, the construction would be: "and I will not be among the polytheists." It was also said: it is coordinated with the object of *qul* on the basis of meaning, and the meaning is: ﴿Say: "Indeed, I [am commanded]"—it was said to me: "Be the first of those who submit, and do not be among the polytheists"—so both are governed by the verb of saying, but the first came without the word of saying while carrying its meaning, so the second is governed by the meaning. It was also said: it is coordinated with *qul* (say), commanded to say such and such, and forbidden from such and such. It was also said: it is a prohibition against allying with polytheists. It was also said: the address is to him in wording, but what is meant is his community. This is the apparent meaning, because of His saying: ﴿If you should associate others with Allah, your deeds will surely be nullified﴾ [Az-Zumar: 65], and infallibility is incompatible with the possibility of association.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 14–16 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Say: Indeed I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous Day.﴾ The apparent meaning is that "fear" (al-khawf) here is in its proper sense, which is the anticipation of something disliked. Ibn 'Abbas said: the meaning of "akhaf" (I fear) is "a'lam" (I know). And "'asaytu" (I disobey) is general in regard to all kinds of sins, but here it refers only to shirk, which was forbidden, as stated by Ibn 'Atiyyah. The fear is not actually realized, due to his infallibility (ismah); rather it is conditional upon a condition that is impossible in his case, and its response (jawab) is omitted. For this reason it came in the past tense. It was said: it is an intervening conditional clause (shart mu'taridah), having no place in i'rab, like an intervening oath. It was also said: it is in a position of nasb as a circumstantial clause (hal), as if it were said: "Indeed I fear, disobeying my Lord." Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: the example of the verse is, if five were an even number, it would be divided into two equal parts; meaning that it is a conditional upon an impossibility. The tremendous Day is the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Whoever is turned away from it on that Day, He has indeed shown him mercy.﴾ Hamzah, Abu Bakr and al-Kisa'i read "man yasrif" in the active voice, so "man" is a fronted object (maf'ul muqaddam), and the pronoun in "yasrif" refers to Allah. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy: "man yasrifi Allah." The pronoun in "'anhu" refers to the punishment, and the hidden pronoun in "rahimahu" refers to the Lord. That is: whoever Allah turns the punishment away from, He has shown him the great mercy, which is salvation from punishment; and when he is saved from punishment, he enters Paradise. It is also permissible to parse "man" as a subject (mubtada'). The pronoun in "'anhu" refers to it, and the object of "yasrif" is omitted for brevity, since it was mentioned earlier in the verse before the estimation; that is: whoever Allah turns the punishment away from, He has shown him mercy. On this view it may also be a case of al-ishtighal, so "man" is in the accusative by an implied verb which is explained by the meaning of "yasrif." It is also permissible, on parsing "man" as a subject, for the object to be mentioned, namely "yawma'idhin," with an omission, meaning "the terror of that Day," so "yawma'idhin" is in the accusative as an object. The rest of the Seven read "man yusraf" in the passive voice, and it is known that the one who turns away is Allah the Exalted, so it was omitted for knowledge of Him, or for brevity, since the Lord was previously mentioned. In this case it is also permissible that the pronoun in "yusraf" refers to "man," and in "'anhu" refers to the punishment; that is: whoever is turned away from the punishment. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to "man," and the object of "yusraf" is "yawma'idhin," which is built (mabni) because it is annexed to "idh," so it is in a position of raf' by "yusraf." The tanwin in "yawma'idhin" is the tanwin of compensation (tanwin 'iwad) for a omitted clause implied by the preceding speech; the estimate is "the Day when the recompense occurs," since no explicit clause preceded it, the tanwin serves as a compensation for it. The grammarians discussed the preference between the two readings, as is their custom. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose... Abu 'Ali pointed to the goodness of reading "yasrif" in the active voice, to suit "fa-qad rahimahu," and he did not come with "fa-qad ruhima," and the reading of 'Abd Allah and Ubayy supports it: "man yasrifi Allah." Al-Tabari preferred the reading "yusraf" in the passive voice, saying: because it involves less implication. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: as for Makki ibn Abi Talib, he was confused in his book al-Hidayah in preferring the reading with the vowel fatha on the ya', and he gave corrupt examples in his argument. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is a verbal justification, whose connection to the preference is weak; as for the meaning, the two readings are one. We have mentioned on more than one occasion that we do not prefer one of the two mutawatir readings over the other. Abu 'Amr al-Zahid related in his book al-Yawaqit that Abu al-'Abbas Ahmad ibn Yahya Tha'lab did not see preference between the seven readings. He said: Tha'lab said from his own words: if the i'rab differs in the Qur'an among the Seven, I do not prefer one i'rab over another in the Qur'an; but when I turn to ordinary speech, the speech of people, I prefer the stronger. The best predecessor for us is Ahmad ibn Yahya, who was knowledgeable in grammar and lexicography, pious and trustworthy.

﴿That is the manifest triumph.﴾ The reference of "dhalika" (that) is to the verbal noun implied by "man yusraf," meaning: that turning away is the success and the salvation from destruction. "Al-mubin" means clear in itself, or making others clear.

[p. 88] Its meaning: if He afflicts you and strikes you with harm. The literal sense of *mass* (al-mass) is the contact of two bodies. It appears that the *ba'* in *bi-durrin* ("with harm") and in *bi-khayrin* ("with good") is for transitivity (al-ta'diya), even though the verb is already transitive. It is as if it were said: "If God touches you for harm," then He has touched you. Transitivity by means of *ba'* in a verb that is already transitive is rare. Among its examples is the Exalted's saying: ﴿Had God not repelled some people by means of others﴾ [al-Baqarah: 251]. [p. 88] Another example is the Arabs' saying: "I struck one of the two stones against the other" (*sakaktu ahada al-hajarayni bi-al-akhar*).

*Al-durr* (with a dammah) is bad condition in the body and elsewhere, while *al-darr* (with a fatha) is the opposite of benefit. Al-Suddi interpreted *al-durr* here as sickness, and *al-khayr* as well-being. It is also said: *al-durr* is poverty, and *al-khayr* is wealth. The best view is that *al-durr* is general, covering sickness, poverty and other things, and *al-khayr* is general, covering wealth, health and other things.

In a hadith of Ibn 'Abbas from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The pen has dried with what is to be. So if all of creation gathered together to harm you with something that God had not decreed for you, they would not be able to do it." Narrated by al-Tirmidhi.

The opposite of *khayr* is *sharr* (evil), but *darr* has taken its place here. The text departed from *sharr* because *sharr* is more general than *darr*. So it used *darr*, which is more specific, and *khayr*, which is general, to match a general term. This gives precedence to the aspect of mercy.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: *darr* here has taken the place of *sharr*, even though *sharr* is more general than it, so that it pairs with *khayr*. This is an element of eloquence, a departure from the rule of artificial constraint (*al-takalluf wa al-san'a*). The door of artificial constraint in ornate prose (*tarsi' al-kalam*) is that a thing be paired with what is specifically associated with it, by some kind of association, either in agreement or in matching. Among this is the Exalted's saying: ﴿That you will not be hungry therein or be naked﴾ [Ta-Ha: 118], ﴿and that you will not be thirsty therein or be exposed to the sun﴾ [Ta-Ha: 119]. Here He brought hunger together with nakedness, though the proper pairing would be with thirst. From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*Kaʼannī lam arkab jawādan li-l-ladhdhati wa-lam atabattan kāʻiban dhāta khalkhāli*
"As if I had never ridden a steed for pleasure, nor embraced a maiden with anklets."

*Wa-lam asba' al-zikka al-rawiyya wa-lam aqul*
*li-khaylī kurrī karratan baʻda ijfāli*
"Nor did I buy the full wineskin, nor did I say to my horses: 'Turn back for a charge after the rout!'"

End of quotation. The common element between hunger and nakedness is that both are emptiness: hunger is emptiness of the inside, and nakedness is emptiness of the outside. Between thirst and exposure to the sun, the common element is that both are burning: thirst is the burning of the inside, and exposure to the sun is the burning of the outside. Do you not see their saying: "The water cooled the heat of my inside"? In the first line, the common element between riding for pleasure, which is hunting, and embracing a maiden is that both share the pleasure of dominance, capture, subjugation, and triumph, like that of riding. Do you not see that they call the woman's mount *rakb*, a word in the sense of *maf'ul*, meaning "ridden"? The poet said:

*Inna lahā larakban irzabbā*
*ka'annahu jabhatu dhurā ḥubbā*
"Indeed she has a rakb, a large one, as if it were the forehead of a tall hill."

In the second line, the common element between buying wine and returning after defeat is that both involve giving. The purchase of wine is the giving of money, and returning after rout is the giving of one's life. How excellent is Imru' al-Qays' reasoning in his two lines, where he moved from the lower to the higher, because victory over a human being is higher and more noble than victory over other than one's kind. Do you not see that the soul's attachment to love is greater than its attachment to hunting? And because giving up life is greater than giving up wealth.

The reason for placing the touching of harm before the touching of good is clear, because it connects with what precedes it, namely the warning indicated by the Exalted's saying: ﴿Say, "Indeed, I fear﴾ [al-An'am: 15], and what precedes that. The answer to the first condition came with restriction in His saying: ﴿there is none to remove it but He﴾, as an intensification of sole power to remove it. The answer to the second condition came with His saying: ﴿then He is over all things capable﴾, indicating His power over all things, so that touching with good or otherwise is included in it.

If it were said that the answer is omitted because the first one indicates it, that would be a good view. Its implied meaning would be: "There is none to bring it to you but He." The better estimate is: "There is none to turn it back," for the sake of clearly stating what resembles it in His saying: "And if He wills good for you, there is none to repel His bounty." Then He followed it with what includes both good and evil, namely His power over all things.

In His saying ﴿there is none to remove it but He﴾ there is an omission, whose implied meaning is: "There is none to remove it from you but He."

﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants, and He is the Wise, the All-Aware﴾. When the Exalted mentioned His sole control over what He wills of harm and good, and His power over things, He mentioned His dominance and triumph, and that the world is subdued, prevented from reaching its aims. Rather, He compels and forces them to what He Himself wills. *Fawq* ("over") is literal in the sense of place. One who made it superfluous here went too far, and the claim that the meaning is "He subdues His servants" is further removed. Even further is the view of one who held that it is literal here, and that He is in a direction above the world, since that implies embodiment (*tajsim*).

As for the majority, they said that the "over" here is figurative. Some said: He is above them by bringing into being and by annihilation. Some said: it is an omitted genitive, whose meaning is "above the subjugation of His servants, by the occurrence of His will rather than theirs." Al-Zamakhshari said: it is a depiction of subjugation, elevation, triumph and power, like His saying: ﴿And indeed, We are above them, subduing﴾ [al-A'raf: 127].

The Arabs use *fawq* to indicate the height of rank and its superiority over other ranks. From this is His saying: ﴿The hand of God is over their hands﴾ [al-Fath: 10], and His saying: ﴿And over every possessor of knowledge is one [more] knowing﴾ [Yusuf: 76]. Al-Nabigha al-Ja'di said:

*Balaghnā al-samā majdan wa-jūdan wa-su'dadan*
*wa-innā li-narjū fawqa dhālika maẓhara*
"We have reached the heavens in glory, generosity and lordship, and we hope for a manifestation beyond that."

He means the height of rank and station.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: the attributes of perfection are confined to knowledge and power. So His saying ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾ indicates perfection of power, and ﴿He is the Wise, the All-Aware﴾ indicates perfection of knowledge. As for His being the Subduer, that is because everything other than Him, the Exalted, is possible in its essence. What is possible in its essence has no preference for existence over non-existence, nor non-existence over existence, except by His preference and bringing into being. So He is, in truth, the One who subdued possible things, sometimes in the ways of preferring existence over non-existence, and sometimes in the ways of preferring non-existence over existence. Included in this is everything the Exalted mentioned in His saying: ﴿Say: "O God, Owner of sovereignty"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 26], and so on.

"The Wise" (*al-hakim*) also means "the one who makes things firm" (*al-muhkim*), that is, His acts are perfectly fashioned, free from all forms of defect and corruption, and not in the sense of "the knowing," because "the All-Aware" (*al-khabir*) indicates knowledge, which would then cause repetition. End of quotation. There is some abridgment and summary in it.

It was also said: "the Wise" means "the knowing," and "the All-Aware" also means "the knowing," mentioned for emphasis.

*Fawq* is in the accusative as an adverb of place. It is either the object of *al-qahir*, meaning "the one who is exalted over His servants," or it is in the nominative position as a second predicate of *huwa* ("He"). He is described by two things: first, that He is the Subduer; second, that He is above His servants in rank, station and nobility, not in direction, since He is the One who brought them into being and brought direction into being, and He does not depend on any of His creatures. So "over" is used figuratively for the meaning, from the literal "over" of place.

Al-Mahdawi related that it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*), as if he said: "He is the Subduer, dominating, over His servants." Abu al-Baqa' said the same, estimating it as "exalted" or "dominating." He also permitted that *fawq 'ibadihi* be in the nominative position as an appositive (*badal*) of *al-qahir*.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: its meaning is the use of "servants" (*ibad*) in the sense of exaltation and honor, and "slaves" (*'abid*) in the sense of contempt, belittling and blame. He mentioned instances of this according to his view. He had already presented this meaning earlier at length, and we responded to him.

It appears that the *ba'* in *bi-durrin* ("with harm") and in *bi-khayrin* ("with good") is for transitivity (al-ta'diya), even though the verb is already transitive. The best view is that *al-durr* is general, covering sickness, poverty and other things, and *al-khayr* is general, covering wealth, health and other things.
