Ibn 'Atiyya said: *darr* here has taken the place of *sharr*, even though *sharr* is more general than it, so that it pairs with *khayr*. This is an element of eloquence, a departure from the rule of artificial constraint (*al-takalluf wa al-san'a*). The door of artificial constraint in ornate prose (*tarsi' al-kalam*) is that a thing be paired with what is specifically associated with it, by some kind of association, either in agreement or in matching. Among this is the Exalted's saying: ﴿That you will not be hungry therein or be naked﴾ [Ta-Ha: 118], ﴿and that you will not be thirsty therein or be exposed to the sun﴾ [Ta-Ha: 119]. Here He brought hunger together with nakedness, though the proper pairing would be with thirst. From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*Kaʼannī lam arkab jawādan li-l-ladhdhati wa-lam atabattan kāʻiban dhāta khalkhāli*
"As if I had never ridden a steed for pleasure, nor embraced a maiden with anklets."

*Wa-lam asba' al-zikka al-rawiyya wa-lam aqul*
*li-khaylī kurrī karratan baʻda ijfāli*
"Nor did I buy the full wineskin, nor did I say to my horses: 'Turn back for a charge after the rout!'"

End of quotation. The common element between hunger and nakedness is that both are emptiness: hunger is emptiness of the inside, and nakedness is emptiness of the outside. Between thirst and exposure to the sun, the common element is that both are burning: thirst is the burning of the inside, and exposure to the sun is the burning of the outside. Do you not see their saying: "The water cooled the heat of my inside"? In the first line, the common element between riding for pleasure, which is hunting, and embracing a maiden is that both share the pleasure of dominance, capture, subjugation, and triumph, like that of riding. Do you not see that they call the woman's mount *rakb*, a word in the sense of *maf'ul*, meaning "ridden"? The poet said:

*Inna lahā larakban irzabbā*
*ka'annahu jabhatu dhurā ḥubbā*
"Indeed she has a rakb, a large one, as if it were the forehead of a tall hill."

In the second line, the common element between buying wine and returning after defeat is that both involve giving. The purchase of wine is the giving of money, and returning after rout is the giving of one's life. How excellent is Imru' al-Qays' reasoning in his two lines, where he moved from the lower to the higher, because victory over a human being is higher and more noble than victory over other than one's kind. Do you not see that the soul's attachment to love is greater than its attachment to hunting? And because giving up life is greater than giving up wealth.

The reason for placing the touching of harm before the touching of good is clear, because it connects with what precedes it, namely the warning indicated by the Exalted's saying: ﴿Say, "Indeed, I fear﴾ [al-An'am: 15], and what precedes that. The answer to the first condition came with restriction in His saying: ﴿there is none to remove it but He﴾, as an intensification of sole power to remove it. The answer to the second condition came with His saying: ﴿then He is over all things capable﴾, indicating His power over all things, so that touching with good or otherwise is included in it.

If it were said that the answer is omitted because the first one indicates it, that would be a good view. Its implied meaning would be: "There is none to bring it to you but He." The better estimate is: "There is none to turn it back," for the sake of clearly stating what resembles it in His saying: "And if He wills good for you, there is none to repel His bounty." Then He followed it with what includes both good and evil, namely His power over all things.

In His saying ﴿there is none to remove it but He﴾ there is an omission, whose implied meaning is: "There is none to remove it from you but He."

﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants, and He is the Wise, the All-Aware﴾. When the Exalted mentioned His sole control over what He wills of harm and good, and His power over things, He mentioned His dominance and triumph, and that the world is subdued, prevented from reaching its aims. Rather, He compels and forces them to what He Himself wills. *Fawq* ("over") is literal in the sense of place. One who made it superfluous here went too far, and the claim that the meaning is "He subdues His servants" is further removed. Even further is the view of one who held that it is literal here, and that He is in a direction above the world, since that implies embodiment (*tajsim*).

As for the majority, they said that the "over" here is figurative. Some said: He is above them by bringing into being and by annihilation. Some said: it is an omitted genitive, whose meaning is "above the subjugation of His servants, by the occurrence of His will rather than theirs." Al-Zamakhshari said: it is a depiction of subjugation, elevation, triumph and power, like His saying: ﴿And indeed, We are above them, subduing﴾ [al-A'raf: 127].

The Arabs use *fawq* to indicate the height of rank and its superiority over other ranks. From this is His saying: ﴿The hand of God is over their hands﴾ [al-Fath: 10], and His saying: ﴿And over every possessor of knowledge is one [more] knowing﴾ [Yusuf: 76]. Al-Nabigha al-Ja'di said:

*Balaghnā al-samā majdan wa-jūdan wa-su'dadan*
*wa-innā li-narjū fawqa dhālika maẓhara*
"We have reached the heavens in glory, generosity and lordship, and we hope for a manifestation beyond that."

He means the height of rank and station.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: the attributes of perfection are confined to knowledge and power. So His saying ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾ indicates perfection of power, and ﴿He is the Wise, the All-Aware﴾ indicates perfection of knowledge. As for His being the Subduer, that is because everything other than Him, the Exalted, is possible in its essence. What is possible in its essence has no preference for existence over non-existence, nor non-existence over existence, except by His preference and bringing into being. So He is, in truth, the One who subdued possible things, sometimes in the ways of preferring existence over non-existence, and sometimes in the ways of preferring non-existence over existence. Included in this is everything the Exalted mentioned in His saying: ﴿Say: "O God, Owner of sovereignty"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 26], and so on.

"The Wise" (*al-hakim*) also means "the one who makes things firm" (*al-muhkim*), that is, His acts are perfectly fashioned, free from all forms of defect and corruption, and not in the sense of "the knowing," because "the All-Aware" (*al-khabir*) indicates knowledge, which would then cause repetition. End of quotation. There is some abridgment and summary in it.

It was also said: "the Wise" means "the knowing," and "the All-Aware" also means "the knowing," mentioned for emphasis.

*Fawq* is in the accusative as an adverb of place. It is either the object of *al-qahir*, meaning "the one who is exalted over His servants," or it is in the nominative position as a second predicate of *huwa* ("He"). He is described by two things: first, that He is the Subduer; second, that He is above His servants in rank, station and nobility, not in direction, since He is the One who brought them into being and brought direction into being, and He does not depend on any of His creatures. So "over" is used figuratively for the meaning, from the literal "over" of place.

Al-Mahdawi related that it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*), as if he said: "He is the Subduer, dominating, over His servants." Abu al-Baqa' said the same, estimating it as "exalted" or "dominating." He also permitted that *fawq 'ibadihi* be in the nominative position as an appositive (*badal*) of *al-qahir*.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: its meaning is the use of "servants" (*ibad*) in the sense of exaltation and honor, and "slaves" (*'abid*) in the sense of contempt, belittling and blame. He mentioned instances of this according to his view. He had already presented this meaning earlier at length, and we responded to him.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 19:**

﴿Say: "What thing is greatest as testimony?" Say: "Allah is witness between me and you."﴾ The exegetes (al-mufassirun) said: The Quraysh asked for a witness to confirm the truth of Muhammad's prophethood (ﷺ). They said: "What proof testifies that Allah bears witness for you?" He said: "This Qur'an, with which I have challenged you, and you were unable to produce its like, or the like of part of it." Al-Kalbi said: The chiefs of Makkah said: "O Muhammad! We do not see anyone who confirms what you say about the matter of the message. We have asked the Jews and the Christians about you, and they claimed that you have no mention or description among them. So show us someone who will testify for you that you are the Messenger of Allah, as you claim." So Allah revealed this [p. 90] verse. It was also said: The polytheists asked when there was revealed ﴿If Allah should touch you with harm﴾ [Al-An'am: 17] and the rest of the verse, and they said: "Who will testify for you that this Qur'an was sent down to you from Allah, and that none but Allah harms or benefits?" So Allah said: "And this Qur'an, which is miraculous."

(Ayyu) is an interrogative. The discussion of the divisions of (ayyu) and the reason for its i'rab (grammatical analysis) is mentioned in the science of grammar (nahw). The matter of shay' (thing) has already been discussed at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah, and the disagreement over its real meaning was mentioned there.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Shay' is the most general of the general terms, since it applies to everything that may be known and spoken of. It therefore applies to the eternal, the substance, the accident, the impossible and the possible. For this reason it is correct to say of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: "a thing unlike other things." It is as if you said: "a known thing, unlike other known things." But it is not correct to say "a body unlike other bodies." He intended (Which thing is greatest as testimony?) and placed shay' in place of shahid (witness), in order to intensify the generality. End of quotation.

Ibn Atiyya said: This verse implies that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, may be described as shay', just as He may be described as mawjud (existent), but "there is nothing like unto Him." Others said here that shay' applies to the eternal and the originated, the substance and the accident, the non-existent and the existent. Since this is its implication, it is permissible to apply it to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and the majority agreed on this. Jahm (Jahm ibn Safwan) disagreed and said: "Shay' is not applied to Allah. He may be called dhat (essence) and mawjud (existent)." He said that shay' was not applied to Him because of His saying ﴿Creator of all things﴾ [Al-An'am: 102]; so applying shay' to Him would imply that He is the creator of Himself, which is impossible. He also cited His saying ﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names﴾ [Al-A'raf: 180]. A name is only beautiful because of the beauty of what it names, namely that it indicates an attribute of perfection and a description of majesty. The word shay' is the most general of things, so it is found in the lowest and most base things. Therefore it does not indicate an attribute of perfection or a description of majesty. Thus it is necessary that it not be permissible to call Allah by it, since it is not among the most beautiful names. He also cited that shay' includes the non-existent, based on His saying ﴿And never say of anything, "I will do that tomorrow"﴾ [Al-Kahf: 23]. So applying shay' to Him does not establish the distinction of His essence from all other essences by a known attribute or a distinctive property, nor does it indicate that He is absolute. Therefore it is necessary that it not be permissible to apply it to Allah, the Most High. He also cited His saying, the Most High: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [Ash-Shura: 11], and the essence of every thing is like its own self. This is an explicit statement that He, the Most High, is not named by the name shay'. He also argued that one cannot say the kaf (in ka-mithlihi) is superfluous, because treating a word of the Qur'an as meaningless and void is unseemly and is not to be resorted to except in dire necessity.

It is answered that the word shay' is the most general of words, and whenever the specific is true, the general is true. So whenever it is true that He is truly a dhat (essence), it must be true that He is a shay'. The majority argued with this verse, its meaning being: "Which of things is greatest as testimony?" Then the answer came: "Say: Allah." This requires applying shay' to Him, and His inclusion in the word shay' which is intended in its generality. If you said: "Which of the people is best?" and it was answered: "Jibril," it would not be correct, because he is not included in the word "people." They also argued with His saying, the Most High: ﴿Everything will perish except His face﴾ [Al-Qasas: 88], where "His face" means His essence, and the exception must be included within what it is an exception from. This indicates that shay' is applied to Him. Jahm could say: This is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), and the first proof did not explicitly state a matching answer, since His saying ﴿Say: Allah is witness between me and you﴾ is a subject and predicate, a predicate that is an independent clause with no grammatical connection to what precedes it. Rather, His saying ﴿What thing is greatest as testimony?﴾ is an interrogative for the purpose of affirmation and stating the matter, then He informed that the Creator of things and witnesses is the witness between me and you. The speech is coherent in meaning, so the clause is not a grammatical answer. What they said would only be complete if the verse were limited to "Say: Allah." Some have taken this view, parsing it as a subject with an omitted predicate, because of what precedes it. The meaning is: "Say: Allah is greatest as testimony," then a subject is implied for which shahid is the predicate, its meaning: "He is ﴿witness between me and you﴾." This is not necessarily the intended reading; rather it is weaker, because it implies an omission both at the end and at the beginning, whereas the earlier reading has no omission with correct meaning. Therefore the Qur'an must be interpreted according to the stronger reading, not the weaker.

Ibn Abbas said: Allah said to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): "Say to them: 'What thing is greatest as testimony?' If they answer you, well; otherwise say to them: ﴿Allah is witness between me and you﴾." Mujahid said: The meaning is that Allah said to His Prophet: "Say to them: ﴿What thing is greatest as testimony?﴾" and say to them: ﴿Allah is witness between me and you﴾, that is, concerning my delivery and your lying and your disbelief.

Ibn Atiyya said: This verse is like His saying [p. 91] ﴿Say: To whom belongs what is in the heavens and the earth? Say: To Allah﴾ [Al-An'am: 12], in that He asked in the form of affirmation and statement, then immediately gave the answer, since no contradiction can be conceived in it. It is like when you ask one with whom you dispute and from whom you suffer injustice: "Who is most powerful in the land?" and then immediately say: "The sultan, for he stands between us." So the sense of the verse is: "Say to them: 'What thing is greatest as testimony? It is the witness between me and you.'" End of quotation.

This verse is not the same as His saying ﴿Say: To whom belongs what is in the heavens and the earth? Say: To Allah﴾, because "To Allah" must be the answer, whereas here it is not necessarily so, since from His saying ﴿Say: Allah is witness between me and you﴾ a subject and predicate can be formed, and this is the apparent reading. Moreover, in this verse the word shay' appears, and there is dispute over applying it to Allah, the Most High; whereas in that verse the word (man) appears, and it is applied to Allah, the Most High.

It was said: The meaning of (akbar) is "greater" and "more correct," because no error, forgetfulness or lying can occur in it. It was also said: Its meaning is "more excellent," because the ranks of testimonies differ in excellence according to the ranks of the witnesses. And shahadatan (testimony) is in the accusative as a tamyiz (specifying accusative). Ibn Atiyya said: It may also be accusative as an object, by treating akbar as resembling the attributive adjective of the active participle form. End of quotation.

This is a strange statement, because it is not correct to make it an object, and because afal (the elative form) of one who is not like the attributive adjective of the active participle form cannot be; nor is it permissible for afal to be of the category of the attributive adjective of the active participle form, because the condition of the attributive adjective of the active participle form is that it inflects for feminine, dual and plural, and the elative form does not take these inflections. This is stated explicitly by the grammarians. Ibn Atiyya therefore made the accusative noun here an object, made akbar resemble the attributive adjective, and made its accusative noun an object. This is a grave confusion, and perhaps it is from the copyist and not from the author.

The meaning of ﴿between me and you﴾ is "between us," but since it was attached to the first person pronoun (ya' of the speaker), it was necessary to repeat bayn. This is like the saying of the poet: "fa-ayyi ma (whichever of us), wa-ayyuka kana sharran (and whichever of you was evil)," and "kilaya wa-kilaka (both of me and both of you)," where the meaning is "fa-ayyuna wa-kilana (whichever of us, and both of us)."

* *

﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me that I may warn you thereby and whoever it reaches﴾. The majority read (wa-uhiya) in the passive voice, with (al-Qur'an) as its nominative. ʿIkrimah, Abu Nuhayk, Ibn al-Samayqa' and al-Jahdari read (wa-awha) in the active voice, with al-Qur'an in the accusative as its object. The meaning is "that I may warn you and that I may give you good news," so the coordinated term was omitted because the meaning indicates it; or he limited it to warning, since it is in a context of frightening these deniers of the message who take other than Allah as god. The apparent reading, which is the view of the majority, is that (man) is in the accusative, coordinated with the object of (li-undhirakum). The pronoun referring back to (man) is an omitted accusative pronoun, and the subject of (balagha) is a pronoun referring to the Qur'an; so whoever it has reached is the Qur'an itself. The address in ﴿that I may warn you thereby﴾ is to the people of Makkah. Muqatil said: [It reaches] whoever among the Arabs and non-Arabs it reaches. It was said: from both humans and jinn. It was said: whoever it reaches until the Day of Resurrection. Sa'id ibn Jubayr reported: Whoever the Qur'an reaches, it is as if he saw Muhammad (ﷺ). In a hadith: "Whoever this Qur'an reaches, I am his warner." Another group said: The subject of (balagha) refers to (man), not to the Qur'an, and the object is omitted; the meaning is "whoever reaches puberty." It may also be that (man) is in the nominative, coordinated with the pronoun hidden within ﴿that I may warn you thereby﴾, the coordination being permitted because of the separation between them by the object pronoun and the prepositional phrase. The sense is: "and that he may warn thereby whoever the Qur'an has reached."

﴿Do you indeed bear witness that there are other gods with Allah?﴾ It was read ﴿Do you indeed bear witness﴾ in affirmative form, so it may be a pure statement, but it may also be an interrogative with its particle omitted. This is shown by the reading in interrogative form, which was read with two clearly articulated hamzas, with an alif inserted between them, with the second hamza eased, and with an alif inserted between the first hamza and the eased hamza. Al-Asma'i transmitted this last reading from Abu 'Amr and Nafi'. This interrogative is meant as rebuke and reproach against them and denunciation of them. If the address is to the people of Makkah, then "gods" means the idols, since they are the owners of idols. If it is to all polytheists, then "gods" means everything worshipped besides Allah, the Most High, whether an idol, a star, a fire, or a human being. "Other" (ukhra) is an attribute of "gods." The attribute of the plural of non-rational things is like the attribute of a feminine singular, as in His saying: ﴿other uses﴾ [Ta-Ha: 18] and ﴿the most beautiful names﴾. Since the gods were stones and wood, they were treated in this way.

﴿Say: I do not bear witness. Say: He is only one God, and I am free from what you associate with Him﴾. Allah, the Most High, commanded him to inform them that he does not bear witness to their testimony, and commanded him secondly to single out Allah, the Most High, for divinity and to disavow their association. How wonderful this arrangement is: he was first commanded to inform them that he does not agree with them in testimony, and this does not necessarily entail the singling out of Allah for divinity; so he was commanded to it secondly, so that the affirmation of the oneness of Allah, the Most High, would be combined with the denial of their agreement. Thirdly, He informed him of disavowing their association, which serves as an emphasis of what came before. It is possible that this is not included within the saying, and it is possible, and this is the apparent reading, that it is included within it, so he was commanded to say both sentences. The apparent meaning of the verse implies that it concerns the worshippers of idols. Al-Tabari mentioned that it was revealed concerning a group of Jews. It is attributed to Ibn Abbas, who said: "al-Nahham ibn Zayd, Qardam ibn Ka'b and Mujazzi' ibn 'Amr came and said: 'O Muhammad, do you know of any god with Allah other than Him?' He said: 'There is no god but Allah; I have been commanded with this.' So the verse was revealed concerning them."

**﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recognize him as they recognize their own sons. Those who have lost their souls, they do not believe.﴾** The explanation of the first clause has already been given in al-Baqarah, and the explanation of the second clause in this surah, shortly before. Some said here that the pronoun in (*yaʿrifunahu*, "they recognize him") refers to the Messenger, as stated by Qatadah, al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj. The majority, including ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, hold that it refers to Tawhid (the oneness of God), because of the nearness of His words: ﴿Say: He is only One God﴾ [al-Anʿam: 19]. It is also said that it refers to the Qur'an, which is a view held by a group, because of His words: ﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me﴾ [al-Anʿam: 19]. It is further said that it refers to all of these things together, namely Tawhid, the Messenger and the Qur'an, as if He had mentioned several things and then said that the People of the Book recognize them (*yaʿrifunahu*), that is, they recognize what We have said and what We have related. It is also said that it refers to their Book, meaning that they recognize their own Book, and in this there is a mention of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). And it is said that it refers to the religion and the Messenger, so the meaning is that they recognize Islam as the religion of God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God.

﴿Those to whom We gave the Book﴾ here is general in wording but particular in meaning, for this recognition is not known to, and does not come near, anyone except those among them who believe, or those who are fair-minded. "The Book" means the Torah and the Gospel, and it is stated in the singular as a reference to the genus. It is also said that "the Book" here means the Qur'an, and the pronoun in (*yaʿrifunahu*) refers to it, as mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said, in a summarized form: If what is written in the Torah and the Gospel is only the coming of a prophet at the end of time, then it is not necessarily the case that this prophet is Muhammad (ﷺ). But if his time, place, lineage, appearance and form were specified, then they would have known him necessarily, and it is not permissible for a great multitude to lie. Moreover, we know necessarily that their Book did not contain these complete details. On these two assumptions, how can it be correct to say: ﴿They recognize him as they recognize their own sons﴾? He answered that they were people capable of reflection and reasoning, and that they had witnessed the manifestation of miracles at the hand of the Messenger, so through the miracles they knew that he was a Messenger from God. Thus the intended meaning is to compare their recognition of him with their recognition of their sons to this extent that we have mentioned, end of quote.

This division which he mentioned does not necessarily follow, because He did not say "they recognize him through the Torah and the Gospel." He only said (*yaʿrifunahu*, "they recognize him"), so it is possible that this recognition is attributed to the Torah and the Gospel from the reports of their prophets and their texts. Thus the details among them come from that, not from the Torah and the Gospel themselves, and their recognition of him is detailed and clear through reports, not through considering the miracles. ﴿As they recognize their own sons﴾. Furthermore, we do not grant him that the division is limited to what he mentioned, because another possibility is admitted, namely that the Torah and the Gospel indicate the coming of a prophet at the end of time and some of his attributes, but not all the attributes that were mentioned, such as the specification of a time, place, lineage, appearance and form. This possibility is supported by the report of ʿUmar with ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam, when ʿUmar said to him: God has revealed to His Prophet in Makkah that you recognize him as you recognize your sons; so how is this recognition? ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam said: Yes, I recognize him by the description with which God described him in the Torah, so I have no doubt about him; as for my son, I do not know what his mother has done. Also, what indicates that their recognition of him does not necessarily rest on the Torah and the Gospel alone is the questions of ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam when he first met the Messenger of God (ﷺ): What is the first food the people of Paradise eat? When he was told the answers to those questions, he embraced Islam immediately, and he knew that he was the Messenger who had been pointed out in the Torah. And there is the report of Zayd ibn Saʿnah, when he mentioned that he had recognized all his attributes, except that he did not know that his forbearance would precede his anger; so he tested this in him, found this quality, and embraced Islam.

﴿Those who have lost﴾ (*al-ladhina khasiru*) is parsed as a subject (*mubtada*', the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence), and the predicate (*khabar*, the complement of that subject) is ﴿they do not believe﴾ (*fahum la yu'minun*). According to this, ﴿those who have lost﴾ is more general than the disbelieving People of the Book and the polytheists. Loss (*khusran*) means being cheated. It is related that each servant has a place in Paradise and a place in the Fire; the believers take the places of the people of disbelief in Paradise, and the disbelievers take the places of the people of Paradise in the Fire, so loss and gain are meant here. They also allowed that ﴿those who have lost﴾ could be a qualifier (*naʿt*, an attributive adjective) of ﴿those to whom We gave the Book﴾. And ﴿they do not believe﴾ is a clause conjoined (*maʿtuf*) to a previous clause, so the context of ﴿those to whom We gave the Book﴾ would be one of censure, not the context of citing them as witnesses against the disbelievers of Quraysh and the other Arabs. They said: this is because it is not correct to cite them as witnesses and also censure them in one verse. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: it is correct, because what they are cited for differs from what they are censured for, and censure and citation are not from the same aspect, end of quote. In that case, ﴿those who have lost﴾ is not general, since the meaning would be "those among them who have lost their souls," that is, from among the People of the Book.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 6, verses 21–23:**

﴿Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God, or denies His signs? Indeed, the wrongdoers will not prosper.﴾ The discussion of ﴿Who is more unjust﴾ has already been given. *Iftira'* (fabrication) means invention, and the meaning is: there is no one more unjust than one who lies against God, or denies the signs of God. Al-Zamakhshari said: "They combined two contradictory things. They lied against God by claiming what has no proof for it, and they denied what is established by clear proof and sound demonstration, when they said: ﴿Had God willed, we would not have associated anything with Him, nor would our fathers﴾ [al-An'am: 148]. They said: 'By God, we were commanded to do it.' They said: 'The angels are the daughters of God,' and 'These are our intercessors with God.' They attributed to Him the prohibition of the *sawa'ib* and *bahair* (certain animals), and they denied the Qur'an and the miracles, calling them magic, and they did not believe in the Messenger (ﷺ)." End of quotation. In this there is a trace of *i'tizal* (the Mu'tazili doctrine): in his words, "when they said: ﴿Had God willed, we would not have associated anything with Him, nor would our fathers﴾ [al-An'am: 148]." Ibn Atiyya said: "*Iftara* means he invented. The one who denies the signs is also a fabricator of lies, but these two are both kinds of disbelief, which is why they were mentioned separately and explicitly." The meaning of ﴿the wrongdoers will not prosper﴾ is that they will not attain their aims in this world or the Hereafter, but will remain in deprivation and abandonment. He denied prosperity to the wrongdoer, so the most unjust is included in that. The wrongdoer is not the same as the most unjust. If this one does not prosper, how could the most unjust prosper?
