﴿And on the Day We gather them all, then We will say to those who associated others with God: "Where are your partners whom you used to claim?"﴾ It has been said that *yawma* (on the day) is an object of a verb omitted, which is *udhkur* (remember), so that it is the object, as Ibn Atiyya and Abu al-Baqa said. It has also been said that the omitted element comes later, its estimate being: ﴿And on the day We gather them﴾ such-and-such happened, and it was left unstated so that it would remain in the vagueness that is more effective in instilling fear, as al-Zamakhshari said. It has been said: the governing element is *unzur kayfa kadhdhabu yawma nahshuruhum* (see how they denied on the day We gather them). It has been said: it is an object of an omitted verb whose estimate is: *wa-liyahdharu yawma nahshuruhum* (and let them beware of the day We gather them). It has been said: it is conjoined to an omitted adverbial phrase, and the governing element of it is the governing element of that adverbial phrase, the estimate being: that the wrongdoers will not prosper today in this world, and on the day We gather them, as al-Tabari said.

The majority read *nahshuruhum* and *thumma naqulu* with *nun* in both. Humayd and Ya'qub read both with *ya'*. Abu Hurayra read *nahshiruhum* with a *kasra* on the *shin*. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in *nahshuruhum* refers to those who fabricated lies against God or denied His signs. The words ﴿Then We will say to those who associated others﴾ mean "Then We will say to them," but it singled out the attribute that makes their rebuke necessary. It is possible that it refers to all people, as they are all included in this generality, and then the rebuke is singled out for the polytheists. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the polytheists and their idols, as you see in their saying: ﴿Gather those who did wrong, along with their companions and what they used to worship﴾ [al-Saffat: 22], besides God. The conjunction *thumma* (then) indicates the interval between the stages of the Day of Resurrection in its standing-places, for there are standing-places on that day, and between each standing-place and the next there is an interval according to the length of that day.

﴿Where are your partners?﴾ is a question of rebuke and reproach. The apparent meaning of ﴿Where are your partners?﴾ is the absence of the partners from them, that is, those idols have vanished and no longer exist. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also possible that they see them, except that when they do not benefit them, and what they hoped for from intercession does not come from them, they are as if they were absent from them; and that they are kept away from them and between them at the time of rebuke, so that they lose them at the very hour in which they had placed their hope in them, and thus the possibility of their disgrace and regret is made clear." End of quotation. The meaning is: "Where are your gods that you made into partners of God?" The word "partners" is attributed to them because there is in reality no partnership between idols and anything, and the name of "partner" was applied to them only by the mere naming of the disbelievers; so it is attributed to them by this relation.

*Za'm* (claim) is the saying that inclines toward falsehood and lying in most speech. For this reason Ibn Abbas said: "Every *za'm* in the Qur'an means *kadhib* (lie)." He specified the Qur'an because it applies to mere mention and speech. From this is the saying of the poet:

*You say: "We perish if you perish," but the provisions of the servants are upon God, as He has claimed.*

Ibn Atiyya said: "On this basis Sibawayh says: *bi-za'm al-Khalil* (on the claim of al-Khalil), but that is used for a strange matter whose responsibility remains upon the one who says it." End of quotation. The two objects of *yaz'umun* (you claim) are omitted for brevity, since what precedes indicates their omission, and the estimate is: *tuz'umunahum shuraka'* (you claim them as partners). It is also good that the estimate be as some of them said: ﴿Where are your partners whom you used to claim﴾ that they would intercede for you with God, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿Then their trial was only that they said: "By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists."﴾ The meaning of *fitna* was already given, and here it is explained as love of a thing and admiration for it, as you say: "I am infatuated with Zayd." On this reading the meaning is: "Then their love for the idols, their admiration for them, and their following of them did not, when they were questioned about them and stood before their powerlessness, amount to anything except disavowing them and denying them. In this there is rebuke for them, just as you say to a man who used to profess affection for another and then turned away from him and became hostile: 'O so-and-so, your affection for so-and-so was nothing but your enmity and separation from him.'" The meaning of ﴿Then their trial was not﴾ as "their affection and admiration for the idols" is: nothing except disavowal of them, with the emphatic oath asserting their disavowal; and the trial occurs in this world. It has also been explained as *ikhtibar* (testing), and the meaning is: "Then our testing of them was not, since the question about the partners and their being made to stand is a test to see their denial of association." And the trial here occurs in the Resurrection; that is: "Then the answer to the test they received by being asked about their partners was nothing but the denial of associating," as summarized from the words of Ibn Atiyya, with some addition.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Fitnatuhum* is their disbelief. The meaning is: then the outcome of their disbelief, to which they clung for their whole lives, for which they fought and of which they boasted, saying, 'the religion of our fathers,' was not anything except its denial, their disavowal of it, and their swearing that they had no connection to practising it. It is also possible that the meaning is: then their answer was nothing except their saying, and so it was named a trial because it is a lie." End of quotation. The first explanation in Ibn Atiyya's exposition is in the sense of al-Zajjaj; the first explanation of al-Zamakhshari's exegesis has its wording from al-Hasan and its meaning from Ibn Abbas; and the second is from Muhammad ibn Ka'b and others. He said: the estimate is: "then their answer was not ﴿except that they said﴾," and this saying was named a trial because it is a fabrication and a lie. Al-Dahhak said: "*Fitna* here means denial, that is: then their denial was not." Qatada said: "Their excuse." Abu al-Aliyya said: "Their saying." Ata and Abu Ubayda said: "Between them." Abu Ubayda added: "That which bound them with the proof, and increased them in blame." It has also been said: "Their argument." The apparent reading is that the pronoun refers to the polytheists, and that it is general to whoever associated others with God. Al-Hasan said: "This is specific to the hypocrites, who acted according to their habit in the world." It has also been said: they are a people who were polytheists and did not know that they were polytheists, so they swear by their belief in this world.

The majority read ﴿then their trial was not﴾ with *ta'*; Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with *ya'*. Ubayy, Ibn Mas'ud and al-A'mash read *ma kana fitnatuhum*; Talha and Ibn Mutarrif read *thumma ma kana*; the two sons (Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr? — the two Ibns) and Hafs read *fitnatuhum* in the nominative. A group read *thumma lam yakun* with *ya'* and *fitnatuhum* in the nominative. The grammatical analysis of these readings is clear. The most common of them is the reading *thumma lam yakun fitnataham* with *ya'* in the accusative, because *an* with what follows it is treated in definiteness as a pronoun. When the more definite and what is less definite are both definite, they mention that the more common practice is to make the more definite the subject and the less definite the predicate. For this reason all seven readers agreed on this in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The answer of his people was only that they said﴾ [al-Naml: 56], and ﴿Their argument was only that they said﴾ [al-Jathiya: 25]. As for one who reads with *ya'* and raises *fitna*, he masculinizes the verb because the feminine marking of *fitna* is metaphorical, or because it occurs in a sense that is masculine. *Fitna* is the subject of *yakun*, and the predicate ﴿except that they said﴾ makes the less definite the subject and the more definite the predicate. As for one who reads ﴿then their trial was not﴾ with *ta'* and raises *fitna*, he feminizes the verb because *fitna* is feminine. Its grammatical analysis is like that of what came before. As for one who reads ﴿then not was﴾ with *ta'* and *fitnatahum* in the accusative, the better view is to estimate ﴿except that they said﴾ as feminine; that is: "then their trial was not except their saying." It was said: this is permitted because *fitna* in meaning is ... Abu Ali said: "This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For him is ten times its like﴾ [al-An'am: 160], where He made *al-amthal* (its likes) feminine, since they were, in meaning, *al-hasanat* (good deeds)." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also read *takun* with *ta'*, and *fitnataham* in the accusative. The verb *an qalu* came because the predicate came feminine, as in His saying: 'Whoever your mother was.'" End of quotation. It has already been stated that the better view is to estimate *an qalu* as feminine, that is, *illa maqalatuhum* (except their saying). Likewise al-Zajjaj estimated it as feminine, that is, *maqalatuhum*. Al-Zamakhshari's grammatical explanation is a patchwork from the words of Abu Ali. As for "Whoever your mother was," he took the subject of *kana* in the sense of *man*, because *man* has a singular form and has meanings according to what is intended of singularity, duality, plurality, masculinity and femininity. The taking into account of meaning is not for the sake of matching the predicate, as you see that it comes where there is no predicate, such as: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾; and *yakun* is like *man* in: "O wolf, they two accompany each other." The *ta'* in *taqnut* in the reading with *ta'* is not the feminine marking of *kanat* for the sake of the feminine predicate; it is only for taking into account the sense of *man* when you intend the feminine by it, as though you said: "What woman was your mother?"

Al-Akhawan (Hamza and al-Kisa'i) read ﴿by God, our Lord﴾ with the *ba'* in the accusative as a vocative, that is, *ya Rabbana* (O our Lord). Ibn Atiyya permitted the accusative here as praise. Abu al-Baqa permitted the implied *a'ni* (I mean). The rest of the seven read it in the genitive as an adjective, and they permitted it to be an apposition and a *'atf al-bayan* (explicative apposition). 'Ikrima and Salam ibn Miskin read ﴿Allah, our Lord﴾ with both nouns in the nominative. Ibn Atiyya said: "This is by inversion of the order, that they said: ﴿we were not polytheists﴾, (Allah is our Lord). The meaning of ﴿we were not polytheists﴾ is that they denied their association in this world." It is narrated that when they see the people of the Fire being brought out from it, the people of faith, they cry out, and they are halted and told: "Where are your partners?" Then they deny, out of a hope that they will be treated as the people of faith were treated. What is narrated here is contrary to the apparent meaning of the verse, which is ﴿And on the day We gather them all﴾, then We say. Its apparent meaning is that the saying does not come so far after the gathering, after the disobedient believers have entered the Fire, remained in it for what God willed, and been brought out of it; then after all of that it is said to them: "Where are your partners?" A man came to Ibn Abbas and said: "I heard God say: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾, and in another place: ﴿and they will not hide from God any matter﴾ [al-Nisa': 42]." Ibn Abbas said: "When they saw that none enters Paradise except a believer, they said: 'Come, let us deny,' and they said: ﴿We were not polytheists﴾, so God sealed their mouths, and their limbs spoke, and so they hide from God no matter."

The address is to the Messenger, peace be upon him, and the "looking" (al-nazar) is of the heart. "How" (kayfa) is in the accusative, governed by "they lied" (kadhdhabu). The clause is in the accusative position as the object of "look," because "look" is suspended (mu'allaqah, meaning its effect on the following clause is blocked while the clause still functions as its object). "They lied" is in the past tense, though the matter has not yet occurred. It is a narration about the Day of Resurrection, and there is no difficulty in using the past tense in place of the future there, to affirm that it will certainly happen.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, how can it be correct that they lie when they see the realities of matters? Moreover, lying and denial have no benefit. I say: the one being tested speaks with what benefits him and with what does not benefit him, without distinguishing between them, out of bewilderment and dismay. Do you not see them saying ﴿Our Lord, bring us out of it, and if we return, then indeed we are wrongdoers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 107]? They had become certain of eternal abiding and did not doubt it, and ﴿they call out, "O Malik, let your Lord decree against us"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 77], while they knew that He would not decree against them. As for the view of those who say that the meaning of ﴿by Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23] is "in our own estimation," or "we did not know that we were in error in our belief," and that His saying ﴿look how they lied against themselves﴾ means in this world, this is an imposition, a strained and distorted reading of the most eloquent speech, turning it into something that is clumsy and confounding. The meaning they adopted is not what this speech translates or corresponds to; it is far removed from it. I do not know what such a person does with His explanation through His saying ﴿On the day when Allah resurrects them all and they swear to Him as they swear to you, and they think that they are upon something. Unquestionably, they are the liars﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 18], after His saying ﴿and they say about Allah the lie while they know﴾ [Al 'Imran: 75]; He likened their lying in the Hereafter to their lying in this world. End of al-Zamakhshari's words.

As for the view of "those who say," this refers to Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i, al-Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar, and those who agreed with them, that the people of the Resurrection cannot be permitted to lie. They relied on matters that return to the question of good and evil (al-qubh wa-l-husn, the Mu'tazilite doctrine that good and evil are known by reason), and built their position upon that. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi mentioned these in his commentary, and they may be consulted there, since the question of good and evil is one in which they opposed Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah). The majority of exegetes say that the disbelievers lie in the Hereafter, and the apparent meanings of the Qur'an indicate this. Al-Zamakhshari here opposed his fellow Mu'tazilites and agreed with Ahl al-Sunnah.

﴿And what they used to fabricate has vanished from them﴾. It is possible that "ma" is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah), and Ibn 'Atiyyah went to this view, saying: its meaning is that their fabrication in the world and their disbelief, by their ascribing partners to Allah, has gone away. It is said: it refers to the false oaths in the Hereafter. It is said: their fabrication has been lost to them because of the bewilderment that overtook them. It is possible that "ma" means "that which" (alladhi), and al-Zamakhshari went to this view. He said: what they used to fabricate, namely His divinity and His intercession, has vanished from them, and this is the meaning of the words of al-Hasan and Abu 'Ali, who said: what they used to worship of idols in the world did not avail them anything. It is said: it is their saying, ﴿we only worship them so that they bring us nearer to Allah in position﴾ [al-Zumar: 3], so it vanished from them when they knew that there was no nearness through them. It is possible that "wa-dalla" (and ... vanished) is conjoined to "kadhdhabu," so that it falls under the report of "look," and it is possible that it is a new, independent report, so that it does not fall within its scope, and the looking does not extend over it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 25–26 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Among them are those who listen to you, but We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness.﴾ Abu Salih narrated from Ibn Abbas that Abu Sufyan, al-Walid, al-Nadr, Utba, Shayba, Umayya and Ubayy listened to the Messenger (ﷺ). They said to al-Nadr, "O Abu Qutayla! What is Muhammad saying?" He replied, "He says nothing but the fables of the ancients, like what I tell you about the past generations." He was a man of poetry who had gathered stories from the lands of the non-Arabs, such as the story of Rustam and Isfandiyar, and he used to tell them to Quraysh, and they would listen to him. Abu Sufyan said, "I see that some of what he says is true." Abu Jahl said, "No! Do not acknowledge any of this. Death is easier than this." Then the verse was revealed.

The pronoun in (ومِنهم) refers to those who associated partners with God (al-ladhina ashraku). He used the singular pronoun in (يَسْتَمِعُ) in agreement with the wording of (مِن) (min), and the plural in ﴿على قلوبهم﴾ in agreement with its meaning. The clause beginning with (وجَعَلْنا) is coordinated with the clause before it, a verbal clause coordinated with a nominal clause, so it is information from God, Exalted, that He made such-and-such. It has also been said that the (و) is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), meaning "while We have placed," i.e., "We listen to your recitation," and they are, in their heedlessness, like one whose heart is in a sheath and whose ear is deaf. The word (جَعَلَ) here may be understood as meaning "cast" (ألقى), so that (على) is attached to it; or as meaning "made" (صيّر), so that it is attached to a omitted element, since it occupies the position of the second object; or as meaning "created" (خلق), in which case it occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (حال), because if it had been placed after its noun it would have been a qualifier, and when it was placed before, it became a circumstance.

(الأكِنَّةُ) is the plural of (كِنانٌ), like (عِنانٌ) and (أعِنَّةٌ). (الكِنانُ) is the all-enveloping covering.

The poet says:
When they draw them out in battle from their sheaths, you think the lightning of rain has flashed, its clouds stirred.

﴿أن يفقهوه﴾ is in the position of the object of purpose (المفعول من أجله); its estimate is: "in their view, disliking that they understand it." It has also been said that the meaning is "lest they understand it," and similar examples of these two interpretations have been mentioned before. Talha ibn Musarrif read (وِقْرًا) with a kasra on the waw, as if he understood that their ears were "loaded" (وُقِرَتْ) with deafness, as a beast is loaded with a burden. The apparent meaning is that the covering and the deafness here are not literal; rather, this is of the type of using a sensible image for an intelligible matter, so that it settles in the soul. He used the image of "sheaths" for turning their hearts away from reflecting on God's signs, and the image of "heaviness" in the ears for their refusal to lend their ears to hearing it. Do you not see that they said: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise about it﴾ (Fussilat 41:26)? When they neither reflected nor listened, they were in the position of one who has a covering on his heart and a load in his ear. Others said: this is literal, and he is unaware of it, like the intrusion of the devil into the inner self of a human being, while he is unaware of it.

Al-Jubba'i took a different path in understanding this verse. He said: they used to listen to the recitation in order to use its hearing to discover the location of the Messenger (ﷺ) at night, so that they could aim to kill him and harm him. At that point God would cast sleep upon their hearts, and this is what is meant by the sheaths, and their ears would become heavy so that they could not hear that recitation because of that sleep, and this is what is meant by His words: "in their ears deafness." It has also been said: the person whom God knows will not believe and will die in disbelief, God marks his heart with a special sign, by which the angels deduce that they do not believe. If this is established, then it is not far-fetched to call that sign "sheaths." It has also been said: when they persisted in disbelief, their turning away from belief became like a sheath preventing belief, so God mentioned that as a metaphor for this meaning. It has also been said: when He withheld from them the favors (الألطاف) that are suitable only to be bestowed upon one who has been guided, He left them alone and entrusted them to themselves so that their conduct would be evil; it is not far-fetched that He attributes this to Himself, saying: ﴿And We have placed over their hearts sheaths﴾. It has also been said: this statement came as a report of what they used to say, and they said: "Our hearts are in sheaths." All these views are attributed to al-Jubba'i, and they are all a flight from attributing the "placing" to God literally, so they interpreted it through these distant figurative senses.

Al-Zamakhshari took a path close to some of these views. He said: the coverings upon the hearts and the heaviness in the ears are an image of the deafness of their hearts and their hearing to accepting it and believing in its truth. The reason for attributing the verb to Himself, namely His saying (وجعلنا), is to indicate that this is a fixed matter in them that does not depart from them, as if they were created upon it; or it is a report of what they used to say: ﴿And in our ears is heaviness, and between us and you is a barrier﴾ (Fussilat 41:5). End of quotation. This follows the doctrine of his companions, the Mu'tazilites. As for the People of the Sunnah, attributing the "placing" to God is literal and not figurative, and this is the question of the creation of human acts, which is discussed in the principles of religion (usul al-din).

Ibn Atiyya said: this is an expression for what God placed in the souls of these people of coarseness and remoteness from accepting good, as if they had not been hearing His words.

﴿And among them are those who listen to you, and We have placed over their hearts﴾. When He mentioned that their intellects do not benefit them, as if there were coverings over their seats, and not their hearing, as if there were heaviness in their ears, He moved to the sense that is more eloquent than the sense of hearing, and He negated what results from perceiving it, which is belief. The seeing here is visual, and the sign is like the splitting of the moon, the water gushing from His fingers, the trunk's lament, the staff turning into a sword, salt water becoming sweet, the little food becoming abundant, and what is similar to that. Ibn Abbas said: ﴿every sign﴾ means every proof and argument; they will not believe in it because of what He placed over their hearts as coverings. End of quotation. The intended meaning of this conditional clause is to report the complete exaggeration and the extreme obstinacy in their unbelief, to the point that when the visible thing that truly indicates the truthfulness of the Messenger comes to them, they do not draw from it its proper consequence, but rather draw from it its opposite.

﴿Until, when they come to you disputing with you, those who disbelieve say: This is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾. (يجادلونك) means they dispute with you in argumentation, and their denial of the signs reached the point of disputation. This refers to the Qur'an, and their describing it as "fables of the ancients" is a disparagement of its being the speech of God. It has been said: al-Nadr used to contest the Qur'an with the stories of Isfandiyar and Rustam. Ibn Abbas said: their disputation was their saying: "You eat what you have killed yourselves, but you do not eat what God has killed." End of quotation. This is far-fetched. The apparent meaning of the disputation is that it concerns what they heard, which they listened to from the Messenger, namely the Qur'an, and the meaning is that in their argumentation their affair ended in disputation and fabrication without evidence.

The occurrence of the conditional clause (إذا) after (حتى) is very common in the Qur'an, and the first occurrence of it is His saying: ﴿And test the orphans until, when they reach marriageable age﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:6). Here (حتى) is a particle of beginning (حرف ابتداء), and it is not a preposition governing (إذا), nor is the conditional clause or the consequent clause in a position of genitive. It is not a condition of (حتى), when it is a particle of beginning, that the noun in the nominative (المبتدأ) follow it; rather, it can be followed by a noun in the nominative. Do you not see that they say in examples like "I struck the people, until even Zayd I struck him," that (حتى) here is a particle of beginning, even though what follows it is in the accusative? When (حتى) is followed by (إذا), it may be understood to have the meaning of (الفاء), and it may be understood to have the meaning of (إلى أن). So the estimate would be: "then when they are averse (لكارهون) [al-Anfal 8:5], they dispute with you [al-Anfal 8:6], he says"; or the estimate would be: ﴿And We have placed over their hearts sheaths, lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness﴾, meaning: We prevented them from understanding the Qur'an and reflecting upon it, until they say: ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾ at the time of their coming to you disputing with you, because the end point (الغاية) is taken only from the consequent of the condition, not from the condition itself. Upon these two meanings the whole of what comes in the Qur'an with His words "until, when" (حتى إذا) is explained. The construction (حتى إذا) must be preceded by an explicit statement, as in this verse, and as in His words: ﴿So they set out, until when they met a boy, he killed him; he said: Did you kill?﴾ (al-Kahf 18:74). Or it must be preceded by an implied statement that the context indicates, as in His words: ﴿Pieces of iron, until when he made them equal between the two cliffs, he said: Blow! until when he made it fire﴾ (al-Kahf 18:96). The estimate is: they brought him the iron, and he placed it between the two cliffs, until when he made them equal, he said: "Blow!" so he blew, until when he made it into fire by His command and permission, he said: "Bring me, I will pour (molten copper upon it)." For this reason al-Farra' said: "until when" (حتى إذا) must be preceded by a statement, either explicitly or by estimate. We have mentioned the rulings of (حتى) fully in the book al-Takmil, and its entry into the conditional, and the views of al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i on that, and the views of others.

Al-Zamakhshari said: here it is the (حتى) after which sentences come, and the sentence (إذا) is in the position of a circumstance. End of quotation. This agrees with what we have mentioned. Then he said: it is also permissible that it be the preposition, and (إذا) be in the position of the genitive, meaning "until the time of their coming," and "(لكارهون) disputing with you" is a circumstance, and his saying "those who disbelieve say" is an explanation. The meaning is that their denial of the signs reached the point that they dispute with you and contest you. He explained their disputation as their saying: ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾, thus making the speech of God and the truest of discourse into superstitions and falsehoods, and this is the extreme of denial. End of quotation.

What al-Zamakhshari permitted regarding (إذا) after (حتى), that it be in the genitive, Ibn Malik required in al-Tashil, claiming that (إذا) is governed by (حتى). He said in al-Tashil: it may also depart from it, meaning the temporal (إذا) as an object, and as a genitive governed by (حتى), or as a subject in the nominative. What al-Zamakhshari went to in permitting that (إذا) be in the genitive governed by (حتى), and Ibn Malik in requiring that, and his not mentioning any view other than it, is an error. We have explained this in the book al-Tadhyil on the explanation of al-Tashil. Al-Hawfi, Abu al-Baqa' and others among the grammarians have correctly arrived at the right view on this. Abu al-Baqa' said here: (يوزعون حتى إذا) is in the position of the accusative for its consequent, which is (يقول), and (حتى) here has no governing function; it merely conveyed the meaning of the end point, just as it does not govern sentences. (يجادلونك) is a circumstance from the subject pronoun in (جاءوك), and it is the governing element of the circumstance; (يقول) is the consequent of (إذا), and it is the governing element of (إذا). End of quotation.

﴿And they forbid others from it and keep away from it﴾. It is reported from Ibn Abbas that it was revealed concerning Abu Talib, who used to forbid the polytheists from harming the Messenger (ﷺ) and his followers, while they were calling him to Islam. Quraysh gathered with Abu Talib, wanting evil for the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and Abu Talib said:

By God, they will not reach you with their gathering, until I am laid down as a buried one in the dust.
So proclaim your command; there is no shame upon you in it, and rejoice, and let your eyes be cooled thereby.
You called me, and you claimed that you were a sincere counselor, and you have indeed spoken truly, and you were trustworthy there.
And you presented a religion that is undoubtedly among the best religions of mankind.
Were it not for the reproach or the fear of insult, you would have found me generous with it, and clear about it.

Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: it was revealed concerning the disbelievers of Makkah, who would forbid people from following the Messenger (ﷺ) and would keep themselves far from him. This is also the view of Ibn ʿAbbas according to the narration of al-Walibi.

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in His saying "and they" (wa-hum) refers to the disbelievers, and this is the view of the majority, which al-Tabari also chose. The pronoun in His saying "from him" ('anhu) refers to the Qur'an, which is the thing the pronoun attached to "yafqahuhu" refers to, and which is indicated by their saying "this is nothing but" (in hadha). This is the view of Qatadah and Mujahid. The meaning is that they forbid others from following and contemplating the Qur'an, and they keep themselves away from it.

It has also been said that the pronoun in "from him" refers to the Messenger (ﷺ), since his mention came earlier in His saying "And among them are those who listen to you, until, when they come to you, they dispute with you." In that case this is an iltifat (a shift from address to third-person reference), that is, a movement from direct address to the third person. The pronoun in "and they" refers to the disbelievers already mentioned. The meaning is that they combined keeping themselves far from the Messenger with forbidding others from following him, so they went astray and led others astray. It has already been noted that this view is one of the reports concerning the occasion of revelation.

It has also been said that the pronoun in "and they" refers to Abu Talib and those who agreed with him in protecting the Messenger (ﷺ). The pronoun in "from him" refers to the Messenger, and the meaning is that "they forbid from him" those who wish to harm him, and they keep away from him by not believing in him and not following him, so they do one thing while doing its opposite. This is also the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, Habib ibn Abi Thabit, ʿAta' ibn Dinar and Muqatil. This view is also one of the reports concerning the occasion of revelation. However, attributing this to Abu Talib and his followers by the wording "and they" apparently means it returns to the whole group of disbelievers, and that the whole group did not forbid harming the Messenger. The attribution is made to all the disbelievers for what was done by some of them, so the expression concerning a part of them is worded in a way that covers all of them, because the reproach in this form is more severe and harsher, since they forbid harming him and keep away from following him. This is like when you censure a group among them by saying: "thieves," "among them are adulterers," "among them are wine-drinkers." These are thieves, adulterers and wine-drinkers, while in reality some of them do one thing and some do another. The meaning here is: "among them are those who listen," "among them are those who forbid harming him and keep away from his guidance."

In His saying "they forbid from him and keep away" (yanhawna ʿanhu wa-yanʾawna) there is tajnis al-tasrif (paronomasia of morphological form), which is when each word differs from the other by one letter. "Yanhawna" differs by the letter ha', and "yanʾawna" differs by the hamza. Similar to it is "wa-hum yahsabuna annahum yuhsinuna" (And they think they are doing good), and "wa-yafrahu wa-yamrahu" (and they exult and swagger), and "al-khayl maʿqud fi nawasiha al-khayr" (good is tied to the forelocks of horses). In the book al-Tahbir it is called tajnis al-tahrif (paronomasia by alteration), which is when a single letter is the difference between the two words. The poet's verse cited for it is:

"If I do not raid the son of Hind,
for the plunder of wealth or the destruction of souls..."

Others have said that tajnis al-tahrif is when the difference between the two words is in the vowel marks (shakl), like the saying of some Arabs when a child of theirs had died: "O God, I am muslim (submitting) and musallim (one who submits others)." And some Arabs said: "al-laha tuftahu al-laha" (Lahá opens the ... [wordplay on two meanings]).

al-Hasan recited "yanawna" with the hamza dropped and its vowel transferred to the nun, which is an analogical (qiyasi) ease of pronunciation.

"And they destroy only themselves, and they do not perceive" (wa-in yuhlikuna illa anfusahum wa-ma yashuruna). Before this there is an omitted element, its estimate being: "and they forbid from him and keep away from him," that is, from the Messenger or the Qur'an, intending that people abandon the Messenger so they would destroy him, while in reality they are destroying themselves. Destruction here does not mean death, but abiding forever in the Fire. The "in" (in) is negating, with the meaning of "ma" (not). Denying them awareness, regarding their destruction of themselves, is a great reproach, because it is more emphatic in negating knowledge, since animals perceive and sense. So the evil consequence of what they intended fell upon themselves and did not extend to others.

"And if you could see when they are made to stand over the Fire" (wa-law tara idh wuqifu ʿala al-nar) [al-An'am: 27]. When He, exalted is He, mentioned the matter of resurrection in His saying "and the day We gather them," and digressed from that to some of their blameworthy attributes in the world, He returned to the first subject. The response to "law" (if) is omitted, its indication being the meaning, and its estimate is: "you would see a dreadful matter and a great terror." Omitting the response of "law" when the speech indicates it is permissible and eloquent, and among its examples is "wa-law anna qur'anan suyyirat bihi al-jibal" (And if a Qur'an were by which the mountains were moved) [al-Ra'd: 31], and the poet's verse:

"By your life, if anything had come to us from a messenger other than you,
but we found no repelling of it for you..."

That is: if anything had come to us from a messenger other than you, we would have repelled it. "Tara" is a present-tense verb with the meaning of the past, that is: "and if you had seen." "Idh" remains a past-time adverb governed by "tara," and this is presented in the form of the past, though the event has not yet occurred, treating what is certainly expected as if it had already happened. The apparent reading is that the seeing here is visual, though it has been permitted that it be seeing of the heart. The meaning is: if you had directed your sound thought to contemplating their condition, you would have gained greater certainty that on the Day of Resurrection they will be in the worst state, so the addressee in this state gathers true report and clear reasoning, and these are two of the sources of certain knowledge. The addressee of "tara" is the Messenger, or the listener. The object of "tara" is omitted, its estimate being: "and if you could see their condition when they were made to stand." It has been said that "tara" remains in the future sense, and "idh" means "idha" (when), so it is a future time adverb, and then "law" here is used in the manner of the conditional "in." Those who held this were compelled to it by the fact that this matter has not yet occurred.

The majority read "wuqifu" in the passive voice, and its meaning according to the majority is: "they were detained over the Fire." Ibn al-Sa'ib said its meaning is: "they were made to sit upon it." "ʿAla" here means "fi" (in), or it stays in its original sense. The meaning of their sitting is that Hell has levels, so when they are on one level, the Fire is beneath them on another level. Muqatil said: they were presented to it, and whoever is presented to something has been made to stand before it. It has been said: they saw it, and whoever sees something stands before it. It has been said: they came to know the measure of its punishment, like the saying "I stood upon what is with so-and-so," meaning "I understood it and made it clear," which al-Zajjaj chose. It has been said: they were made guardians over it, like perpetual endowments upon its paths, mentioned by al-Mawardi. It has been said: they were made to stand near it. In a hadith: "that people will be made to stand upon the edge of Hell." al-Tabari said: they were made to enter it, and "waqafa" in this reading is transitive. Ibn al-Sumayfa and Zayd ibn ʿAli read "waqafu" in the active voice from the intransitive "waqafa," whose verbal noun is "al-wuquf" for this and "al-waqf" for that. The transitive form "awqafa" has been heard, though it is a rare dialect, which Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla did not know. He said: I have not heard in the speech of the Arabs "awqaftu fulanan" (I made so-and-so stand), but if I met a man standing and said to him "what made you stand here?", it would be good in my view, end of quote. Abu ʿAmr went to its goodness because it is analogically applicable to every intransitive verb, that it be made transitive by the hamza, as in "daHika Zaydun" (Zayd laughed) and "aDHhakTuhu" (I made him laugh).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 25–26 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Among them are those who listen to you, but We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness.﴾ Abu Salih narrated from Ibn Abbas that Abu Sufyan, al-Walid, al-Nadr, Utba, Shayba, Umayya and Ubayy listened to the Messenger (ﷺ). They said to al-Nadr, "O Abu Qutayla! What is Muhammad saying?" He replied, "He says nothing but the fables of the ancients, like what I tell you about the past generations." He was a man of poetry who had gathered stories from the lands of the non-Arabs, such as the story of Rustam and Isfandiyar, and he used to tell them to Quraysh, and they would listen to him. Abu Sufyan said, "I see that some of what he says is true." Abu Jahl said, "No! Do not acknowledge any of this. Death is easier than this." Then the verse was revealed.

The pronoun in (ومِنهم) refers to those who associated partners with God (al-ladhina ashraku). He used the singular pronoun in (يَسْتَمِعُ) in agreement with the wording of (مِن) (min), and the plural in ﴿على قلوبهم﴾ in agreement with its meaning. The clause beginning with (وجَعَلْنا) is coordinated with the clause before it, a verbal clause coordinated with a nominal clause, so it is information from God, Exalted, that He made such-and-such. It has also been said that the (و) is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), meaning "while We have placed," i.e., "We listen to your recitation," and they are, in their heedlessness, like one whose heart is in a sheath and whose ear is deaf. The word (جَعَلَ) here may be understood as meaning "cast" (ألقى), so that (على) is attached to it; or as meaning "made" (صيّر), so that it is attached to a omitted element, since it occupies the position of the second object; or as meaning "created" (خلق), in which case it occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (حال), because if it had been placed after its noun it would have been a qualifier, and when it was placed before, it became a circumstance.

(الأكِنَّةُ) is the plural of (كِنانٌ), like (عِنانٌ) and (أعِنَّةٌ). (الكِنانُ) is the all-enveloping covering.

The poet says:
When they draw them out in battle from their sheaths, you think the lightning of rain has flashed, its clouds stirred.

﴿أن يفقهوه﴾ is in the position of the object of purpose (المفعول من أجله); its estimate is: "in their view, disliking that they understand it." It has also been said that the meaning is "lest they understand it," and similar examples of these two interpretations have been mentioned before. Talha ibn Musarrif read (وِقْرًا) with a kasra on the waw, as if he understood that their ears were "loaded" (وُقِرَتْ) with deafness, as a beast is loaded with a burden. The apparent meaning is that the covering and the deafness here are not literal; rather, this is of the type of using a sensible image for an intelligible matter, so that it settles in the soul. He used the image of "sheaths" for turning their hearts away from reflecting on God's signs, and the image of "heaviness" in the ears for their refusal to lend their ears to hearing it. Do you not see that they said: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise about it﴾ (Fussilat 41:26)? When they neither reflected nor listened, they were in the position of one who has a covering on his heart and a load in his ear. Others said: this is literal, and he is unaware of it, like the intrusion of the devil into the inner self of a human being, while he is unaware of it.

Al-Jubba'i took a different path in understanding this verse. He said: they used to listen to the recitation in order to use its hearing to discover the location of the Messenger (ﷺ) at night, so that they could aim to kill him and harm him. At that point God would cast sleep upon their hearts, and this is what is meant by the sheaths, and their ears would become heavy so that they could not hear that recitation because of that sleep, and this is what is meant by His words: "in their ears deafness." It has also been said: the person whom God knows will not believe and will die in disbelief, God marks his heart with a special sign, by which the angels deduce that they do not believe. If this is established, then it is not far-fetched to call that sign "sheaths." It has also been said: when they persisted in disbelief, their turning away from belief became like a sheath preventing belief, so God mentioned that as a metaphor for this meaning. It has also been said: when He withheld from them the favors (الألطاف) that are suitable only to be bestowed upon one who has been guided, He left them alone and entrusted them to themselves so that their conduct would be evil; it is not far-fetched that He attributes this to Himself, saying: ﴿And We have placed over their hearts sheaths﴾. It has also been said: this statement came as a report of what they used to say, and they said: "Our hearts are in sheaths." All these views are attributed to al-Jubba'i, and they are all a flight from attributing the "placing" to God literally, so they interpreted it through these distant figurative senses.

Al-Zamakhshari took a path close to some of these views. He said: the coverings upon the hearts and the heaviness in the ears are an image of the deafness of their hearts and their hearing to accepting it and believing in its truth. The reason for attributing the verb to Himself, namely His saying (وجعلنا), is to indicate that this is a fixed matter in them that does not depart from them, as if they were created upon it; or it is a report of what they used to say: ﴿And in our ears is heaviness, and between us and you is a barrier﴾ (Fussilat 41:5). End of quotation. This follows the doctrine of his companions, the Mu'tazilites. As for the People of the Sunnah, attributing the "placing" to God is literal and not figurative, and this is the question of the creation of human acts, which is discussed in the principles of religion (usul al-din).

Ibn Atiyya said: this is an expression for what God placed in the souls of these people of coarseness and remoteness from accepting good, as if they had not been hearing His words.

﴿And among them are those who listen to you, and We have placed over their hearts﴾. When He mentioned that their intellects do not benefit them, as if there were coverings over their seats, and not their hearing, as if there were heaviness in their ears, He moved to the sense that is more eloquent than the sense of hearing, and He negated what results from perceiving it, which is belief. The seeing here is visual, and the sign is like the splitting of the moon, the water gushing from His fingers, the trunk's lament, the staff turning into a sword, salt water becoming sweet, the little food becoming abundant, and what is similar to that. Ibn Abbas said: ﴿every sign﴾ means every proof and argument; they will not believe in it because of what He placed over their hearts as coverings. End of quotation. The intended meaning of this conditional clause is to report the complete exaggeration and the extreme obstinacy in their unbelief, to the point that when the visible thing that truly indicates the truthfulness of the Messenger comes to them, they do not draw from it its proper consequence, but rather draw from it its opposite.

﴿Until, when they come to you disputing with you, those who disbelieve say: This is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾. (يجادلونك) means they dispute with you in argumentation, and their denial of the signs reached the point of disputation. This refers to the Qur'an, and their describing it as "fables of the ancients" is a disparagement of its being the speech of God. It has been said: al-Nadr used to contest the Qur'an with the stories of Isfandiyar and Rustam. Ibn Abbas said: their disputation was their saying: "You eat what you have killed yourselves, but you do not eat what God has killed." End of quotation. This is far-fetched. The apparent meaning of the disputation is that it concerns what they heard, which they listened to from the Messenger, namely the Qur'an, and the meaning is that in their argumentation their affair ended in disputation and fabrication without evidence.

The occurrence of the conditional clause (إذا) after (حتى) is very common in the Qur'an, and the first occurrence of it is His saying: ﴿And test the orphans until, when they reach marriageable age﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:6). Here (حتى) is a particle of beginning (حرف ابتداء), and it is not a preposition governing (إذا), nor is the conditional clause or the consequent clause in a position of genitive. It is not a condition of (حتى), when it is a particle of beginning, that the noun in the nominative (المبتدأ) follow it; rather, it can be followed by a noun in the nominative. Do you not see that they say in examples like "I struck the people, until even Zayd I struck him," that (حتى) here is a particle of beginning, even though what follows it is in the accusative? When (حتى) is followed by (إذا), it may be understood to have the meaning of (الفاء), and it may be understood to have the meaning of (إلى أن). So the estimate would be: "then when they are averse (لكارهون) [al-Anfal 8:5], they dispute with you [al-Anfal 8:6], he says"; or the estimate would be: ﴿And We have placed over their hearts sheaths, lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness﴾, meaning: We prevented them from understanding the Qur'an and reflecting upon it, until they say: ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾ at the time of their coming to you disputing with you, because the end point (الغاية) is taken only from the consequent of the condition, not from the condition itself. Upon these two meanings the whole of what comes in the Qur'an with His words "until, when" (حتى إذا) is explained. The construction (حتى إذا) must be preceded by an explicit statement, as in this verse, and as in His words: ﴿So they set out, until when they met a boy, he killed him; he said: Did you kill?﴾ (al-Kahf 18:74). Or it must be preceded by an implied statement that the context indicates, as in His words: ﴿Pieces of iron, until when he made them equal between the two cliffs, he said: Blow! until when he made it fire﴾ (al-Kahf 18:96). The estimate is: they brought him the iron, and he placed it between the two cliffs, until when he made them equal, he said: "Blow!" so he blew, until when he made it into fire by His command and permission, he said: "Bring me, I will pour (molten copper upon it)." For this reason al-Farra' said: "until when" (حتى إذا) must be preceded by a statement, either explicitly or by estimate. We have mentioned the rulings of (حتى) fully in the book al-Takmil, and its entry into the conditional, and the views of al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i on that, and the views of others.

Al-Zamakhshari said: here it is the (حتى) after which sentences come, and the sentence (إذا) is in the position of a circumstance. End of quotation. This agrees with what we have mentioned. Then he said: it is also permissible that it be the preposition, and (إذا) be in the position of the genitive, meaning "until the time of their coming," and "(لكارهون) disputing with you" is a circumstance, and his saying "those who disbelieve say" is an explanation. The meaning is that their denial of the signs reached the point that they dispute with you and contest you. He explained their disputation as their saying: ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾, thus making the speech of God and the truest of discourse into superstitions and falsehoods, and this is the extreme of denial. End of quotation.

What al-Zamakhshari permitted regarding (إذا) after (حتى), that it be in the genitive, Ibn Malik required in al-Tashil, claiming that (إذا) is governed by (حتى). He said in al-Tashil: it may also depart from it, meaning the temporal (إذا) as an object, and as a genitive governed by (حتى), or as a subject in the nominative. What al-Zamakhshari went to in permitting that (إذا) be in the genitive governed by (حتى), and Ibn Malik in requiring that, and his not mentioning any view other than it, is an error. We have explained this in the book al-Tadhyil on the explanation of al-Tashil. Al-Hawfi, Abu al-Baqa' and others among the grammarians have correctly arrived at the right view on this. Abu al-Baqa' said here: (يوزعون حتى إذا) is in the position of the accusative for its consequent, which is (يقول), and (حتى) here has no governing function; it merely conveyed the meaning of the end point, just as it does not govern sentences. (يجادلونك) is a circumstance from the subject pronoun in (جاءوك), and it is the governing element of the circumstance; (يقول) is the consequent of (إذا), and it is the governing element of (إذا). End of quotation.

"By your life, if anything had come to us from a messenger other than you,
but we found no repelling of it for you..."

That is: if anything had come to us from a messenger other than you, we would have repelled it. "Tara" is a present-tense verb with the meaning of the past, that is: "and if you had seen." "Idh" remains a past-time adverb governed by "tara," and this is presented in the form of the past, though the event has not yet occurred, treating what is certainly expected as if it had already happened. The apparent reading is that the seeing here is visual, though it has been permitted that it be seeing of the heart. The meaning is: if you had directed your sound thought to contemplating their condition, you would have gained greater certainty that on the Day of Resurrection they will be in the worst state, so the addressee in this state gathers true report and clear reasoning, and these are two of the sources of certain knowledge. The addressee of "tara" is the Messenger, or the listener. The object of "tara" is omitted, its estimate being: "and if you could see their condition when they were made to stand." It has been said that "tara" remains in the future sense, and "idh" means "idha" (when), so it is a future time adverb, and then "law" here is used in the manner of the conditional "in." Those who held this were compelled to it by the fact that this matter has not yet occurred.

The majority read "wuqifu" in the passive voice, and its meaning according to the majority is: "they were detained over the Fire." Ibn al-Sa'ib said its meaning is: "they were made to sit upon it." "ʿAla" here means "fi" (in), or it stays in its original sense. The meaning of their sitting is that Hell has levels, so when they are on one level, the Fire is beneath them on another level. Muqatil said: they were presented to it, and whoever is presented to something has been made to stand before it. It has been said: they saw it, and whoever sees something stands before it. It has been said: they came to know the measure of its punishment, like the saying "I stood upon what is with so-and-so," meaning "I understood it and made it clear," which al-Zajjaj chose. It has been said: they were made guardians over it, like perpetual endowments upon its paths, mentioned by al-Mawardi. It has been said: they were made to stand near it. In a hadith: "that people will be made to stand upon the edge of Hell." al-Tabari said: they were made to enter it, and "waqafa" in this reading is transitive. Ibn al-Sumayfa and Zayd ibn ʿAli read "waqafu" in the active voice from the intransitive "waqafa," whose verbal noun is "al-wuquf" for this and "al-waqf" for that. The transitive form "awqafa" has been heard, though it is a rare dialect, which Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla did not know. He said: I have not heard in the speech of the Arabs "awqaftu fulanan" (I made so-and-so stand), but if I met a man standing and said to him "what made you stand here?", it would be good in my view, end of quote. Abu ʿAmr went to its goodness because it is analogically applicable to every intransitive verb, that it be made transitive by the hamza, as in "daHika Zaydun" (Zayd laughed) and "aDHhakTuhu" (I made him laugh).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 27:

﴿So they will say: "Would that we could be returned, and not deny the signs of our Lord, and be among the believers."﴾ Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah and Ḥafṣ read (wa-lā nukadhdhiba wa-nakūna) with the accusative (naṣb) in both. According to the majority of the Basran grammarians, this accusative is by the implied (an) after the waw, so that it forms with the implied (an) and the verb after it a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the nominative, conjoined to an assumed, implied verbal noun from the preceding clause. The sense is: "Would that for us there were a return, and the absence of denial, and being among the believers." Many grammar books state that the accusative after this waw is an answer to the wish (jawāb al-tamannī), as al-Zamakhsharī said: "(wa-lā nukadhdhiba wa-nakūna) in the accusative by the implied (an), as an answer to the wish, meaning: if we are returned, we will not deny and we will be among the believers." End of quotation. But this is not as he mentioned, for the accusative of the verb after the waw is not by way of answer, because the waw does not occur in the answer to a conditional, so a conditional and its answer are not formed from what precedes it or what follows it. Rather it is the waw of joining, by which what follows is conjoined to the assumed verbal noun before it. It is the waw of conjunction, and with the accusative one of its three meanings is necessarily fixed, namely accompaniment (maʿiyyah). What distinguishes it from the fāʾ is assuming a conditional before it, or a circumstantial (ḥāl) in its place. The basis of the view that it is an answer is that it puts the verb in the accusative in the places where the fāʾ does, so it was thought to be an answer. Sībawayh said: The waw puts into the accusative what follows it wherever the fāʾ and waw put into the accusative what follows them, but its meaning and the meaning of the fāʾ differ. Do you not see: "Do not forbid a character trait, and come to be like it." If the fāʾ were inserted here, it would corrupt the meaning; he meant that the prohibition and the doing cannot be combined. And you say: "Do not eat fish and drink milk"; if you insert the fāʾ the meaning is corrupted. End of Sībawayh's words, summarized and in his wording. What makes clear to you that it is not an answer is that the fāʾ alone, without it, when removed, makes the verb after it jussive (majzūm) with what precedes it, because of the conditional sense in it, except when it puts the verb in the accusative after a negation and the fāʾ drops, then it is not jussive. Having established this, the three verbs in meaning are wished for in a joint manner, not that each one is wished for alone, since the sense, as we said, is: "Would that for us there were a return with the absence of denial and being among the believers." Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: Ibn ʿĀmir, in the transmission of Hishām ibn ʿAmmār from his companions from Ibn ʿĀmir, read (wa-lā nukadhdhibu) with the nominative and (wa-nakūna) with the accusative, and that is explained by what preceded. End of quotation. He had earlier stated that the nominative of (wa-lā nukadhdhiba wa-nakūna) in the reading of the rest of the seven has two aspects: first, conjunction with (nuradd), so that the two are included in the wish; second, resumption and severance (istiʾnāf wa-qaṭʿ). Both aspects are acceptable for the nominative of (wa-lā nukadhdhiba) in this reading. In the codex of ʿAbd Allāh it reads "fa-lā nukadhdhiba" with the fāʾ, and in the reading of Ubayy: "fa-lā nukadhdhiba biāyāti rabbinā abadan wa-nakūna." Abū ʿAmr related that in the reading of Ubayy it is "wa-naḥnu nakūnu min al-mu'minīn." They also permitted, for the nominative of (wa-lā nukadhdhiba wa-nakūna), that they be in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Thus three aspects are established for the nominative.

The first: that it is conjoined to (nuradd), so that the absence of denial and the being among the believers are both included in the wish; i.e., "Would that we did not deny, and would that we were among the believers." In this aspect the nominative is equal to the accusative, since both involve conjunction, though their basis differs: in the accusative it is conjoined to an assumed verbal noun of return, and in the nominative to the verb itself. If you say: the wish is an utterance (inshāʾ), and an utterance is not subject to truth or falsehood, so how did His saying "And indeed they are liars" come as a report from God that the disposition of these disbelievers is lying, so that this is a narration and report of their state in the world, and has no connection to the object of the wish? The second aspect: this wish has included the meaning of a report and a promise. When a person's disposition is something, and then he wishes for what contradicts that disposition and what is far from it to occur from him, it is correct to call him a liar by way of figurative speech, like: "Would that God gave me wealth so that I might do good to you and reward you for your kindness." This is a wisher in the sense of one promising and reporting. When God gives him wealth and he does not do good to his companion and does not reward him, he has lied, and his wish is in the position of one who says: "If God gives me wealth, I will reward you for your kindness." Like the words of a wicked man far from acts of obedience: "Would that I performed the pilgrimage, struggled, and stood the night in prayer," so it is permissible to say to such a one, by figurative speech, "You have lied," i.e., you are not fit to do good, and it is not fit for you. The second of the aspects of the nominative: that the nominative of (wa-lā nukadhdhiba wa-nakūna) is by resumption, so they report about themselves this, and it falls under "they said": i.e., they said, "Would that we were returned," and they said, "We do not deny the signs of our Lord, and we will be among the believers," reporting that this proceeds from them in every state. On this basis their lying in this report is correct. Sībawayh preferred this aspect and compared it to his saying "Leave me and I will not return," meaning "and I do not return," whether you left me or did not leave me. The third aspect of the nominative: that (wa-lā nukadhdhiba wa-nakūna) is in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial clause, the sense being: "Would that we were returned not denying, and being among the believers," so that it falls as a restriction on the wished-for return, and the subject of the circumstance is the concealed pronoun in (nuradd). The saying "And indeed they are liars" may be answered by the two aspects mentioned in the parsing of (wa-lā nukadhdhiba wa-nakūna) when they are conjoined to (nuradd). It is related that some reciter read (wa-lā nukadhdhiba) with the accusative and (wa-nakūna) with the nominative: the accusative is conjunction with an assumed verbal noun, and the nominative in (wa-nakūna) is conjunction with (nuradd), or resumption, i.e., "and we will be." The circumstantial reading is weak here, because it is an affirmative present verb, so it does not take the circumstantial form with the waw, except on the supposition of a deleted subject, as in: "I was saved and I pledge to them my property," and "I pledge to them my property." The apparent meaning is that they wished for return from the Hereafter to the world. Al-Ṭabarī related an interpretation of "return": that they wished to be returned from the torment of the Fire to standing at the Fire where they were made to stand, so the meaning is: "Would that we were made to stand this standing, not denying the signs of our Lord, being among the believers." He said: this interpretation is weakened in several respects that invalidate it; if they were returned they would return to what they were forbidden, and denial is not correct in this wish either, because it is a wish for what has already passed; denial, as we mentioned, is correct only before this, figuratively, in wishes about future things. End of quotation. Some of them raised here a question, saying: If it is said, how do they wish for return while knowing it is impossible to obtain? He answered: We say, perhaps they did not know that return would not take place. Second: knowledge of non-return does not prevent wanting, as in His saying: "They wish to come out of the Fire" [al-Māʾidah 37] and "Pour upon us some of the water" [al-Aʿrāf 50]. End of quotation. This question does not arise, because the wish may apply to the possible and the impossible, unlike the hope (tarajjī), which applies only to the possible. So the wish here is applied to the impossible, which is one of the two kinds for which the wish is used in the Arabic language. The more correct view is that the (yā) in His saying "Yā layta" is a particle of alerting (ḥarf tanbīh), not a particle of calling (ḥarf nidāʾ), and the vocative object is deleted, because in this there is the deletion of the whole calling clause and the deletion of its complement altogether, and that is a great deal of omission.

**Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 6, verse 28:**

﴿Nay, there has become apparent to them what they used to conceal before.﴾ *Bal* (بَلْ) here marks *idrab* (a turning from one matter to another, glossed as "transition") and *intiqal* (a move from one thing to another), without cancelling what came before. This is how it occurs in the Book of God Most High: when what follows it is a report from God Most High, not a narration about a people, *bal* in it is for *idrab*, as in His saying: ﴿Nay, he has invented it; nay, he is a poet﴾ [al-Anbiya': 5]. The meaning of *bada* (بَدا) is "became apparent" (ظَهَرَ).

Al-Zajjaj said: *bal* here is *istidrak* (a correction, glossed as "qualification") and an affirmation after a negation, like their saying: "Zayd did not stand, but 'Amr stood." End of quote. I do not know what negation preceded it, for *bal* to affirm it. Others said: *bal* is a rejection of what they wished for, meaning: the matter is not as they said, because they did not say that out of desire for faith, but said it out of fear of punishment and hope for mercy. End of quote. I do not know what this statement means.

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in *lahum* ("to them") refers to the same ones to whom the pronoun in *wuqifu* ("they were made to stand") refers. Abu Rawq said: They are all the disbelievers, whom God will gather, and He will say: ﴿Where are your partners?﴾ (the verse), and they will say: ﴿By God, our Lord﴾ (the verse), and their limbs will speak and testify that they used to associate partners in the world, and [will testify] to what they concealed. This is His saying: ﴿Nay, there has become apparent to them﴾. According to this, *min qabl* ("before") refers to the Hereafter, meaning: before its becoming apparent in the Hereafter.

Qatada said: ﴿what they used to conceal﴾ becomes apparent, namely their polytheism.

Ibn Abbas said: They are the Jews and Christians, because if they were asked in the world, "Will you be punished for what you are upon?" they would say, "No." Then the punishment for their polytheism became apparent to them in the Hereafter. This is His saying: ﴿Nay, there has become apparent to them﴾.

It was said: they are the disbelievers of Makkah, to whom there became apparent what they had concealed concerning the resurrection, through their saying: ﴿There is nothing but our life of this world; we die and we live, and we are not to be resurrected﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 37] after death.

It was said: the hypocrites used to conceal disbelief, and its consequence became apparent to them on the Day of Resurrection.

It was said: the disbelievers who, when the Messenger admonished them, were afraid, and concealed that fear so that their followers would not perceive it; that fear will become apparent to them on the Day of Resurrection.

It was said: they are the Jews, the Christians and the rest of the disbelievers, and what they concealed is the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ and his circumstances. The meaning is: there became apparent to them your truthfulness in prophethood and your warning of God's punishment. These statements, on the basis that the pronoun in *lahum* and in *yukhfuna* ("they conceal") refers to one category.

It was said: the pronoun differs; meaning: there became apparent to the followers what the leaders used to conceal from them of corruption. This is related from al-Hasan in a similar sense.

It was said: there became apparent to the Arab polytheists what the People of the Book used to conceal from them concerning the resurrection and the matter of the Fire, because the People of the Book were mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿those whom We gave the Book recognize it﴾ [al-An'am: 20].

It was said: ﴿Nay, there has become apparent to them﴾ means: to some of them, what some of them used to conceal from others. So it applied "all" to "some" figuratively.

Al-Zahrawi said: It is also possible that the purpose of the verse is to report the terror of the Day of Resurrection, expressing it by saying that their hidden things from the world became apparent to them (p-104), such as sins and other things. How, then, will it be concerning what they used to disclose, such as disbelief and the like? In support of this interpretation, consider His saying, magnifying the Day of Resurrection: ﴿the Day when the secrets are tested﴾ [al-Tariq: 9].

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿what they used to conceal﴾ from people, of their ugly deeds and disgraces in their records, and the testimony of their limbs against them. Therefore they wished what they wished out of distress, though they were resolved that, if they were returned, they would believe. End of quote.

* *

﴿And if they were returned, they would certainly revert to what they were forbidden﴾. That is: if they were returned (*wa law ruddu*) to the world after standing before the Fire and wishing to be returned, they would revert to what they were forbidden of disbelief. Al-Zamakhshari said: and the sins. End of quote. Thus he included the sinners who did not repent among those standing before the Fire who wish to be returned, in accordance with his Mu'tazili doctrine (*al-i'tizali*, the Mu'tazili school). This sentence reports a matter that will not occur, how it would have been had it occurred. This is among the things that God has kept for Himself as knowledge; if He informs of something of it, it is known; otherwise it is not spoken about.

Ibn al-Qushayri said: ﴿they would revert to what they were forbidden﴾ (of polytheism), because of God's knowledge concerning them and His will that they would not believe in the world. Iblis witnessed what he witnessed of God's signs and then was obstinate.

Al-Wahidi said: this verse is among the clear proofs against the Mu'tazila for the corruption of their view, for God Most High informed of a people upon whom His decree had passed in pre-eternity (*al-azal*, glossed as "pre-eternity") with polytheism. Then He made clear that if they witnessed the Fire and the punishment, and then asked to return, and were returned to the world, they would revert to polytheism, and that is because of the prior decree concerning them. Otherwise, a rational person would not doubt what he has witnessed. End of quote.

Here he raised a question, which I think is for the Mu'tazila: how can it be said: "If they were returned to the world, they would revert to disbelief in God and to disobeying Him, when they have known God by necessity and witnessed the kinds of punishment?" The Qadi answered: the assumption is, "if they were returned to the state of moral responsibility (*al-taklif*, glossed as "legal accountability"), and the return to this state occurs only if there did not occur on the Day of Resurrection a knowledge of God by necessity and the witnessing of the terrors and the punishment of Hell. So this condition is necessarily implied in the verse." The Qadi's answer was judged weak, because the purpose of the verse is their extreme persistence in disbelief and their lack of desire for faith. Even if we assume the absence of knowledge of God on the Day of Resurrection and the absence of witnessing its terrors, there would be no extra astonishment in the people's persistence in their disbelief, since their persistence in disbelief runs in the same way as the persistence of all other disbelievers in disbelief in the world. So we know that the condition the Qadi mentioned cannot be considered at all. End of quote.

Rather, the meaning is: "And if they were returned," though they have known God by necessity, have witnessed the punishment, are keeping it in mind, and are mindful of it, they would revert to what they were forbidden of disbelief.

Ibrahim, Yahya ibn Waththab and al-A'mash recited (*wa law ridduu*, glossed as "a variant reading") with a kasra on the *ra*, by transferring the vowel of the *dal* from *radida* to the *ra*.

﴿And indeed they are liars.﴾ The discussion of this sentence has already been given. Is the lying related to what the wish contained, namely the promise of faith? Or is it a report from God Most High about their habit and custom, and what they are upon of lying in addressing the Messenger of God ﷺ? In that case it is cut off from what precedes it in speech.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 29:

﴿And they said: There is nothing but our life of this world.﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said: "And they said" is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon "they would have gone back" (laʿādū), meaning: if they were returned, they would disbelieve, and they would say "there is nothing but our life of this world," as they used to say before witnessing the Resurrection (qiyamah). It is also permissible that it be coordinated upon His saying "and indeed they are liars," with the meaning: "and indeed they are a people who lie in everything, and they are the ones who said: ﴿There is nothing but our life of this world﴾," and this is sufficient as proof of their lying, end of quote. The first opinion, which he presented, that it falls within the answer of (law, "if"), is the opinion of Ibn Zayd. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: God's confronting them in the verse after it regarding the Resurrection, and the indication to it in His saying: ﴿Is this not the truth?﴾ [al-Anʿam: 30], is a refutation of this interpretation, end of quote. What Ibn ʿAtiyyah mentioned does not refute it, because the two situations differ: their affirmation of the truth of the Resurrection is in the Hereafter, and their denial of it is in this world, on the assumption of their being returned, and it is a denial born of obstinacy. Thus their affirmation of it in the Hereafter does not contradict their denial of it in this world on the assumption of their return. Do you not see His saying: ﴿And they denied them while their souls were certain of them﴾ [al-Naml: 14], and the saying of Abu Jahl, while he knew that what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) brought was true, meaning that he would never believe in it? This, and that, are in one situation, namely this world. The second opinion that al-Zamakhshari mentioned is the opinion of the majority, and it is that His saying: ﴿And indeed they are liars﴾ [al-Anʿam: 28] is a statement separate from what precedes it, and "they said" is a report about what proceeded from them in the state of the world. Muqatil said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) informed the disbelievers of Mecca about the Resurrection, they said: "This..." and the meaning of the verse is the denial of gathering and return. In this verse it is made clear that what they used to fear was the gathering and return, according to some of the earlier exegetes' statements. Here "in" (in) is negating. They did not suffice with reporting the restricted matter, saying "it is our life of this world," until they brought negation and restriction; that is, there is no life except this life of the world only, and "it" is a pronoun for the life, and the predicate after it explains it. The estimate is: "and what is life except our life of this world." So said some of our companions, that the pronoun is placed first and is not intended to be delayed, when the apparent noun is made a predicate of the implied subject, and they counted it along with the pronoun attached to "rubba" (many a), like: rubbahu rajulan akramta, and the nominative after "niʿma" (how excellent) according to the Basrans' school, like: niʿma rajulun Zayd, or with the first of two competing verbs according to Sibawayh's school, like: darabani wa darabtu al-Zaydayn, or the explained term is substituted for it according to al-Akhfash's school, like: marartu bihi Zayd. He said: or its predicate is made, and he illustrated it with His saying: ﴿It is nothing but our life of this world﴾; the estimate is two: "the life, is nothing but our life of this world," so the stating of the predicate indicates it and clarifies it. None of our other companions mentioned this category, or it is the pronoun of the matter according to the Basrans, and the pronoun of the unspecified according to the Kufans, like: hadha Zayd qa'im, against Ibn al-Tarawah's denial of this category. The clarification of these hidden pronouns is mentioned in books of grammar. "Of this world" (al-dunya) is an adjective of His saying "our life" (hayatuna), and it was not brought as an adjective to remove an accidental commonality in a definite noun, because they do not acknowledge that there is another life other than the worldly one; rather that is a description by way of emphasis, since there is no life for them except this life.

﴿And we are not to be resurrected﴾. When the statement indicated the negation of resurrection by what it included of restriction, they explicitly stated the pure negation indicating the absence of resurrection by explicit wording, and they emphasized that with the bāʾ (ba) entering the predicate, by way of exaggeration in denial. This indicates that this verse concerns the polytheists of the Arabs and those who agreed with them in denying resurrection.

﴿Had you seen when they were made to stand before their Lord. He will say, "Is this not the truth?" They will say, "Yes, by our Lord."﴾ The response to "law" (if/had) is omitted, as it was omitted in His saying "had you seen" earlier. This is a metaphor for detention, rebuke and questioning, like a wrongdoing servant standing before his master to be punished. Some of the anthropomorphists (al-Mushabbihah, those who liken Allah to created things) have relied on this verse and said: its apparent meaning indicates that Allah is in a place and direction, since the people of the Resurrection stand before Him and near Him, and this indicates that He is in a place, appearing there at times and absent from it at others. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: This is an error, because the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that they are standing "over" Allah, as one of us stands over the ground, and this indicates that He is elevated over the essence of Allah, exalted far above that, and this is invalid by consensus. Therefore it is necessary to resort to interpretation (ta'wil), so the meaning is: when they are made to stand over what their Lord promised them of the punishment of the disbelievers and the reward of the believers, and over what He informed them of concerning the Hereafter; or the meaning is the standing of knowledge (wuquf al-ma'rifah). These two interpretations were mentioned by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "over His judgment and His command." It was also said: "over the questioning of their Lord concerning their deeds." It was said: "for the questioning of the angels of their Lord." It was said: "over the reckoning of their Lord." [p. 106]

He says: ﴿Is this not the truth?﴾ The apparent reading is that the agent of "qal" (said) is Allah Himself, so the question is from Him, the Exalted, to them. It was said the question is from the angels, so the pronoun is returned to the one who made them stand before Allah among the angels, i.e., "the one who made them stand among the angels said." Al-Zamakhshari said: "qal" (he said) is an answer to one who asks, "What did their Lord say to them when they stood before Him?" So it is said: "Is this not the truth?" This is a reproach from Allah to them for their denial and their saying, since they used to hear talk of resurrection and recompense, which is truth, and they thought it was nothing but falsehood.
