In my view it is possible that the clause is circumstantial (hal), the estimate being: "when they were made to stand before their Lord," saying to them: "Is this not the truth?" The reference of "this" is to the resurrection and its related matters. Abu al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi said: "Is this punishment not the truth?" It seems he had in mind His saying "so taste the punishment." They said: "Yes, by our Lord." The discussion of "bala" (yes, in answer to a negative question) has already been made. They confirmed their answer with an oath in their saying "by our Lord," which is an admission of faith at a time when it does not benefit them. The emphasis with their saying "by our Lord" corresponds to the beginning of the verse, "made to stand before their Lord." Mentioning the Lord is a reminder to them that He used to nurture them and set right their condition, since He was their master and they were His servants, but they disobeyed Him and opposed His command.

* *

﴿He will say, "Taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve."﴾ That is, because of your disbelief in the punishment. The "ba'" (bi-) is causal. It was said that the object of the disbelief is the resurrection, meaning: because of your disbelief in the resurrection. It was said that its object is the punishment, meaning: because of your disbelief in the punishment. The "tasting" of the punishment is an eloquent metaphor, and the meaning is: engage with it as the taster engages, for it is the most intense form of engagement.

﴿Those have lost who denied the meeting with Allah, until when the Hour came upon them suddenly, they said, "Alas for us over what we neglected concerning it."﴾ [al-An'am: 31] This is a resumed statement from Allah, the Exalted, about the condition of the deniers of the resurrection and their loss: they took disbelief in exchange for faith, so this resembles the state of a merchant who took and gave, and what he took of disbelief was a cause of his destruction, and what he gave of faith was a cause of his salvation. So he resembles one who has lost in his transaction, having no profit and no capital. The meaning of "the meeting with Allah" is reaching the Hereafter and what occurs there of recompense, and their return to His judgments in it. "Until" (hatta) is the limit of their denial, not of their loss, because loss has no limit, while the denial is limited by the regret, since the denial does not cease to be with them until their saying "Alas for us" at the time the Hour comes. The discussion of "until when" (hatta idha) has already been made in His saying: ﴿until when they come to you disputing with you﴾ [al-An'am: 25]. The meaning of "meeting with Allah" is the meeting of His recompense, and the annexation is for magnifying and honouring the matter of the recompense. It is similar to "he met Allah while He was angry with him," meaning he met its recompense. Whoever affirms that Allah is in a direction has relied on this and said: "the meeting" is literal. "The Hour" is the Day of Resurrection, named "the Hour" because of the swiftness with which the reckoning in it is completed for the recompense, in accordance with His saying: ﴿the swiftest of reckoners﴾ [al-An'am: 62]. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the definite article was placed on it as a definiteness of reference without prior mention, because of its fame, its settledness in souls, and the spread of its mention; and also because His saying "the meeting with Allah" includes it. Then the usage of "the Hour" became dominant for the Day of Resurrection, so the "al" in it is for dominance, as it is in "al-bayt" (the house) for the Ka'bah, and "al-najm" (the star) for the Pleiades.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "They only regret at their death," I say: since death is an occurrence among the events of the Hereafter and its preliminaries, it was made of the kind of the Hour and named by its name. For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever dies, his resurrection has come." The coming of the Hour is put after death because of its swiftness, so what happens is without any interval. End of quotation. The application of "the Hour" to the time of death is a metaphor. It is possible to take "the Hour" literally, meaning the Day of Resurrection, and their regret at the time of death does not necessitate that they will not regret on the Day of Resurrection. Rather, the apparent meaning is that, in accordance with His saying: ﴿while they bear their burdens upon their backs﴾ [al-An'am: 31], since this is a circumstance of their saying: ﴿they said, "Alas for us over what we neglected concerning it"﴾ [al-An'am: 31], and it is a circumstance of concomitance. If we take "the Hour" as the time of death, it becomes a projected circumstance (hal muqaddarah), and the coming of the projected circumstance in relation to the concomitant is rare. Thus their denial continues with them, limited by the regret until the Day of Resurrection, since their stay in the barzakh (intermediate realm), according to the opinion of the most moderate of them in terms of method, is one day, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿You did not remain except a day﴾ [Ta-Ha: 104]. So when the Hour came upon them, the denial ceased, and they witnessed directly what the messengers had informed them of, so they said, "Alas for us." [p. 107]

As for the accusative of "suddenly" (baghtah), it may be a verbal noun in the place of a circumstance from "the Hour," meaning "surprising," or a circumstance from the object of "came upon them," meaning "taken by surprise," or a verbal noun of "came" (jaa'a) from a root other than its own wording, as if it were said: "until when the Hour surprised them with a surprise," or a verbal noun of a deleted verb, meaning "it will surprise them with a surprise." They call upon regret, although it does not answer, in the manner of exalting it. Sibawayh said: It is as if the one who calls upon regret, or wonder, or joy, or woe, says: "Come near," or "be present," for this is your time and your moment. In this there is an exaltation of the matter for the speaker himself and for his hearer, if there is a hearer. This exaltation for the self and the hearer is also the intended purpose in calling inanimate things, as when you say, "O house! O dwelling!" and in calling what does not reason, as when they say, "O camel!" "Fararna" means "we fell short," and "tafrit" is falling short while having the ability to avoid it. The pronoun in "fiha" (concerning it) refers to "the Hour," meaning concerning the preparation for it. This was said by al-Hasan (al-Basri), or to the transaction which the mention of loss includes, as said by al-Tabari. Al-Zamakhshari said: the pronoun refers to "the worldly life," and it is brought in with its pronoun although it has not been mentioned, because it is known; or it refers to "the Hour," meaning we fell short in its matter and in belief in it, as you say, "I fell short regarding so-and-so," and from it: "I fell short in the side of Allah." End of quotation. Its referring to the world is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, and reason indicates that the place of shortfall is nothing but the world, so it is good to return it to the world for this meaning. Ibn 'Atiyyah presented this view as a possibility, saying: "It may be that the pronoun refers to the world, since the meaning requires it, and the sense of place is more apt, like 'Zayd is in the house.'" Its referring to "the Hour" is the saying of al-Hasan, and the meaning is in preparing provision and readiness for it. It was also said: the pronoun refers to "ma" (what), which is a relative pronoun, and it returns to the meaning, i.e., "Alas for us" over the deeds and acts of obedience which we neglected. The "ma" in the previous possibilities is verbal (masdariyyah), the estimate being "over our shortfall in the world," or "in the Hour," or "in the transaction," according to the estimate mentioned earlier. The apparent reading is that it returns to "the Hour." Anyone who went to the view that it refers to their dwellings in Paradise, when they see their dwellings in it had they believed, is further from the correct meaning.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 31:**

﴿وهم يَحْمِلُونَ أوْزارَهم عَلى ظُهُورِهِمْ﴾ ("while they carry their burdens on their backs"). *Al-awzar* means the sins and misdeeds, as stated by Ibn Abbas. The apparent meaning is that this carrying is literal. This is the view of Umayr ibn Hani', Amr ibn Qays al-Mula'i, and al-Suddi, and al-Tabari chose it. What its substance conveys is that a person's deed takes the form of a man with an ugly face and appearance and a foul smell. He asks the person, "I am your deed. You rode me in the world, so today I will ride you." He then mounts him, strides over the necks of the people, and drives him until he brings him into the Fire. Abu Hurayrah narrated the same meaning from the Prophet (ﷺ), though the wording differs. It has also been said that this is a figurative usage (*majaz*), in which "carrying the burden" is an expression for the hardship and pain that a person experiences because of his sins. The meaning is that they suffer the punishment for their sins as a heavy suffering upon them. Ibn Atiyya began with this view, and al-Zamakhshari mentioned no other. He said it is like His saying ﴿فَبِما كَسَبَتْ أيْدِيكُمْ﴾ ("for what your hands have earned", 42:30), because carrying loads on the back is customary, just as earning is associated with the hands. The *wa* in (*wa-hum*) is the *wāw al-ḥāl* (the "circumstantial *wāw*", introducing a clause describing the state of the subject). The clause begins with the pronoun because this is more emphatic in attribution, since the subject (*dhū al-ḥāl*) is effectively mentioned twice in meaning. The back is singled out because it is usually the place where loads are habitually carried, and because it implies an emphasis on the heaviness of what is carried, for it can bear a heavy load that neither the head nor the shoulders can bear. This is like His saying ﴿فَلَمَسُوهُ بِأيْدِيهِمْ﴾ ("and they touched it with their hands", 6:7), because touching is most often done with the hand, and because the hand is stronger in perception.

﴿ألا ساءَ ما يَزِرُونَ﴾ ("Unquestionably evil is what they bear"). Here *sā'a* admits three possibilities. The first is that it is the transitive, conjugated verb, whose pattern is *fa'ala* with an open ʿayn, and the meaning is "Unquestionably what they bear has distressed them." On this view, *mā* may be a relative pronoun meaning "that which," in which case it is the subject. It may also be a verbal *mā* (*mā maṣdariyyah*), in which case it and what follows form a verbal noun that is the subject; that is, "Unquestionably their burden has distressed them." The second possibility is that the verb has been transformed into *fa'ula*, with a *ḍamma* on the ʿayn, and has taken on the sense of wonder (*taʿajjub*). The meaning is "Unquestionably how bad is that which they bear," or "how bad is their burden," depending on the two possibilities for *mā*. The third possibility is also that it has been transformed into *fa'ula* with a *ḍamma* on the ʿayn, but it is intended to express emphatic censure. It is then equivalent in meaning and rulings to *bi'sa* ("how evil"). The application of the relative *mā*, as in His saying ﴿بِئْسَما اشْتَرَوْا بِهِ أنْفُسَهُمْ﴾ ("evil is that for which they sold their souls", 2:90), applies here too. The difference between this third possibility and the one before it is that the previous one does not require the conditions that apply to the subject of *bi'sa*, and it is not a nominal sentence formed of a subject and predicate; rather, it is formed of a verb and its subject. The difference between these two possibilities and the first is that in the first the verb is transitive, whereas in these two it is intransitive, and that in the first the statement is an assertion, whereas in these two it is a formulation of praise or blame. Al-Zamakhshari took it as belonging only to the category of *bi'sa*, saying: "*sā'a mā yazirūn*" means "*bi'sa shay'an yazirūna wizrahum*" ("how evil is the thing they bear as their burden"), like His saying ﴿ساءَ مَثَلًا القَوْمُ﴾ ("evil is the example of the people", 7:177). Ibn Atiyya mentioned this possibility as a final option. He began by saying that *sā'a* is transitive and *mā* is its subject, as you say "*sā'a fī hādhā al-amr*" ("it distressed him in this matter"), and that the statement is a pure report. He said, like the words of the poet:

*"You accepted a humiliating plan, of no benefit; so evil is this acceptance, O Qays of Ghaylan."*

What he said about the line, that the statement is a pure report, is not required. Rather, the phrase "*fa-sā'a hādhā riḍan*" in the line admits all three possibilities. This sentence is introduced with *ألا* ("unquestionably") as an alert and a signal of the evil of their deed. *Alā* indicates what follows it, as in His saying "*Alā fal-yuballigh al-shāhid al-ghā'ib*" ("Let the one present convey it to the one absent"), and ﴿ألا إنَّهم يَثْنُونَ صُدُورَهم لِيَسْتَخْفُوا مِنهُ﴾ ("Unquestionably they fold their chests to hide from Him", 11:5), and "*Alā lā yajhalanna aḥadun ʿalaynā*" ("Let no one act ignorantly toward us").

﴿Wa-ma al-hayatu al-dunya illa la'ibun wa-lahwun wa-la-l-darul-akhiratu khayrun lilladhina yattaqun. Afala ta'qilun﴾. Translation: "The life of this world is nothing but play and diversion. But the Abode of the Hereafter is better for those who are mindful (of God). Will you not then reason?"

When He mentioned their saying, "There is only our life of this world" [al-An'am: 29], He mentioned its end and the final outcome of its affairs: that it is transient and comes to an end soon. Thus it resembles diversion and play, since both do not last and have no benefit, just as this world has no benefit. Diversion and play are occupation with what brings no sustenance and no profit. So is this world. This is unlike occupation with the deeds of the Hereafter, which bring about benefits and goods.

Al-Hasan said: there is an ellipsis in the speech. The estimate is: "And the people of the life are only people of play and diversion." It was also said: the estimate is "And the deeds of the life are..."

Ibn 'Abbas said: this is the life of the disbeliever, because he spends it in delusion and falsehood. As for the life of the believer, it is folded over with righteous deeds, so it is not play and diversion.

In a hadith: "I am not of the *dadd*, nor is the *dadd* of me." *Al-dadd* means play, and play and diversion. It was said: they both have one meaning, and it was repeated for emphasis in condemning this world.

Al-Rummani said: play (la'ib) is an action that distracts from what benefits toward what does not benefit, and diversion (lahw) is turning the self away from seriousness toward jest. It is said: *lahitu 'anhu*, meaning I turned my self away from it.

Al-Mahdawi refuted him, saying: "This is weak and far-fetched, because the one whose meaning is turning away (*al-sarf*) has a *ya'* as its third radical, as evidenced by their saying *lahayan*, while the first radical of the (other) is a *waw*."

But this objection is not valid, because *fa'ila* is from roots with a *waw*, in which the *waw* becomes a *ya'*, as you say: *shaqiya fulanun* (he was miserable), and it is from *al-shiqwa* (misery). Likewise *lahiya*, whose origin is *lahiwa*, from roots with a *waw*; the *waw* became a *ya'* because of the kasra before it, so they said *lahiya*, just as they said *haliya bi-'ayni* (he was pleased with my eye), and it is from *al-halw* (sweetness).

As for his argument from their saying in the dual *lahayan*, it is invalid, because the dual is like the verb, in which the *waw* becomes a *ya'*, since its base is the singular. And in the singular it changes in their saying *lahin* (an active participle from *lahiya*), just as they said *shajja* (he was sad), and it is from *al-shajw* (grief), and they said in its dual *shajayan* with a *ya'*. Some of this has already been mentioned in the discussion of vocabulary.

Ibn 'Amir alone read *wa-la-daru al-akhirati* (with the definite article attached to *dar* and) in the construct form (idafa). They said: it is like their saying *masjidu al-jami'* (the congregational mosque). It was said that it is the addition of the qualified to its qualifier. Al-Farra' said: it is the addition of a thing to itself, like your saying *barihatu al-uwla* (the calamity of the first), *yawmu al-khamis* (the day of Thursday), and *haqqu al-yaqin* (the truth of certainty), and this is permissible only when the two expressions differ.

It was also said: it is by omitting the qualified noun and placing the qualifier in its position, meaning "and the abode of the life of the Hereafter," and what indicates it is "the life of this world." This is the view of the Basrans. It is good for this reason: this adjective has come to be used as a noun, so it takes governing words, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed to Us belong the Hereafter and the first﴾ [al-Layl: 13], and His saying: ﴿And the Hereafter is better for you than the first﴾ [al-Duha: 4].

The rest of the seven readers read ﴿wa-la-daru al-akhirah﴾ with the definiteness of *al-dar* by the article *al-*, and the raising of *al-akhirah* as an attributive qualifier of it.

*Khayrun* here is the superlative (af'al al-tafdil), and omitting the thing compared with is good because it occurs as the predicate. The estimate is "better than the life of this world." It was also said: *khayrun* here is not for comparison, but is like His saying: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that day are better in resting place﴾ [al-Furqan: 24], since the believer and the disbeliever share no part in the essence of good, so that the believer would exceed him in it. Rather, this is specific to the believer.

As for "the Abode of the Hereafter," Ibn 'Abbas said: it is Paradise. It was also said: this is a metaphor by which residing in bliss is expressed, as the poet said:

*By God, the days of Najd and its delight, where it was once our abode—how noble an abode it was!*

The meaning of "those who are mindful" (alladhina yattaquna) is those who are mindful of shirk, because the believing sinner, even if we assume he enters the Fire, will afterwards enter Paradise, so the Abode of the Hereafter becomes better for him than the abode of this world. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "better for one who is mindful of disbelief and sins." He said in *al-Muntakhab* something similar, saying: God the Exalted has shown that this superiority is attained only by those who are among the righteous who avoid sins and major sins. As for disbelievers and transgressors, no, because for them this world is better than the Hereafter. This is closer to the speech of the Mu'tazilah.

Al-Zamakhshari said: His saying "for those who are mindful" is evidence that everything other than the deeds of the mindful is diversion and play.

Al-Fakhr al-Razi has explained the superiority here, saying: The good things of this world are base, and the good things of the Hereafter are noble. Its explanation is that the good things of this world are nothing but the satisfaction of the two appetites, and this is at the utmost baseness, as evidenced by the sharing of base animals in that, and some of them exceeding man in it: like the camel in abundance of eating, the rooster in abundance of copulation, the wolf in the strength to corrupt and tear, and the scorpion in the strength to inflict pain. And as evidence that increasing in that does not bring about honor; rather, one who increases in it is hated, disgusting, and despised, described as a beast. And as evidence that people do not boast of these states; rather, rational people conceal them, hide when doing them, and speak of them only by euphemism, mentioning them openly only when reviling someone with them. And because the reality of pleasures is the removal of pains, and they end quickly. Thus by these aspects the baseness of these pleasures is established.

As for spiritual felicities, they are lofty, noble, lasting, and sacred felicities. This is because if all creatures imagine in a human being great knowledge and strong withdrawal from bodily pleasures, they naturally honor him, serve him, and count themselves slaves to him and wretched in comparison to him. And if we assume that the good things of this world and the good things of the Hereafter share in preference, the good things of the Hereafter would be more excellent, because arriving at them is certain. The good things of this world are not known, nor even presumed. How many a mighty ruler at the morning of a day was under the dust by its evening! And how many a morning-bound great commander became an abject captive by evening! And if we assume that one finds after the joy of a day another day, he does not know whether he will benefit on that day from what he gathered of wealth, good things, and pleasures. Unlike the requirement of the otherworldly felicities, for it is certain that one benefits from them in the Hereafter. And suppose he benefited from them; that benefit is not free of the admixture of disliked and grieving things. And suppose he benefited tomorrow; they will end, and he will grieve at their ending, as the poet said:

*The greatest grief to me in a joy whose ending its owner is certain of is the departure.*

(p-110)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 33:

﴿We certainly know that what they say grieves you. Yet it is not you they deny, but it is the signs of Allah that the wrongdoers reject.﴾

Al-Naqqash said: It was revealed concerning al-Harith ibn 'Amr ibn Nawfal ibn 'Abd Manaf, for he used to deny [the Prophet] openly, but affirm him in secret, and he would say: "We fear that the Arabs will snatch us away, and we are a people who eat from the head [of the sheep]." Others said: It is narrated that al-Akhnas ibn Shariq said to Abu Jahl: "O Abu al-Hakam, tell me about Muhammad: is he truthful or a liar? For there is no one here but us." He said to him: "By Allah, Muhammad is truthful, and he has never lied. But if the Banu Qusayy take the standard, the water-supply, the guardianship of the Ka'bah and prophethood, what will remain for the rest of Quraysh?" So it was revealed.

"Qad" (قَدْ) is a particle of expectation (tawaqqu') when it enters upon the future tense; the expectation then comes from the speaker, as in your saying: "Rain may fall in such-and-such a month." When it is in the past tense, or the present tense with the meaning of the past, the expectation lies with the listener, while the speaker is certain of what he reports. Here it is expressed with the present tense (al-mudari'), since the intended meaning is the attribute of knowledge and its continuity, and time is not considered in it, as in their saying: "He gives and withholds."

Al-Zamakhshari and al-Tibrizi said: "Qad na'lamu" (قَدْ نَعْلَمُ) carries the meaning of "rubba ma" (رُبَّما), which comes to indicate the frequency and abundance of the action, as in his saying: "But he may waste wealth with his gifts." End of quotation.

What he mentioned, that (qad) comes to denote abundance and increase in the action, is a view not well known among the grammarians, although some of them have said so, citing the poet's verse:

"I often leave the opponent with fingertips yellowed, as though his garments were stained with saffron."

And his saying:

"A trustworthy brother whom wine does not ruin his wealth... but rather his giving may waste the wealth."

Our view is that abundance is not understood from (qad) itself, but from the context of the speech, since glory and praise are not achieved by killing a single opponent or by generosity only once; they are achieved only through the frequent occurrence of such acts. Even if we grant that (qad) denotes abundance and increase in the action, that cannot apply to his saying "qad na'lamu," since His knowledge, may He be exalted, does not admit of increase or abundance. As for his saying that it carries the meaning of "rubba ma," which indicates increase and abundance of the action, the well-known view is that "rubba" denotes paucity, not abundance. The "ma" that enters upon it is a preparatory particle (muhayyi'ah) which makes it suitable for a verb to follow it, and a preparatory "ma" does not remove the word from its meaning. Do you not see that in "ka'annama yaqumu Zayd" and "la'allama yakhruju Bakr," the "ma" has not removed "ka'anna" from comparison nor "la'alla" from hope?

One of our companions said: "Qad" has in its denotation of paucity and its turning of the verb toward the past (i.e., when it enters upon the present tense) — he means — this is the apparent view of Sibawayh. If it is free of the meaning of paucity, it is generally free of turning the verb toward the past, and it is then used for confirmation and emphasis, as in His saying: "We certainly know that it grieves you" (﴿قَدْ نَعْلَمُ إنَّهُ لَيَحْزُنُكَ﴾), and His saying: "Why do you hurt me, when you know that I am the Messenger of Allah to you?" (﴿لِمَ تُؤْذُونَنِي وقَدْ تَعْلَمُونَ أنِّي رَسُولُ اللَّهِ إلَيْكُمْ﴾) [al-Saff: 5], and the poet's verse:

"Surely the mercy of his Lord reaches a person, even if he were beneath the earth seventy valleys deep."

Sometimes it is free of paucity while still turning the meaning toward the past, as in His saying: "We see the turning of your face" (﴿قَدْ نَرى تَقَلُّبَ وجْهِكَ﴾) [al-Baqarah: 144]. End of quotation.

Makki said: "Qad" here and similar uses come to confirm the thing, affirm it, and attest to it, and "na'lamu" carries the meaning of "'alimna" (we knew).

Ibn Abi al-Fadl said in "Ri Al-Zaman" (Ray al-Zam'an): The word "qad" comes for expectation, comes for proximity to the present, and comes for paucity. End of quotation. Such as the saying: "Indeed the liar may be believed, and indeed the coward may become brave."

The pronoun in "annahu" is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), and the clause after it explains it, occupying the position of the predicate of "inna." The active participle cannot be used here in the place of the present tense, with its following word functioning as its subject, because that would require the predicate of the pronoun of the matter to be singular, and this is not permitted according to the Basrans.

The discussion of the reading of those who read "yahzunka" (﴿يَحْزُنُكَ﴾) in the fourth form and in the first form was presented at the end of Surah Al 'Imran, and the justification of that has been given, so there is no need to repeat it here. "Alladhi yaqulun" means what contradicts what you are upon.

Al-Hasan said: They used to say that he is a sorcerer, a poet, a soothsayer, and a madman. It was said: They used to openly state that they do not believe in him and do not accept his religion. It was said: They used to attribute to him lying and fabrication. It was said: Some of the disbelievers of Quraysh used to say: "He has a companion from the jinn who tells him what he tells."

'Ali, Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read "yukadhdhibunaka" with light (takhfif) pronunciation. The rest of the seven and Ibn 'Abbas read it with emphasis (tashdid). It is said that the two have one meaning, like "kathura" and "akthara." It is also said that there is a difference between them. Al-Kisa'i related that the Arabs say: "Kadhdhabtu al-rajul" when you attribute lying to him, and "akdhabtuhu" when you attribute lying to what he brought, without attributing it to him personally. The Arabs also say: "Akdhabtu al-rajul" when you find him to be a liar, just as you say: "Ahmadtu al-rajul" when you find him praiseworthy. According to the view of the difference, the meaning of the light reading is: they do not find you a liar, or they do not attribute lying to you. According to the meaning of the emphatic reading, it may be either a purely factual report about their not denying him, and this is attributing it to all of them in a figurative sense, while what is meant is some of them, because it is known with certainty that some of them did deny him and deny what he brought; or the negation of denial may be for the absence of what would follow from it of harms, as if it were said: "They do not deny you" in a way that harms you, because you are not a liar, so their denial is like non-denial.

Al-Muntakhab said: By His saying "They do not deny you" is not meant the specific denial of him personally, but the meaning is that they deny the indication of the miracle as proof of truthfulness in general, so the meaning is that they do not deny you in particular, but they deny all the prophets and messengers.

Qatadah and al-Suddi said: They do not deny you with an argument; rather it is a denial of stubbornness and slander. Najiyah ibn Ka'b said: They do not say that you are a liar, knowing your truthfulness, but they deny what you have brought. Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil said: "They do not deny you" in secret, but they deny you openly out of enmity. And [someone] said: They are not able to say to you, regarding what you have informed them of from their books, "You have lied." This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj. Some of them preferred the light reading of 'Ali, but there is no preference between two mutawatir readings.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is that your denial is a matter referring back to Allah, the Exalted, because you are His messenger, attested by the miracles. So they do not really deny you; rather, they deny Allah by rejecting His signs. So desist from grieving for yourself, and that they have denied you while you are truthful. Let something more important occupy you, namely your great concern over their rejection of Allah's signs and their contempt for His Book. This is like the words of a master to his servant when some people have insulted him: "They have not insulted you, but they have insulted me." In this same manner is His saying: "Indeed those who pledge allegiance to you, they are pledging allegiance only to Allah" (﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ يُبايِعُونَكَ إنَّما يُبايِعُونَ اللَّهَ﴾) [al-Fath: 10]. End of quotation.

From Ibn 'Abbas: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was called "the Trustworthy," so they knew that he did not lie about anything, but they were denying out of obstinacy. Abu Jahl used to say: "We do not deny you, and indeed you are truthful among us, but we deny what you have brought us." End of quotation.

In the passage there is an omission; its implied sense is: "So do not grieve, for they do not deny you." The apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun, to alert that the cause of their rejection is injustice (zulm), which is transgressing the limit in aggression. That is, "But they, with the signs of Allah, reject."

As for "his signs" (ayatuhu): al-Suddi said: Muhammad (ﷺ). Ibn al-Sa'ib said: Muhammad and the Qur'an. Muqatil said: The Qur'an. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The signs of Allah are His marks and the evidences of His Prophet. Juhud (juhud, rejection) is denying a thing after knowing it, and it is the opposite of affirmation. If the verse was revealed concerning disbelievers in general, then "juhud" is used figuratively, since not all of them disbelieved after knowledge; but when they denied his prophethood and sought to refute him with false claims, He described their denial with the most ugly form of denial, which is jahd (outright rejection), to make them out as gravely culpable and to condemn their deed, since his miracles and signs are radiant, and every person of sound nature is obliged to acknowledge them and know them. If the verse was revealed concerning the stubborn opponents, then juhud occurs in its true sense. Obstinate disbelief (kufr al-'inad) is indicated by the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, and it indeed occurs, as in the story of Abu Jahl with al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, the story of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt, and his saying: "I would not believe in a prophet who was not from Thaqif." Some theologians denied the permissibility of obstinate disbelief, because knowledge requires faith and denial requires disbelief, so the two cannot coexist; they interpreted the apparent verses of the Qur'an, saying that His saying: "They denied them, though their souls were convinced of them" (﴿وجَحَدُوا بِها واسْتَيْقَنَتْها أنْفُسُهُمْ﴾) [al-Naml: 14] refers to the rulings of the Torah which they altered, such as the verse of stoning and the like. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Obstinate disbelief from one who knows Allah and prophethood is far-fetched. End of quotation.

The interpretations concerning the negation of denial refer only to their inner beliefs. As for their statements, their statements are indeed denying, either of him or of what he brought.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 34:

﴿And messengers were denied before you, but they were patient over what they were denied and were harmed until Our help reached them.﴾ Al-Dahhak and Ibn Jurayj said: God consoled His Prophet (ﷺ) with this verse. According to their view, he (ﷺ) was himself denied, and this contradicts His saying: ﴿for they do not deny you﴾. The contradiction is removed by the interpretations already mentioned, such as the view of al-Zamakhshari and others that His saying ﴿they do not deny you﴾ is not a literal negation of denial against him. He said: it is only of the type of your saying to your servant: "They did not insult you, but they insulted me." The saying ﴿And messengers were denied before you﴾ comes as consolation for him (ﷺ). When God consoled him by saying that when they denied you, they were in fact denying God, He consoled him a second time by saying that it is the habit of the followers of messengers before you to deny their messengers, and that the messengers were patient, so take them as your model in patience. The ﻣﺎ (ma) in His saying ﴿over what they were denied﴾ is a verbal-source particle (maṣdariyyah), meaning: they were patient over their being denied. The meaning is: take them as your model in patience over denial and harm, until victory and triumph come to you as they came to them. Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿they were patient over what they were denied﴾ seeking My reward, ﴿and were harmed until they were sawn apart with saws and burned with fire, until Our help reached them by punishing those who denied them.﴾ End of quotation. The word (wa-ūdhū, "and were harmed") may be coordinated with His saying ﴿were denied﴾, or with His saying ﴿they were patient﴾, and it is unlikely to be coordinated with ﴿were denied﴾ in the sense of ﴿over what they were denied﴾. The meaning would then be: they were patient over their denial and their harming. It is reported from Ibn ʿAmir that he read (wa-ūdhū) without a waw after the hamza, taking it as a triliteral verb, from ādhaytu fulānan (I harmed so-and-so), not as a quadriliteral verb from ādhaytu (I harmed). In His saying ﴿Our help﴾ there is an iltifāt (shift of grammatical person), since the preceding verses speak of God in the third person. The eloquence of this shift is that He attributed the help to the pronoun that suggests majesty, in which one (singular) is treated as many. Naṣr (help) is a verbal noun attributed to its agent, and the object is omitted; the meaning is: Our help for them against those who denied and harmed them. The apparent reading is that the limit (ghāyah) here applies to the patience and the harming, because of the apparent coordination of (wa-ūdhū) with (fa-ṣabarū). If it is coordinated with (kudhdhibū), the limit applies to the patience. If it is coordinated with (kudhdhibat), the limit applies to that and to the denial, or to the harming alone.

* *

﴿And none can alter the words of God.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: that is, the promises of God. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned no other interpretation and said: His promises, from His saying: ﴿And Our word had already preceded for Our servants the messengers, that they would surely be helped﴾ [al-Saffat: 171–172]. Al-Zajjaj said: what He reported and what He commanded, and reports and commands are among the words of God. Ibn ʿAtiyya limited himself to part of what al-Zajjaj said, saying: none can reject His commands. It was also said: the meaning is His judgments and decrees, as in His saying: ﴿But the word of punishment has come into effect upon the disbelievers﴾ [al-Zumar: 71], that is, what He decreed against them became obligatory. It was also said: the meaning is that no one is able to alter the words of God, however much one embellishes and strives, because He protected them with firm wording and upright meaning from being mixed with the speech of the people of deviation. It was also said: the wording is a report, but the meaning is a prohibition; that is, no one should alter the words of God. This is like His saying: (there is no doubt in it), meaning they should not doubt it, according to one of the views.

* *

﴿And there has certainly come to you some of the news of the messengers.﴾ This contains a strengthening confirmation of what was previously reported: the denial of the messengers by their followers, their harming of them, their patience, until help came to them against them. The subject (fāʿil) is (naba', "news"). Al-Farisi said: it is (min naba'), with (min) being superfluous, meaning: the news of the messengers had come to you. This view is weak because of the addition of (min) in an obligatory position. It was also said: it is definite, but this is only permissible according to the view of al-Akhfash. Moreover, the meaning is not general; only part of their news had come, not all their news, as shown by His saying: ﴿Among them are those We have related to you, and among them are those We have not related to you﴾ [Ghafir: 78]. Al-Rummani said: the subject of (jā'aka, "came to you") is a pronoun, its implied meaning being: there had come to you news. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: in my view the correct position is to assume a pronoun meaning clarification (jalā') or explanation (bayān). The full version of this view and of the previous one is that the implied meaning is: there had come to you this, from the news of the messengers, meaning news or explanation; so the subject is an implied pronoun explained by "news" or "explanation," not an omitted subject, since the subject cannot be omitted. What appears to me is that the subject is an implied pronoun whose implied meaning is "he" (huwa), and what the meaning of the previous sentence indicates: that is, there had come to you this report of the denial of the followers of the messengers toward the messengers, and the patience and harming, until they were helped; and this report is part of the news of the messengers whom you are to take as models. Here (min naba') is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), its anaphor (dhū al-ḥāl) being that implied pronoun, and the governing word for both it and the circumstantial clause being (jā'aka). On this reading the meaning is not "there had come to you news or explanation," unless by "news" and "explanation" is meant this earlier news or earlier explanation. As for al-Zamakhshari, he did not address the subject of (jā'a), but said: ﴿And there has certainly come to you some of the news of the messengers﴾ means some of their reports and stories. This is an interpretation of meaning, not a grammatical parsing (i'rāb), because (min) cannot function as a subject.

﴿Wa in kana kabura 'alayka i'radWhum fa-in istatha'ta an tabtaghiya nafaqan fi al-ardi aw sullaman fi al-sama'i fa-ta'tiyahum bi-ayah﴾ ("And if their turning away is hard for you, then if you are able to seek a tunnel into the earth or a ladder into the sky and bring them a sign…"). (*Kabura*) means it became great and hard: their turning away from faith and from believing in what you brought was grievous. It was indeed grievous to him, but the conditional here carries the sense of clarification and manifestation, and it is in the future tense. The conditional that has not occurred, namely His saying ﴿fa-in istatha'ta﴾ ("then if you are able"), is joined to it, yet it is not the sole object of the answer. So the two conditions together, by interpretation, have not occurred; rather the whole is in the future, even though the apparent occurrence of one of them taken alone may be realized. A parallel is ﴿in kana qamisuhu qudda min qubulin﴾ ("if his shirt was torn from the front") [Yusuf: 26] and ﴿wa in kana qamisuhu qudda min dubrin﴾ ("and if his shirt was torn from the back") [Yusuf: 27]. It is known that one of them did occur, but the meaning is that it be made clear and manifest that it was torn in such-and-such a way. This is how what comes with the conditional *in* before the form *kana* is interpreted according to the view of the majority of grammarians, contrary to Abu al-Abbas al-Mubarrad, who claimed that *in*, when it precedes *kana*, remains in its past meaning without interpretation.

*Naft* (tunnel) is the passage inside the earth in which one hides. Nubayh al-Ghanawi read ﴿an tabtaghiya nafiqan fi al-ardi﴾, with *nafiqa'* (a tunnel-exit), which is a long vowel form and is one of the exits of the burrow of the jerboa (*yarbu'*). The jerboa comes out from the inner earth to its surface and thins the layer facing the earth, and makes two doors for the burrow: one is the *nafiqa'*, the other is the *qasi'a'*. When something alarms it from one of them, it pushes out the layer that troubled it from one of them and exits through it. It was said: its burrow has three doors.

Al-Suddi said: *al-sullam* is the means of ascent. Qatada said: the steps. Abu 'Ubayda said: the cause and the rung. The Arabs say: "Take me as a ladder for your need," meaning a means. From this is the verse of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr:

*Nor for you two is there an escape from the earth, so seek by it a tunnel or a ladder in the heavens.*

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-sullam* derives from *al-salamah* (safety), and it is that thing which delivers you to your place of ascent; and *al-sullam* is that on which one climbs and ascends, and it is masculine. Al-Farra' related that it may be feminine. Some said: its feminine usage is according to the meaning of *al-mirqah* (rung), not by lexical assignment, just as the word *al-sawt* (voice) is feminine in the sense of *al-sayhah* (cry) and *al-istighathah* (call for help) in the verse: "Ask the Banu Asad: what is this voice?"

As for the meaning of the verse, al-Zamakhshari said: it means that you are not able to do that, and the purpose is to show his eagerness for the Islam of his people and his fervent desire for it, and that if he were able to bring them a sign from beneath the earth or from above the sky, he would bring it, hoping for their faith. It was also said: they used to demand signs, and he would wish to be answered in them, due to the extent of his eagerness for their faith. So it was said to him: "If you are able to do such and such, then do it," indicating that his eagerness had reached the point that if he were able to do that, he would do it, until he brought them what they asked for, perhaps they would believe. End of quotation.

The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿fa-ta'tiyahum bi-ayah﴾ ("then bring them a sign") is that the sign is other than seeking a tunnel in the earth or a ladder in the sky, and that the meaning is: that you seek a tunnel in the earth, and enter it, or a ladder in the sky, and ascend on it to it, ﴿then bring them a sign﴾ other than entering the tunnel and ascending to the sky, of the kind by which their faith is hoped for, or of what they proposed, hoping for their faith; and that sign is from one of the two directions.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: His saying ﴿wa in kana kabura 'alayka i'raduhum﴾ is an imposition of proof upon the Prophet (ﷺ), and a division of the situations upon them, until it becomes clear that there is no way except patience and proceeding in God's command. The meaning is: if you magnify their denial and their disbelief upon yourself, and bind yourself to grief over it, then if you are able to enter a passage in the depths of the earth, or to climb a ladder in the sky, then go ahead with it; that is, you are not able to do any of this, and it is necessary to commit to patience and bear hardship, and to confront them with the signs that God set up for the observers and the reflecting ones, for He, there is no god but He, did not intend to gather them upon guidance, but intended to set up of the signs that a people may be guided by contemplating them, by the truth of His dominion ﴿fa-la takununna mina al-jahilin﴾ ("so do not be among the ignorant"), that is, in that you would grieve and sorrow over a matter that God willed and enforced, and knew the benefit in it. End of quotation.

Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya permitted that the sign he brings might be the very act itself. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that seeking a tunnel in the earth or a ladder in the sky be the bringing of the sign, as if it were said: if you were able to penetrate beneath the earth or ascend in the sky, perhaps that would be a sign for you by which they would believe. Ibn 'Atiyya said: ﴿fa-ta'tiyahum bi-ayah﴾ means "with a sign," and he intends either in your doing that, that is, the sign would be the very act of entering the earth and ascending in the sky; or in your bringing them the sign from one of the two directions. End of quotation.

What they permitted in this does not appear from the indication of the wording, for if it were as they permitted, the construction would be ﴿fa-ta'tiyahum bi-dhalika ayah﴾ ("then bring them that as a sign"). Moreover, what sign is there in entering a passage into the earth? As for ascending in the sky, that would be a sign.

It was also said: His saying ﴿an tabtaghiya nafaqan fi al-ardi﴾ is an allusion to their saying: ﴿wa qalu lan nu'mina laka hatta tafjura lana mina al-ardi yanbu'an﴾ ("and they said: 'We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush for us from the earth'") [al-Isra': 90]. And His saying ﴿aw sullaman fi al-sama'i﴾ is an allusion to their saying: ﴿aw tarqa fi al-sama'i wa lan nu'mina liruqiyyika﴾ ("or you ascend into the sky, and we will not believe in your ascent") [al-Isra': 93].

In it is the pronoun of the matter (*damir al-sha'n*), and the clause introduced by ﴿kabura 'alayka i'raduhum﴾ is in the position of the predicate of *kana*. In this is evidence that the predicate of *kana* and its sisters may be a past verb, and there is no need to presuppose *qad* (indeed) with it, because of the abundance of such usage in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech, contrary to one who claimed that *qad* must necessarily appear or be presupposed with it, and contrary to one who restricted this to *kana* without its sisters. They also permitted that its subject be ﴿i'raduhum﴾ ("their turning away"), so it would not be in the nominative case by *kabura*, as in the first view; and *kabura* in that case contains a pronoun referring to the turning away, and it is in the position of the predicate. This is a matter of disagreement. The answer to the conditional is omitted, because the meaning indicates it, and its estimate is: "then do so," as you say: "If you wish, stand with us and visit so-and-so," meaning: then do so. That is why the conditional verb came in the past form, or the present form negated by *lam*, because it is past, and it does not come in the present form except in poetry.

* *

﴿Wa law sha'a Allahu la-jama'ahum 'ala al-huda﴾ ("And if God had willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance"). That is, either He creates that in their hearts first, so that no one would go astray, or He creates it in them after their going astray. This conditional indicates that He, exalted is He, did not will guidance for all of them, but rather intended to leave the disbeliever in his disbelief. Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi said: This apparent meaning confirms that: if the disbeliever's capacity for disbelief is not capable of faith, then the capacity for disbelief necessitates disbelief, which is not capable of faith, so the Creator of that capacity has intended disbelief without doubt. If it is capable of faith as it is capable of disbelief, then the relation of capacity to both is equal, and preponderance is impossible except by a motive that preponderates, and it is not from the servant, otherwise an infinite regress would occur. So it is established that the Creator of that motive is God, and it is established that the totality of the sufficient motive necessitates the act, and it is established that the Creator of the totality of that motive which necessitates that disbelief intends that disbelief and does not intend that faith. This certain proof strengthens the apparent meaning of this verse, and there is no clarification stronger than the agreement of proof with the apparent meaning of the Qur'an.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: This verse refutes the Qadariyyah (those who deny divine decree) who say that capacity does not require that the disbeliever believe, and that what a person does of all his actions has no creation in it. Exalted is God above their saying.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Wa law sha'a Allahu la-jama'ahum 'ala al-huda﴾ by a compelling sign, but He does not do so, because that would take it out of wisdom. End of quotation. This is the view of the Mu'tazilah. Al-Qadi said: Compulsion (*al-ilja'*) is that He informs them that if they attempt anything other than faith, He would prevent them from it, and then they would refrain from doing anything other than faith. He, exalted is He, only abandoned doing this compulsion, because that would remove their obligation, so what occurred from them would be as if it had not occurred. He, exalted is He, only intended that they benefit from what they choose themselves, from the connection to reward through it, and that would not be except by choice.

Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi answered that He, exalted is He, intended of them that they undertake faith while the motive toward faith and toward disbelief is equal, or while that preponderance is present. The first is charging with what cannot be borne, because commanding the attainment of preponderance while equality is present is charging with the combination of two contradictories, which is impossible. If it is the second, then the preponderant side would be necessarily occurring, and the non-preponderant side would be impossible to occur, and all these divisions contradict what they claimed of power and free choices, so their statement falls entirely.

* *

﴿Fa-la takununna mina al-jahilin﴾ ("so do not be among the ignorant"). The statement of Ibn 'Atiyya has preceded: that you would grieve and sorrow over a matter that God willed and enforced, and knew the benefit in it.

Abu Hayyan also said: "'[Do not be] among the ignorant' (*min al-jahilin*) may mean: do not be ignorant that God, ﴿if God had willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance﴾. It may also mean: do not be concerned with the existence of their disbelief, which God has decreed and willed, and let your soul take you toward what God has not decreed." End of quote. The first possibility has been regarded as weak, because with the perfection of His essence, the abundance of His knowledge, the vastness of His awareness of what befits the power of the Real, may He be exalted, and His dominion over all that He can determine, He should not be described as ignorant. For if He willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance. This is a matter of religion and creed, so it is not permissible that the Prophet (ﷺ) be ignorant of it. It seems that al-Zamakhshari interpreted His words, ﴿if God had willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance﴾, as meaning that a compelling sign (*ayah mulji'ah*) would come to them, but He does not do so because it would depart from wisdom. So he said, regarding His words ﴿so do not be among the ignorant﴾, "[meaning] among those who are ignorant of that and seek what is contrary to it." By this he pointed to bringing a compelling sign that forces belief, and the discussion of compulsion (*ilja'*) has already preceded.

It was also said: "Do not be ignorant that some of them will believe in you and some of them will disbelieve." This has been regarded as weak, because this is not something the Prophet (ﷺ) would be ignorant of.

It was also said: "Do not be among those who lack patience, for lack of patience is among the traits of the ignorant." This has been regarded as weak, because He, may He be exalted, has commanded him to be patient in many verses, and given the command to be patient together with the statement that it is good, it is far-fetched to describe him, after his patience, as lacking patience.

It was also said: "Do not let your grief intensify over their disbelief, lest you come close to the state of one who is ignorant of God's rulings and decree." This has been stated explicitly in His words, ﴿so do not let your soul go out in sorrow over them﴾ [Fatir: 8].

Some people said: this address is permissible because of his nearness to God and his standing with Him; this manner of addressing him is like how a reasonable person speaks to a close relative more sternly than to strangers, out of concern for him lest he be singled out for humiliation.

Makki and al-Mahdawi said: the address is to him, but what is meant is his community (*ummah*). They completed this view by saying that the persistence of some of them in disbelief and their being deprived of the fruits of faith used to grieve him.

Ibn Atiyya said: this is weak, and the wording does not require it. End of quote.

It was also said: the Messenger is protected from ignorance and doubt without any disagreement, but protection does not prevent being tested through command and prohibition; or because constriction of his chest and abundance of grief are among human natural dispositions, which protection does not remove, as shown by the hadith: "O God, I am a human being, and I become angry as humans become angry," and the hadith: "I am only a human being, so when I forget, remind me." End of quote.

What I choose is that this address is not directed to the Messenger. This is because He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿if God had willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance﴾. This is a report and a universal principle that nothing comes into existence except what He wills to occur. This report is not specific to the Messenger in this address; rather, the Messenger already knows the content of this report. Therefore, it is directed to the listener, and the prohibition in ﴿so do not be﴾ is addressed to the listener, not to the Messenger. It is as if it were said: "If God had willed, O listener who does not know that what has occurred in existence occurs by God's will, He would have gathered them upon guidance. So do not be, O listener, among the ignorant regarding the fact that what God has willed to occur has occurred, and that all beings hang upon His will."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 36:

﴿Only those who listen will respond. As for the dead, God will raise them up; then to Him they will be returned.﴾ ﴿They say, "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say: "God is certainly able to send down a sign, but most of them do not know."﴾ [al-An'am: 37] ﴿There is no creature on the earth, nor any bird that flies on its two wings, but they are communities like you. We have neglected nothing in the Book. Then to their Lord they will be gathered.﴾ [al-An'am: 38] ﴿Those who deny Our signs are deaf and dumb, in darknesses. Whomever God wills, He leaves astray; and whomever He wills, He places on a straight path.﴾ [al-An'am: 39] ﴿Say: "Tell me, if the punishment of God comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you, would you call upon other than God, if you are truthful?"﴾ [al-An'am: 40] ﴿Rather, it is Him you call upon, and He removes what you call upon Him for, if He wills, and you forget what you associate with Him.﴾ [al-An'am: 41] ﴿We certainly sent messengers to communities before you, and We seized them with misfortune and adversity, that they might humble themselves.﴾ [al-An'am: 42] ﴿Why, when Our might came upon them, did they not humble themselves? But their hearts became hardened, and Satan made attractive to them what they used to do.﴾ [al-An'am: 43] ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened to them the gates of everything, until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and they were then in despair.﴾ [al-An'am: 44] ﴿So the last remnant of the people who did wrong was cut off. And praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds.﴾ [al-An'am: 45] ﴿Say: "Tell me, if God took away your hearing and your sight and sealed your hearts, what god other than God could bring them back to you?" Look how We vary the signs, yet they turn away.﴾ [al-An'am: 46] ﴿Say: "Tell me, if the punishment of God comes upon you suddenly or openly, will anyone be destroyed except the wrongdoing people?"﴾ [al-An'am: 47] ﴿We send the messengers only as bringers of good news and warners. Whoever believes and acts righteously, no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.﴾ [al-An'am: 48] ﴿As for those who deny Our signs, punishment will touch them for what they used to defy.﴾ [al-An'am: 49] ﴿Say: "I do not tell you that I have the treasuries of God, nor that I know the unseen, nor do I tell you that I am an angel. I only follow what is revealed to me." Say: "Are the blind and the seeing equal? Will you not reflect?"﴾ [al-An'am: 50] ﴿Warn with it those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord, for them there is no protector or intercessor apart from Him, so that they may fear God.﴾ [al-An'am: 51] ﴿Do not drive away those who call upon their Lord at dawn and dusk, seeking His face. You are not accountable for their reckoning in any way, nor are they accountable for yours in any way, so that you would drive them away and be among the wrongdoers.﴾ [al-An'am: 52]

Al-tadarru' (humbling oneself): a form of tafa''ul from al-diraʿah, which means humiliation; one says ḍaraʿa yaḍraʿu ḍaraʿah. The poet said:

"Let Yazid be wept for by one who is humbled by a dispute, and by one who is bewildered by what the calamities strike."

That is, one who is humiliated and weak.

Ṣadafa ʿan al-shay' means he turned away from it, ṣadfan and ṣudūfan, and ṣādaftuhu means I met him while turning away from his direction. Ibn al-Riqa' said:

"When they mention a story, they say the best of it, and they are turned away from every evil that is avoided."

Ṣudufun is the plural of ṣadūf, like ṣabūr and ṣubur. It has been said that ṣadafa means to incline, taken from the ṣadaf of a camel, which is when its foot leans from the hand toward the leg on the outer side. Ṣadafah is the singular of ṣadaf, which is the oyster shell that contains the pearl. The poet said:

"It increased my wonder that I came to be among fish, and I did not turn around like a pearl in a shell."

Al-khazanah is what is kept safe in something lest it be taken. From this comes the hadith: "Their udders are the stores for their livestock..." And: "Does any of you like that his storehouse be broken into and his stores taken?" It is pronounced with a fatḥah on the khāʾ. The poet said:

"When a man does not guard his tongue, he is not a guard over anything else."

Al-ṭard is expulsion with humiliation, and al-ṭarīd is the one expelled. Banū Maṭrūd and Banū Ṭirād are two clans of Iyad.

﴿Only those who listen will respond﴾: only those who listen with acceptance and attentiveness respond to faith, as He said: ﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart, or gives ear while he is a witness.﴾ [Qaf: 37]. Yastajību means yujību. Al-Rummani distinguished between ajāba and istajāba: istajāba implies acceptance of what one is called to. He said: ﴿So their Lord responded to them﴾ [Al ʿImran: 195], and ﴿So We responded to him and saved him from distress﴾ [al-Anbiya': 88]. This is not so for ajāba, since one may answer with opposition.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is that those whom you are eager to make believe you are like the dead who do not hear, and only one who hears responds, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ [al-Naml: 80].

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: This is from the type that came earlier in al-tasliyah (consolation), meaning: do not be concerned with those who turn away, for only those who respond to the call of faith respond, those who understand the signs and receive the proofs with acceptance. He expressed all of that by "they hear," since it is the path to knowledge of prophethood and the miraculous signs. This is a term the Sufis use when admonition reaches someone to a healing degree; they say: "he listened."

﴿And the dead, God will raise them up﴾: The apparent meaning is that this is an independent sentence, consisting of a subject and predicate (mubtada' wa khabar). The apparent meaning of death and resurrection here is literal. This is a report from God Most High that the dead in general, whether responders or non-responders, God will raise, and He will recompense them for their deeds. The word "the dead" came general to indicate the generality in what preceded it, in His saying: ﴿Only those who listen will respond﴾, since restriction implies the other category, namely that whoever does not listen with acceptance does not respond to faith, and these are the disbelievers. In the report about all of them being raised and returned to God's recompense is a threat and a severe warning to whoever does not respond.

The statements of the exegetes agree that His saying "and the dead" refers to the disbelievers. They were called "the dead" just as they were called "the deaf, the dumb, and the blind" (p-118).

The comparison of the disbeliever to the dead is that the body of a dead person is empty of the soul, so there appear from it stench, pus, discharge, and kinds of decay, and the best state of it is burial under the earth. The disbeliever's soul is empty of intellect, so there appears from him his ignorance of God Most High, his opposition to His command, and his refusal to accept the miracles of the messengers. If his soul is empty of intellect, he is like a madman, and the best state for him is to be restrained and confined. Thus intellect is to the soul as the soul is to the body.

If "the dead" here means the disbelievers, then "raising" may mean its literal sense of gathering on the Day of Resurrection. "Return" means their return to His might and punishment; this was said by Mujahid and Qatadah. In this case the sentence contains a threat to the disbelievers.

It has also been said: death and raising are literal, and the sentence is an illustration (mathal) of His power to compel them to respond, in that He is the One who raises the dead from their graves on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿Then to Him they will be returned﴾ for recompense. So He is capable of giving life to these dead by disbelief through faith, while you are not able to do that. This was said by al-Zamakhshari.

It has also been said: death and raising are figurative (majaz). Death is borrowed (istiʿarah) for disbelief, and raising for faith. So it has been said: the sentence "And the dead, God will raise them up" is a subject and predicate, meaning: the dead by disbelief, God gives life to them by faith.

It has been said: it is not a sentence at all; rather "the dead" is coordinated (maʿtūf) with "those who listen," and "God will raise them up" is a circumstantial clause (jumlah ḥāliyyah). The meaning is: only those who listen with acceptance respond, believing at first instance, and the disbelievers, until God Most High guides them and enables them to have faith. So do not grieve, and do not hasten what has not been decreed.

It was also read: ﴿Then to Him they will return﴾, with a fatḥah on the yāʾ, from the intransitive rajaʿa.

﴿They say, "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?"﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: It was revealed concerning the leaders of Quraysh, who asked the Messenger for a sign out of obstinacy, though he had already brought them many signs that were convincing. End of quote. The pronoun in "they say" (wa-qālū) refers to the disbelievers, and "lawlā" (why not) is an expression of urging (taḥḍīḍ), meaning "hallā" (why not then).

﴿Say, "Indeed, Allah is able to send down a sign"﴾, meaning: whatever sign you ask Him to send down, Allah is able to do so, just as He sent down the previous signs. There is no difference in the power of Allah over the signs demanded out of obstinacy and the signs that were not demanded. You have demanded signs, such as the splitting of the moon, but they did not benefit you and did not affect you. You said, "This is continuous magic," and you did not take account of what was sent down despite its abundance, as if no sign had been sent down at all, because your habit is stubbornness toward the signs of Allah. Al-Zamakhshari said: "to send down a sign" means a sign that would compel them to believe, like the lifting of the mountain over the Children of Israel, or a sign that, if they denied it, would bring them punishment.

﴿But most of them do not know﴾ that Allah is able to send down that sign, and that even if He does, it is wisdom for Him to withhold sending it. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: They do not know that if it were sent down and they did not believe, they would be hastened to punishment. It may also be that they do not know that Allah, exalted is He, has made the benefit lie in signs that are open to reflection and contemplation, so that some people may be guided and others go astray. End of quote. What appears to be the case is that "they do not know" negates knowledge from them, since they distinguished between the power of Allah over the signs that were sent down and its power over the signs that were demanded. Yet the power of Allah extends equally to both, since the demanded and the non-demanded are alike in being possible. Whoever distinguishes between things that are alike, and is not content with what has been reported of them, is without doubt ignorant.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 38 (part 1 of 2):

﴿There is no creature on the earth, nor bird that flies with its two wings, but they are communities like you.﴾ Ibn al-Anbari said: The point of argument in this verse is that God has furnished the polytheists with intellects and given them understandings by which He holds them responsible for reflecting on the matter of the Messenger (ﷺ), just as He has given the beasts and birds understandings by which some of them recognize the signals of others, and He guided the male among them to approach the female. In this there is evidence of the penetrating power of the One who has endowed them with this. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The meaning of this verse is to draw attention to the signs of God present in the varieties of His creatures. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "What is the purpose of mentioning this?" I say: it indicates the greatness of His power, the subtlety of His knowledge, the vastness of His dominion, and His management of those creatures that differ in kinds and multiply in species; He is watchful over their conditions, for what belongs to them and what is upon them, and no affair preoccupies Him from another affair; and that the obligated ones are not singled out for this above the rest of the animals. End of quotation.

What appears is that when He, exalted is He, related of these people their saying, ﴿Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ [al-An'am: 37], and they did not take heed of the signs that had been sent down, they were answered that power is capable of sending down a sign, namely the one you have proposed; and they were alerted to their ignorance in distinguishing one sign from another. They were informed that they themselves and all other animals are alike in that divine power is related to all of them equally. There is no difference between the creation of one who is obligated and one who is not obligated in terms of the relation of power to both, and their bringing forth from the state of non-existence to the state of existence. So it is as if it were said: power is related to all the signs, those proposed and those not proposed, just as it is related to your creation and the creation of all other animals. Thus possibility is what unites all of that; for this reason God, exalted is He, said: ﴿but they are communities like you﴾, meaning in the relation of power to bringing them into being, just as it is related to bringing you into being, and likewise the signs. In this there is an indication that the signs that occur at the hands of the prophets, peace be upon them, may be by bringing forth substances, such as the water that gushed from between the fingers and the food that multiplied from a little, just as created beings are substances brought forth by God, exalted is He. It seems that the comparison by likeness is drawn between animals and humans, without mention of inanimate things and without mention of what encompasses them, because of the strength of resemblance in awareness of things and guidance to many benefits, unlike inanimate matter, although power relates to all created beings. ﴿Creature﴾ (dabba) has already been explained; here, in the context of negation, it is accompanied by (min), which indicates the comprehensiveness of the genus; so it is general, including everything that crawls, and the bird falls within it. Thus mentioning the bird after mentioning the creature is specification after generalization, and the mention of a part of a whole, and it becomes of the type of isolation, like His saying: ﴿and Gabriel and Michael﴾ [al-Baqara: 98], after the mention of the angels. The bird was singled out because its movement in existence, unlike other animals, is more eloquent in power and more indicative of its greatness than the movement of other animals on the earth. The earth is a dense body upon which the movement of bodies is possible, whereas air is a subtle body in which the movement of dense bodies is ordinarily not possible except by overwhelming divine power; for this reason God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Have they not seen the birds made subservient in the atmosphere of heaven? None holds them but God﴾ [al-Nahl: 79]. His saying "on the earth" comes as an indication of the generalization of all places. Since the word "creature" (min dabba) refers to the one who moves, He brought the object of movement in general terms, namely the earth, and the earth encompasses land and sea. ﴿Flies with its two wings﴾ is an emphasis on His saying "nor bird," because there is no bird that does not fly with its two wings; and it removes the metaphor that His saying "nor bird" might have carried if it were left alone. Do you not see the metaphorical use of "bird" for deeds in His saying: ﴿And every human being We have fastened his bird to his neck﴾ [al-Isra: 13]? And their saying: "such-and-such flew to so-and-so in the division," meaning his share; and "the bird of good fortune and misfortune." In it is an alert to imagining its form in the state of flight, and a summoning of the sight of this remarkable act. The description with the word "flies" came because it suggests permanence and predominance, since most of the bird's states are flying, and it rarely remains still; even the caged one often delights in flying within the place where it is confined, whether in a cage or otherwise.

Ibn Abi 'Abla read "nor bird" (wa-la ta'irun) in the nominative, as a conjunction with the position of "creature" (dabba). They also permitted that "on the earth" be in the position of a nominative attribute relative to the position of "creature"; likewise it requires that "flies" be so, and this is required in the reading of Ibn Abi 'Abla. The (bi-) in (bi-janahayhi) is for instrumentality, as in His saying: "I wrote with the pen." And "communities like you" (ummun amthaluKum) is the predicate of the subject which is "creature" and "nor bird." The predicate was made plural though the subject is singular, following the sense, because the singular here is for comprehensiveness. As for likeness here, al-Zamakhshari said: "Your likenesses are written in their provisions, their terms, and their deeds, just as your provisions, your terms, and your deeds are written." End. Ibn 'Atiyya said: alike to humans in creation, provision, life, death, and gathering. Al-Tabari and others said, and it is related from Abu Hurayra, and al-Zajjaj chose, that the likeness is that they are recompensed for their deeds and called to account, and retribution is exacted for some of them from others, according to what is reported in the hadiths. Makki said: in that they know God, exalted is He, and worship Him. This is the view of Abu 'Ubayda, who said: its meaning is "except kinds who know God and worship Him." al-Wahidi related it from Ibn 'Abbas that the likeness arises from the fact that they know God, affirm His unity, praise Him, and glorify Him. A group of exegetes went this way, citing His saying: ﴿There is not a thing but it glorifies Him with His praise﴾ [al-Isra: 44], and His saying about the animals: ﴿Each has known its prayer and its glorification﴾ [al-Nur: 41], and what He addressed the ant with, and what He addressed the hoopoe with. Ibn 'Atiyya said, regarding Makki's view: this is the view of Khalaf. End. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is possible that the likeness is only in their being communities, and nothing else, just as you mean by saying: "I passed by a man like you," that is, in that he is a man. It is valid in other attributes as well, but the benefit in this is that the likeness be in attributes other than their being communities. Mujahid said: "except classes arranged in categories." Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas: the likeness occurred between them and the children of Adam because some of them understand from others. Ibn 'Isa said: they are like you in need of a manager who manages for them what they need: food that sustains them, clothing that covers them, and shelter that shields them. It is related from Abu al-Darda' that he said: The intellects of the dumb animals are blinded regarding everything except four things: God, glorified and exalted is He; the seeking of provision; knowledge of male and female; and the readiness of each of the two for its partner. It was said: the likeness lies in their being created groups, some resembling others, becoming familiar with one another, and reproducing like humankind. Abu Sulayman al-Khattabi related from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna that he recited this verse and said: there is no human on earth but that there is in him some resemblance to some of the beasts: some advance like the lion, some run like the wolf, some bark like dogs, some strut like the peacock, and some are greedy like the pig. In another narration: some of them resemble the pig, which, when good food is placed before him, leaves it, and when a man rises from his excrement, he laps at it. Likewise you find among the children of Adam one who, if he hears fifty wise sayings, does not retain a single one of them; and if a single one of them is wrong, he retains it, and he does not sit in a gathering where it is narrated from you.

﴿We have not neglected in the Book anything﴾ means: We have not left out nor omitted; and "the Book" is the Preserved Tablet. The meaning: We did not neglect in it anything that We did not record, nor did We establish what ought to be established, as al-Zamakhshari said, and he mentioned no other; or it is the Qur'an, which is what the context and sense of the verse require. He began with this view from Ibn 'Atiyya, and mentioned the Preserved Tablet; according to this, His saying "anything" is on its generality, and according to the first view it is of the general that is intended as the particular, the meaning being "anything that calls to knowledge of God and His obligations." Some of the Zahiriyya often cite His saying: ﴿We have not neglected in the Book anything﴾ to indicate that the Book comprised all the obligatory rulings. "Neglect" (tafrit) is shortcoming, so its proper transitive particle is "fi" (in), as in His saying: ﴿over what I neglected in regard to God's side﴾ [al-Zumar: 56]. If that is so, then the verb carries the sense of omitting and leaving, and "min shay'" (anything) is in the position of the direct object, with "min" being superfluous; the meaning: We did not leave out nor omit in the Book any thing needed of divine indications and obligations. It is improbable to make "min" here partitive, and to take the sense to be: We did not neglect in the Book part of anything the obligated one needs, although some have said so. Abu al-Baqa' made "min shay'" here occupy the position of the verbal noun, i.e., "neglect"; he said: according to this interpretation, there remains in the verse no proof for one who thinks that the Book explicitly contains mention of everything. A parallel is His saying: ﴿Their scheming will not harm you at all﴾ [Al 'Imran: 120], i.e., any harm. End. What he mentioned, that on this interpretation no proof remains for the one he mentioned, is not as he stated; for when negation applies to the verbal noun, the verbal noun is negated in a general way, and from the negation of this generality follows the negation of the kinds of the verbal noun and its particular instances. A parallel is "there is no standing" (la qiyam): this is a general negation, so all kinds of standing are negated along with its particular instances, such as the standing of Zayd and the standing of 'Amr and the like. So when neglect is negated in the manner of generality, that is a negation of all kinds of neglect, its particular instances, and its related matters; it follows from this that the Book comprises mention of every thing. Ibn Abi 'Abla, al-A'raj and 'Alqama read "ma farratna" with a light "ra'," and the meaning is the same. Al-Naqqash said: the meaning of "farratna," when light, is "we delayed," as they say: "God removed the illness from you" (farrata Allahu 'anka al-maradh), meaning He removed it.

Then to their Lord they will be gathered.

The apparent reading of the pronoun is that it refers to what was mentioned before, namely all the communities of birds and beasts. Some scholars said: it refers to the disbelievers, not to communities, and what came between them is an interjected statement, an argument and proofs. What favours this view is that it says "they" (bihim) and uses the plural form of the "waw" which is used for rational beings. Had it referred to the communities of birds and beasts, the construction would have been "then to their Lord it [feminine] will be gathered." This is answered: since they (the animals) were obedient to what God willed of them, they were treated as rational beings.

The root of al-hashr (gathering) is to assemble, as in "so he gathered and called out" (fa-hashara fa-nada). The apparent meaning is that it means resurrection on the Day of Judgment, which is the view of the majority: the beasts, animals and birds will be gathered. On this there is a hadith narrated by Yazid ibn al-Asamm from Abu Hurayrah, who said: God will gather all creation on the Day of Judgment, the beasts, animals, birds and everything, and on that day God, Mighty and Majestic, will reach such justice that He will take retribution for the hornless (sheep) from the horned, and then He will say: "Be dust," and that is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the disbeliever will say: Would that I were dust﴾ [an-Naba': 40].

Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and others said: the gathering of the animals is their death, because animals have no obligation upon them, do not hope for reward, do not fear punishment, and do not understand address. End of quote.
