Whoever adopts this position interprets the hadith of Abu Hurayrah as a figurative expression of reckoning and retribution, so that every responsible person understands that he cannot escape it and there is no escape, and that it is pure justice. Ibn Atiyyah said: the statement in the hadiths containing that God takes retribution for the hornless from the horned is a metaphor for justice, not a literal statement; it is a despised view that tends toward the belief in symbols and the like. End of quote. Ibn Furak said: the view that they are gathered together with the children of Adam is more apparent. End of quote.

Regarding the view that beasts are gathered together with people, they differed about the purpose for which they are gathered. The People of the Sunnah held that it is to demonstrate the power of restoration, and in that there is a rebuke to whoever denies it, who says: "Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?" The Mu'tazilah said: God gathers the beasts and birds in order to deliver compensation (iwad) to them. Likewise al-Zamakhshari said: "So He compensates them and gives justice to some of them from others," as is narrated: He takes retribution for the hornless from the horned. End of quote. The Mu'tazilah elaborated at length on delivering compensation for the pains and harms suffered by animals, and that this is obligatory upon God, and they derived many branches, and differed about the compensation: is it cut off, or is it everlasting? Al-Qadi and most Mu'tazilah of Basra held that it is cut off, so after the compensation is fulfilled, He turns them into dust. Abu al-Qasim al-Balkhi said: the compensation must be everlasting. It was also said: the beasts enter Paradise and are compensated for what pains they suffered. All that the Mu'tazilah said is based on the premise that God is obliged to deliver compensation to animals for the pains that befell them in this world. The position of the People of the Sunnah is that obligation upon God, Exalted is He, is impossible.

(p-122) ﴿Those who deny Our signs are deaf and dumb, in darkness.﴾ Al-Naqqash said: It was revealed concerning the Banu Abd al-Dar, and then it extended to others besides them. End of quotation. The connection of this verse to what precedes it: when His saying ﴿Only those who hear respond﴾ [al-An'am: 36] had come before, He informed that those who deny the signs are deaf, not hearing those who admonish them, so none of them responds. And since His saying ﴿There is no creature crawling upon the earth...﴾ [al-An'am: 38] and so on was an admonition to the immense power of Allah the Exalted, His subtle workmanship and wondrous creation, He mentioned that the one who denies His signs is deaf to hearing the truth and mute in speaking it. Here "the signs" means the Qur'an, or the miracles that appeared at the hands of the Messenger (ﷺ), or the proofs and arguments; there are three opinions. As for the description of them as ﴿deaf and dumb, in darkness﴾, the apparent meaning is that it is a metaphor for the failure to benefit mentally from these faculties, not that they are literally deaf and dumb in darkness. His saying ﴿in darkness﴾ is a kinaya (allusion) for blindness of insight, so that it is as if they see, like His saying ﴿deaf, dumb, blind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 18]. However, His saying ﴿in darkness﴾ is more eloquent than saying "blind," since it makes it a container for them, and it is plural because the directions of disbelief differ, as it was said regarding His saying ﴿and made the darknesses and the light﴾ [al-An'am: 1], according to one of the opinions, and regarding His saying ﴿He brings them out of the light into the darknesses﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257].

Al-Jubba'i said: The description of them as ﴿deaf and dumb, in darkness﴾ is literal, and that is on the Day of Resurrection, when He makes them deaf and dumb in darkness, misguiding them thereby away from Paradise and bringing them to the Fire. This interpretation is supported by His saying the Exalted: ﴿And We shall gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, dumb and deaf; their abode is Hell﴾ [al-Isra': 97] and so on.

Al-Ka'bi said: "deaf and dumb" is to be taken as insult and humiliation, on the basis that they were indeed like that in reality. End of quotation.

The "darknesses" are the darknesses of disbelief, or veils cast over the heart so that it becomes dark and is screened from the light of faith, or the darknesses of the Day of Resurrection, and from this it was said: "Return behind you and seek light" [al-Hadid: 13], or they are hardships, because the Arabs used to express hardship by darkness; they say "a dark day" when they encounter hardship in it. From this is his saying:

"O Banu Asad, do you know our trial, when there was a day with stars, dark?"

That makes four opinions; the fourth was stated by al-Layth.

﴿Whomever Allah wills to misguide, He misguides; and whomever He wills, He places him upon a straight path.﴾ The object of (yasha') is omitted; its estimated form is: whomever Allah wills to misguide him (yudlilhu), and whomever He wills to guide him (yaj'alhu). It is not permissible for (man) in both to be an object of (yasha') because of the mutual opposition between the two willings. If you say, it would be an object of (yasha') with an omitted modifier, its estimate being: the misguidance of whom Allah wills, and the guidance of whom Allah wills, so the modifier was deleted and (man) was placed in its position, and the verb of the response indicates this object — the answer is that this is not permissible, because Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash related from the Arabs that a conditional noun other than a time adverb, and a noun annexed to a conditional noun, must have in the response a pronoun referring to the conditional noun or to the annexed noun. The pronoun in (yudlilhu) either refers to the omitted misguidance, or to (man). It is not permissible that it refer to misguidance, which would be like His saying ﴿covering him, a wave from above it﴾ [al-Nur: 40], since the pronoun refers to the omitted (dhi) from His saying "or like darknesses," as the estimate is "or like one of darknesses"; because the estimate would become: the misguidance of whom Allah wills — He misguides him, i.e., He misguides the misguidance, and this is not valid. Nor is it permissible that it refer to the conditional (man), because then the response clause would be devoid of a pronoun referring to the annexed noun to the conditional noun, and that is not permissible. If you say: the estimate is "whom Allah wills with misguidance," so it would then be a fronted object, because shā' means arāda (wills), and one says "Allah willed him with such-and-such"; the poet said:

"She desired 'Irar with humiliation, and whoever desires 'Irar with humiliation, by my life, has wronged."

The answer: it is not preserved from Arabic speech that shā' is transitive with bi-, one does not preserve "shā'a Allahu bi-kadha." It does not follow that because a thing has the meaning of another thing, it is transitive in the same way; rather the transitivity of a single word may differ according to its complement. Do you not see that you say "dakhaltu al-dar" (I entered the house) and "dakhaltu fi ghimar al-nas" (I entered into the crowd of people)? And one does not say "dakhaltu ghimar al-nas." If this occurs with a single verb, it is all the more so with two verbs. Having established this, the i'rab (grammatical parsing) of (man) admits two possibilities: the first, which is preferable, is that it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is the conditional clause; the second is that it is an object of a verb that is omitted and comes after it, explained by the conditional verb in meaning, and the matter is of the type of al-ishtighal (verbal preoccupation), the estimate being: whomever Allah makes wretched, He wills his misguidance; and whomever He makes happy, He wills his guidance ﴿and places him upon a straight path﴾.

The apparent meaning of the verse indicates the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah, that Allah the Exalted is the Guide and He is the Misguider, and that this is tied to His will, and He is not questioned about what He does. The Mu'tazilah interpreted this verse as they interpreted other verses, saying: the meaning of (yudlilhu) is that He forsakes him and corrupts him, and his straying is because He did not show him favor (lutf), since he is not among those who merit His favor; and the meaning of ﴿places him upon a straight path﴾ is that He shows him favor, since favor applies to him. This is according to al-Zamakhshari. Others said: He misguides him from the path of Paradise, and ﴿places him upon a straight path﴾ is the path which the believers travel to Paradise. They said: It has been established by proof that He, the Exalted, does not will this misguidance except for one who deserves punishment, just as He does not will guidance except for the believers.

[p. 124] This is the beginning of an argument against the disbelievers who ascribe partners to Allah.

﴿Say: Tell me, if the punishment of Allah comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you, will you call upon other than Allah, if you are truthful?﴾

Al-Kirmani said: *(ara'aytakum)* is an interrogative and expressive of wonder, and it has no parallel.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: The meaning is: Tell me, if you fear the punishment of Allah, or you fear destruction, or you fear the Hour, will you call upon your idols and seek refuge in them to remove that, if you are truthful in your saying that they are gods? Rather, you call upon Allah, the Creator, the Provider, and He removes what you fear if He wills. And you forget your idols, meaning you abandon them. He expressed abandonment by its most extreme form, which, together with abandonment, is heedlessness and inattention. So how can one who is in this state in times of hardship be made a god?

*(Atakum 'adhabu Allah)*, "the punishment of Allah has come upon you," means that its fear and its signs and its beginnings have come upon you, such as drought, distress, and illnesses from which destruction is feared, like colic (*qawlanj*). What supports this interpretation is that if we assume the coming and arrival of the punishment, it would not follow that He says afterward, "then He removes what you call upon," because what has already arrived and passed cannot be removed.

It is possible that by "the Hour" in this verse he means the hour of a person's death, and this is the end of his statement. But this interpretation he mentioned is not necessary. Rather, when punishment befalls a person and continues upon him, he calls upon none but Allah. His statement, "because what has already arrived and passed cannot be removed," is not as he said, because the punishment that befalls a person is of a kind: some of it has passed and ended, and that cannot be removed; and some of it is still clinging to the person in the present, so it can be removed and lifted by Allah cutting it off from the person. This verse refers to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When harm touches man, he calls upon Us, lying on his side or sitting or standing; but when We remove his harm from him, he passes on as if he had never called upon Us about a harm that touched him﴾ [Yunus: 12]. So what has passed of the harm that touched him cannot be removed, and what still clings to him, Allah Exalted removes. Harm is a genus, just as punishment here is a genus.

Muqatil said: The punishment of Allah is the punishment that used to come upon the earlier nations. Ibn 'Abbas said: It is death, and he means, and Allah knows best, its preliminaries of hardships.

The majority hold that *(al-sa'a)*, "the Hour," is the Resurrection. In *(ara'ayt)*, the hamza is for interrogation. If it is the visual *(basariyya)* or the one meaning to strike sight, or the cognitive *('ilmiyya)* that remains in its original usage, then it is not permitted except to make the hamza clear or to soften it *(bayn bayn)*, and it is not permitted to drop it. The *ta'* [in *ara'aytum*] varies with the addressee, and it is not permitted to attach the *kaf* to it. But if it is the cognitive one that means "inform me" *(akhbirni)*, then it is permitted to make the hamza clear, and the majority read it this way in *ara'aytakum*, *ara'aytum*, and *ara'ayta*. It is also permitted to soften it *bayn bayn*, and Nafi' read it this way. It was also narrated from him that he replaced it with a pure alif, and its vowel is lengthened because of its sukun and the sukun of what follows it. This replacement is weak according to the grammarians, but it has been heard from the speech of the Arabs; Qutrub and others reported it. Dropping it is also permitted, and al-Kisa'i read it this way, and this has occurred in Arabic speech. The reciter said:

*"Tell me, if she brings forth a slender boy."*

Indeed al-Farra' claimed that this is the dialect of most Arabs. Al-Farra' said: The Arabs have two dialects and two meanings for *ara'ayta*. One: you ask a man, "Did you see Zayd?" meaning with your own eyes; this is with a hamza. The second: you say *ara'ayta*, meaning "inform me," and in this sense you may drop the hamza if you wish, and this is the more common in Arabic speech, pointing to dropping the hamza in order to distinguish the two meanings. And when it means "inform me," the *ta'* may vary with the addressee, and the *kaf* may be attached to it, indicating the variation of the addressee, while the *ta'* remains open, as it is for the masculine singular.

The view of the Basrans is that the *ta'* is the subject, and what is attached to it is a particle indicating the variation of the addressee, and its variation has made the variation of the *ta'* unnecessary. The view of al-Kisa'i is that the subject is the *ta'*, and the attached particle of address is in the place of the first object. The view of al-Farra' is that the *ta'* is a particle of address like it is in *anta* ("you"), and the particle of address after it is in the place of the subject; the accusative pronouns were borrowed for the nominative. The discussion of these views, substitution and correctness, is mentioned in the science of grammar *(al-nahw)*. That *ara'ayta* and *ara'aytaka* mean "inform me" is explicitly stated by Sibawayh, al-Akhfash, al-Farra', al-Fārisi, Ibn Kaysan, and others. This is an explanation of meaning, not an explanation of *i'rab* (grammatical case-analysis). They said: The Arabs say, *"Ara'ayta Zaydan ma sana'a"* ("Tell me about Zayd: what did he do?"). The first object here is necessarily in the accusative, and it is not permitted to be nominative according to the consideration of suspension *(ta'liq)* of *ara'ayta*. This is permitted with *'alimta* and *ra'aytu* when they remain in the meaning of "knowing" stripped of the meaning of "inform me," because "inform me" is not suspended, and so what has its meaning is likewise. The interrogative clause is in the position of the second object. Sibawayh said: And you say, *"Ara'aytaka Zaydan abu man huwa?"* ("Tell me about Zayd: who is his father?") and *"Ara'aytaka 'Amran a'indaka huwa am 'inda fulan?"* ("Tell me about 'Amr: is he with you or with so-and-so?"). In it, the accusative is the only good option for Zayd. Do you not see that if you said, *"Ara'ayta abu man anta?"* and *"Ara'ayta azayd thamma am fulan?"* it would not be good, because it contains the meaning of "inform me about Zayd." Then Sibawayh said: The interrogative has become in the position of the second object.

Many grammarians have objected to Sibawayh and disagreed with him, saying: *(ara'ayta)* is often suspended, and the Qur'an contains much of this, including: ﴿Say: Tell me, if the punishment of Allah comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you, will you call upon other than Allah﴾; ﴿Have you seen the one who forbids﴾ [al-'Alaq: 9]; ﴿a servant when he prays﴾ [al-'Alaq: 10]; ﴿Have you seen if he denies and turns away﴾ [al-'Alaq: 13]; ﴿Does he not know﴾ [al-'Alaq: 14]. And the poet said:

*"Tell me, if she brings forth a slender boy,*
*Well-groomed, wearing striped cloaks,*
*Do you say, 'Summon the witnesses'?"*

Ibn Kaysan held that the interrogative clause in *ara'ayta Zaydan ma sana'a?* is a substitute *(badal)* for *ara'ayta*. Abu al-Hasan claimed that when *ara'aytaka* means "inform me," there must be after it the noun about which one is informed, and the clause that follows it must be interrogative, because "inform me" agrees with the meaning of interrogation. He also claimed that it leaves its original usage entirely and is used with the meaning of *(amma)* ("as for") or *(tanabbah)* ("take note"). He made this the case in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿He said: Tell me, when we took refuge at the rock, indeed I forgot the fish﴾ [al-Kahf: 63]. We have gone deeply into the discussion of *ara'ayta* and its questions in our book called *al-Tadhyil fi Sharh al-Tashil*, in which we gathered what is not found collected in one book, so that one may consult it there. We will speak about every place where *ara'ayta* occurs in the Qur'an individually.

We say: What we choose is that it remains in its ruling of transitivity to two objects; the first is in the accusative, and what we have not found by induction except as an interrogative or oath clause is the second. Once this is established, we say: The first object in this verse is omitted, and the matter falls under the category of *tanazu'* (grammatical contention), where *(ara'aytakum)* and the condition are in contention over "the punishment of Allah." The second was made to operate, which is *(atakum)*, so *'adhab* was raised by it. Had the first been made to operate, the construction would be *('adhaba)* in the accusative. Its parallel is *idrib in jaa'aka Zaydun* ("strike, if Zayd comes to you") with *(jaa'aka)* operating. If it were in the accusative, it would be permitted, and it would be an application of the first. As for the second object, it is the interrogative clause from ﴿Is it other than Allah you call upon﴾, and the linking pronoun for this clause to the first object is omitted, its estimate being: ﴿Is it other than Allah you call upon﴾ to remove it. The meaning is: Say: Tell me, the punishment of Allah, if it comes upon you, or the Hour, if it comes upon you, is it other than Allah you call upon to remove it, or to remove a fire that it has?

Abu al-Hasan claimed that *ara'aytakum* in this verse means *amma* ("as for"). He said: It is always after the conditional and time expressions, and the estimate is: As for if His punishment comes upon you... and the interrogation is the answer to *ara'ayta*, not the answer to the condition. This is removing *ara'ayta* from its meaning entirely, and we have already mentioned its explanation according to what is established for it, so we have no need for this distant interpretation. According to what Abu al-Hasan claimed, *ara'ayta* would have neither two objects nor one object.

Some held that the object of *(ara'aytakum)* is omitted and indicated by the speech, its estimate being: Tell me your worship of the idols, will it benefit you at the coming of the Hour? This is indicated by His saying: ﴿Is it other than Allah you call upon﴾. Others said: Here there is no need for an object answer, because the condition and its answer have already made up the meaning of the object. These two views are weak.

As for the answer to the condition, al-Hawfi held that its answer is *(ara'aytakum)*, placed first because the interrogative hamza entered upon it. This is not permitted according to us. It is only permitted to place the answer of the condition before it according to the view of the Kufans, Abu Zayd, and al-Mubarrad. Others held that it is omitted, and al-Zamakhshari estimated it, saying: If the punishment of Allah comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you, whom do you call upon? And its correction is by inserting the *fa'* (then), i.e., *"fa-man tad'un?"* ("then whom do you call upon?"), because when the interrogative clause falls as the answer to the condition, the *fa'* must be in it. Others estimated it: If the punishment of Allah comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you, you call upon Allah; and this is indicated by the interrogation in His saying: ﴿Is it other than Allah you call upon﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permitted that the condition be connected to His saying: ﴿Is it other than Allah you call upon﴾, as if it were said: Is it other than Allah you call upon if the punishment of Allah comes upon you? End of his statement. But it is not permitted that the condition be connected to His saying: ﴿Is it other than Allah﴾, because if it were connected to it, it would be the answer to the condition, and it is not permitted for it to be the answer to the condition, because when the answer to the condition is an interrogative with a particle, it can only be with *hal* ("is it that"), with *fa'* placed before it, as in: *"In qama Zaydun fa-hal tukrimuhu?"* ("If Zayd stands, will you honor him?"). This is not permitted with the hamza: the *fa'* cannot come before the hamza or after it. So it is not permitted to say: *"In qama Zaydun fa-a-tukrimuhu?"* or *"a-fa-tukrimuhu?"* or *"a-tukrimannahu?"* Rather, when an interrogative comes as the answer to the condition, it can only be with what is correct to occur after *fa'*, not before it. This is how al-Akhfash transmitted it from the Arabs. It is also impermissible from another angle, because we have established that *(ara'aytaka)* is transitive to two objects: one of them in this verse is omitted, and it falls under *tanazu'*; the other is the position of the interrogative clause. So if you made it the answer to the condition, *(ara'aytakum)* would remain transitive to only one object, and that is not permitted. Also, the Arabs' practice with a condition that comes after *ara'ayta* is the past tense of the verb, which is evidence that the answer to the condition is omitted, because the answer to the condition is only omitted when its verb is in the past. The Exalted said: ﴿Say: Tell me, if the punishment of Allah comes upon you﴾; ﴿Say: Tell me, if Allah takes away your hearing and your sight﴾ [al-An'am: 46]; ﴿Say: Tell me, if His punishment comes upon you by night﴾ [Yunus: 50]; ﴿Say: Tell me, if Allah takes away﴾ [al-An'am: 46]; ﴿Then have you seen, if We let them enjoy for years﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 205]; ﴿Have you seen if he denies and turns away﴾ [al-'Alaq: 13]; ﴿Does he not know﴾ [al-'Alaq: 14]; and other verses. And the poet said:

*"Tell me, if she brings forth a slender boy."*

Also, the interrogative clauses beginning with the interrogative hamza are evidence that they are not the answer (*jawab*) to the condition (*shart*), since it is not valid for them to function as its answer. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: if the conditional clause is linked, meaning by His words ﴿Other than Allah?﴾, then what do you make of His words ﴿He will remove that for which you call upon Him﴾ together with His words (p-128) ﴿Or the Hour comes upon you﴾? The calamities of the Hour are not removed from the polytheists." I say: He has made the removal conditional on His will, which is His words ﴿if He wills﴾, indicating that if He were to do it, there would be a wisdom in it, but He does not do it because of another wisdom that outweighs it, end of quote. This is based on the view that the condition may be linked to His words ﴿Other than Allah?﴾, and the one who holds that this is not permissible has argued for it.

Several views on the answer to the condition have been summarized. The first: it is mentioned, and it is the earlier ﴿Tell me﴾ (*ara'aytakum*). The second: it is mentioned, and it is ﴿Other than Allah do you call upon?﴾. The third: it is omitted, its estimated form being: "whom do you call upon?" The fourth: it is omitted, its estimated form being: "you called upon Allah." This is what we have found transmitted. What we hold to is other than these views: that it is omitted, because of the indication of ﴿Tell me﴾ upon it, and its estimated form is: ﴿If the punishment of Allah comes upon you, then inform me about it: do you call upon other than Allah to remove it?⁠﴾ As you say: "Tell me about Zayd if he comes to you, what will you do with him?" The estimate is: "If he comes to you, then inform me," so the answer was omitted because "inform me" indicates it. A parallel to this is: "You are a wrongdoer if you do it," the estimate being: "then you are a wrongdoer," so "then you are a wrongdoer" was omitted, and it is the answer to the condition because of what precedes it indicating it. This estimate that we have made is what the rules of Arabic grammar require.

By "other than Allah" is meant the idols they used to worship. The fronting of the object here after the hamza indicates denunciation of them for calling upon idols, since calling upon is not what is denied; rather, what is denied is that idols are called upon. As you say: "Zayd you strike?" You do not deny the striking, but you deny that its object is Zayd. Al-Zamakhshari said: "He rebuked them with His words ﴿Other than Allah do you call upon?⁠﴾, meaning: do you single out your gods for supplication in what is your custom when harm befalls you, or do you call upon Allah apart from them?" End of quote. He estimated it to mean "do you single out," because for him the fronting of the object indicates restriction and exclusivity. We have already discussed this earlier, and that it does not indicate restriction and exclusivity.

This verse, according to the scholars of rhetoric (*'ulama al-bayan*), belongs to the category of *istidraj al-mukhatab* (gradually drawing in the addressee), which is to soften the address and mix it with a kind of gentleness and tenderness, until the addressee is brought to a matter which he acknowledges, whereupon the proof is established against him. Allah Most High addressed these disbelievers with gentle speech, and mentioned to them a matter they do not dispute: that whenever harm touched them, they called upon Allah alone and not others.

The answer to ﴿If you are truthful⁠﴾ is omitted; its estimated form is: "If you are truthful in your claim that other than Allah is a god, then do you call upon him to remove the punishment that will befall you?" ﴿Rather, it is Him you call upon, and He removes that for which you call upon Him, if He wills, and you forget what you associate.⁠﴾ (*Iyyahu*) is a detached pronoun in the accusative, and its discussion was already covered in full in His words ﴿You alone we worship⁠﴾ (al-Fatiha: 5).

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Here *iyyahu* is a pronoun treated as the nouns which are made possessive, in that it is always attached (to something)," end of quote. This contradicts the view of Sibawayh, because Sibawayh's view is that what is attached to *iyya* of the indication of speech, address, or absence is a particle, not a noun, and *iyya* is attached to it; for the pronoun, in his view, is not made possessive, because it is the most definite of definites. If it were made possessive, it would follow that it becomes indefinite until it is made possessive, and then it becomes definite through the possessive construction, and is no longer a pronoun. This is invalid.

Its coming here, fronted before its verb, is evidence of concern with mentioning the object. For al-Zamakhshari, its fronting is evidence of restriction and exclusivity, and for this reason he said: "Rather, you single Him out for supplication, apart from the gods." Our view is that exclusivity and restriction are understood from the context of the speech, not from fronting the object before the governing element.

Here *bal* is for *idrab* (transition from one matter to another without negation of the first), and for the transition from one thing to another without annulment, because the preceding speech contains the sense of negation, since the meaning of the preceding clause is negation, and its estimate is: "You do not call upon your idols to remove the punishment." This is a true statement in which *idrab*, meaning annulment, is not possible.

The *ma* in His words ﴿that for which you call upon Him⁠﴾ is most apparently a relative pronoun, meaning: "He removes the one you call upon Him for." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is also valid for it to be temporal," end of quote. Then the object of *yakshifu* would be omitted, meaning: "He removes the punishment for the duration of your calling upon Him," i.e., as long as you are calling upon Him. This involves omitting the object and departing from the apparent meaning without need, and it is weakened by joining the temporal *ma* to the present tense, which is very rare; its usual form is to be joined to the past tense. You say: "I will not speak to you as long as the sun has risen." For this reason the grammatical rule for it has been mentioned in the science of grammar. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is also valid for it to be verbal-nominal (*masdariyya*) with an omission in the speech." Al-Zajjaj said: "It is like ﴿Ask the town⁠﴾" (Yusuf: 82), end of quote. Then the estimate of the omitted element would be: "He removes the cause of your calling upon Him, which is the punishment." This is a claim of an unspecified omitted element, and it contradicts the apparent meaning.

The pronoun in *ilayhi* refers back to the relative *ma*, meaning: "to its removal." *Da'a* (to call) is used with *ila* (to) with respect to the object of the supplication, as Allah Most High said: ﴿And when they are called to Allah⁠﴾ (al-Nur: 48), and as the poet said:

*And if you call to glory and nobility, one day, the chiefs of noble people, then call us.*

It is also used with *li* (for), as the poet said:

*And if I am called to the great deeds, I will be among their defenders.*

Another said:

*I called out when Musawwar's lot befell me.*

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The pronoun in *ilayhi* may refer to Allah, with the estimate: 'He removes that in which you call upon Allah.'" End of quote. This is not sound, because *da'a* with respect to the one who answers the supplication is used with a direct object without a preposition, as Allah Most High said: ﴿Call upon Me, I will answer you⁠﴾ (Ghafir: 60), and ﴿I answer the supplication of the supplicant when he calls upon Me⁠﴾ (al-Baqara: 186). From the speech of the Arabs: "I called upon Allah, the All-Hearing." You do not say, with this meaning, "I called to Allah." However, his statement could be corrected by the claim of *tadmin* (lexical implication): *yad'una* is taken to imply the meaning of *yalja'una* (to seek refuge), as if it were said: "He removes that to which they seek refuge by supplication to Allah." But *tadmin* is not a rule of analogy and is not resorted to except in cases of necessity, and there is no necessity here that calls for it.

Allah Most High made the removal conditional upon His will: if He wills to show favor by removing it, He does so, and if He does not will, He does not do it; nothing is obligatory upon Him. Al-Zamakhshari said: "*In sha'a* (if He wills): if He intends to show favor to you, and it would not be a corruption," end of quote. In his words "and it would not be a corruption" there is the hidden ideological leaning of the Mu'tazila.

The apparent meaning of His words ﴿and you forget what you associate⁠﴾ is that forgetting is literal, and it means heedlessness and unawareness of the idols. This is because when a person is overwhelmed by what he has no power to repel, his thoughts are stripped of everything except Allah, who removes that overwhelming affliction, so he nearly comes to cling to Allah alone and to be oblivious of anyone else, and thus he does not mention anyone other than Allah who is capable of removing what has overwhelmed him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "*And you forget what you associate*: and you dislike your gods." There is a distance in this. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "You leave them," and he had already stated this view; al-Zajjaj preceded him to it, saying: "You leave them, because you know that in reality they neither harm nor benefit." Al-Nahhas said: "It is like His words ﴿And We had already made a covenant with Adam before, but he forgot⁠﴾" (Ta-Ha: 115). It has been said: "They turn away with the turning away of one who forgets, out of despair of salvation from it before." The *ma* is a relative pronoun, meaning: "and you forget that which you associate." It has also been said that *ma* is verbal-nominal, meaning: "and you forget your association." The meaning of these clauses is: "Rather, there is no refuge for you except Allah Most High, and your idols are cast aside and forgotten," as Ibn 'Atiyya said.

[p. 124] This is the beginning of an argument against the disbelievers who ascribe partners to Allah.

﴿Say: Tell me, if the punishment of Allah comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you, will you call upon other than Allah, if you are truthful?﴾

Al-Kirmani said: *(ara'aytakum)* is an interrogative and expressive of wonder, and it has no parallel.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: The meaning is: Tell me, if you fear the punishment of Allah, or you fear destruction, or you fear the Hour, will you call upon your idols and seek refuge in them to remove that, if you are truthful in your saying that they are gods? Rather, you call upon Allah, the Creator, the Provider, and He removes what you fear if He wills. And you forget your idols, meaning you abandon them. He expressed abandonment by its most extreme form, which, together with abandonment, is heedlessness and inattention. So how can one who is in this state in times of hardship be made a god?

*(Atakum 'adhabu Allah)*, "the punishment of Allah has come upon you," means that its fear and its signs and its beginnings have come upon you, such as drought, distress, and illnesses from which destruction is feared, like colic (*qawlanj*). What supports this interpretation is that if we assume the coming and arrival of the punishment, it would not follow that He says afterward, "then He removes what you call upon," because what has already arrived and passed cannot be removed.

It is possible that by "the Hour" in this verse he means the hour of a person's death, and this is the end of his statement. But this interpretation he mentioned is not necessary. Rather, when punishment befalls a person and continues upon him, he calls upon none but Allah. His statement, "because what has already arrived and passed cannot be removed," is not as he said, because the punishment that befalls a person is of a kind: some of it has passed and ended, and that cannot be removed; and some of it is still clinging to the person in the present, so it can be removed and lifted by Allah cutting it off from the person. This verse refers to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When harm touches man, he calls upon Us, lying on his side or sitting or standing; but when We remove his harm from him, he passes on as if he had never called upon Us about a harm that touched him﴾ [Yunus: 12]. So what has passed of the harm that touched him cannot be removed, and what still clings to him, Allah Exalted removes. Harm is a genus, just as punishment here is a genus.

We will speak about every place where *ara'ayta* occurs in the Qur'an individually.

We say: What we choose is that it remains in its ruling of transitivity to two objects; the first is in the accusative, and what we have not found by induction except as an interrogative or oath clause is the second. Once this is established, we say: The first object in this verse is omitted, and the matter falls under the category of *tanazu'* (grammatical contention), where *(ara'aytakum)* and the condition are in contention over "the punishment of Allah." The second was made to operate, which is *(atakum)*, so *'adhab* was raised by it. Had the first been made to operate, the construction would be *('adhaba)* in the accusative. Its parallel is *idrib in jaa'aka Zaydun* ("strike, if Zayd comes to you") with *(jaa'aka)* operating. If it were in the accusative, it would be permitted, and it would be an application of the first. As for the second object, it is the interrogative clause from ﴿Is it other than Allah you call upon﴾, and the linking pronoun for this clause to the first object is omitted, its estimate being: ﴿Is it other than Allah you call upon﴾ to remove it. The meaning is: Say: Tell me, the punishment of Allah, if it comes upon you, or the Hour, if it comes upon you, is it other than Allah you call upon to remove it, or to remove a fire that it has?

Abu al-Hasan claimed that *ara'aytakum* in this verse means *amma* ("as for"). He said: It is always after the conditional and time expressions, and the estimate is: As for if His punishment comes upon you... and the interrogation is the answer to *ara'ayta*, not the answer to the condition. This is removing *ara'ayta* from its meaning entirely, and we have already mentioned its explanation according to what is established for it, so we have no need for this distant interpretation. According to what Abu al-Hasan claimed, *ara'ayta* would have neither two objects nor one object.

Some held that the object of *(ara'aytakum)* is omitted and indicated by the speech, its estimate being: Tell me your worship of the idols, will it benefit you at the coming of the Hour? This is indicated by His saying: ﴿Is it other than Allah you call upon﴾. Others said: Here there is no need for an object answer, because the condition and its answer have already made up the meaning of the object. These two views are weak.

As for the answer to the condition, al-Hawfi held that its answer is *(ara'aytakum)*, placed first because the interrogative hamza entered upon it. This is not permitted according to us. It is only permitted to place the answer of the condition before it according to the view of the Kufans, Abu Zayd, and al-Mubarrad. Others held that it is omitted, and al-Zamakhshari estimated it, saying: If the punishment of Allah comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you, whom do you call upon? And its correction is by inserting the *fa'* (then), i.e., *"fa-man tad'un?"* ("then whom do you call upon?"), because when the interrogative clause falls as the answer to the condition, the *fa'* must be in it. Others estimated it: If the punishment of Allah comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you, you call upon Allah; and this is indicated by the interrogation in His saying: ﴿Is it other than Allah you call upon﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permitted that the condition be connected to His saying: ﴿Is it other than Allah you call upon﴾, as if it were said: Is it other than Allah you call upon if the punishment of Allah comes upon you? End of his statement. But it is not permitted that the condition be connected to His saying: ﴿Is it other than Allah﴾, because if it were connected to it, it would be the answer to the condition, and it is not permitted for it to be the answer to the condition, because when the answer to the condition is an interrogative with a particle, it can only be with *hal* ("is it that"), with *fa'* placed before it, as in: *"In qama Zaydun fa-hal tukrimuhu?"* ("If Zayd stands, will you honor him?"). This is not permitted with the hamza: the *fa'* cannot come before the hamza or after it. So it is not permitted to say: *"In qama Zaydun fa-a-tukrimuhu?"* or *"a-fa-tukrimuhu?"* or *"a-tukrimannahu?"* Rather, when an interrogative comes as the answer to the condition, it can only be with what is correct to occur after *fa'*, not before it. This is how al-Akhfash transmitted it from the Arabs. It is also impermissible from another angle, because we have established that *(ara'aytaka)* is transitive to two objects: one of them in this verse is omitted, and it falls under *tanazu'*; the other is the position of the interrogative clause. So if you made it the answer to the condition, *(ara'aytakum)* would remain transitive to only one object, and that is not permitted. Also, the Arabs' practice with a condition that comes after *ara'ayta* is the past tense of the verb, which is evidence that the answer to the condition is omitted, because the answer to the condition is only omitted when its verb is in the past. The Exalted said: ﴿Say: Tell me, if the punishment of Allah comes upon you﴾; ﴿Say: Tell me, if Allah takes away your hearing and your sight﴾ [al-An'am: 46]; ﴿Say: Tell me, if His punishment comes upon you by night﴾ [Yunus: 50]; ﴿Say: Tell me, if Allah takes away﴾ [al-An'am: 46]; ﴿Then have you seen, if We let them enjoy for years﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 205]; ﴿Have you seen if he denies and turns away﴾ [al-'Alaq: 13]; ﴿Does he not know﴾ [al-'Alaq: 14]; and other verses. And the poet said:

*"Tell me, if she brings forth a slender boy."*

Also, the interrogative clauses beginning with the interrogative hamza are evidence that they are not the answer (*jawab*) to the condition (*shart*), since it is not valid for them to function as its answer. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: if the conditional clause is linked, meaning by His words ﴿Other than Allah?﴾, then what do you make of His words ﴿He will remove that for which you call upon Him﴾ together with His words (p-128) ﴿Or the Hour comes upon you﴾? The calamities of the Hour are not removed from the polytheists." I say: He has made the removal conditional on His will, which is His words ﴿if He wills﴾, indicating that if He were to do it, there would be a wisdom in it, but He does not do it because of another wisdom that outweighs it, end of quote. This is based on the view that the condition may be linked to His words ﴿Other than Allah?﴾, and the one who holds that this is not permissible has argued for it.

Several views on the answer to the condition have been summarized. The first: it is mentioned, and it is the earlier ﴿Tell me﴾ (*ara'aytakum*). The second: it is mentioned, and it is ﴿Other than Allah do you call upon?﴾. The third: it is omitted, its estimated form being: "whom do you call upon?" The fourth: it is omitted, its estimated form being: "you called upon Allah." This is what we have found transmitted. What we hold to is other than these views: that it is omitted, because of the indication of ﴿Tell me﴾ upon it, and its estimated form is: ﴿If the punishment of Allah comes upon you, then inform me about it: do you call upon other than Allah to remove it?⁠﴾ As you say: "Tell me about Zayd if he comes to you, what will you do with him?" The estimate is: "If he comes to you, then inform me," so the answer was omitted because "inform me" indicates it. A parallel to this is: "You are a wrongdoer if you do it," the estimate being: "then you are a wrongdoer," so "then you are a wrongdoer" was omitted, and it is the answer to the condition because of what precedes it indicating it. This estimate that we have made is what the rules of Arabic grammar require.

By "other than Allah" is meant the idols they used to worship. The fronting of the object here after the hamza indicates denunciation of them for calling upon idols, since calling upon is not what is denied; rather, what is denied is that idols are called upon. As you say: "Zayd you strike?" You do not deny the striking, but you deny that its object is Zayd. Al-Zamakhshari said: "He rebuked them with His words ﴿Other than Allah do you call upon?⁠﴾, meaning: do you single out your gods for supplication in what is your custom when harm befalls you, or do you call upon Allah apart from them?" End of quote. He estimated it to mean "do you single out," because for him the fronting of the object indicates restriction and exclusivity. We have already discussed this earlier, and that it does not indicate restriction and exclusivity.

This verse, according to the scholars of rhetoric (*'ulama al-bayan*), belongs to the category of *istidraj al-mukhatab* (gradually drawing in the addressee), which is to soften the address and mix it with a kind of gentleness and tenderness, until the addressee is brought to a matter which he acknowledges, whereupon the proof is established against him. Allah Most High addressed these disbelievers with gentle speech, and mentioned to them a matter they do not dispute: that whenever harm touched them, they called upon Allah alone and not others.

The answer to ﴿If you are truthful⁠﴾ is omitted; its estimated form is: "If you are truthful in your claim that other than Allah is a god, then do you call upon him to remove the punishment that will befall you?" ﴿Rather, it is Him you call upon, and He removes that for which you call upon Him, if He wills, and you forget what you associate.⁠﴾ (*Iyyahu*) is a detached pronoun in the accusative, and its discussion was already covered in full in His words ﴿You alone we worship⁠﴾ (al-Fatiha: 5).

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Here *iyyahu* is a pronoun treated as the nouns which are made possessive, in that it is always attached (to something)," end of quote. This contradicts the view of Sibawayh, because Sibawayh's view is that what is attached to *iyya* of the indication of speech, address, or absence is a particle, not a noun, and *iyya* is attached to it; for the pronoun, in his view, is not made possessive, because it is the most definite of definites. If it were made possessive, it would follow that it becomes indefinite until it is made possessive, and then it becomes definite through the possessive construction, and is no longer a pronoun. This is invalid.

Its coming here, fronted before its verb, is evidence of concern with mentioning the object. For al-Zamakhshari, its fronting is evidence of restriction and exclusivity, and for this reason he said: "Rather, you single Him out for supplication, apart from the gods." Our view is that exclusivity and restriction are understood from the context of the speech, not from fronting the object before the governing element.

Here *bal* is for *idrab* (transition from one matter to another without negation of the first), and for the transition from one thing to another without annulment, because the preceding speech contains the sense of negation, since the meaning of the preceding clause is negation, and its estimate is: "You do not call upon your idols to remove the punishment." This is a true statement in which *idrab*, meaning annulment, is not possible.

The *ma* in His words ﴿that for which you call upon Him⁠﴾ is most apparently a relative pronoun, meaning: "He removes the one you call upon Him for." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is also valid for it to be temporal," end of quote. Then the object of *yakshifu* would be omitted, meaning: "He removes the punishment for the duration of your calling upon Him," i.e., as long as you are calling upon Him. This involves omitting the object and departing from the apparent meaning without need, and it is weakened by joining the temporal *ma* to the present tense, which is very rare; its usual form is to be joined to the past tense. You say: "I will not speak to you as long as the sun has risen." For this reason the grammatical rule for it has been mentioned in the science of grammar. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is also valid for it to be verbal-nominal (*masdariyya*) with an omission in the speech." Al-Zajjaj said: "It is like ﴿Ask the town⁠﴾" (Yusuf: 82), end of quote. Then the estimate of the omitted element would be: "He removes the cause of your calling upon Him, which is the punishment." This is a claim of an unspecified omitted element, and it contradicts the apparent meaning.

The pronoun in *ilayhi* refers back to the relative *ma*, meaning: "to its removal." *Da'a* (to call) is used with *ila* (to) with respect to the object of the supplication, as Allah Most High said: ﴿And when they are called to Allah⁠﴾ (al-Nur: 48), and as the poet said:

*And if you call to glory and nobility, one day, the chiefs of noble people, then call us.*

It is also used with *li* (for), as the poet said:

*And if I am called to the great deeds, I will be among their defenders.*

Another said:

*I called out when Musawwar's lot befell me.*

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The pronoun in *ilayhi* may refer to Allah, with the estimate: 'He removes that in which you call upon Allah.'" End of quote. This is not sound, because *da'a* with respect to the one who answers the supplication is used with a direct object without a preposition, as Allah Most High said: ﴿Call upon Me, I will answer you⁠﴾ (Ghafir: 60), and ﴿I answer the supplication of the supplicant when he calls upon Me⁠﴾ (al-Baqara: 186). From the speech of the Arabs: "I called upon Allah, the All-Hearing." You do not say, with this meaning, "I called to Allah." However, his statement could be corrected by the claim of *tadmin* (lexical implication): *yad'una* is taken to imply the meaning of *yalja'una* (to seek refuge), as if it were said: "He removes that to which they seek refuge by supplication to Allah." But *tadmin* is not a rule of analogy and is not resorted to except in cases of necessity, and there is no necessity here that calls for it.

Allah Most High made the removal conditional upon His will: if He wills to show favor by removing it, He does so, and if He does not will, He does not do it; nothing is obligatory upon Him. Al-Zamakhshari said: "*In sha'a* (if He wills): if He intends to show favor to you, and it would not be a corruption," end of quote. In his words "and it would not be a corruption" there is the hidden ideological leaning of the Mu'tazila.

The apparent meaning of His words ﴿and you forget what you associate⁠﴾ is that forgetting is literal, and it means heedlessness and unawareness of the idols. This is because when a person is overwhelmed by what he has no power to repel, his thoughts are stripped of everything except Allah, who removes that overwhelming affliction, so he nearly comes to cling to Allah alone and to be oblivious of anyone else, and thus he does not mention anyone other than Allah who is capable of removing what has overwhelmed him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "*And you forget what you associate*: and you dislike your gods." There is a distance in this. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "You leave them," and he had already stated this view; al-Zajjaj preceded him to it, saying: "You leave them, because you know that in reality they neither harm nor benefit." Al-Nahhas said: "It is like His words ﴿And We had already made a covenant with Adam before, but he forgot⁠﴾" (Ta-Ha: 115). It has been said: "They turn away with the turning away of one who forgets, out of despair of salvation from it before." The *ma* is a relative pronoun, meaning: "and you forget that which you associate." It has also been said that *ma* is verbal-nominal, meaning: "and you forget your association." The meaning of these clauses is: "Rather, there is no refuge for you except Allah Most High, and your idols are cast aside and forgotten," as Ibn 'Atiyya said.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 42–45:

﴿And We certainly sent [messengers] to communities before you, and We seized them with adversity and hardship, that perhaps they might humble themselves.﴾ This is a consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ). The habit of nations toward their messengers is denial and extreme hardness of hearts, to the point that when they are seized by calamities, they do not humble themselves before Allah, nor do they ask Him to remove them. These nations to whom Allah Almighty sent the messengers were more extreme in deviation, more stubborn, and more hardened than those to whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sent, when He addressed them with His saying: ﴿Say: "Have you seen...?"﴾ [al-An'am: 40], and so on. He informed that in times of crisis they call upon no one to remove them except Allah Almighty. (p-130) In the speech there is an ellipsis; the estimated meaning is: "And We certainly sent messengers to communities before you, so they denied, and We seized them." The explanation of al-ba'sa' (adversity) and al-darra' (hardship) has already been given. The expression of hope (al-taraji) here is with reference to humans; that is, if anyone saw what befell them, he would hope for their humbling themselves and their supplication to Allah for its removal. Al-akhdh (seizing) means holding with strength, force, and subjugation, and here it is a metaphor for the continuation of punishment and its persistence; the meaning is: We punished them in this world.

﴿Why, then, when Our might came upon them, did they not humble themselves?﴾ Here (law-la) is a particle of exhortation (tahdid), followed by the verb, either explicitly or implicitly, or separated from it by a complement of the verb, such as an object or an adverbial phrase, as in this verse, where (law-la) and (tadarra'u) are separated by (idh), which functions as a complement of (tadarra'u). The exhortation indicates that their humbling did not occur when the might came; its meaning is to express reproach toward a guilty absent party and to display the evil of his action, so that the addressee may feel regret over it. Attributing the coming (al-maji') to might (al-ba's) is a metaphor for its reaching them, and what is meant is the first signs of might and its indications.

﴿But their hearts became hard﴾: that is, they were hardened and endured the encounter with punishment, because of what Allah willed of their disbelief. The use of (lakin) here is appropriate, because the meaning is the absence of humbling at the coming of might and the presence of hardness indicating obstinacy and arrogance; thus (lakin) falls between two opposites, namely softness and hardness. Likewise, if hardness is an expression for disbelief, then by mentioning the cause the effect is expressed, and if humbling is an expression for faith, then by mentioning the cause the effect is expressed, it is also situated between two opposites. You say: "His heart hardened, so he disbelieved; and he believed, so he humbled himself."

﴿And Satan made attractive to them what they were doing﴾: It is possible that this sentence falls under the (istidrak) (corrective contrast), and it is possible that it is a new statement. The apparent is the first, so the cause of abandoning humbling is the hardness of their hearts and their admiration of their deeds, which Satan caused to be made attractive to them.

﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the gates of everything﴾: that is, when they abandoned admonition and restraint by what they had been reminded of regarding might, We led them on gradually by facilitating their worldly aims. He expressed this by His saying: ﴿We opened for them the gates of everything﴾, since it implies the comprehensiveness of goods and the attainment of desires.

﴿Until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly﴾: The meaning of these clauses is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And let not those who disbelieve think that Our giving them respite is good for them. We only give them respite that they may increase in sin﴾ [Al 'Imran: 178]. In the authentic hadith from Uqba ibn Amir, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If you see Allah giving servants what they wish despite their disobedience, then that is indeed a respite from Him for them," and then he recited: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of﴾, to the end of the verse. The gates (al-abwab) are a metaphor for the causes that Allah prepared for them, which necessitate the expansion of provision upon them. The vagueness in this generality is to magnify and exalt what was opened for them. The opening is limited by their rejoicing in what they were given, and their being seized suddenly is consequent upon their rejoicing; that is, their destruction unexpectedly, which is the most severe destruction, since no feeling of it had preceded, so that the soul could prepare to meet it. He tested them first with adversity and hardship, but they did not take admonition; then He moved them to what caused their joy through the abundance of blessings upon them, but this did not find in them any gratitude, nor did they intend thanks, nor did they incline to repentance; rather they attained nothing but joy at what was lavished upon them. Muhammad ibn al-Nadr al-Harithi said: These people were given respite for twenty years.

﴿Then they were in despair﴾: that is, astonished, wretched, unable to produce an answer. Ibn Amir read (fattahna) with a doubled ta', and the doubling is for intensifying the action. (Idha) here is the sudden (fuja'iyya), and according to the Kufan school it is a particle, and it is reported from Sibawayh that it is an adverb of place; and according to al-Riyashi it is an adverb of time. The governing element in it, if we say it is an adverb, is the predicate of the subject, meaning: "In that place they are in despair," that is, the place of their residence, and at that time they are in despair. The original meaning of (iblas) is lowering the gaze upon the arrival of retribution or the loss of blessing. Al-Hasan said: "Dejected." As-Suddi said: "Destroyed." Ibn Kaysan and Qutrub said: "Humbled." Ibn Abbas said: "Bewildered." Az-Zajjaj said: "Regretful." Ibn Jarir said: "The one who is silent when the proof is cut off."

﴿So the last remnant of the people who did wrong was cut off﴾: This is an expression for their annihilation by destruction; the meaning is: "So their remnant was cut off," and the cause of the annihilation is mentioned by naming the attribute, which is wrongdoing, here meaning disbelief. Al-dabir is that which follows a thing from behind; it is said: "The child followed the parent" (dabara al-walid al-walada yadburuhu), and "So-and-so was the last of the people" (dabara al-qawm dubüran wa dabaran) when he was their last. Umayya ibn Abi as-Salt said:

"They were uprooted by a punishment that reached their last remnant, so they could neither avert it nor defend themselves."

Abu Ubayda said: "The dabir of a people is their last member who follows them." Al-Asmai said: "Al-dabir is the origin; it is said: 'Allah cut off his dabir,' that is, removed his root." Ikrima read: (fa-qata'a dabira) with fatha on the qaf, ta' and ra', meaning "so Allah cut off," and this is an iltifat (shift), since it involves moving from the first-person pronoun to the third-person pronoun.

﴿And praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾: Az-Zamakhshari said: "It is a notification of the obligation of praising Allah at the destruction of wrongdoers, and that it is among the greatest blessings and most abundant portions." End. What appears is that when Allah sent the messengers to these nations, they denied and harmed them, and Allah tested them sometimes with calamity and sometimes with ease, but they did not believe, so He destroyed them, and the messengers were relieved of their evil and denial, and that became a blessing regarding the messengers, since Allah fulfilled His promise through their tongues by the destruction of the deniers. Therefore this whole action was fittingly concluded with praise to Him.

[There is also evidence] that their gods cannot avail them anything at all. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿if Allah took away your hearing and your sight﴾ is that the faculties of hearing and sight are actually removed, so the taking away is literal. The discussion of the singular "hearing" and the plural "sights," and of the sealing upon the hearts, has already been covered at the beginning of al-Baqarah, so there is no need to repeat it.

The first object of ﴿Tell me﴾ is omitted, and the estimated sense is: "Tell me your hearing and your sights, if Allah takes them away." The second object is the interrogative clause, as you say: "Tell me about Zayd, what is he doing?" We have established that this belongs to the category of i'mal (the grammatical principle of letting one of two governing verbs work on a shared object, the second verb being the one that governs it, while the first omits it). We have clarified how this works in the verse before this one. The pronoun in (bihi) ("with it") is in the singular, treating it as if it were like a demonstrative noun, as though it were said: "He brings you with that." Or the estimated sense is: "with what He took away and sealed upon." It has been said that it refers to hearing, explicitly, and that the hearts and sights are included in it. It has also been said that it refers to the guidance that the meaning indicates, because the taking away of hearing and sight and the sealing upon the hearts is the cause of misguidance and the blocking of the paths of guidance. As for (man ilahun ghayru Allah) ("who is a god other than Allah"), it is an interrogative whose meaning is to make them acknowledge that there is no other god besides Him, so attachment to anyone else does not benefit them. Al-Hawfi said: The particle of condition and what is joined to it are in a position of the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), and the governing element of the circumstantial clause is "Tell me," like His saying: "Strike him if he goes out," meaning "going out." The answer to the condition is what preceded it, of that which the interrogative hamzah has entered upon. End of quote. This parsing is a confusion.

"Unzur" ("look") is an address to the listener. The "variation of the signs": Muqatil said: We frighten them by taking away their hearing, sights and hearts, and by what was done to the earlier nations. Ibn Furak said: Its variation is that sometimes it comes with vengeance, sometimes with blessing, sometimes with encouragement, and sometimes with intimidation. It has been said: We follow up the proofs for them and strike examples for them. It has been said: We direct them toward origination, extinction and destruction. It has been said: the signs are [evidence] for the soundness of His Oneness and the truthfulness of His Prophet. Al-sadf and al-sudud mean turning away and aversion. Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 47–49:

﴿Say, "Have you considered: if the punishment of Allah came upon you suddenly or openly, would any be destroyed except the wrongdoing people?"﴾ This is a third threat. The first was with one of two things: the punishment or the Hour (al-sa'ah). The second was with seizing (al-akhdh) and sealing (al-khatm). The third is with the punishment alone. It was said: ﴿suddenly﴾ (baghtah) means unexpectedly, without any prior knowledge reaching you of it. And ﴿openly﴾ (jahrah) means that its signs appear to you and then it descends. Al-Hasan said: ﴿suddenly﴾ means at night, and ﴿openly﴾ means by day. Mujahid said: ﴿suddenly﴾ means unexpectedly while you are secure, and ﴿openly﴾ means while you are watching. Since baghtah includes the meaning of concealment, its being contrasted with jahrah is valid, and it was mentioned first because it is more deterrent than jahrah. The clause ﴿would any be destroyed﴾ (hal yuhlaku) carries the sense of negation, i.e., none will be destroyed except the wrongdoing people. For this reason, illa entered while it occupies the position of the second object of ara'aytakum, and the connecting pronoun is omitted, i.e., "would any be destroyed by it." The first object of ﴿ara'aytakum﴾ is omitted by the rule of al-i'mal (operating one of two verbs on a shared complement), for the reason we have established. Since the threat is severe, it combined the two particles of address in it. The address is to the disbelievers of Quraysh and the Arabs. Mention of wrongdoing is an indication of the cause of destruction, and the meaning is: "Would any be destroyed except you, because of your wrongdoing?" Ibn Muhaysin recited (hal yahlik) with the verb in the active voice.

﴿And We do not send the messengers except as bearers of good news and warners﴾ That is, bearers of good news of reward and warners of punishment. ﴿Bearers of good news and warners﴾ is in the accusative as circumstantial states (hal), and in them is the sense of causation, i.e., We sent them for giving good news and warning, not so that signs be demanded from them after the clarity of what they brought and the manifestation of its truth.

﴿So whoever believes and does righteousness﴾ That is, whoever affirms with his heart and makes good in his deeds.

﴿There will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.﴾ ﴿And those who deny Our signs, the punishment will touch them for what they used to defiantly disobey.﴾ He made the punishment "touching" as if it were a living thing that does to them whatever it wills of pains. Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash recited (yafsiqun) with a kasrah on the sin.

(p-133) Alqamah recited (numessihumu al-'adhab) with the nun, from amassa. Al-A'mash assimilated al-'adhab bima as Abu 'Amr did. Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash recited (yafsiqun) with a kasrah on the sin.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 6, Verse 50:**

﴿Say: I do not tell you that with me are the treasures of God, nor do I know the unseen, nor do I tell you that I am an angel. I only follow what is revealed to me.﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, I do not claim what the minds find improbable, that a human being could possess the treasures of God, which are His distribution among creation and His provisions, or knowledge of the unseen, or that I am one of the angels, who are the noblest kind God created, the most excellent, and the closest in rank to Him. That is, I have not claimed divinity, nor angelhood, because there is no rank higher than the rank of the angels after divinity, so that you would find my claim improbable and reject it. I only claim what is similar to what many humans have, which is prophethood. End of quote. As for what he said, that the meaning is "I tell you: I am not a god, so I do not possess its attributes, such as having its treasures with me or knowledge of the unseen," this is the view of al-Tabari. The more apparent meaning is that he means he is a human being, with nothing of God's treasures in his possession, nor of His power, and he knows nothing of what is hidden from him. This is what Ibn Atiyyah said. As for al-Zamakhshari's statement about the angels, that they are the noblest kind God created, the most excellent, and the closest in rank, it follows the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazilites), that the angel is the most excellent of God's creation. Al-Juba'i (al-Jubba'i) used this verse as evidence that the angels are more excellent than the prophets, saying: "Because the meaning of the verse is, I do not claim a rank above my rank. Had the angel not been more excellent, this would not be valid." Al-Qadi said: If the purpose of what he negated is the way of humility, then the closer view is that it indicates the angel is more excellent. If the negation is of his power over actions that only the angels can perform, it does not indicate that they are more excellent. End of quote. We have discussed this point at His words: ﴿nor the angels who are brought near﴾ [al-Nisa': 172]. Ibn Atiyyah said: The force of the wording in this verse suggests that the angel is more excellent than the human, but this does not necessarily follow from this context. What necessarily follows from it is that the angel holds a greater position in their souls and is closer to God. Preference is conveyed by the meaning in a subtle way, and it is apparent from other verses, though it is a matter of disagreement. By ﴿what is revealed﴾ he means the Qur'an and everything else the angel brings. That is, in this there are lessons and signs for whoever reflects and considers. End of quote.

Al-Kalbi said: ﴿the treasures of God﴾ are His decrees, such as enriching the poor and impoverishing the rich. Muqatil said: they are mercy and punishment. It was also said: they are His signs. And it was said: they are all of this together, based on His words: ﴿And there is nothing but that its treasures are with Us﴾ [al-Hijr: 21]. It was said: these three answers respond to what the polytheists asked. The first answers their saying: "If you are a messenger, then ask God to widen the treasures of this world for us." The second answers their saying: "If you are a messenger, then tell us what will happen in the future of benefits and harms, so that we may prepare to obtain the former and repel the latter." The third answers their saying: "What is wrong with this messenger, that he eats food and walks in the markets?" End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): what is the grammatical position (i'rab, the analysis of the case endings and syntactic function of words) of ﴿nor do I know the unseen﴾? I say: it is in the accusative case, coordinated with the position of His words ﴿the treasures of God﴾, because it is part of what is said, as if he said: "I do not say to you this statement, nor this statement." End of quote. What he said is not necessarily fixed. Rather, the apparent view is that it is coordinated with ﴿I do not say﴾, not a complement of it. He was commanded to inform about himself through these three sentences, so they are governed by the command, which is ﴿Say﴾. He varied the object of the negation: he negated his saying ﴿with me are the treasures of God﴾ and his saying ﴿I am an angel﴾, and he negated knowledge of the unseen. He did not say ﴿I do not say that I know the unseen﴾, because his not having the treasures of God, the provisions and distribution of His servants, is known to all people. So he negated his claim to that. And his being in human form is also known to them, through their knowledge of his birth and upbringing among them. So he also negated his claim to that. He did not negate these two from their root, because the absence of these from their root is known to them. So he negated that he would deceive them in claiming something they know to be false with certainty.

Since knowledge of the unseen is something that can appear through a human being, and many people claim it, such as fortune-tellers, sand-diviners, and astrologers, and since he had informed about some unseen matters and what he reported matched, he negated knowledge of the unseen from its root, saying ﴿nor do I know the unseen﴾, explicitly affirming pure servanthood and dependence. What he said of unseen matters comes only from the revelation sent to him, not from himself, so he said ﴿I only follow what is revealed to me﴾, as God related about him: ﴿Had I known the unseen, I would have acquired much good, and no harm would have touched me﴾ [al-A'raf: 188]. And as transmitted from him, peace be upon him: "I do not know what is behind this wall, except that my Lord informs me." This negation came in a progressive order. First he negated what all people desire of provisions, which are the sustenance of bodily life. Then he negated second what noble souls aspire to, such as knowing what they do not know and learning what will happen in the future. Then he negated third what is specific to his own self, the attribute of the angels, which is distinct from the attribute of humanity. He ascended in negation from general to specific to more specific. Then he confined what he is in all his states by his saying ﴿I only follow what is revealed to me﴾, meaning: I am a follower of what God has revealed, not legislating anything from myself. Its apparent meaning is a proof for those who deny analogy (qiyas, reasoning by analogy in law).

﴿Say: Are the blind and the seeing equal?﴾ That is, the one who looks and reflects on the signs is not equal to the disbelieving turner-away who neglects to look. Ibn Abbas said: the disbeliever and the believer. Ibn Jubayr said: the misguided and the guided. It was also said: the ignorant and the knowledgeable. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is an example for the misguided and the guided. It may also be an example for one who follows what is revealed to him and one who does not follow it, or for one who claims the straight path, which is prophethood, and one who claims the impossible, which is divinity and angelhood.

﴿Will you not then reflect?﴾ This is an offer and urging, its meaning being a command. That is: so reflect, and do not be misguided like the blind. Or: reflect, so that you will know that I only follow what is revealed to me. Or: so that you will know that I do not claim what is not fitting for a human being. [p. 134]

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 51–52 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And warn thereby those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord﴾. When He had informed that he (the Prophet ﷺ) follows only what is revealed to him, God, exalted is He, commanded him to warn by it, so He said: ﴿And warn thereby﴾, i.e., by what has been revealed to you. It was also said: the pronoun refers to God, i.e., by the punishment of God. It was also said: it refers to the Gathering (al-hashr), and he is commanded to warn all creatures. The warning is specifically directed here at those who fear the Gathering, because it is the most likely place for faith. It is as if it were said: as for the disbelieving rejecters, leave them and their opinion, and warn with the Qur'an those whose faith is hoped for. Abu Salih reported from Ibn Abbas that this verse was revealed concerning the freed slaves among them: Bilal, Suhayb, Khabbab, Ammar, Mihja', Salman, Amir ibn Fuhayra, and Salim, the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfa. The apparent sense of His words ﴿those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord﴾ is the generality of whoever fears the Gathering and believes in the Resurrection, whether Muslim, Jew (p. 135) or Christian. It is therefore not restricted to Muslims who affirm the Resurrection, except that they are negligent in action, so he warns them with what has been revealed to him, ﴿so that they may become mindful﴾, i.e., enter the group of the people of taqwa (God-consciousness). It does not (apply) to the People of the Book, nor to some of the polytheists, of whom it is known from their state that when they hear of the Resurrection they fear it may be true and that they will perish. Thus they are among those in whom the warning is hoped to take effect, unlike the obstinate rebels among them. The word ﴿fear﴾ remains in its literal sense, i.e., they fear what follows from the Gathering, namely being held to account for their sins, whereas the Gathering itself is certain. Al-Tabari said: "fear" here means "know," and the meaning of ﴿to their Lord﴾ is "to the recompense of their Lord," i.e., His promise. The anthropomorphists (al-mujassima) have clung to this verse, claiming that God is in a place, in a specific direction and a particular location, because the word ﴿ilā﴾ (to) indicates the end of a limit.

﴿They will have no protector or intercessor besides Him﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to ﴿yuḥsharū﴾ (be gathered), meaning: they fear they will be gathered unaided and without anyone to intercede for them. This circumstance is necessary, because everyone is gathered, so the fear is of being gathered in this state. Ibn Atiyya said: if we take it as part of the fear, it is in the position of a circumstantial clause, i.e., they fear being gathered in the state of one who has no protector or intercessor. It is then specific to the believing Muslims, because the Jews and Christians claim that they have intercessors and that they are the sons of God, and similar falsehoods. If, however, we take it as an informational statement from God about the state of that Day, then it is general to Muslims and the People of the Book.

﴿so that they may become mindful﴾. This is a hope for the realization of their God-consciousness, if the warning takes effect.

﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face﴾. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas said: this was revealed concerning six of us: myself, Ibn Mas'ud, Suhayb, Ammar, al-Miqdad, and Bilal. The Quraysh said: "We will not accept being followers of these people, so drive them away from you," and so it was revealed. Khabbab ibn al-Aratt said: it was revealed about us. We were weak in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), who taught us morning and evening what benefits us. Al-Aqra' ibn Habis and Uyayna ibn Husayn said: "We are among the nobles of our people, and we dislike that they should see us with them, so drive them away when we sit with you," and so it was revealed. Khabbab said: "We came to him while he was saying: ﴿Peace be upon you; your Lord has prescribed mercy upon Himself﴾ [al-An'am: 54], and we drew close to him until we placed our knees against his knee." This has a problem, because the surah is Meccan, and those nobles were not warned except in Medina. In another report from Khabbab: "Whenever he wished to rise, he rose and left us, so God, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening﴾ [al-Kahf: 28], and so he would sit with us, and when the time came for him to rise, we rose and left him until he got up." Al-Awfi reported from Ibn Abbas that some of the nobles said: "We will believe in you, but when we pray behind you, put these people who are with you at the back, so that they pray behind us." Thus the "driving away" means their being placed at the back of the row, not their being expelled from the gathering. These causes of revelation have been reported with additions and omissions, but their substance is that some noble Arabs asked the Messenger (ﷺ) to drive away the poor believers from him, and so this was revealed. When God commanded the warning of those who are not mindful, "so that they may become mindful," He followed this with bringing near the mindful and honouring them, forbidding him to drive them away, and describing them as those whose outward conduct conforms to their inward state in calling upon their Lord and in the sincerity of their intentions. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿they call upon their Lord﴾ is that they ask Him, turn to Him, and aim at Him with supplication and longing. ﴿Morning and evening﴾ is an expression for continuous time, and these two are not meant in their particular times, just as you say "Praise be to God at dawn and at dusk," meaning in every state. So "morning" stands for the daytime and "evening" for the night. Or they are singled out because occupation is dominant among people in these two times, and whoever is in these two times and is dominated by the remembrance and supplication of God is more dominated by it when free. It was also said: the intended "supplication" is the obligatory prayer. Al-Hasan and Muqatil said: it is the prayer at Mecca which was performed twice a day, morning and evening. Qatada and Mujahid in one report said: it is the Dawn and Afternoon prayers. Ibn Umar, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid in one report, and Ibrahim said: it is the five daily prayers. Some storytellers (qussas) said: it means gathering with them morning and evening, but Ibn al-Musayyab, Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Amra, and others rejected this, saying: the verse concerns the prayers in congregation. Abu Ja'far said: it means the recitation of the Qur'an and learning it. Al-Dahhak said: worship. Ibrahim in one report said: the remembrance of God. Al-Zajjaj said: calling upon God, exalted is He, with monotheism and sincerity, and worshipping Him.

The majority read ﴿bi-l-ghadāh﴾ (with the morning). Ibn Amir, Abu Abd al-Rahman, Malik ibn Dinar, al-Hasan, Nasr ibn Asim, and Abu Raja al-Utaridi read ﴿bi-l-ghuduwa﴾. It was also reported from Abu Abd al-Rahman: ﴿bi-l-ghudu﴾ without the ending hā'. Ibn Abi Abla read ﴿bi-l-ghadawāt wa-l-ʿashiyyāt﴾ with the alif in both, in the plural. The well-known form of غَدْوَة (ghadwa) is definite by being a proper noun (ʿalamiyya) and not declined (mamnūʿ al-ṣarf). Al-Farra' said: I heard Abu al-Jarrah say: "I have never seen anything like غَدْوَة," meaning the morning of his day.
