He said: do you not see that the Arabs do not add to it (the genitive), so the definite article (al-) does not enter it either; they only say: "I came to you غَدَاةَ الخَمِيس (on the morning of Thursday)." End of quotation. Sibawayh and al-Khalil related that some of them use it as an indefinite, saying رَأَيْتُهُ غَدْوَةً with tanwin, and on this dialect Ibn Amir and those mentioned with him read; in that case it is like فَيْنَةَ. Abu Zayd related: "I met him فَيْنَةَ (at a time), not declined," and "I met him الفَيْنَةَ بَعْدَ الفَيْنَةِ," i.e., the time after time. Since this dialect was obscure to Abu Ubayd, he thought badly of those who recited this reading and said: "We only see that Ibn Amir and al-Sulami recited that reading by following the script; the presence of the waw in the written text is no evidence for reciting it that way, because they wrote الصَّلاة and الزَّكاة with a waw, while their pronunciation is without it, and likewise الغَداة. On this basis we found the Arabs." End of quotation. This is ignorance on Abu Ubayd's part of this dialect, which Sibawayh and al-Khalil recorded and which these reciters used. How could it be thought of these reciters that they recited thus only because it is written with a waw in the mushaf (the written codex)? Recitation is only a transmitted sunna that is followed. Moreover, Ibn Amir was a pure Arab who existed before any lahn (grammatical error) appeared, because he recited the Qur'an to Uthman ibn Affan. Nasr ibn Asim is one of the Arab imams in grammar, and he was among those who took the science of grammar from Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali, the originator of the science of grammar. Al-Hasan al-Basri was of such eloquence that his speech is cited as evidence. How then can these be thought to have committed lahn? End of quotation. They were deceived by the script of the mushaf. But Abu Ubayda was ignorant of this dialect and of the transmission of this reading, so he dared to reject it, may God pardon him.

The apparent sense is that ﴿al-ʿashiyy﴾ is a synonym of ﴿al-ʿashiyya﴾, and you can see His words: ﴿when there were displayed before him in the evening the poised, swift steeds﴾ [Sad: 31]. It was also said: it is the plural of ʿashiyya. The meaning of ﴿seeking His face﴾ is that they sincerely direct their intentions to Him in their worship. The essence and reality of a thing is expressed by "face." Ibn Abbas said: they seek the reward of God. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause. Whoever affirmed organs for God has used His words ﴿His face﴾ as evidence, exalted is God far above that by a great exaltation.

﴿You are not accountable for their reckoning at all, nor are they accountable for yours at all﴾. Al-Hasan and the majority said: "reckoning" here means the reckoning of deeds. It was also said: it means the reckoning of provision, i.e., you do not provide for them and they do not provide for you; this was related by al-Tabari. Al-Zamakhshari said: like His words: ﴿Their reckoning is only with my Lord﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 113]. That is because they (the disbelievers) disparaged their religion and their sincerity, so He said: ﴿You are not accountable for their reckoning at all﴾, after testifying for them to their sincerity and to their intention of seeking the face of God in their deeds. Even if the matter is as they say in God's sight, you are only bound to observe the outward and to adopt the conduct of the mindful. If they have an inward state that is not pleasing, their reckoning is incumbent upon them alone and does not extend to you, just as your reckoning is upon you and does not extend to them, like His words: ﴿no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164]. End of quotation. What he mentioned of the alternation in his words "even if the matter is as they say," up to the end, is not possible, because God has informed that they ﴿call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face﴾, and God's information is the truth about which there is no doubt. So one cannot say concerning them "even if the matter is as they say, and even if they have an inward state that is not pleasing," because that is a supposition contrary to what God, exalted is He, has informed about the sincerity of their inward states and intentions toward Him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): Was not His words ﴿You are not accountable for their reckoning at all﴾ sufficient, that ﴿nor are they accountable for yours at all﴾ had to be added to it? (I answer): The two clauses have been made as one clause, and their purpose is one meaning, which is what is intended in His words ﴿no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164]. This meaning is not complete except by the two clauses together, as if it were said: neither you nor they shall be held to account for the reckoning of the other. End of quotation. His words "as if it were said: neither you nor they shall be held to account for the reckoning of the other" is a non-Arabic construction. The pronoun here cannot be returned as third person or second person. If it is returned as third person, there is no preceding singular third-person noun to which it refers; what precedes is only ﴿nor they﴾, and it cannot refer back to it on the belief that the singular is sufficient in place of the plural, because the construction would become "for the reckoning of their companion." If it is returned as second person, there is no preceding second-person addressee to which it refers; what precedes is only "neither you shall be held to account," and it cannot refer back to it because it is a second person, so it cannot be referred to as third person. Even if you made it second person, the construction would still not be correct. The correction of this construction is to say: "Neither shall each one of you nor of them be held to account for the reckoning of the other," or "You shall not be held to account for their reckoning, nor they for yours," or "Neither you nor they shall be held to account for your reckoning," where the address (khitab) overrides the third person, as you say: "You and Zayd are striking." The apparent sense is that all the pronouns refer to ﴿those who call﴾. It was also said: the pronoun in ﴿their reckoning﴾ and in (upon them) refers to the polytheists, and the two clauses would be a parenthetical insertion between the prohibition and its answer. Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is: "They shall not be held to account for your reckoning, nor shall you be held to account for theirs, so that their faith concerns you and the eagerness for it moves you to drive away the believers." Ibn Atiyya said: it is possible that the pronoun in ﴿their reckoning﴾ and in (upon them) refers to the disbelievers who wanted to drive away the believers, i.e., "there is nothing upon you from them, whether they believed or disbelieved, so that you drive these away in order to please them." The pronoun in ﴿you drive them away﴾ refers to the weak among the believers. This interpretation is supported by the fact that what follows the fā' (so) is always the cause of what precedes it, and that does not become clear if all the pronouns refer to the believers. Al-Tabari related that the reckoning here is only about worldly provision, i.e., you do not provide for them and they do not provide for you. He said: on this interpretation all the pronouns refer to the believers. End of quotation.

The "min" in ﴿min ḥisābihim﴾ and in ﴿min ḥisābika﴾ is partitive (mubaʿḍiyya), and in ﴿min ḥisābihim﴾ it stands in the accusative position of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). Its dhū al-ḥāl (the noun it describes) is "min shay'" (anything), because if ﴿min ḥisābihim﴾ had come after it, it would have been in the position of a qualifier (naʿt) of "shay'." Since it came first, it became accusative as a ḥāl. The "ʿalayka" in ﴿mā ʿalayka﴾ is in the position of the predicate (khabar) of "mā," if "mā" is Ḥijāzī (the Hijazi usage of negative "mā," which makes it work like "laysa"). We permit placing the predicate of this "mā" in the middle when it is an adverbial phrase or a prepositional phrase. Otherwise it is in the position of the predicate of the subject (mubtadaʾ), if we do not permit that, or if we hold that "mā" is Tamīmī (the Tamimi usage, in which "mā" does not govern the predicate).

As for ﴿min ḥisābika﴾, it has been said that it stands in the accusative position of a ḥāl. This is weak, because when the element that governs the ḥāl carries the sense of a verb, the ḥāl may not be placed before it, especially when it precedes both its governor and its dhū al-ḥāl.

It has also been said that the predicate may be ﴿min ḥisābika﴾, and "ʿalayhim" is a qualifier (ṣifa) of "shay'" that came before it, so it became accusative as a ḥāl. This is weak, because "ʿalayhim" is the focus of the meaning (maḥaṭṭ al-fāʾida), so it is more likely to be the predicate. On this view, "min ḥisābika" is an explanatory specification (tabyīn), neither a ḥāl nor a predicate.

Observe the care He shows for His Prophet and the honour He gives him by addressing him, for He began with him in both clauses together. He said: ﴿mā ʿalayka min ḥisābihim min shay'﴾ ("You bear no accountability for their reckoning in any way"), then He said: ﴿wa-mā min ḥisābika ʿalayhim min shay'﴾ ("and none of their reckoning is upon you in any way"). So He placed the address to Him first in both clauses. According to the first structure, if it were considered, the second structure would be "wa-mā ʿalayhim min ḥisābika min shay'," but He placed the address to the Messenger and his affair first, to honour him over them and to show care in addressing him. In these two clauses there is also radd al-ʿajuz ʿala al-ṣadr (the device of returning the end of a phrase to its beginning), and an example of it is the poet's words:

"The one you made lawful is not made lawful, and the one you made unlawful is not made unlawful."

As for ﴿fa-taṭrudahum fa-takūna mina al-ẓālimīn﴾ ("so that you would drive them away and be among the wrongdoers"): the apparent view is that His saying ﴿fa-taṭrudahum﴾ is the answer (jawāb) to His saying ﴿mā ʿalayka min ḥisābihim min shay'﴾, and the accusative here is in one of the two senses of the accusative in your saying: "mā taʾtīnā fa-tuḥaddithanā" (you do not come to us so that you speak to us). One of the two senses of this is: "You do not come to us speaking; you only come and do not speak." This meaning is not valid in the verse. The second sense is: "You do not come to us, so how would you speak to us?", meaning: this does not happen, so how could this happen? This second meaning is the one that is valid in the verse: that their reckoning is not upon you, so that the driving away would have an effect. They gave the answer to "that it be ﴿fa-taṭrudahum﴾" as an answer to a negation without explaining how it could serve as an answer.

The apparent view of His saying ﴿fa-takūna mina al-ẓālimīn﴾ is that it is conjoined (maʿṭūf) to ﴿fa-taṭrudahum﴾. The meaning is the report that their reckoning is not upon him, and that driving them away and the wrongdoing that results from driving them away do not occur. They also permitted that "fa-takūna" be an answer to the prohibition in His saying ﴿wa-lā taṭrudi﴾ ("and do not drive away"), like His saying ﴿lā taftarū ʿalā Allāhi kadhiban fa-yusḥitakum bi-ʿadhāb﴾ ("Do not invent a lie against God, lest He destroy you with a punishment") [Ṭā-Hā: 61]. In that case the two clauses, and the answer to the first, form a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ) between the prohibition and its answer. The meaning of "mina al-ẓālimīn" is: among those who place a thing in other than its proper place.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 51–52 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And warn thereby those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord﴾. When He had informed that he (the Prophet ﷺ) follows only what is revealed to him, God, exalted is He, commanded him to warn by it, so He said: ﴿And warn thereby﴾, i.e., by what has been revealed to you. It was also said: the pronoun refers to God, i.e., by the punishment of God. It was also said: it refers to the Gathering (al-hashr), and he is commanded to warn all creatures. The warning is specifically directed here at those who fear the Gathering, because it is the most likely place for faith. It is as if it were said: as for the disbelieving rejecters, leave them and their opinion, and warn with the Qur'an those whose faith is hoped for. Abu Salih reported from Ibn Abbas that this verse was revealed concerning the freed slaves among them: Bilal, Suhayb, Khabbab, Ammar, Mihja', Salman, Amir ibn Fuhayra, and Salim, the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfa. The apparent sense of His words ﴿those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord﴾ is the generality of whoever fears the Gathering and believes in the Resurrection, whether Muslim, Jew (p. 135) or Christian. It is therefore not restricted to Muslims who affirm the Resurrection, except that they are negligent in action, so he warns them with what has been revealed to him, ﴿so that they may become mindful﴾, i.e., enter the group of the people of taqwa (God-consciousness). It does not (apply) to the People of the Book, nor to some of the polytheists, of whom it is known from their state that when they hear of the Resurrection they fear it may be true and that they will perish. Thus they are among those in whom the warning is hoped to take effect, unlike the obstinate rebels among them. The word ﴿fear﴾ remains in its literal sense, i.e., they fear what follows from the Gathering, namely being held to account for their sins, whereas the Gathering itself is certain. Al-Tabari said: "fear" here means "know," and the meaning of ﴿to their Lord﴾ is "to the recompense of their Lord," i.e., His promise. The anthropomorphists (al-mujassima) have clung to this verse, claiming that God is in a place, in a specific direction and a particular location, because the word ﴿ilā﴾ (to) indicates the end of a limit.

﴿They will have no protector or intercessor besides Him﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to ﴿yuḥsharū﴾ (be gathered), meaning: they fear they will be gathered unaided and without anyone to intercede for them. This circumstance is necessary, because everyone is gathered, so the fear is of being gathered in this state. Ibn Atiyya said: if we take it as part of the fear, it is in the position of a circumstantial clause, i.e., they fear being gathered in the state of one who has no protector or intercessor. It is then specific to the believing Muslims, because the Jews and Christians claim that they have intercessors and that they are the sons of God, and similar falsehoods. If, however, we take it as an informational statement from God about the state of that Day, then it is general to Muslims and the People of the Book.

﴿so that they may become mindful﴾. This is a hope for the realization of their God-consciousness, if the warning takes effect.

﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face﴾. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas said: this was revealed concerning six of us: myself, Ibn Mas'ud, Suhayb, Ammar, al-Miqdad, and Bilal. The Quraysh said: "We will not accept being followers of these people, so drive them away from you," and so it was revealed. Khabbab ibn al-Aratt said: it was revealed about us. We were weak in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), who taught us morning and evening what benefits us. Al-Aqra' ibn Habis and Uyayna ibn Husayn said: "We are among the nobles of our people, and we dislike that they should see us with them, so drive them away when we sit with you," and so it was revealed. Khabbab said: "We came to him while he was saying: ﴿Peace be upon you; your Lord has prescribed mercy upon Himself﴾ [al-An'am: 54], and we drew close to him until we placed our knees against his knee." This has a problem, because the surah is Meccan, and those nobles were not warned except in Medina. In another report from Khabbab: "Whenever he wished to rise, he rose and left us, so God, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening﴾ [al-Kahf: 28], and so he would sit with us, and when the time came for him to rise, we rose and left him until he got up." Al-Awfi reported from Ibn Abbas that some of the nobles said: "We will believe in you, but when we pray behind you, put these people who are with you at the back, so that they pray behind us." Thus the "driving away" means their being placed at the back of the row, not their being expelled from the gathering. These causes of revelation have been reported with additions and omissions, but their substance is that some noble Arabs asked the Messenger (ﷺ) to drive away the poor believers from him, and so this was revealed. When God commanded the warning of those who are not mindful, "so that they may become mindful," He followed this with bringing near the mindful and honouring them, forbidding him to drive them away, and describing them as those whose outward conduct conforms to their inward state in calling upon their Lord and in the sincerity of their intentions. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿they call upon their Lord﴾ is that they ask Him, turn to Him, and aim at Him with supplication and longing. ﴿Morning and evening﴾ is an expression for continuous time, and these two are not meant in their particular times, just as you say "Praise be to God at dawn and at dusk," meaning in every state. So "morning" stands for the daytime and "evening" for the night. Or they are singled out because occupation is dominant among people in these two times, and whoever is in these two times and is dominated by the remembrance and supplication of God is more dominated by it when free. It was also said: the intended "supplication" is the obligatory prayer. Al-Hasan and Muqatil said: it is the prayer at Mecca which was performed twice a day, morning and evening. Qatada and Mujahid in one report said: it is the Dawn and Afternoon prayers. Ibn Umar, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid in one report, and Ibrahim said: it is the five daily prayers. Some storytellers (qussas) said: it means gathering with them morning and evening, but Ibn al-Musayyab, Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Amra, and others rejected this, saying: the verse concerns the prayers in congregation. Abu Ja'far said: it means the recitation of the Qur'an and learning it. Al-Dahhak said: worship. Ibrahim in one report said: the remembrance of God. Al-Zajjaj said: calling upon God, exalted is He, with monotheism and sincerity, and worshipping Him.

The majority read ﴿bi-l-ghadāh﴾ (with the morning). Ibn Amir, Abu Abd al-Rahman, Malik ibn Dinar, al-Hasan, Nasr ibn Asim, and Abu Raja al-Utaridi read ﴿bi-l-ghuduwa﴾. It was also reported from Abu Abd al-Rahman: ﴿bi-l-ghudu﴾ without the ending hā'. Ibn Abi Abla read ﴿bi-l-ghadawāt wa-l-ʿashiyyāt﴾ with the alif in both, in the plural. The well-known form of غَدْوَة (ghadwa) is definite by being a proper noun (ʿalamiyya) and not declined (mamnūʿ al-ṣarf). Al-Farra' said: I heard Abu al-Jarrah say: "I have never seen anything like غَدْوَة," meaning the morning of his day. He said: do you not see that the Arabs do not add to it (the genitive), so the definite article (al-) does not enter it either; they only say: "I came to you غَدَاةَ الخَمِيس (on the morning of Thursday)." End of quotation. Sibawayh and al-Khalil related that some of them use it as an indefinite, saying رَأَيْتُهُ غَدْوَةً with tanwin, and on this dialect Ibn Amir and those mentioned with him read; in that case it is like فَيْنَةَ. Abu Zayd related: "I met him فَيْنَةَ (at a time), not declined," and "I met him الفَيْنَةَ بَعْدَ الفَيْنَةِ," i.e., the time after time. Since this dialect was obscure to Abu Ubayd, he thought badly of those who recited this reading and said: "We only see that Ibn Amir and al-Sulami recited that reading by following the script; the presence of the waw in the written text is no evidence for reciting it that way, because they wrote الصَّلاة and الزَّكاة with a waw, while their pronunciation is without it, and likewise الغَداة. On this basis we found the Arabs." End of quotation. This is ignorance on Abu Ubayd's part of this dialect, which Sibawayh and al-Khalil recorded and which these reciters used. How could it be thought of these reciters that they recited thus only because it is written with a waw in the mushaf (the written codex)? Recitation is only a transmitted sunna that is followed. Moreover, Ibn Amir was a pure Arab who existed before any lahn (grammatical error) appeared, because he recited the Qur'an to Uthman ibn Affan. Nasr ibn Asim is one of the Arab imams in grammar, and he was among those who took the science of grammar from Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali, the originator of the science of grammar. Al-Hasan al-Basri was of such eloquence that his speech is cited as evidence. How then can these be thought to have committed lahn? End of quotation. They were deceived by the script of the mushaf. But Abu Ubayda was ignorant of this dialect and of the transmission of this reading, so he dared to reject it, may God pardon him.

The apparent sense is that ﴿al-ʿashiyy﴾ is a synonym of ﴿al-ʿashiyya﴾, and you can see His words: ﴿when there were displayed before him in the evening the poised, swift steeds﴾ [Sad: 31]. It was also said: it is the plural of ʿashiyya. The meaning of ﴿seeking His face﴾ is that they sincerely direct their intentions to Him in their worship. The essence and reality of a thing is expressed by "face." Ibn Abbas said: they seek the reward of God. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause. Whoever affirmed organs for God has used His words ﴿His face﴾ as evidence, exalted is God far above that by a great exaltation.

﴿You are not accountable for their reckoning at all, nor are they accountable for yours at all﴾. Al-Hasan and the majority said: "reckoning" here means the reckoning of deeds. It was also said: it means the reckoning of provision, i.e., you do not provide for them and they do not provide for you; this was related by al-Tabari. Al-Zamakhshari said: like His words: ﴿Their reckoning is only with my Lord﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 113]. That is because they (the disbelievers) disparaged their religion and their sincerity, so He said: ﴿You are not accountable for their reckoning at all﴾, after testifying for them to their sincerity and to their intention of seeking the face of God in their deeds. Even if the matter is as they say in God's sight, you are only bound to observe the outward and to adopt the conduct of the mindful. If they have an inward state that is not pleasing, their reckoning is incumbent upon them alone and does not extend to you, just as your reckoning is upon you and does not extend to them, like His words: ﴿no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164]. End of quotation. What he mentioned of the alternation in his words "even if the matter is as they say," up to the end, is not possible, because God has informed that they ﴿call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face﴾, and God's information is the truth about which there is no doubt. So one cannot say concerning them "even if the matter is as they say, and even if they have an inward state that is not pleasing," because that is a supposition contrary to what God, exalted is He, has informed about the sincerity of their inward states and intentions toward Him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): Was not His words ﴿You are not accountable for their reckoning at all﴾ sufficient, that ﴿nor are they accountable for yours at all﴾ had to be added to it? (I answer): The two clauses have been made as one clause, and their purpose is one meaning, which is what is intended in His words ﴿no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164]. This meaning is not complete except by the two clauses together, as if it were said: neither you nor they shall be held to account for the reckoning of the other. End of quotation. His words "as if it were said: neither you nor they shall be held to account for the reckoning of the other" is a non-Arabic construction. The pronoun here cannot be returned as third person or second person. If it is returned as third person, there is no preceding singular third-person noun to which it refers; what precedes is only ﴿nor they﴾, and it cannot refer back to it on the belief that the singular is sufficient in place of the plural, because the construction would become "for the reckoning of their companion." If it is returned as second person, there is no preceding second-person addressee to which it refers; what precedes is only "neither you shall be held to account," and it cannot refer back to it because it is a second person, so it cannot be referred to as third person. Even if you made it second person, the construction would still not be correct. The correction of this construction is to say: "Neither shall each one of you nor of them be held to account for the reckoning of the other," or "You shall not be held to account for their reckoning, nor they for yours," or "Neither you nor they shall be held to account for your reckoning," where the address (khitab) overrides the third person, as you say: "You and Zayd are striking." The apparent sense is that all the pronouns refer to ﴿those who call﴾. It was also said: the pronoun in ﴿their reckoning﴾ and in (upon them) refers to the polytheists, and the two clauses would be a parenthetical insertion between the prohibition and its answer. Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is: "They shall not be held to account for your reckoning, nor shall you be held to account for theirs, so that their faith concerns you and the eagerness for it moves you to drive away the believers." Ibn Atiyya said: it is possible that the pronoun in ﴿their reckoning﴾ and in (upon them) refers to the disbelievers who wanted to drive away the believers, i.e., "there is nothing upon you from them, whether they believed or disbelieved, so that you drive these away in order to please them." The pronoun in ﴿you drive them away﴾ refers to the weak among the believers. This interpretation is supported by the fact that what follows the fā' (so) is always the cause of what precedes it, and that does not become clear if all the pronouns refer to the believers. Al-Tabari related that the reckoning here is only about worldly provision, i.e., you do not provide for them and they do not provide for you. He said: on this interpretation all the pronouns refer to the believers. End of quotation.

The "min" in ﴿min ḥisābihim﴾ and in ﴿min ḥisābika﴾ is partitive (mubaʿḍiyya), and in ﴿min ḥisābihim﴾ it stands in the accusative position of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). Its dhū al-ḥāl (the noun it describes) is "min shay'" (anything), because if ﴿min ḥisābihim﴾ had come after it, it would have been in the position of a qualifier (naʿt) of "shay'." Since it came first, it became accusative as a ḥāl. The "ʿalayka" in ﴿mā ʿalayka﴾ is in the position of the predicate (khabar) of "mā," if "mā" is Ḥijāzī (the Hijazi usage of negative "mā," which makes it work like "laysa"). We permit placing the predicate of this "mā" in the middle when it is an adverbial phrase or a prepositional phrase. Otherwise it is in the position of the predicate of the subject (mubtadaʾ), if we do not permit that, or if we hold that "mā" is Tamīmī (the Tamimi usage, in which "mā" does not govern the predicate).

As for ﴿min ḥisābika﴾, it has been said that it stands in the accusative position of a ḥāl. This is weak, because when the element that governs the ḥāl carries the sense of a verb, the ḥāl may not be placed before it, especially when it precedes both its governor and its dhū al-ḥāl.

It has also been said that the predicate may be ﴿min ḥisābika﴾, and "ʿalayhim" is a qualifier (ṣifa) of "shay'" that came before it, so it became accusative as a ḥāl. This is weak, because "ʿalayhim" is the focus of the meaning (maḥaṭṭ al-fāʾida), so it is more likely to be the predicate. On this view, "min ḥisābika" is an explanatory specification (tabyīn), neither a ḥāl nor a predicate.

Observe the care He shows for His Prophet and the honour He gives him by addressing him, for He began with him in both clauses together. He said: ﴿mā ʿalayka min ḥisābihim min shay'﴾ ("You bear no accountability for their reckoning in any way"), then He said: ﴿wa-mā min ḥisābika ʿalayhim min shay'﴾ ("and none of their reckoning is upon you in any way"). So He placed the address to Him first in both clauses. According to the first structure, if it were considered, the second structure would be "wa-mā ʿalayhim min ḥisābika min shay'," but He placed the address to the Messenger and his affair first, to honour him over them and to show care in addressing him. In these two clauses there is also radd al-ʿajuz ʿala al-ṣadr (the device of returning the end of a phrase to its beginning), and an example of it is the poet's words:

"The one you made lawful is not made lawful, and the one you made unlawful is not made unlawful."

As for ﴿fa-taṭrudahum fa-takūna mina al-ẓālimīn﴾ ("so that you would drive them away and be among the wrongdoers"): the apparent view is that His saying ﴿fa-taṭrudahum﴾ is the answer (jawāb) to His saying ﴿mā ʿalayka min ḥisābihim min shay'﴾, and the accusative here is in one of the two senses of the accusative in your saying: "mā taʾtīnā fa-tuḥaddithanā" (you do not come to us so that you speak to us). One of the two senses of this is: "You do not come to us speaking; you only come and do not speak." This meaning is not valid in the verse. The second sense is: "You do not come to us, so how would you speak to us?", meaning: this does not happen, so how could this happen? This second meaning is the one that is valid in the verse: that their reckoning is not upon you, so that the driving away would have an effect. They gave the answer to "that it be ﴿fa-taṭrudahum﴾" as an answer to a negation without explaining how it could serve as an answer.

The apparent view of His saying ﴿fa-takūna mina al-ẓālimīn﴾ is that it is conjoined (maʿṭūf) to ﴿fa-taṭrudahum﴾. The meaning is the report that their reckoning is not upon him, and that driving them away and the wrongdoing that results from driving them away do not occur. They also permitted that "fa-takūna" be an answer to the prohibition in His saying ﴿wa-lā taṭrudi﴾ ("and do not drive away"), like His saying ﴿lā taftarū ʿalā Allāhi kadhiban fa-yusḥitakum bi-ʿadhāb﴾ ("Do not invent a lie against God, lest He destroy you with a punishment") [Ṭā-Hā: 61]. In that case the two clauses, and the answer to the first, form a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ) between the prohibition and its answer. The meaning of "mina al-ẓālimīn" is: among those who place a thing in other than its proper place.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 53:

﴿Thus We tested some of them by means of others, that they might say: "Are these the ones on whom Allah has bestowed favour from among us?"﴾ The kaf (ك) is for comparison (tashbih), in a position of nasb (accusative). The demonstrative "dhalika" (that) refers to a previous trial. Earlier, the mention was made of the nations of the messengers and their being sent as bearers of good tidings and warners, and the division of their nations into believers and deniers. This indicates that the followers of the messengers differ, and that trial (fitan) inevitably befalls them, as it has befallen this nation. Thus, Allah, exalted is He, compares the testing and examination of this nation with the testing of the earlier nations. That is, the condition of this nation is like the condition of the earlier nations in that some are tried by others. The trial may be by wealth and poverty, or by nobility and lowliness, and by strength and weakness.

Al-Zamakhshari (ت) said: "The like of that great trial is the trial of some people by others, meaning We tested them with it. This is because the polytheists would say to the Muslims: ﴿Are these the ones on whom Allah has bestowed favour from among us?﴾, meaning: He has favoured them with the guidance to attain the truth and with what makes them happy with Him, rather than us, while we are the foremost and the leaders, and they are the slaves and the poor, denying that such people could be upon the truth, or that they could be favoured with good from among us, like His saying: ﴿Has the Reminder been cast upon him from among us?﴾ [al-Qamar: 25], and ﴿Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 11]. The meaning of 'We tested them so that they would say that' is: abandonment (khidhlan) of them, so they fell into trial, until their being tried became a cause for this saying, because no one says a statement like this except one who is forsaken and fabricates speech." End of his words.

The last part of his speech follows the method of the Mu'tazila (al-Mu'tazila) in interpreting the trial that He, exalted is He, attributed to Himself as abandonment, in accordance with his custom.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The testing of the believers by the polytheists is what they suffer from them of harm. The testing of the polytheists by the believers is that a noble man among the polytheists sees people who have no nobility, whom this religion has honoured and given a standing and rank with their Prophet. The reference of 'dhalika' is to their injustice in wanting the weak to be driven away." End of his words.

This comparison does not fit well, for the sense becomes: "The like of that, i.e., the request to drive them away, We tested some of them by means of others." What the mind immediately grasps when you say "I struck the like of that" is that it understands the like of that striking, not that the likeness occurs in something else.

The lam in ﴿li-yaqulu﴾ (that they might say) is apparently the lam of purpose (lam kay), meaning: this trial is so that they would say this statement in the form of a question addressed to themselves, as a private muttering to themselves. The meaning becomes: We tested the nobles of the disbelievers by the weak believers, so that they would marvel within themselves at this, and it would be a cause for reflection for whoever is guided. Whoever affirms that the lam can denote becoming (lam al-sayrura) permits here that it be the lam of becoming, and their saying would be in the manner of deserving (istihqaq). The word "ha'ulaa'" (these) refers to the believers, and ﴿manna Allahu 'alayhim﴾ (Allah has bestowed favour upon them) means, in their claim, that their religion is from Him, exalted is He.

﴿Is not Allah most knowing of the grateful?﴾ This is an interrogative whose meaning is affirmation (taqrir) and a rebuttal of those who made that statement. That is: Allah knows best who gives thanks, so He places His guidance in him, rather than in the one who disbelieves, so He does not guide him. The word "al-shukr" (gratitude) comes here in the utmost beauty, since in their statement ﴿Are these the ones on whom Allah has bestowed favour?﴾ the term "manna" (bestowed favour) occurred, so mentioning bestowal matches the word "gratitude." The meaning is: He, exalted is He, knows those favoured who are grateful for His blessings, and knowledge includes the meaning of reward and recompense for them for their gratitude, so they are not an object of your contempt or your wonder.

It has been said: "The grateful" are those upon whom faith was bestowed, not the leaders whose disbelief He knows. It has been said: "Those who give thanks for Islam when I guide them." It has been said: "Those who are granted success in faith, like Bilal and those beneath him." Al-Zamakhshari said: "That is, Allah knows best who will have faith and gratitude, so He grants him success in faith, and who will persist in his disbelief, so He forsakes him and withholds from him success." End of his words. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 6, Verse 54:**

﴿When those who believe in Our signs come to you, say: "Peace be upon you."﴾ The majority of scholars hold that it was revealed concerning those whom God forbade him to drive away. Whenever he saw them, he would greet them with peace first and say: "Praise be to God who has placed in my community those whom I greet first with peace." It was also said: it refers to those who approved the opinion of Abu Talib on driving away the weak. Al-Fudayl ibn Iyad said: some people said, "We have committed sins, so ask forgiveness for us," and he turned away from them, and so it was revealed. It was also said: it was revealed concerning Umar, when he advised accepting the disbelievers, not knowing that this was corrupting. According to these occasions of revelation, the interpretation of ﴿those who believe﴾ is as follows. If by them he meant the six whom he was forbidden to drive away, then this is of the category of the general term (ʿāmm) used to mean the specific (khāṣṣ). And the words ﴿Peace be upon you﴾ will be a command to honour them and an indication of the special distinction of honouring them in this way. If he meant Umar, when he apologised, asked forgiveness, and said, "I intended nothing by that except good," then it is the use of the plural for a single, honoured person. The apparent meaning is that the believers are meant in general, without restriction either to the six or to others. And the sentence is a new statement (istiʾnaf) from God, Exalted is He, after the account of those whom He forbade him to drive away has ended. Had they been the ones meant, the more eloquent construction would have been: "and when they come to you." The "signs" here are the verses of the Qur'an and the marks of prophethood. Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: the signs of God are the signs of His existence, and the signs of His attributes of majesty, generosity, greatness, and oneness. Nothing other than God is limitless, and there is no way for the intellects to comprehend it in complete detail. But it is possible for a person to become aware of some of the signs and then believe in the rest in summary. Then, throughout his life, he is like one swimming in those seas and wandering in those deserts. Since these have no end, there is likewise no end to the servant's ascent through the ladders of those signs. This is a general outline whose details have no limit. Then, when the servant is described by these qualities, God commanded His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) to say to them: "Peace be upon you." This greeting is thus good news of attaining honour after that safety and deliverance from the sea of the world of darkness, the centre of corporeal things, the source of calamities and fears, and the place of change and transformation. As for the honour of arriving at the everlasting, pure, immaterial, and holy things, and reaching the expanse of the world of lights, and ascending to the ladders of the pavilions of majesty... the end of his words. This is much talk with no benefit, overflowing with the allusions of the philosophers, far from the methods of those who follow the Sharia and from the paths of Arabic speech, and whoever is overcome by something will be carried away even outside its proper place. How apt is the saying of the one who urged the Mansur of the Unitarians against the philosophers, in a qasida:

*"Burn their books, east and west, for within them lies hidden the worst of knowledge.*
*Their poison creeps into beliefs, and beliefs are like bodies."*

Al-Mubarrad said: "Salam" in the language is one of the names of God, Exalted is He; its plural is salamah; it is also a verbal noun and the name of a tree. Al-Zajjaj said: it is a verbal noun of sallama, *taslim* and *salam*, like *sarah* from *sarrah* and *ada'* from *addā*. ʿIkrima and al-Hasan said: he was commanded to begin the greeting of peace to them, as an honour to them. Ibn Zayd said: he was commanded to convey the peace to them from God. It was also said: the meaning of "peace" here is a supplication for protection from calamities. Abu al-Haytham said: "salam" and "tahiyya" have the same meaning, and the meaning of "Peace be upon you" is: may God give you life. Al-Zamakhshari said: either he was commanded to convey God's greeting of peace to them, or he was commanded to begin the greeting with them, as an honour and to comfort their hearts. End of his words. His use of "either... or" refers to the first being the view of Ibn Zayd and the second the view of ʿIkrima. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: its wording is that of a statement, but its meaning is supplication, and this is one of the places where it is permitted to begin with an indefinite noun (nakira), since it has become specific. End of his words. The specification that the grammarians mean for an indefinite noun with which a sentence may begin is that it be specified by a qualifier, by an operating word, or by an annexation (idafa). But ﴿salam﴾ has none of these specifications. Some grammarians have tried to make the permissibility of beginning with an indefinite noun depend on specification and generality. What appears from Ibn ʿAtiyya's words is that by his saying "since it has become specific," he means that it has been used for supplication, so the indefinite noun no longer retains its general descriptive meaning, since it has been used to mean one of the things that an indefinite noun may signify.

* *

﴿Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾: that is, He made it obligatory. The Creator, Exalted is He, has nothing obligatory upon Him by reason, except when He informs us that He has decreed something; then that thing becomes obligatory. It was also said: *kataba* means *waʿada* (promised), and the writing here is in the Preserved Tablet. It was also said: it is in another book. In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, it is related that God, Exalted is He, wrote a book, which is with Him above the Throne: "Indeed My mercy precedes My anger." This sentence is one that he was commanded to say, as good news to them of the vastness of God's mercy and to gladden their hearts.

﴿that whoever among you does evil in ignorance﴾: The "evil" (suʾ): it was said to be shirk, and it was said to be sins. The interpretation of "doing evil in ignorance" has already been given in His saying: ﴿The acceptance of repentance from God is only for those who do evil in ignorance﴾ [al-Nisa': 17], so there is no need to repeat it.

﴿then repents after it and makes amends, then indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful﴾: that is, after doing evil. "And makes amends": he made the continuation of reform a condition regarding the thing from which he repented. ʿAsim and Ibn ʿAmir read *annahu* (أنَّهُ) with the two hamzas open. The first is a substitution (badal) for "mercy," and the second is the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimated form being: "his affair is that He, that is God, is Forgiving and Merciful to him." Al-Nahhas erred when he claimed that *fa-innahu* is coordinated with *annahu* and repeated for the length of the speech; but this, as we have mentioned, is a mistake, because *man* is a subject whether it is a relative pronoun or a conditional, so if it is a relative it remains without a predicate, and if it is a conditional it remains without an apodosis. It was also said: *innahu* is a subject with an omitted predicate, its estimated form being: "upon Himself: that whoever does..." It was also said: *fa-innahu* is a substitution for *annahu*, but this is not correct, because the *fa* enters into it and because *man* lacks a predicate or an apodosis. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, and the two brothers (al-Kisa'i and Hamza) read the hamza in both with a kasra. The first is by way of explanation (tafsir) of "mercy," and the second is in the position of the predicate or apodosis. Nafi' read the first with a fatha according to the two previously mentioned possibilities, and the second with a kasra according to its own construction as well. A group read the first with a kasra and the second with a fatha; al-Zahrawi related this from al-Aʿraj. Sibawayh related from him something like the reading of Nafiʿ. Al-Dani said: the reading of al-Aʿraj is the opposite of the reading of Nafiʿ. And "bi-jahalah" (in ignorance) is in the position of an accusative of circumstance (ḥāl), meaning: "while he is ignorant." How excellent is the arrangement of this speech! He first commanded him to say to the believers, "Peace be upon you," so he began first with safety and security for those who believed. Then he addressed them, second, with the obligation of mercy, and attributed the writing to their Lord, meaning: the one who looks after your interests, who nurtures you and owns you, has written mercy for you. This is good news of the general mercy. Then he substituted for it something specific, namely His forgiveness and mercy for whoever repents and makes amends. Had someone gone so far as to say that *al-rahma* is an object of purpose (mafʿul li-ajlihi), and that *annahu* is in the accusative position governed by *kataba* (meaning: for the sake of His mercy toward you), it would not have been far-fetched. But the apparent reading is that *al-rahma* is the object of *kataba*. The Mu'tazila used as evidence His saying ﴿Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾ to argue that He does not create disbelief in the disbeliever, because mercy contradicts that, and contradicts His punishing him forever and ever.

﴿And thus We detail the verses, that the way of the criminals may become clear﴾. The *kaf* (الكاف) is for comparison (*li-l-tashbih*), and (ذَلِكَ) refers to the detailing that occurs in this surah. That is: in the same clear manner of this detailing, We detail the verses of the Qur'an and summarize them in describing the states of the criminals: one whose heart is sealed, whose Islam is not hoped for; one in whom you see signs of acceptance, who fears when he hears the mention of the Resurrection; and one who has entered Islam but does not observe its limits. It has also been said: the meaning is, just as We detailed in this surah the evidence for the soundness of monotheism, prophethood, divine decree and destiny, We detail for you Our proof and Our arguments in establishing every truth that the people of falsehood deny.

It has also been said: it refers to the detailing for the earlier nations, and "like that detailing for those before you, We detail for you."

Al-Tibrizi said: its meaning is, "just as We made it clear to the grateful and to the disbelievers."

Ibn Qutaybah said: its detailing is its coming in separate parts, one thing after another.

Taj al-Qurra' said: *al-fasl* is the separation between two things, and *al-tafsil* is the clarification of meanings that are ambiguous.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the reference in His words (وكذلك) is to what preceded of the prohibition against driving away the believers and the explanation of the corruption of the view of those who oppose that. And *tafsil al-ayat* is their clarification, their explanation and their manifestation. End of quote.

*Istabana* can be intransitive and transitive. The Tamim and the people of Najd treat *al-sabil* as masculine, while the people of the Hijaz treat it as feminine.

Al-'Arabiyyan (Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir), Ibn Kathir and Hafs read (ولِتَسْتَبِينَ) with *ta'* and (سَبِيلُ) with *raf'* (nominative). Al-Akhawan (Hamza and al-Kisa'i) and Abu Bakr read (ولِيَسْتَبِينَ) with *ya'* and (سَبِيلُ) with *raf'*. Here *istabana* is intransitive, meaning: "that the way of the criminals may become manifest." Nafi' reads (ولِتَسْتَبِينَ) with the *ta'* of address and (سَبِيلَ) with *nasb* (accusative), so *istabana* here is transitive.

It has been said: it is addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ). It has also been said: it is outwardly addressed to him, but the intended meaning is his community, because the Prophet (ﷺ) had already made it clear.

The way of the criminals is singled out because making their way clear entails making the way of the believers clear too; or it is an omitted conjunction understood from the meaning, the estimated sense being: "the way of the criminals and the believers."

It has been said: the way of the criminals is singled out because they are the ones who raised the statements mentioned earlier, and they are more important in this context, since these are verses of refutation against them. The apparent meaning of ﴿المُجْرِمِينَ﴾ is general, but Ibn Zayd interpreted it to mean, by "the criminals," those who commanded the driving away of the weak.

The *lam* in (لِتَسْتَبِينَ) is connected to a later verb, meaning: "that the way of the criminals may become clear, We detailed it for you." Or there is a suppressed cause before it, which is the view of the Kufans, the estimated sense being: "so that We may make clear to you, and that it may become manifest."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "that he may clearly understand their way, and so treat each of them in the manner that he ought to be treated, We detailed that detailing."

Abu Hayyan, *al-Bahr al-Muhit* (The Surging Sea), on surah 6, verse 56:

﴿Say: Indeed I have been forbidden to worship those whom you invoke besides God.﴾ God commanded him to declare openly his disavowal of their worship of other than God. When God mentioned the detailed explanation of the verses, so that the path of the one who falsifies (*mubtil*) would be distinguished from the path of the one who is right (*muhiqq*), He forbade him from following their path. The meaning of ﴿nuhitu﴾ (I have been forbidden) is "I have been restrained." Al-Zamakhshari said: "By the faculties of reason that God placed within me, and by the evidences of revelation (*sam'*) that I have been given."

﴿Alladhina tad'una﴾ (those whom you invoke) refers to the idols. He referred to them with *alladhina* (those, for the masculine plural rational) according to the claim of the disbelievers, when they gave them the status of those who understand.

As for ﴿tad'una﴾ (you invoke), Ibn Abbas said: its meaning is "you worship." It was also said: "you name them gods." It derives from "I called my son Zayd," meaning "I named him." It was also said: "you call upon them in your affairs and needs."

In His saying ﴿those whom you invoke besides God﴾ there is a rebuke to them and a description of them as rushing headlong into what they were in without insight. The wording ﴿nuhitu﴾ (I have been forbidden) is more emphatic than the negation with *la a'budu* (I do not worship), because it implies that a binding obligation has come down.

﴿Say: I do not follow your desires﴾, that is, what your souls incline toward of worshipping other than God. Since their idols were varied, each worshipper had a desire-idol specific to him, and therefore the word was made plural. The word *ahwa'akum* (your desires) is general, and what it is normally used for is what is other than good. It includes the worship of idols and what they were commanded to do, such as driving away the weak believers, and other things that are not true. It is more general than the preceding clause and more explicit in opposing them. In His saying ﴿ahwa'akum﴾ there is an alert to the cause from which the error arose, and a warning to whoever wishes to follow the truth and avoid falsehood, as Ibn Durayd said:

*The bane of the intellect is desire, so whoever rises above his desire, his intellect has saved him.*

﴿Then indeed I would have gone astray, and I would not be among the guided﴾. The meaning: if I followed your desires, I would have gone astray and would not have been guided. The clause ﴿wa ma ana min al-muhtadin﴾ (and I am not among the guided) reinforces His saying ﴿qad dalaltu﴾ (I would have gone astray). The first is a verbal sentence (*fi'liyya*), indicating renewal, and this one is a nominal sentence (*ismiyya*), indicating permanence. Thus the negation of the renewal of error and of its persistence is achieved, and it came at the end of a verse.

Al-Sulami, Ibn Wathhab and Talha read ﴿daliltu﴾ with the vowel of the lam changed to kasra (*dalilt*), and this is a dialect form. In *al-Tahrir* it is stated: Yahya and Ibn Abi Layla read here, and in the prostration verse in ﴿a-idha sallalna﴾ (when we have decayed?), with the letter *sad* unpointed (*sallalna*, from *salla*). It is said that *salla al-lahm* means the meat became putrid. It is also narrated as *salalna*, meaning we were buried in *al-sallah*, which is hard ground. Abu al-Abbas related this from Mujahid ibn al-Furat in the book *Kitab al-Shawadh* (the book of anomalous readings, those readings that are not transmitted by the widely accepted channels).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 57:

﴿Say: Indeed I am upon clear evidence from my Lord﴾ i.e., upon a clear sharia (divine law) and a sound religion (millah). It was also said: al-bayyinah is the miracle that demonstrates my truthfulness, and it is the Qur'an. They said: the ta' in (bayyinah) may be for emphasis (mubalaghah), and the meaning is "upon a matter that is clear." When He negated that he follows desires, He drew attention to what must be followed, which is the clear matter from Allah the Exalted.

﴿But you have denied it﴾ This is a report from Him about them, that they denied it. The apparent reading is that the pronoun returns to Allah, i.e., "and you have denied Allah." It was also said: it returns to (bayyinah), because its meaning is "upon a clear matter." It was also said: it returns to the clarity (al-bayan) indicated by (bayyinah). It was also said: it returns to the Qur'an.

﴿What you are hastening for is not with me﴾ That which they were hastening for: it was said to be the proposed signs (al-ayat al-muqtarahah), as said by al-Zajjaj. It was also said: it is the punishment, and this was preferred on the grounds that the word "hastening" (al-isti'jal) in the Qur'an only occurs regarding punishment, since they did not hasten for the proposed signs; and on the grounds that the wording ﴿and you have denied it﴾ implies that you have committed what makes you deserving of punishment, except that this is not in my hands. Al-Zamakhshari said: he means the punishment they hastened for in their saying: ﴿So rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾ [al-Anfal: 32].

﴿Judgment belongs only to Allah﴾ i.e., judgment belongs to Allah absolutely, and it is the decisive separation between the two disputing parties (p-143) by imposing reward and punishment. It was also said: it is the decree of sending punishment, and in it is the general entrusting of matters to Allah the Exalted.

"Yaqdi al-haqq" (He decides the truth) is the reading of the two Arab readers (al-'Arabiyyan) and the two brothers, i.e., He decrees the true decision in everything He decides concerning it, whether delay or hastening. Some took (yaqdi) to imply the meaning of "yunfidh" (executes), so it governed a direct object. It was also said: (yaqdi) means "yasna'" (makes/does), i.e., whatever He makes is true. al-Hudhali said:

"And upon them are two coats of mail; Dawud decreed them, or Tubba' made the full coats."

i.e., he made them. It was also said that the preposition (ba') was omitted and the original is "bil-haqq" (with the truth), and this is supported by the reading of Abdullah, Ubayy, Ibn Thabit, al-Nakha'i, Talhah and al-A'mash: (yaqdi bil-haqq) with the preposition of genitive, and the letter yaʼ was dropped in writing because it was dropped in pronunciation due to the meeting of two sukun. Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr read yaqdi bil-haqq.

(And He is the best of deciders) and in the Codex of Abdullah it reads: "and He is the swiftest of deciders."

Ibn 'Abbas, the two Haramis, and 'Asim read (yaqussu al-haqq) from qassa al-hadith (to relate a narrative), like His saying: ﴿We relate to you the best of narratives﴾ [Yusuf: 3], or from qassa al-athar, i.e., he followed it. It is reported that Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' was asked: "Is it yaqussu al-haqq or yaqdi al-haqq?" He said: "If it were yaqussu, it would say 'and He is the best of narrators' — has anyone read it this way?" And since He said "and He is the best of deciders," the separation is in judgment. End. It did not reach Abu 'Amr that it was read with it, and this is indicated by his saying "has anyone read it?" This does not necessarily follow from what he said, for separation (fasl) occurs in speech too; He said: ﴿Indeed it is a decisive word﴾ [al-Tariq: 13], and He said: (its verses were made firm, then detailed), and He said: ﴿We detail the verses﴾ [al-An'am: 55]. So mentioning "the deciders" does not necessitate that it specifies (yaqdi).

Here (khayr) is the superlative (af'al al-tafdil) in its proper usage. It was also said: it is not in its proper usage, because His judgment does not resemble any judgment, and no one separates as He separates; but this argument indicates that it is in its proper usage.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 58:

﴿Say: "If I had what you are hastening for, the matter would already have been decided between me and you."﴾ That is: if it were within my power to bring about what you are hastening for, namely the sending of signs you propose or the descent of punishment, I would hasten to it, and the separation between me and you would take place.

It is narrated from ʿIkrima regarding ﴿the matter would already have been decided between me and you﴾ that it means: the Resurrection would have taken place. What is narrated from Ibn Jurayj, that the meaning is "death would have been slaughtered" (ladhabaḥa al-mawt), is not sound, and it has no meaning here.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "And ﴿what you are hastening for﴾ [al-Anʿam: 57], of the punishment, I would have destroyed you quickly, out of anger for my Lord and indignation at your denial of Him, and I would have rid myself of you swiftly." End of quote. This is also the view of Ibn ʿAbbas: "I would not have given you a moment's respite, and I would have destroyed you."

﴿And Allah knows best the wrongdoers﴾. The apparent meaning is that the sense is: "and Allah knows best about you" (God, most high, knows best). The apparent noun describing them as wrongdoers has been placed in the position of the pronoun. The meaning of "knows" regarding them is: knows their recompense, so there is in it a warning and a threat. It has also been said: He knows the timing of their punishment; and it has been said: He knows the outcome of their affair, whether some will be guided and some will persist; and it has been said: He knows who ought to be seized and who should be given respite; and it has been said: He knows what wisdom requires of their punishment.

[p. 144]

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 6, verses 59–73**

﴿With Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He. He knows what is on the land and in the sea. Not a leaf falls but He knows it, nor is there a grain in the darkness of the earth, nor anything moist or dry, but it is in a Clear Record.﴾ [Al-An'am 6:59]

﴿It is He who takes your souls by night, and He knows what you have committed by day. Then He raises you up therein, that a term appointed may be fulfilled. Then to Him is your return; then He will inform you of what you used to do.﴾ [Al-An'am 6:60]

﴿He is the Subduer over His servants, and He sends over you guardians, until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him, and they do not fail.﴾ [Al-An'am 6:61]

﴿Then they are returned to Allah, their true Master. Surely judgement belongs to Him, and He is the swiftest of reckoners.﴾ [Al-An'am 6:62]

﴿Say: "Who rescues you from the darkness of land and sea, when you call upon Him humbly and secretly, saying, 'If He delivers us from this, we will surely be among the thankful'?"﴾ [Al-An'am 6:63]

﴿Say: "Allah rescues you from it and from every distress, yet you still associate partners with Him."﴾ [Al-An'am 6:64]

﴿Say: "He is able to send upon you a punishment from above you or from beneath your feet, or to confound you into factions and make some of you taste the violence of others. Observe how We vary the signs, that perhaps they may understand."﴾ [Al-An'am 6:65]

﴿Your people denied it, though it is the truth. Say: "I am not a guardian over you."﴾ [Al-An'am 6:66]

﴿For every news there is a fixed time, and you will come to know.﴾ [Al-An'am 6:67]

﴿When you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our signs, turn away from them until they engage in some other discourse. And if Satan causes you to forget, then do not sit, after the reminder, with the wrongdoing people.﴾ [Al-An'am 6:68]

﴿Those who are mindful of Allah are not accountable for them in any way, but it is a reminder, that perhaps they may be mindful.﴾ [Al-An'am 6:69]

﴿Leave those who have taken their religion as play and diversion, and whom the worldly life has deceived. But remind them thereby, lest a soul be given up to destruction for what it has earned; it will have, apart from Allah, no protector and no intercessor; and if it offers every ransom, none will be accepted from it. Those are the ones who are given up to destruction for what they earned; for them is a drink of scalding water and a painful punishment, for what they used to disbelieve.﴾ [Al-An'am 6:70]

﴿Say: "Shall we call upon other than Allah that which neither benefits us nor harms us, and be turned back on our heels after Allah has guided us, like one whom the devils have enticed in the earth, bewildered, who has companions calling him to guidance, saying, 'Come to us'?" Say: "Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the guidance, and we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds."﴾ [Al-An'am 6:71]

﴿And establish prayer and fear Him; and it is He to whom you will be gathered.﴾ [Al-An'am 6:72]

﴿It is He who created the heavens and the earth in truth; and on the day He says, "Be," and it is, His word is the truth. His is the dominion on the day the Trumpet is blown. He is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He is the Wise, the All-Aware.﴾ [Al-An'am 6:73]

(p-١٤٤) *Al-suqut* (السُّقُوطُ): falling from a height. *Al-waraqa* (الوَرَقَةُ): a single leaf of a plant, or a sheet of paper, and it is well known. *Al-ratb* and *al-yabis* (الرَّطْبُ واليابِسُ) are both well known. It is said: *ratb*, so he is *ratib* and *ratib* (رَطِيبٌ); and *yabis* and *yabis* (يَبِيسٌ). The form *yabs* (يَبْسٌ) with the *ya* dropped and the *ba* vowelled with kasra is anomalous. *Al-karb* (الكَرْبُ): grief that seizes the soul; *karaba al-rajul*, so he is *makrub* (مَكْرُوبٌ). The poet said:

*A distressed man whom I relieved of distress by a spear-thrust of decisive force, when he called upon me.*

*Al-shi'a* (الشِّيعَةُ): a group that follows another; its plural is *ashya'*. *Shayya'tu fulanan*: I followed him. The Arabs say: *sha'akum al-salam*, meaning, "May peace follow you," and *ash'akumu Allahu al-salam*, meaning, "May Allah cause peace to follow you." *Al-ibsal* (الإبْسالُ): a person surrendering himself to destruction. It is said: *absaltu waladi*, I pledged my son as a pledge. The poet said:

*And my giving up my son without a crime, they committed no offence against him, nor was there any spilt blood.*

*Ba'awnahu*: "they gained him" (*janaynahu*). *Al-ba'w* (البَعْوُ): a crime. *Al-hamim* (الحَمِيمُ): hot water. *Al-hayra* (الحَيْرَةُ): hesitation in a matter, not finding a way out of it; from this comes "the water was bewildered in the clouds." It is said: *haara yahiru hayratan, hayran, hayaranan, hayrura*. *Al-sur* (الصُّورُ): the plural of *suratun*, and *al-sur* is the horn in the dialect of the people of Yemen. The poet said:

*We struck them on the morning of the two hosts, with lofty ones amid the dust of the two clouds of dust, a fierce striking, unlike the striking of the two horns.*

﴿With Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He.﴾ When He, Exalted, said: ﴿The judgement belongs only to Allah﴾ [Al-An'am 6:57], and said: ﴿He knows best the wrongdoers﴾ [Al-An'am 6:58], after His words: ﴿What you are hastening for﴾ [Al-An'am 6:57], He moved from the particular to the general, which is His knowledge of all unseen matters. He used the metaphor of *keys* (*al-mafatih*) for the power over them, since keys are the means of reaching a thing. Thus included in this general statement are what they were hastening for and other things. *Al-mafatih* is the plural of *mift'h*, with a kasra on the *mim*, which is the instrument by which what has been locked is opened. Al-Zamakhshari (الزَّهْراوِيُّ) said: *mift'h* is more eloquent than *miftah*. It is possible that it is the plural of *miftah*, because in such forms it is permissible not to include the *ya*; they say *masabih, mahareb, and qaraqir* as plurals of *misbah* and *qurqur*. Ibn al-Sumayqa' read *mafatih* with a *ya*. It is also reported from some of them: *miftah al-ghayb*, in the singular. It is also said that it is the plural of *maftah* with a fatha on the *mim*, which denotes a place: the places of the unseen and their locations from which the hidden things are opened. This is supported by what is reported from Ibn Abbas: they are the treasuries of rain, plants, and the descent of punishment. Al-Suddi and others said: the treasuries of the unseen. It is reported from Ibn Umar, from him (peace be upon him), that he said: "The keys of the unseen are five, which none knows but Allah," then: ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Luqman 31:34] to the end of the surah. It is also said: the keys of the unseen are the matters by which the absent is inferred, so that its reality is known; from your saying: *fataħtu 'ala al-imam*, I prompted the imam when he forgot. Abu Mas'ud said: "Your Prophet (peace be upon him) was given everything except the keys of the unseen." It is reported from Ibn Abbas: they are the treasuries of the unseen of the heavens and the earth, of destinies and provisions. Ata' said: what is hidden of reward and punishment, and what matters will come to. Al-Zajjaj said: the means to knowledge of the unseen when it is sought. It is also said: the ends of lifespans and the conclusions of deeds. It is also said: what has not yet occurred, whether it will occur or not; and what will occur, how it will occur; and what will not occur, if it were to occur, how it would occur. And ﴿none knows them but He﴾ restricts that none knows those keys and none is acquainted with them besides Him, Exalted. Indeed, there appear from those who claim affiliation with Sufism (*al-sufi*, the mystical tradition) things such as claiming knowledge of hidden matters and being acquainted with the knowledge of the ends of their followers, and that they are with them in Paradise, a matter definitely decided for them and their followers. They announce this from the pulpits, and no one denies it. Even though they are empty of knowledge, they give the impression that they know the unseen. In the Sahih of Muslim, from A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her): "Whoever claims that Muhammad knows what will happen tomorrow has greatly slandered Allah," and Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾ [Al-Naml 27:65]. These claims and superstitions have multiplied in the lands of Egypt, and there have arisen people of childish minds who are called "shaykhs," who have failed to grasp the faculties of reason and transmitted knowledge, and whom the pursuit of knowledge has wearied:

*They boast, claiming a great matter that was not for the Friend (Abraham) nor for the Interlocutor (Moses).*

*While a man among them was in lowliness, he saw the Tablet and what marks were on it.*

*So he plucked knowledge from it fresh and tender, and he knew what would happen before the attack.*

*Indeed, my intellect is in fetters whenever I believe in a great fabrication.*

﴿And He knows what is on the land and in the sea.﴾ Since His mention of the keys of the unseen was a matter of intellection, and He informed us that He alone possesses knowledge of it and is specially singled out for it, He mentioned the connection of His knowledge to this perceptible reality in general terms. Then He mentioned His knowledge of the leaf, the grain, the moist and the dry in particular terms. Thus it is established that He, Exalted, informs us that He knows the universals and particulars, and holds exclusive knowledge of them, while we know only part of them. He placed land first because we see much of what it contains: cities, villages, deserts, mountains, animals, plants, and minerals. Or it is an ascent to what is more wondrous in general, because what it contains of kinds of animals is more wondrous, and its length and breadth are greater. Land stands against sea. It is also said: *al-barr* means barren wastes and *al-bahr* means the known sea. So the meaning is: and He knows what is in the land of plants, creatures, stones, minerals, and other things, and what is in the sea of animals, jewels, and other things. Mujahid said: *al-barr* is the barren earth in which there is no water, and *al-bahr* is every village and place in which there is water. It is also said: He did not mean the apparent land and sea, but rather that His knowledge encompasses us and what has been prepared for our welfare of their benefits. They were singled out for mention because they are the greatest creation that is adjacent to us.

﴿Not a leaf falls but He knows it.﴾ The *min* (مِن) here is extra, for the generality of the class of leaf. He knows it absolutely, before its falling, during it, and after it. Al-Zajjaj said: He knows it falling and remaining, just as you say: "No one comes to you but I know him," and it does not mean only at the time of his coming. It is also said: He knows when it falls, where it falls, and how much it turns in the air. It is also said: He knows how it turned from back to front until it fell upon the earth. *Yalamuha* (يَعْلَمُها) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relative to *waraqa*, and it is a circumstantial clause from an indefinite noun, as you say: "No one came except riding."

﴿Nor is there a grain in the darkness of the earth.﴾ It is said: beneath the seventh earth. It is said: beneath the dust. It is said: the seed that is sown, which farmers bury beneath the earth. It is said: beneath the rock at the bottom of the lands. It is said: and not a grain but He knows when it sprouts, and who will eat it. Consider the excellent arrangement of these known things. He began first with a matter of intellection that we do not perceive by the senses, which is His saying: ﴿With Him are the keys of the unseen﴾; then second with a matter of which we perceive much by the senses, which is ﴿He knows what is on the land and in the sea﴾, which contains generality; then third with two subtle parts, one higher, which is the falling of a leaf from above to below, and the second lower, which is the hiddenness of a grain in the belly of the earth. These sentences indicate that He, Exalted, knows universals and particulars. They also contain a refutation of the philosophers, who claim that Allah does not know particulars. Some of them claim that He, Exalted, knows neither universals nor particulars, not even His own essence. Exalted is Allah above that.

﴿Nor anything moist or dry, but it is in a Clear Record.﴾ *Al-ratb* and *al-yabis* are two well-known attributes, and the intended meaning is the generality of what is characterized by them. The commentators have illustrated this with examples: what grows and what does not grow; the tongue of the believer and the tongue of the disbeliever; the eye that weeps from fear of Allah and the eye that is dry from hardness. As for what al-Naqqash related from Ja'far al-Sadiq, that the leaf is the miscarriage of the children of Adam, the grain refers to that which is not a miscarriage, the moist refers to the living, and the dry refers to the dead, this is not authentically attributed to Ja'far; it is from the esoteric interpretation of the Batiniyya (an esoteric sect), may Allah curse them. Muqatil said: ﴿in a Clear Record﴾ is the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh al-mahfuz*). Al-Zajjaj said: it is a metaphor for the certain knowledge of Allah. This exception serves as emphasis, because His saying ﴿nor a grain﴾ and ﴿nor anything moist or dry﴾ is conjoined to His saying ﴿of a leaf﴾, and the first exception applies to them as well, just as you say: "No man came to me that I did not honour him, nor a woman," meaning "that I did not honour her." But since the speech was long, the exception was repeated for emphasis, and what made it good is that it is the *fasila* (فاصِلَةُ), the rhyme-final word of the verse.

Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and Ibn al-Sumayqa' read ﴿nor anything moist nor anything dry﴾ with *raf'* (nominative) in both. The preferred view is that they are conjoined to the position of ﴿of a leaf﴾, and it is possible that the nominative is by way of a beginning (*mubtada'*), with its predicate being ﴿but it is in a Clear Record﴾.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 60–62 (part 1 of 2):

﴿It is He who takes your souls by night, and knows what you have earned by day. Then He raises you up therein, that a term appointed may be fulfilled. Then to Him is your return. Then He will inform you of what you used to do.﴾ The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that, when He (exalted is He) mentioned His exclusive possession of complete knowledge of universals and particulars, He mentioned His exclusive possession of complete power, as an alert to what divinity specifically entails. He mentioned something perceptible that overpowers humankind, namely the taking of souls by night and the raising up by day, neither of which lies within human power. Rather, it is a matter that Allah, exalted is He, brings upon a person. In common usage, "tawaffi" (taking in full, causing to die) refers to death, but here it means sleep, by way of metaphor, because of the link between sleep and death, which is the cessation of its perception, awareness and thought. Since the "tawaffi" meant here as sleep is a cause of rest, He (exalted is He) attributed it to Himself, and since it is painful in the sense of death, He said: ﴿Say: The angel of death will take you﴾ [al-Sajdah: 11], and ﴿Our messengers took him in full﴾, and ﴿The angels take them in full﴾ [al-Nahl: 28]. The apparent meaning is that the address is general to every hearer. Al-Zamakhshari said: The address is to the disbelievers, and the night was specified for sleep and the day for raising up, although one may sleep by day and be raised up by night, in keeping with what is usual. The meaning of "jaraḥtum" is "you earned," and from it come "jawarih al-tayr" (the birds of prey), that is, its hunters, and "ijtarahu al-sayyi'at" (they earned the evil deeds), meaning they acquired them. What is meant by it is the deeds of the limbs, and from this the limbs are called "jawarih." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It may be that it derives from "jarh" (wound), as if sin is a wound in the religion, and the Arabs say: the wound of the tongue is like the wound of the hand. Makki said: The origin of "ijtirah" is a man acting with one of his limbs, his hand or his foot, then it became common until every earner is called "mujtarih" and "jarih." The apparent sense of His words ﴿what you have earned﴾ is generality regarding what is acquired, whether good or bad. Al-Zamakhshari said: [it means] what you have earned of sins. End. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. Qatadah said: what you have done. Mujahid said: what you have earned. "Al-ba'th" here is the waking from sleep. The pronoun in "fihi" refers to the day, as said by Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Suddi; it refers to it verbally, and the meaning is on another day, as you say: "I have a dirham and its half." 'Abd Allah ibn Kathir said it refers to the taking in full, that is, He wakes you during the taking in full, meaning within its course and interstices. It was also said that it refers to the night. Al-Zamakhshari said: Then He raises you from the graves, regarding that by which you have ended your lifespans through sleep by night and earning sins by day and because of it, like your saying: "For what did you call me?" and you reply: "For such and such a matter." End. Taking it to mean raising from the graves is rejected by His words ﴿that a term appointed may be fulfilled﴾, because the meaning, and Allah knows best, is that He gives them life in these two states of sleep and wakefulness so that they may complete what has been decreed for them of their terms and written deeds. The fulfilment of the term is the separation of the lifespan's duration from what is other than it. "Musamma" (appointed) is in the knowledge of Allah, or in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), or at the completion of creation and the breathing of the spirit. In the Sahih it is reported that the angel says at the completion of that: "What is the provision? What is the term?" Al-Zamakhshari said: It is the term which He named and set for the resurrection of the dead and their recompense for their deeds. ﴿Then to Him is your return﴾ is the return to the station of reckoning. ﴿Then He will inform you of what you used to do﴾ in your nights and your days. End. Others, such as Ibn Jubayr, said: ﴿your return﴾ is by true death. When He (exalted is He) mentioned sleep and wakefulness, this was an alert to death and resurrection, and that their ruling with respect to Him (exalted is He) is one. Just as He puts to sleep and wakes, He causes to die and gives life. Talhah and Abu Raja' read: (liyaqdiya ajalan musamman), making the verb active and putting "ajal" in the accusative, meaning that Allah may complete their terms, like His words ﴿When Musa had fulfilled the term﴾ [al-Qasas: 29] in the reading of the majority. It is possible that the omitted subject is His pronoun or their pronoun.

﴿He is the Subduer over His servants, and He sends over you guardians﴾. The discussion of ﴿He is the Subduer over His servants﴾ has already passed. Ibn 'Atiyyah said here: "al-Qahir" (the Subduer), if it is taken as a verbal attribute, meaning the manifester of subjugation through thunderbolts, winds and punishment, then it is correct to make "fawq" (over) a locative of direction, because these things are only sent to the servants from above them. If "al-Qahir" is taken as an essential attribute, in the sense of power and dominance, then "fawq" cannot be of direction but is for elevation of rank and status, as you say: "The ruby is above iron." End. The apparent sense of ﴿and He sends﴾ is that it is conjoined to ﴿He is the Subduer﴾ [al-An'am: 18], a verbal clause conjoined to a nominal clause, and it is among the effects of subjugation. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be conjoined to His words ﴿takes you in full﴾ and what follows it of verbs, and that it be conjoined to ﴿the Subduer﴾, the sense being: He who subdues and sends, and that it be a circumstantial clause with an omitted subject, that is, "and He sends." The subject of the circumstantial clause is either the pronoun in ﴿the Subduer﴾ or the pronoun in the adverbial expression. This is the weakest of these analyses. ﴿Over you﴾ apparently relates to "yursilu" (sends), as in His words ﴿There will be sent against you both a flame﴾ [al-Rahman: 35]. The word "'ala" (over) indicates elevation and dominance, since they have power over us, so it is as if that is over us. It is possible that it relates to "ḥafazah" (guardians), meaning: and He sends guardians over you, that is, they guard over you your deeds, as He said: ﴿Indeed over you are guardians﴾ [al-Infitar: 10], as you say: "I kept watch over you for what you do."
