They permitted that it be a circumstantial clause, because if it were placed after, it would be an attribute, meaning guardians present over you, that is, having authority over you. "Hafazah" is the plural of "hafiz," and it is a regular plural of the pattern "fa'il" as a masculine adjective with a sound middle radical, rational, and rarely of what is not rational. Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, angels guarding your deeds, and they are the noble scribes. End. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: What is meant by that is the angels appointed to write down the deeds. End. What these two said is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. The apparent sense of the plural is that it corresponds to a plural, and the verse does not address how many are assigned to each person, nor what they guard. From Ibn 'Abbas: there are two angels with every person, one at his right for good deeds and the other at his left for evil deeds. When he commits an evil deed, the one on the right says: "Wait for him, perhaps he will repent of it; if he does not repent, it is written against him." It was also said: two angels by night and two by day, one of whom writes the good and the other writes the evil. When he walks, one of them is before him and the other behind him; when he sits, one is at his right and the other at his left. It was also said: five angels, two by night, two by day, and one who never leaves him by night or day, and what is written is the good deed and the bad deed. It was said: the acts of obedience, the acts of disobedience, and the permissible acts. It was said: they only observe speech and action, because of His words ﴿Not a word does he utter but there is with him a watcher ready﴾ [Qaf: 18], and His words ﴿They know what you do﴾ [al-Infitar: 12]. As for the deeds of the heart, their knowledge belongs to Allah, exalted is He. It was also said: they observe them in general, not in detail; so when one resolves upon an evil deed, a foul wind comes out of his mouth, and when one resolves upon a good deed, a pleasant wind comes out. Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): Allah is independent of the scribes by His knowledge, so what is the benefit of them? (I answer): In them is a kindness to the servants, for when they know that Allah is watchful over them, and that the angels, who are the noblest of His creation, are appointed over them to guard their deeds and write them down in scrolls displayed before the heads of the witnesses on the standing of the Resurrection, that is more restraining for them from ugliness and further from evil. End. His words "the angels who are the noblest of His creation" follow the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school) concerning the angels, and this benefit is not fixed, since it is possible that its benefit is that the scrolls of deeds will be weighed on the Day of Resurrection, because the weighing of deeds by their mere existence is impossible. This benefit follows the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah (the people of the Sunnah). As for the Mu'tazilah, they interpreted the weighing and the balance figuratively. His word "ḥafazah" does not imply that this guarding is by writing, as they explained. Rather, it has been said: they are the angels of whom the Prophet ﷺ said: "Angels succeed one another among you by night and angels by day." This was said by Qatadah and al-Suddi. It was also said: they guard the person from every thing until his term comes.

﴿Until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him in full﴾. That is, the causes of death; "tawaffathu" means they seize his soul. "Rusulunā" (Our messengers) came in the plural. It was said: he means by it the Angel of Death (peace be upon him), and the plural is used for him as a mark of honour. It was also said: the Angel of Death and his helpers. Most scholars hold that "Rusulunā" is the same as the guardians, who guard them throughout the period of life, and when the causes of death come, they take them in full. There is no contradiction between His words ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ [al-Zumar: 42], His words ﴿Say: The angel of death will take you﴾ [al-Sajdah: 11], and His words ﴿Our messengers take him in full﴾, because the attribution of this to Allah (exalted is He) is in truth, and to others by direct action; it is attributed to the Angel of Death because he is the one who commands his helpers, and it is attributed to him and to them because they are those who undertake the seizing of souls. From Mujahid: the earth is made for him like a basin, from which he takes whomever he takes, and there is no household but that he circles around them every day twice. Hamzah read: "tawaffāhu" with a long alif, imala-ed, and its apparent form is a past verb like "tawaffathu," except that it is masculine in form on the sense of the plural. Whoever reads "tawaffathu" with the feminine form takes it according to the sense of the group. It is possible that it is an imperfect, and its original form is "tatawaffāhu," then one of the two tā' is deleted, according to the disagreement over which is deleted. Al-A'mash read: "yatawaffāhu" with the prefix yā' of the imperfect, in the masculine.

﴿And they do not fail﴾. This is a circumstantial clause, and its governing element is "tawaffathu," or it is a resumptive clause informing about them that they do not fail in anything of what they were commanded regarding the guarding and the taking in full. Its meaning is: they do not fall short. Al-A'raj and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read: "lā yufrifūna" with the light form, meaning they do not exceed the limit in what they were commanded. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Tafrit" is neglect and falling behind the limit, while "ifrāt" is exceeding the limit, meaning they neither diminish from what they were commanded nor add to it. End. This is the meaning of the words of Ibn Jinni. Ibn Bahr said: "yufarrirūna" means they do not allow anyone to fall behind them, that is, to precede them and escape them. It was said that the light reading may mean they do not go ahead of Allah's command, but this is only valid if it is transmitted that "afrata" means "farrata," that is, to go ahead. Al-Hasan said: When the dying person is at the point of death, five hundred angels attend him, take his soul and then ascend with it.

﴿Then they are returned to God, their true Master.﴾ The apparent sense is that the pronoun refers to the servants, and the address "your" (in ﴿عَلَيْكم﴾, "over you") comes as a shift from third person to second person (*iltifat*, a shift in address), because direct address brings the admonition closer to the listeners. It is also possible that the pronoun in *ruddū* refers to *aḥadikum* ("one of you") according to its meaning, since by *aḥadukum* he does not mean the singular in its literal sense but its plural meaning, as if it were said: "until death comes to you." It is read as *riddū* with a kasra on the *rāʾ*, the vowel of the *dāl* that was assimilated having been transferred to the *rāʾ*. The one who returns them (*al-rādd*) is the one who warns them of God, or it refers to the resurrection in the Hereafter, or the angels return them by death to God. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to "Our messengers," meaning the angels, who die as the children of Adam die and are returned to God, exalted is He. Its reference to the servants is more evident. *Mawlāhum* ("their Master") is a general term for the kinds of guardianship that exist between God and His servants, such as sovereignty, support, provision, and reckoning, and other things. In the annexation (*iḍāfa*) there is an indication of His mercy toward them. The apparent meaning of the statement about being returned to God is that it refers to resurrection, return to the judgment of God, and His recompense on the Day of Resurrection, and the end of the verse indicates this.

Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi) said: The explicit wording of the verse indicates that death occurs to the servant and that he is returned to God. The dead person, being dead, cannot be returned to God; rather, what is returned is the soul (*nafs*) and the spirit (*rūḥ*). Here there is death and life: death is the share of the body, and life is the share of the soul and the spirit. Thus it is established that the human being is nothing but the soul and the spirit, and is not merely a designation for this bodily structure. In His saying ﴿Be returned to God﴾ there is an indication that the spirit existed before the body, because the return from this world to the presence of Majesty happens only if it existed before attachment to the body. A parallel is ﴿Return to your Lord﴾ [al-Fajr: 28], and ﴿To God is your return, all of you﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 48]. There is also a hadith: "The spirits were created two thousand years before the bodies." The argument of the philosophers that souls did not exist before the existence of the body is weak, and we have shown its weakness in the rational books. End of his words, and there is some abridgement in it. He also said: ﴿To God﴾ indicates direction, and that is false, so it is necessary to interpret it as meaning that they are returned to a place where there is no owner and no judge other than Him. End.

The apparent meaning is that this return is by resurrection on the Day of Judgment, not what al-Razi intended. His description of God as *al-Ḥaqq* ("the True") means the justice that is not void nor metaphorical. Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: In this world they were under the control of false masters, which are the self (*nafs*), desire (*shahwa*), and anger (*ghaḍab*), as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Have you seen him who has taken his own desire as his god?﴾ [al-Jathiya: 23]. When he died, he was freed from the control of the false masters and passed to the control of the True Master. End of his words. His interpretation lies outside the ways and purposes of Arabic speech, and for the most part it resembles the words of those who call themselves sages (*ḥukamāʾ*). Al-Hasan and al-Aʿmash read *al-Ḥaqqa* with a fatḥa (*naṣb*). The apparent analysis is that it is an adjective that has been detached and put in the accusative for praise, and its accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) was permitted, with the sense: "the true return."

﴿Ah! To Him belongs the judgment﴾. This is an alert from Him, exalted is He, to His servants that all kinds of disposal belong to Him. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Ah! To Him belongs the judgment that day; no judgment belongs to anyone else."

﴿And He is the swiftest of reckoners﴾. The discussion of the swiftness of His reckoning has already been given in His saying: ﴿And God is swift in reckoning﴾ [al-Baqara: 202].

It was said: the acts of obedience, the acts of disobedience, and the permissible acts. It was said: they only observe speech and action, because of His words ﴿Not a word does he utter but there is with him a watcher ready﴾ [Qaf: 18], and His words ﴿They know what you do﴾ [al-Infitar: 12]. As for the deeds of the heart, their knowledge belongs to Allah, exalted is He. It was also said: they observe them in general, not in detail; so when one resolves upon an evil deed, a foul wind comes out of his mouth, and when one resolves upon a good deed, a pleasant wind comes out. Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): Allah is independent of the scribes by His knowledge, so what is the benefit of them? (I answer): In them is a kindness to the servants, for when they know that Allah is watchful over them, and that the angels, who are the noblest of His creation, are appointed over them to guard their deeds and write them down in scrolls displayed before the heads of the witnesses on the standing of the Resurrection, that is more restraining for them from ugliness and further from evil. End. His words "the angels who are the noblest of His creation" follow the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school) concerning the angels, and this benefit is not fixed, since it is possible that its benefit is that the scrolls of deeds will be weighed on the Day of Resurrection, because the weighing of deeds by their mere existence is impossible. This benefit follows the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah (the people of the Sunnah). As for the Mu'tazilah, they interpreted the weighing and the balance figuratively. His word "ḥafazah" does not imply that this guarding is by writing, as they explained. Rather, it has been said: they are the angels of whom the Prophet ﷺ said: "Angels succeed one another among you by night and angels by day." This was said by Qatadah and al-Suddi. It was also said: they guard the person from every thing until his term comes.

﴿Until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him in full﴾. That is, the causes of death; "tawaffathu" means they seize his soul. "Rusulunā" (Our messengers) came in the plural. It was said: he means by it the Angel of Death (peace be upon him), and the plural is used for him as a mark of honour. It was also said: the Angel of Death and his helpers. Most scholars hold that "Rusulunā" is the same as the guardians, who guard them throughout the period of life, and when the causes of death come, they take them in full. There is no contradiction between His words ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ [al-Zumar: 42], His words ﴿Say: The angel of death will take you﴾ [al-Sajdah: 11], and His words ﴿Our messengers take him in full﴾, because the attribution of this to Allah (exalted is He) is in truth, and to others by direct action; it is attributed to the Angel of Death because he is the one who commands his helpers, and it is attributed to him and to them because they are those who undertake the seizing of souls. From Mujahid: the earth is made for him like a basin, from which he takes whomever he takes, and there is no household but that he circles around them every day twice. Hamzah read: "tawaffāhu" with a long alif, imala-ed, and its apparent form is a past verb like "tawaffathu," except that it is masculine in form on the sense of the plural. Whoever reads "tawaffathu" with the feminine form takes it according to the sense of the group. It is possible that it is an imperfect, and its original form is "tatawaffāhu," then one of the two tā' is deleted, according to the disagreement over which is deleted. Al-A'mash read: "yatawaffāhu" with the prefix yā' of the imperfect, in the masculine.

﴿And they do not fail﴾. This is a circumstantial clause, and its governing element is "tawaffathu," or it is a resumptive clause informing about them that they do not fail in anything of what they were commanded regarding the guarding and the taking in full. Its meaning is: they do not fall short. Al-A'raj and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read: "lā yufrifūna" with the light form, meaning they do not exceed the limit in what they were commanded. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Tafrit" is neglect and falling behind the limit, while "ifrāt" is exceeding the limit, meaning they neither diminish from what they were commanded nor add to it. End. This is the meaning of the words of Ibn Jinni. Ibn Bahr said: "yufarrirūna" means they do not allow anyone to fall behind them, that is, to precede them and escape them. It was said that the light reading may mean they do not go ahead of Allah's command, but this is only valid if it is transmitted that "afrata" means "farrata," that is, to go ahead. Al-Hasan said: When the dying person is at the point of death, five hundred angels attend him, take his soul and then ascend with it.

﴿Then they are returned to God, their true Master.﴾ The apparent sense is that the pronoun refers to the servants, and the address "your" (in ﴿عَلَيْكم﴾, "over you") comes as a shift from third person to second person (*iltifat*, a shift in address), because direct address brings the admonition closer to the listeners. It is also possible that the pronoun in *ruddū* refers to *aḥadikum* ("one of you") according to its meaning, since by *aḥadukum* he does not mean the singular in its literal sense but its plural meaning, as if it were said: "until death comes to you." It is read as *riddū* with a kasra on the *rāʾ*, the vowel of the *dāl* that was assimilated having been transferred to the *rāʾ*. The one who returns them (*al-rādd*) is the one who warns them of God, or it refers to the resurrection in the Hereafter, or the angels return them by death to God. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to "Our messengers," meaning the angels, who die as the children of Adam die and are returned to God, exalted is He. Its reference to the servants is more evident. *Mawlāhum* ("their Master") is a general term for the kinds of guardianship that exist between God and His servants, such as sovereignty, support, provision, and reckoning, and other things. In the annexation (*iḍāfa*) there is an indication of His mercy toward them. The apparent meaning of the statement about being returned to God is that it refers to resurrection, return to the judgment of God, and His recompense on the Day of Resurrection, and the end of the verse indicates this.

Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi) said: The explicit wording of the verse indicates that death occurs to the servant and that he is returned to God. The dead person, being dead, cannot be returned to God; rather, what is returned is the soul (*nafs*) and the spirit (*rūḥ*). Here there is death and life: death is the share of the body, and life is the share of the soul and the spirit. Thus it is established that the human being is nothing but the soul and the spirit, and is not merely a designation for this bodily structure. In His saying ﴿Be returned to God﴾ there is an indication that the spirit existed before the body, because the return from this world to the presence of Majesty happens only if it existed before attachment to the body. A parallel is ﴿Return to your Lord﴾ [al-Fajr: 28], and ﴿To God is your return, all of you﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 48]. There is also a hadith: "The spirits were created two thousand years before the bodies." The argument of the philosophers that souls did not exist before the existence of the body is weak, and we have shown its weakness in the rational books. End of his words, and there is some abridgement in it. He also said: ﴿To God﴾ indicates direction, and that is false, so it is necessary to interpret it as meaning that they are returned to a place where there is no owner and no judge other than Him. End.

The apparent meaning is that this return is by resurrection on the Day of Judgment, not what al-Razi intended. His description of God as *al-Ḥaqq* ("the True") means the justice that is not void nor metaphorical. Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: In this world they were under the control of false masters, which are the self (*nafs*), desire (*shahwa*), and anger (*ghaḍab*), as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Have you seen him who has taken his own desire as his god?﴾ [al-Jathiya: 23]. When he died, he was freed from the control of the false masters and passed to the control of the True Master. End of his words. His interpretation lies outside the ways and purposes of Arabic speech, and for the most part it resembles the words of those who call themselves sages (*ḥukamāʾ*). Al-Hasan and al-Aʿmash read *al-Ḥaqqa* with a fatḥa (*naṣb*). The apparent analysis is that it is an adjective that has been detached and put in the accusative for praise, and its accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) was permitted, with the sense: "the true return."

﴿Ah! To Him belongs the judgment﴾. This is an alert from Him, exalted is He, to His servants that all kinds of disposal belong to Him. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Ah! To Him belongs the judgment that day; no judgment belongs to anyone else."

﴿And He is the swiftest of reckoners﴾. The discussion of the swiftness of His reckoning has already been given in His saying: ﴿And God is swift in reckoning﴾ [al-Baqara: 202].

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 60–62 (part 1 of 2):

﴿It is He who takes your souls by night, and knows what you have earned by day. Then He raises you up therein, that a term appointed may be fulfilled. Then to Him is your return. Then He will inform you of what you used to do.﴾ The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that, when He (exalted is He) mentioned His exclusive possession of complete knowledge of universals and particulars, He mentioned His exclusive possession of complete power, as an alert to what divinity specifically entails. He mentioned something perceptible that overpowers humankind, namely the taking of souls by night and the raising up by day, neither of which lies within human power. Rather, it is a matter that Allah, exalted is He, brings upon a person. In common usage, "tawaffi" (taking in full, causing to die) refers to death, but here it means sleep, by way of metaphor, because of the link between sleep and death, which is the cessation of its perception, awareness and thought. Since the "tawaffi" meant here as sleep is a cause of rest, He (exalted is He) attributed it to Himself, and since it is painful in the sense of death, He said: ﴿Say: The angel of death will take you﴾ [al-Sajdah: 11], and ﴿Our messengers took him in full﴾, and ﴿The angels take them in full﴾ [al-Nahl: 28]. The apparent meaning is that the address is general to every hearer. Al-Zamakhshari said: The address is to the disbelievers, and the night was specified for sleep and the day for raising up, although one may sleep by day and be raised up by night, in keeping with what is usual. The meaning of "jaraḥtum" is "you earned," and from it come "jawarih al-tayr" (the birds of prey), that is, its hunters, and "ijtarahu al-sayyi'at" (they earned the evil deeds), meaning they acquired them. What is meant by it is the deeds of the limbs, and from this the limbs are called "jawarih." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It may be that it derives from "jarh" (wound), as if sin is a wound in the religion, and the Arabs say: the wound of the tongue is like the wound of the hand. Makki said: The origin of "ijtirah" is a man acting with one of his limbs, his hand or his foot, then it became common until every earner is called "mujtarih" and "jarih." The apparent sense of His words ﴿what you have earned﴾ is generality regarding what is acquired, whether good or bad. Al-Zamakhshari said: [it means] what you have earned of sins. End. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. Qatadah said: what you have done. Mujahid said: what you have earned. "Al-ba'th" here is the waking from sleep. The pronoun in "fihi" refers to the day, as said by Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Suddi; it refers to it verbally, and the meaning is on another day, as you say: "I have a dirham and its half." 'Abd Allah ibn Kathir said it refers to the taking in full, that is, He wakes you during the taking in full, meaning within its course and interstices. It was also said that it refers to the night. Al-Zamakhshari said: Then He raises you from the graves, regarding that by which you have ended your lifespans through sleep by night and earning sins by day and because of it, like your saying: "For what did you call me?" and you reply: "For such and such a matter." End. Taking it to mean raising from the graves is rejected by His words ﴿that a term appointed may be fulfilled﴾, because the meaning, and Allah knows best, is that He gives them life in these two states of sleep and wakefulness so that they may complete what has been decreed for them of their terms and written deeds. The fulfilment of the term is the separation of the lifespan's duration from what is other than it. "Musamma" (appointed) is in the knowledge of Allah, or in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), or at the completion of creation and the breathing of the spirit. In the Sahih it is reported that the angel says at the completion of that: "What is the provision? What is the term?" Al-Zamakhshari said: It is the term which He named and set for the resurrection of the dead and their recompense for their deeds. ﴿Then to Him is your return﴾ is the return to the station of reckoning. ﴿Then He will inform you of what you used to do﴾ in your nights and your days. End. Others, such as Ibn Jubayr, said: ﴿your return﴾ is by true death. When He (exalted is He) mentioned sleep and wakefulness, this was an alert to death and resurrection, and that their ruling with respect to Him (exalted is He) is one. Just as He puts to sleep and wakes, He causes to die and gives life. Talhah and Abu Raja' read: (liyaqdiya ajalan musamman), making the verb active and putting "ajal" in the accusative, meaning that Allah may complete their terms, like His words ﴿When Musa had fulfilled the term﴾ [al-Qasas: 29] in the reading of the majority. It is possible that the omitted subject is His pronoun or their pronoun.

﴿He is the Subduer over His servants, and He sends over you guardians﴾. The discussion of ﴿He is the Subduer over His servants﴾ has already passed. Ibn 'Atiyyah said here: "al-Qahir" (the Subduer), if it is taken as a verbal attribute, meaning the manifester of subjugation through thunderbolts, winds and punishment, then it is correct to make "fawq" (over) a locative of direction, because these things are only sent to the servants from above them. If "al-Qahir" is taken as an essential attribute, in the sense of power and dominance, then "fawq" cannot be of direction but is for elevation of rank and status, as you say: "The ruby is above iron." End. The apparent sense of ﴿and He sends﴾ is that it is conjoined to ﴿He is the Subduer﴾ [al-An'am: 18], a verbal clause conjoined to a nominal clause, and it is among the effects of subjugation. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be conjoined to His words ﴿takes you in full﴾ and what follows it of verbs, and that it be conjoined to ﴿the Subduer﴾, the sense being: He who subdues and sends, and that it be a circumstantial clause with an omitted subject, that is, "and He sends." The subject of the circumstantial clause is either the pronoun in ﴿the Subduer﴾ or the pronoun in the adverbial expression. This is the weakest of these analyses. ﴿Over you﴾ apparently relates to "yursilu" (sends), as in His words ﴿There will be sent against you both a flame﴾ [al-Rahman: 35]. The word "'ala" (over) indicates elevation and dominance, since they have power over us, so it is as if that is over us. It is possible that it relates to "ḥafazah" (guardians), meaning: and He sends guardians over you, that is, they guard over you your deeds, as He said: ﴿Indeed over you are guardians﴾ [al-Infitar: 10], as you say: "I kept watch over you for what you do." They permitted that it be a circumstantial clause, because if it were placed after, it would be an attribute, meaning guardians present over you, that is, having authority over you. "Hafazah" is the plural of "hafiz," and it is a regular plural of the pattern "fa'il" as a masculine adjective with a sound middle radical, rational, and rarely of what is not rational. Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, angels guarding your deeds, and they are the noble scribes. End. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: What is meant by that is the angels appointed to write down the deeds. End. What these two said is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. The apparent sense of the plural is that it corresponds to a plural, and the verse does not address how many are assigned to each person, nor what they guard. From Ibn 'Abbas: there are two angels with every person, one at his right for good deeds and the other at his left for evil deeds. When he commits an evil deed, the one on the right says: "Wait for him, perhaps he will repent of it; if he does not repent, it is written against him." It was also said: two angels by night and two by day, one of whom writes the good and the other writes the evil. When he walks, one of them is before him and the other behind him; when he sits, one is at his right and the other at his left. It was also said: five angels, two by night, two by day, and one who never leaves him by night or day, and what is written is the good deed and the bad deed. It was said: the acts of obedience, the acts of disobedience, and the permissible acts. It was said: they only observe speech and action, because of His words ﴿Not a word does he utter but there is with him a watcher ready﴾ [Qaf: 18], and His words ﴿They know what you do﴾ [al-Infitar: 12]. As for the deeds of the heart, their knowledge belongs to Allah, exalted is He. It was also said: they observe them in general, not in detail; so when one resolves upon an evil deed, a foul wind comes out of his mouth, and when one resolves upon a good deed, a pleasant wind comes out. Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): Allah is independent of the scribes by His knowledge, so what is the benefit of them? (I answer): In them is a kindness to the servants, for when they know that Allah is watchful over them, and that the angels, who are the noblest of His creation, are appointed over them to guard their deeds and write them down in scrolls displayed before the heads of the witnesses on the standing of the Resurrection, that is more restraining for them from ugliness and further from evil. End. His words "the angels who are the noblest of His creation" follow the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school) concerning the angels, and this benefit is not fixed, since it is possible that its benefit is that the scrolls of deeds will be weighed on the Day of Resurrection, because the weighing of deeds by their mere existence is impossible. This benefit follows the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah (the people of the Sunnah). As for the Mu'tazilah, they interpreted the weighing and the balance figuratively. His word "ḥafazah" does not imply that this guarding is by writing, as they explained. Rather, it has been said: they are the angels of whom the Prophet ﷺ said: "Angels succeed one another among you by night and angels by day." This was said by Qatadah and al-Suddi. It was also said: they guard the person from every thing until his term comes.

﴿Until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him in full﴾. That is, the causes of death; "tawaffathu" means they seize his soul. "Rusulunā" (Our messengers) came in the plural. ﴿And they do not fail﴾. This is a circumstantial clause, and its governing element is "tawaffathu," or it is a resumptive clause informing about them that they do not fail in anything of what they were commanded regarding the guarding and the taking in full. Its meaning is: they do not fall short. Al-A'raj and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read: "lā yufrifūna" with the light form, meaning they do not exceed the limit in what they were commanded. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Tafrit" is neglect and falling behind the limit, while "ifrāt" is exceeding the limit, meaning they neither diminish from what they were commanded nor add to it. End. This is the meaning of the words of Ibn Jinni. Ibn Bahr said: "yufarrirūna" means they do not allow anyone to fall behind them, that is, to precede them and escape them. It was said that the light reading may mean they do not go ahead of Allah's command, but this is only valid if it is transmitted that "afrata" means "farrata," that is, to go ahead. Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi) said: The explicit wording of the verse indicates that death occurs to the servant and that he is returned to God. Thus it is established that the human being is nothing but the soul and the spirit, and is not merely a designation for this bodily structure. In His saying ﴿Be returned to God﴾ there is an indication that the spirit existed before the body, because the return from this world to the presence of Majesty happens only if it existed before attachment to the body. A parallel is ﴿Return to your Lord﴾ [al-Fajr: 28], and ﴿To God is your return, all of you﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 48]. There is also a hadith: "The spirits were created two thousand years before the bodies." The argument of the philosophers that souls did not exist before the existence of the body is weak, and we have shown its weakness in the rational books. End of his words, and there is some abridgement in it. End.

﴿Ah! To Him belongs the judgment﴾. This is an alert from Him, exalted is He, to His servants that all kinds of disposal belong to Him. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Ah! To Him belongs the judgment that day; no judgment belongs to anyone else."

﴿And He is the swiftest of reckoners﴾. The discussion of the swiftness of His reckoning has already been given in His saying: ﴿And God is swift in reckoning﴾ [al-Baqara: 202].

Say: "Who delivers you from the darknesses of land and sea?" When the proofs of His divinity, namely His perfect knowledge and complete power, had been mentioned, He mentioned one of their effects, which is deliverance from calamities. This is an interrogative used to express affirmation, denunciation, reproach, and making them stop, regarding the corruption of their belief when they worship idols and abandon the One who delivers from calamities and to whom one turns for their removal. It has been said that the literal meaning of "darknesses" is intended, and it was made plural in view of its sources. On land and at sea there is the darkness of night, the darkness of clouds, and the darkness of thunderbolts; on land there is also the darkness of dust, the darkness of overcast sky, and the darkness of wind; and at sea there is also the darkness of waves. This would be by omitting a modifier, the estimate being: the perils of the darkness of land and sea and their dangers. Most exegetes hold that "darknesses" is a metaphor for the hardships of land and sea, their dangers, and their terrors. The Arabs say "a black day," "a dark day," and "a day with stars," as if, because of its darkness and the setting of its sun, stars appeared in it; they mean by this that the day was severe for them. Qatada and al-Zajjaj said: "from the distresses of land and sea." Al-Tabari related it as the going astray on the way in the darknesses. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also possible that what is intended is what they are threatened with of being swallowed by the earth on land and drowned at sea because of their sins; so when they call out and humble themselves, God removes from them the sinking and the drowning, and they are saved from its darknesses." End.

Calling Him with humility and in secrecy: that is, you call on Him, showing your need for Him and concealing it. Humility (tadarru') is an attribute that appears on a person, and secrecy (khufyah) is concealment. Al-Hasan said: "tadarru'an" means openly, and "khufyatan" means inwardly, in intention. Both are in the accusative as verbal nouns (masadir). "Tad'unahu" is a circumstantial clause. "Khufyatan" is read with a damma on the kha', which is the recitation of the majority, and with a kasra, which is the recitation of Abu Bakr. Al-A'mash read "wa-kheefatan" (with fear), from fear. The Kufan readers read "man yunajjikum" and "qul Allahu yunajjikum" with doubled letters (tashdid) in both. Hamid ibn Qays, Ya'qub, and Ali ibn Nasr transmitted from Abu 'Amr with light (takhfif) in both. The two Harams (the readers of Mecca and Medina) and the two Arabs read "man yunajjikum" with tashdid and "qul Allahu yunajjikum" with takhfif. Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 66–69:

﴿But your people have denied it, though it is the truth.﴾ Al-Suddi said: "it" (bihi) refers to the Qur'an, in which the clarification of the signs came. Al-Zamakhshari said: "it" refers to the punishment, and it is the truth, meaning it must certainly descend upon them. Ibn Atiyya said: It is possible that it refers to the threat contained in the verse, and al-Tabari inclined to this view. It was also said: it refers to the Prophet ﷺ (p-152), and this is because he is addressed with the second person (kaf) shortly after. End of quotation. Ibn Abi 'Abla read: "And your people have denied it" with a ta' (wa-kadhdhabat bihi qawmuk), as in His saying: ﴿The people of Noah denied [the messengers]﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 105]. Apparently, His saying ﴿and it is the truth﴾ is a resumptive (istinaf) sentence, not a circumstantial clause (hal).

﴿Say: I am not a guardian over you﴾, meaning: I am not one who stands over you to compel you to monotheism. It was also said: "a guardian" (wakil) means "one with authority"; and it was said: I am not able to prevent you from denial by compulsion; I am only a warner. Ibn Atiyya said: This was before the revelation of jihad and the command to fight, and then it was abrogated (nusikha). It was also said: there is no abrogation in this, since it is a statement of fact. Abrogation is applicable to it, because what is necessarily implied by the wording is: "I am not now," and it does not imply that he will not be in the future.

﴿For every news there is a fixed time﴾, meaning: for every term there is something by which it is announced, that is, from his announcing to them that they will be punished, and his threatening them with it, at a time of settlement and occurrence that is inevitable. It was also said: for every deed there is a recompense, but this is not the apparent meaning. Al-Suddi said: the news of the Qur'an settled with what he threatened them with of punishment on the day of Badr. Muqatil said: its fulfillment is in this world on the day of Badr, and in the Hereafter, Hell.

﴿And you will soon know﴾ is an intensification in threat and warning, so it may be a threat of the punishment of the Hereafter, and it may be a threat of war and of seizing them in faith by way of compulsion and conquest.

﴿And when you see those who engage in vain talk about Our signs, turn away from them until they engage in a different discourse﴾. This is an address to the Messenger ﷺ, and the believers are included in it, because the reason for the prohibition, which is hearing vain talk about the signs of Allah, encompasses him and them. It was also said: it is specific to him alone, because his standing up from them would be difficult for him, and his leaving those who are angry with him; the believers, with them, are not like him. It was also said: it is an address to the listener, and "those who engage in vain talk" are the polytheists, or the Jews, or the people of desires: three opinions.
