Whoever said that the address in ﴿And when you see﴾ is specific to the Messenger said that ﴿those who are mindful﴾ refers to the believers apart from him, and its meaning is permission for them but not for him, as if he said: "O Muhammad, do not sit with them; as for the believers, nothing of their reckoning is upon them; so if they sit, let them remind them, perhaps they will be mindful of Allah in abandoning what they are upon." This speaker also said: this permission which this verse entails was abrogated by the verse of al-Nisa. ﴿Reminder﴾ may be in the accusative position, meaning: "but you remind them"; and whoever said that the permission was due to acts of worship said: that was abrogated by the verse of al-Nisa. Or it may be in the nominative position, meaning: "but upon them is a reminder"; some estimated it as: "but it is a reminder," meaning: the obligation is a reminder. It was also said: "this is a reminder," meaning the prohibition is a reminder. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is not permissible that it be conjoined to the location of ﴿of anything﴾ as in your saying: "There is no one in the house but Zayd," because His saying ﴿of their reckoning﴾ prevents that. End of quotation. It seems he imagined that in conjunction the restriction of the conjoined term must apply to the first term, which is ﴿of their reckoning﴾, since it is a restriction on something, so he holds it impermissible that it be a conjunction of single words conjoined to ﴿of anything﴾ by location, because the sense would then become: "But a reminder of their reckoning." That is not the meaning, and what he imagined is not valid. Conjunction with *wa-lakin* does not entail what he mentioned: you say: "We have no bad man, but a good man"; "We have no man from Tamim, but a man from Quraysh"; "No learned man stood up, but an ignorant man." Based on what we have established, it may be a conjunction of sentences, as previously mentioned, and it may be a conjunction of single words. Conjunction is only by *wa*, and *lakin* is used for the sense of correction (istidrak). Ibn Atiyya said: The believer should follow the ruling of this verse with the atheists, the disputers, and those who engage in vain talk about it. Al-Tabari related from Abu Ja'far that he said: "Do not sit with the people of disputations, for they are those who engage in vain talk about the signs of Allah, exalted is He."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 66–69:

﴿But your people have denied it, though it is the truth.﴾ Al-Suddi said: "it" (bihi) refers to the Qur'an, in which the clarification of the signs came. Al-Zamakhshari said: "it" refers to the punishment, and it is the truth, meaning it must certainly descend upon them. Ibn Atiyya said: It is possible that it refers to the threat contained in the verse, and al-Tabari inclined to this view. It was also said: it refers to the Prophet ﷺ (p-152), and this is because he is addressed with the second person (kaf) shortly after. End of quotation. Ibn Abi 'Abla read: "And your people have denied it" with a ta' (wa-kadhdhabat bihi qawmuk), as in His saying: ﴿The people of Noah denied [the messengers]﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 105]. Apparently, His saying ﴿and it is the truth﴾ is a resumptive (istinaf) sentence, not a circumstantial clause (hal).

﴿Say: I am not a guardian over you﴾, meaning: I am not one who stands over you to compel you to monotheism. It was also said: "a guardian" (wakil) means "one with authority"; and it was said: I am not able to prevent you from denial by compulsion; I am only a warner. Ibn Atiyya said: This was before the revelation of jihad and the command to fight, and then it was abrogated (nusikha). It was also said: there is no abrogation in this, since it is a statement of fact. Abrogation is applicable to it, because what is necessarily implied by the wording is: "I am not now," and it does not imply that he will not be in the future.

﴿For every news there is a fixed time﴾, meaning: for every term there is something by which it is announced, that is, from his announcing to them that they will be punished, and his threatening them with it, at a time of settlement and occurrence that is inevitable. It was also said: for every deed there is a recompense, but this is not the apparent meaning. Al-Suddi said: the news of the Qur'an settled with what he threatened them with of punishment on the day of Badr. Muqatil said: its fulfillment is in this world on the day of Badr, and in the Hereafter, Hell.

﴿And you will soon know﴾ is an intensification in threat and warning, so it may be a threat of the punishment of the Hereafter, and it may be a threat of war and of seizing them in faith by way of compulsion and conquest.

﴿And when you see those who engage in vain talk about Our signs, turn away from them until they engage in a different discourse﴾. This is an address to the Messenger ﷺ, and the believers are included in it, because the reason for the prohibition, which is hearing vain talk about the signs of Allah, encompasses him and them. It was also said: it is specific to him alone, because his standing up from them would be difficult for him, and his leaving those who are angry with him; the believers, with them, are not like him. It was also said: it is an address to the listener, and "those who engage in vain talk" are the polytheists, or the Jews, or the people of desires: three opinions.

Here "you see" (ra'ayta) is visual (basariyya), and for this reason it is transitive to one object, and it is necessary to posit an omitted circumstantial clause, meaning: "And when you see those who engage in vain talk about Our signs while they are engaged in it," that is: "And when you see them occupied with this state." It was also said: "you see" is cognitive ('ilmiyya), because engaging in vain talk about the signs is not something perceived by sight; but this is far-fetched, because it would require omitting the second object of the verbs of knowing, so the sense would be: "And when you see those who engage in vain talk about Our signs as engaging in it." Omitting it as a restriction is not permissible, and omitting it as an abbreviation is very rare, to the point that some grammarians forbade it. Engaging in vain talk about the signs is a metaphor for mocking them and slandering them. Quraysh used to do this in their assemblies. ﴿So turn away from them﴾, meaning: do not sit with them and get up from them; it is not merely turning away in the heart, as He clarified: ﴿And it has already been revealed to you in the Book that when you hear the signs of Allah being denied and mocked, do not sit with them until they engage in a different discourse; otherwise, you would be like them﴾ [al-Nisa: 140]. It has been mentioned previously from the statements of the exegetes on this verse that His saying ﴿And it has already been revealed to you in the Book﴾ [al-Nisa: 140] refers to what was revealed in the Book, namely His saying: ﴿And when you see those who engage in vain talk﴾ and ﴿until they engage in﴾; "until" is the limit of turning away from them, meaning: there is no harm in your sitting with them.

As for the pronoun in (ghayrihi) "other than it," al-Hawfi said it refers to the vain talk, as the poet said:

*When the foolish one is forbidden, he rushes toward it and opposes, while the foolish one is in opposition.*

That is, he rushes toward foolishness. Abu al-Baqa' said: he mentioned the ha' because he returned it to the meaning of the signs, and because it is a discourse (hadith).

His saying: ﴿And if Satan causes you to forget, then do not sit after the reminder with the wrongdoing people﴾, meaning: if Satan preoccupies you with his whispering until you forget the prohibition on sitting with them, then do not sit with them after the reminder, that is, after your remembering the prohibition. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that it means: even if Satan makes you forget before the prohibition the ugliness of sitting with the mockers, since it is something the intellects reject, then do not sit after the reminder, that is, after We have reminded you of its ugliness and alerted you to it, with them. End of quotation. This contradicts the apparent sense of the condition, because they were already prohibited from sitting with them, and then this condition is conjoined to the previous condition, so all of it is future. How excellent is the coming of the first condition with *idha*, which is used for what is certain, because their engaging in vain talk about the signs is certain; and the coming of the second condition with *in*, because *in* is used for what is uncertain. The phrase ﴿with the wrongdoing people﴾ comes as an indication of the reason for engaging in vain talk about the signs and slandering them, and that the cause of this is their wrongdoing, which is exceeding the limit and placing things other than in their proper places. Ibn Atiyya said: *Imma* is a conditional particle, and it is generally followed by the heavy nun (nun al-tawkid al-thaqila), though it is sometimes not, as the poet said:

*Imma yusibka 'aduwwun fi munawa'a…*

and other examples. End of quotation. This question is disputed. Some grammarians held that when *ma* is added after *in*, the emphatic nun is obligatory and may not be omitted except in poetic necessity; others held that it is not obligatory and that it is permissible in speech. His restricting it to the heavy nun is not good; rather the correct view is the emphatic nun whether heavy or light, and it seems he considered its occurrences in the Qur'an, where after *imma* only the heavy nun appears.

Ibn Amir read: (yunassiyannaka) with a shadda, making it transitive by doubling; the majority read it with the hamza. Ibn Atiyya, mentioning the two readings, said: "However, the doubling is more intensive." End of quotation. This is not as he stated: there is no difference between the transitivity by doubling and by the hamza. The second object of *yunsiyannaka* is omitted, its estimate being: "if Satan causes you to forget our prohibiting you from sitting with them." *Al-dhikra* is a verbal noun of *dhakara*, formed on the pattern *fu'la* with its alif for feminine; no other verbal noun comes on the pattern *fu'la* except this one.

﴿And nothing of their reckoning falls upon those who are mindful of Allah﴾. Those who are mindful (alladhina yattaqun) are the believers, and the pronoun in ﴿their reckoning﴾ refers to the mockers who engage in vain talk about the signs. It was narrated that when the verse ﴿So do not sit with them﴾ [al-Nisa: 140] was revealed, the believers said: "We cannot circumambulate or worship in the Sacred Precinct," so the verse ﴿And nothing of their reckoning falls upon those who are mindful of Allah﴾ was revealed, and thus a measure of what they need in dealing with them in worship and the like was permitted. The apparent view is that the ruling of the Messenger ﷺ agrees with the ruling for others, since he is included in His saying ﴿those who are mindful﴾. He was commanded to turn away from them, so that if forgetfulness occurred and he remembered, then do not sit with them. It was also said: it is for the mindful, and he is their head, meaning: nothing of their reckoning is upon you.

﴿But it is a reminder﴾, meaning: but upon you is to remind them, a reminder, when you hear them engaging in vain talk, by standing up from them, showing your dislike of their action, and admonishing them.

﴿Perhaps they will be mindful﴾, meaning: perhaps they will refrain from engaging in vain talk about the signs out of shame before you and desire for your company, as Muqatil said; or perhaps they will be mindful of the threat through your reminding them. It was also said: the meaning is: do not sit with them nor approach them, until you do not hear their mockery and vain talk; and your prohibition from sitting is not because anything of their reckoning falls upon you; rather it is a reminder for you, so that perhaps you will be steadfast in your piety and increase it, meaning: you will remain firm in your mindfulness. Thus the pronoun in (la'allahum) "perhaps they" refers to ﴿those who are mindful﴾. Whoever said that the address in ﴿And when you see﴾ is specific to the Messenger said that ﴿those who are mindful﴾ refers to the believers apart from him, and its meaning is permission for them but not for him, as if he said: "O Muhammad, do not sit with them; as for the believers, nothing of their reckoning is upon them; so if they sit, let them remind them, perhaps they will be mindful of Allah in abandoning what they are upon." This speaker also said: this permission which this verse entails was abrogated by the verse of al-Nisa. ﴿Reminder﴾ may be in the accusative position, meaning: "but you remind them"; and whoever said that the permission was due to acts of worship said: that was abrogated by the verse of al-Nisa. Or it may be in the nominative position, meaning: "but upon them is a reminder"; some estimated it as: "but it is a reminder," meaning: the obligation is a reminder. It was also said: "this is a reminder," meaning the prohibition is a reminder. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is not permissible that it be conjoined to the location of ﴿of anything﴾ as in your saying: "There is no one in the house but Zayd," because His saying ﴿of their reckoning﴾ prevents that. End of quotation. It seems he imagined that in conjunction the restriction of the conjoined term must apply to the first term, which is ﴿of their reckoning﴾, since it is a restriction on something, so he holds it impermissible that it be a conjunction of single words conjoined to ﴿of anything﴾ by location, because the sense would then become: "But a reminder of their reckoning." That is not the meaning, and what he imagined is not valid. Conjunction with *wa-lakin* does not entail what he mentioned: you say: "We have no bad man, but a good man"; "We have no man from Tamim, but a man from Quraysh"; "No learned man stood up, but an ignorant man." Based on what we have established, it may be a conjunction of sentences, as previously mentioned, and it may be a conjunction of single words. Conjunction is only by *wa*, and *lakin* is used for the sense of correction (istidrak). Ibn Atiyya said: The believer should follow the ruling of this verse with the atheists, the disputers, and those who engage in vain talk about it. Al-Tabari related from Abu Ja'far that he said: "Do not sit with the people of disputations, for they are those who engage in vain talk about the signs of Allah, exalted is He."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 70:

﴿Leave alone those who have taken their religion as amusement and play.﴾ This is a command to leave them, and it was so because the followers of Islam were few at that time. Qatada said: "Then this was abrogated (naskh, the cancellation of a earlier ruling by a later one), along with similar instances, by fighting." Mujahid said: "It is only a command of threat and warning, like His saying, ﴿Leave Me with the one whom I created alone﴾ (74:11). There is no abrogation in it, because it contains a statement, which is the threat." Their religion refers to what they were upon: the bahira (a she-camel whose ears were slit and released), the sa'iba (a camel released to roam freely), the hami and the wasila (pre-Islamic animal-related practices), worship of idols, and circumambulating the House naked, whistling and clapping. Or it refers to the religion they were commanded and called to, which is the religion of Islam, ﴿as amusement and play﴾ in that they mocked it and ridiculed it. Or it refers to their worship, because they were absorbed in idle play, games, drinking wine, lute-playing and dancing, and had no worship except that. These are three opinions. ﴿Amusement and play﴾ is in the accusative as the second object of ﴿taken﴾.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: "The more likely view is that the one who truly upholds the religion is the one who supports it because evidence has established that it is true, right and correct. As for those who support it in order to use it as a means to attain positions and leadership, to overcome an opponent and to gather wealth, they have supported the religion for the sake of this world. God has judged this world in all the verses to be amusement and play. So the verse is an indication of the one who uses his religion as a means to his worldly life, and most of creation is described by this attribute." End of quote. There is some abridgement in it. The apparent meaning of his interpretation requires that ﴿taken﴾ here is transitive to one object, and that ﴿amusement and play﴾ is in the accusative as an object of purpose (object of cause), so the meaning becomes: they acquired their religion, practised it and displayed amusement and play, that is, for the sake of this world and gaining it. From some of the words of al-Zamakhshari [p. 155] and Ibn 'Ata'iyya it appears that ﴿amusement and play﴾ is the first object of ﴿taken﴾ and ﴿their religion﴾ is the second object. Al-Zamakhshari said: "That is, their religion, which they were obliged to follow, [they made] ﴿amusement and play﴾, because their worship and what they were upon, such as forbidding the bahira and the sa'iba and other things, were of the kind of play, following of desire and acting on lust, and of the category of jest rather than seriousness. They took what was play and amusement, such as the worship of idols and other things, as their religion. And they took their religion, which they were obliged to follow and called to, which is the religion of Islam, as ﴿amusement and play﴾, in that they mocked it and ridiculed it." End of quote. The apparent meaning of his second interpretation is what we have mentioned from him. Ibn 'Ata'iyya said: "He attributed the religion to them in the sense that they made idle play and amusement a religion. It may also be that the meaning is: they took their religion, which ought to have been for them, as amusement and play." End of quote. So his first interpretation is what we have mentioned from him. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It was also said: God appointed for every people a festival which they honour, pray in and fill with the remembrance of God. All people, polytheists and People of the Book, took their festivals as amusement and play, except the Muslims, who took their religion as their festival, as God prescribed it."

The meaning of ﴿Leave them﴾ (6:91) is: turn away from them, do not care about their denial and mockery, and do not occupy your heart with them. End of quote.

﴿And the life of this world has deceived them﴾ may be coordinated with the relative clause, or it may be a new statement, meaning: the deceptions deceived them, and these are the hopes in what cannot be attained, so they were deceived by God's blessings, His provision and His giving them respite. It was said: it deceived them by their denial of the Resurrection. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: "Because the love of this world took hold of them, they turned away from the reality of the religion and confined themselves to adorning outward appearances, in order to reach the trash of this world by them." End of quote. It was also said: ﴿garrat-hum﴾ comes from ghar with a fatha on the ghayn, meaning: it filled their mouths and satisfied them. From this is the poet's saying:

"When we met at al-Hulayba, he filled me with his kindness until I came out staggering."

And from this: the bird ghharra its chick (it filled the chick's mouth with food).

﴿And warn by it, lest a soul be delivered to destruction for what it has earned﴾. The pronoun in (bihi) refers either to the Qur'an, to the religion, or to ﴿their reckoning﴾ (6:69). There are three opinions, the first of which is the first, like His saying, ﴿So remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning﴾ (50:45). As for ﴿tubsala﴾, Ibn Abbas said: it is disgraced. Al-Hasan and Ikrima said: it is handed over. Qatada said: it is detained and held as a pledge. Al-Kalbi, Ibn Zayd and al-Akhfash said: it is requited. Al-Dahhak said: it is burned. Ibn Zayd also said: it is seized. Muwarrij said: it is punished. It was said: deliverance and entry into Paradise are forbidden to it. Abu Bakr said: some of our shaykhs approved the view of the one who said: it is handed over (to destruction) by its deeds, unable to escape, because it is said: istabsala lil-mawt (he faced death), meaning he saw what he could not repel. They agreed that ﴿tubsala﴾ is in the place of the object of purpose, and they estimated: out of dislike that ﴿tubsala﴾, out of fear that ﴿tubsala﴾, and lest ﴿tubsala﴾. In my view it is also permissible that it occupies the place of the genitive as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun, the pronoun being explained by the substitute, and the verb of destruction (al-ibsal) is left implicit because of the grandeur implied in an implicit reference, just as the affair and the matter are left implicit and explained by the substitute, which is the ibsal. So the sense is: and warn of the pledging and detention of souls by what they have earned, just as they said: "O God, bless him, the compassionate, the merciful." Sibawayh permitted this. He said: "If you say: darabtu wa darabuni qawmaka (I struck and they struck me, your people), you put it in the accusative, except in the view of the one who said: akaluni al-baraghith (the fleas ate me), or you take it as a substitute for the implicit pronoun." He also said: "If you say: daraba-ni wa daraba-tu-hum qawmuka (he struck me and I struck them, your people), you put it in the nominative by inversion of order, unless you make the substitute here as you did in the nominative." The following line has also been transmitted:

"She was combed, then she cleaned her teeth with a twig of iskhil wood."

with ʻūdi read in the genitive, as a substitute for the pronoun. The meaning is: lest a soul be handed over, abandoning faith, for what it has earned of disbelief or by its evil deeds.

﴿For it there is no protector other than God﴾, meaning: other than God's punishment, ﴿nor any intercessor﴾ who would avert it by asking on its behalf. This sentence is a descriptive clause, or a circumstantial clause, or a new statement; the last is the most apparent. (Min) here indicates the starting point. Ibn 'Ata'iyya said: "It may be superfluous." End of quote. This is weak.

﴿And if it offers every ransom, it will not be accepted from it﴾, meaning: if it offers every ransom. The 'adl here means ransom, because the one who ransoms equals the ransom with its like. It is reported from Abu 'Ubayda that the intended meaning of 'adl here is the opposite of injustice, which is equity, meaning: if it acts equitably in every matter by monotheism and submission after obstinacy. Al-Tabari rejected this view on the basis of consensus that the repentance of a disbeliever is accepted. This does not follow, because it is a statement about its condition on the Day of Resurrection, which is a state of direct witnessing and compulsion, in which faith does not benefit a soul that had not believed before. They said: ﴿every ransom﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun, and the pronoun in (yu'khadh) refers to the thing being ransomed, understood from the context, and does not refer to the verbal noun, because taking cannot be attributed to it. As for ﴿it will not be accepted from it, those are they﴾, the meaning is of what is ransomed. So it is correct to attribute the taking to it. It is also permissible that ﴿every ransom﴾ be in the accusative as the object, meaning: and if it ransoms itself (every ransom), i.e., every thing it ransoms itself with will not be accepted from it, and the pronoun on this reading refers to ﴿every ransom﴾. This conditional sentence is by way of supposition and assumption, not by way of the possibility of its occurrence.

﴿Those are they who have been delivered to destruction for what they earned﴾. The apparent meaning is that it refers to ﴿those who took﴾, as al-Hawfi said, and al-Zamakhshari followed him. Ibn 'Ata'iyya said: ﴿Those﴾ is a reference to the category implied by His saying, ﴿lest a soul be delivered﴾.

﴿For them is a drink of scalding water and a painful punishment for what they used to disbelieve﴾. The apparent view is that it is a new statement, though it may be a circumstantial clause. (Sharab) is on the pattern fa'al in the sense of maf'ul, like ta'am in the sense of ma'tum (food). The pattern fi'al in the sense of maf'ul is not regular: one does not say dirab or qital in the sense of madrub or maqtul.

**[Commentary of Abu Hayyan on al-Bahr al-Muhit, Surah al-An'am 6:71–73, part 1 of 2]**

﴿Say, "Shall we call upon, besides Allah, that which neither benefits us nor harms us, and be turned back on our heels after Allah has guided us?"﴾ That is: besides Allah, the One who benefits and harms, the Originator of things, the All-Powerful, [do we call upon] that which has no power to benefit or harm, since they are idols: wood, stone, and other such things. "And be turned back" to polytheism "on our heels": the *qahqarā* (retreat backwards) is to go back, and it is the base way of walking after Allah has guided us to the path of truth, and to the upright, lofty way of walking. "And be turned back" is coordinated (*ma'ṭūf*) with "Shall we call upon" (*a-nadʿū*), meaning: would this happen? This is an interrogative used in the sense of denial, i.e., nothing of this sort occurs. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the *wāw* in it be a *wāw* of circumstance (*ḥāl*), meaning: "while we are being turned back," i.e., would this matter occur in this condition? But this is weak, because it requires an implied subject (*mubtada'*) and because it would be an emphasizing circumstantial clause. The expression "returning on one's heels" is used of one who returns from good to evil. Al-Tabari and others said: returning on one's heels is used of one who hoped for something and was disappointed.

﴿Like one whom the devils have enticed on the earth, bewildered, having companions who call him to guidance, "Come to us."﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said: "Like one" (*ka-lladhī*) [p. 157] whom the rebellious jinn and the ghouls have taken away on the earth, in the desert, bewildered, wandering, astray from the road, not knowing what to do. "Him" (*lahu*): i.e., for this one who has been enticed, "companions" means a group of companions, "who call him to guidance," i.e., to show him the straight path. Or "the straight path" is called "guidance." They say to him, "Come to us," while he has gone astray in the wilderness, following the jinn, not answering them nor coming to them. This is based on what the Arabs assume and believe, that jinn lead humans astray and ghouls take control of them, like His saying: ﴿those who are driven to madness by the Devil﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:275). Thus the one who strays from the path of Islam and follows the steps of Satan is compared to such a person, while Muslims call him to it and he does not heed them. End of quote. The essence of his words is taken from the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, but he lengthened and refined it. Ibn 'Abbas said: The likeness of one who worships an idol is like one whom the ghoul has called, so he follows it, and in the morning it has cast him into a wilderness and a place of destruction, so he is bewildered in those deserts. Al-Zamakhshari took *istahwathu* (enticed him) to derive from *hawā*, which is affection and inclination, as if it were said: "like one whom the devils have inclined away from the clear road into the barren desert." Others, such as Abu 'Ali, took it to derive from *huwiyy* (falling), meaning they threw him into a pit, and *istaf'ala* would be used in the sense of *af'ala*, like *istazalla* and *azalla* (both meaning to cause to slip). The Arabs say: *hawā al-rajul* (the man fell) and *ahwāhu ghayruhu* (another made him fall), and *istahwāhu* means he asked him to fall: *hawā* and *yahwī* (to fall) something. *Al-huwiyy* is falling from a height to a low place. The poet said:

*My son fell from the peaks of nobility, so his foot and his hand slipped.*

*Al-huwiyy* is also used of rushing headlong toward something one desires, and from this comes: ﴿So make hearts from among people yearn toward them﴾ (Ibrahim 14:37). And he said:

*They yearn toward Makkah seeking guidance; the believers of the jinn are not like its disbelievers.*

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: This parable is extremely beautiful, because one who falls from a high place into a deep hollow falls toward it while turning around on himself, since a stone, in its descent from above to below, descends in a spiral, and this causes complete turmoil and bewilderment. When he descends from above to below, he does not know on what position he will land, whether his affliction will increase because of his fall or decrease. Nothing is more complete or better suited to describe the bewildered and frightened person than this parable. End of quote. This is a speech of excessive elaboration with no real benefit in it. Al-Zamakhshari made His saying "having companions" mean "having a group of companions," and set against them, in the form of the comparison, the Muslims who call him to guidance and whom he does not heed. This is the interpretation of Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. Others made "having companions" refer to the devils who call to it, or who do not call him to guidance according to their claim and what they lead him to believe. Thus "companions" here is likened to the disbelievers who confirm in apostasy those who have turned away from Islam. This interpretation is also related from Ibn 'Abbas. Makki and others mention that the one whom the devils enticed is 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr al-Siddiq, and the "companions" are his father and mother. The people of biography mention that this verse was revealed about him: he invited his father Abu Bakr to worship idols. He was the eldest son of Abu Bakr and full brother of 'A'ishah; their mother was Umm Ruman bint al-Harith ibn Ghanm al-Kinaniyyah. He witnessed Badr and Uhud with his people while still a disbeliever, and he challenged to single combat, whereupon his father Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) rose to face him in single combat. It is mentioned that the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "Spare me yourself." Then he embraced Islam and his Islam was good, and he accompanied the Messenger (peace be upon him) during the truce of al-Hudaybiyah. His name had been 'Abd al-Ka'bah, and the Messenger (ﷺ) named him 'Abd al-Rahman. In the Sahih it is reported that 'A'ishah heard someone say that His saying: ﴿And one who said to his parents, "Uff to you both"﴾ (al-Ahqaf 46:17) was revealed about 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr. She said: "They lied. By Allah, nothing of the Qur'an was revealed about us except my innocence."

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: If this is about Abu Bakr, how is it that the Messenger was told: ﴿Say, "Shall we call upon..."﴾? I say: Because of the closeness that existed between the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers, and especially between him and al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him). [p. 158] End of quote. This question only arises if it is correct that it was revealed about Abu Bakr and his son 'Abd al-Rahman, but that is not established.

The position of "like one" (*ka-lladhī*) is in the accusative. It was said that it is an adjective (*na't*) of an omitted verbal noun (*maṣdar*), meaning: a return like the return of the one [who was enticed]. The better view is that it is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), meaning: being like the one [who was enticed]. Apparently *alladhī* (the one) is singular, but it may mean the plural sense, i.e., like the group who. Hamzah recited *istahwāhu* with an inclined *alif*. Al-Sulami, al-A'mash and Talhah recited *istahwathu al-shaytān* with a *tā'* and the singular *al-shaytān*. Al-Kisa'i said: It is so in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud. End of quote. However, those who transmitted to us the recitation from Ibn Mas'ud transmitted *al-shayāṭīn* in the plural. Al-Hasan recited *al-shayāṭūn*, and its parallel has been mentioned previously, and he has been regarded as having erred in this. It has been said that it is anomalous and ugly. The apparent sense of His saying "on the earth" is that it relates to *istahwathu* (enticed him). It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause from the object of *istahwathu*, meaning: being on the earth. It was also said that it relates to *ḥayrān* (bewildered). It was also said that it relates to the pronoun in *ḥayrān*. *Ḥayrān* is not declined (*lā yanṣarif*), its feminine is *ḥayrā*, and *ḥayrān* is a circumstantial clause from the object of *istahwathu*. It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause from *alladhī* (the one), with the governing element being the implied return. The clause "having companions" is either a circumstantial clause, or an adjective of *ḥayrān*, or a new independent clause. "To the guidance" (*ilā al-hudā*) relates to *yad'ūnahu* (call him), and *ātinā* (come to us) is from *al-ityān* (coming). In the codex of 'Abd Allah it is *ataynā* as a past verb, not an imperative, so *ilā al-hudā* relates to it.

﴿Say, "Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the [true] guidance."﴾ Those who said that "having companions" means the devils, and that His saying "to the guidance" is according to their claim, took this sentence as a refutation of them, meaning: what you claim is not guidance; rather it is disbelief, and guidance is only the guidance of Allah, which is faith. Those who said that "companions" is a parable for the believers who call to the guidance which is faith, took it as an announcement that the guidance is the guidance of Allah, given to whomever He wills. It does not follow from their calling to guidance that guidance necessarily occurs; rather that is in the hand of Allah. Whomever He guides is guided.

﴿And we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds.﴾ Apparently the *lām* is the *lām* of purpose (*kay*), and the second object of *umirnā* (we have been commanded) is omitted, and they estimated it as: "and we have been commanded with sincerity, so that we may submit and surrender to the Lord of the worlds." The clause is included within what is said, coordinated with "Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the [true] guidance." Al-Zamakhshari said: It is a cause for the command, so the meaning of "we have been commanded" is: it was said to us, "Submit, so that we may submit." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The view of Sibawayh is that "that we may submit" (*li-nuslima*) is in the position of the object (*mafʿūl*), and that your saying "I have been commanded *li-aqūma*" and "I have been commanded *an aqūma*" (that I stand) are the same. Similar to it is the poet's saying:

*I want to forget her memory, but it is as if Layla appears to me on every path.*

And other such examples. End of quote. On the apparent sense of his words, the *lām* is extra (*zā'idah*), and *an nuslima* is the complement of *umirnā*, as a second object after dropping the preposition. It was also said that the *lām* has the meaning of *bāʾ* (with), as if it were said: "and we have been commanded *bi-an nuslima*" (to submit). The *lām* in the sense of *bāʾ* is a strange opinion. What Ibn 'Atiyyah attributed to Sibawayh is not as he stated. Rather, that is the view of al-Kisa'i and al-Farra', who claimed that the *lām* of purpose falls in the position of *an* after *arada* (wanted) and *amara* (commanded). God the Exalted said: ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:26); ﴿They desire to extinguish﴾ (al-Saff 61:8), meaning *an yuṭfi'ū*; ﴿Allah only desires to remove from you the impurity﴾ (al-Ahzab 33:33); and "I want to forget her memory." Abu Ishaq refuted this for both of them. Sibawayh and his companions held that the *lām* here is connected to an omitted element, and that the verb before it is meant as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), and the meaning is: the desire is for the clarification, and the command is for submission. Thus the two are a subject and predicate. So the following views are reached concerning this *lām*: first, it is extra; second, it has the meaning of *kay* (purpose), either for the verb itself or for the verbal noun formed from the verb; third, it is the *lām* of *kay*, treated as if it were *an*; fourth, it has the meaning of *bāʾ*. We have discussed this issue in the book *al-Takmil*.

The phrase "to the Lord of the worlds" (*li-rabbi al-ʿālamīn*) is a reminder that He is the Owner of the entire world, including what they worship, such as idols and others.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah al-An'am (6), verses 71–73 (part 2 of 2)**

﴿And that you establish the prayer and fear Him.﴾ Here *an* (أنْ) is *masdariyyah* (the verbal particle that forms a verbal noun). Scholars differ over what it is coordinated with. Al-Zajjaj said: it is coordinated with his statement "*li-nuslima*" (that we may submit), so the sense is "*li-an nuslima wa-an aqimu*" (that we submit and that you establish). Ibn Atiyya said: "The wording rules this out, because *nuslima* is *mu'rab* (inflected, *i'rab* being grammatical case-inflection) while *aqimu* is *mabni* (indeclinable), and coordinating an indeclinable word with an inflected one is not permitted, since coordination requires sharing the same governing element." End of quote. But what he mentioned, that an indeclinable word may not be coordinated with an inflected one and that this is impermissible, is not as he stated. Rather, it is permissible, as in *qama Zaydun wa-hadha* (Zayd stood and this one [stood]). God Most High says: ﴿He will go before his people on the Day of Resurrection and lead them into the Fire﴾ [11:98]. The most that this shows is that when the governing element meets an inflected word it affects it, and when it meets an indeclinable word it does not affect it. It is also permissible to say *in qama Zaydun wa-yaqsidni uhsin ilayhi* (if Zayd stands and visits me, be kind to him), with *yaqsidni* in the jussive. Here *in* (if) has no effect on *qama* because it is indeclinable, but it does have an effect on *yaqsidni* because it is inflected.

Ibn Atiyya then said: "Unless the coordination is taken to be with *in* alone, which is awkward. It is more properly explained by supposing that his statement *an aqimu* [42:13] has the meaning of *wa-li-yuqim* (and let him establish), and then it came out in the form of a command for the sake of the eloquence of the expression. So coordination became permissible, on the basis that we disregard the grammatical rule of the wording and rely on the meaning. This resembles, in one respect, what Yunus reported from the Arabs: *udkhulu al-awwalu fa-al-awwalu* (enter, the first, then the next), whereas otherwise the only correct form would be *udkhulu al-awwala fa-al-awwala* with the accusative." End of quote. What Ibn Atiyya corrected with his statement "Unless... to the end" is precisely what al-Zajjaj meant: that *an aqimu* is coordinated with *an nuslima*, and both are a reason for the implied command. Ibn Atiyya found it awkward because he wished *an aqimu* to retain the meaning of a command. This is not so, because when *an* (in its verbal-noun function) enters upon an imperative verb, the particle and the imperative combine to form a verbal noun, and once they form a verbal noun the sense of command is removed from them. Grammarians, including Sibawayh and others, have permitted *an* (the verbal-noun particle that governs the subjunctive) to be connected to the past tense and to the imperative. Sibawayh said: "You say *katabtu ilayhi bi-an qum*," meaning "with standing." When this is the case, his statement *li-nuslima* and *an aqimu* are in the sense of "for submission and for the establishment of the prayer." As for Ibn Atiyya's comparison with *udkhulu al-awwalu fa-al-awwalu* with the nominative, it does not resemble it, because *udkhulu* cannot, if the pronoun is removed from it, govern what follows it. This differs from *an*, which is connected to the imperative. So there is no real resemblance between them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, to what is his statement *wa-an aqimu* coordinated? I say: to the position of *li-nuslima*, as if it were said: 'And we were commanded that we submit and that you establish [the prayer].'" End of quote. The apparent sense of this explanation is that *an nuslima* is in the position of the second object of *wa-umirna* (we were commanded), and *wa-an aqimu* is coordinated with it. In this case the *lam* would be superfluous. But he had earlier stated that the *lam* indicates the reason for the command, so his speech is self-contradictory, since what is a reason cannot be an object. What shows that by his statement *an nuslima* he meant that it stands in the position of the second object is his statement after that: "It is also possible that the sense is: 'And we were commanded *li-an nuslima* and *li-an aqimu*,' i.e., for submission and for the establishment of the prayer." End of quote. This is the view of al-Zajjaj. If this view were not different from his first view, his two statements would be the same, and that is contradictory.

Al-Zajjaj also said: "It is possible that *wa-an aqimu* is coordinated with *i'tina* (come to us)." It has also been said that it is coordinated with his statement: ﴿Indeed the guidance of God is the [true] guidance﴾, and the sense is: "Say, *an aqimu*..." Both of these views are very weak, and the structure of the speech does not support them. Ibn Atiyya said: "It is appropriate that it be [understood] with the interpretation: '*wa-iqamah*' (and establishment), so it is coordinated with the implied object of *umirna*." End of quote. He had supposed: "And we were commanded with sincerity or with faith *li-an nuslima*." This view is not objectionable, and it is closer than the two views before it, since a second object for *umirna* must be supposed in any case. It is also permissible to omit the word coordinated-to when the meaning is understood. You say: *a-darabta Zaydan?* (Did you strike Zayd?) and he answers: *na'am wa-Amran* (yes, and Amr), meaning: "I struck him and Amr." Al-Farra' also permitted: *ja'ani alladhi wa-Zaydun qa'imani* (the one who came to me and Zayd are two standing [men]), meaning: "the one who came to me, he, and Zayd are two standing [men]," so that *huwa* (he) is omitted because the sense indicates it. The pronoun in the accusative in ﴿wa-ittaquhu﴾ (and fear Him) refers to the Lord of the worlds.

﴿And it is He to whom you will be gathered.﴾ This is a declarative sentence that contains both an admonition and a warning to those who abandon compliance with what they have been commanded: submission, prayer, and fear of God. The fruits of performing these deeds and the regrets of neglecting them appear only on the Day of Gathering and Resurrection.

﴿And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in truth.﴾ When God Most High mentioned that He gathers all creation to His recompense, which is the ultimate end to which their affair returns, He mentioned the beginning of the existence of the world and His bringing it into being *bi-l-haqq* (in truth). That is, with what is true, having no vanity in it, nor is it false. That is, He did not create them in vain or for play, but they issued from wisdom and rightness. And it is so that these two may be taken as evidence of the existence of the Creator, since these great created things, upon which are the marks of origination, must have one originator who is knowing, powerful, willing, glorified and exalted. It has also been said: the meaning of *bi-l-haqq* is "by His word," in His saying to the created things "Be!" and in His saying: ﴿Come, willingly or unwillingly﴾ [41:11]. What is meant in this and similar passages is only the manifestation of the responsiveness of what God wills to do, and its bringing forth into existence swiftly, and placing it in the position of what is commanded and so complies.

﴿And the day He says "Be!" and it is, His word is the truth.﴾ Scholars permitted *yawma* (the day) to be the object of an implied verb, and they supposed the sense: "Mention the resurrection, the day He says 'Be!'", i.e., the day He says to bodies "Be!", being brought back. The sentence is complete at His statement "Be!" Then He informed that His word will be the truth, which was in this world, a report of the resurrection. In this case *qawluhu* ("His word") is the subject of *fa-yakun* ("and it is"). Or the sentence is complete at His statement "Be! and it is," and *qawluhu al-haqq* ("His word is the truth") is a nominal sentence with subject and predicate. Al-Zajjaj said: *yawma yaqu* (the day He says) is coordinated with the pronoun in His statement *wa-ittaquhu* (and fear Him), i.e., "fear His punishment and the terrors, and the day," so its accusative case is that of a direct object, not an adverb of time. It has also been said: *wa-yawma* is coordinated with "the heavens and the earth," and the governing element is *khalaqa* (He created). It has also been said: the governing element is *udhkur* (mention). Or it is coordinated with *bi-l-haqq*, since that is in the position of the accusative, and *yaquolu* has the sense of the past tense, as if he said: "And He is the One who created the heavens and the earth in truth, and the day He said to them 'Be!'" The sentence is complete at His statement *fa-yakun* (and it is), and *qawluhu al-haqq* is a nominal sentence. Or it is complete at *kun* (Be!), and *fa-yakunu qawluhu al-haqq* begins anew, i.e., "what appears appears," with *qawluhu* as the subject of *yakunu*, *al-haqq* as an adjective, and *yakunu* as a complete verb (meaning "to happen" or "to come into being"). All these grammatical analyses are remote, and the structure of the speech does not accept them. The closest of what has been said is that of al-Zamakhshari: that *qawluhu al-haqq* is a subject, *al-haqq* is its adjective, and *yawma yaquolu* is the predicate of the subject, so that it is attached to an implied stable element, as you say: *yawma al-jumu'ati al-qitalu* (on Friday is the fighting). *Al-yawm* here means "the time," and the meaning is that He created the heavens and the earth standing in truth and wisdom, and at the time He says to any thing among things "Be!", that thing comes to be. *Qawluhu al-haqq* means that nothing among the heavens, the earth, and all other created things exists except out of wisdom and rightness. Al-Zamakhshari also permitted another view: that *qawluhu al-haqq* is the subject of *fa-yakun*, so that the accusative of *yawma* is governed by an implied element indicated by His statement *bi-l-haqq*, as if it were said: "Be, on the day, in truth." This is a strained analysis.

﴿And to Him belongs the dominion on the day the Horn is blown.﴾ It has been said that *yawma* is a substitute for *wa-yawma yaquolu*. It has also been said that it is in the accusative governed by *al-mulk* (dominion). Specifying that day with it is like specifying it with His statement ﴿To whom belongs the dominion today?﴾ [40:16] and with His statement ﴿And the command on that day belongs to God﴾ [82:19]. Its benefit is to inform that He alone holds dominion at a time when no claim of dominion can be made. It has also been said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial element (*hal*), its referent being *al-mulk* and its governing element being *lahu*. It has also been said that it is in the position of the predicate of His statement *qawluhu al-haqq*, i.e., "on the day the Horn is blown." It has also been said that it is an adverb of time governing *tuhsharun* (you will be gathered), or governing *yaquolu* (He says), or governing *'alimu al-ghaybi wa-al-shahadah* (Knower of the unseen and the witnessed). Al-Hasan read *fi al-suwar* (in the trumpets, plural of *sur*, which is the variant reading) and this was reported by Amr ibn Ubayd from Iyad. The reading *al-suwar* supports the interpretation of those who understood it this way, since *al-suwar* is the plural of *surah* (form), as in *thawmah* and *thuwam* (garlic, plural). The apparent meaning is that there is literally a blowing. It has also been said that it is a metaphor for the arrival of the Hour and the passing away of this world. It was also transmitted from Abd al-Warith, from Abu Amr, that he read *nanfukhu* (We blow) with the first person plural of majesty.

﴿The Knower of the unseen and the witnessed.﴾ That is, He is the Knower. Or it is a subject, on the supposition of the question "Who is the one blowing?" Or it is the subject of *yaquolu* or of *yunfakhu*, with an omitted element indicated by *yunfakhu*, like *rijalun* (men) after His statement *yusabbihu* (is glorified) with the *ba'* vowelled with a fatha; and *shuraka'uhum* (their associates) after *zuyyina* (was made attractive), in the passive, with *qatlu* (killing) in the nominative; and like *da'i'un li-khusumatin* (a suppliant in dispute) after *liyabki Yazidu* (Let Yazid weep):

*Let Yazid weep, a suppliant in dispute, and a weeping man who was cast down.*

The supposition is: "He is glorified by men" (*yusabbihu lahu rijalun*), "their associates made it attractive" (*zayyanahu shurakauhum*), and "a suppliant weeps for him" (*yubkihi da'i'un*). Or it is an adjective of *alladhi* (the one who). These are several views, and the first is the best. The unseen and the witnessed encompass all existing things. Al-A'mash read *'alimi* (Knower) in the genitive, and it has been explained as a substitute for the pronoun in *lahu* (to Him) or for "Lord of the worlds," or as an adjective of the pronoun in *lahu*. The first view is better, because the substituted-for noun is far off in the second, and because an absent pronoun is being described, which is not the position of the majority of scholars; it was permitted only by al-Kisai alone.

﴿And He is the Wise, the All-Aware.﴾ Since He mentioned the creation of creatures and the swiftness of His bringing into being whatever He wills, and since the resurrection entails the annihilation of creatures before it, the attribute *al-Hakim* (the Wise) is fitting. And since He mentioned that He is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the attribute *al-Khabir* (the All-Aware) is fitting, since it is an attribute indicating knowledge of what is subtle in perception among things.

(p. 160) (p. 161) (p. 162)

**[Commentary of Abu Hayyan on al-Bahr al-Muhit, Surah al-An'am 6:71–73, part 1 of 2]**

﴿Say, "Shall we call upon, besides Allah, that which neither benefits us nor harms us, and be turned back on our heels after Allah has guided us?"﴾ That is: besides Allah, the One who benefits and harms, the Originator of things, the All-Powerful, [do we call upon] that which has no power to benefit or harm, since they are idols: wood, stone, and other such things. "And be turned back" to polytheism "on our heels": the *qahqarā* (retreat backwards) is to go back, and it is the base way of walking after Allah has guided us to the path of truth, and to the upright, lofty way of walking. "And be turned back" is coordinated (*ma'ṭūf*) with "Shall we call upon" (*a-nadʿū*), meaning: would this happen? This is an interrogative used in the sense of denial, i.e., nothing of this sort occurs. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the *wāw* in it be a *wāw* of circumstance (*ḥāl*), meaning: "while we are being turned back," i.e., would this matter occur in this condition? But this is weak, because it requires an implied subject (*mubtada'*) and because it would be an emphasizing circumstantial clause. The expression "returning on one's heels" is used of one who returns from good to evil. Al-Tabari and others said: returning on one's heels is used of one who hoped for something and was disappointed.

﴿Like one whom the devils have enticed on the earth, bewildered, having companions who call him to guidance, "Come to us."﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said: "Like one" (*ka-lladhī*) [p. 157] whom the rebellious jinn and the ghouls have taken away on the earth, in the desert, bewildered, wandering, astray from the road, not knowing what to do. "Him" (*lahu*): i.e., for this one who has been enticed, "companions" means a group of companions, "who call him to guidance," i.e., to show him the straight path. Or "the straight path" is called "guidance." They say to him, "Come to us," while he has gone astray in the wilderness, following the jinn, not answering them nor coming to them. This is based on what the Arabs assume and believe, that jinn lead humans astray and ghouls take control of them, like His saying: ﴿those who are driven to madness by the Devil﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:275). Thus the one who strays from the path of Islam and follows the steps of Satan is compared to such a person, while Muslims call him to it and he does not heed them. End of quote. The essence of his words is taken from the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, but he lengthened and refined it. Ibn 'Abbas said: The likeness of one who worships an idol is like one whom the ghoul has called, so he follows it, and in the morning it has cast him into a wilderness and a place of destruction, so he is bewildered in those deserts. Al-Zamakhshari took *istahwathu* (enticed him) to derive from *hawā*, which is affection and inclination, as if it were said: "like one whom the devils have inclined away from the clear road into the barren desert." Others, such as Abu 'Ali, took it to derive from *huwiyy* (falling), meaning they threw him into a pit, and *istaf'ala* would be used in the sense of *af'ala*, like *istazalla* and *azalla* (both meaning to cause to slip). The Arabs say: *hawā al-rajul* (the man fell) and *ahwāhu ghayruhu* (another made him fall), and *istahwāhu* means he asked him to fall: *hawā* and *yahwī* (to fall) something. *Al-huwiyy* is falling from a height to a low place. The poet said:

*My son fell from the peaks of nobility, so his foot and his hand slipped.*

*Al-huwiyy* is also used of rushing headlong toward something one desires, and from this comes: ﴿So make hearts from among people yearn toward them﴾ (Ibrahim 14:37). And he said:

*They yearn toward Makkah seeking guidance; the believers of the jinn are not like its disbelievers.*

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: This parable is extremely beautiful, because one who falls from a high place into a deep hollow falls toward it while turning around on himself, since a stone, in its descent from above to below, descends in a spiral, and this causes complete turmoil and bewilderment. When he descends from above to below, he does not know on what position he will land, whether his affliction will increase because of his fall or decrease. Nothing is more complete or better suited to describe the bewildered and frightened person than this parable. End of quote. This is a speech of excessive elaboration with no real benefit in it. Al-Zamakhshari made His saying "having companions" mean "having a group of companions," and set against them, in the form of the comparison, the Muslims who call him to guidance and whom he does not heed. This is the interpretation of Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. Others made "having companions" refer to the devils who call to it, or who do not call him to guidance according to their claim and what they lead him to believe. Thus "companions" here is likened to the disbelievers who confirm in apostasy those who have turned away from Islam. This interpretation is also related from Ibn 'Abbas. Makki and others mention that the one whom the devils enticed is 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr al-Siddiq, and the "companions" are his father and mother. The people of biography mention that this verse was revealed about him: he invited his father Abu Bakr to worship idols. He was the eldest son of Abu Bakr and full brother of 'A'ishah; their mother was Umm Ruman bint al-Harith ibn Ghanm al-Kinaniyyah. He witnessed Badr and Uhud with his people while still a disbeliever, and he challenged to single combat, whereupon his father Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) rose to face him in single combat. It is mentioned that the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "Spare me yourself." Then he embraced Islam and his Islam was good, and he accompanied the Messenger (peace be upon him) during the truce of al-Hudaybiyah. His name had been 'Abd al-Ka'bah, and the Messenger (ﷺ) named him 'Abd al-Rahman. In the Sahih it is reported that 'A'ishah heard someone say that His saying: ﴿And one who said to his parents, "Uff to you both"﴾ (al-Ahqaf 46:17) was revealed about 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr. She said: "They lied. By Allah, nothing of the Qur'an was revealed about us except my innocence."

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: If this is about Abu Bakr, how is it that the Messenger was told: ﴿Say, "Shall we call upon..."﴾? I say: Because of the closeness that existed between the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers, and especially between him and al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him). [p. 158] End of quote. This question only arises if it is correct that it was revealed about Abu Bakr and his son 'Abd al-Rahman, but that is not established.

The position of "like one" (*ka-lladhī*) is in the accusative. It was said that it is an adjective (*na't*) of an omitted verbal noun (*maṣdar*), meaning: a return like the return of the one [who was enticed]. The better view is that it is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), meaning: being like the one [who was enticed]. Apparently *alladhī* (the one) is singular, but it may mean the plural sense, i.e., like the group who. Hamzah recited *istahwāhu* with an inclined *alif*. Al-Sulami, al-A'mash and Talhah recited *istahwathu al-shaytān* with a *tā'* and the singular *al-shaytān*. Al-Kisa'i said: It is so in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud. End of quote. However, those who transmitted to us the recitation from Ibn Mas'ud transmitted *al-shayāṭīn* in the plural. Al-Hasan recited *al-shayāṭūn*, and its parallel has been mentioned previously, and he has been regarded as having erred in this. It has been said that it is anomalous and ugly. The apparent sense of His saying "on the earth" is that it relates to *istahwathu* (enticed him). It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause from the object of *istahwathu*, meaning: being on the earth. It was also said that it relates to *ḥayrān* (bewildered). It was also said that it relates to the pronoun in *ḥayrān*. *Ḥayrān* is not declined (*lā yanṣarif*), its feminine is *ḥayrā*, and *ḥayrān* is a circumstantial clause from the object of *istahwathu*. It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause from *alladhī* (the one), with the governing element being the implied return. The clause "having companions" is either a circumstantial clause, or an adjective of *ḥayrān*, or a new independent clause. "To the guidance" (*ilā al-hudā*) relates to *yad'ūnahu* (call him), and *ātinā* (come to us) is from *al-ityān* (coming). In the codex of 'Abd Allah it is *ataynā* as a past verb, not an imperative, so *ilā al-hudā* relates to it.

﴿Say, "Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the [true] guidance."﴾ Those who said that "having companions" means the devils, and that His saying "to the guidance" is according to their claim, took this sentence as a refutation of them, meaning: what you claim is not guidance; rather it is disbelief, and guidance is only the guidance of Allah, which is faith. Those who said that "companions" is a parable for the believers who call to the guidance which is faith, took it as an announcement that the guidance is the guidance of Allah, given to whomever He wills. It does not follow from their calling to guidance that guidance necessarily occurs; rather that is in the hand of Allah. Whomever He guides is guided.

﴿And we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds.﴾ Apparently the *lām* is the *lām* of purpose (*kay*), and the second object of *umirnā* (we have been commanded) is omitted, and they estimated it as: "and we have been commanded with sincerity, so that we may submit and surrender to the Lord of the worlds." The clause is included within what is said, coordinated with "Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the [true] guidance." Al-Zamakhshari said: It is a cause for the command, so the meaning of "we have been commanded" is: it was said to us, "Submit, so that we may submit." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The view of Sibawayh is that "that we may submit" (*li-nuslima*) is in the position of the object (*mafʿūl*), and that your saying "I have been commanded *li-aqūma*" and "I have been commanded *an aqūma*" (that I stand) are the same. Similar to it is the poet's saying:

*I want to forget her memory, but it is as if Layla appears to me on every path.*

And other such examples. End of quote. On the apparent sense of his words, the *lām* is extra (*zā'idah*), and *an nuslima* is the complement of *umirnā*, as a second object after dropping the preposition. It was also said that the *lām* has the meaning of *bāʾ* (with), as if it were said: "and we have been commanded *bi-an nuslima*" (to submit). The *lām* in the sense of *bāʾ* is a strange opinion. What Ibn 'Atiyyah attributed to Sibawayh is not as he stated. Rather, that is the view of al-Kisa'i and al-Farra', who claimed that the *lām* of purpose falls in the position of *an* after *arada* (wanted) and *amara* (commanded). God the Exalted said: ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:26); ﴿They desire to extinguish﴾ (al-Saff 61:8), meaning *an yuṭfi'ū*; ﴿Allah only desires to remove from you the impurity﴾ (al-Ahzab 33:33); and "I want to forget her memory." Abu Ishaq refuted this for both of them. Sibawayh and his companions held that the *lām* here is connected to an omitted element, and that the verb before it is meant as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), and the meaning is: the desire is for the clarification, and the command is for submission. Thus the two are a subject and predicate. So the following views are reached concerning this *lām*: first, it is extra; second, it has the meaning of *kay* (purpose), either for the verb itself or for the verbal noun formed from the verb; third, it is the *lām* of *kay*, treated as if it were *an*; fourth, it has the meaning of *bāʾ*. We have discussed this issue in the book *al-Takmil*.

The phrase "to the Lord of the worlds" (*li-rabbi al-ʿālamīn*) is a reminder that He is the Owner of the entire world, including what they worship, such as idols and others.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah al-An'am (6), verses 71–73 (part 2 of 2)**

﴿And that you establish the prayer and fear Him.﴾ Here *an* (أنْ) is *masdariyyah* (the verbal particle that forms a verbal noun). Scholars differ over what it is coordinated with. Al-Zajjaj said: it is coordinated with his statement "*li-nuslima*" (that we may submit), so the sense is "*li-an nuslima wa-an aqimu*" (that we submit and that you establish). Ibn Atiyya said: "The wording rules this out, because *nuslima* is *mu'rab* (inflected, *i'rab* being grammatical case-inflection) while *aqimu* is *mabni* (indeclinable), and coordinating an indeclinable word with an inflected one is not permitted, since coordination requires sharing the same governing element." End of quote. But what he mentioned, that an indeclinable word may not be coordinated with an inflected one and that this is impermissible, is not as he stated. Rather, it is permissible, as in *qama Zaydun wa-hadha* (Zayd stood and this one [stood]). God Most High says: ﴿He will go before his people on the Day of Resurrection and lead them into the Fire﴾ [11:98]. The most that this shows is that when the governing element meets an inflected word it affects it, and when it meets an indeclinable word it does not affect it. It is also permissible to say *in qama Zaydun wa-yaqsidni uhsin ilayhi* (if Zayd stands and visits me, be kind to him), with *yaqsidni* in the jussive. Here *in* (if) has no effect on *qama* because it is indeclinable, but it does have an effect on *yaqsidni* because it is inflected.

Ibn Atiyya then said: "Unless the coordination is taken to be with *in* alone, which is awkward. It is more properly explained by supposing that his statement *an aqimu* [42:13] has the meaning of *wa-li-yuqim* (and let him establish), and then it came out in the form of a command for the sake of the eloquence of the expression. So coordination became permissible, on the basis that we disregard the grammatical rule of the wording and rely on the meaning. This resembles, in one respect, what Yunus reported from the Arabs: *udkhulu al-awwalu fa-al-awwalu* (enter, the first, then the next), whereas otherwise the only correct form would be *udkhulu al-awwala fa-al-awwala* with the accusative." End of quote. What Ibn Atiyya corrected with his statement "Unless... to the end" is precisely what al-Zajjaj meant: that *an aqimu* is coordinated with *an nuslima*, and both are a reason for the implied command. Ibn Atiyya found it awkward because he wished *an aqimu* to retain the meaning of a command. This is not so, because when *an* (in its verbal-noun function) enters upon an imperative verb, the particle and the imperative combine to form a verbal noun, and once they form a verbal noun the sense of command is removed from them. Grammarians, including Sibawayh and others, have permitted *an* (the verbal-noun particle that governs the subjunctive) to be connected to the past tense and to the imperative. Sibawayh said: "You say *katabtu ilayhi bi-an qum*," meaning "with standing." When this is the case, his statement *li-nuslima* and *an aqimu* are in the sense of "for submission and for the establishment of the prayer." As for Ibn Atiyya's comparison with *udkhulu al-awwalu fa-al-awwalu* with the nominative, it does not resemble it, because *udkhulu* cannot, if the pronoun is removed from it, govern what follows it. This differs from *an*, which is connected to the imperative. So there is no real resemblance between them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, to what is his statement *wa-an aqimu* coordinated? I say: to the position of *li-nuslima*, as if it were said: 'And we were commanded that we submit and that you establish [the prayer].'" End of quote. The apparent sense of this explanation is that *an nuslima* is in the position of the second object of *wa-umirna* (we were commanded), and *wa-an aqimu* is coordinated with it. In this case the *lam* would be superfluous. But he had earlier stated that the *lam* indicates the reason for the command, so his speech is self-contradictory, since what is a reason cannot be an object. What shows that by his statement *an nuslima* he meant that it stands in the position of the second object is his statement after that: "It is also possible that the sense is: 'And we were commanded *li-an nuslima* and *li-an aqimu*,' i.e., for submission and for the establishment of the prayer." End of quote. This is the view of al-Zajjaj. If this view were not different from his first view, his two statements would be the same, and that is contradictory.

Al-Zajjaj also said: "It is possible that *wa-an aqimu* is coordinated with *i'tina* (come to us)." It has also been said that it is coordinated with his statement: ﴿Indeed the guidance of God is the [true] guidance﴾, and the sense is: "Say, *an aqimu*..." Both of these views are very weak, and the structure of the speech does not support them. Ibn Atiyya said: "It is appropriate that it be [understood] with the interpretation: '*wa-iqamah*' (and establishment), so it is coordinated with the implied object of *umirna*." End of quote. He had supposed: "And we were commanded with sincerity or with faith *li-an nuslima*." This view is not objectionable, and it is closer than the two views before it, since a second object for *umirna* must be supposed in any case. It is also permissible to omit the word coordinated-to when the meaning is understood. You say: *a-darabta Zaydan?* (Did you strike Zayd?) and he answers: *na'am wa-Amran* (yes, and Amr), meaning: "I struck him and Amr." Al-Farra' also permitted: *ja'ani alladhi wa-Zaydun qa'imani* (the one who came to me and Zayd are two standing [men]), meaning: "the one who came to me, he, and Zayd are two standing [men]," so that *huwa* (he) is omitted because the sense indicates it. The pronoun in the accusative in ﴿wa-ittaquhu﴾ (and fear Him) refers to the Lord of the worlds.

﴿And it is He to whom you will be gathered.﴾ This is a declarative sentence that contains both an admonition and a warning to those who abandon compliance with what they have been commanded: submission, prayer, and fear of God. The fruits of performing these deeds and the regrets of neglecting them appear only on the Day of Gathering and Resurrection.

﴿And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in truth.﴾ When God Most High mentioned that He gathers all creation to His recompense, which is the ultimate end to which their affair returns, He mentioned the beginning of the existence of the world and His bringing it into being *bi-l-haqq* (in truth). That is, with what is true, having no vanity in it, nor is it false. That is, He did not create them in vain or for play, but they issued from wisdom and rightness. And it is so that these two may be taken as evidence of the existence of the Creator, since these great created things, upon which are the marks of origination, must have one originator who is knowing, powerful, willing, glorified and exalted. It has also been said: the meaning of *bi-l-haqq* is "by His word," in His saying to the created things "Be!" and in His saying: ﴿Come, willingly or unwillingly﴾ [41:11]. What is meant in this and similar passages is only the manifestation of the responsiveness of what God wills to do, and its bringing forth into existence swiftly, and placing it in the position of what is commanded and so complies.

﴿And the day He says "Be!" and it is, His word is the truth.﴾ Scholars permitted *yawma* (the day) to be the object of an implied verb, and they supposed the sense: "Mention the resurrection, the day He says 'Be!'", i.e., the day He says to bodies "Be!", being brought back. The sentence is complete at His statement "Be!" Then He informed that His word will be the truth, which was in this world, a report of the resurrection. In this case *qawluhu* ("His word") is the subject of *fa-yakun* ("and it is"). Or the sentence is complete at His statement "Be! and it is," and *qawluhu al-haqq* ("His word is the truth") is a nominal sentence with subject and predicate. Al-Zajjaj said: *yawma yaqu* (the day He says) is coordinated with the pronoun in His statement *wa-ittaquhu* (and fear Him), i.e., "fear His punishment and the terrors, and the day," so its accusative case is that of a direct object, not an adverb of time. It has also been said: *wa-yawma* is coordinated with "the heavens and the earth," and the governing element is *khalaqa* (He created). It has also been said: the governing element is *udhkur* (mention). Or it is coordinated with *bi-l-haqq*, since that is in the position of the accusative, and *yaquolu* has the sense of the past tense, as if he said: "And He is the One who created the heavens and the earth in truth, and the day He said to them 'Be!'" The sentence is complete at His statement *fa-yakun* (and it is), and *qawluhu al-haqq* is a nominal sentence. Or it is complete at *kun* (Be!), and *fa-yakunu qawluhu al-haqq* begins anew, i.e., "what appears appears," with *qawluhu* as the subject of *yakunu*, *al-haqq* as an adjective, and *yakunu* as a complete verb (meaning "to happen" or "to come into being"). All these grammatical analyses are remote, and the structure of the speech does not accept them. The closest of what has been said is that of al-Zamakhshari: that *qawluhu al-haqq* is a subject, *al-haqq* is its adjective, and *yawma yaquolu* is the predicate of the subject, so that it is attached to an implied stable element, as you say: *yawma al-jumu'ati al-qitalu* (on Friday is the fighting). *Al-yawm* here means "the time," and the meaning is that He created the heavens and the earth standing in truth and wisdom, and at the time He says to any thing among things "Be!", that thing comes to be. *Qawluhu al-haqq* means that nothing among the heavens, the earth, and all other created things exists except out of wisdom and rightness. Al-Zamakhshari also permitted another view: that *qawluhu al-haqq* is the subject of *fa-yakun*, so that the accusative of *yawma* is governed by an implied element indicated by His statement *bi-l-haqq*, as if it were said: "Be, on the day, in truth." This is a strained analysis.

﴿And to Him belongs the dominion on the day the Horn is blown.﴾ It has been said that *yawma* is a substitute for *wa-yawma yaquolu*. It has also been said that it is in the accusative governed by *al-mulk* (dominion). Specifying that day with it is like specifying it with His statement ﴿To whom belongs the dominion today?﴾ [40:16] and with His statement ﴿And the command on that day belongs to God﴾ [82:19]. Its benefit is to inform that He alone holds dominion at a time when no claim of dominion can be made. It has also been said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial element (*hal*), its referent being *al-mulk* and its governing element being *lahu*. It has also been said that it is in the position of the predicate of His statement *qawluhu al-haqq*, i.e., "on the day the Horn is blown." It has also been said that it is an adverb of time governing *tuhsharun* (you will be gathered), or governing *yaquolu* (He says), or governing *'alimu al-ghaybi wa-al-shahadah* (Knower of the unseen and the witnessed). Al-Hasan read *fi al-suwar* (in the trumpets, plural of *sur*, which is the variant reading) and this was reported by Amr ibn Ubayd from Iyad. The reading *al-suwar* supports the interpretation of those who understood it this way, since *al-suwar* is the plural of *surah* (form), as in *thawmah* and *thuwam* (garlic, plural). The apparent meaning is that there is literally a blowing. It has also been said that it is a metaphor for the arrival of the Hour and the passing away of this world. It was also transmitted from Abd al-Warith, from Abu Amr, that he read *nanfukhu* (We blow) with the first person plural of majesty.

﴿The Knower of the unseen and the witnessed.﴾ That is, He is the Knower. Or it is a subject, on the supposition of the question "Who is the one blowing?" Or it is the subject of *yaquolu* or of *yunfakhu*, with an omitted element indicated by *yunfakhu*, like *rijalun* (men) after His statement *yusabbihu* (is glorified) with the *ba'* vowelled with a fatha; and *shuraka'uhum* (their associates) after *zuyyina* (was made attractive), in the passive, with *qatlu* (killing) in the nominative; and like *da'i'un li-khusumatin* (a suppliant in dispute) after *liyabki Yazidu* (Let Yazid weep):

*Let Yazid weep, a suppliant in dispute, and a weeping man who was cast down.*

The supposition is: "He is glorified by men" (*yusabbihu lahu rijalun*), "their associates made it attractive" (*zayyanahu shurakauhum*), and "a suppliant weeps for him" (*yubkihi da'i'un*). Or it is an adjective of *alladhi* (the one who). These are several views, and the first is the best. The unseen and the witnessed encompass all existing things. Al-A'mash read *'alimi* (Knower) in the genitive, and it has been explained as a substitute for the pronoun in *lahu* (to Him) or for "Lord of the worlds," or as an adjective of the pronoun in *lahu*. The first view is better, because the substituted-for noun is far off in the second, and because an absent pronoun is being described, which is not the position of the majority of scholars; it was permitted only by al-Kisai alone.

﴿And He is the Wise, the All-Aware.﴾ Since He mentioned the creation of creatures and the swiftness of His bringing into being whatever He wills, and since the resurrection entails the annihilation of creatures before it, the attribute *al-Hakim* (the Wise) is fitting. And since He mentioned that He is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the attribute *al-Khabir* (the All-Aware) is fitting, since it is an attribute indicating knowledge of what is subtle in perception among things.
