He argued by the setting rather than the rising, though both are a movement from state to state, because argument by setting is clearer, as it is a movement with concealment and hiding. He used the plural "those that set" to indicate that there are many that set, and this star shared with them in setting, so it has no distinction over them in being worshipped, due to sharing in the attribute that indicates origination.

﴿So when he saw the moon rising, he said: "This is my lord."﴾ Not in the case of the stars does "he saw a star rising" come, because he did not at first watch until the star rose, since with the darkening of the night stars appear, unlike his situation with the moon and the sun. When he had made clear to them that this luminary, which is the star he saw, is not fit to be a lord, he watched for what is brighter than it and more luminous, in the manner of attaching it to the star and inferring that it is not fit for worship. So he saw it at its first rising, which is the rising (buzugh), and then he did the same with the sun. He watched for it since it was brighter than the moon, more luminous, larger in body, and more widely beneficial, and it is said that the moon draws its light from it. So he said that as an argument against them, and he showed that it is equal to the moon and the stars in the attribute of origination.

﴿So when it set, he said: "If my Lord does not guide me, I shall surely be among the people who go astray."﴾ "The people who go astray" here means the worshippers of created things such as idols and others. Whoever claims that the saying "This is my lord" is on its outward meaning and that the incident was in childhood uses this as evidence. Al-Zamakhshari said: "'If my Lord does not guide me' is an admonition to his people that whoever takes the moon as a god, which is like the star in setting, is astray, for guidance to the truth is by the grace and kindness of Allah."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 75–78 (part 2 of 2):

﴿So when he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my lord; this is greater."﴾ It is well known that the sun (al-shams) is feminine. It has been said that it may be both masculine and feminine. It is therefore feminine at first, according to the well-known usage, but it is masculine in the demonstrative (هذا, "this"), following a less common dialect, out of consideration for and in agreement with the predicate. Thus the masculine dialect, which is the rarer one, is preferred over the feminine dialect. As for those who see only the feminine, Ibn 'Atiyya said: "He used the masculine, i.e., 'this thing that is seen' or 'this luminous thing.'" Al-Akhfash estimated it as "this rising one." It has also been said that al-shams here means "the light" (al-diya'), and God the Exalted said: ﴿He made the sun a radiance﴾ [Yunus: 5], so he pointed to the light, and the light is masculine. Al-Zamakhshari said: "He made the subject (al-mubtada') like the predicate (al-khabar), because they are both expressions of one thing, as in the saying of the Arabs: 'Your need did not come' (ما جاءت حاجتك) and 'Your mother was not' (وما كانت أمك), and ﴿Their trial was only that they said﴾ [al-An'am: 23]." He said that choosing this method was necessary to protect the Lord from the suspicion of femininity. Do you not see that they said of the attribute of God: 'Allam' (the All-Knowing, an intensive form in masculine), and did not say 'Allama,' even though 'Allama' is more emphatic, to avoid the feminine marker (ta' al-ta'nith)? End of quotation. It is possible that most of the languages of non-Arabs do not distinguish between masculine and feminine in pronouns or in demonstratives, and they have no marker for the feminine. Rather, masculine and feminine are the same in this respect for them. Therefore, when God related the words of Abraham, he referred to the feminine in our language with what is used for the masculine. Indeed, if the feminine had a distinct form, they would have no sign in their speech that indicates it. When God the Exalted reported about it with His saying "rising" (بازغة) and "set" (أفلت), He used the feminine according to the requirement of Arabic grammar, since that is not a quotation.

﴿So when it set, he said, "O my people, I am free from what you associate [with God]."﴾ That is, from the heavenly bodies that you make into partners with their Creator. When the sun set, nothing remained for them that could represent (their god) to them, and his argument was made manifest. Thereby he grew strong in opposing them, and he disowned their associating (others with God). Al-Maturidi said: "The preferred view is that it be said: he proved that these (bodies) are not fit for divinity, since the light of the moon overcame the light of Venus, and the light of the sun (overcame) its light, and one was overpowered by the other. The Lord is not overpowered, and darkness overcame the light of the sun and subdued it." End of the summary. Ibn Abi al-Fadl said: "Darkness only came after the sun had gone, so it did not coincide with it, so that one could say it overpowered it and overpowered its light." End of quotation.

Others among the exegetes (mufassirun) said: he gave as proof what appeared in them of the nature of coming into being (huduth) and of moving from one state to another, and that is one of the attributes of bodies. It is as if he said: if it becomes clear in these lofty luminaries that they are not fit for lordship, then your idols, which are made of wood and stone, are more deserving that this be made clear regarding them. He presented these luminaries as an example to them because they were people concerned with observing the spheres and attached to the stars.

The exegetes agreed that the seeing of these luminaries occurred on one night. He saw the star Venus or Jupiter, according to the previous disagreement, inclining toward setting. When it set, the moon rose; that is, at its first rising. Then the night spread entirely. When the sun rose, the light of the moon disappeared before it because of the spread of morning, and its light faded and it also drew near its place of setting. That was called "setting" (ufūl) because it was close to complete setting, by a figurative use in naming. Then the sun rose upon that.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This sequence works on the fifteenth night of the month up to the twentieth night, and it does not follow in one night as the exegetes unanimously agreed, except on these nights, and by that figurative use regarding the setting of the moon." End of quotation.

The apparent meaning, and that which the exegetes hold, is that the intended meaning of the star, the moon, and the sun is what the Arabs laid down for them in applying these words to these luminaries. It is related from some Arabs (a view that is probably not authentically attributed to him) that the seeing is seeing of the heart. The star is taken to mean the animal soul (al-nafs al-hayawaniyya) which every star has; the moon is taken to mean the rational soul (al-nafs al-natiqa) which every sphere has; and the sun is taken to mean the abstract intellect (al-'aql al-mujarrad) which every sphere has. Ibn Sina used to interpret the setting (ufūl) as contingency (imkan). Al-Ghazali claimed that the meaning of its setting is its contingency in itself, and every contingent thing necessarily has an effector and necessarily ends at the Necessary Existent (wajib al-wujud). Some people took the star to mean the senses, the moon to mean imagination and the estimative faculty (al-wahm), and the sun to mean the intellect. They meant that these three perceiving faculties are deficient and of limited power, and that the Governor of the world has dominion over them and is victorious over them. End of quotation.

These two interpretations resemble the interpretation of the Batiniyya, may God curse them, since both are riddles and symbols, and the Book of God is far too exalted for them. Had it not been that Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi and others had transmitted them in their tafsir, I would have turned away from transmitting them entirely, since they are things we are certain are false. Among the esoteric interpretation of the Imamiyya, which they attribute to 'Ali, is that the star is the one given permission (al-ma'dhun), who is the summoner (al-da'i); the moon is the one following (al-lahiq), who is above the one given permission in rank, like the vizier to the imam; the sun is the imam; and Abraham was in the rank of the one who responds (al-mustajib). So he said to the one given permission, "This is my lord," meaning the lord of nurturing in knowledge, for he nurtures the one who responds with knowledge and calls him to it. When it set, what the one given permission possessed of knowledge was exhausted, so he turned away from it and clung to the one following. When what he possessed was exhausted, he turned away from him and turned toward the one who follows (al-tali), who is the silent one (al-samit) who accepts knowledge from the Messenger, who is called the speaker (al-natiq), because he speaks all that the Messenger speaks. When what he possessed was exhausted, he ascended to the speaker, who is the Messenger, and who, according to them, is the one who shapes the laws (al-musawwir li-l-shara'i'). End of quotation of this confusion. The riddle to which the verse does not point in any way, in any of the modes of indication or interpretation, is that before this there are two interpretations resembling this impossible interpretation. The Sufis, in their interpretation of the Book of God the Exalted, have various kinds of these interpretations.

Al-Qushayri said: "When the night covered him, the veils of seeking enveloped him, and the dawn of existence had not yet been revealed to him. Then the star of intellects rose for him, and he witnessed the Truth by His secret through the light of proof, and he said, 'This is my lord.' Then its light increased, and the moon of knowledge rose, and he gazed upon it by the secret of exposition, and he said, 'This is my lord.' Then the morning brightened, the day was enjoyed, and the sun of recognition (al-'irfan) rose from the tower of its nobility. Then there was no place left for seeking, no room for conjecture, and no place for suspicion to dwell. So he said: ﴿I am free from what you associate﴾, for after resurrection there is no doubt, and after manifestation there is no concealment." End of quotation.

It is a great wonder, indeed the greatest of wonders, that people claim that these who are attributed to Sufism are the elite servants of God the Exalted, while their speech on the Book of God the Exalted is this speech.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 75–78 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And thus We showed Abraham the dominion (malakut) of the heavens and the earth﴾. This is a parenthetical clause (jumla i'tiradiyya) between His saying: ﴿And when Abraham said﴾ (Al-An'am 6:74), rebuking his father for worshipping idols, and the clause of argument against them by means of the singularity of the One worshipped and His not resembling created things, which is His saying: ﴿So when the night covered him﴾. [p. 165] "We showed" (nurī) means "We caused him to see" (arayna-hu), and it is a narration of a past state (hikayat hal). It is transitive to two objects, so the apparent meaning is that it is of sight (basariyya). Ibn Atiyya said: "Or it is from ura, which is in the sense of 'to know' (arafa)." The claim that ra'a means 'to know' and then becomes transitive to two objects through the hamza requires that this be transmitted from the Arabs, and what the grammarians have transmitted is that ra'a, when it means sight, is transitive to one object, and when it means 'to know', governing two objects, it is transitive to two objects.

On the reading that it is of sight, Salman al-Farisi, Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid said: the heavens and the earth were opened up for him, so he saw with his eyes the higher dominion and the lower dominion, and he saw his station in Paradise. Ibn Atiyya said: "If this transmission is sound, then in it there is a specification of Abraham with what no one else before him or after him attained." It is narrated from Ali, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Allah unveiled for him the heavens and the earth, even the Throne and the lowest of the earths." If it is sight, then the meaning is not mere seeing, but there occurred to him along with it reflection and knowledge that did not occur to anyone of the people of his time to whom he was sent. This was said by Ibn Abbas and others. In this there is a specification of him, restricted to the people of his time, and that it is of the sight of the heart. Ibn Atiyya permitted this, and al-Zamakhshari mentioned nothing other than it. Ibn Atiyya said: He saw through them the dominion of the heavens and the earth by his reflection and his contemplation, and this necessarily builds upon what came before of his seeing with his eyes and his perception in general by his senses. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Like that instruction and enlightenment, We inform Abraham and show him the dominion of the heavens and the earth, meaning the lordship (rububiyya) and the divinity (ilahiyya), and We grant him success in knowing them, and We guide him with what We have expanded his breast by and directed his gaze to the path of inference. 'We showed' is a narration of a past state." The reference of "that" (dhalika) is to the guidance, or: like his guidance to the oneness of Allah, the Exalted, and his calling his father and people to the worship of Allah, the Exalted, and rejecting the idols, We caused him to witness the dominion of the heavens and the earth. Al-Mahdawi related that the meaning is: "And just as We guided you, O Muhammad, We showed Abraham." This is far from the indication of the wording. It is also permissible that the kaf is for causation, meaning: "And for this reason, the denunciation and the calling to Allah at the time of the claim of others to lordship, We caused him to witness the dominion of the heavens and the earth, so that he came to have a special distinction by that." Ibn Abbas said: "[He was shown] the great matters, their secret and their open aspects, so nothing of the deeds of the creatures was hidden from him. When he saw that, he began to curse the sinners. Allah said: 'You are not able to bear this,' so He returned him, so that he would not see their deeds." Al-Zajjaj and others said: "Malakut is the kingdom, like rahabut and rahbut and jabarut, and it is a form of intensification. From their speech: 'He has the malakut of Yemen and Iraq.'" Mujahid said: "By it he means the signs of the heavens and the earth." Qatada said: "The malakut of the heavens: the sun, the moon and the stars; and the malakut of the earth: the mountains, the trees and the seas." It was also said: "The worship of the angels and the disobedience of the children of Adam." Abu al-Sammal read malkut with a sukun on the lam, which is a dialect meaning 'kingdom'. Ikrima read malakut with the triangular tha (malakuth), and said: "Malakuth in Greek or Coptic." Al-Nakha'i said: "It is malakutha in Hebrew." And it was read: "And thus You show" with the ta on top, and "Ibrahima malakuta" with the ta raised, meaning: "You show him the indications of lordship."

﴿And that he might be among the certain﴾. That is: We showed him the dominion. It was said: there is a hidden cause to which this is joined, and it was estimated as: "to establish the proof against his people." Others said: "so that he would infer by it the Creator." It was said: the waw is superfluous. The object of "certain" (muqinin) was said to be the oneness of Allah and His power, and it was said: His prophethood and His messengership. It was also said: "by direct sight, just as he had certainty by demonstration," so he passed from the knowledge of certainty (ilm al-yaqin) to the eye of certainty (ayn al-yaqin), as he asked in His saying: ﴿Show me how You give life to the dead﴾ (Al-Baqara 2:260). The meaning of "iqan" (certainty) has been explained at the beginning of Al-Baqara. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: "Certainty is an expression for knowledge that arises after the removal of doubt through reflection. For this reason the knowledge of Allah is not described as certainty, because His knowledge is not preceded by doubt, nor derived from thought and reflection. When the proofs are many, agree and correspond, they become a cause for the arising of certainty, since from each one of them there arises a kind of influence and strength, so it increases until one is decided." [p. 166]

﴿So when the night covered him, he saw a star and said: "This is my lord."﴾ This clause is joined to His saying: ﴿And when Abraham said﴾ (Al-An'am 6:74), according to the view of those who made ﴿And thus We show﴾ a parenthesis, and this is the view of al-Zamakhshari. Ibn Atiyya said: "The fa in His saying 'so when' links what follows to what came before, and it favours the view that the intended dominion is this detail in this verse." Al-Zamakhshari said: "His father and his people used to worship idols and the sun, the moon and the stars. He wanted to alert them to the error in their religion, and to guide them to the way of looking and inference, and to make them know that correct looking leads to the conclusion that none of them can be a god, because of the evidence of origination (hudath) in them, and that behind them is an originator who originated them, and a maker who made them, and a manager who manages their rising, their setting, their movement, their course, and all their conditions." The star is Venus, as said by Ibn Abbas and Qatada, or Jupiter, said by Mujahid and al-Suddi. It is quadriliteral, and the waw in it is original, and the fa is repeated in it, so its measure is fa'fal, like qawqal, and this is a rare construction. The apparent view is that the answer to "so when" is "he saw a star," and on this basis they permitted that "This is my lord" be an attribute of the star, which is problematic, or that it be a new sentence, which is the apparent view. It is also permissible that the answer is "he said: 'This is my lord,'" and "he saw a star" is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: the night covered him while he was seeing a star. As for "This is my lord," the apparent view is that it is a declarative sentence. It was said: it is interrogative in the sense of denial, with the hamza omitted from it, like the poet's line:

"Did they cast the pebbles with seven or with eight?"

Ibn al-Anbari said: "This is anomalous, because it is not permissible to omit the particle except when there is a distinction between the declarative and the interrogative. If it is declarative, it is impossible for this statement to be made as a matter of conviction and resolve, given the infallibility of the prophets from sins, let alone shirk with Allah." As for what is narrated from Ibn Abbas, that this occurred to him in his childhood and before his puberty, and that he worshipped it until it set, and worshipped the moon until it set, and worshipped the sun until it set, perhaps it is not sound. And what has been said by some that this was after puberty and legal responsibility is nothing. And what they recount, that his mother hid him in a cave at the time of his birth out of fear of Nimrod, because the astrologers had informed him that a boy would be born in such a year who would ruin his kingdom at his hands, and that he issued a decree that whoever was born of a female should be abandoned and whoever was born of a male should be slaughtered, until he became ten years old, or it was said fifteen, and that he looked, when he first understood, from the cave and saw the star: this is a narration that the context of the verse repels, and His saying: ﴿Indeed I am free of what you associate﴾ (Al-An'am 6:78), and His saying: ﴿That is Our argument, which We gave to Abraham against his people﴾ (Al-An'am 6:83). Some interpreted that on the basis of a hidden saying, which is frequent, its estimate being: "He said: 'They say, This is my lord,'" as a narration of their saying. Its corruption is clarified by what appears upon it of the marks of origination. This does not need the hidden saying, but it is sound that this be like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Where are My associates?﴾ (Al-Nahl 16:27), meaning: according to your claim. Al-Zamakhshari said: "'This is my lord' is the saying of one who does justice to his opponent while knowing that he is in error, so he recounts his saying as it is, without being partisan to his doctrine, because that is more likely to lead to the truth and further from contention. Then he turns against it after recounting it and nullifies it by proof." Thus this statement from him is a means of drawing them out (istidraj) to show the proof and a way to it, just as he used a means to break the idols with his saying: ﴿So he looked a look at the stars﴾ (Al-Saffat 37:88), ﴿and said: "Indeed I am ill"﴾ (Al-Saffat 37:89). He agreed with them outwardly about looking at the stars, and gave them the impression that his saying "I am ill" arose from his looking at them.

﴿So when it set, he said: "I do not love those that set."﴾ That is: I do not love the worship of those that set, that change from state to state, that move from place to place, that are hidden by a veil, for that is a characteristic of bodies. He argued by the setting rather than the rising, though both are a movement from state to state, because argument by setting is clearer, as it is a movement with concealment and hiding. He used the plural "those that set" to indicate that there are many that set, and this star shared with them in setting, so it has no distinction over them in being worshipped, due to sharing in the attribute that indicates origination.

﴿So when he saw the moon rising, he said: "This is my lord."﴾ Not in the case of the stars does "he saw a star rising" come, because he did not at first watch until the star rose, since with the darkening of the night stars appear, unlike his situation with the moon and the sun. When he had made clear to them that this luminary, which is the star he saw, is not fit to be a lord, he watched for what is brighter than it and more luminous, in the manner of attaching it to the star and inferring that it is not fit for worship. So he saw it at its first rising, which is the rising (buzugh), and then he did the same with the sun. He watched for it since it was brighter than the moon, more luminous, larger in body, and more widely beneficial, and it is said that the moon draws its light from it. So he said that as an argument against them, and he showed that it is equal to the moon and the stars in the attribute of origination.

﴿So when it set, he said: "If my Lord does not guide me, I shall surely be among the people who go astray."﴾ "The people who go astray" here means the worshippers of created things such as idols and others. Whoever claims that the saying "This is my lord" is on its outward meaning and that the incident was in childhood uses this as evidence. Al-Zamakhshari said: "'If my Lord does not guide me' is an admonition to his people that whoever takes the moon as a god, which is like the star in setting, is astray, for guidance to the truth is by the grace and kindness of Allah."

Then the star of intellects rose for him, and he witnessed the Truth by His secret through the light of proof, and he said, 'This is my lord.' Then its light increased, and the moon of knowledge rose, and he gazed upon it by the secret of exposition, and he said, 'This is my lord.' Then the morning brightened, the day was enjoyed, and the sun of recognition (al-'irfan) rose from the tower of its nobility. Then there was no place left for seeking, no room for conjecture, and no place for suspicion to dwell. So he said: ﴿I am free from what you associate﴾, for after resurrection there is no doubt, and after manifestation there is no concealment." End of quotation.

It is a great wonder, indeed the greatest of wonders, that people claim that these who are attributed to Sufism are the elite servants of God the Exalted, while their speech on the Book of God the Exalted is this speech.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 79–82:

He suffices with the container (az-zarf) instead of what is contained (al-mazruf) because of its generality, since these shining bodies are contained within the heavens. And since the idols his people worshipped were of wood and stone, and he mentioned the container of the shining bodies, he joined to it the earth, which is the container of wood and stone. "Hanifan" means inclining away from every religion to the religion of truth, which is the worship of God, exalted is He. "Musliman" means submitting to Him, surrendering to Him. ﴿Wa ma ana minal-mushrikin﴾ — "And I am not among the polytheists."

When he denounced his father's worship of idols and declared him and his people misguided, and then argued for their error through rational premises (since they would not submit to a transmitted proof, whose establishment depends on many premises), and presented those premises as grounded in sound sense perception, he disavowed their worship and emphasized this with "inna" (indeed). Then he informed them that he had directed his worship to the Originator of the world, of which these shining bodies, by which part of it is inferred, are a part. Then he negated of himself that he should be among the polytheists, as an intensification of his disavowal of them.

﴿Wa hajjahu qawmuhu, qala atuhajjunni fillahi wa qad hadan﴾ — "Ḥājjahu" is a reciprocal form (mufa'ala) from two parties who differ in a ruling, each presenting his argument for the soundness of his claim. The meaning: his people argued with him about God's oneness and the negation of partners from Him, denying that. Arguing with such people consists only in clinging to following their forefathers through imitation (taqlid), and in intimidation by what they worship of idols, like the saying of the people of Hud: ﴿In naqulu illa i'taraka ba'du alihatina bi-su'[in]﴾ [Hud: 54] — "We say only that some of our gods have struck you with evil." So he answered them that God had guided him by the decisive proof of His oneness and the rejection of all else, and that he does not fear their gods.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir, with a variant from Hisham, read ﴿Atuhajjunni﴾ with the nun lightened. Its origin is with two nuns: the first is the sign of the nominative (raf') and the second is the nun of protection (nun al-wiqaya). The disagreement about which of the two is omitted is mentioned in the science of grammar (nahw). Some grammarians considered the one who reads with lightening to be in error and mistaken in this. Makki said: deletion is remote in Arabic, ugly and disliked; it is permissible only in poetry for the sake of meter, and the Qur'an does not admit of that, since there is no necessity calling for it. Makki's statement is not accepted. It is also said that lightening is a dialect of Ghatafan. The rest of the seven read with a doubled nun, its origin being ﴿Atuhajjunana﴾, and it was assimilated (idgham) to avoid the heaviness of two identical moving consonants, so it was lightened by assimilation. It was not read there with unassimilated form (fakk), though that is the original and is permissible in speech.

The phrase "fillah" (concerning God) is connected to "atuhajjunni", not to his people's saying "wa hajjahu qawmuhu". This is a case of i'mal (government), specifically the governing of the second verb. Had it been connected to the first, a pronoun would have been placed in the second, and its parallel is: ﴿Yastaftunaka, qul Allahu yuftikum fil-kalalah﴾ [an-Nisa: 176]. The clause ﴿wa qad hadan﴾ is in the status of a circumstantial clause (hal). He denounced that they should argue with him when God had already granted him guidance to His oneness, so their argument is of no avail, for it is refuted.

﴿Wa la akhafu ma tushrikuna bihi illa an yasha'a rabbi shay'a﴾ — It is related that the disbelievers said to Abraham, peace be upon him: "Were you not afraid that our gods would afflict you with leprosy or disease, for your harming them and disparaging them?" He said to them: "I do not fear what you associate with Him, because it has no power and no independent sufficiency." "Ma" here means "alladhi" (that which), and the pronoun in "bihi" refers back to it, i.e., "that which you associate with God, exalted is He." It may also refer back to God, i.e., "that which you associate with God in lordship." As for ﴿illa an yasha'a rabbi﴾, Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is an exception not from the first part; since the force of the statement is that he does not fear harm, he excepted the will of his Lord, exalted is He, that He should will harm for him. End of quote. Thus it is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), and al-Ḥawfi said the same, so the meaning becomes: "But God's will to harm me is what I fear." Al-Zamakhshari said: "illa an yasha'a rabbi" means "except at the time of my Lord's will for some feared thing," the time being omitted, meaning: I do not fear your objects of worship at any time whatsoever, for they cannot benefit or harm, except that my Lord wills that I be struck with something dreadful from their direction if I commit a sin that deserves the descent of something disliked, such as their striking me with a star, or with a fragment of the sun and moon, or making them capable of harming me. End of quote. Thus it is a connected exception from the generality of times implied by the negation. Abu al-Baqa' allowed that it may be connected or disjunctive, but he made it connected, an exception from the circumstances, estimating: "except in the state of my Lord's will," meaning: I do not fear them in every state except in this state. "Shay'an" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maf'ul mutlaq), i.e., "willing," or as a direct object.

"'Ilman" is in the accusative as a transferred specification (tamyiz mahwwal min al-fa'il), the original being: "The knowledge of my Lord encompassed everything."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Will you not remember, so that you may distinguish between the sound and the corrupt, and the capable and the incapable?" It is also said: "Will you not take heed to what I tell you?" Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi said: "Will you not remember that negating partners, rivals and equals from God does not necessitate the descent of punishment and the arrival of retribution?"

﴿Wa kayfa akhafu ma ashraktum wa la takhafuna annakum ashraktum billahi ma lam yunazzil bihi 'alaykum sultanan﴾ — This is an interrogative whose meaning is wonder and denial, as if he marvels at the corruption of their minds, that they frighten him with wood and stone that neither harm nor benefit, while they do not fear the consequence of their associating partners with God, who holds in His hand benefit, harm and the whole affair. "Wa la takhafuna" is conjoined to "akhafu," so it falls within the wonder and denial. The object of fear varies: in relation to Abraham he attached fear to the idols, and in relation to them he attached it to their associating with God, exalted is He, avoiding parallelism; and so that God would not be made the equal of their idols, had the construction been "and you do not fear God." He used the word "ma," which is set for what has no intellect, because the idols have no intellect, being stone, wood and stars. "Sultan" means proof, and association cannot be supported by proof. It seems that when he had established the rational proof against the partners and their lordship, he also negated that there could be a transmitted proof for it. So the meaning is that this is impossible both by reason and by revelation, and therefore it must be discarded. It was also read "sulutanan" with a damma on the lam; the disagreement is whether this is a dialect, thereby establishing the pattern fu'lan with damma on the first and middle letters, or whether it is a case of imitation (ittiba'), in which case it is not established by it.

﴿Fa ayyu al-fariqayni ahaqqu bil-amni in kuntum ta'lamun﴾ — When they frightened him in a place of safety, and did not fear in a place of fear, the interrogative was presented in the form of a possibility, though it was known with certainty that he is the one secure and not they, as the poet said:

*Fa-la-in laqaytuka khaliyayni latalamanna ayyi wa ayyaka fari al-ahzab*

meaning: "Ayyana" (which of us). It is known to him that he is the horseman of the factions, not the one addressed. He added "ayya" to "al-fariqayn," meaning the group of polytheists and the group of monotheists. He turned away from saying "ayyuna ahaqqu bil-amni, ana am antum," out of caution against stripping himself of it, so that this would be a self-praise. The answer to the condition is omitted, meaning: "If you are of those who possess knowledge and insight, then tell me which of these two groups is more deserving of security."

﴿Alladhina amanu wa lam yalbisu imanahum bizulmin ula'ika lahumu al-amnu wa hum muhtadun﴾ — The apparent sense is that this is from Abraham's speech: when he asked them as one knowing who is the secure one, and presented it in the form of an inquirer who does not know, he resumed the answer to the question and made explicit that possibility, saying: the group most deserving of security is "those who believed." It is also said that it is from the speech of Abraham's people, who answered with something that was a proof against them. It is also said that it is from God's speech, commanding Abraham to say it to his people, or saying it by way of judgment between His creatures and those who argued with him, his people. "Al-labs" means mixing. "Alladhina amanu" are Abraham and his companions, and they are not in this community, so said 'Ali; and from him: Abraham specifically, or those who emigrated to Medina, so said 'Ikrima; or it is general, so said some, and this is the apparent sense. Injustice here is shirk, so said Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy. From a group of Companions it is related that when this verse was revealed, the Companions became fearful and said: "Which of us has not wronged himself?" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "It is only as Luqman said: ﴿Indash-shirka laz-zulmun 'azim﴾ [Luqman: 13]." Something similar occurred to Zayd ibn Suhan with Salman as occurred to 'Umar with Ubayy. Mujahid read "wa lam yalbisu imanahum bishirkin," and perhaps that is an interpretation of meaning, since it is a reading that contradicts the consensus text. Al-Zamakhshari said: i.e., they did not mix their faith with disobedience that makes them transgressors. The word "labs" refuses the interpretation of injustice as disbelief. End of quote. This is a hidden Mu'tazili doctrine, namely that the transgressor does not have security if he dies persisting in a major sin. His saying "the word labs refuses the interpretation of injustice as disbelief" is a rejection of those who interpret injustice as disbelief and polytheism, and they are the majority. Perhaps al-Zamakhshari did not have this transmitted from the Messenger, and what led him to reject it is only the word labs, since labs means mixing; it is possible for a person at one time to be a believer yet a disobedient one with a sin that makes him a transgressor, but it is not possible to be a believer and a polytheist at the same time.

'Ikrima read "wa lam yulbisu" with a damma on the ya'. "Alladhina" may be the predicate of an omitted subject, or its predicate may be the subject, with the predicate being "ula'ika lahumu al-amnu." Makki said: deletion is remote in Arabic, ugly and disliked; it is permissible only in poetry for the sake of meter, and the Qur'an does not admit of that, since there is no necessity calling for it. Makki's statement is not accepted. It is also said that lightening is a dialect of Ghatafan. This is a case of i'mal (government), specifically the governing of the second verb. Had it been connected to the first, a pronoun would have been placed in the second, and its parallel is: ﴿Yastaftunaka, qul Allahu yuftikum fil-kalalah﴾ [an-Nisa: 176]. He denounced that they should argue with him when God had already granted him guidance to His oneness, so their argument is of no avail, for it is refuted.

He said to them: "I do not fear what you associate with Him, because it has no power and no independent sufficiency." "Ma" here means "alladhi" (that which), and the pronoun in "bihi" refers back to it, i.e., "that which you associate with God, exalted is He." It may also refer back to God, i.e., "that which you associate with God in lordship." End of quote. Thus it is a connected exception from the generality of times implied by the negation. Abu al-Baqa' allowed that it may be connected or disjunctive, but he made it connected, an exception from the circumstances, estimating: "except in the state of my Lord's will," meaning: I do not fear them in every state except in this state. "'Ilman" is in the accusative as a transferred specification (tamyiz mahwwal min al-fa'il), the original being: "The knowledge of my Lord encompassed everything."

﴿Afala tatadhakkarun﴾ — an admonition to them concerning their heedlessness in worshipping what neither harms nor benefits, and in associating partners with God, and concerning what he argued against them by manifesting the proofs he established for the invalidity of these idols for lordship. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Will you not remember, so that you may distinguish between the sound and the corrupt, and the capable and the incapable?" It is also said: "Will you not take heed to what I tell you?" Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi said: "Will you not remember that negating partners, rivals and equals from God does not necessitate the descent of punishment and the arrival of retribution?"

﴿Wa kayfa akhafu ma ashraktum wa la takhafuna annakum ashraktum billahi ma lam yunazzil bihi 'alaykum sultanan﴾ — This is an interrogative whose meaning is wonder and denial, as if he marvels at the corruption of their minds, that they frighten him with wood and stone that neither harm nor benefit, while they do not fear the consequence of their associating partners with God, who holds in His hand benefit, harm and the whole affair. "Wa la takhafuna" is conjoined to "akhafu," so it falls within the wonder and denial. The object of fear varies: in relation to Abraham he attached fear to the idols, and in relation to them he attached it to their associating with God, exalted is He, avoiding parallelism; and so that God would not be made the equal of their idols, had the construction been "and you do not fear God." He used the word "ma," which is set for what has no intellect, because the idols have no intellect, being stone, wood and stars. "Sultan" means proof, and association cannot be supported by proof. It seems that when he had established the rational proof against the partners and their lordship, he also negated that there could be a transmitted proof for it. So the meaning is that this is impossible both by reason and by revelation, and therefore it must be discarded. It was also read "sulutanan" with a damma on the lam; the disagreement is whether this is a dialect, thereby establishing the pattern fu'lan with damma on the first and middle letters, or whether it is a case of imitation (ittiba'), in which case it is not established by it.

*Fa-la-in laqaytuka khaliyayni latalamanna ayyi wa ayyaka fari al-ahzab*

meaning: "Ayyana" (which of us). It is known to him that he is the horseman of the factions, not the one addressed. He added "ayya" to "al-fariqayn," meaning the group of polytheists and the group of monotheists. He turned away from saying "ayyuna ahaqqu bil-amni, ana am antum," out of caution against stripping himself of it, so that this would be a self-praise. The answer to the condition is omitted, meaning: "If you are of those who possess knowledge and insight, then tell me which of these two groups is more deserving of security."

﴿Alladhina amanu wa lam yalbisu imanahum bizulmin ula'ika lahumu al-amnu wa hum muhtadun﴾ — The apparent sense is that this is from Abraham's speech: when he asked them as one knowing who is the secure one, and presented it in the form of an inquirer who does not know, he resumed the answer to the question and made explicit that possibility, saying: the group most deserving of security is "those who believed." It is also said that it is from the speech of Abraham's people, who answered with something that was a proof against them. It is also said that it is from God's speech, commanding Abraham to say it to his people, or saying it by way of judgment between His creatures and those who argued with him, his people. "Al-labs" means mixing. "Alladhina amanu" are Abraham and his companions, and they are not in this community, so said 'Ali; and from him: Abraham specifically, or those who emigrated to Medina, so said 'Ikrima; or it is general, so said some, and this is the apparent sense. Injustice here is shirk, so said Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy. From a group of Companions it is related that when this verse was revealed, the Companions became fearful and said: "Which of us has not wronged himself?" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "It is only as Luqman said: ﴿Indash-shirka laz-zulmun 'azim﴾ [Luqman: 13]." Something similar occurred to Zayd ibn Suhan with Salman as occurred to 'Umar with Ubayy. Mujahid read "wa lam yalbisu imanahum bishirkin," and perhaps that is an interpretation of meaning, since it is a reading that contradicts the consensus text. Al-Zamakhshari said: i.e., they did not mix their faith with disobedience that makes them transgressors. The word "labs" refuses the interpretation of injustice as disbelief. End of quote. This is a hidden Mu'tazili doctrine, namely that the transgressor does not have security if he dies persisting in a major sin. His saying "the word labs refuses the interpretation of injustice as disbelief" is a rejection of those who interpret injustice as disbelief and polytheism, and they are the majority. The Messenger (ﷺ) himself interpreted it as shirk, so it must be accepted. Perhaps al-Zamakhshari did not have this transmitted from the Messenger, and what led him to reject it is only the word labs, since labs means mixing; it is possible for a person at one time to be a believer yet a disobedient one with a sin that makes him a transgressor, but it is not possible to be a believer and a polytheist at the same time.

"Lam yalbisu" may be conjoined to the relative clause, or may be a circumstantial clause, the circumstantial waw entering a negated sentence with "lam," as in His saying: ﴿Anna yakunu li ghulamun wa lam yamsasni bashar﴾ [Maryam: 20]. 'Ikrima read "wa lam yulbisu" with a damma on the ya'. "Alladhina" may be the predicate of an omitted subject, or its predicate may be the subject, with the predicate being "ula'ika lahumu al-amnu." **Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 83–90 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And that was Our argument, which We gave to Abraham against his people.﴾ The demonstrative "that" (tilka) refers to the argument that occurred from His saying ﴿So when the night covered him﴾ (6:76) up to His saying ﴿and they are the guided﴾ (6:82). This is the apparent meaning. He attributed it to Himself as a mark of honour, and the pronoun of attribution is the plural of majesty (nun al-'azama), not the first-person singular (ta' al-mutakallim). "We gave it" (atayna-ha) means: We brought it to his mind and created it in his soul, since it is among the rational proofs. Or it means: We gave it by revelation from Us and taught it to him.

If tilka is parsed as a subject (mubtada'), and hujjatuna as an apposition (badal), and atayna-ha as the predicate (khabar) of tilka, then 'ala qawmihi ("against his people") cannot be connected to hujjatuna. The same applies if tilka hujjatuna is parsed as subject and predicate, and atayna-ha as a circumstantial clause (hal). In that case the governing element is the demonstrative, because hujjah is not a verbal noun (masdar). Rather, it is the composed speech used to argue for a point. Even if we took it as a figurative verbal noun, this would still not be permitted, because a predicate or a circumstantial clause of this kind may not separate the verbal noun from what it governs.

Al-Hawfi permitted atayna-ha to be in the position of a qualifier (na't) of hujjatuna, with the intention of separation, the meaning being: "And that is an argument of Ours which We gave." End of quote. This is very far-fetched.

Al-Hawfi said: ha is the first object and Ibrahim is the second object. We have already mentioned that this is the view of al-Suhayli. As for the view of the majority, ha is the second object and Ibrahim is the first object.

Al-Hawfi and Ibn 'Atiyya said: 'ala qawmihi ("against his people") is connected to atayna-ha. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "We made it manifest to Ibrahim against his people." Abu al-Baqa' said: it is connected to a deleted element, its estimate being "an argument against his people and a proof." Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿We gave it to Ibrahim﴾ means "We guided him to it and enabled him to it." This is an explanation of meaning. It is also permitted that it be in the position of a circumstantial clause, with a deleted genitive (idafah) construction, meaning: "We gave it to Ibrahim, establishing supremacy over the arguments of his people, overpowering them."

﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾: that is, ranks and stations of whom We will. The original sense of darajat ("degrees") is spatial. Raising them may be by knowledge, or by prophethood, or by good character, or by sincerity of works in the Hereafter, or by prophethood and wisdom in this world, or by reward and Paradise in the Hereafter, or by argument and eloquence. These are opinions, the closest of which is the last, due to the context of the verse.

The Kufans read darajatin with tanwin (nunation), while the rest read it as an idafah (construction of annexation). Those who read it with tanwin put the noun in the accusative, either as an adverb of place (zarf) or as a second object. This view requires the verb narfa'u ("We raise") to be taken as implying a meaning that governs two objects, i.e. "We give whom We will degrees."

﴿Indeed your Lord is Wise, Knowing﴾: that is, Wise in the management of His servants, Knowing of their deeds. Or: Wise in dividing His servants into worshippers of idols and worshippers of God, Knowing of the arguments that occur between them. It is possible that the address in "your Lord" is to the Messenger, and it is possible that the intended person is Ibrahim, in which case it is an instance of iltifat (shift from third-person reference to second-person address), a shift from the pronoun of absence to the pronoun of address, as a mark of honour through direct address.

﴿And We gave him Ishaq and Ya'qub﴾: Ishaq was his son by his loins through Sarah, and Ya'qub was the son of Ishaq, as God the Exalted said: ﴿So We gave her good news of Ishaq, and after Ishaq, Ya'qub﴾ (11:71). God the Exalted enumerated His blessings upon Ibrahim: He mentioned giving him the argument against his people, and pointed to the raising of his ranks. He also mentioned what He bestowed upon him by giving him this prophet from whom the prophets of the Children of Israel descended. Among the greatest favours is that prophets and messengers should come from a man's offspring. He did not mention Isma'il together with Ishaq. It was said: the purpose of the mention here is the prophets of the Children of Israel, all of whom are the children of Ishaq and Ya'qub. No prophet came from the loins of Isma'il except Muhammad (ﷺ), and He did not mention him in this context, because He commanded him (peace be upon him) to argue against the Arabs regarding the denial of associating partners with God, saying that their forefather Ibrahim, when he was a monotheist devoted to God and free of polytheism, God granted him first kingship and prophethood.

The clause "And We gave him" (wa-wahabna) is coordinated with His saying ﴿And that was Our argument﴾, a verbal clause coordinated with a nominal clause. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "wa-wahabna" is coordinated with "atayna-ha." End of quote. This is not correct, because "atayna-ha" has a place in the grammatical structure, either as a predicate or as a circumstantial clause, and neither of these can apply to "wa-wahabna."

﴿Each We guided﴾: that is, each one of Ishaq and Ya'qub We guided.

﴿And Nuh We guided before﴾: When He mentioned the nobility of the sons of Ibrahim, He mentioned the nobility of his forefathers. He mentioned Nuh, who is "the second Adam," and said "before" (min qabl), to draw attention to his antiquity. [p. 173] There is a subtle point in mentioning him: Nuh (peace be upon him) lived when idols were worshipped, and his people were the first people to worship idols. He affirmed the oneness of God the Exalted, called to His worship, and rejected those idols. God related his supplication to his Lord concerning his people, where they said: ﴿Do not abandon your gods, nor abandon Wadd, nor Suwa', nor Yaghuth, nor Ya'uq, nor Nasr﴾ (71:23). Ibrahim lived when idols were worshipped, and he affirmed the oneness of God the Exalted and called to abandoning them. So God the Exalted mentioned Nuh and that He guided him, just as He guided Ibrahim.

﴿And from his offspring, Dawud and Sulayman﴾: It was said: "from the offspring of Nuh," the pronoun referring to him because he is the nearest mentioned person, and because among them is Lut, who was the son of Ibrahim's brother, so he is from the offspring of Nuh and not from the offspring of Ibrahim. It was also said: "from the offspring of Ibrahim," the pronoun referring to him because he is the intended subject of mention. Ibn 'Abbas said: all these prophets are attributed to the offspring of Ibrahim, even though some of them are not connected to him by birth from either mother or father, because Lut was the son of Ibrahim's brother, and the Arabs call an uncle a father. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: "And We gave him Lut" in support and assistance. End of quote.

They said: the meaning is "And We guided, or gave, from his offspring Dawud and Sulayman." He joined them because they were father and son, and because they were both kings and prophets. He placed Dawud first because he came earlier in time, because he was the possessor of a scripture, and because he was the origin of Sulayman, who was his branch.

﴿And Ayyub and Yusuf﴾: He joined them because they shared in trial. Ayyub was tested with affliction in his body and the rejection of his people. Yusuf was tested with imprisonment and with being far from his family. In their outcome both were given safety and well-being. He placed Ayyub first because his trial was greater.

﴿And Musa and Harun﴾: He joined them because they shared in brotherhood. He placed Musa first because he was the one who spoke with God (Kalim Allah).

﴿Thus do We reward the good-doers﴾: that is, like that reward, namely giving the argument and bestowing righteous offspring, We reward whoever is a good-doer in His worship, mindful of Us in his deeds.

﴿And Zakariyya and Yahya and 'Isa and Ilyas﴾: He joined them among themselves because they shared in intense asceticism and turning away from the world. He began with Zakariyya and Yahya because they preceded 'Isa in time. He placed Zakariyya first because he was the father of Yahya, so he was the origin and Yahya the branch. He joined 'Isa and Ilyas because both had not yet died. He placed 'Isa first because he was the possessor of a scripture and had a wide sphere of influence. The genealogies of these prophets were mentioned, except for Ilyas. He is Ilyas son of Bashir son of Finhas son of al-'Ayzar son of Harun son of 'Imran. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud that Idris is Ilyas, but this was rejected on the grounds that Idris is the grandfather of Nuh (peace be upon them both), as the reports concur on this. It was also said that Ilyas is al-Khidr.

The disagreement of the readers regarding Zakariyya, whether with a long or short vowel, has already been mentioned. Ibn 'Abbas, with a variant from him, and al-Hasan and Qatada read the hamza of Ilyas with facilitation (tashil). In the mention of 'Isa here there is evidence that the son of a daughter is included in "offspring" (dhurriyyah). By this verse, it was used as evidence for his inclusion in a waqf (endowment) made for "offspring." Whether the pronoun in ﴿from his offspring﴾ refers to Nuh or to Ibrahim, we say: al-Hasan and al-Husayn, the sons of Fatima (may God be pleased with them both), are from the offspring of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). By this verse Abu Ja'far al-Baqir and Yahya ibn Ya'mur argued for this. al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf had demanded from them evidence for this, since he denied it, and they remained silent in two incidents that occurred between them and him.

﴿Each is of the righteous﴾: "each" does not restrict to these four, but includes all those previously mentioned of the fourteen prophets.

﴿And Isma'il and al-Yasa' and Yunus and Lut﴾: It is well known that Isma'il is the son of Ibrahim by Hajar, and he was the eldest of his sons. It was said he was a prophet of the Children of Israel who lived in the time of Talut, and he is the one meant by the words ﴿when they said to a prophet of theirs: "Raise up for us a king that we may fight in the way of God"﴾ (2:246).

As for al-Yasa', Zayd ibn Aslam said: he is Yusha' ibn Nun. Others said: he is al-Yasa' ibn Akhtub, son of the old woman. The majority read "al-Yasa'" (with the definite article), as if the article were added to the present-tense form of the verb wasi'a. The two brothers (Hamza and al-Kisa'i) read "al-Layasa'" on the pattern fay'al, like "al-Dayghim." It is disputed whether this is Arabic or foreign. As for the reading of the majority and the view of those who say it is Arabic, they said: it is a present-tense verb used as a proper name, and it has no pronoun in it, so it is declined as a noun, then made indefinite and definite with the article. It was also said it was named by the verb, like Yazid, and then the article was added to it as an irregular extra element, like "al-Yazid" in the poet's verse:

I saw al-Walid ibn al-Yazid blessed.

And it was fixed as it was fixed in "al-An" (now). As for those who say it is foreign, they said: the article was added to it and became fixed irregularly. Among those who explicitly stated the addition of the article to al-Yasa' is Abu 'Ali al-Farisi. As for the reading of the two brothers, Abu 'Ali considered that the article in it is like its occurrence in al-Harith and al-'Abbas, since these are from the patterns of adjectives. But the addition of the article to it is irregular with respect to the rule followed by foreign proper names, since nothing of this pattern came in them, just as nothing with the article for definiteness came in them.

Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Malik al-Jayyani said: whatever the article accompanies in its transferred form, like the one named al-Nadr or al-Nu'man, or in its original form, like al-Yasa' and al-Samaw'al, the article is most usually fixed in it, though it may be permitted to omit it. Accordingly, the article is not necessarily obligatory in it. From his saying that al-Yasa' is not transferred from fa'ala, as some said, it is clear.

It was mentioned that he (al-Jayyani) said: Yunus is with a damma, fatha, and kasra on the nun, and likewise Yusuf. With a fatha on the nun and on the sin of Yusuf, al-Hasan, Talha, Yahya, al-A'mash, and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read throughout the Qur'an.

These four were gathered together because no creatures remained who were their followers or partisans. These are six ranks. The rank of kingship and power, in which He mentioned Dawud and Sulayman. The rank of severe trial, in which He mentioned Ayyub. The rank of combining trial with attaining kingship, in which He mentioned Yusuf. The rank of the strength of proofs, miracles, fighting and dominance, in which He mentioned Musa and Harun. The rank of severe asceticism and separation from people for worship, in which He mentioned Zakariyya, Yahya, 'Isa and Ilyas. The rank of the absence of followers, in which He mentioned Isma'il, al-Yasa', Yunus and Lut.

These names are non-Arabic (a'jamiyyah). They are not put in the genitive with a kasra and do not take tanwin, except al-Yasa', which is put in the genitive with a kasra and does not take tanwin. Lut, however, is declined (masrufa), because of the lightness of its structure with a sukun in the middle, and because it is masculine, even though it has what its brothers have of the prohibition of declension, namely being a proper name and a personal foreign form. The Muslims have shunned this noble name, so few of them have been named with it, such as Abu Mikhnaf Lut ibn Yahya. The prophet Lut is Lut ibn Harun ibn Azar, who is Tarakh, and the raising of his lineage has already been mentioned.

﴿And each We preferred over the worlds﴾: In this there is evidence that prophets are superior to saints (awliya'), contrary to some who claim to belong to the Sufis, in their assertion that the saint is superior to the prophet. Among them is Muhammad ibn al-'Arabi al-Hatimi, author of al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya, 'Anqa' Maghrib and other books of error. In this there is also evidence that prophets are superior to angels, since "the worlds" includes all that exists apart from God the Exalted, so angels are included in the generality. Ibn 'Atiyya said: its meaning is "the worlds of their times."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 83–90 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿And [We guided] some of their fathers, their offspring and their brothers﴾. The genitive (al-majrur) here is in the accusative position (mawdi' nasb). Al-Zamakhshari said: it is coordinated (ma'tufan) with "kullan" (each), meaning: and We preferred some of their fathers. Ibn Atiyyah said: "We guided from among their fathers, their offspring and their brothers groups (jama'at)," so "min" is partitive (li-l-tab'id). The intended meaning is whoever believed, whether a prophet or not, and 'Isa enters within the reference of "from among their fathers." For this reason Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "the maternal uncle and the maternal aunt." End of quotation.

﴿From among their fathers﴾ such as Adam, Idris, Nuh, Hud and Salih. "Their offspring" such as the believing offspring of Nuh, peace be upon him. "Their brothers" such as the brothers of Yusuf. He mentioned the roots (usul), the branches (furu') and the relatives (hawashi).

﴿And We chose them and guided them to a straight path﴾. The apparent reading is that "wa-ijtabaynahum" (and We chose them) is coordinated with "fadilna" (We preferred), meaning: We selected them. He repeated the guidance by way of clarifying the earlier guidance, and that it is guidance to the path of truth that is straight, upright, with no crookedness in it, which is the Oneness of God, exalted is He, and His transcendence above association (shirk).

﴿That is the guidance of God; He guides with it whom He wills of His servants﴾. That is, that guidance to the straight path is the guidance of God. Ibn Atiyyah said: "That" refers to the blessing mentioned in His words "and We chose them." End of quotation. In the verse there is evidence that guidance is by the will of God, exalted is He.

﴿And if they had associated [others with God], what they used to do would have been nullified for them﴾. That is: even if they had associated, along with their merit, their elevation, and the ranks raised for them, they would have been like others in the nullification of their deeds, just as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿If you associate [others with God], your deeds will surely be nullified﴾ [al-Zumar: 65]. In His words "And if they had associated" there is an indication that the earlier guidance is Oneness and the negation of association.

﴿Those are the ones to whom We gave the Book, the judgment (al-hukm) and prophethood﴾. When He mentioned that He preferred them, chose them and guided them, He mentioned what they were preferred with. "Al-Kitab" (the Book) is a genus of the divine scriptures, such as the scrolls of Ibrahim, the Torah, the Psalms and the Gospel. "Al-hukm" means wisdom (al-hikmah), or judgment between disputants, or what they legislated, or understanding of the Book, or jurisprudence in the religion of God; these are opinions. Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi said: "We gave them the Book" is the rank of knowledge by which they judge the inner states and spirits of people; "al-hukm" is the rank of the enforcement of judgment according to the outward; and "prophethood" is the third rank, upon the attainment of which the attainment of the two ranks follows. Thus the judges over creation are three groups. End of quotation, summarized.

﴿So if these disbelieve in them, We have already entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them﴾. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in "bihā" (in them) refers to prophethood, since it is the nearest thing mentioned. Al-Zamakhshari said: "bihā" refers to the Book, the judgment and prophethood, so he made the pronoun refer to all three, and this also has a clear basis. The demonstrative "these" (ha'ulā') refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh and every disbeliever of that era; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, al-Suddi and others. Al-Zamakhshari said: "these" means the people of Mecca. End of quotation. Al-Suddi also said this. Al-Hasan said: the nation of the Messenger. The meaning of "wakkalna" (We entrusted) is: We prepared (arsadna) them for belief in them. Entrustment here is a metaphor for enabling (tawfiq) belief in them and fulfilling their rights, just as a man is entrusted with a matter so that he will carry it out, look after it and guard it. The people entrusted with them here are the angels, said by Abu Raja'; or the believers of Medina, said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi. Al-Zamakhshari said: "a people" are the prophets mentioned and those who followed them, based on the proof of His words: ﴿Those are the ones whom God guided﴾. End of quotation. This is also the view of al-Hasan and Qatadah; they said: the intended people are those whose mention preceded, of the prophets and the believers. It was also said: the eighteen prophets mentioned earlier, and al-Zajjaj and Ibn Jarir chose this, because of His later words: ﴿Those are the ones whom God guided﴾. It was said: the Emigrants (muhajirun) and the Helpers (ansar). It was said: everyone who believed in the Messenger. Mujahid said: they are the Persians. Although some specific people have been named as the explanation of this verse, its meaning is general to the disbelievers and the believers until the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance﴾. The demonstrative "those" (ulā'ika) refers to those indicated by the first "ulā'ika," namely the prophets mentioned earlier, and He commanded him, exalted is He, that he follow their guidance. The earlier guidance is the Oneness of God, exalted is He, and sanctifying Him above any partner. So the meaning is: follow their path in belief in God, exalted is He, His Oneness and the foundations of the religion, not the legislations (shara'i'), for these differ, and so it is not possible to command following what differs. The legislations are guidance only so long as they are not abrogated (lam tunsakh), and when they are abrogated they no longer remain guidance, unlike the foundations of the religion, which are always guidance in their entirety. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a way﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48]. Ibn Atiyyah said: "It is possible that the demonstrative 'those' refers to 'a people' [in the previous verse], and this follows from some interpretations of the intended 'people' and not from others." End of quotation. He means that if "the people" are explained as the prophets mentioned or as the angels, then it is possible for the demonstrative to refer to "a people"; but if they are explained otherwise, it is not valid. It was also said: the following is in patience, as the one before him was patient. It was said: it is to be taken as all their guidance except what the evidence specifies. It was said: it is in noble character, of patience in the face of harm and forgiveness. In "Ray al-Zam'an" it is said: God, exalted is He, commanded His Prophet in this verse to noble character. He commanded the repentance of Adam, the gratitude of Nuh, the fidelity of Ibrahim, the truthfulness of his promise by Isma'il, the forbearance of Ishaq, the good opinion of Ya'qub, the forbearance of Yusuf, the patience of Ayyub, the penitence of Dawud, the humility of Sulayman, the sincerity of Musa, the worship of Zakariyya, the chastity of Yahya and the asceticism of 'Isa. These noble qualities that are in all the prophets were gathered in the Messenger ﷺ, and upon all of them be peace. For this reason God, exalted is He, described him with His words: ﴿And indeed, you are of a great moral character﴾ [al-Qalam: 4]. Al-Zamakhshari said: "So follow their guidance" singles out their guidance for following, and none is followed except them. This is in the sense of fronting the object, and this is in accordance with his view that fronting the object entails exclusivity; we have already refuted him on this in the discussion of ﴿You alone we worship﴾ [al-Fatihah: 5]. The two Harams (al-Haramayn, the readers of Mecca and Medina) and the people of their two sanctuaries, and Abu 'Amr, read "iqtadih" with the "ha'" silent both in continuous reading and in pause; it is the silent ha' (ha' al-saktah), and they treated it in continuous reading the way it is treated in pause. The two brothers (al-Akhawan, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i) read it by omitting it in continuous reading and affirming it in pause, and this is the analogical form. Hisham read "iqtadihi" with the vowel of the ha' rapidly weakened (ikhtilas) in continuous reading and the ha' silent in pause. Ibn Dhakwan read it with a kasrah on the ha' and joined it with a ya' in continuous reading, and silent in pause; it is interpreted as the pronoun of the verbal noun, not the silent ha'. Ibn Mujahid's dismissal of the kasrah reading is an error on his part, and interpreting it as the silent ha' is weak.

﴿Say: I do not ask you for any wage for it; it is only a reminder to the worlds﴾. That is: for calling to the Qur'an, which is guidance and the straight path. "Ajran" (wage) means a payment by which I would increase my wealth or be particularly favored. The Qur'an is only a reminder, an admonition, for all the worlds.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 83–90 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And that was Our argument, which We gave to Abraham against his people.﴾ The demonstrative "that" (tilka) refers to the argument that occurred from His saying ﴿So when the night covered him﴾ (6:76) up to His saying ﴿and they are the guided﴾ (6:82). This is the apparent meaning. He attributed it to Himself as a mark of honour, and the pronoun of attribution is the plural of majesty (nun al-'azama), not the first-person singular (ta' al-mutakallim). "We gave it" (atayna-ha) means: We brought it to his mind and created it in his soul, since it is among the rational proofs. Or it means: We gave it by revelation from Us and taught it to him.

If tilka is parsed as a subject (mubtada'), and hujjatuna as an apposition (badal), and atayna-ha as the predicate (khabar) of tilka, then 'ala qawmihi ("against his people") cannot be connected to hujjatuna. The same applies if tilka hujjatuna is parsed as subject and predicate, and atayna-ha as a circumstantial clause (hal). In that case the governing element is the demonstrative, because hujjah is not a verbal noun (masdar). Rather, it is the composed speech used to argue for a point. Even if we took it as a figurative verbal noun, this would still not be permitted, because a predicate or a circumstantial clause of this kind may not separate the verbal noun from what it governs.

Al-Hawfi permitted atayna-ha to be in the position of a qualifier (na't) of hujjatuna, with the intention of separation, the meaning being: "And that is an argument of Ours which We gave." End of quote. This is very far-fetched.

Al-Hawfi said: ha is the first object and Ibrahim is the second object. We have already mentioned that this is the view of al-Suhayli. As for the view of the majority, ha is the second object and Ibrahim is the first object.

Al-Hawfi and Ibn 'Atiyya said: 'ala qawmihi ("against his people") is connected to atayna-ha. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "We made it manifest to Ibrahim against his people." Abu al-Baqa' said: it is connected to a deleted element, its estimate being "an argument against his people and a proof." Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿We gave it to Ibrahim﴾ means "We guided him to it and enabled him to it." This is an explanation of meaning. It is also permitted that it be in the position of a circumstantial clause, with a deleted genitive (idafah) construction, meaning: "We gave it to Ibrahim, establishing supremacy over the arguments of his people, overpowering them."

﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾: that is, ranks and stations of whom We will. The original sense of darajat ("degrees") is spatial. Raising them may be by knowledge, or by prophethood, or by good character, or by sincerity of works in the Hereafter, or by prophethood and wisdom in this world, or by reward and Paradise in the Hereafter, or by argument and eloquence. These are opinions, the closest of which is the last, due to the context of the verse.

The Kufans read darajatin with tanwin (nunation), while the rest read it as an idafah (construction of annexation). Those who read it with tanwin put the noun in the accusative, either as an adverb of place (zarf) or as a second object. This view requires the verb narfa'u ("We raise") to be taken as implying a meaning that governs two objects, i.e. "We give whom We will degrees."

﴿Indeed your Lord is Wise, Knowing﴾: that is, Wise in the management of His servants, Knowing of their deeds. Or: Wise in dividing His servants into worshippers of idols and worshippers of God, Knowing of the arguments that occur between them. It is possible that the address in "your Lord" is to the Messenger, and it is possible that the intended person is Ibrahim, in which case it is an instance of iltifat (shift from third-person reference to second-person address), a shift from the pronoun of absence to the pronoun of address, as a mark of honour through direct address.

﴿And We gave him Ishaq and Ya'qub﴾: Ishaq was his son by his loins through Sarah, and Ya'qub was the son of Ishaq, as God the Exalted said: ﴿So We gave her good news of Ishaq, and after Ishaq, Ya'qub﴾ (11:71). God the Exalted enumerated His blessings upon Ibrahim: He mentioned giving him the argument against his people, and pointed to the raising of his ranks. He also mentioned what He bestowed upon him by giving him this prophet from whom the prophets of the Children of Israel descended. Among the greatest favours is that prophets and messengers should come from a man's offspring. He did not mention Isma'il together with Ishaq. It was said: the purpose of the mention here is the prophets of the Children of Israel, all of whom are the children of Ishaq and Ya'qub. No prophet came from the loins of Isma'il except Muhammad (ﷺ), and He did not mention him in this context, because He commanded him (peace be upon him) to argue against the Arabs regarding the denial of associating partners with God, saying that their forefather Ibrahim, when he was a monotheist devoted to God and free of polytheism, God granted him first kingship and prophethood.

The clause "And We gave him" (wa-wahabna) is coordinated with His saying ﴿And that was Our argument﴾, a verbal clause coordinated with a nominal clause. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "wa-wahabna" is coordinated with "atayna-ha." End of quote. This is not correct, because "atayna-ha" has a place in the grammatical structure, either as a predicate or as a circumstantial clause, and neither of these can apply to "wa-wahabna."

﴿Each We guided﴾: that is, each one of Ishaq and Ya'qub We guided.

﴿And Nuh We guided before﴾: When He mentioned the nobility of the sons of Ibrahim, He mentioned the nobility of his forefathers. He mentioned Nuh, who is "the second Adam," and said "before" (min qabl), to draw attention to his antiquity. [p. 173] There is a subtle point in mentioning him: Nuh (peace be upon him) lived when idols were worshipped, and his people were the first people to worship idols. He affirmed the oneness of God the Exalted, called to His worship, and rejected those idols. God related his supplication to his Lord concerning his people, where they said: ﴿Do not abandon your gods, nor abandon Wadd, nor Suwa', nor Yaghuth, nor Ya'uq, nor Nasr﴾ (71:23). Ibrahim lived when idols were worshipped, and he affirmed the oneness of God the Exalted and called to abandoning them. So God the Exalted mentioned Nuh and that He guided him, just as He guided Ibrahim.

﴿And from his offspring, Dawud and Sulayman﴾: It was said: "from the offspring of Nuh," the pronoun referring to him because he is the nearest mentioned person, and because among them is Lut, who was the son of Ibrahim's brother, so he is from the offspring of Nuh and not from the offspring of Ibrahim. It was also said: "from the offspring of Ibrahim," the pronoun referring to him because he is the intended subject of mention. Ibn 'Abbas said: all these prophets are attributed to the offspring of Ibrahim, even though some of them are not connected to him by birth from either mother or father, because Lut was the son of Ibrahim's brother, and the Arabs call an uncle a father. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: "And We gave him Lut" in support and assistance. End of quote.

They said: the meaning is "And We guided, or gave, from his offspring Dawud and Sulayman." He joined them because they were father and son, and because they were both kings and prophets. He placed Dawud first because he came earlier in time, because he was the possessor of a scripture, and because he was the origin of Sulayman, who was his branch.

﴿And Ayyub and Yusuf﴾: He joined them because they shared in trial. Ayyub was tested with affliction in his body and the rejection of his people. Yusuf was tested with imprisonment and with being far from his family. In their outcome both were given safety and well-being. He placed Ayyub first because his trial was greater.

﴿And Musa and Harun﴾: He joined them because they shared in brotherhood. He placed Musa first because he was the one who spoke with God (Kalim Allah).

﴿Thus do We reward the good-doers﴾: that is, like that reward, namely giving the argument and bestowing righteous offspring, We reward whoever is a good-doer in His worship, mindful of Us in his deeds.

﴿And Zakariyya and Yahya and 'Isa and Ilyas﴾: He joined them among themselves because they shared in intense asceticism and turning away from the world. He began with Zakariyya and Yahya because they preceded 'Isa in time. He placed Zakariyya first because he was the father of Yahya, so he was the origin and Yahya the branch. He joined 'Isa and Ilyas because both had not yet died. He placed 'Isa first because he was the possessor of a scripture and had a wide sphere of influence. The genealogies of these prophets were mentioned, except for Ilyas. He is Ilyas son of Bashir son of Finhas son of al-'Ayzar son of Harun son of 'Imran. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud that Idris is Ilyas, but this was rejected on the grounds that Idris is the grandfather of Nuh (peace be upon them both), as the reports concur on this. It was also said that Ilyas is al-Khidr.

The disagreement of the readers regarding Zakariyya, whether with a long or short vowel, has already been mentioned. Ibn 'Abbas, with a variant from him, and al-Hasan and Qatada read the hamza of Ilyas with facilitation (tashil). In the mention of 'Isa here there is evidence that the son of a daughter is included in "offspring" (dhurriyyah). By this verse, it was used as evidence for his inclusion in a waqf (endowment) made for "offspring." Whether the pronoun in ﴿from his offspring﴾ refers to Nuh or to Ibrahim, we say: al-Hasan and al-Husayn, the sons of Fatima (may God be pleased with them both), are from the offspring of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). By this verse Abu Ja'far al-Baqir and Yahya ibn Ya'mur argued for this. al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf had demanded from them evidence for this, since he denied it, and they remained silent in two incidents that occurred between them and him.

﴿Each is of the righteous﴾: "each" does not restrict to these four, but includes all those previously mentioned of the fourteen prophets.

﴿And Isma'il and al-Yasa' and Yunus and Lut﴾: It is well known that Isma'il is the son of Ibrahim by Hajar, and he was the eldest of his sons. It was said he was a prophet of the Children of Israel who lived in the time of Talut, and he is the one meant by the words ﴿when they said to a prophet of theirs: "Raise up for us a king that we may fight in the way of God"﴾ (2:246).

As for al-Yasa', Zayd ibn Aslam said: he is Yusha' ibn Nun. Others said: he is al-Yasa' ibn Akhtub, son of the old woman. The majority read "al-Yasa'" (with the definite article), as if the article were added to the present-tense form of the verb wasi'a. The two brothers (Hamza and al-Kisa'i) read "al-Layasa'" on the pattern fay'al, like "al-Dayghim." It is disputed whether this is Arabic or foreign. As for the reading of the majority and the view of those who say it is Arabic, they said: it is a present-tense verb used as a proper name, and it has no pronoun in it, so it is declined as a noun, then made indefinite and definite with the article. It was also said it was named by the verb, like Yazid, and then the article was added to it as an irregular extra element, like "al-Yazid" in the poet's verse:

I saw al-Walid ibn al-Yazid blessed.

And it was fixed as it was fixed in "al-An" (now). As for those who say it is foreign, they said: the article was added to it and became fixed irregularly. Among those who explicitly stated the addition of the article to al-Yasa' is Abu 'Ali al-Farisi. As for the reading of the two brothers, Abu 'Ali considered that the article in it is like its occurrence in al-Harith and al-'Abbas, since these are from the patterns of adjectives. But the addition of the article to it is irregular with respect to the rule followed by foreign proper names, since nothing of this pattern came in them, just as nothing with the article for definiteness came in them.

Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Malik al-Jayyani said: whatever the article accompanies in its transferred form, like the one named al-Nadr or al-Nu'man, or in its original form, like al-Yasa' and al-Samaw'al, the article is most usually fixed in it, though it may be permitted to omit it. Accordingly, the article is not necessarily obligatory in it. From his saying that al-Yasa' is not transferred from fa'ala, as some said, it is clear.

It was mentioned that he (al-Jayyani) said: Yunus is with a damma, fatha, and kasra on the nun, and likewise Yusuf. With a fatha on the nun and on the sin of Yusuf, al-Hasan, Talha, Yahya, al-A'mash, and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read throughout the Qur'an.

These four were gathered together because no creatures remained who were their followers or partisans. These are six ranks. The rank of kingship and power, in which He mentioned Dawud and Sulayman.
