﴿Say, "Who sent down the Book which Musa brought, a light and guidance for the people?"﴾ If the deniers are the Children of Israel, the argument against them is clear, because they uphold the sending down of the Book upon Musa. If they are the Arabs, the basis of the argument against them is that the sending down of the Book upon Musa is a well-known matter, transmitted by a people whom the Arabs did not dispute. They used to say: "If the Book had been sent down to us, we would have been better guided than them." Abu Hamid al-Ghazali said: this verse is built upon the second figure of the logical syllogisms, because its outcome returns to the point that Musa, upon whom something was sent down from God, is a human being, and that whom God sent nothing is not a human being. This yields by the second figure that Musa was not a human being, and this is an impossible absurdity. This impossibility is not due to the form of the syllogism, nor to the soundness of the premise. Nothing remains except that assuming the soundness of the premise, which is their saying "God has not sent down anything upon any human being," necessarily leads to it being false. So the evidence of this verse for the intended conclusion is valid only upon acknowledging the soundness of the second figure of the logical syllogisms and upon acknowledging the soundness of reductio ad absurdum (qiyas al-khulf). End of his statement. In the verse there is evidence that contradiction undermines the soundness of speech, because He contradicted their saying "God has not sent down anything" with His saying "Who sent down the Book?" If contradiction were not a proof of the invalidity of a statement, this argument would not be effective for this purpose. The Book here is the Torah. "Light and guidance" is in the accusative of circumstance (ḥāl), and the governing element is either "anzala" or "jā'a."

﴿You make it into scrolls, showing some and concealing much﴾. The ta' is the reading of the majority in all three verbs. Its apparent meaning is that it addresses the Children of Israel. The meaning is: you make it into scrolls, i.e. pages and sheets, and you conceal much, like their concealing of the signs that indicate the sending of the Messenger and other signs that they concealed. God included in the obligation their reproach, even though He condemned them for their bad handling of their Book, their distortion of it, and their revealing of some parts while concealing others. It was said: Musa brought it, and it is a light and guidance for the people, but you changed it and made it into scrolls and sheets so that you could carry out what you intended of revealing and concealing. The reading with ta' accords with His saying "you were taught." As for those who say that if the deniers are the Arabs or the disbelievers of Quraysh, the address cannot be directed to them, but rather it would be an interruption of the Children of Israel, saying in the midst of the question and the answer: "You, O Children of Israel, make it into scrolls," such a thing is unlikely, because it disrupts the composition and structure of the verse, making the speech first an address to the disbelievers and then an address to the Jews. It has been answered that since all of them shared in denying the prophethood of the Messenger, part of the speech was an address to the Arabs and part an address to the Children of Israel. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with the ya' in the third person in all three verbs.

﴿And you were taught what you did not know, neither you nor your fathers﴾. Its apparent meaning is that it is an address to the Children of Israel, intended as a favour upon them and upon their fathers, that they came to know of God's religion and His guidance what they had not known, because their fathers had also known and some of them had known. This does not apply to the fathers of the Arabs. Alternatively, it is intended as a reproach against them, because they did not benefit from it due to their aversion and misguidance. It was said: the address is to the Arabs, reported by Mujahid. God mentioned His favour upon them, i.e., you were taught, O company of Arabs, guidance, monotheism and direction to the truth that you did not know, ﴿neither you nor your fathers﴾. It was said: the address is to those Jews who believed. It was said: to those among Quraysh who believed. The explanation of ﴿what you did not know﴾ is derived according to the addressees: the Torah, or the religion of Islam and its laws, or both, or the Qur'an. Al-Zamakhshari said: the address is to the Jews, i.e., you were taught through the tongue of Muhammad (ﷺ) what was revealed to him, what you did not know, although you are the bearers of the Torah, and your ancient fathers, who were more knowledgeable than you, did not know that this Qur'an recounts to the Children of Israel most of what they differ about. It was said: the address is to those among Quraysh who believed, ﴿that you may warn a people whose fathers were not warned﴾ [Ya Sin: 6]. End of quotation.

﴿Say, "God."﴾ He commanded him to hasten to the answer, i.e., say: God sent it down. For they cannot deny you, because the Book described with light and guidance that has been brought by one supported with miracles, its evidence has reached such clarity that it is necessary to acknowledge that its sender is God, whether or not the opponent admits it. A parallel is His saying: ﴿Say, "What thing is greatest in testimony?" Say, "God"﴾ [al-An'am: 19]. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it may be that the meaning is: if they are ignorant, or perplexed, or ask and the like, then say "God." End of quotation. This assumption is not needed, because the speech is self-sufficient without it.

﴿Then leave them in their plunging, playing﴾. That is, in their falsehood in which they plunge. It is said of one who is engaged in an activity that brings him no benefit: "You are only playing." "Playing" (yal'abūna) is an accusative of circumstance from the object of "leave them" or from the pronoun of "their plunging." "In their plunging" is connected to "leave them," or to "playing," or is an accusative of circumstance from "playing." The apparent meaning of the command is conciliation (muwādaʿa), so it would be abrogated (naskh) by the verses of fighting. If it is taken as a threat or a warning free of conciliation, then there is no abrogation.

﴿And this is a blessed Book which We have sent down﴾ [p. 179] That is: this Qur'an. When He mentioned and established that those who deny that God sent down anything upon a human being are denying, and argued against them with what they cannot deny, He informed that this Book sent down upon the Messenger is blessed, abundant in benefit and usefulness. Since the denial fell upon the sending down, as they said "God has not sent down," and it was said: "Who sent down the Book?", the mention of its description with sending down was more emphatic than the description of it as blessed. Also, whatever God sends down is necessarily blessed, so the description of it as blessed becomes like an emphatic attribute, since what precedes it includes it. As for His saying: ﴿And this is a blessed reminder which We have sent down﴾ [al-Anbiya': 50], it did not occur in a context of denying that God sends down anything; rather it came after His saying: ﴿And We gave Musa and Harun the criterion and a light and a reminder for the righteous﴾ [al-Anbiya': 48]. He mentioned that what He gave to the Messenger is a blessed reminder. Since the sending down is renewed, He expressed the description with a verb, and since the description of it with blessing is a permanent attribute that does not depart, He expressed it with the noun that indicates permanence.

﴿Confirming what was before it﴾. That is, of the Books of God that were sent down. It was said: the Torah. It was said: the Resurrection. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is not correct, because the Qur'an is before the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around it.﴾ The Mother of Cities is Makkah. It was so called because it is the source of the religion, because the earth was spread out (*dahw*) from it, because it is the center of the earth, and because it is the qiblah, the place of the Hajj, and the site of the first House set up for people. The meaning is: that you may warn the people of the Mother of Cities and those around it, and they are all the rest of the inhabitants of the earth. This is what Ibn ʿAbbas said. It was also said that it refers to the Arabs. A group of Jews used this verse, ﴿the Mother of Cities and those around it﴾, to argue that he was a messenger only to the Arabs. They said: "those around it" are the surrounding towns, which is the Arabian Peninsula. It is answered that "those around it" is general and covers the whole earth. Even if we assume it is specific, mentioning the Arabian Peninsula would be evidence for the exclusion of the ruling from everything else only through *mafhūm* (implicit meaning), which is weak. The omission of *ahl* (people) is because the meaning indicates it, since buildings cannot be warned, as in His saying: ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], since the town cannot be asked. The word *man* (those) was not omitted so that *ḥawlahā* (around it) could be conjoined to *Umma al-Qurā* (the Mother of Cities). Although in terms of meaning it would be valid, *ḥawl* is an adverb (*ẓarf*, adverb of place) that does not vary in its usage. So if it were conjoined to *Umm al-Qurā*, it would have to be an object (*mafʿūl bihi*) because it is conjoined to the object, and that is not permissible, because using it as an object means departing from its adverbial function, and that is not allowed for it, since, as we have said, the Arabs did not use it except in its necessary adverbial function, not varied with anything else. Abu Bakr read *li-yundhira* (that it may warn), meaning: the Qur'an with its admonitions and commands. The majority read *wa-litundhira* (and that you may warn) addressed to the Messenger, and the meaning is: and that you may warn with what We have sent down. So the *lām* is connected to a deleted word that comes later, indicated by what precedes it. Al-Zamakhsharī said: *wa-litundhira* is conjoined to what is indicated by the description of the Book, as if it were said: We sent it down for blessings, and confirming what came before it of the Books, and for warning.

﴿Those who believe in the Hereafter believe in it.﴾ It is apparent that the pronoun in *bihi* (in it) refers to the Book, meaning: those who affirm that there will be a gathering, a resurrection and a recompense for them, believe in this Book because of what it contains of promise and threat, glad tidings and warning. For there is no book among the divine Books and no law among the laws that contains what is in this Book, nor what is in this law concerning the Day of Resurrection and the raising of the dead. The meaning is: they believe in it with the faith supported by sound proof. Otherwise, the People of the Book believe in the resurrection but do not believe in the Qur'an. He mentioned only belief in the resurrection, which is one of the six pillars, which are: the necessarily existent being, the angels, the books, the messengers, the Last Day, and divine decree, because belief in it entails belief in the rest. It also serves to inform the disbelieving Arabs and others who do not believe in the resurrection that whoever believes in the resurrection believes in this Book. The root of religion is fear of the consequence, so whoever opposes it, fear does not cease to be with him until he believes. It was also said that the pronoun refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿And they are over their prayer they guard.﴾ He singled out the prayer because it is the pillar of religion, and whoever guards it is guarding its counterparts. The meaning of guarding is persevering in performing it at its times in the best manner in which it is performed. Prayer is the most noble of the acts of worship after faith in Allah, and for this reason the name of faith was not applied to any act of worship except it. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And Allah would not let your faith go to waste﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], meaning: your prayer. Disbelief was not applied to any sin except the abandonment of it. It was narrated: "Whoever abandons the prayer deliberately has disbelieved." The majority read *ʿalā ṣalātihim* (over their prayer) in the singular, and what is meant by it is the genus. Khalaf narrated from Yahya from Abu Bakr: *ṣalawātihim* (their prayers) in the plural. Abu ʿAlī al-Ḥasan ibn Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm al-Baghdādī mentioned this in his book *al-Rawḍa* (The Garden), which he composed, and he said: he was alone in this among all people.

﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah, or says: "It has been revealed to me," when nothing has been revealed to him, or who says: "I will send down the like of what Allah has sent down."﴾ Al-Zahrāwī and al-Mahdawī mentioned that the verse was revealed concerning al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith. It was said: and concerning those who mocked along with him, because he opposed the Qur'an with his saying: "By those who sow seed, sowing; by those who bake bread, baking; by those who cook, cooking; by those who grind, grinding; by those who morsel, morseling," and other such nonsense. Qatāda and others said: what is meant by it is Musaylima al-Ḥanafī and al-Aswad al-ʿAnsī, and they mentioned the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) vision of the two bracelets. Al-Zamakhsharī said: it is Musaylima al-Ḥanafī, or the liar of Ṣanʿā', al-Aswad al-ʿAnsī. Al-Suddī said: "What is meant by it is ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿd ibn Abī Sarḥ al-ʿĀmirī, the foster brother of ʿUthmān. He was writing the verse ﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾ before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and when he dictated to him ﴿Then We produced it as another creation﴾ [al-Muʾminūn: 14], he marvelled at the detail of the creation of man, and said: ﴿So blessed be Allah, the best of creators﴾. The Messenger said: 'Write it, for thus it was revealed.' ʿAbd Allāh imagined [that it was his own speech], apostatized, and fled to Makkah, and said: 'I will send down the like of what Allah has sent down.'" Ikrimah said: its first part was about Musaylima, and its last part about Ibn Abī Sarḥ. It was narrated from him that when he was dictated ﴿All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 148], he would write: "All-Knowing, All-Wise," and when he was dictated "All-Knowing, All-Wise," he would write: "All-Forgiving, All-Merciful." Shurahbīl ibn Saʿd said: it was revealed concerning Ibn Abī Sarḥ, and whoever says: "I will send down the like of what Allah has sent down" apostatizes. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered Makkah in the year of the Conquest, and ʿUthmān hid him until the people of Makkah were reassured. Then he brought him to the Messenger, and he asked the Messenger for his protection, and the Messenger granted him security. End of quotation. ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān appointed him in his days, and the cities were opened at his hands. He conquered Ifriqiya in the year thirty-one, and raided the Asāwid of the land of Nubia, and he was the one who made the truce with them that remains to this day. He raided the Ṣawārī of the land of the Romans. His Islam had become good, and nothing objectionable appeared from him. He was one of the noble, wise and generous men of Quraysh and the knight of the Banū ʿĀmir ibn Lu'ayy. He stayed in ʿAsqalān, it was said, or al-Ramla, fleeing from the strife when ʿUthmān was killed, and he died there in the year thirty-six, it was said, or thirty-seven. He supplicated his Lord and said: "O Allah, make the last of my deeds the dawn prayer." He died at the end of the dawn, and he had already given the salām to his right, and was about to give the salām to his left, and that was before the people gathered around Muʿāwiya.

When He mentioned the Qur'an, and that it is a blessed Book sent down from Him, He followed it with a threat against the one who claims prophethood and messengership by way of fabrication. The discussion of *wa-man aẓlamu* (and who is more unjust) has already occurred. They interpreted it as an interrogative whose meaning is negation, that is: no one is more unjust. He began first with the general, which is inventing a lie against Allah, and this is more general than whether that invention is by claiming a revelation or otherwise. Then secondly with the specific, which is an invention attributed to a revelation from Allah, the Exalted.

﴿or says: "It has been revealed to me," when nothing has been revealed to him﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*jumla ḥāliyya*), or it means: not one to whom anything has been revealed. For whoever says "It has been revealed to me" while it has been revealed to him is truthful. Then secondly he mentioned something more specific than what precedes it, because revelation may be by the sending down of a Qur'an and by other than that. The story of Ibn Abī Sarḥ is his claim that he would send down a Qur'an like what Allah has sent down. His saying ﴿the like of what Allah has sent down﴾ is not his belief that Allah had sent down something; rather the meaning is: ﴿the like of what Allah has sent down﴾ according to your claim. The repetition of *man* (whoever) indicates that its referent is different from the referent of the earlier *man*. So the one who said "I will send down" is other than the one who invented or said "it has been revealed," even though what precedes him applies to him in the manner of the general applying to the specific. His saying "I will send down" is a false promise, and calling it sending down is a metaphor; the meaning is: I will arrange speech that resembles what you claimed Allah had sent down. Abū Ḥaywa read *mā nazzala* with the intensive form. And although the cause of the revelation of this verse was particular persons, it encompasses everyone who claims a claim like theirs, such as Ṭulayḥa al-Asadī, al-Mukhtār ibn Abī ʿUbayd al-Thaqafī, Sajāḥ, and others. Many learned men have claimed prophethood. Among those whom we have known in our own time was Ibrāhīm al-Ghāzāzī the poor, who claimed that in the city of Mālaqa, and the Sultan Abū ʿAbd Allāh Muḥammad ibn Yūsuf ibn Naṣr al-Khazrajī, king of al-Andalus, killed him at Gharnāṭa and crucified him. And Barqashāṭ ibn Qasīm al-Nīlī the poet claimed prophethood in the city of al-Nīl in the land of Iraq, and he had a Qur'an that he composed. He was not killed, because he was mocked and considered weak in his mind.

﴿And if you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death﴾. *Al-ẓālimūn* (the wrongdoers) is general, and it includes the Jews, the false prophets and others. It was also said that the *alif-lām* is for prior reference, meaning: from among the Jews and those who claimed prophethood, and they are the ones previously mentioned.

﴿while the angels extend their hands﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās said: with beating, meaning: the angels of seizing the soul strike their faces and their backs at its seizing. Al-Farrāʾ also said this. The meaning is not merely the extending of the hand, since believers and disbelievers share that. This is the beginning of the punishment and its signs. Ibn ʿAbbās also said: on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Ḥasan and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: with punishment. Al-Ḥasan also said: this occurs in the Fire.

﴿"Bring forth your souls."﴾ Al-Zamakhsharī said: they extend their hands to them, saying: "Hand over your spirits, bring them out to us from your bodies." This is an expression of harshness in the drive and intense insistence on taking out the soul without respite or delay, and that they treat them like a creditor who extends his hand to one who owes him a debt, presses him in demanding it, does not grant him time, and says to him: "Give me what you owe me now, or I will remain here until I pull it from your friends." Whoever says that the extending of hands is in the Fire, the meaning is: bring yourselves out from these calamities and trials and free yourselves, if what you claimed were true in the world. In this there is rebuke and reproach for their past evil deeds. It was also said: it is a command in the manner of humiliation and terrifying, and that they are like one who has been charged with taking his own soul.

﴿Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation﴾. *Al-hūn* means *al-hawān* (humiliation). ʿAbd Allāh and ʿIkrima read *ʿadhāba l-hawān* with an *alif* and an open *hāʾ*. As for *al-yawm* (today): whoever says that this is in the world, it is an expression for the time of death, and the punishment is what they were punished with from the severity of the extraction, or the extended lengthy period in which they are afflicted with punishment in the barzakh. Whoever says that this is in the Resurrection, it is an expression for the Day of Resurrection or for the time of their address in the Fire. The punishment is attributed to humiliation because it is established in it, since the chastising may be in the manner of reproof and discipline, and there is no humiliation in it, and it may be in the manner of humiliation.

﴿for what you used to say about Allah other than the truth﴾. Saying about Allah other than the truth includes every kind of disbelief, and whoever was previously mentioned among those who invent lies against Allah enters into it with a stronger entry.

﴿And you used to be arrogant towards His signs﴾, meaning: arrogant regarding belief in His signs. The answer to *law* (if) is deleted, its estimate being: you would have seen a great matter and you would have seen a marvel. Its deletion is more eloquent than its mention. *Tarā* (you see) is in the sense of *ra'ayta* (you saw), because it governs the past adverb *idh* (when). *Al-malāʾika bāsiṭū* (the angels extending) is a circumstantial clause, and *akhrijū* (bring forth) is an object governed by a deleted circumstantial word, meaning: saying "bring forth." And *mā* in *bi-mā* is a verbal-noun particle (*maṣdariyya*).

And ﴿You have come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾. ʿIkrima said: al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith said: "Al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā will intercede for me," so it was revealed.

When He said ﴿Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation﴾, He made them acknowledge that they would come on the Day of Resurrection alone, with no helper for them, needing Him, after they had been masters of servants and intercessors in the world. It appears that this speech is from the address of the angels appointed to punish them. It was also said: it is Allah's speech to them. This is based on the premise that Allah, the Exalted, speaks to the disbelievers, and it is evident from His saying ﴿Surely We will question those to whom messengers were sent﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 6], and from His saying ﴿We will surely question them all﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 92].

And you have come to Us [as] you were created the first time, alone (*furada*), as We created you at first. Others say that this is a past tense that is still in its literal sense, reported (*mahkiy*), so that they are told this while standing before God for recompense and reckoning. Ibn Abbas said: "*furada*" means being without family, wealth and children. Al-Hasan said: each one alone, without helpers or intercessors. Muqatil said: nothing of the world that you used to boast of is with you. Al-Zajjaj said: each one is singular, apart from his partner and intercessor. Ibn Kaysan said: "*furada*" means apart from the one worshipped. It was also said: We have brought you without any helper or supporter. These statements are close in meaning. When they were in the world they strove to obtain status, wealth and intercessors, and in the Hereafter they come isolated from everything they had acquired in the world.

It is read as *furada* (without tanwin, not declined), and Isa ibn Umar and Abu Haywa read *furadan* with tanwin. Abu Amr and Nafi, in a report transmitted from other than them, read *fardaa* like *sakraa*, as in the verse ﴿And you see people as drunken﴾ [22:2], and it is feminine in accordance with the meaning of a group. The *kaf* in *kama* (as) is in the accusative position. It was said that it is a substitute (*badal*) for *furada*. It was also said that it is an adjective (*na't*) of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning "coming," ﴿as We created you﴾, meaning like your coming on the day We created you. This resembles the first isolation at the time of creation, so it restricts the state of isolation by comparing it to the state of creation, because a person is created bare, without wealth, child or retinue. It was also said: naked and uncircumcised. Whoever said "in the condition in which you were born, in isolation" includes both of these statements. *Awwala marra* ("the first time") is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*zarf*), meaning the first time. It is not to be understood as "the first of God's creation," because "first creation" would require a second creation, and a second creation does not occur; that is rather a restoration (*i'adah*), not a creation.

﴿And you left behind what We had bestowed upon you, behind your backs﴾. That is, what We had favoured you with in the world did not benefit you, and you did not carry any of it, not even a speck, nor did you send it ahead for yourselves. By His words ﴿behind your backs﴾ He indicated the world, because they leave behind what they were given while it still exists.

﴿And We do not see with you your intercessors whom you claimed to be partners among you﴾. He made them acknowledge their error in worshipping the idols and venerating them. Muqatil said: they believed in the intercession of the angels and said: ﴿We only worship them so that they bring us near to God in closeness﴾ [39:3]. "*Fikum*" (among you) is connected to "*shurakaa*" (partners). The meaning is: in your subjugation (*isti'bad*), because when they called them gods and worshipped them, they made them partners of God in themselves and in their subjugation. It was also said: they made them partners of God in the sense that they intercede for them with Him, so they are partners in this sense. It is possible that the meaning is: partners of God in delivering you from punishment, and that their worship benefits you as His worship benefits you. It was also said: "*fikum*" means "with you." Ibn Qutaybah said: they are partners with me in your creation. It was also said: they bear for you a share of the punishment.

﴿Indeed, your connection has been cut off, and what you used to claim has gone astray from you﴾. The majority of the Seven Readers (*jumhur al-sab'a*, the seven canonical reciters) read *baynukum* with a *damma*, on the basis that the word *bayn* was used as a noun by extension of its use as an adverb (*zarf*), and the verb was ascribed to it so that it became a noun, just as they used it as a noun in the verse ﴿And between us and you there is a barrier﴾ [41:5], and as Sibawayh reported: "He is red between the two eyes." Al-Farisi preferred this reading. Or it means that *al-bayn* refers to connection, i.e. your connection has been cut off. Abu al-Fath, al-Zahrawi and al-Mahdawi said this. Ibn Atiyyah rejected this and claimed that *al-bayn* in the sense of connection was not heard from the Arabs, and that it was derived only from this verse. Or it means that *al-bayn* refers to separation, and this is a metaphor for a distant matter; the meaning is: the distance between you has been cut off because of its length, so this is expressed by *al-bayn*. Nafi, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read *baynakum* with a *fatha* on the *nun*. Al-Akhfash interpreted it as the subject, but it is built on the *fatha* in view of the most common uses of this adverb. It is also said that it is because it is attached to an indeclinable word, as in the verse ﴿and among us are some other than that﴾ [72:11]. Others interpreted it as accusative in the sense of an adverb. The subject of *taqatta'a* (was cut off) is the cutting-off (*taqatta'*). Al-Zamakhshari said: the cutting-off happened between you, as you say: "He joined between the two things," meaning: he caused the joining between them, the verb being ascribed to its verbal noun by this interpretation. End of quote. Its apparent sense is not good. Its precise analysis is that he attributed the verb to a pronoun referring to its verbal noun and omitted it within it, because if he attributed it to the explicit verbal noun, it would be omitted, and the omission of the subject is not permitted. Even with this assumption it is not correct, because the condition of attribution is absent in it, namely the difference between the predicate and the thing predicated of. For this reason one cannot say "stood" or "sat" while meaning "he stood, that is, the standing." It was also said that the subject is a hidden pronoun referring to the connection indicated by the word "*shurakaa'*" (partners). The subject is not to be taken as the explicit verbal noun, as Ibn Atiyyah said. He said: the verb is attributed to something omitted, its estimate being: "the connection and the bond among you has been cut off," or something like this. This is a clear view, and on this basis the people interpreted it, Mujahid, al-Suddi and others. End of quote. His statement "to something omitted" is not correct, because the subject is not omitted. Abu al-Baqa permitted that *baynakum* be an adjective of an omitted subject, meaning: "something between you was cut off, or a connection." This is also not correct, because the subject is not omitted. What appears to me is that the matter falls under the principle of *i'mal* (operating two verbs on one noun): the cutting-off (*taqatta'*) and the going-astray (*dalla*) both govern "*ma kuntum taz'umun*" (what you used to claim). The second verb, *dalla*, is made to operate, and in *taqatta'* a pronoun referring to *ma* (what) is understood, which is the idols. The meaning is: what you used to claim was cut off between you, and they went astray from you, as He said: ﴿and the means were cut off from them﴾ [2:166], meaning: no connection remained between you and "*ma kuntum taz'umun*" (what you used to claim), that they were partners, so you worshipped them. This is an easy analysis that no one has noticed. Abd Allah, Mujahid and al-A'mash read *ma baynakum* (what was between you), and the meaning is: what was between you and what you used to claim perished and vanished. The two objects of *taz'umun* are omitted, the estimate being: "you claimed them to be intercessors," omitted because of the indication of them, as the poet said:

*You see their love as a shame upon me, and you reckon it*

meaning: and you reckon it a shame. Abu Abd Allah al-Razi has a discussion on this verse that resembles the opinions of the philosophers. At its end he said: and it is to this that His words refer: "Indeed, your connection has been cut off," and the meaning is that the connection between the soul and the body has been severed, and there is no way to restore it a second time. End of quote. This is not understood from the verse.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 91–94 (part 1 of 3):

﴿They did not measure God with His true measure when they said, "God has not sent down anything upon any human being."﴾ It was revealed concerning the Jews. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Muhammad ibn Ka'b. Another view is that it was revealed concerning Malik ibn al-Sayf, the Jewish scholar, when the Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: "I adjure you by God, who sent down the Torah to Musa, do you find in it that God hates the fat rabbi?" He said: "Yes." He said: "You are the fat rabbi." He became angry and then said: "God has not sent down anything upon any human being." This is reported by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Ikrimah. Another view is that it was revealed concerning Finhas ibn 'Azura among them; this is reported by al-Suddi. Another view is that it was revealed concerning the Jews and Christians; this is reported by Qatadah. Another view is that it was revealed concerning the polytheist Arabs; this is reported by Mujahid and others. Some scholars restricted it, from this view, to the polytheists of Quraysh; this is the narration of Ibn Abi Najih from him. In the narration of Ibn Kathir from Mujahid, from its beginning up to "upon any human being," it refers to the polytheists of Quraysh, and His saying "Who sent down the Book" refers to the Jews.

When God mentioned concerning Ibrahim the proof of monotheism and the foolishness of the opinion of the people of polytheism, and mentioned the favour God bestowed upon Ibrahim by placing prophethood among his descendants, and that Nuh (peace be upon him) was his forefather, whom God had guided and who had been sent to his people, and when He commanded the Messenger to follow the guidance of the prophets, [p. 177] He began to establish prophethood and to refute those who deny revelation. He said: ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure.﴾ The root meaning of qadr is knowing the quantity. It is said: "He measured (qadara) the thing" when he estimated it, tested it, and wished to know its measure. It is conjugated as yaqduruhu, with a dammah, qadran and qadaran. From this is His saying: ﴿If it is obscured for you, then estimate for it﴾, meaning: seek to know it. Then the word was extended, until it was said of everyone who knows something that he "measures its measure," and of one who does not know it through its attributes that he "does not measure its measure." Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said, and al-Farra', Tha'lab and al-Zajjaj preferred, that its meaning is: they did not magnify God with His true magnification. Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash said: they did not know Him with His true knowledge. Al-Maturidi said: "Who magnifies God with His true greatness, or knows Him with His true knowledge? The angels said: 'We did not worship You with Your true worship,' and the Messenger (ﷺ) said: 'I cannot count praise upon You.'" This is resolved by saying that the meaning is: they did not magnify Him with the magnification within their capacity and within what is in their power, and they did not know Him in that way. Abu al-'Aliyah said, and al-Khalil ibn Ahmad preferred: its meaning is: they did not describe Him with His true description regarding what is obligatory for Him, what is impossible for Him, and what is permissible for Him. Ibn 'Abbas also said: they did not believe in God with His true belief, and they did not know that God is powerful over all things. Abu 'Ubaydah also said: they did not worship Him with His true worship. It was also said: they did not honour Him with His true honour; this is related by Ibn Abi al-Fadl in Ri alzam'an, and it has the same meaning as magnification. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is from fulfilling the measure, so it is general, and it includes whoever does not know Him, whoever does not magnify Him, and other things. However, his explanation with their saying "God has not sent down anything" requires that they were ignorant and did not know God with His true knowledge, since they denied that God sends messengers. Al-Zamakhshari said: they did not know God with His true knowledge in respect of His mercy upon His servants and His kindness to them, when they denied the sending of messengers and the revelation to them, and that is among the greatest of His mercy and the most glorious of His blessings. ﴿We did not send you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 107]. Or: they did not know Him with His true knowledge in respect of His wrath upon the disbelievers and the severity of His seizing them, and they did not fear Him when they dared to utter that monstrous statement denying prophethood. The speakers were the Jews, as evidenced by the reading of the one who read "you make it" with the letter ta', and likewise "you show them" and "you conceal." They said that only to exaggerate in denying the sending down of the Qur'an upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ), so they were compelled to admit what they could not avoid admitting: the sending down of the Torah to Musa. End of quotation. The pronoun in ﴿They did not measure﴾ refers to those concerning whom the verse was revealed, according to the earlier disagreement. Whoever says it is about the Children of Israel must hold that it is Medinan, and for this reason al-Naqqash reported that it is Medinan. Al-Hasan and 'Isa al-Thaqafi read "wa ma qaddaru" with the shaddah, and "haqqa qadarihi" with a fatha on the dal. ﴿haqqa qadrihi﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar); originally it is an attribute, meaning: they estimated Him with the truth. When the attribute of the verbal noun is annexed to it, it takes the accusative of the verbal noun. The governing element of "idh" is "qadaru." In Ibn 'Atiyyah's statement there is an indication that "idh" is causal.

﴿Say, "Who sent down the Book which Musa brought, a light and guidance for the people?"﴾ If the deniers are the Children of Israel, the argument against them is clear, because they uphold the sending down of the Book upon Musa. If they are the Arabs, the basis of the argument against them is that the sending down of the Book upon Musa is a well-known matter, transmitted by a people whom the Arabs did not dispute. They used to say: "If the Book had been sent down to us, we would have been better guided than them." Abu Hamid al-Ghazali said: this verse is built upon the second figure of the logical syllogisms, because its outcome returns to the point that Musa, upon whom something was sent down from God, is a human being, and that whom God sent nothing is not a human being. This yields by the second figure that Musa was not a human being, and this is an impossible absurdity. This impossibility is not due to the form of the syllogism, nor to the soundness of the premise. Nothing remains except that assuming the soundness of the premise, which is their saying "God has not sent down anything upon any human being," necessarily leads to it being false. So the evidence of this verse for the intended conclusion is valid only upon acknowledging the soundness of the second figure of the logical syllogisms and upon acknowledging the soundness of reductio ad absurdum (qiyas al-khulf). End of his statement. In the verse there is evidence that contradiction undermines the soundness of speech, because He contradicted their saying "God has not sent down anything" with His saying "Who sent down the Book?" If contradiction were not a proof of the invalidity of a statement, this argument would not be effective for this purpose. The Book here is the Torah. "Light and guidance" is in the accusative of circumstance (ḥāl), and the governing element is either "anzala" or "jā'a."

﴿You make it into scrolls, showing some and concealing much﴾. The ta' is the reading of the majority in all three verbs. Its apparent meaning is that it addresses the Children of Israel. The meaning is: you make it into scrolls, i.e. pages and sheets, and you conceal much, like their concealing of the signs that indicate the sending of the Messenger and other signs that they concealed. God included in the obligation their reproach, even though He condemned them for their bad handling of their Book, their distortion of it, and their revealing of some parts while concealing others. It was said: Musa brought it, and it is a light and guidance for the people, but you changed it and made it into scrolls and sheets so that you could carry out what you intended of revealing and concealing. The reading with ta' accords with His saying "you were taught." As for those who say that if the deniers are the Arabs or the disbelievers of Quraysh, the address cannot be directed to them, but rather it would be an interruption of the Children of Israel, saying in the midst of the question and the answer: "You, O Children of Israel, make it into scrolls," such a thing is unlikely, because it disrupts the composition and structure of the verse, making the speech first an address to the disbelievers and then an address to the Jews. It has been answered that since all of them shared in denying the prophethood of the Messenger, part of the speech was an address to the Arabs and part an address to the Children of Israel. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with the ya' in the third person in all three verbs.

﴿And you were taught what you did not know, neither you nor your fathers﴾. Its apparent meaning is that it is an address to the Children of Israel, intended as a favour upon them and upon their fathers, that they came to know of God's religion and His guidance what they had not known, because their fathers had also known and some of them had known. This does not apply to the fathers of the Arabs. Alternatively, it is intended as a reproach against them, because they did not benefit from it due to their aversion and misguidance. It was said: the address is to the Arabs, reported by Mujahid. God mentioned His favour upon them, i.e., you were taught, O company of Arabs, guidance, monotheism and direction to the truth that you did not know, ﴿neither you nor your fathers﴾. It was said: the address is to those Jews who believed. It was said: to those among Quraysh who believed. The explanation of ﴿what you did not know﴾ is derived according to the addressees: the Torah, or the religion of Islam and its laws, or both, or the Qur'an. Al-Zamakhshari said: the address is to the Jews, i.e., you were taught through the tongue of Muhammad (ﷺ) what was revealed to him, what you did not know, although you are the bearers of the Torah, and your ancient fathers, who were more knowledgeable than you, did not know that this Qur'an recounts to the Children of Israel most of what they differ about. It was said: the address is to those among Quraysh who believed, ﴿that you may warn a people whose fathers were not warned﴾ [Ya Sin: 6]. End of quotation.

﴿Say, "God."﴾ He commanded him to hasten to the answer, i.e., say: God sent it down. For they cannot deny you, because the Book described with light and guidance that has been brought by one supported with miracles, its evidence has reached such clarity that it is necessary to acknowledge that its sender is God, whether or not the opponent admits it. A parallel is His saying: ﴿Say, "What thing is greatest in testimony?" Say, "God"﴾ [al-An'am: 19]. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it may be that the meaning is: if they are ignorant, or perplexed, or ask and the like, then say "God." End of quotation. This assumption is not needed, because the speech is self-sufficient without it.

﴿Then leave them in their plunging, playing﴾. That is, in their falsehood in which they plunge. It is said of one who is engaged in an activity that brings him no benefit: "You are only playing." "Playing" (yal'abūna) is an accusative of circumstance from the object of "leave them" or from the pronoun of "their plunging." "In their plunging" is connected to "leave them," or to "playing," or is an accusative of circumstance from "playing." The apparent meaning of the command is conciliation (muwādaʿa), so it would be abrogated (naskh) by the verses of fighting. If it is taken as a threat or a warning free of conciliation, then there is no abrogation.

﴿And this is a blessed Book which We have sent down﴾ [p. 179] That is: this Qur'an. When He mentioned and established that those who deny that God sent down anything upon a human being are denying, and argued against them with what they cannot deny, He informed that this Book sent down upon the Messenger is blessed, abundant in benefit and usefulness. Since the denial fell upon the sending down, as they said "God has not sent down," and it was said: "Who sent down the Book?", the mention of its description with sending down was more emphatic than the description of it as blessed. Also, whatever God sends down is necessarily blessed, so the description of it as blessed becomes like an emphatic attribute, since what precedes it includes it. As for His saying: ﴿And this is a blessed reminder which We have sent down﴾ [al-Anbiya': 50], it did not occur in a context of denying that God sends down anything; rather it came after His saying: ﴿And We gave Musa and Harun the criterion and a light and a reminder for the righteous﴾ [al-Anbiya': 48]. He mentioned that what He gave to the Messenger is a blessed reminder. Since the sending down is renewed, He expressed the description with a verb, and since the description of it with blessing is a permanent attribute that does not depart, He expressed it with the noun that indicates permanence.

﴿Confirming what was before it﴾. That is, of the Books of God that were sent down. It was said: the Torah. It was said: the Resurrection. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is not correct, because the Qur'an is before the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around it.﴾ The Mother of Cities is Makkah. It was so called because it is the source of the religion, because the earth was spread out (*dahw*) from it, because it is the center of the earth, and because it is the qiblah, the place of the Hajj, and the site of the first House set up for people. The meaning is: that you may warn the people of the Mother of Cities and those around it, and they are all the rest of the inhabitants of the earth. This is what Ibn ʿAbbas said. It was also said that it refers to the Arabs. A group of Jews used this verse, ﴿the Mother of Cities and those around it﴾, to argue that he was a messenger only to the Arabs. They said: "those around it" are the surrounding towns, which is the Arabian Peninsula. It is answered that "those around it" is general and covers the whole earth. Even if we assume it is specific, mentioning the Arabian Peninsula would be evidence for the exclusion of the ruling from everything else only through *mafhūm* (implicit meaning), which is weak. The omission of *ahl* (people) is because the meaning indicates it, since buildings cannot be warned, as in His saying: ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], since the town cannot be asked. The word *man* (those) was not omitted so that *ḥawlahā* (around it) could be conjoined to *Umma al-Qurā* (the Mother of Cities). Although in terms of meaning it would be valid, *ḥawl* is an adverb (*ẓarf*, adverb of place) that does not vary in its usage. So if it were conjoined to *Umm al-Qurā*, it would have to be an object (*mafʿūl bihi*) because it is conjoined to the object, and that is not permissible, because using it as an object means departing from its adverbial function, and that is not allowed for it, since, as we have said, the Arabs did not use it except in its necessary adverbial function, not varied with anything else. Abu Bakr read *li-yundhira* (that it may warn), meaning: the Qur'an with its admonitions and commands. The majority read *wa-litundhira* (and that you may warn) addressed to the Messenger, and the meaning is: and that you may warn with what We have sent down. So the *lām* is connected to a deleted word that comes later, indicated by what precedes it. Al-Zamakhsharī said: *wa-litundhira* is conjoined to what is indicated by the description of the Book, as if it were said: We sent it down for blessings, and confirming what came before it of the Books, and for warning.

﴿Those who believe in the Hereafter believe in it.﴾ It is apparent that the pronoun in *bihi* (in it) refers to the Book, meaning: those who affirm that there will be a gathering, a resurrection and a recompense for them, believe in this Book because of what it contains of promise and threat, glad tidings and warning. For there is no book among the divine Books and no law among the laws that contains what is in this Book, nor what is in this law concerning the Day of Resurrection and the raising of the dead. The meaning is: they believe in it with the faith supported by sound proof. Otherwise, the People of the Book believe in the resurrection but do not believe in the Qur'an. He mentioned only belief in the resurrection, which is one of the six pillars, which are: the necessarily existent being, the angels, the books, the messengers, the Last Day, and divine decree, because belief in it entails belief in the rest. It also serves to inform the disbelieving Arabs and others who do not believe in the resurrection that whoever believes in the resurrection believes in this Book. The root of religion is fear of the consequence, so whoever opposes it, fear does not cease to be with him until he believes. It was also said that the pronoun refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿And they are over their prayer they guard.﴾ He singled out the prayer because it is the pillar of religion, and whoever guards it is guarding its counterparts. The meaning of guarding is persevering in performing it at its times in the best manner in which it is performed. Prayer is the most noble of the acts of worship after faith in Allah, and for this reason the name of faith was not applied to any act of worship except it. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And Allah would not let your faith go to waste﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], meaning: your prayer. Disbelief was not applied to any sin except the abandonment of it. It was narrated: "Whoever abandons the prayer deliberately has disbelieved." The majority read *ʿalā ṣalātihim* (over their prayer) in the singular, and what is meant by it is the genus. Khalaf narrated from Yahya from Abu Bakr: *ṣalawātihim* (their prayers) in the plural. Abu ʿAlī al-Ḥasan ibn Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm al-Baghdādī mentioned this in his book *al-Rawḍa* (The Garden), which he composed, and he said: he was alone in this among all people.

﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah, or says: "It has been revealed to me," when nothing has been revealed to him, or who says: "I will send down the like of what Allah has sent down."﴾ Al-Zahrāwī and al-Mahdawī mentioned that the verse was revealed concerning al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith. It was said: and concerning those who mocked along with him, because he opposed the Qur'an with his saying: "By those who sow seed, sowing; by those who bake bread, baking; by those who cook, cooking; by those who grind, grinding; by those who morsel, morseling," and other such nonsense. Qatāda and others said: what is meant by it is Musaylima al-Ḥanafī and al-Aswad al-ʿAnsī, and they mentioned the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) vision of the two bracelets. Al-Zamakhsharī said: it is Musaylima al-Ḥanafī, or the liar of Ṣanʿā', al-Aswad al-ʿAnsī. Al-Suddī said: "What is meant by it is ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿd ibn Abī Sarḥ al-ʿĀmirī, the foster brother of ʿUthmān. He was writing the verse ﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾ before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and when he dictated to him ﴿Then We produced it as another creation﴾ [al-Muʾminūn: 14], he marvelled at the detail of the creation of man, and said: ﴿So blessed be Allah, the best of creators﴾. The Messenger said: 'Write it, for thus it was revealed.' ʿAbd Allāh imagined [that it was his own speech], apostatized, and fled to Makkah, and said: 'I will send down the like of what Allah has sent down.'" Ikrimah said: its first part was about Musaylima, and its last part about Ibn Abī Sarḥ. It was narrated from him that when he was dictated ﴿All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 148], he would write: "All-Knowing, All-Wise," and when he was dictated "All-Knowing, All-Wise," he would write: "All-Forgiving, All-Merciful." Shurahbīl ibn Saʿd said: it was revealed concerning Ibn Abī Sarḥ, and whoever says: "I will send down the like of what Allah has sent down" apostatizes. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered Makkah in the year of the Conquest, and ʿUthmān hid him until the people of Makkah were reassured. Then he brought him to the Messenger, and he asked the Messenger for his protection, and the Messenger granted him security. End of quotation. ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān appointed him in his days, and the cities were opened at his hands. He conquered Ifriqiya in the year thirty-one, and raided the Asāwid of the land of Nubia, and he was the one who made the truce with them that remains to this day. He raided the Ṣawārī of the land of the Romans. His Islam had become good, and nothing objectionable appeared from him. He was one of the noble, wise and generous men of Quraysh and the knight of the Banū ʿĀmir ibn Lu'ayy. He stayed in ʿAsqalān, it was said, or al-Ramla, fleeing from the strife when ʿUthmān was killed, and he died there in the year thirty-six, it was said, or thirty-seven. He supplicated his Lord and said: "O Allah, make the last of my deeds the dawn prayer." He died at the end of the dawn, and he had already given the salām to his right, and was about to give the salām to his left, and that was before the people gathered around Muʿāwiya.

When He mentioned the Qur'an, and that it is a blessed Book sent down from Him, He followed it with a threat against the one who claims prophethood and messengership by way of fabrication. The discussion of *wa-man aẓlamu* (and who is more unjust) has already occurred. They interpreted it as an interrogative whose meaning is negation, that is: no one is more unjust. He began first with the general, which is inventing a lie against Allah, and this is more general than whether that invention is by claiming a revelation or otherwise. Then secondly with the specific, which is an invention attributed to a revelation from Allah, the Exalted.

﴿or says: "It has been revealed to me," when nothing has been revealed to him﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*jumla ḥāliyya*), or it means: not one to whom anything has been revealed. For whoever says "It has been revealed to me" while it has been revealed to him is truthful. Then secondly he mentioned something more specific than what precedes it, because revelation may be by the sending down of a Qur'an and by other than that. The story of Ibn Abī Sarḥ is his claim that he would send down a Qur'an like what Allah has sent down. His saying ﴿the like of what Allah has sent down﴾ is not his belief that Allah had sent down something; rather the meaning is: ﴿the like of what Allah has sent down﴾ according to your claim. The repetition of *man* (whoever) indicates that its referent is different from the referent of the earlier *man*. So the one who said "I will send down" is other than the one who invented or said "it has been revealed," even though what precedes him applies to him in the manner of the general applying to the specific. His saying "I will send down" is a false promise, and calling it sending down is a metaphor; the meaning is: I will arrange speech that resembles what you claimed Allah had sent down. Abū Ḥaywa read *mā nazzala* with the intensive form. And although the cause of the revelation of this verse was particular persons, it encompasses everyone who claims a claim like theirs, such as Ṭulayḥa al-Asadī, al-Mukhtār ibn Abī ʿUbayd al-Thaqafī, Sajāḥ, and others. Many learned men have claimed prophethood. Among those whom we have known in our own time was Ibrāhīm al-Ghāzāzī the poor, who claimed that in the city of Mālaqa, and the Sultan Abū ʿAbd Allāh Muḥammad ibn Yūsuf ibn Naṣr al-Khazrajī, king of al-Andalus, killed him at Gharnāṭa and crucified him. And Barqashāṭ ibn Qasīm al-Nīlī the poet claimed prophethood in the city of al-Nīl in the land of Iraq, and he had a Qur'an that he composed. He was not killed, because he was mocked and considered weak in his mind.

﴿And if you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death﴾. *Al-ẓālimūn* (the wrongdoers) is general, and it includes the Jews, the false prophets and others. It was also said that the *alif-lām* is for prior reference, meaning: from among the Jews and those who claimed prophethood, and they are the ones previously mentioned.

﴿while the angels extend their hands﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās said: with beating, meaning: the angels of seizing the soul strike their faces and their backs at its seizing. Al-Farrāʾ also said this. The meaning is not merely the extending of the hand, since believers and disbelievers share that. This is the beginning of the punishment and its signs. Ibn ʿAbbās also said: on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Ḥasan and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: with punishment. Al-Ḥasan also said: this occurs in the Fire.

﴿"Bring forth your souls."﴾ Al-Zamakhsharī said: they extend their hands to them, saying: "Hand over your spirits, bring them out to us from your bodies." This is an expression of harshness in the drive and intense insistence on taking out the soul without respite or delay, and that they treat them like a creditor who extends his hand to one who owes him a debt, presses him in demanding it, does not grant him time, and says to him: "Give me what you owe me now, or I will remain here until I pull it from your friends." Whoever says that the extending of hands is in the Fire, the meaning is: bring yourselves out from these calamities and trials and free yourselves, if what you claimed were true in the world. In this there is rebuke and reproach for their past evil deeds. It was also said: it is a command in the manner of humiliation and terrifying, and that they are like one who has been charged with taking his own soul.

﴿Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation﴾. *Al-hūn* means *al-hawān* (humiliation). ʿAbd Allāh and ʿIkrima read *ʿadhāba l-hawān* with an *alif* and an open *hāʾ*. As for *al-yawm* (today): whoever says that this is in the world, it is an expression for the time of death, and the punishment is what they were punished with from the severity of the extraction, or the extended lengthy period in which they are afflicted with punishment in the barzakh. Whoever says that this is in the Resurrection, it is an expression for the Day of Resurrection or for the time of their address in the Fire. The punishment is attributed to humiliation because it is established in it, since the chastising may be in the manner of reproof and discipline, and there is no humiliation in it, and it may be in the manner of humiliation.

﴿for what you used to say about Allah other than the truth﴾. Saying about Allah other than the truth includes every kind of disbelief, and whoever was previously mentioned among those who invent lies against Allah enters into it with a stronger entry.

﴿And you used to be arrogant towards His signs﴾, meaning: arrogant regarding belief in His signs. The answer to *law* (if) is deleted, its estimate being: you would have seen a great matter and you would have seen a marvel. Its deletion is more eloquent than its mention. *Tarā* (you see) is in the sense of *ra'ayta* (you saw), because it governs the past adverb *idh* (when). *Al-malāʾika bāsiṭū* (the angels extending) is a circumstantial clause, and *akhrijū* (bring forth) is an object governed by a deleted circumstantial word, meaning: saying "bring forth." And *mā* in *bi-mā* is a verbal-noun particle (*maṣdariyya*).

And ﴿You have come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾. ʿIkrima said: al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith said: "Al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā will intercede for me," so it was revealed.

When He said ﴿Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation﴾, He made them acknowledge that they would come on the Day of Resurrection alone, with no helper for them, needing Him, after they had been masters of servants and intercessors in the world. It appears that this speech is from the address of the angels appointed to punish them. It was also said: it is Allah's speech to them. This is based on the premise that Allah, the Exalted, speaks to the disbelievers, and it is evident from His saying ﴿Surely We will question those to whom messengers were sent﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 6], and from His saying ﴿We will surely question them all﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 92].

And you have come to Us [as] you were created the first time, alone (*furada*), as We created you at first. Others say that this is a past tense that is still in its literal sense, reported (*mahkiy*), so that they are told this while standing before God for recompense and reckoning. Ibn Abbas said: "*furada*" means being without family, wealth and children. Al-Hasan said: each one alone, without helpers or intercessors. Muqatil said: nothing of the world that you used to boast of is with you. Al-Zajjaj said: each one is singular, apart from his partner and intercessor. Ibn Kaysan said: "*furada*" means apart from the one worshipped. It was also said: We have brought you without any helper or supporter. These statements are close in meaning. When they were in the world they strove to obtain status, wealth and intercessors, and in the Hereafter they come isolated from everything they had acquired in the world.

It is read as *furada* (without tanwin, not declined), and Isa ibn Umar and Abu Haywa read *furadan* with tanwin. Abu Amr and Nafi, in a report transmitted from other than them, read *fardaa* like *sakraa*, as in the verse ﴿And you see people as drunken﴾ [22:2], and it is feminine in accordance with the meaning of a group. The *kaf* in *kama* (as) is in the accusative position. It was said that it is a substitute (*badal*) for *furada*. It was also said that it is an adjective (*na't*) of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning "coming," ﴿as We created you﴾, meaning like your coming on the day We created you. This resembles the first isolation at the time of creation, so it restricts the state of isolation by comparing it to the state of creation, because a person is created bare, without wealth, child or retinue. It was also said: naked and uncircumcised. Whoever said "in the condition in which you were born, in isolation" includes both of these statements. *Awwala marra* ("the first time") is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*zarf*), meaning the first time. It is not to be understood as "the first of God's creation," because "first creation" would require a second creation, and a second creation does not occur; that is rather a restoration (*i'adah*), not a creation.

﴿And you left behind what We had bestowed upon you, behind your backs﴾. That is, what We had favoured you with in the world did not benefit you, and you did not carry any of it, not even a speck, nor did you send it ahead for yourselves. By His words ﴿behind your backs﴾ He indicated the world, because they leave behind what they were given while it still exists.

﴿And We do not see with you your intercessors whom you claimed to be partners among you﴾. He made them acknowledge their error in worshipping the idols and venerating them. Muqatil said: they believed in the intercession of the angels and said: ﴿We only worship them so that they bring us near to God in closeness﴾ [39:3]. "*Fikum*" (among you) is connected to "*shurakaa*" (partners). The meaning is: in your subjugation (*isti'bad*), because when they called them gods and worshipped them, they made them partners of God in themselves and in their subjugation. It was also said: they made them partners of God in the sense that they intercede for them with Him, so they are partners in this sense. It is possible that the meaning is: partners of God in delivering you from punishment, and that their worship benefits you as His worship benefits you. It was also said: "*fikum*" means "with you." Ibn Qutaybah said: they are partners with me in your creation. It was also said: they bear for you a share of the punishment.

﴿Indeed, your connection has been cut off, and what you used to claim has gone astray from you﴾. The majority of the Seven Readers (*jumhur al-sab'a*, the seven canonical reciters) read *baynukum* with a *damma*, on the basis that the word *bayn* was used as a noun by extension of its use as an adverb (*zarf*), and the verb was ascribed to it so that it became a noun, just as they used it as a noun in the verse ﴿And between us and you there is a barrier﴾ [41:5], and as Sibawayh reported: "He is red between the two eyes." Al-Farisi preferred this reading. Or it means that *al-bayn* refers to connection, i.e. your connection has been cut off. Abu al-Fath, al-Zahrawi and al-Mahdawi said this. Ibn Atiyyah rejected this and claimed that *al-bayn* in the sense of connection was not heard from the Arabs, and that it was derived only from this verse. Or it means that *al-bayn* refers to separation, and this is a metaphor for a distant matter; the meaning is: the distance between you has been cut off because of its length, so this is expressed by *al-bayn*. Nafi, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read *baynakum* with a *fatha* on the *nun*. Al-Akhfash interpreted it as the subject, but it is built on the *fatha* in view of the most common uses of this adverb. It is also said that it is because it is attached to an indeclinable word, as in the verse ﴿and among us are some other than that﴾ [72:11]. Others interpreted it as accusative in the sense of an adverb. The subject of *taqatta'a* (was cut off) is the cutting-off (*taqatta'*). Al-Zamakhshari said: the cutting-off happened between you, as you say: "He joined between the two things," meaning: he caused the joining between them, the verb being ascribed to its verbal noun by this interpretation. End of quote. Its apparent sense is not good. Its precise analysis is that he attributed the verb to a pronoun referring to its verbal noun and omitted it within it, because if he attributed it to the explicit verbal noun, it would be omitted, and the omission of the subject is not permitted. Even with this assumption it is not correct, because the condition of attribution is absent in it, namely the difference between the predicate and the thing predicated of. For this reason one cannot say "stood" or "sat" while meaning "he stood, that is, the standing." It was also said that the subject is a hidden pronoun referring to the connection indicated by the word "*shurakaa'*" (partners). The subject is not to be taken as the explicit verbal noun, as Ibn Atiyyah said. He said: the verb is attributed to something omitted, its estimate being: "the connection and the bond among you has been cut off," or something like this. This is a clear view, and on this basis the people interpreted it, Mujahid, al-Suddi and others. End of quote. His statement "to something omitted" is not correct, because the subject is not omitted. Abu al-Baqa permitted that *baynakum* be an adjective of an omitted subject, meaning: "something between you was cut off, or a connection." This is also not correct, because the subject is not omitted. What appears to me is that the matter falls under the principle of *i'mal* (operating two verbs on one noun): the cutting-off (*taqatta'*) and the going-astray (*dalla*) both govern "*ma kuntum taz'umun*" (what you used to claim). The second verb, *dalla*, is made to operate, and in *taqatta'* a pronoun referring to *ma* (what) is understood, which is the idols. The meaning is: what you used to claim was cut off between you, and they went astray from you, as He said: ﴿and the means were cut off from them﴾ [2:166], meaning: no connection remained between you and "*ma kuntum taz'umun*" (what you used to claim), that they were partners, so you worshipped them. This is an easy analysis that no one has noticed. Abd Allah, Mujahid and al-A'mash read *ma baynakum* (what was between you), and the meaning is: what was between you and what you used to claim perished and vanished. The two objects of *taz'umun* are omitted, the estimate being: "you claimed them to be intercessors," omitted because of the indication of them, as the poet said:

*You see their love as a shame upon me, and you reckon it*

meaning: and you reckon it a shame. Abu Abd Allah al-Razi has a discussion on this verse that resembles the opinions of the philosophers. At its end he said: and it is to this that His words refer: "Indeed, your connection has been cut off," and the meaning is that the connection between the soul and the body has been severed, and there is no way to restore it a second time. End of quote. This is not understood from the verse.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 91–94 (part 1 of 3):

﴿They did not measure God with His true measure when they said, "God has not sent down anything upon any human being."﴾ It was revealed concerning the Jews. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Muhammad ibn Ka'b. Another view is that it was revealed concerning Malik ibn al-Sayf, the Jewish scholar, when the Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: "I adjure you by God, who sent down the Torah to Musa, do you find in it that God hates the fat rabbi?" He said: "Yes." He said: "You are the fat rabbi." He became angry and then said: "God has not sent down anything upon any human being." This is reported by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Ikrimah. Another view is that it was revealed concerning Finhas ibn 'Azura among them; this is reported by al-Suddi. Another view is that it was revealed concerning the Jews and Christians; this is reported by Qatadah. Another view is that it was revealed concerning the polytheist Arabs; this is reported by Mujahid and others. Some scholars restricted it, from this view, to the polytheists of Quraysh; this is the narration of Ibn Abi Najih from him. In the narration of Ibn Kathir from Mujahid, from its beginning up to "upon any human being," it refers to the polytheists of Quraysh, and His saying "Who sent down the Book" refers to the Jews.

When God mentioned concerning Ibrahim the proof of monotheism and the foolishness of the opinion of the people of polytheism, and mentioned the favour God bestowed upon Ibrahim by placing prophethood among his descendants, and that Nuh (peace be upon him) was his forefather, whom God had guided and who had been sent to his people, and when He commanded the Messenger to follow the guidance of the prophets, [p. 177] He began to establish prophethood and to refute those who deny revelation. He said: ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure.﴾ The root meaning of qadr is knowing the quantity. It is said: "He measured (qadara) the thing" when he estimated it, tested it, and wished to know its measure. It is conjugated as yaqduruhu, with a dammah, qadran and qadaran. From this is His saying: ﴿If it is obscured for you, then estimate for it﴾, meaning: seek to know it. Then the word was extended, until it was said of everyone who knows something that he "measures its measure," and of one who does not know it through its attributes that he "does not measure its measure." Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said, and al-Farra', Tha'lab and al-Zajjaj preferred, that its meaning is: they did not magnify God with His true magnification. Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash said: they did not know Him with His true knowledge. Al-Maturidi said: "Who magnifies God with His true greatness, or knows Him with His true knowledge? The angels said: 'We did not worship You with Your true worship,' and the Messenger (ﷺ) said: 'I cannot count praise upon You.'" This is resolved by saying that the meaning is: they did not magnify Him with the magnification within their capacity and within what is in their power, and they did not know Him in that way. Abu al-'Aliyah said, and al-Khalil ibn Ahmad preferred: its meaning is: they did not describe Him with His true description regarding what is obligatory for Him, what is impossible for Him, and what is permissible for Him. Ibn 'Abbas also said: they did not believe in God with His true belief, and they did not know that God is powerful over all things. Abu 'Ubaydah also said: they did not worship Him with His true worship. It was also said: they did not honour Him with His true honour; this is related by Ibn Abi al-Fadl in Ri alzam'an, and it has the same meaning as magnification. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is from fulfilling the measure, so it is general, and it includes whoever does not know Him, whoever does not magnify Him, and other things. However, his explanation with their saying "God has not sent down anything" requires that they were ignorant and did not know God with His true knowledge, since they denied that God sends messengers. Al-Zamakhshari said: they did not know God with His true knowledge in respect of His mercy upon His servants and His kindness to them, when they denied the sending of messengers and the revelation to them, and that is among the greatest of His mercy and the most glorious of His blessings. ﴿We did not send you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 107]. Or: they did not know Him with His true knowledge in respect of His wrath upon the disbelievers and the severity of His seizing them, and they did not fear Him when they dared to utter that monstrous statement denying prophethood. The speakers were the Jews, as evidenced by the reading of the one who read "you make it" with the letter ta', and likewise "you show them" and "you conceal." They said that only to exaggerate in denying the sending down of the Qur'an upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ), so they were compelled to admit what they could not avoid admitting: the sending down of the Torah to Musa. End of quotation. The pronoun in ﴿They did not measure﴾ refers to those concerning whom the verse was revealed, according to the earlier disagreement. Whoever says it is about the Children of Israel must hold that it is Medinan, and for this reason al-Naqqash reported that it is Medinan. Al-Hasan and 'Isa al-Thaqafi read "wa ma qaddaru" with the shaddah, and "haqqa qadarihi" with a fatha on the dal. ﴿haqqa qadrihi﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar); originally it is an attribute, meaning: they estimated Him with the truth. When the attribute of the verbal noun is annexed to it, it takes the accusative of the verbal noun. The governing element of "idh" is "qadaru." In Ibn 'Atiyyah's statement there is an indication that "idh" is causal.

﴿Say, "Who sent down the Book which Musa brought, a light and guidance for the people?"﴾ If the deniers are the Children of Israel, the argument against them is clear, because they uphold the sending down of the Book upon Musa. If they are the Arabs, the basis of the argument against them is that the sending down of the Book upon Musa is a well-known matter, transmitted by a people whom the Arabs did not dispute. They used to say: "If the Book had been sent down to us, we would have been better guided than them." Abu Hamid al-Ghazali said: this verse is built upon the second figure of the logical syllogisms, because its outcome returns to the point that Musa, upon whom something was sent down from God, is a human being, and that whom God sent nothing is not a human being. This yields by the second figure that Musa was not a human being, and this is an impossible absurdity. This impossibility is not due to the form of the syllogism, nor to the soundness of the premise. Nothing remains except that assuming the soundness of the premise, which is their saying "God has not sent down anything upon any human being," necessarily leads to it being false. So the evidence of this verse for the intended conclusion is valid only upon acknowledging the soundness of the second figure of the logical syllogisms and upon acknowledging the soundness of reductio ad absurdum (qiyas al-khulf). End of his statement. In the verse there is evidence that contradiction undermines the soundness of speech, because He contradicted their saying "God has not sent down anything" with His saying "Who sent down the Book?" If contradiction were not a proof of the invalidity of a statement, this argument would not be effective for this purpose. The Book here is the Torah. "Light and guidance" is in the accusative of circumstance (ḥāl), and the governing element is either "anzala" or "jā'a."

﴿You make it into scrolls, showing some and concealing much﴾. The ta' is the reading of the majority in all three verbs. Its apparent meaning is that it addresses the Children of Israel. The meaning is: you make it into scrolls, i.e. pages and sheets, and you conceal much, like their concealing of the signs that indicate the sending of the Messenger and other signs that they concealed. God included in the obligation their reproach, even though He condemned them for their bad handling of their Book, their distortion of it, and their revealing of some parts while concealing others. It was said: Musa brought it, and it is a light and guidance for the people, but you changed it and made it into scrolls and sheets so that you could carry out what you intended of revealing and concealing. The reading with ta' accords with His saying "you were taught." As for those who say that if the deniers are the Arabs or the disbelievers of Quraysh, the address cannot be directed to them, but rather it would be an interruption of the Children of Israel, saying in the midst of the question and the answer: "You, O Children of Israel, make it into scrolls," such a thing is unlikely, because it disrupts the composition and structure of the verse, making the speech first an address to the disbelievers and then an address to the Jews. It has been answered that since all of them shared in denying the prophethood of the Messenger, part of the speech was an address to the Arabs and part an address to the Children of Israel. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with the ya' in the third person in all three verbs.

﴿And you were taught what you did not know, neither you nor your fathers﴾. Its apparent meaning is that it is an address to the Children of Israel, intended as a favour upon them and upon their fathers, that they came to know of God's religion and His guidance what they had not known, because their fathers had also known and some of them had known. This does not apply to the fathers of the Arabs. Alternatively, it is intended as a reproach against them, because they did not benefit from it due to their aversion and misguidance. It was said: the address is to the Arabs, reported by Mujahid. God mentioned His favour upon them, i.e., you were taught, O company of Arabs, guidance, monotheism and direction to the truth that you did not know, ﴿neither you nor your fathers﴾. It was said: the address is to those Jews who believed. It was said: to those among Quraysh who believed. The explanation of ﴿what you did not know﴾ is derived according to the addressees: the Torah, or the religion of Islam and its laws, or both, or the Qur'an. Al-Zamakhshari said: the address is to the Jews, i.e., you were taught through the tongue of Muhammad (ﷺ) what was revealed to him, what you did not know, although you are the bearers of the Torah, and your ancient fathers, who were more knowledgeable than you, did not know that this Qur'an recounts to the Children of Israel most of what they differ about. It was said: the address is to those among Quraysh who believed, ﴿that you may warn a people whose fathers were not warned﴾ [Ya Sin: 6]. End of quotation.

﴿Say, "God."﴾ He commanded him to hasten to the answer, i.e., say: God sent it down. For they cannot deny you, because the Book described with light and guidance that has been brought by one supported with miracles, its evidence has reached such clarity that it is necessary to acknowledge that its sender is God, whether or not the opponent admits it. A parallel is His saying: ﴿Say, "What thing is greatest in testimony?" Say, "God"﴾ [al-An'am: 19]. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it may be that the meaning is: if they are ignorant, or perplexed, or ask and the like, then say "God." End of quotation. This assumption is not needed, because the speech is self-sufficient without it.

﴿Then leave them in their plunging, playing﴾. That is, in their falsehood in which they plunge. It is said of one who is engaged in an activity that brings him no benefit: "You are only playing." "Playing" (yal'abūna) is an accusative of circumstance from the object of "leave them" or from the pronoun of "their plunging."
