So it is not permissible for it to govern, nor for its genitive to have a position. They have stated this and cited:

Alqaytu kāsibahum fī qaʿri muẓlimatin

Here "al-kāsib" is not restricted to a time. When it is restricted to a time, it is either past without the definite article, in which case by the Basrans it does not govern, or with the definite article, or present or future, in which case governing is permissible, and the genitive construction with it is as established and detailed in the science of grammar. Even granting that it is present, in the sense of continuity across times, and governs, it is still not permissible to conjoin to the position of its genitive; rather, if it were present or future, that would not be permissible according to the correct view, which is the position of Sibawayh. So if you say "Zayd ḍāribun ʿamran al-āna aw ghadan wa-khālidan" (Zayd is hitting ʿAmr now or tomorrow, and Khalid), it is not permissible to conjoin "wa-khālidan" to the position of "ʿamran". According to Sibawayh's position you must rather estimate: "wa-taḍribu khālidan" (and he hits Khalid), because the condition for conjoining to the position is absent, namely that the position be fixed and not subject to change. This is explained in the science of grammar. It is also read irregularly (shādhdh): "wa-al-shamsu wa-al-qamaru" in the nominative, as a subject, with the predicate omitted, its estimate being "majʿūlāni ḥusbānan" (they are made a reckoning) or "maḥsūbāni ḥusbānan" (they are reckoned as a reckoning).

﴿Dhālika taqdīru al-ʿazīzi al-ʿalīm﴾ (That is the decree of the Mighty, the Knowing). That is, that making, or that splitting, or the making and the splitting. "Dhālika" is a reference to all the reports from His words ﴿the Splitter of the grain﴾ [al-An'am: 95] to the end of them: it is the decree of the Mighty, the Dominant, to whom everything in these matters is subject and under control, the Knowing, from whom nothing in these states or anything else is hidden. In making all of that by His decree is proof that He is the one who alone is the Doer, the Chooser, not that these things have it by their nature or by an inherent property.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 97–99 (part 1 of 2):

﴿It is He who made for you the stars, that you may be guided by them in the darkness of the land and the sea.﴾ He draws attention to the greatest of the benefits of their creation, which is guidance to the paths, the routes, the directions that are intended, and the qibla. For the movements of the stars at night are used as indicators for the qibla, just as the movement of the sun during the day is used as an indicator for it. The address is general to all people. ﴿That you may be guided﴾ is connected to a verb "ja'ala" (made) that is implied, since it (the phrase) is a substitute (badal) for "lakum" (for you). That is, He made that for your being guided. And "ja'ala" here may mean "khalaqa" (created), in which case it takes only one object. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is possible that it means 'sayyara' (made/rendered), and the second object is understood from ﴿that you may be guided﴾, that is: He made the stars for you as a guidance." End of quotation. This is weak, because the omission of one of the two objects of the verbs of the "zanna" class is rare. The apparent meaning is that "the darknesses" here is to be taken literally. He is more distant who said: it is possible that "the darknesses" here means the hardships in the situations in which it happens that one is guided by them. He attributed the darknesses to the land and the sea because of their association with them, or he likened the confusing paths to darknesses. God, exalted is He, mentioned the stars in His Book for adornment, for hurling at devils, and for guidance; whatever else is said about them is fabrication against God and slander.

﴿We have indeed detailed the signs for a people who know.﴾ That is, We have made clear and divided them. He singled out those who know because they are the ones who benefit from their detailing; as for others, they turn away from the signs and from reasoning by them.

﴿It is He who produced you from a single soul﴾, which is Adam, peace be upon him.

﴿So there is a place of lodging and a place of storing﴾. The majority read the qaf with a fatha, taking it as a place (noun of place), that is, a place of settling and a place of depositing, or as a verbal noun, that is, so there is settling and depositing. Musta-qarr cannot be a passive participle, because its verb is not transitive, so a passive participle cannot be formed from it. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read the qaf with a kasra as an active participle, and on this reading "mustawda'" (with fatha on the dal) is a passive participle. When He mentioned their creation, He mentioned their division into "mustaqarr and mustawda'", that is: among you is the one who settles and the one who is deposited. Harun al-A'war related from Abu 'Amr: "mustawdi'" with a kasra on the dal, an active participle. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, 'Ata', al-Nakha'i, al-Dahhak, Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: the one who settles is in the womb and the one who is deposited is in the loins. Ibn Bahr said the reverse, saying: the meaning is that He mentioned the masculine and the feminine; He expressed the male by "mustaqarr" because the drop is formed in his loins, and He expressed the female by "mustawda'" because her womb is a place of deposit for the drop. Ibn Mas'ud said: the one who settles is in the womb and the one who is deposited is in the grave. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: the one who settles is in the earth and the one who is deposited is in the loins; and from him both are in the womb; and from him the one who settles is where he dwells and the one who is deposited is where he dies; and from him the one who settles is the one who has been created and the one who is deposited is the one who has not yet been created. Mujahid said: the one who settles is in this world and the one who is deposited is with God. It was said: both are in this world. It was said: the one who settles is in Paradise and the one who is deposited is in the Fire. It was said: "mustaqarr" is in the Hereafter by his deeds, and "mustawda'" is in his origin, moving from state to state and from time to time, until the end of his term. End of quotation. What the reflection requires is that settling and depositing are two states that succeed one another upon the human being, from the loins to the womb, to this world, to the grave, to the gathering, to Paradise or to the Fire; and in each stage he attains a settling and a depositing: settling in relation to what precedes it, and depositing in relation to what follows it. The word "wadi'ah" (deposit) implies transfer.

﴿We have indeed detailed the signs for a people who understand.﴾ Since guidance by the stars is evident, He concluded it with His saying "who know" (ya'lamun), that is: whoever has even a little perception benefits by considering the stars and their benefit. And since production from a single soul, and the disposition through many states, requires thought and precision of reflection, He concluded it with His saying "who understand" (yafqahun), for "fiqh" is the employment of acuteness, precision of observation and thought. So it was fitting to end each sentence with what corresponds to what the discourse began with.

﴿It is He who sent down water from the sky, and We brought forth by it the growth of everything﴾. When He mentioned His favour in creating us, He mentioned His favour upon us by that which sustains our welfare and our interests. "The sky" here means the cloud. The apparent meaning of "the growth of everything" is what is called growth in the language, namely that which grows of grains, fruits, herbs, grasses and trees; and "everything" means of what grows. He indicated that the cause is one while the effects are many, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿watered with one water, yet We make some of them excel others in fruit﴾.

Al-Tabari said: ﴿the growth of everything﴾ is all that grows of animals, plants, minerals and other things, because all of that is nourished and grows by the descent of water from the sky. Al-Farra' said: its meaning is "the provision of everything", that is, what is suitable as nourishment for everything, so "everything" is restricted to what is nourished, and the annexation of "growth" to it is an explanatory annexation in the generality. On both of the preceding interpretations, the annexation returns in meaning to the annexation of what resembles an adjective to the qualified noun, since the meaning becomes: We brought forth by it every growing thing. In His saying "We brought forth" there is an iltifat (shift) from the third person to the first person plural of majesty.

﴿Then We brought forth from it green (foliage)﴾, that is, of the plants, tender, lush, fresh. "Fa-akhrajna" (then We brought forth) is conjoined to the preceding "fa-akhrajna". Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a substitute (badal) for the preceding "fa-akhrajna".

﴿We bring forth from it grain piled up﴾, that is, from the green (foliage) such as wheat, barley and all pulses, and from fruits such as pomegranates, pine nuts and others, whatever has its grain piled and one part rests upon another. "Nukhriju" (We bring forth) is a clause in place of a qualifier for "khadir" (green), or it may be a resumptive statement. Al-A'mash and Ibn Muhaysin read: "yakhruju minhu habbun mutarakib", taking it as nominative by "yakhruju", with "mutarakib" as an adjective in its accusative and nominative cases.

﴿And from the palm trees, from their spathe, are clusters hanging low﴾, that is, near to the one who reaches, because of their shortness and the adherence of their roots to the earth. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Bara' and al-Dahhak. al-Zamakhshari approved it, saying: easy to pick, presented to the picker like a near thing that is within reach; and because the palm, even if small, can be reached by one sitting, yet it bears fruit. al-Hasan said: some of them are near to others. It was also said: "hanging low" means inclined. It was said: the mention of "hanging low" without mention of "tall" is because the blessing in them is more manifest, or "tall" is omitted because "hanging low" indicates it, like His saying: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81], meaning and the cold. The majority read "qinwan" with a kasra on the qaf. al-A'mash and al-Khaffaf, from Abu 'Amr al-A'raj in one narration, read it with a damma; it is related from al-Sulami from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. al-A'raj in one narration and Harun from Abu 'Amr read "qanwan" with a fatha on the qaf, and Abu al-Fath explained it as a collective noun of the pattern "fa'lan", since "fa'lan" is not among the patterns of broken plurals. In Ibn 'Atiyya's book it is related from al-A'raj that the qaf is read with a damma, as the plural of "qinw" with a damma on the qaf. al-Farra' said: this is the dialect of Qays and the people of the Hijaz, and the kasra is more famous among the Arabs, and "qinw" is the singular of "qinwan". End of quotation. This differs from what we related in "al-Mufradat" that the dialect of the Hijaz is "qinwan" with a kasra on the qaf. This phrase is a subject and predicate, and "min tal'iha" (from its spathe) is a substitute for "wa-min al-nakhl" (and from the palm trees), and the construction is: "qinwan daniyah" (clusters hanging low) which come from the spathe of the palm. The mention of "qinwan" is singled out and detached from His saying "the growth of everything, from which We bring forth green", because of the great favour and blessing in detaching them, since they are among the greatest, or among the greatest, of the sustenance of the Arabs; and they are presented in the form of subject and predicate to indicate permanence and stability, and that this is a settled matter. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "wa-min al-nakhl" is to be taken as "We bring forth from the palm trees and from its spathe clusters"; "qinwan" is a subject whose predicate is preceded, and the clause is in the place of the object of "nukhriju". End of quotation. This is an error, because what is transitive to one object does not have a clause in the place of its object unless the verb is one that suspends, and the clause contains something that prevents the verb from governing any of its single words, from among the impediments explained in the science of grammar. "Nukhriju" is not one that suspends, and there is nothing in the clause that prevents the verb from governing any of its words; for if the verb were implied here, it would govern what follows it, and the construction and its implication would be: "wa-nukhriju min al-nakhl min tal'iha qinwanan daniyatan" in the accusative. al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible that the predicate be omitted, since "akhrajna" indicates it, its implication being: "and produced from the spathe of the palm are clusters". End of quotation. There is no need for this implication, since the clause is self-contained in its information without it. Abu al-Baqa' said: it is permissible that "qinwan" be a subject whose predicate is "min tal'iha", and in "min al-nakhl" there is a pronoun whose implication is "and there grows from the palm trees a thing or fruit", so "min tal'iha" is a substitute for it; and it is permissible that "qinwan" be nominative as a subject of "min tal'iha", so that in "min al-nakhl" there is a pronoun explained by "qinwan"; and if you make "qinwan" nominative by His saying "min al-nakhl", on the view of those who make the first of the two verbs operate, it is permissible, and in "min tal'iha" there would be a pronoun in the nominative. End of quotation. This is an analysis mixed with confusion that does not befit the Qur'an. As for one who reads "yakhruju minhu habbun mutarakib", it is permissible that His saying "min al-nakhl min tal'iha qinwan daniyah" be conjoined to it, as one says "yadribu fi al-dar Zayd, wa-fi al-suq 'Amr"; and it is permissible that it be a subject and predicate, which is the more apt.

﴿And gardens of grapevines﴾. The reading of the majority is with a kasra on the ta' (wa-jannatin), conjoined to "nabat" (growth), and this is the conjunction of the particular to the general for its nobility, the same as when the palm was singled out, the gardens of grapevines are singled out for the nobility of both, as He said: ﴿Would any of you like to have a garden of palms and grapevines?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 266]. Muhammad ibn Abi Layla, al-A'mash and Abu Bakr in one narration from 'Asim read "wa-jannatun" with a damma (nominative). Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim rejected this reading, to the point that Abu Hatim said: it is impossible, since gardens of grapes do not come from the palm. This reading should not be rejected, and it has a good grammatical justification: it is taken as a subject whose predicate is omitted, which al-Nahhas estimated as "for them are gardens", Ibn 'Atiyya estimated as "for you are gardens", Abu al-Baqa' estimated as "and from the vine are gardens", and it was estimated as "and from the vine" to correspond to "wa-min al-nakhl"; al-Zamakhshari estimated it as "and there are gardens" meaning "with the palm". A parallel to this is the reading of one who reads "wa-hurun 'in" [al-Waqi'ah: 22] with a damma, after His saying "They are served with a cup from a spring" [al-Saffat: 45] and so on, its estimate being: "for them are houris". Sibawayh, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' permitted the like of this, and there are many like it. The predicate was also estimated as postponed, its estimate being: "and gardens of grapevines" we brought forth, and His earlier saying "fa-akhrajna" indicates its estimate, as one says: "I honoured 'Abd Allah and his brother", the estimate being: "and his brother I honoured him", so "akramtuhu" is omitted, indicated by "akramtu" before it. al-Tabari construed it as "wa-jannatun" being conjoined to "qinwan". Ibn 'Atiyya said: "his saying is weak". Abu al-Baqa' said: it is not permissible that it be conjoined to "qinwan", because grapes do not come out of the palm. al-Zamakhshari said: it has been mentioned that in its nominative there are two possibilities, one of which is that it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, its estimate being: "and there are gardens", and this estimate was mentioned from him earlier. He said: the second is that it is conjoined to "qinwan" in the sense of: "and its produce from the palm is clusters" (and gardens of grapevines), that is, of the growth of grapevines. End of quotation. This conjunction is on the basis that the restriction "from the palm" is not taken into account in it, as if he said: "from the palm are clusters hanging low, and gardens of grapevines" are existing, just as you say: "from the Banu Tamim is a wise man, and a man from Quraysh who are departing".

**[p-191]** ﴿And the olive and the pomegranate, resembling one another and not resembling one another﴾. It is read with the accusative (*naṣb*) by consensus. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "as a coordination (*ʿaṭf*) upon (*ḥabban*)." It was also said: "as a coordination upon (*nabāta*)." Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It is also read *wa-jannātin* with the accusative, as a coordination upon *nabāta kulli shay'* (the plants of every thing), meaning: and We brought forth by it ﴿gardens of grapevines﴾, and likewise His saying: ﴿and the olive and the pomegranate﴾." End of quotation. The apparent meaning is that it is coordinated upon *nabāta*, just as *wa-jannātin* is coordinated upon it. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "The best reading is that it be in the accusative of specification (*al-ikhtiṣāṣ*), as in His saying: ﴿and those who establish the prayer﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 162], due to the excellence of these two categories." End of quotation.

Qatādah said: "It resembles in its leaves and differs in its fruit. The resemblance of the leaves is in size and in the fact that it covers the whole branch." Ibn Jurayj said: "Resembling in appearance and not resembling in taste, like two pomegranates whose color is one and whose taste differs." Al-Ṭabarī said: "It is possible that it resembles in the fruit and differs in taste, and it may be that he means resemblance in taste and difference in appearance. These conditions are all found in consideration of the kinds of fruits." Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Some of it resembles and some of it does not resemble in quantity, color and taste, and that is evidence that the intent is deliberate and not neglect." End of quotation.

The majority (*al-Jumhūr*) read *mushtabihan*. It was read anomalously (*shādhdhan*) as *mutashābihan*. Both have the same meaning, like *ikhtaṣama* and *takhāṣama*, *ishtaraka* and *istawā* and *tasāwā*, and similar forms in which the *ifti‘āl* (a verbal pattern of the form *if‘āl*) and *tafāʿul* patterns share meaning. *Mushtabihan* is in the accusative as a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative, describing the state of the noun) of *al-rummān* because it is nearer, and the *ḥāl* of the first noun is omitted; or it is a *ḥāl* of the first noun because it precedes. The estimate is: "and the olive (being) resembling and not resembling, and the pomegranate likewise." Al-Zamakhsharī estimated it this way, and said: "Like his saying: *kuntu minhu wa-wālidī barīʾan* (I was free of him and my father likewise, free)." End of quotation. According to his estimate, the meaning of the verse of poetry is: "I was free of him, and my father likewise, that is, free." The verse does not necessarily have what he mentioned, because *barīʾan* is on the pattern *faʿīl*, like *ṣadīq* and *rafīq*, so it may be used of the singular, the dual and the plural. It is possible that *barīʾan* is the predicate of *kāna* with the pronoun shared, and the apparent coordinated noun is in it, since it may be a predicate about both of them. It is not permissible for it to be a *ḥāl* of both, although some have permitted it, for if it were a *ḥāl* of both the construction would be *mutashābihīna wa-ghayru mutashābihīn*.

Al-Zajjāj said: "He joined the olive with the pomegranate because they are two trees whose leaves, the Arabs know, cover the branch from its beginning to its end." The poet said:

*Blessed is the stranger who died, as the ripening of the pomegranate and the olive was blessed.*

﴿Look at its fruit when it bears fruit, and at its ripening﴾. The "looking" (*al-naẓar*) is the looking of the eye's seeing, and for that reason he transitive it with *ilā* (to). But there follows from it reflection (*al-fikr*), consideration (*al-iʿtibār*), insight (*al-istibṣār*) and inference (*al-istidlāl*) upon a dazzling power that transfers it from one state to another. He drew attention to two states: the beginning, which is the time of the beginning of bearing fruit, and the end, which is the time of its ripening. That is: how does He bring it forth small and weak, from which hardly any benefit is gained, and how does it return ripe, containing benefits? He drew attention to these two states, though between them there are states through which consideration and insight occur, because these two are more remarkable in occurrence and more evident for inference.

Ibn Thawwāb, Mujāhid and Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read ﴿ thumurihi ﴾ with a *ḍamma* on the *thāʾ* and the *mīm*. Ibn Thawwāb and Mujāhid said: "They are the kinds of wealth, meaning the wealth that is obtained from it." Abū ʿAlī said: "The better view is that it is the plural of *thamara* (a fruit), like *khashaba* and *khushub*, *ukama* and *ukum*; and its parallel among the weak-lettered roots is *lābah* and *lūb*, *nāqah* and *nūq*, *sāḥah* and *sūḥ*." A group read with a *ḍamma* on the *thāʾ* and a sukūn on the *mīm*, seeking lightness, as you say *kutub* for *kutub* (books), i.e. *kutb*. The rest of the seven read *thamarihi* with a *fatḥa* on the *thāʾ* and the *mīm*, and it is a noun of genus (*ism al-jins*), like *shajarah* and *shajar*. *Al-thamar* is the harvest of the tree and what appears on it; if the tree is called *thamar*, it is a metaphor (*majāz*). The governing element of *idhā* (when) is *unẓurū* (look).

The majority read *wa-yanʿihi* with a *fatḥa* on the *yāʾ* and a sukūn on the *nūn*. Qatādah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Muḥayṣin read it with a *ḍamma* on the *yāʾ* and a sukūn on the *nūn*. Ibn Abī ʿAblah and al-Yamānī read *wa-yāniʿihi*, the active participle of *yanaʿa* (to ripen). Al-Zamakhsharī attributed this to Ibn Muḥayṣin.

Al-Marwazī said: "﴿When it bears fruit﴾ [happens] where there is no constant shade, so it does not ripen, nor constant sun, so it does not burn. He sent upon every fruit two different winds: a wind that moves the leaves so the fruit appears and the sun strikes it, and another wind that moves the leaves and shades the fruit so that it does not burn." End of quotation.

﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe﴾. The demonstrative *dhālikum* refers to everything previously mentioned, from the splitting of the grain and the date-stone to the end of what God created and of what He bestowed as a favour. The "signs" (*al-āyāt*) are the indications that point to the perfection of His power, the precision of His craftsmanship, and His singularity in creating, to the exclusion of others. The manifestation of signs benefits only those for whom God has decreed faith. As for those whom God's decree has preceded with disbelief, they do not benefit from these signs. So by specifying *belief* He drew attention to this meaning. Consider the excellence of the sequence of this arrangement with respect to what came before: ﴿Indeed God is the splitter of the grain and the date-stone﴾ [al-Anʿām: 95]. The arrangement that followed is consistent with this arrangement. When He mentioned that He brought forth the vegetation of everything, He mentioned sown crops, which is what is meant by His saying ﴿green, from which We bring forth clustered grain﴾, and He began with it as He began with it in His saying ﴿splitter of the grain﴾ [al-Anʿām: 95]. Then He followed with what has a stone, so He said ﴿from the palm-trees, from its spathe, clusters hanging low﴾ to the end, as He followed with it in His saying *wa-l-nawā* (and the date-stone). He placed the crops before the trees because they are food, while fruit is a delicacy, and food takes precedence over fruit. He placed the palm before the rest of the fruits because it functions as food in relation to the Arabs. He placed the grape because it is the most noble of fruits, and it is beneficial in all its stages: first *ḥanūṭ* (the bud), then *ḥiṣrim* (the unripe grape), then *ʿinab* (the grape); then, if it is pressed, there comes from it vinegar and syrup (*dibs*), and if it is dried, there comes from it raisins (*zabīb*). He placed the olive because it is very beneficial for eating, and in the great-benefit oil pressed from it, for eating, for lighting lamps, and other uses. He mentioned the pomegranate because of the wonder of its condition and its strangeness, for it is composed of skin, flesh, seeds and water. The three (skin, flesh, seeds) are cold, dry, earthy, dense, astringent, and strong in these qualities; its water is the opposite: the most pleasant and most subtle of drinks, and closest to the state of moderation, and in it is a strengthening of the weak temperament: nourishment from one aspect and medicine from another. Thus He, exalted is He, gathered in it the two opposites that are contrary to each other. How dazzling is His power, and how wondrous is what He created.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 97–99 (part 1 of 2):

﴿It is He who made for you the stars, that you may be guided by them in the darkness of the land and the sea.﴾ He draws attention to the greatest of the benefits of their creation, which is guidance to the paths, the routes, the directions that are intended, and the qibla. For the movements of the stars at night are used as indicators for the qibla, just as the movement of the sun during the day is used as an indicator for it. The address is general to all people. ﴿That you may be guided﴾ is connected to a verb "ja'ala" (made) that is implied, since it (the phrase) is a substitute (badal) for "lakum" (for you). That is, He made that for your being guided. And "ja'ala" here may mean "khalaqa" (created), in which case it takes only one object. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is possible that it means 'sayyara' (made/rendered), and the second object is understood from ﴿that you may be guided﴾, that is: He made the stars for you as a guidance." End of quotation. This is weak, because the omission of one of the two objects of the verbs of the "zanna" class is rare. The apparent meaning is that "the darknesses" here is to be taken literally. He is more distant who said: it is possible that "the darknesses" here means the hardships in the situations in which it happens that one is guided by them. He attributed the darknesses to the land and the sea because of their association with them, or he likened the confusing paths to darknesses. God, exalted is He, mentioned the stars in His Book for adornment, for hurling at devils, and for guidance; whatever else is said about them is fabrication against God and slander.

﴿We have indeed detailed the signs for a people who know.﴾ That is, We have made clear and divided them. He singled out those who know because they are the ones who benefit from their detailing; as for others, they turn away from the signs and from reasoning by them.

﴿It is He who produced you from a single soul﴾, which is Adam, peace be upon him.

﴿So there is a place of lodging and a place of storing﴾. The majority read the qaf with a fatha, taking it as a place (noun of place), that is, a place of settling and a place of depositing, or as a verbal noun, that is, so there is settling and depositing. Musta-qarr cannot be a passive participle, because its verb is not transitive, so a passive participle cannot be formed from it. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read the qaf with a kasra as an active participle, and on this reading "mustawda'" (with fatha on the dal) is a passive participle. When He mentioned their creation, He mentioned their division into "mustaqarr and mustawda'", that is: among you is the one who settles and the one who is deposited. Harun al-A'war related from Abu 'Amr: "mustawdi'" with a kasra on the dal, an active participle. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, 'Ata', al-Nakha'i, al-Dahhak, Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: the one who settles is in the womb and the one who is deposited is in the loins. Ibn Bahr said the reverse, saying: the meaning is that He mentioned the masculine and the feminine; He expressed the male by "mustaqarr" because the drop is formed in his loins, and He expressed the female by "mustawda'" because her womb is a place of deposit for the drop. Ibn Mas'ud said: the one who settles is in the womb and the one who is deposited is in the grave. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: the one who settles is in the earth and the one who is deposited is in the loins; and from him both are in the womb; and from him the one who settles is where he dwells and the one who is deposited is where he dies; and from him the one who settles is the one who has been created and the one who is deposited is the one who has not yet been created. Mujahid said: the one who settles is in this world and the one who is deposited is with God. It was said: both are in this world. It was said: the one who settles is in Paradise and the one who is deposited is in the Fire. It was said: "mustaqarr" is in the Hereafter by his deeds, and "mustawda'" is in his origin, moving from state to state and from time to time, until the end of his term. End of quotation. What the reflection requires is that settling and depositing are two states that succeed one another upon the human being, from the loins to the womb, to this world, to the grave, to the gathering, to Paradise or to the Fire; and in each stage he attains a settling and a depositing: settling in relation to what precedes it, and depositing in relation to what follows it. The word "wadi'ah" (deposit) implies transfer.

﴿We have indeed detailed the signs for a people who understand.﴾ Since guidance by the stars is evident, He concluded it with His saying "who know" (ya'lamun), that is: whoever has even a little perception benefits by considering the stars and their benefit. And since production from a single soul, and the disposition through many states, requires thought and precision of reflection, He concluded it with His saying "who understand" (yafqahun), for "fiqh" is the employment of acuteness, precision of observation and thought. So it was fitting to end each sentence with what corresponds to what the discourse began with.

﴿It is He who sent down water from the sky, and We brought forth by it the growth of everything﴾. When He mentioned His favour in creating us, He mentioned His favour upon us by that which sustains our welfare and our interests. "The sky" here means the cloud. The apparent meaning of "the growth of everything" is what is called growth in the language, namely that which grows of grains, fruits, herbs, grasses and trees; and "everything" means of what grows. He indicated that the cause is one while the effects are many, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿watered with one water, yet We make some of them excel others in fruit﴾.

Al-Tabari said: ﴿the growth of everything﴾ is all that grows of animals, plants, minerals and other things, because all of that is nourished and grows by the descent of water from the sky. Al-Farra' said: its meaning is "the provision of everything", that is, what is suitable as nourishment for everything, so "everything" is restricted to what is nourished, and the annexation of "growth" to it is an explanatory annexation in the generality. On both of the preceding interpretations, the annexation returns in meaning to the annexation of what resembles an adjective to the qualified noun, since the meaning becomes: We brought forth by it every growing thing. In His saying "We brought forth" there is an iltifat (shift) from the third person to the first person plural of majesty.

﴿Then We brought forth from it green (foliage)﴾, that is, of the plants, tender, lush, fresh. "Fa-akhrajna" (then We brought forth) is conjoined to the preceding "fa-akhrajna". Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a substitute (badal) for the preceding "fa-akhrajna".

﴿We bring forth from it grain piled up﴾, that is, from the green (foliage) such as wheat, barley and all pulses, and from fruits such as pomegranates, pine nuts and others, whatever has its grain piled and one part rests upon another. "Nukhriju" (We bring forth) is a clause in place of a qualifier for "khadir" (green), or it may be a resumptive statement. Al-A'mash and Ibn Muhaysin read: "yakhruju minhu habbun mutarakib", taking it as nominative by "yakhruju", with "mutarakib" as an adjective in its accusative and nominative cases.

﴿And from the palm trees, from their spathe, are clusters hanging low﴾, that is, near to the one who reaches, because of their shortness and the adherence of their roots to the earth. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Bara' and al-Dahhak. al-Zamakhshari approved it, saying: easy to pick, presented to the picker like a near thing that is within reach; and because the palm, even if small, can be reached by one sitting, yet it bears fruit. al-Hasan said: some of them are near to others. It was also said: "hanging low" means inclined. It was said: the mention of "hanging low" without mention of "tall" is because the blessing in them is more manifest, or "tall" is omitted because "hanging low" indicates it, like His saying: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81], meaning and the cold. The majority read "qinwan" with a kasra on the qaf. al-A'mash and al-Khaffaf, from Abu 'Amr al-A'raj in one narration, read it with a damma; it is related from al-Sulami from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. al-A'raj in one narration and Harun from Abu 'Amr read "qanwan" with a fatha on the qaf, and Abu al-Fath explained it as a collective noun of the pattern "fa'lan", since "fa'lan" is not among the patterns of broken plurals. In Ibn 'Atiyya's book it is related from al-A'raj that the qaf is read with a damma, as the plural of "qinw" with a damma on the qaf. al-Farra' said: this is the dialect of Qays and the people of the Hijaz, and the kasra is more famous among the Arabs, and "qinw" is the singular of "qinwan". End of quotation. This differs from what we related in "al-Mufradat" that the dialect of the Hijaz is "qinwan" with a kasra on the qaf. This phrase is a subject and predicate, and "min tal'iha" (from its spathe) is a substitute for "wa-min al-nakhl" (and from the palm trees), and the construction is: "qinwan daniyah" (clusters hanging low) which come from the spathe of the palm. The mention of "qinwan" is singled out and detached from His saying "the growth of everything, from which We bring forth green", because of the great favour and blessing in detaching them, since they are among the greatest, or among the greatest, of the sustenance of the Arabs; and they are presented in the form of subject and predicate to indicate permanence and stability, and that this is a settled matter. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "wa-min al-nakhl" is to be taken as "We bring forth from the palm trees and from its spathe clusters"; "qinwan" is a subject whose predicate is preceded, and the clause is in the place of the object of "nukhriju". End of quotation. This is an error, because what is transitive to one object does not have a clause in the place of its object unless the verb is one that suspends, and the clause contains something that prevents the verb from governing any of its single words, from among the impediments explained in the science of grammar. "Nukhriju" is not one that suspends, and there is nothing in the clause that prevents the verb from governing any of its words; for if the verb were implied here, it would govern what follows it, and the construction and its implication would be: "wa-nukhriju min al-nakhl min tal'iha qinwanan daniyatan" in the accusative. al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible that the predicate be omitted, since "akhrajna" indicates it, its implication being: "and produced from the spathe of the palm are clusters". End of quotation. There is no need for this implication, since the clause is self-contained in its information without it. Abu al-Baqa' said: it is permissible that "qinwan" be a subject whose predicate is "min tal'iha", and in "min al-nakhl" there is a pronoun whose implication is "and there grows from the palm trees a thing or fruit", so "min tal'iha" is a substitute for it; and it is permissible that "qinwan" be nominative as a subject of "min tal'iha", so that in "min al-nakhl" there is a pronoun explained by "qinwan"; and if you make "qinwan" nominative by His saying "min al-nakhl", on the view of those who make the first of the two verbs operate, it is permissible, and in "min tal'iha" there would be a pronoun in the nominative. End of quotation. This is an analysis mixed with confusion that does not befit the Qur'an. As for one who reads "yakhruju minhu habbun mutarakib", it is permissible that His saying "min al-nakhl min tal'iha qinwan daniyah" be conjoined to it, as one says "yadribu fi al-dar Zayd, wa-fi al-suq 'Amr"; and it is permissible that it be a subject and predicate, which is the more apt.

﴿And gardens of grapevines﴾. The reading of the majority is with a kasra on the ta' (wa-jannatin), conjoined to "nabat" (growth), and this is the conjunction of the particular to the general for its nobility, the same as when the palm was singled out, the gardens of grapevines are singled out for the nobility of both, as He said: ﴿Would any of you like to have a garden of palms and grapevines?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 266]. Muhammad ibn Abi Layla, al-A'mash and Abu Bakr in one narration from 'Asim read "wa-jannatun" with a damma (nominative). Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim rejected this reading, to the point that Abu Hatim said: it is impossible, since gardens of grapes do not come from the palm. This reading should not be rejected, and it has a good grammatical justification: it is taken as a subject whose predicate is omitted, which al-Nahhas estimated as "for them are gardens", Ibn 'Atiyya estimated as "for you are gardens", Abu al-Baqa' estimated as "and from the vine are gardens", and it was estimated as "and from the vine" to correspond to "wa-min al-nakhl"; al-Zamakhshari estimated it as "and there are gardens" meaning "with the palm". A parallel to this is the reading of one who reads "wa-hurun 'in" [al-Waqi'ah: 22] with a damma, after His saying "They are served with a cup from a spring" [al-Saffat: 45] and so on, its estimate being: "for them are houris". Sibawayh, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' permitted the like of this, and there are many like it. The predicate was also estimated as postponed, its estimate being: "and gardens of grapevines" we brought forth, and His earlier saying "fa-akhrajna" indicates its estimate, as one says: "I honoured 'Abd Allah and his brother", the estimate being: "and his brother I honoured him", so "akramtuhu" is omitted, indicated by "akramtu" before it. al-Tabari construed it as "wa-jannatun" being conjoined to "qinwan". Ibn 'Atiyya said: "his saying is weak". Abu al-Baqa' said: it is not permissible that it be conjoined to "qinwan", because grapes do not come out of the palm. al-Zamakhshari said: it has been mentioned that in its nominative there are two possibilities, one of which is that it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, its estimate being: "and there are gardens", and this estimate was mentioned from him earlier. He said: the second is that it is conjoined to "qinwan" in the sense of: "and its produce from the palm is clusters" (and gardens of grapevines), that is, of the growth of grapevines. End of quotation. This conjunction is on the basis that the restriction "from the palm" is not taken into account in it, as if he said: "from the palm are clusters hanging low, and gardens of grapevines" are existing, just as you say: "from the Banu Tamim is a wise man, and a man from Quraysh who are departing".

**[p-191]** ﴿And the olive and the pomegranate, resembling one another and not resembling one another﴾. It is read with the accusative (*naṣb*) by consensus. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "as a coordination (*ʿaṭf*) upon (*ḥabban*)." It was also said: "as a coordination upon (*nabāta*)." Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It is also read *wa-jannātin* with the accusative, as a coordination upon *nabāta kulli shay'* (the plants of every thing), meaning: and We brought forth by it ﴿gardens of grapevines﴾, and likewise His saying: ﴿and the olive and the pomegranate﴾." End of quotation. The apparent meaning is that it is coordinated upon *nabāta*, just as *wa-jannātin* is coordinated upon it. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "The best reading is that it be in the accusative of specification (*al-ikhtiṣāṣ*), as in His saying: ﴿and those who establish the prayer﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 162], due to the excellence of these two categories." End of quotation.

Qatādah said: "It resembles in its leaves and differs in its fruit. The resemblance of the leaves is in size and in the fact that it covers the whole branch." Ibn Jurayj said: "Resembling in appearance and not resembling in taste, like two pomegranates whose color is one and whose taste differs." Al-Ṭabarī said: "It is possible that it resembles in the fruit and differs in taste, and it may be that he means resemblance in taste and difference in appearance. These conditions are all found in consideration of the kinds of fruits." Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Some of it resembles and some of it does not resemble in quantity, color and taste, and that is evidence that the intent is deliberate and not neglect." End of quotation.

The majority (*al-Jumhūr*) read *mushtabihan*. It was read anomalously (*shādhdhan*) as *mutashābihan*. Both have the same meaning, like *ikhtaṣama* and *takhāṣama*, *ishtaraka* and *istawā* and *tasāwā*, and similar forms in which the *ifti‘āl* (a verbal pattern of the form *if‘āl*) and *tafāʿul* patterns share meaning. *Mushtabihan* is in the accusative as a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative, describing the state of the noun) of *al-rummān* because it is nearer, and the *ḥāl* of the first noun is omitted; or it is a *ḥāl* of the first noun because it precedes. The estimate is: "and the olive (being) resembling and not resembling, and the pomegranate likewise." Al-Zamakhsharī estimated it this way, and said: "Like his saying: *kuntu minhu wa-wālidī barīʾan* (I was free of him and my father likewise, free)." End of quotation. According to his estimate, the meaning of the verse of poetry is: "I was free of him, and my father likewise, that is, free." The verse does not necessarily have what he mentioned, because *barīʾan* is on the pattern *faʿīl*, like *ṣadīq* and *rafīq*, so it may be used of the singular, the dual and the plural. It is possible that *barīʾan* is the predicate of *kāna* with the pronoun shared, and the apparent coordinated noun is in it, since it may be a predicate about both of them. It is not permissible for it to be a *ḥāl* of both, although some have permitted it, for if it were a *ḥāl* of both the construction would be *mutashābihīna wa-ghayru mutashābihīn*.

Al-Zajjāj said: "He joined the olive with the pomegranate because they are two trees whose leaves, the Arabs know, cover the branch from its beginning to its end." The poet said:

*Blessed is the stranger who died, as the ripening of the pomegranate and the olive was blessed.*

﴿Look at its fruit when it bears fruit, and at its ripening﴾. The "looking" (*al-naẓar*) is the looking of the eye's seeing, and for that reason he transitive it with *ilā* (to). But there follows from it reflection (*al-fikr*), consideration (*al-iʿtibār*), insight (*al-istibṣār*) and inference (*al-istidlāl*) upon a dazzling power that transfers it from one state to another. He drew attention to two states: the beginning, which is the time of the beginning of bearing fruit, and the end, which is the time of its ripening. That is: how does He bring it forth small and weak, from which hardly any benefit is gained, and how does it return ripe, containing benefits? He drew attention to these two states, though between them there are states through which consideration and insight occur, because these two are more remarkable in occurrence and more evident for inference.

Ibn Thawwāb, Mujāhid and Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read ﴿ thumurihi ﴾ with a *ḍamma* on the *thāʾ* and the *mīm*. Ibn Thawwāb and Mujāhid said: "They are the kinds of wealth, meaning the wealth that is obtained from it." Abū ʿAlī said: "The better view is that it is the plural of *thamara* (a fruit), like *khashaba* and *khushub*, *ukama* and *ukum*; and its parallel among the weak-lettered roots is *lābah* and *lūb*, *nāqah* and *nūq*, *sāḥah* and *sūḥ*." A group read with a *ḍamma* on the *thāʾ* and a sukūn on the *mīm*, seeking lightness, as you say *kutub* for *kutub* (books), i.e. *kutb*. The rest of the seven read *thamarihi* with a *fatḥa* on the *thāʾ* and the *mīm*, and it is a noun of genus (*ism al-jins*), like *shajarah* and *shajar*. *Al-thamar* is the harvest of the tree and what appears on it; if the tree is called *thamar*, it is a metaphor (*majāz*). The governing element of *idhā* (when) is *unẓurū* (look).

The majority read *wa-yanʿihi* with a *fatḥa* on the *yāʾ* and a sukūn on the *nūn*. Qatādah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Muḥayṣin read it with a *ḍamma* on the *yāʾ* and a sukūn on the *nūn*. Ibn Abī ʿAblah and al-Yamānī read *wa-yāniʿihi*, the active participle of *yanaʿa* (to ripen). Al-Zamakhsharī attributed this to Ibn Muḥayṣin.

Al-Marwazī said: "﴿When it bears fruit﴾ [happens] where there is no constant shade, so it does not ripen, nor constant sun, so it does not burn. He sent upon every fruit two different winds: a wind that moves the leaves so the fruit appears and the sun strikes it, and another wind that moves the leaves and shades the fruit so that it does not burn." End of quotation.

﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe﴾. The demonstrative *dhālikum* refers to everything previously mentioned, from the splitting of the grain and the date-stone to the end of what God created and of what He bestowed as a favour. The "signs" (*al-āyāt*) are the indications that point to the perfection of His power, the precision of His craftsmanship, and His singularity in creating, to the exclusion of others. The manifestation of signs benefits only those for whom God has decreed faith. As for those whom God's decree has preceded with disbelief, they do not benefit from these signs. So by specifying *belief* He drew attention to this meaning. Consider the excellence of the sequence of this arrangement with respect to what came before: ﴿Indeed God is the splitter of the grain and the date-stone﴾ [al-Anʿām: 95]. The arrangement that followed is consistent with this arrangement. When He mentioned that He brought forth the vegetation of everything, He mentioned sown crops, which is what is meant by His saying ﴿green, from which We bring forth clustered grain﴾, and He began with it as He began with it in His saying ﴿splitter of the grain﴾ [al-Anʿām: 95]. Then He followed with what has a stone, so He said ﴿from the palm-trees, from its spathe, clusters hanging low﴾ to the end, as He followed with it in His saying *wa-l-nawā* (and the date-stone). He placed the crops before the trees because they are food, while fruit is a delicacy, and food takes precedence over fruit. He placed the palm before the rest of the fruits because it functions as food in relation to the Arabs. He placed the grape because it is the most noble of fruits, and it is beneficial in all its stages: first *ḥanūṭ* (the bud), then *ḥiṣrim* (the unripe grape), then *ʿinab* (the grape); then, if it is pressed, there comes from it vinegar and syrup (*dibs*), and if it is dried, there comes from it raisins (*zabīb*). He placed the olive because it is very beneficial for eating, and in the great-benefit oil pressed from it, for eating, for lighting lamps, and other uses. He mentioned the pomegranate because of the wonder of its condition and its strangeness, for it is composed of skin, flesh, seeds and water. The three (skin, flesh, seeds) are cold, dry, earthy, dense, astringent, and strong in these qualities; its water is the opposite: the most pleasant and most subtle of drinks, and closest to the state of moderation, and in it is a strengthening of the weak temperament: nourishment from one aspect and medicine from another. Thus He, exalted is He, gathered in it the two opposites that are contrary to each other. How dazzling is His power, and how wondrous is what He created.

For the movements of the stars at night are used as indicators for the qibla, just as the movement of the sun during the day is used as an indicator for it. The address is general to all people. ﴿That you may be guided﴾ is connected to a verb "ja'ala" (made) that is implied, since it (the phrase) is a substitute (badal) for "lakum" (for you). That is, He made that for your being guided. And "ja'ala" here may mean "khalaqa" (created), in which case it takes only one object. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is possible that it means 'sayyara' (made/rendered), and the second object is understood from ﴿that you may be guided﴾, that is: He made the stars for you as a guidance." End of quotation. This is weak, because the omission of one of the two objects of the verbs of the "zanna" class is rare. The apparent meaning is that "the darknesses" here is to be taken literally. Harun al-A'war related from Abu 'Amr: "mustawdi'" with a kasra on the dal, an active participle. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, 'Ata', al-Nakha'i, al-Dahhak, Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: the one who settles is in the womb and the one who is deposited is in the loins. Ibn Bahr said the reverse, saying: the meaning is that He mentioned the masculine and the feminine; He expressed the male by "mustaqarr" because the drop is formed in his loins, and He expressed the female by "mustawda'" because her womb is a place of deposit for the drop. Ibn Mas'ud said: the one who settles is in the womb and the one who is deposited is in the grave. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: the one who settles is in the earth and the one who is deposited is in the loins; and from him both are in the womb; and from him the one who settles is where he dwells and the one who is deposited is where he dies; and from him the one who settles is the one who has been created and the one who is deposited is the one who has not yet been created. Mujahid said: the one who settles is in this world and the one who is deposited is with God. It was said: both are in this world. It was said: the one who settles is in Paradise and the one who is deposited is in the Fire. It was said: "mustaqarr" is in the Hereafter by his deeds, and "mustawda'" is in his origin, moving from state to state and from time to time, until the end of his term. End of quotation. What the reflection requires is that settling and depositing are two states that succeed one another upon the human being, from the loins to the womb, to this world, to the grave, to the gathering, to Paradise or to the Fire; and in each stage he attains a settling and a depositing: settling in relation to what precedes it, and depositing in relation to what follows it. The word "wadi'ah" (deposit) implies transfer.

﴿We have indeed detailed the signs for a people who understand.﴾ Since guidance by the stars is evident, He concluded it with His saying "who know" (ya'lamun), that is: whoever has even a little perception benefits by considering the stars and their benefit. And since production from a single soul, and the disposition through many states, requires thought and precision of reflection, He concluded it with His saying "who understand" (yafqahun), for "fiqh" is the employment of acuteness, precision of observation and thought. So it was fitting to end each sentence with what corresponds to what the discourse began with.

﴿It is He who sent down water from the sky, and We brought forth by it the growth of everything﴾. When He mentioned His favour in creating us, He mentioned His favour upon us by that which sustains our welfare and our interests. "The sky" here means the cloud. The apparent meaning of "the growth of everything" is what is called growth in the language, namely that which grows of grains, fruits, herbs, grasses and trees; and "everything" means of what grows. He indicated that the cause is one while the effects are many, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿watered with one water, yet We make some of them excel others in fruit﴾.

Al-Tabari said: ﴿the growth of everything﴾ is all that grows of animals, plants, minerals and other things, because all of that is nourished and grows by the descent of water from the sky. Al-Farra' said: its meaning is "the provision of everything", that is, what is suitable as nourishment for everything, so "everything" is restricted to what is nourished, and the annexation of "growth" to it is an explanatory annexation in the generality. On both of the preceding interpretations, the annexation returns in meaning to the annexation of what resembles an adjective to the qualified noun, since the meaning becomes: We brought forth by it every growing thing. In His saying "We brought forth" there is an iltifat (shift) from the third person to the first person plural of majesty.

﴿Then We brought forth from it green (foliage)﴾, that is, of the plants, tender, lush, fresh. "Fa-akhrajna" (then We brought forth) is conjoined to the preceding "fa-akhrajna". Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a substitute (badal) for the preceding "fa-akhrajna".

﴿We bring forth from it grain piled up﴾, that is, from the green (foliage) such as wheat, barley and all pulses, and from fruits such as pomegranates, pine nuts and others, whatever has its grain piled and one part rests upon another. "Nukhriju" (We bring forth) is a clause in place of a qualifier for "khadir" (green), or it may be a resumptive statement. Al-A'mash and Ibn Muhaysin read: "yakhruju minhu habbun mutarakib", taking it as nominative by "yakhruju", with "mutarakib" as an adjective in its accusative and nominative cases.

﴿And from the palm trees, from their spathe, are clusters hanging low﴾, that is, near to the one who reaches, because of their shortness and the adherence of their roots to the earth. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Bara' and al-Dahhak. al-Zamakhshari approved it, saying: easy to pick, presented to the picker like a near thing that is within reach; and because the palm, even if small, can be reached by one sitting, yet it bears fruit. al-Hasan said: some of them are near to others. It was also said: "hanging low" means inclined. It was said: the mention of "hanging low" without mention of "tall" is because the blessing in them is more manifest, or "tall" is omitted because "hanging low" indicates it, like His saying: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81], meaning and the cold. The majority read "qinwan" with a kasra on the qaf. al-A'mash and al-Khaffaf, from Abu 'Amr al-A'raj in one narration, read it with a damma; it is related from al-Sulami from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. al-A'raj in one narration and Harun from Abu 'Amr read "qanwan" with a fatha on the qaf, and Abu al-Fath explained it as a collective noun of the pattern "fa'lan", since "fa'lan" is not among the patterns of broken plurals. In Ibn 'Atiyya's book it is related from al-A'raj that the qaf is read with a damma, as the plural of "qinw" with a damma on the qaf. al-Farra' said: this is the dialect of Qays and the people of the Hijaz, and the kasra is more famous among the Arabs, and "qinw" is the singular of "qinwan". End of quotation. This differs from what we related in "al-Mufradat" that the dialect of the Hijaz is "qinwan" with a kasra on the qaf. This phrase is a subject and predicate, and "min tal'iha" (from its spathe) is a substitute for "wa-min al-nakhl" (and from the palm trees), and the construction is: "qinwan daniyah" (clusters hanging low) which come from the spathe of the palm. The mention of "qinwan" is singled out and detached from His saying "the growth of everything, from which We bring forth green", because of the great favour and blessing in detaching them, since they are among the greatest, or among the greatest, of the sustenance of the Arabs; and they are presented in the form of subject and predicate to indicate permanence and stability, and that this is a settled matter. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "wa-min al-nakhl" is to be taken as "We bring forth from the palm trees and from its spathe clusters"; "qinwan" is a subject whose predicate is preceded, and the clause is in the place of the object of "nukhriju". End of quotation. This is an error, because what is transitive to one object does not have a clause in the place of its object unless the verb is one that suspends, and the clause contains something that prevents the verb from governing any of its single words, from among the impediments explained in the science of grammar. "Nukhriju" is not one that suspends, and there is nothing in the clause that prevents the verb from governing any of its words; for if the verb were implied here, it would govern what follows it, and the construction and its implication would be: "wa-nukhriju min al-nakhl min tal'iha qinwanan daniyatan" in the accusative. al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible that the predicate be omitted, since "akhrajna" indicates it, its implication being: "and produced from the spathe of the palm are clusters". End of quotation. There is no need for this implication, since the clause is self-contained in its information without it. Abu al-Baqa' said: it is permissible that "qinwan" be a subject whose predicate is "min tal'iha", and in "min al-nakhl" there is a pronoun whose implication is "and there grows from the palm trees a thing or fruit", so "min tal'iha" is a substitute for it; and it is permissible that "qinwan" be nominative as a subject of "min tal'iha", so that in "min al-nakhl" there is a pronoun explained by "qinwan"; and if you make "qinwan" nominative by His saying "min al-nakhl", on the view of those who make the first of the two verbs operate, it is permissible, and in "min tal'iha" there would be a pronoun in the nominative. End of quotation. This is an analysis mixed with confusion that does not befit the Qur'an. As for one who reads "yakhruju minhu habbun mutarakib", it is permissible that His saying "min al-nakhl min tal'iha qinwan daniyah" be conjoined to it, as one says "yadribu fi al-dar Zayd, wa-fi al-suq 'Amr"; and it is permissible that it be a subject and predicate, which is the more apt.

﴿And gardens of grapevines﴾. The reading of the majority is with a kasra on the ta' (wa-jannatin), conjoined to "nabat" (growth), and this is the conjunction of the particular to the general for its nobility, the same as when the palm was singled out, the gardens of grapevines are singled out for the nobility of both, as He said: ﴿Would any of you like to have a garden of palms and grapevines?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 266]. Muhammad ibn Abi Layla, al-A'mash and Abu Bakr in one narration from 'Asim read "wa-jannatun" with a damma (nominative). Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim rejected this reading, to the point that Abu Hatim said: it is impossible, since gardens of grapes do not come from the palm. This reading should not be rejected, and it has a good grammatical justification: it is taken as a subject whose predicate is omitted, which al-Nahhas estimated as "for them are gardens", Ibn 'Atiyya estimated as "for you are gardens", Abu al-Baqa' estimated as "and from the vine are gardens", and it was estimated as "and from the vine" to correspond to "wa-min al-nakhl"; al-Zamakhshari estimated it as "and there are gardens" meaning "with the palm". A parallel to this is the reading of one who reads "wa-hurun 'in" [al-Waqi'ah: 22] with a damma, after His saying "They are served with a cup from a spring" [al-Saffat: 45] and so on, its estimate being: "for them are houris". Sibawayh, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' permitted the like of this, and there are many like it. The predicate was also estimated as postponed, its estimate being: "and gardens of grapevines" we brought forth, and His earlier saying "fa-akhrajna" indicates its estimate, as one says: "I honoured 'Abd Allah and his brother", the estimate being: "and his brother I honoured him", so "akramtuhu" is omitted, indicated by "akramtu" before it. al-Tabari construed it as "wa-jannatun" being conjoined to "qinwan". Ibn 'Atiyya said: "his saying is weak". Abu al-Baqa' said: it is not permissible that it be conjoined to "qinwan", because grapes do not come out of the palm. al-Zamakhshari said: it has been mentioned that in its nominative there are two possibilities, one of which is that it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, its estimate being: "and there are gardens", and this estimate was mentioned from him earlier. He said: the second is that it is conjoined to "qinwan" in the sense of: "and its produce from the palm is clusters" (and gardens of grapevines), that is, of the growth of grapevines. End of quotation. This conjunction is on the basis that the restriction "from the palm" is not taken into account in it, as if he said: "from the palm are clusters hanging low, and gardens of grapevines" are existing, just as you say: "from the Banu Tamim is a wise man, and a man from Quraysh who are departing".

**[p-191]** ﴿And the olive and the pomegranate, resembling one another and not resembling one another﴾. It is read with the accusative (*naṣb*) by consensus. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "as a coordination (*ʿaṭf*) upon (*ḥabban*)." It was also said: "as a coordination upon (*nabāta*)." Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It is also read *wa-jannātin* with the accusative, as a coordination upon *nabāta kulli shay'* (the plants of every thing), meaning: and We brought forth by it ﴿gardens of grapevines﴾, and likewise His saying: ﴿and the olive and the pomegranate﴾." End of quotation. The apparent meaning is that it is coordinated upon *nabāta*, just as *wa-jannātin* is coordinated upon it. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "The best reading is that it be in the accusative of specification (*al-ikhtiṣāṣ*), as in His saying: ﴿and those who establish the prayer﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 162], due to the excellence of these two categories." End of quotation.

Qatādah said: "It resembles in its leaves and differs in its fruit. The resemblance of the leaves is in size and in the fact that it covers the whole branch." Ibn Jurayj said: "Resembling in appearance and not resembling in taste, like two pomegranates whose color is one and whose taste differs." Al-Ṭabarī said: "It is possible that it resembles in the fruit and differs in taste, and it may be that he means resemblance in taste and difference in appearance. These conditions are all found in consideration of the kinds of fruits." Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Some of it resembles and some of it does not resemble in quantity, color and taste, and that is evidence that the intent is deliberate and not neglect." End of quotation.

The majority (*al-Jumhūr*) read *mushtabihan*. It was read anomalously (*shādhdhan*) as *mutashābihan*. Both have the same meaning, like *ikhtaṣama* and *takhāṣama*, *ishtaraka* and *istawā* and *tasāwā*, and similar forms in which the *ifti‘āl* (a verbal pattern of the form *if‘āl*) and *tafāʿul* patterns share meaning. *Mushtabihan* is in the accusative as a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative, describing the state of the noun) of *al-rummān* because it is nearer, and the *ḥāl* of the first noun is omitted; or it is a *ḥāl* of the first noun because it precedes. The estimate is: "and the olive (being) resembling and not resembling, and the pomegranate likewise." Al-Zamakhsharī estimated it this way, and said: "Like his saying: *kuntu minhu wa-wālidī barīʾan* (I was free of him and my father likewise, free)." End of quotation. According to his estimate, the meaning of the verse of poetry is: "I was free of him, and my father likewise, that is, free." The verse does not necessarily have what he mentioned, because *barīʾan* is on the pattern *faʿīl*, like *ṣadīq* and *rafīq*, so it may be used of the singular, the dual and the plural. It is possible that *barīʾan* is the predicate of *kāna* with the pronoun shared, and the apparent coordinated noun is in it, since it may be a predicate about both of them. It is not permissible for it to be a *ḥāl* of both, although some have permitted it, for if it were a *ḥāl* of both the construction would be *mutashābihīna wa-ghayru mutashābihīn*.

Al-Zajjāj said: "He joined the olive with the pomegranate because they are two trees whose leaves, the Arabs know, cover the branch from its beginning to its end." The poet said:

*Blessed is the stranger who died, as the ripening of the pomegranate and the olive was blessed.*

﴿Look at its fruit when it bears fruit, and at its ripening﴾. The "looking" (*al-naẓar*) is the looking of the eye's seeing, and for that reason he transitive it with *ilā* (to). But there follows from it reflection (*al-fikr*), consideration (*al-iʿtibār*), insight (*al-istibṣār*) and inference (*al-istidlāl*) upon a dazzling power that transfers it from one state to another. He drew attention to two states: the beginning, which is the time of the beginning of bearing fruit, and the end, which is the time of its ripening. That is: how does He bring it forth small and weak, from which hardly any benefit is gained, and how does it return ripe, containing benefits? He drew attention to these two states, though between them there are states through which consideration and insight occur, because these two are more remarkable in occurrence and more evident for inference.

Ibn Thawwāb, Mujāhid and Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read ﴿ thumurihi ﴾ with a *ḍamma* on the *thāʾ* and the *mīm*. Ibn Thawwāb and Mujāhid said: "They are the kinds of wealth, meaning the wealth that is obtained from it." Abū ʿAlī said: "The better view is that it is the plural of *thamara* (a fruit), like *khashaba* and *khushub*, *ukama* and *ukum*; and its parallel among the weak-lettered roots is *lābah* and *lūb*, *nāqah* and *nūq*, *sāḥah* and *sūḥ*." A group read with a *ḍamma* on the *thāʾ* and a sukūn on the *mīm*, seeking lightness, as you say *kutub* for *kutub* (books), i.e. *kutb*. The rest of the seven read *thamarihi* with a *fatḥa* on the *thāʾ* and the *mīm*, and it is a noun of genus (*ism al-jins*), like *shajarah* and *shajar*. *Al-thamar* is the harvest of the tree and what appears on it; if the tree is called *thamar*, it is a metaphor (*majāz*). The governing element of *idhā* (when) is *unẓurū* (look).

The majority read *wa-yanʿihi* with a *fatḥa* on the *yāʾ* and a sukūn on the *nūn*. Qatādah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Muḥayṣin read it with a *ḍamma* on the *yāʾ* and a sukūn on the *nūn*. Ibn Abī ʿAblah and al-Yamānī read *wa-yāniʿihi*, the active participle of *yanaʿa* (to ripen). Al-Zamakhsharī attributed this to Ibn Muḥayṣin.

Al-Marwazī said: "﴿When it bears fruit﴾ [happens] where there is no constant shade, so it does not ripen, nor constant sun, so it does not burn. He sent upon every fruit two different winds: a wind that moves the leaves so the fruit appears and the sun strikes it, and another wind that moves the leaves and shades the fruit so that it does not burn." End of quotation.

﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe﴾. The demonstrative *dhālikum* refers to everything previously mentioned, from the splitting of the grain and the date-stone to the end of what God created and of what He bestowed as a favour. The "signs" (*al-āyāt*) are the indications that point to the perfection of His power, the precision of His craftsmanship, and His singularity in creating, to the exclusion of others. The manifestation of signs benefits only those for whom God has decreed faith. As for those whom God's decree has preceded with disbelief, they do not benefit from these signs. So by specifying *belief* He drew attention to this meaning. Consider the excellence of the sequence of this arrangement with respect to what came before: ﴿Indeed God is the splitter of the grain and the date-stone﴾ [al-Anʿām: 95]. The arrangement that followed is consistent with this arrangement. When He mentioned that He brought forth the vegetation of everything, He mentioned sown crops, which is what is meant by His saying ﴿green, from which We bring forth clustered grain﴾, and He began with it as He began with it in His saying ﴿splitter of the grain﴾ [al-Anʿām: 95]. Then He followed with what has a stone, so He said ﴿from the palm-trees, from its spathe, clusters hanging low﴾ to the end, as He followed with it in His saying *wa-l-nawā* (and the date-stone). He placed the crops before the trees because they are food, while fruit is a delicacy, and food takes precedence over fruit. He placed the palm before the rest of the fruits because it functions as food in relation to the Arabs. He placed the grape because it is the most noble of fruits, and it is beneficial in all its stages: first *ḥanūṭ* (the bud), then *ḥiṣrim* (the unripe grape), then *ʿinab* (the grape); then, if it is pressed, there comes from it vinegar and syrup (*dibs*), and if it is dried, there comes from it raisins (*zabīb*). He placed the olive because it is very beneficial for eating, and in the great-benefit oil pressed from it, for eating, for lighting lamps, and other uses. He mentioned the pomegranate because of the wonder of its condition and its strangeness, for it is composed of skin, flesh, seeds and water. The three (skin, flesh, seeds) are cold, dry, earthy, dense, astringent, and strong in these qualities; its water is the opposite: the most pleasant and most subtle of drinks, and closest to the state of moderation, and in it is a strengthening of the weak temperament: nourishment from one aspect and medicine from another. Thus He, exalted is He, gathered in it the two opposites that are contrary to each other. How dazzling is His power, and how wondrous is what He created.

[Commentary of Abu Hayyan on al-Bahr al-Muhit, on surah 6, verses 100–102]

﴿They have made the jinn partners with God, though He created them﴾. When God mentioned what is specific to Him of His manifest power and perfect craftsmanship, and His bounty upon the human world in what He brought into being for them of what they need for the maintenance of their lives, and clarified that in signs for a people who know, for a people who understand, and for a people who believe [p. 193], He mentioned how they dealt with their Originator who created them from non-existence and the Provider of their sustenance: by associating others with Him in worship, and by attributing to Him what is impossible for Him, describing Him with the marks of createdness, such as sons and daughters.

Al-Kalbi said: it was revealed concerning the zanadiqah (heretics). They said: God is the creator of humans and animals, and Iblis is the creator of snakes, scorpions and beasts of prey. Close to this is the doctrine of the Magians, who said: the world has two makers, an eternal god, and a second, a created devil, arising from a thought of the eternal god. Likewise the Ha'itiyyah among the Mu'tazilah, the followers of Ahmad ibn Ha'it, claimed that the world has two makers: the eternal God, and another, created one whom God first created and then entrusted with the management of the world, and who calls creation to account in the Hereafter.

The pronoun in (wa-ja'alu, "they made") refers to the disbelievers, because they are polytheists and People of the Book. It has been said that it refers to the worshippers of idols. The Christians said: the Messiah is the son of God; the Jews said: 'Uzayr is the son of God; and groups of the Arabs made the angels daughters of God, Exalted is He. The Banu Mudlij claimed that God, Exalted is He, intermarried with the jinn and that the angels were born from her. It has also been said that among the angels there is a group called the jinn, and Iblis is among them, and they are the guardians of Paradise.

Al-Hasan said: all these groups obeyed Satan in the worship of idols and believed in divinity for those who did not possess it, so they made them partners with God in worship. The apparent meaning of the statement is that they made the jinn themselves partners with God, and what al-Hasan said contradicts this apparent meaning, since the apparent meaning of his words is that the partners are the idols, and that obeying Satan was made into an association with Him, Exalted is He, since the association arose from his command and seduction. Similarly Isma'il al-Darir said: by the jinn he meant Iblis, whom they obeyed when he commanded them. The apparent sense of the word "jinn" is that they are those whom the mind immediately thinks of as the counterpart of humankind, in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind﴾ [al-An'am: 130], and that they are not the angels, due to His saying: (Then He will say to the angels: "Were these the ones who used to worship you?" They will say: "Glory be to You, You are our Protector, not them; rather they used to worship the jinn") [Saba': 40–41]. So the verse refers to those who made the jinn partners with God in worshipping them, and who believed that they know the unseen. Groups of the Arabs used to do this, seeking refuge with the jinn of the valleys during their journeys.

The majority read (al-jinn) in the accusative case. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah parsed it (i'rab, grammatical analysis) as the first object of (ja'alu), with (ja'alu) meaning "made" (sayyaru). (Shuraka'a) is the second object, and (lillahi) is connected to (shuraka'a). Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the benefit of the fronting? I say: its benefit is to magnify that anyone should be taken as a partner of God, whether he be an angel, a jinni, a human, or otherwise; for this reason the name of God was placed before the partners." End of quotation. Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' allowed that (al-jinn) could be a substitute (badal) for (shuraka'a), with (lillahi) in the position of the second object and (shuraka'a) the first object. But what they allowed is not permissible, because for a substitute it is valid that it take the place of the thing it substitutes; so if you say "they made for God the jinn," the sentence would be sound—but it is not sound. And the condition of a substitute is that it be intended as a repetition of the governing verb, according to the more famous of the two opinions, or that it be governed by the verb governing the substituted noun according to another opinion, and this is not valid at all here, as we have mentioned. Al-Hawfi allowed that (shuraka'a) be the first object and (al-jinn) the second object, as is the order of the arrangement. Abu al-Baqa' allowed that (lillahi shuraka'a) be a circumstantial clause (hal), and it would have been (lil-shuraka'a) had it been placed later. But the best of what they parsed is what I heard from our teacher, the scholar Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Ibrahim ibn al-Zubayr al-Thaqafi, saying about it: (al-jinn) is in the accusative by an implied verb, answering an assumed question, as if it were said: "Whom did they make partners with God?" It is answered: "The jinn," meaning: "They made the jinn." This meaning is supported by the reading of Abu Haywah and Yazid ibn Qutayb: (al-jinnu) in the nominative, by supposing it as the answer to someone who asks: "Who is the one they made a partner?" and it is said to him: "They are the jinn." This would be by way of magnifying what they did and belittling those they made partners with God. Shu'ayb ibn Abi Hamzah read (al-jinni) in the genitive, and this was also transmitted from Abu Haywah and Ibn Qutayb. Al-Zamakhshari said: it was also read with the genitive of specification [p. 194], and the meaning is: they made them partners in His worship, because they obeyed them as God is obeyed. End of quotation. The meaning of this reading is not clear, since the construction would be: "They made the partners of the jinn to God," and this meaning does not appear.

The pronoun in (wa-khalaqahum, "though He created them") refers to those who make the partners, since they are the ones spoken of. It is a circumstantial clause, meaning: "And He has created them, and He alone brought them into being, not the one they took as a partner, namely the jinn; so they made one who did not create them a partner to their Creator. This is the utmost ignorance." It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the jinn: that is, God created the ones they took as partners, so both are equal in that the one who makes and the one made are created by God. How, then, is it fitting that some of the created be made a partner to God, Exalted is He?

Yahya ibn Ya'mur read (wa-khalqahum) with a sukun on the lam, and likewise it is in the Mushaf of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud). The apparent sense is that it is conjoined to (al-jinn), meaning: "They made their created things, which they carve as idols, partners to God," as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Do you worship what you carve?﴾ [al-Saffat: 95] ﴿And God created you and what you do﴾ [al-Saffat: 96]. So "creation" here falls upon the made object, in the sense of the created thing. Ibn 'Atiyyah said this is its meaning. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is also read (wa-khalqahum), that is, their fabrication of falsehood, meaning: they made their fabrication (khalq) a partner to God, in that they attributed their ugly deeds to God, saying: "God commanded us to do them." End of quotation. So "creation" here is a verbal noun in the sense of fabrication (ikhtilaq).

﴿And they attributed to Him, falsely and without knowledge, sons and daughters﴾. That is, they invented and fabricated. It is said: kharaqa, khalaqa, ikhtalaqa, ikhtaraqa, iqtala'a, iftaraa and kharasa "al-ifk" when one lies about it, as al-Farra' said. ﴿And He created every thing﴾. The first: the Originator of the heavens and the earth, which are great bodies, cannot properly be described as begetting, since begetting is an attribute of bodies, and the originator of bodies cannot be a body so as to be a begetter. The second: begetting occurs only between two spouses of one kind, and He, Exalted is He, is exalted above any kin; so it is not valid that He have a consort, and so begetting is not valid. The third: there is nothing except that He is its Creator and knows it, and whoever has this attribute is free of need of everything; a son is sought only by one in need.
