"Clear proofs have come to you from your Lord" [al-An'am: 104]. This is spoken on the tongue of the Messenger, as shown by the final words: "and I am not a guardian over you" [al-An'am: 104]. Basirah (insight) is the light of the heart by which one gains insight, just as basar (sight) is the light of the eye by which one sees. That is: there has come to you, through revelation and admonition, that which is permissible for Allah, may He be exalted, and that which is not, the things that belong to the hearts, like insights. So said al-Zamakhshari. Ibn Atiyyah said: "Basirah is that which strives toward the intellect's acquisition of things considered through reflection. It is as if He said: there have come to you in the Qur'an and the signs the paths of seeing the truth and what helps toward it. Basirah for the heart is borrowed from sight of the eye." Al-Hawfi said: "Basirah is the clear, manifest proof, as Allah, may He be exalted, said: 'I call to Allah with insight' [Yusuf: 108], and 'Man is a witness against himself' [al-Qiyamah: 14]." Al-Kalbi said: "The basair are the verses of the Qur'an which contain clarification, clear proofs and admonition about what is permissible for Allah and what is impossible for Him." Attributing the coming to the basair is a metaphor to magnify their status, since they are like an absent thing whose arrival is expected, as one says: "Well-being has come."

"So whoever sees, it is for his own benefit" [al-An'am: 104]. That is: the seeing is for his own self, that is, its benefit and fruit.

"And whoever is blind, it is to his own detriment" [al-An'am: 104]. That is: the blindness is against himself, that is, the consequence of blindness returns to his own self. Seeing and blindness are metaphors for guidance and misguidance. The meaning is that the fruit of guidance and misguidance belongs only to the one who is guided or who goes astray, because He, may He be exalted, is free of need from His creation. This is one of the excellent metaphors. When He mentioned the insights, He followed them with seeing and blindness, and this is a correspondence. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "whoever sees" the truth and believes, "for his own self he sees," and by it he benefits himself; "and whoever is blind" to it, "against his own self he is blind." What we have estimated from the verbal noun is preferable, namely "so seeing and blindness are..." for two reasons. The first is that the omitted element is a single word rather than a clause, and the prepositional phrase is a core element rather than a supplement. In his estimation, the omitted element is a clause and the prepositional phrase is a supplement. The second, which is stronger, is that if the estimate were a verb, the fa' (then) would not enter, whether man is conditional or relative resembling the conditional. This is because a past-tense verb, if it is not a supplication or a fixed form, and comes as the response of a conditional or as the predicate of a subject resembling a conditional noun, does not take fa' in the response of the condition or in the predicate. If you said: "Whoever came to me, I honored him," it would not be permissible, unlike our estimate, for which fa' is necessary. Omitting it is permissible only in poetry. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: "Basirah is the name of complete perception that arises in the heart. The preceding verses are not themselves insights, but because of their strength and clarity they bring about insights for whoever recognizes them. Since they were causes of the arising of insights, they were called insights."

"And I am not a guardian over you" [al-An'am: 104]. That is: I am not a watcher who keeps account of your deeds; or a trustee who takes you to faith; or a protector for you from the punishment of Allah; or a lord who will recompense you; or a witness. These are sayings, the fourth of which is from al-Hasan and the fifth from al-Zajjaj. Al-Zamakhshari said: "(a guardian) I guard your deeds and recompense you for them. I am only a warner, and Allah is the Guardian over you." End of quotation. This is an expansion of al-Hasan's statement. Ibn Atiyyah said: "Before the rise of Islam, he was a guardian, and after that he was a guardian over the world, taking them to Islam by the sword."

"Thus do We vary the signs" [al-An'am: 105]. That is: and in the same way as We have made clear those signs, which are insights, and turned them about, We vary the signs and repeat them in many ways.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 103–110 (part 2 of 4):

﴿And they will say, "You have studied"﴾: meaning the people of Makkah, when the Qur'an was recited to them. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read دَارَسْتَ (dārasta), meaning: "You, O Muhammad, have studied with others these matters," that is, you have read it and debated it with them. This was a hint from them toward Salman and others among the non-Arabs and the Jews. Ibn 'Amir and a group outside the seven readers read دَرَسَتْ (darasat), in the active form with a hidden subject, meaning: "The verses have been studied," that is, they have been repeated upon their ears until they wore out, became old in their souls, and were effaced. The rest of the seven read دَرَسْتَ (darasta), meaning: "You, O Muhammad, have studied in the ancient books what you bring to us," just as they said: ﴿These are fables of the ancients, which he has had written down﴾ [al-Furqan: 5]. Al-Dahhak said: دَرَسْتَ means "you read and learned from Abu Fukayhah, Jabr and Yasar." It was also read دَرَّسْتَ (darrasta) with a shadda and the second person, meaning: "You studied the ancient books." It was read دُرِّسْتَ (durrista), with a shadda, in the passive form addressed to the second person. It was read دُورِسْتَ (dūrista), with no shadda and with a waw, in the passive form; the waw is substituted for the alif of dārasta. A group read دَارَسْتَ, meaning: the group from whom you learn "studied with you," and the hidden subject is permissible because the fame of studying was held by the Jews among them. It is also possible that the verb refers to the verses while its real subject is their people, meaning: "the people of the verses studied." A group read دُرِسَتْ (durisat), with a damma on the rā' and a third-person feminine subject, as an intensive form of darasat, meaning: its studying and decay became intense. Qatadah, al-Hasan and Zayd ibn 'Ali read دُرِسَتْ (durisat) in the passive, with a pronoun for the verses, a third-person form. This is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, with a variant attributed to him. Abu al-Fath said: it may be understood as meaning "it was effaced" or "it was recited." Al-Zamakhshari said the same, and said: in the sense of "it was recited" or "it was effaced." As for the sense "it was recited," it is clear, since darasa in the sense of "repeating the recitation" is transitive. As for darasa in the sense of "it decayed and was obliterated," I do not know of it being transitive, and I have not found in the poetry of the Arabs that I have examined anything but intransitive usage. Ubayy read دَرَسَ (darasa), meaning: "Muhammad studied," or "the Book studied." This is in the codex of 'Abd Allah. It is narrated from al-Hasan: دَرَسْنَ (darasna), in the active form with the feminine plural (nūn) as subject, meaning: the verses studied. It is also so in some codices of 'Abd Allah. A group read دَرَّسْنَ (darrasna), with a shadda on the rā', as an intensive of darasna. It was also read دَارِسَاتٌ (dārisāt), meaning: they are ancient, or possessing study, like ﴿a pleasing life﴾ (ʿīshatin rāḍiyatin). These are thirteen readings of this word.

A group read وَلْيَقُولُوا (wa-liyaqūlū), with a sukūn on the lām, as an imperative carrying rebuke and threat. The majority read it with a kasra on the lām. They said: this lām is the one after which an implied anna is hidden, and the verb is in the accusative by the implied anna. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is the lām of purpose (kay), and on this view it is the lām of consequence (al-ṣayrūra), like His saying: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8], meaning: because their affair came to that. Al-Zamakhshari said: the answer (jawāb) of "liyaqūlū" is omitted; its estimate is: "and that they may say, 'You have studied,' their manipulation of it." He asked: what is the difference between the two lāms in "liyaqūlū" and "linubayyinahu"? He answered: the difference between them is that the first is metaphorical and the second is literal, because the verses were varied for the sake of clarification and were not varied so that they might say "You have studied." But since this saying resulted from the variation of the verses, just as clarification resulted, it was likened to it and followed its course. It was also said: "liyaqūlū" is like "linubayyinahu." End of quotation. Calling what depends on "liyaqūlū" an answer is a strange terminology, and such a thing is not called an answer. You do not say, in "I came" from your saying "I came that you might stand," that it is an answer. This which al-Zamakhshari mentioned about the analysis of "liyaqūlū" is the view of those who deny the lām of consequence, which is also called the lām of outcome and end. It means that since its result after picking him up was that he became for them an enemy and a grief, it is made as if it were the cause of picking him up; so it is a metaphorical cause. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: the lām in "liyaqūlū," on the reading of Ibn 'Amir and those who agree with him, means "lest they say," meaning: the verses were varied and made firm lest they say, "These are fables of the ancients, old, and they have been recited and repeated upon the ears." The lām in the other readings is the lām of consequence. What Abu 'Ali permitted, namely the implied lā after the implied lām, which is an implied anna after it, is the view of some Kufans. The estimate of the speech is: "lest they say," just as they used anna explicitly in His saying: "that you may not go astray." The Basrans do not permit the hiding of lā except in an oath, as made clear there. Some scholars have taken it to be the lām of purpose in its literal sense, and said: the meaning is that these proofs are varied from state to state, so that some of them say, "You have studied," and so they increase in disbelief upon disbelief, and as a warning to others so that they increase in faith upon faith. A parallel is His saying: ﴿He leads many astray by it and guides many by it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26], and ﴿As for those in whose hearts is a disease, it adds uncleanness to their uncleanness﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125]. It is not necessarily so that what the grammarians and exegetes have mentioned, that the lām in "wa-liyaqūlū" is the lām of purpose or the lām of consequence, is correct. Rather, the apparent meaning is that it is the imperative lām, and the verb is jussive by it, not accusative by an implied anna. This is supported by the reading of the one who made the lām quiescent, and the meaning fits it well, as if it were said: "And in the same way We vary the verses, and let them say what they say, that you have studied them and learned them, or that they have studied themselves, meaning they have decayed and become old." He does not heed them, and does not pay attention to their saying. It is a command whose meaning is a threat with warning and indifference toward them and toward what they say about the verses, meaning: We vary them so that they may claim in them whatever they wish, so there is no concern with their claim.

﴿And that We may make it clear to a people who know﴾: meaning, We vary the verses. He returned the pronoun in the singular. They said: this is in the sense of the verses, because they are the Qur'an, as if He had said: "Thus We vary the Qur'an," or it refers to the Qur'an, which is indicated by "the verses" or by "you have studied," or to the verbal noun implied by "linubayyinahu" (that We may make clear), meaning: "that We may make the clarifying clear," as you say, "I struck him, Zayd," when you mean "I struck the striking, Zayd." Or it refers to the verbal noun implied by "nuṣarrifu" (We vary). Ibn 'Abbas said: "for a people" means the allies of those whom He guided to the path of right guidance.

﴿Follow what has been revealed to you from your Lord; there is no god but Him; and turn away from the polytheists﴾: He, exalted is He, commanded him to follow what was revealed to him, and to turn away from those who associated others with God. The command to turn away from them was before its abrogation (naskh, the replacement of an earlier ruling by a later one) by fighting and by driving them to the religion willingly or unwillingly. The sentence between the two commands is a parenthetical clause that emphasizes the obligation to follow what is revealed, or it stands in the position of an emphatic circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

﴿Had God willed, they would not have associated others with Him﴾: meaning, their association is not in reality by their own will, but by the will of God, exalted is He. The apparent meaning of the verse refutes the Mu'tazilah, who interpret it as the will of compulsion and coercion.

﴿We have not made you a guardian over them﴾: meaning, a watcher who keeps them from associating.

﴿Nor are you a manager over them﴾: meaning, one who has power over them. The two clauses are close in meaning, except that the first negates that God has made you a guardian over them, and the second negates that you are a manager over them. The meaning is: We have not empowered you, nor are you by yourself empowered. It fits that you turn away from them, since you are not commanded by Us to be a guardian over them, nor are you a manager over them of your own accord.

﴿Do not revile those whom they call upon besides God, lest they revile God in enmity without knowledge﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: the occasion of its revelation was that the disbelievers of Quraysh said to Abu Talib: "Either Muhammad and his companions stop reviling our gods and disparaging them, or we will revile his God and mock him." So it was revealed. It was also said: they said this when the verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides God are fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya': 98]. It was also said: the Muslims used to revile their idols, so they were forbidden, lest their reviling become a cause of reviling God, exalted is He. The ruling of this verse remains in effect for this nation. If the unbeliever is in a position of strength, and it is feared that Islam, the Messenger, or God will be reviled, then it is not lawful for a Muslim to disparage the religion of the unbeliever, nor his idol, nor his cross, nor to bring up anything that leads to that. When God, exalted is He, commanded the following of what was revealed to him and the peaceful dealing with the polytheists, He shifted from addressing him to addressing the believers, so they were forbidden to revile the idols of the polytheists. The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, was not addressed directly, although it was he on whose tongue the idols were reviled, and his companions followed him in that. This was because addressing him alone with the prohibition would contradict the noble character that he, peace be upon him, possessed, since he, peace be upon him, was neither foul-mouthed, nor clamorous, nor a reviler. Therefore the address came to the believers, saying: ﴿Do not revile﴾. The construction was not "Do not revile" (singular), as in the case of "and turn away" (singular). When obedience leads to a corruption, it ceases to be obedience, and so it is obligatory to forbid it, just as disobedience is forbidden. ﴿Those whom they call upon﴾ are the idols, meaning: the polytheists call upon them. He referred to the idols, which do not reason, with the relative pronoun for those who reason, treating what does not reason as if it reasoned, since they treated them in their worship and belief as if they were beings who reason, believing that they are intercessors for them with God, exalted is He. It was also said: it is possible that "those who call upon" refers to the disbelievers. The apparent meaning of His saying "lest they revile God" is that they would proceed to revile God if their gods were reviled, even though they acknowledge God, exalted is He. But their partisanship for their gods and their intense anger on their behalf drives them to this, so they go beyond moderation to what contradicts reason, just as happens with some Muslims when their anger becomes intense and deviates; they may utter what leads to disbelief. We seek refuge in God from that. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: perhaps some of them were holding to the doctrine of the eternity of time and denying the Creator, so they would commit this kind of outrage. Or the Muslims used to revile the idols, and the idolaters used to revile the Messenger, so the reviling of the Messenger was treated as the reviling of God, exalted is He, just as He said: ﴿Indeed those who pledge allegiance to you pledge allegiance only to God﴾ [al-Fath: 10], and as He said: ﴿Indeed those who injure God and His Messenger﴾ [al-Ahzab: 57]. Or some disbelievers believed that a devil drove the Messenger to claim prophethood and messengership, and out of their ignorance they cursed that devil by saying that he was the god of Muhammad. End of quotation. These are possibilities that contradict the apparent meaning, and he mentioned them only because he stated that those who acknowledge the existence of the Creator do not dare to revile Him, exalted is He. We have already mentioned what can be taken as keeping the words to their apparent meaning. Some Sufis said: the meaning is: address them with the language of argument and the binding of proof, and do not speak to them according to the impulses of the self and custom. The word "fa-yasubbū" (so that they revile) is in the accusative as a response to the prohibition. It was also said that it is jussive by coordination, as in your saying: "Do not stretch it, so that you tear it." ʿAdwan is a verbal noun of 'adā, and likewise ʿadwa and ʿudwān, in the sense of "transgressed," meaning "wronged." Al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Qatadah, Ya'qub, Sallam and 'Abd Allah ibn Yazid read it with a damma on the ʿayn and the dāl and a shadda on the wāw, and it is a verbal noun of 'adā, as we have mentioned. They allowed for both of them to be in the accusative as a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause, or as a verbal noun from a word other than the verb itself, since reviling God is transgression, or as an object of purpose. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: some Meccans read it, and al-Zamakhshari specified it, saying of Ibn Kathir: with a fatha on the ʿayn and a damma on the dāl and a shadda on the wāw, meaning "enemies." It is in the accusative as an emphatic circumstantial clause, and ʿadūw (enemy) is predicated of a plural, as He said: ﴿They are the enemy﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 4]. The meaning of "without knowledge" is in ignorance of what is due to God, exalted is He, that He should be mentioned by it, and this explains the meaning of transgression.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 103–110 (part 3 of 4):

﴿Thus We have made attractive to every nation their deeds﴾: that is, like the making attractive of the worship of idols to the polytheists, ﴿We have made attractive to every nation﴾. The apparent sense of ﴿to every nation their deeds﴾ is generality, both regarding the nations and regarding the deeds. Thus believers and disbelievers are included. Its making attractive (tazyin) is what He creates and originates in souls of love for good or evil and of following its paths. The making attractive by Satan (tazyin al-shaytan) is what he casts into souls of whisperings and evil thoughts. Al-Zamakhshari specified ﴿to every nation their deeds﴾, and said: among the nations of the disbelievers, their evil deeds. That is, We left them to themselves and their affairs, and did not restrain them, until their evil deeds became good in their eyes, and We gave Satan respite until he made them attractive, or We made him attractive in their claim and their saying: "Indeed Allah commanded us with this and made it attractive for us." End. And this is in accordance with his Mu'tazili method. Al-Hasan said: that is, ﴿We made attractive to every nation﴾ the deed which We made obligatory upon them, so he made (zayyana) mean (shara'a), prescribed, and ﴿every nation﴾ is general, while the deed is specific to what Allah the Exalted has made obligatory. Al-Zajjaj denied this and said: it means "Allah sealed their hearts," and the evidence for it is: ﴿Is then one to whom the evil of his deed is made attractive so that he sees it as good [equal to one who is rightly guided]? For indeed, Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾ [Fatir: 8]. End. What al-Hasan explained has been clarified by some of the Mu'tazilah, who said: the intended meaning of the making attractive of the deed is the making attractive of what is commanded, not what is forbidden, and it is to be understood as specific, even though it is general, lest it lead to contradiction between the texts; for it is stated that Allah made faith attractive and disliked disbelief, in His saying: ﴿But Allah has endeared to you the faith and made it attractive in your hearts, and has made hateful to you disbelief﴾ [al-Hujurat: 7]. So if the making attractive of disbelief entered into the meaning of this verse, there would necessarily be a contradiction between the two verses. For this reason, He attributed the making attractive to Satan, in His saying: ﴿Satan made their deeds attractive to them﴾ [al-Anfal: 48]. So Allah does not make attractive what Satan made attractive. Thus we say: Allah makes attractive what He commands, and Satan makes attractive what He forbids, so that this is acting in accordance with all the texts. End. It was answered that there is no contradiction because the making attractive differs: Allah's making attractive through creation of desires, and Satan's making attractive through calling to acts of disobedience. So the verse is on its generality, for every nation and for their deeds.

﴿Then to their Lord is their return, and He will inform them of what they used to do﴾: that is, their affair is entrusted to Allah, and He is Knowing of their conditions, aware of their inner selves, and their turning back on the Day of Resurrection is to Him, so each will be recompensed according to what their deeds require. In that is a beautiful promise for the good-doer and a warning for the wrongdoer.

﴿And they swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that if a sign came to them, they would surely believe in it﴾: that is, a sign of their own suggestion, like their saying: "Until you send down..." ﴿If We willed, We would send down upon them from the sky a sign, so that their necks would remain humbly subjected to it﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 4]. "Send it down upon us so that we may believe in it." The Muslims said: "O Messenger of Allah, send it down upon them," so this verse was revealed; this is related from Ibn Abbas. Or like their saying: "Let al-Safa become gold," until they mentioned the miracles of Musa in the rock, of Isa in raising the dead, and of Salih in the she-camel. The Messenger stood supplicating, and Jibril (peace be upon him) (p-201) came to him and said: "If you wish, al-Safa will become gold; but if they do not believe, they will all be destroyed immediately, as was done to the previous nations, since they did not believe in the suggested signs. And if you wish, leave them until whoever among them repents turns in repentance." So he said: "Rather, until whoever among them repents turns in repentance." They suggested a specific sign only because they doubted the Qur'an, and for this they said: "You have studied," i.e., with the scholars, and you have discussed with the People of the Torah and the Gospel. Most of them were arrogant and obstinate. The meaning is that they swore their utmost oath. The oath was called qasam because it occurs when people divide into those who affirm and those who deny, so it is as if it strengthens the side one chooses. Al-Tibrizi said: al-iqsam is an form (if'al) from al-qasam, which means portion and division. Their swearing by Allah was the utmost in oath-taking, and they used to swear by their fathers and their gods, but when the matter was great they swore by Allah the Exalted. Al-jahd, with a fatha on the jim, means hardship, and with a damma means capacity; some treat them as having one meaning. (Jahda) is in the accusative as a verbal noun governed by (aqsamu), meaning: they swore with the utmost of their oaths; and al-aymān means the oaths, as you say: "I struck him with the strongest of blows." Al-Hawfi said it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in (aqsamu), meaning: striving in their oaths. Al-Mubarrad said it is a verbal noun governed by a verb of its own root. The discussion of ﴿jahda aymanihim﴾ has already occurred in al-Ma'idah. And ﴿la'in ja'athum﴾ is a report about them, not a quotation of their statement; for had their statement been quoted, it would be: "la'in ja'atna ayah". He treated the report of the oath as the quotation of the oath in the wording of what the swearer uttered, and that it is not meant by it any sign in general, since many signs had come to them, but they wanted a suggested sign, as we have mentioned. Talhah ibn Musarrif read: ﴿la-yu'manna bihā﴾ in the passive voice and with the light nun.

﴿Say: Indeed the signs are with Allah﴾: this is a command to respond to them, and that the coming of the signs is not in my hands; rather that belongs to Allah the Exalted, who is capable of them, and He sends them down in the way of wisdom as He wills for His wisdom, and they are not with me so that they may be demanded of me.

﴿And what will make you aware that when they come they will not believe?﴾ It is interrogative, and the pronoun of the subject in (yush'irukum) refers back to it. Some read it with the damma of the ra' omitted, and it is read with its partial suppression. As for the address, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said it is addressed to the disbelievers; al-Farra' and others said the one addressed is the believers. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-Alimi and al-A'sha from Abu Bakr read it, and Ibn 'Atiyyah, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim in the narration of Dawud al-Iyadi said that it is with a kasra on the hamza, while the rest of the seven read it with a fatha. Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah read: (la yu'minun) with the second-person ta' of address, and the rest of the seven read it with the third-person ya' of absence. Thus four readings arise. The first: kasra on the hamza and the ya', and this is the reading of Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Abu Bakr in one narration on the kasra of the hamza. This is a clear reading: Allah the Exalted informed that they "do not believe" definitively, on the assumption of the coming of the sign, and the sentence is complete at His saying: ﴿And what will make you aware﴾, and the complement of (yush'irukum) is omitted, meaning: ﴿and what will make you aware﴾ of what will happen. If the address is to the disbelievers, the implied meaning is: ﴿and what will make you aware﴾ of what will happen from you. Then He informed them by way of iltifat (a shift) of what He knows of their state if the signs came to them. If the address is to the believers, the implied meaning is: ﴿and what will make you aware﴾, O believers, of what will happen from them; then He informed the believers of His knowledge about them. The second reading: kasra on the hamza and the ta', and this is the narration of al-Alimi and al-A'sha from Abu Bakr from 'Asim. The suitable reading is that the address is to the disbelievers in this reading, as if it were said: "And what will make you know, O disbelievers, what will happen from you?" Then He informed them with certainty that they "will not believe" on the assumption of the coming of it. It is very remote that the address in ﴿and what will make you aware﴾ is to the believers while in "they will not believe" it is to the disbelievers. The third reading: fatha on the hamza and the ta', and this is the reading of Nafi', al-Kisa'i and Hafs. The apparent sense is that the address is to the believers, and the meaning: "And what will make you know, O believers, that the sign which you propose, when it comes (p-202) they will not believe in it," meaning: I know that when it comes they will not believe, while you do not know this. The believers were hoping for their faith when that sign came, and wishing for its coming, so He said: "And what will make you know that they will not believe," in the sense that you do not know what My knowledge has preceded concerning them, that they will not believe. Do you not see His saying: "as they did not believe in it the first time"? It is very remote that the address in ﴿and what will make you aware﴾ is to the disbelievers. In this reading, the (anna) is verbal (masdariyyah), and not in the sense of negation. Some exegetes took (anna) here to mean (la'alla), and that usage has been reported from their speech: they say: "Go to the market, for you are buying meat," meaning "perhaps you are." Imru' al-Qays said:
"Halt upon the ruined abode, for we weep for the dwellings as Ibn Haram wept."
Abu 'Ubaydah and others mention this, and (la'alla) often occurs in such a context; Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself﴾ [Abasa: 3], ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ [al-Shura: 17]. In the codex of Ubayy: "And what will make you know? Perhaps it, when it comes, they will not believe." Abu 'Ali weakened this view on the ground that the expectation indicated by (la'alla) does not suit the reading with kasra, since that reading indicates a judgement from Him, the Exalted, upon them that they will not believe. But he did not make (anna-ha) governed by (yush'irukum); rather he made it a reason with its preposition elided, and the implied sense for him is: ﴿Say: Indeed the signs are with Allah﴾ because when they come they will not believe. So He does not bring them because of their insistence upon their disbelief, and this is like "And nothing prevented Us from sending the signs except that the earlier peoples denied them" — that is, the suggested signs. End. And ﴿And what will make you aware﴾ would be a parenthesis between the caused and its cause, since the meaning becomes: ﴿Say: Indeed the signs are with Allah﴾, that is, the suggested ones, He does not bring them, because of the absence of their faith and their insistence on their error. Some made (la) superfluous, so the meaning would be: "And what will make you know of their faith," as they said: "when it comes." He made it superfluous only because if it remained in negation, the statement would be an excuse for the disbelievers, and the intended meaning of the sign would be corrupted. This is from Ibn 'Atiyyah, who said: al-Zajjaj and others weakened the superfluity of (la). End of Ibn 'Atiyyah's words. The one who holds that (la) is superfluous is al-Kisa'i and al-Farra'. Al-Zajjaj said: Sibawayh claimed that its meaning is "perhaps it, when it comes, they will not believe," and this is the reading of the people of Madinah. He said: this view is stronger in Arabic. As for the one who said that (la) is idle, he is mistaken, because what is idle cannot be non-idle; and whoever reads with the kasra, there is consensus that (la) is not idle, so it is not permissible that the meaning be affirmative at one time and otherwise in the context of one speech. Some exegetes interpreted the verse by supposing an elided conjunct which removes (la) from being superfluous, and its estimated form: ﴿And what will make you aware that when they come they will not believe﴾ or they will believe, meaning: what will make you know of the absence of faith or its occurrence? This was mentioned by al-Nahhas and others. The statement does not need the superfluity of (la), nor this supposition, nor for (anna) to mean (la'alla). All this is a departure from the apparent sense for the sake of an assumed meaning; rather, taking it in its apparent sense is better, and it is clear and permissible, as we have investigated at the outset, namely: ﴿And what will make you aware﴾ and inform you, by knowledge of the absence of their faith, there is no way for you to become aware of it.

The fourth reading: opening the hamza and the taa (أَنَّهَا read as إِنَّهَا... no, fathah on both). This is the reading of Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah. The apparent meaning is that it is addressed to the disbelievers. The sense of this reading becomes clear if "لا" is taken as an extra particle (ziyadah), i.e., "And what makes you know that you will believe when it comes, as you swore by it?" It also works if "أنّ" is taken to mean "لعلّ" (perhaps) and "لا" as a negation, i.e., "And what makes you know about their condition? Perhaps when it comes they will not believe in it." Likewise, the meaning is sound if the conjunct is omitted, i.e., "And what makes you know about the absence of your belief when it comes, or its occurrence? For the outcome of your affair is hidden from you, so how do you swear by belief when the sign comes to you?" It is also sound if "أنّ" is taken as a causal particle ('illah), i.e., "Say: The signs are only with God" (﴿قُلْ إِنَّمَا الْآيَاتُ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ﴾), so He does not bring them to you, "for when they come, they will not believe" (﴿إِذَا جَاءَتْ لَا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾), and what makes you aware that you will believe? But if "أنّ" (anna-ha) is kept as the object of "يُشْعِرُكم" and "لا" is kept as a negation, then the meaning of this reading becomes problematic, because it would mean "And what makes you aware, O disbelievers, of the absence of your belief when the proposed sign comes to you?" Whereas what fits the beginning of the verse is "And what makes you aware" of belief occurring from you when it comes. It may also be that the sense is: "And what could make you aware of the absence of belief when it comes?" That is, such a thought does not occur to your minds; rather, you are resolved to believe when it comes. Yet I know that you will not believe when it comes, because you have a seal upon your hearts, and how many signs have come to you without your believing. Some exegetes held that "ما" in His saying "وما يُشْعِرُكم" is a negation, and the subject of "يُشْعِرُكم" is a pronoun referring to God. Taking it as a negation strains the meaning of the verse, whether "أنّ" is opened or kept with a kasrah. The complement of "لا يُؤْمِنُونَ" is omitted, and what justified its omission is that the word it would depend on falls at the verse-end (fasilah); its implied form is: "they will not believe" in it. It has become clear from the ordering of these four readings that the address cannot be to the believers absolutely, nor to the disbelievers absolutely; rather, the address is according to what makes the meaning of the reading correct.

﴿And We turn their hearts and their eyes, as they did not believe in it the first time, and We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾

The apparent meaning is that "وَنُقَلِّبُ" is a resumptive sentence (jumlah isti'nafiyyah), in which God informs that He does this to them. It indicates bewilderment, hesitation, and turning a thing away from its direction. The meaning is that He turns them away from guidance and leaves them in error and disbelief. "كَمَا" is causal (lil-ta'lil), i.e., He does this to them because they did not believe in it the first time the guidance of God came to them, as He said: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is a disease, it adds filth to their filth, and they die while they are disbelievers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125]. The end of the verse confirms this meaning: ﴿And We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾, i.e., We leave them to plunge into evil, and in excess of it they become bewildered. All this is a report from God of what He does to them in this world. Another group said this report is on the presumption that if the sign they proposed came, We would do this to them. For this reason al-Zamakhshari said: "And We turn their hearts and We leave them" is coordinated (ma'tuf) on "لا يُؤْمِنُونَ" and falls under the ruling of "وَمَا يُشْعِرُكُمْ", in the sense: "And what makes you aware that they will not believe, and what makes you aware that We turn their hearts and their eyes?" That is, We set a seal on their eyes and hearts so they neither understand nor see the truth, as they were when Our signs first came, not believing in them, because of which "and what makes you aware that We leave them in their transgression?" That is, We leave them to themselves and do not restrain them or turn them away from transgression until they wander blindly in it. End of quotation. This is the meaning of what Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Ibn Zayd said. They said: "If We brought them a sign as they asked, We would turn their hearts and eyes away from believing in it and We would stand between them and guidance, so they would not believe, just as they did not believe in what they had seen before it, as a punishment for them for that." The difference between this view and the one we began with is that the first is a resumed report of what God does to them in this world, whereas this is a report on the presumption that the proposed sign comes. The first is actual, and this is not actual, because the proposed sign did not occur, so what was consequent upon it did not occur. Muqatil said: "We turn the hearts and eyes of these people away from belief and from the signs, as their predecessors among the earlier nations did not believe in the signs they saw." It was also said: the turning is by disturbing their souls with worry and grief. Al-Kirmani said: its meaning is that We encompass with knowledge what is in their breasts and the treachery of their eyes. End of quotation. This interpretation does not fit His saying "as they did not believe in it the first time", neither as causal nor as comparative, except if it is made dependent on the phrase "that when they come they will not believe", i.e., "as they did not believe in it the first time," so that the interpretation of this turning as encompassing knowledge is possible, though far-fetched.

Al-Ka'bi said: the intended meaning is that We do not do to them what We do to the believers of benefits and graces, because they removed themselves from guidance by means of disbelief. End of quotation. This is in keeping with his Mu'tazili method.

The meaning of turning the heart and the eye is what arises from the heart and eye of motives toward bewilderment and error, because the heart and eye do not turn by themselves; so ascribing the turning to them is metaphorical (majaz). The hearts (al-af'idah) are mentioned first because the locus of motives and deterrents is the heart; when the motive takes hold in the heart, the eye turns to it whether it wills or not, and when deterrents take hold in the heart, the eye turns away from it, even if the gaze is visibly fixed upon it. These interpretations take the matter to be in this world. Another group said it is a report that God does this to them in the Hereafter. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it is an answer to their request in the Hereafter to return to the world, and the meaning is: If they were returned, We would stand between them and guidance as We stood between them and it the first time while they were in the world. End of quotation. This is at odds with the structure of the sentence.

It was also said: their turning is in Hell, upon its flames and embers, so that they are punished, as they did not believe in it the first time, meaning in this world. This was said by al-Jubba'i. Abu al-Hudhayl said: the turning of their hearts is their hearts reaching their throats, as He said: ﴿And warn them of the Day of the Imminent﴾ [Ghafir: 18]. It was also said: the turning of their eyes is into blueness. Taking this to refer to the Hereafter is weak and the composition is strained, because the turning would be in the Hereafter while leaving them in transgression would be in this world, so the two times differ without evidence for their difference. Rather, the apparent meaning is that this is a resumed report, as we established at first. The particle "كَمَا" — we said it is causal, and this is clear in it, though its use in that sense is rare. Another group said "كَمَا" has the meaning of recompense (mujazah), i.e., since they did not believe in it the first time, We requite them by turning their hearts away from guidance and sealing their hearts, as if He said: "And We turn their hearts and eyes as recompense for their not believing the first time in what they were called to of the law." This was said by Ibn 'Atiyyah. This is the meaning of causation that we mentioned, except that calling it recompense is strange; it is not known in the speech of the grammarians that the kaf is for recompense. It was also said: it is for comparison. It was also said: there is an omission in the speech, its implied form being: "So they will not believe in it a second time, as they did not believe in it the first time." It was also said: the kaf is an adjective (na't) of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), i.e., a turning in proportion to their disbelief, that is, a punishment equal to their disobedience. This was said by Abu al-Baqa'. Al-Hawfi said: it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, the implied form being: "They will not believe in it with a second belief, as they did not believe in it the first time." End of quotation. The pronoun refers to God, or the Qur'an, or the Messenger; these are the views. Whoever held that it refers to the turning is further removed. "أَوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ" is in the accusative as a time adverb (zarf zaman).

Al-Nakha'i read: "وَيُقَلِّبُ وَيَذَرُهُمْ" with ya' in both, the subject being the pronoun of God. He also read, according to what Mughirah narrated from him: "وَتُقَلَّبُ أَفْئِدَتُهُمْ وَأَبْصَارُهُمْ", with raf' in both, in the passive voice, and "وَيَذَرُهُمْ" with ya' and sukun on the ra'. Al-A'mash and al-Hamadani agreed with him on "وَيَذَرُهُمُ". Al-Zamakhshari said: al-A'mash read: "وَتُقَلَّبُ أَفْئِدَتُهُمْ وَأَبْصَارُهُمْ", in the passive voice.

That is Allah, your Lord; there is no god but Him, the Creator of all things, so worship Him, and He is the Custodian over all things [al-An'am: 102]. (That) refers to the One described by the attributes mentioned earlier, that He is the Originator who has taken no consort and no son, the Creator of existing things, the One who knows everything: He is Allah. He began with the proper name, then said "your Lord," meaning your Owner and the One who looks after your interests. Then He confined divinity to Himself, then repeated the description of His creation of "all things" [al-An'am: 102], then commanded that He be worshipped, because whoever has these attributes combined in him is deserving of worship and of being singled out for it, so that no partner is taken alongside Him. Then He informed that, together with those earlier attributes, among which is the creation of all things, and as the One who owns all things, including provisions and lifespans, He is a watcher over deeds.

"No vision can encompass Him, while He encompasses vision" [al-An'am: 103]. It has been said that al-idrak (perception, "encompassing") means the comprehensive grasp of a thing. Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, Atiyyah al-Awfi, Ibn al-Musayyib and al-Zajjaj interpreted it this way here. Ibn al-Musayyib said: "vision does not encompass Him," and al-Zajjaj said: "it does not encompass His reality." Idrak includes encompassing a thing, reaching its depths, and containing it from all its sides. Alternatively, "vision" is a metonymy for persons, because through their eyes persons perceive things, so the meaning would be: "creation does not perceive Him, while He perceives them." Or the meaning may be the vision of the heart, that is, the knowledge of creatures does not grasp Him, while He grasps their knowledge and their selves, because He is not encompassed by them. On this reading, it is impossible for Allah according to the Muslims. Seeing (ru'yah) is not contradicted by the negation of idrak. It has also been said that idrak here means ru'yah (seeing). This is a matter on which the Muslims differ. The Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school) deny that it is possible, while Ahl al-Sunnah (the Sunni majority) hold that it is possible by reason and that it occurs by revelation. This is a question discussed in the science of Usul al-Din (the principles of religion), where the proofs of both sides are fully presented. I have seen in it a large book by Abu Ja'far al-Tusi, one of the intellectuals of the Imamiyyah (Twelver Shi'ah), in which he supports the view of his companions who deny seeing. Those who deny seeing have used this verse as evidence for their position, and they have been answered that idrak is other than ru'yah. Even if we accept that idrak is ru'yah, the "vision" here is restricted, that is, the vision of the disbelievers already mentioned, or it means that He is not perceived in this world. Al-Maturidi said: "Vision (basar) is the subtle substance that Allah, may He be exalted, placed in the faculty of sight, by which visible things are perceived." His saying "and He perceives vision" indicates that idrak here does not mean merely ru'yah, for if it meant merely seeing, there would be no particular distinction for Him in it and no praise, since we ourselves see vision. This shows that the meaning of idrak is encompassing the reality of a thing. So vision cannot encompass His reality, while He encompasses its reality. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The meaning is that vision does not attach to Him and does not perceive Him, because He is too exalted to be seen in His essence, since vision only attaches to what is in a direction, either originally or derivatively, such as bodies and forms. 'And He perceives vision': and because of the subtlety of His perception of perceived things, He perceives those subtle substances which no perceiver can perceive."

"He is the Subtle, the All-Aware" [al-An'am: 103]. He is too subtle to be perceived by vision, the All-Aware of everything subtle, "and He perceives vision" [al-An'am: 103], nothing subtle escapes His perception. This is an instance of al-laff (the wrapping of two matters in one expression). End of quotation. This is in line with his Mu'tazili position. Reports from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about believers seeing Allah in the Hereafter are abundant. But they differ over whether the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw Him in this world with his eyes on the night of the Mi'raj (Ascension). A group of hadith scholars, jurists and theologians denied this. Aishah, Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Hurayrah are reported to have said so, though with variant reports from them. Ibn Abbas, Ka'b, al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari and a group of the Companions held that he saw Him with his eyes and the sight of his head. This is also reported from Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Hurayrah, but the first view from Ibn Mas'ud is more widely known. It has been said: "And He perceives vision" means nothing escapes His knowledge. The word "vision" was specified for the sake of rhetorical balance (tajnis), that is, the antithesis. Al-Zajjaj said: "In this is evidence that creatures do not perceive vision," that is, they do not know the true nature of the sight by which a person sees through his two eyes, and not through any other of his bodily organs.

"And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware" [al-An'am: 103]. Abu al-Aliyah said: "Subtle in extracting things, All-Aware of their places."

"Clear proofs have come to you from your Lord" [al-An'am: 104]. This is spoken on the tongue of the Messenger, as shown by the final words: "and I am not a guardian over you" [al-An'am: 104]. Basirah (insight) is the light of the heart by which one gains insight, just as basar (sight) is the light of the eye by which one sees. That is: there has come to you, through revelation and admonition, that which is permissible for Allah, may He be exalted, and that which is not, the things that belong to the hearts, like insights. So said al-Zamakhshari. Ibn Atiyyah said: "Basirah is that which strives toward the intellect's acquisition of things considered through reflection. It is as if He said: there have come to you in the Qur'an and the signs the paths of seeing the truth and what helps toward it. Basirah for the heart is borrowed from sight of the eye." Al-Hawfi said: "Basirah is the clear, manifest proof, as Allah, may He be exalted, said: 'I call to Allah with insight' [Yusuf: 108], and 'Man is a witness against himself' [al-Qiyamah: 14]." Al-Kalbi said: "The basair are the verses of the Qur'an which contain clarification, clear proofs and admonition about what is permissible for Allah and what is impossible for Him." Attributing the coming to the basair is a metaphor to magnify their status, since they are like an absent thing whose arrival is expected, as one says: "Well-being has come."

"So whoever sees, it is for his own benefit" [al-An'am: 104]. That is: the seeing is for his own self, that is, its benefit and fruit.

"And whoever is blind, it is to his own detriment" [al-An'am: 104]. That is: the blindness is against himself, that is, the consequence of blindness returns to his own self. Seeing and blindness are metaphors for guidance and misguidance. The meaning is that the fruit of guidance and misguidance belongs only to the one who is guided or who goes astray, because He, may He be exalted, is free of need from His creation. This is one of the excellent metaphors. When He mentioned the insights, He followed them with seeing and blindness, and this is a correspondence. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "whoever sees" the truth and believes, "for his own self he sees," and by it he benefits himself; "and whoever is blind" to it, "against his own self he is blind." What we have estimated from the verbal noun is preferable, namely "so seeing and blindness are..." for two reasons. The first is that the omitted element is a single word rather than a clause, and the prepositional phrase is a core element rather than a supplement. In his estimation, the omitted element is a clause and the prepositional phrase is a supplement. The second, which is stronger, is that if the estimate were a verb, the fa' (then) would not enter, whether man is conditional or relative resembling the conditional. This is because a past-tense verb, if it is not a supplication or a fixed form, and comes as the response of a conditional or as the predicate of a subject resembling a conditional noun, does not take fa' in the response of the condition or in the predicate. If you said: "Whoever came to me, I honored him," it would not be permissible, unlike our estimate, for which fa' is necessary. Omitting it is permissible only in poetry. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: "Basirah is the name of complete perception that arises in the heart. The preceding verses are not themselves insights, but because of their strength and clarity they bring about insights for whoever recognizes them. Since they were causes of the arising of insights, they were called insights."

"And I am not a guardian over you" [al-An'am: 104]. That is: I am not a watcher who keeps account of your deeds; or a trustee who takes you to faith; or a protector for you from the punishment of Allah; or a lord who will recompense you; or a witness. These are sayings, the fourth of which is from al-Hasan and the fifth from al-Zajjaj. Al-Zamakhshari said: "(a guardian) I guard your deeds and recompense you for them. I am only a warner, and Allah is the Guardian over you." End of quotation. This is an expansion of al-Hasan's statement. Ibn Atiyyah said: "Before the rise of Islam, he was a guardian, and after that he was a guardian over the world, taking them to Islam by the sword."

"Thus do We vary the signs" [al-An'am: 105]. That is: and in the same way as We have made clear those signs, which are insights, and turned them about, We vary the signs and repeat them in many ways.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 103–110 (part 2 of 4):

﴿And they will say, "You have studied"﴾: meaning the people of Makkah, when the Qur'an was recited to them. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read دَارَسْتَ (dārasta), meaning: "You, O Muhammad, have studied with others these matters," that is, you have read it and debated it with them. This was a hint from them toward Salman and others among the non-Arabs and the Jews. Ibn 'Amir and a group outside the seven readers read دَرَسَتْ (darasat), in the active form with a hidden subject, meaning: "The verses have been studied," that is, they have been repeated upon their ears until they wore out, became old in their souls, and were effaced. The rest of the seven read دَرَسْتَ (darasta), meaning: "You, O Muhammad, have studied in the ancient books what you bring to us," just as they said: ﴿These are fables of the ancients, which he has had written down﴾ [al-Furqan: 5]. Al-Dahhak said: دَرَسْتَ means "you read and learned from Abu Fukayhah, Jabr and Yasar." It was also read دَرَّسْتَ (darrasta) with a shadda and the second person, meaning: "You studied the ancient books." It was read دُرِّسْتَ (durrista), with a shadda, in the passive form addressed to the second person. It was read دُورِسْتَ (dūrista), with no shadda and with a waw, in the passive form; the waw is substituted for the alif of dārasta. A group read دَارَسْتَ, meaning: the group from whom you learn "studied with you," and the hidden subject is permissible because the fame of studying was held by the Jews among them. It is also possible that the verb refers to the verses while its real subject is their people, meaning: "the people of the verses studied." A group read دُرِسَتْ (durisat), with a damma on the rā' and a third-person feminine subject, as an intensive form of darasat, meaning: its studying and decay became intense. Qatadah, al-Hasan and Zayd ibn 'Ali read دُرِسَتْ (durisat) in the passive, with a pronoun for the verses, a third-person form. This is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, with a variant attributed to him. Abu al-Fath said: it may be understood as meaning "it was effaced" or "it was recited." Al-Zamakhshari said the same, and said: in the sense of "it was recited" or "it was effaced." As for the sense "it was recited," it is clear, since darasa in the sense of "repeating the recitation" is transitive. As for darasa in the sense of "it decayed and was obliterated," I do not know of it being transitive, and I have not found in the poetry of the Arabs that I have examined anything but intransitive usage. Ubayy read دَرَسَ (darasa), meaning: "Muhammad studied," or "the Book studied." This is in the codex of 'Abd Allah. It is narrated from al-Hasan: دَرَسْنَ (darasna), in the active form with the feminine plural (nūn) as subject, meaning: the verses studied. It is also so in some codices of 'Abd Allah. A group read دَرَّسْنَ (darrasna), with a shadda on the rā', as an intensive of darasna. It was also read دَارِسَاتٌ (dārisāt), meaning: they are ancient, or possessing study, like ﴿a pleasing life﴾ (ʿīshatin rāḍiyatin). These are thirteen readings of this word.

A group read وَلْيَقُولُوا (wa-liyaqūlū), with a sukūn on the lām, as an imperative carrying rebuke and threat. The majority read it with a kasra on the lām. They said: this lām is the one after which an implied anna is hidden, and the verb is in the accusative by the implied anna. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is the lām of purpose (kay), and on this view it is the lām of consequence (al-ṣayrūra), like His saying: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8], meaning: because their affair came to that. Al-Zamakhshari said: the answer (jawāb) of "liyaqūlū" is omitted; its estimate is: "and that they may say, 'You have studied,' their manipulation of it." He asked: what is the difference between the two lāms in "liyaqūlū" and "linubayyinahu"? He answered: the difference between them is that the first is metaphorical and the second is literal, because the verses were varied for the sake of clarification and were not varied so that they might say "You have studied." But since this saying resulted from the variation of the verses, just as clarification resulted, it was likened to it and followed its course. It was also said: "liyaqūlū" is like "linubayyinahu." End of quotation. Calling what depends on "liyaqūlū" an answer is a strange terminology, and such a thing is not called an answer. You do not say, in "I came" from your saying "I came that you might stand," that it is an answer. This which al-Zamakhshari mentioned about the analysis of "liyaqūlū" is the view of those who deny the lām of consequence, which is also called the lām of outcome and end. It means that since its result after picking him up was that he became for them an enemy and a grief, it is made as if it were the cause of picking him up; so it is a metaphorical cause. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: the lām in "liyaqūlū," on the reading of Ibn 'Amir and those who agree with him, means "lest they say," meaning: the verses were varied and made firm lest they say, "These are fables of the ancients, old, and they have been recited and repeated upon the ears." The lām in the other readings is the lām of consequence. What Abu 'Ali permitted, namely the implied lā after the implied lām, which is an implied anna after it, is the view of some Kufans. The estimate of the speech is: "lest they say," just as they used anna explicitly in His saying: "that you may not go astray." The Basrans do not permit the hiding of lā except in an oath, as made clear there. Some scholars have taken it to be the lām of purpose in its literal sense, and said: the meaning is that these proofs are varied from state to state, so that some of them say, "You have studied," and so they increase in disbelief upon disbelief, and as a warning to others so that they increase in faith upon faith. A parallel is His saying: ﴿He leads many astray by it and guides many by it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26], and ﴿As for those in whose hearts is a disease, it adds uncleanness to their uncleanness﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125]. It is not necessarily so that what the grammarians and exegetes have mentioned, that the lām in "wa-liyaqūlū" is the lām of purpose or the lām of consequence, is correct. Rather, the apparent meaning is that it is the imperative lām, and the verb is jussive by it, not accusative by an implied anna. This is supported by the reading of the one who made the lām quiescent, and the meaning fits it well, as if it were said: "And in the same way We vary the verses, and let them say what they say, that you have studied them and learned them, or that they have studied themselves, meaning they have decayed and become old." He does not heed them, and does not pay attention to their saying. It is a command whose meaning is a threat with warning and indifference toward them and toward what they say about the verses, meaning: We vary them so that they may claim in them whatever they wish, so there is no concern with their claim.

﴿And that We may make it clear to a people who know﴾: meaning, We vary the verses. He returned the pronoun in the singular. They said: this is in the sense of the verses, because they are the Qur'an, as if He had said: "Thus We vary the Qur'an," or it refers to the Qur'an, which is indicated by "the verses" or by "you have studied," or to the verbal noun implied by "linubayyinahu" (that We may make clear), meaning: "that We may make the clarifying clear," as you say, "I struck him, Zayd," when you mean "I struck the striking, Zayd." Or it refers to the verbal noun implied by "nuṣarrifu" (We vary). Ibn 'Abbas said: "for a people" means the allies of those whom He guided to the path of right guidance.

﴿Follow what has been revealed to you from your Lord; there is no god but Him; and turn away from the polytheists﴾: He, exalted is He, commanded him to follow what was revealed to him, and to turn away from those who associated others with God. The command to turn away from them was before its abrogation (naskh, the replacement of an earlier ruling by a later one) by fighting and by driving them to the religion willingly or unwillingly. The sentence between the two commands is a parenthetical clause that emphasizes the obligation to follow what is revealed, or it stands in the position of an emphatic circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

﴿Had God willed, they would not have associated others with Him﴾: meaning, their association is not in reality by their own will, but by the will of God, exalted is He. The apparent meaning of the verse refutes the Mu'tazilah, who interpret it as the will of compulsion and coercion.

﴿We have not made you a guardian over them﴾: meaning, a watcher who keeps them from associating.

﴿Nor are you a manager over them﴾: meaning, one who has power over them. The two clauses are close in meaning, except that the first negates that God has made you a guardian over them, and the second negates that you are a manager over them. The meaning is: We have not empowered you, nor are you by yourself empowered. It fits that you turn away from them, since you are not commanded by Us to be a guardian over them, nor are you a manager over them of your own accord.

﴿Do not revile those whom they call upon besides God, lest they revile God in enmity without knowledge﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: the occasion of its revelation was that the disbelievers of Quraysh said to Abu Talib: "Either Muhammad and his companions stop reviling our gods and disparaging them, or we will revile his God and mock him." So it was revealed. It was also said: they said this when the verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides God are fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya': 98]. It was also said: the Muslims used to revile their idols, so they were forbidden, lest their reviling become a cause of reviling God, exalted is He. The ruling of this verse remains in effect for this nation. If the unbeliever is in a position of strength, and it is feared that Islam, the Messenger, or God will be reviled, then it is not lawful for a Muslim to disparage the religion of the unbeliever, nor his idol, nor his cross, nor to bring up anything that leads to that. When God, exalted is He, commanded the following of what was revealed to him and the peaceful dealing with the polytheists, He shifted from addressing him to addressing the believers, so they were forbidden to revile the idols of the polytheists. The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, was not addressed directly, although it was he on whose tongue the idols were reviled, and his companions followed him in that. This was because addressing him alone with the prohibition would contradict the noble character that he, peace be upon him, possessed, since he, peace be upon him, was neither foul-mouthed, nor clamorous, nor a reviler. Therefore the address came to the believers, saying: ﴿Do not revile﴾. The construction was not "Do not revile" (singular), as in the case of "and turn away" (singular). When obedience leads to a corruption, it ceases to be obedience, and so it is obligatory to forbid it, just as disobedience is forbidden. ﴿Those whom they call upon﴾ are the idols, meaning: the polytheists call upon them. He referred to the idols, which do not reason, with the relative pronoun for those who reason, treating what does not reason as if it reasoned, since they treated them in their worship and belief as if they were beings who reason, believing that they are intercessors for them with God, exalted is He. It was also said: it is possible that "those who call upon" refers to the disbelievers. The apparent meaning of His saying "lest they revile God" is that they would proceed to revile God if their gods were reviled, even though they acknowledge God, exalted is He. But their partisanship for their gods and their intense anger on their behalf drives them to this, so they go beyond moderation to what contradicts reason, just as happens with some Muslims when their anger becomes intense and deviates; they may utter what leads to disbelief. We seek refuge in God from that. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: perhaps some of them were holding to the doctrine of the eternity of time and denying the Creator, so they would commit this kind of outrage. Or the Muslims used to revile the idols, and the idolaters used to revile the Messenger, so the reviling of the Messenger was treated as the reviling of God, exalted is He, just as He said: ﴿Indeed those who pledge allegiance to you pledge allegiance only to God﴾ [al-Fath: 10], and as He said: ﴿Indeed those who injure God and His Messenger﴾ [al-Ahzab: 57]. Or some disbelievers believed that a devil drove the Messenger to claim prophethood and messengership, and out of their ignorance they cursed that devil by saying that he was the god of Muhammad. End of quotation. These are possibilities that contradict the apparent meaning, and he mentioned them only because he stated that those who acknowledge the existence of the Creator do not dare to revile Him, exalted is He. We have already mentioned what can be taken as keeping the words to their apparent meaning. Some Sufis said: the meaning is: address them with the language of argument and the binding of proof, and do not speak to them according to the impulses of the self and custom. The word "fa-yasubbū" (so that they revile) is in the accusative as a response to the prohibition. It was also said that it is jussive by coordination, as in your saying: "Do not stretch it, so that you tear it." ʿAdwan is a verbal noun of 'adā, and likewise ʿadwa and ʿudwān, in the sense of "transgressed," meaning "wronged." Al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Qatadah, Ya'qub, Sallam and 'Abd Allah ibn Yazid read it with a damma on the ʿayn and the dāl and a shadda on the wāw, and it is a verbal noun of 'adā, as we have mentioned. They allowed for both of them to be in the accusative as a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause, or as a verbal noun from a word other than the verb itself, since reviling God is transgression, or as an object of purpose. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: some Meccans read it, and al-Zamakhshari specified it, saying of Ibn Kathir: with a fatha on the ʿayn and a damma on the dāl and a shadda on the wāw, meaning "enemies." It is in the accusative as an emphatic circumstantial clause, and ʿadūw (enemy) is predicated of a plural, as He said: ﴿They are the enemy﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 4]. The meaning of "without knowledge" is in ignorance of what is due to God, exalted is He, that He should be mentioned by it, and this explains the meaning of transgression.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 103–110 (part 3 of 4):

﴿Thus We have made attractive to every nation their deeds﴾: that is, like the making attractive of the worship of idols to the polytheists, ﴿We have made attractive to every nation﴾. The apparent sense of ﴿to every nation their deeds﴾ is generality, both regarding the nations and regarding the deeds. Thus believers and disbelievers are included. Its making attractive (tazyin) is what He creates and originates in souls of love for good or evil and of following its paths. The making attractive by Satan (tazyin al-shaytan) is what he casts into souls of whisperings and evil thoughts. Al-Zamakhshari specified ﴿to every nation their deeds﴾, and said: among the nations of the disbelievers, their evil deeds. That is, We left them to themselves and their affairs, and did not restrain them, until their evil deeds became good in their eyes, and We gave Satan respite until he made them attractive, or We made him attractive in their claim and their saying: "Indeed Allah commanded us with this and made it attractive for us." End. And this is in accordance with his Mu'tazili method. Al-Hasan said: that is, ﴿We made attractive to every nation﴾ the deed which We made obligatory upon them, so he made (zayyana) mean (shara'a), prescribed, and ﴿every nation﴾ is general, while the deed is specific to what Allah the Exalted has made obligatory. Al-Zajjaj denied this and said: it means "Allah sealed their hearts," and the evidence for it is: ﴿Is then one to whom the evil of his deed is made attractive so that he sees it as good [equal to one who is rightly guided]? For indeed, Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾ [Fatir: 8]. End. What al-Hasan explained has been clarified by some of the Mu'tazilah, who said: the intended meaning of the making attractive of the deed is the making attractive of what is commanded, not what is forbidden, and it is to be understood as specific, even though it is general, lest it lead to contradiction between the texts; for it is stated that Allah made faith attractive and disliked disbelief, in His saying: ﴿But Allah has endeared to you the faith and made it attractive in your hearts, and has made hateful to you disbelief﴾ [al-Hujurat: 7]. So if the making attractive of disbelief entered into the meaning of this verse, there would necessarily be a contradiction between the two verses. For this reason, He attributed the making attractive to Satan, in His saying: ﴿Satan made their deeds attractive to them﴾ [al-Anfal: 48]. So Allah does not make attractive what Satan made attractive. Thus we say: Allah makes attractive what He commands, and Satan makes attractive what He forbids, so that this is acting in accordance with all the texts. End. It was answered that there is no contradiction because the making attractive differs: Allah's making attractive through creation of desires, and Satan's making attractive through calling to acts of disobedience. So the verse is on its generality, for every nation and for their deeds.

﴿Then to their Lord is their return, and He will inform them of what they used to do﴾: that is, their affair is entrusted to Allah, and He is Knowing of their conditions, aware of their inner selves, and their turning back on the Day of Resurrection is to Him, so each will be recompensed according to what their deeds require. In that is a beautiful promise for the good-doer and a warning for the wrongdoer.

﴿And they swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that if a sign came to them, they would surely believe in it﴾: that is, a sign of their own suggestion, like their saying: "Until you send down..." ﴿If We willed, We would send down upon them from the sky a sign, so that their necks would remain humbly subjected to it﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 4]. "Send it down upon us so that we may believe in it." The Muslims said: "O Messenger of Allah, send it down upon them," so this verse was revealed; this is related from Ibn Abbas. Or like their saying: "Let al-Safa become gold," until they mentioned the miracles of Musa in the rock, of Isa in raising the dead, and of Salih in the she-camel. The Messenger stood supplicating, and Jibril (peace be upon him) (p-201) came to him and said: "If you wish, al-Safa will become gold; but if they do not believe, they will all be destroyed immediately, as was done to the previous nations, since they did not believe in the suggested signs. And if you wish, leave them until whoever among them repents turns in repentance." So he said: "Rather, until whoever among them repents turns in repentance." They suggested a specific sign only because they doubted the Qur'an, and for this they said: "You have studied," i.e., with the scholars, and you have discussed with the People of the Torah and the Gospel. Most of them were arrogant and obstinate. The meaning is that they swore their utmost oath. The oath was called qasam because it occurs when people divide into those who affirm and those who deny, so it is as if it strengthens the side one chooses. Al-Tibrizi said: al-iqsam is an form (if'al) from al-qasam, which means portion and division. Their swearing by Allah was the utmost in oath-taking, and they used to swear by their fathers and their gods, but when the matter was great they swore by Allah the Exalted. Al-jahd, with a fatha on the jim, means hardship, and with a damma means capacity; some treat them as having one meaning. (Jahda) is in the accusative as a verbal noun governed by (aqsamu), meaning: they swore with the utmost of their oaths; and al-aymān means the oaths, as you say: "I struck him with the strongest of blows." Al-Hawfi said it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in (aqsamu), meaning: striving in their oaths. Al-Mubarrad said it is a verbal noun governed by a verb of its own root. The discussion of ﴿jahda aymanihim﴾ has already occurred in al-Ma'idah. And ﴿la'in ja'athum﴾ is a report about them, not a quotation of their statement; for had their statement been quoted, it would be: "la'in ja'atna ayah". He treated the report of the oath as the quotation of the oath in the wording of what the swearer uttered, and that it is not meant by it any sign in general, since many signs had come to them, but they wanted a suggested sign, as we have mentioned. Talhah ibn Musarrif read: ﴿la-yu'manna bihā﴾ in the passive voice and with the light nun.

﴿Say: Indeed the signs are with Allah﴾: this is a command to respond to them, and that the coming of the signs is not in my hands; rather that belongs to Allah the Exalted, who is capable of them, and He sends them down in the way of wisdom as He wills for His wisdom, and they are not with me so that they may be demanded of me.

﴿And what will make you aware that when they come they will not believe?﴾ It is interrogative, and the pronoun of the subject in (yush'irukum) refers back to it. Some read it with the damma of the ra' omitted, and it is read with its partial suppression. As for the address, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said it is addressed to the disbelievers; al-Farra' and others said the one addressed is the believers. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-Alimi and al-A'sha from Abu Bakr read it, and Ibn 'Atiyyah, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim in the narration of Dawud al-Iyadi said that it is with a kasra on the hamza, while the rest of the seven read it with a fatha. Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah read: (la yu'minun) with the second-person ta' of address, and the rest of the seven read it with the third-person ya' of absence. Thus four readings arise. The first: kasra on the hamza and the ya', and this is the reading of Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Abu Bakr in one narration on the kasra of the hamza. This is a clear reading: Allah the Exalted informed that they "do not believe" definitively, on the assumption of the coming of the sign, and the sentence is complete at His saying: ﴿And what will make you aware﴾, and the complement of (yush'irukum) is omitted, meaning: ﴿and what will make you aware﴾ of what will happen. If the address is to the disbelievers, the implied meaning is: ﴿and what will make you aware﴾ of what will happen from you. Then He informed them by way of iltifat (a shift) of what He knows of their state if the signs came to them. If the address is to the believers, the implied meaning is: ﴿and what will make you aware﴾, O believers, of what will happen from them; then He informed the believers of His knowledge about them. The second reading: kasra on the hamza and the ta', and this is the narration of al-Alimi and al-A'sha from Abu Bakr from 'Asim. The suitable reading is that the address is to the disbelievers in this reading, as if it were said: "And what will make you know, O disbelievers, what will happen from you?" Then He informed them with certainty that they "will not believe" on the assumption of the coming of it. It is very remote that the address in ﴿and what will make you aware﴾ is to the believers while in "they will not believe" it is to the disbelievers. The third reading: fatha on the hamza and the ta', and this is the reading of Nafi', al-Kisa'i and Hafs. The apparent sense is that the address is to the believers, and the meaning: "And what will make you know, O believers, that the sign which you propose, when it comes (p-202) they will not believe in it," meaning: I know that when it comes they will not believe, while you do not know this. The believers were hoping for their faith when that sign came, and wishing for its coming, so He said: "And what will make you know that they will not believe," in the sense that you do not know what My knowledge has preceded concerning them, that they will not believe. Do you not see His saying: "as they did not believe in it the first time"? It is very remote that the address in ﴿and what will make you aware﴾ is to the disbelievers. In this reading, the (anna) is verbal (masdariyyah), and not in the sense of negation. Some exegetes took (anna) here to mean (la'alla), and that usage has been reported from their speech: they say: "Go to the market, for you are buying meat," meaning "perhaps you are." Imru' al-Qays said:
"Halt upon the ruined abode, for we weep for the dwellings as Ibn Haram wept."
Abu 'Ubaydah and others mention this, and (la'alla) often occurs in such a context; Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself﴾ [Abasa: 3], ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ [al-Shura: 17]. In the codex of Ubayy: "And what will make you know? Perhaps it, when it comes, they will not believe." Abu 'Ali weakened this view on the ground that the expectation indicated by (la'alla) does not suit the reading with kasra, since that reading indicates a judgement from Him, the Exalted, upon them that they will not believe. But he did not make (anna-ha) governed by (yush'irukum); rather he made it a reason with its preposition elided, and the implied sense for him is: ﴿Say: Indeed the signs are with Allah﴾ because when they come they will not believe. So He does not bring them because of their insistence upon their disbelief, and this is like "And nothing prevented Us from sending the signs except that the earlier peoples denied them" — that is, the suggested signs. End. And ﴿And what will make you aware﴾ would be a parenthesis between the caused and its cause, since the meaning becomes: ﴿Say: Indeed the signs are with Allah﴾, that is, the suggested ones, He does not bring them, because of the absence of their faith and their insistence on their error. Some made (la) superfluous, so the meaning would be: "And what will make you know of their faith," as they said: "when it comes." He made it superfluous only because if it remained in negation, the statement would be an excuse for the disbelievers, and the intended meaning of the sign would be corrupted. This is from Ibn 'Atiyyah, who said: al-Zajjaj and others weakened the superfluity of (la). End of Ibn 'Atiyyah's words. The one who holds that (la) is superfluous is al-Kisa'i and al-Farra'. Al-Zajjaj said: Sibawayh claimed that its meaning is "perhaps it, when it comes, they will not believe," and this is the reading of the people of Madinah. He said: this view is stronger in Arabic. As for the one who said that (la) is idle, he is mistaken, because what is idle cannot be non-idle; and whoever reads with the kasra, there is consensus that (la) is not idle, so it is not permissible that the meaning be affirmative at one time and otherwise in the context of one speech.
