Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: It is the plural of *qabil* in the sense of *kafil* (guarantor), i.e., guarantors of the truthfulness of Muhammad. It is said: "I *qabiltu* the man, *uqabiluhu qubalatan*," meaning I stood surety for him. *Al-qabil*, *al-kafil*, *al-za'im*, *al-adin*, *al-hamil* and *al-damin* have one meaning. It was also said: *qubulan* has the meaning of *qibalan*, i.e., facing and confronting. From it: "I came to you *qubulan* not *dubura*," meaning from the direction of your face. God said: ﴿if his shirt was torn from the front﴾ [Yusuf: 26]. It is also read: ﴿for the *qubul* of their waiting period﴾, meaning for facing and confronting it. In my view this opinion is the best, because it agrees with both readings.

Al-Hasan, Abu Raja' and Abu Haywa read *qubla* with a damma on the *qaf* and a sukun on the *ba'*, as a lightening of the damma. Ubayy and al-A'mash read *qabilan* with a fatha on the *qaf*, a kasra on the *ba'*, and a *ya'* after it, and in this reading it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. Ibn Musarrif read it with a fatha on the *qaf* and a sukun on the *ba'*.

The answer to *law* (if) is: ﴿they would not have believed﴾. Al-Hawfi estimated it as: "*lama kanu*" (they would not have). He said: The *lam* is omitted, although it is intended. This statement is not sound, because when a negated clause with *ma* is the answer to *law*, the most common usage in the Arabic language is that the *lam* does not enter upon *ma*, and it rarely enters upon it. So we do not say that the *lam* was omitted from it. Rather, they introduced the *lam* upon *ma* by analogy with the negated being like the affirmed. Do you not see that when the negation is with *lam*, the *lam* does not enter upon *lam*? This shows that the original form of the negated is that the *lam* does not enter upon it. And ﴿they would not have believed﴾ is more emphatic in negation than "they did not believe," because it contains negation of capacity and suitability for faith; for this reason the *lam* of denial (*lam al-juhud*) appears in the predicate.

The exception ﴿unless God wills﴾ is a continuous exception (*istithna' muttasil*) from an omitted element that is a cause and reason. The estimate is: ﴿they would not have believed﴾ for any thing, except by God's will. Some estimated it as: "In every state except the state of God's will." As for those who held that it is a discontinuous exception (*istithna' munqati'*), like al-Karmani, Abu al-Baqa' and al-Hawfi, their view is far-fetched, since the connection is apparent. Or, the making of their faith conditional upon God's will is evidence for what the People of the Sunnah (*Ahl al-Sunnah*) maintain, namely that the servant's faith occurs by God's will. The Mu'tazilah interpreted this as the will of compulsion and force. For this reason al-Zamakhshari said: It is a will of coercion and compulsion.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿most of them﴾ refers to what the pronouns before it refer to. It was said: they are among the disbelievers, i.e., they ignore the truth, or they are ignorant that it is not permitted to demand signs after they have seen a single sign, or they are ignorant that both faith and disbelief are by God's will and decree. Al-Zamakhshari said: They are ignorant, so they swear by God with their most emphatic oaths that they are upon something of which they are unaware about the state of their hearts when the signs descend. He said: Or, most of the Muslims are ignorant that these people will not believe unless He compels them, so they hope for their faith when the demanded sign comes. Others among the Mu'tazilah said: They are ignorant that they will remain disbelievers when the signs they demanded appear. Al-Jubba'i said: ﴿unless God wills﴾ indicates that God's will is originated, because if it were eternal it would not be permissible for the originated to be made conditional upon it, since it is a condition, and the attainment of the conditioned requires the attainment of the condition. Sensation shows that faith is originated, so it is necessary that the condition be originated, and that is the will. Abu Abd Allah al-Razi answered that the will, although eternal, its connection to bringing that originated thing into being at the time is an originated relation. End of quote.

This verse is a discouragement of faith for those who demanded the signs, except whoever God wills from among them. For this reason His words come: ﴿unless God wills﴾, and they are those who were sealed with happiness and so believed from among them.

﴿وكَذَلِكَ جَعَلْنا لِكُلِّ نَبِيٍّ عَدُوًّا شَياطِينَ الإنْسِ والجِنِّ يُوحِي بَعْضُهم إلى بَعْضٍ زُخْرُفَ القَوْلِ غُرُورًا ولَوْ شاءَ رَبُّكَ ما فَعَلُوهُ فَذَرْهم وما يَفْتَرُونَ﴾ [الأنعام: ١١٢] (And thus We appointed for every prophet an enemy: devils among men and jinn, who inspire one another with flowery speech as deception. Had your Lord willed, they would not have done it, so leave them and what they fabricate.) [Al-An'am: 112]

﴿ولِتَصْغى إلَيْهِ أفْئِدَةُ الَّذِينَ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِالآخِرَةِ ولِيَرْضَوْهُ ولِيَقْتَرِفُوا ما هم مُقْتَرِفُونَ﴾ [الأنعام: ١١٣] (And so that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter incline to it, and so that they are pleased with it, and so that they earn what they are earning.) [Al-An'am: 113]

﴿أفَغَيْرَ اللَّهِ أبْتَغِي حَكَمًا وهو الَّذِي أنْزَلَ إلَيْكُمُ الكِتابَ مُفَصَّلًا والَّذِينَ آتَيْناهُمُ الكِتابَ يَعْلَمُونَ أنَّهُ مُنَزَّلٌ مِن رَبِّكَ بِالحَقِّ فَلا تَكُونَنَّ مِنَ المُمْتَرِينَ﴾ [الأنعام: ١١٤] (Shall I seek a judge other than God, when it is He who has sent down to you the Book made detailed? Those to whom We gave the Book know that it is sent down from your Lord in truth, so do not be among the doubters.) [Al-An'am: 114]

﴿وتَمَّتْ كَلِمَةُ رَبِّكَ صِدْقًا وعَدْلًا لا مُبَدِّلَ لِكَلِماتِهِ وهو السَّمِيعُ العَلِيمُ﴾ [الأنعام: ١١٥] (The word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice. None can change His words, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.) [Al-An'am: 115]

﴿وإنْ تُطِعْ أكْثَرَ مَن في الأرْضِ يُضِلُّوكَ عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ إنْ يَتَّبِعُونَ إلّا الظَّنَّ وإنْ هم إلّا يَخْرُصُونَ﴾ [الأنعام: ١١٦] (If you obey most of those on earth, they will lead you astray from the way of God. They follow only conjecture, and they only guess.) [Al-An'am: 116]

﴿إنَّ رَبَّكَ هو أعْلَمُ مَن يَضِلُّ عَنْ سَبِيلِهِ وهو أعْلَمُ بِالمُهْتَدِينَ﴾ [الأنعام: ١١٧] (Indeed your Lord knows best who strays from His way, and He knows best those who are guided.) [Al-An'am: 117]

﴿فَكُلُوا مِمّا ذُكِرَ اسْمُ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهِ إنْ كُنْتُمْ بِآياتِهِ مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ [الأنعام: ١١٨] (So eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned, if you are believers in His signs.) [Al-An'am: 118]

﴿وما لَكم ألّا تَأْكُلُوا مِمّا ذُكِرَ اسْمُ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهِ وقَدْ فَصَّلَ لَكم ما حَرَّمَ عَلَيْكم إلّا ما اضْطُرِرْتُمْ إلَيْهِ وإنَّ كَثِيرًا لَيُضِلُّونَ بِأهْوائِهِمْ بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ إنَّ رَبَّكَ هو أعْلَمُ بِالمُعْتَدِينَ﴾ [الأنعام: ١١٩] (What is the matter with you that you do not eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned, when He has already detailed for you what He has forbidden to you, except what you are compelled to? Indeed many lead others astray by their desires without knowledge. Indeed your Lord knows best the transgressors.) [Al-An'am: 119]

﴿وذَرُوا ظاهِرَ الإثْمِ وباطِنَهُ إنَّ الَّذِينَ يَكْسِبُونَ الإثْمَ سَيُجْزَوْنَ بِما كانُوا يَقْتَرِفُونَ﴾ [الأنعام: ١٢٠] (Leave the outward and the inward of sin. Indeed those who earn sin will be recompensed for what they have been earning.) [Al-An'am: 120]

﴿ولا تَأْكُلُوا مِمّا لَمْ يُذْكَرِ اسْمُ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهِ وإنَّهُ لَفِسْقٌ وإنَّ الشَّياطِينَ لَيُوحُونَ إلى أوْلِيائِهِمْ لِيُجادِلُوكم وإنْ أطَعْتُمُوهم إنَّكم لَمُشْرِكُونَ﴾ [الأنعام: ١٢١] (And do not eat of that over which the name of God has not been mentioned, for indeed it is wickedness. Indeed the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you, and if you obey them, indeed you are polytheists.) [Al-An'am: 121]

﴿أوَمَن كانَ مَيْتًا فَأحْيَيْناهُ وجَعَلْنا لَهُ نُورًا يَمْشِي بِهِ في النّاسِ كَمَن مَثَلُهُ في الظُّلُماتِ لَيْسَ بِخارِجٍ مِنها كَذَلِكَ زُيِّنَ لِلْكافِرِينَ ما كانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ﴾ [الأنعام: ١٢٢] (Is one who was dead and We gave him life, and made for him a light by which he walks among the people, like one whose likeness is in darkness, from which he cannot emerge? Thus the deeds they were doing have been made attractive to the disbelievers.) [Al-An'am: 122]

﴿وكَذَلِكَ جَعَلْنا في كُلِّ قَرْيَةٍ أكابِرَ مُجْرِمِيها لِيَمْكُرُوا فِيها وما يَمْكُرُونَ إلّا بِأنْفُسِهِمْ وما يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ [الأنعام: ١٢٣] (And thus We placed in every town the greatest of its criminals, so that they might scheme therein. But they scheme only against themselves, and they do not perceive.) [Al-An'am: 123]

﴿وإذا جاءَتْهم آيَةٌ قالُوا لَنْ نُؤْمِنَ حَتّى نُؤْتى مِثْلَ ما أُوتِيَ رُسُلُ اللَّهِ اللَّهُ أعْلَمُ حَيْثُ يَجْعَلُ رِسالَتَهُ سَيُصِيبُ الَّذِينَ أجْرَمُوا صَغارٌ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ وعَذابٌ شَدِيدٌ بِما كانُوا يَمْكُرُونَ﴾ [الأنعام: ١٢٤] (When a sign comes to them, they say: "We will not believe until we are given what the messengers of God were given." God knows best where to place His message. Those who committed crime will be struck with humiliation before God and severe punishment for what they used to scheme.) [Al-An'am: 124]

﴿فَمَن يُرِدِ اللَّهُ أنْ يَهدِيَهُ يَشْرَحْ صَدْرَهُ لِلْإسْلامِ ومَن يُرِدْ أنْ يُضِلَّهُ يَجْعَلْ صَدْرَهُ ضَيِّقًا حَرَجًا كَأنَّما يَصَّعَّدُ في السَّماءِ كَذَلِكَ يَجْعَلُ اللَّهُ الرِّجْسَ عَلى الَّذِينَ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ [الأنعام: ١٢٥] (So whomever God wills to guide, He expands his breast for Islam; and whomever He wills to lead astray, He makes his breast narrow and constricted, as if he were climbing up into the sky. Thus God places defilement upon those who do not believe.) [Al-An'am: 125]

﴿وهَذا صِراطُ رَبِّكَ مُسْتَقِيمًا قَدْ فَصَّلْنا الآياتِ لِقَوْمٍ يَذَّكَّرُونَ﴾ [الأنعام: ١٢٦] (And this is the straight path of your Lord. We have detailed the signs for a people who remember.) [Al-An'am: 126]

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 112–113:

﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy: devils of mankind and jinn, inspiring one another with ornamented speech as deception.﴾ The meaning: just as these disbelievers who demand signs, and others, are enemies to you, so We appointed for those before you among the prophets enemies, devils of mankind and jinn, that is, the rebellious of both kinds. (يُوحِي) means: he casts secretly, one to another, that is, some of the jinn kind to some of the human kind, or the devils of the jinn inspire the devils of mankind with (زُخْرُفَ القَوْلِ) "ornamented speech," that is, its embellished and adorned form. The fruit of this appointing is a trial, so that patience is shown in what they were afflicted with from those who oppose them, and thus the reward and recompense become great. In this is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and an example to follow of the prophets who preceded him, and that you are not alone in enmity from those contemporary with you; rather this is the custom of the prophets before you. (عَدُوٌّ) as we said before is in the sense of (أعداء) "enemies." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they are an enemy to you; evil is the exchange for the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Kahf: 50]. And the poet said:

*If I do not benefit my friend with my affection, then my enmity will not harm my enemies.*

Al-Hawfi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu al-Baqa' parsed it here in the same way as their parsing of ﴿And they made the jinn partners to Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 100], and permitted in (شَياطِينَ) that it is a badal (substitute/apposition) for (عَدُوًّا), just as they permitted there the badal relation of (الجِنَّ) to (شُرَكاءَ). We have refuted this against them. The apparent reading is that his saying "devils of mankind and jinn" is an idafa (construct phrase) of an attribute to the thing described, that is, "mankind and the jinn, the devils," so it follows that there are devils among mankind and devils among the jinn, and the shaytan is the rebel of both kinds, as we explained. This is the view of Qatada, Mujahid and al-Hasan. Likewise Abu Dharr understood it from the Messenger's saying to him: "Have you sought refuge from the devils of the jinn and mankind?" I said: "O Messenger of Allah, are there devils among mankind?" He said: "Yes, and they are worse than the devils of the jinn." Malik ibn Dinar said: "The devil of mankind is harder on me than the devil of the jinn, because when I seek refuge in Allah, the devil of the jinn departs from me, while the devil of mankind comes to me and drags me openly to sins."

'Ata said: As for the enemies of the Prophet (ﷺ) from the devils of mankind, they are al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-'As ibn Wa'il, Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, al-'Asi ibn 'Amr, Zam'a ibn al-Aswad, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, al-Aswad ibn 'Abd al-Asad, 'Utba and Shayba, the sons of Rabi'a, 'Utba ibn Abi Mu'ayt, al-Walid ibn 'Utba, Ubayy and Umayya, the sons of Khalaf, Nabih and Munabbih, the sons of al-Hajjaj, 'Utba ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza and Ma'attib ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza.

In the hadith: "There is none of you but that his companion from the jinn has been assigned to him." It was said: "And not you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Nor I, except that Allah has protected me and helped me against him, so he submits, and he does not command me except to good."

It was also said: the idafa is not of the kind of attribute-to-described-thing, but rather of the kind of "the slave of Zayd," meaning: the devils of mankind and jinn, that is, rebellious ones who lead them astray. On this interpretation 'Ikrima, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and al-Kalbi explained it. They said: there are no devils from mankind as such; the meaning is: the devils of mankind who are with mankind, and the devils of the jinn who are with the jinn. Iblis divided his troops into one group to mankind and one group to the jinn, and they meet, and one commands the other to mislead his companion with what he himself misled his companion with. This idafa was preferred because it makes the two terms of the idafa distinct, while the earlier idafa was preferred because the purpose is consolation and taking the example of the prophets who came before, since among their peoples there were those who opposed them, as in the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) there were those who opposed him, and they are the devils of mankind. Regarding (جَعَلْنا) the apparent meaning is that He, the Exalted, is the one who makes them enemies of the prophets, and enmity toward the prophets is disobedience and disbelief, so it requires that He is the creator of that. The Mu'tazila interpreted this apparent meaning. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Just as We left you and your enemies unrestrained, so We did with the prophets before you and their enemies; He did not prevent them from enmity." End of quote. This is the view of al-Ka'bi, who said: "He left between him and them."

Al-Jubba'i said: (الجَعْل) here means judgment and declaration; it is said: "He declared him a disbeliever," meaning he judged him to be a disbeliever; and "He declared him just," meaning he reported his justice. When he made clear to the Messenger that they were enemies to them, he said: "He made them enemies to them." Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: when Allah sent him to all the worlds and singled him out with miracles, they envied him, and envy became a clear sign of strong enmity. Therefore, on this interpretation, He said: "He made them to him enemies," as the poet said:

*You made them envious of me.*

And this requires that they become enemies of the prophets. (غُرُورًا) is in the accusative as a maf'ul lahu (object of purpose). They also permitted it to be a maṣdar (verbal noun) of (يُوحِي), since it has the sense of "deceiving one another," or a maṣdar in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), meaning "deceiving."

﴿And if your Lord had willed, they would not have done it﴾, that is: they did not do the enmity, or the inspiring, or the ornamentation, or the speech, or the deception. These are the possibilities they mentioned.

﴿So leave them and what they fabricate﴾, that is: leave them and what they fabricate of denial of you. It includes a warning and a threat. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means what Iblis adorned for them and what deceived them. End of quote. The apparent meaning of the command is conciliation, and this has been abrogated (naskh, abrogation) by the verses of fighting. Qatada said: every (ذَرْ) in the Book of Allah is abrogated by fighting. (ما) is in the sense of (الذي) "that which," or is a descriptive (مَوْصُوفَة), or a maṣdariyya (verbal-noun particle).

﴿And that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it, and that they may be pleased with it, and that they may earn what they are earning﴾, that is: and that they may incline to it. The pronoun returns to what it refers to in (فَعَلُوهُ). And that they may be pleased with it, and that they may acquire what they are acquiring of sins. The lam here is lam kay (the lam of purpose), and it is conjoined with his saying "deception," since its meaning is "for deception," so it is connected to (يُوحِي). The accusative of (غُرُورًا) is because all the conditions of the accusative are met in it. (يُوحِي) was made to take this with the lam because there is no clear maṣdariyya condition, and because the subject differs: the subject of (يُوحِي) is (بَعْضُهم) and the subject of (تَصْغى) is (أفْئِدَةُ). The ordering of these objects is in the highest eloquence, because first there is deception, then inclination, then approval, then the act; so each is caused by what precedes it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (وَلِتَصْغى) has an omitted answer (جواب), its estimate being: "and so that this should be what We appointed for every prophet an enemy," the lam being lam al-ṣayrūra (the lam of consequence), and the pronoun in (إلَيْهِ) refers to what the pronoun in (فَعَلُوهُ) refers to; that is: "and so that the hearts of the disbelievers may incline to what has been mentioned of the enmity of the prophets and the whisperings of the devils." End of quote. Calling what the lam relates to an "answer" is a strange terminology. What he said is the view of al-Zajjaj, who said: its estimate is ﴿and so that it may incline to it﴾ they did that, so it is lam of consequence. Al-Akhfash held that the lam of (وَلِتَصْغى) is lam kay, and it is the answer of an omitted oath, its estimate: "by Allah, (and so that it may incline)" in the place of "you will surely incline," so the answer of the oath is of the single-word type, and you say: "By Allah, Zayd will surely stand," the estimate being: "I swear by Allah to the standing of Zayd." This was supported by the poet's verse:

*When she says "Leave me," Allah swears an oath, that he may make me independent of her, he is unique and all-encompassing.*

And by his saying (وَلِتَصْغى). The refutation of this is mentioned in the books of grammar.

al-Nakha'i and al-Jarrah ibn 'Abd Allah read (وَلِتُصْغِي) with the fourth form (ascaya). al-Hasan read with the lam pronounced with sukun in all three. It was reported from him: in (لِيَرْضَوْهُ وَلِيَقْتَرِفُوا) with kasra in (وَلِتَصْغى). Abu 'Amr al-Dani said: al-Hasan's reading is only (وَلِتَصْغِي) with the kasra on the ghayn. End of quote. The sukun of the lam in all three is explained as an anomaly in lam kay, and it is lam kay in all three, being conjoined with (غُرُورٍ), or the sukun of lam kay in this kind is anomalous in what was heard but strong in analogy, as Abu al-Fath said. Others said: it is the lam of command (lām al-amr) in all three, but this is far in (وَلِتَصْغى) with the retention of the yā', although it has come in a little speech. Qunbul read: ﴿Indeed, whoever fears and is patient﴾ with the understanding that it allows the interpretation. It was said: in (وَلِتَصْغى) it is lam kay with sukun, anomalously, while in (لِيَرْضَوْهُ وَلِيَقْتَرِفُوا) it is lam al-amr, implying threat and warning, like his saying: ﴿Do what you will﴾ [Fussilat: 40]; and in his saying ﴿what they are earning﴾ it indicates magnification and emphasis of what they do, like his saying: ﴿So there covered them of the sea what covered them﴾ [Ta-Ha: 78].

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 114–117:**

﴿Shall I seek a judge other than God, when it is He who has sent down to you the Book, fully explained?﴾ "The polytheists of Quraysh said to the Messenger: 'Appoint between us and you a judge from the rabbis of the Jews, or, if you wish, from the bishops of the Christians, so that he may inform us about you from what is in their book concerning your affair.' So it was revealed." The connection of its composition (nazm) with what precedes it is that when He related the oaths of the disbelievers, and answered them by saying that there is no benefit in showing them the signs they propose, since they would not stop persisting in disbelief, He made clear the proof of his prophethood by sending down the Qur'an to him, which creation has been unable to match, and He judged concerning it that it proves his prophethood, and by the fact that the Torah and the Gospel contain that he is a true messenger and that the Qur'an is a book from God that is true. Another connection: when He mentioned their enmity and threatened them, they said what we have mentioned as the occasion of revelation. It was their custom, when a matter became unclear to them and they disagreed about it, to make a soothsayer (kahin) their judge. So God commanded him to say: ((p-209) ﴿Shall I seek a judge other than God?﴾). This is an interrogative whose meaning is negation, i.e., "I do not seek a judge other than God." Al-Kirmani said: "Al-hakam (the judge, in the form of intensive) is more emphatic than al-hakim (the judge, active participle), because one who is known for judging again and again is a hakam, whereas hakim is an active participle that applies even to a single instance." Isma'il al-Darir said: "The difference between them is that the hakam judges only with truth, while the hakim judges with truth and without truth." Ibn 'Atiyya said something similar, saying: "Al-hakam is more emphatic than al-hakim, since it is a form denoting justice among judges, whereas al-hakim is a participle derived from the verb, and it may be said of one who is unjust." End of quotation. It seems to be an allusion to God's judgment against them that they will not believe even if He sent them every sign, or to His judgment by appointing enemies for the prophets. And ﴿judge﴾ means one who separates between truth and falsehood. They allowed, in the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of (ghayr), that it be an object of (abtaghi) with ﴿judge﴾ as a circumstantial accusative (hal), or the reverse. Al-Hawfi and Ibn 'Atiyya permitted that it be in the accusative of specification (tamyiz) after "other than them," as in the saying: "Indeed for us other than her are camels," and this is sound; Abu al-Baqa' also reported it. So "the Book" is the Qur'an, and ﴿fully explained﴾ means clarified, removing ambiguity; or "favored" with promise and threat; or "divided" into parts according to what suits the interests, i.e., He did not send it down all together; or "in which the rulings are detailed," from prohibition and command, the lawful and the unlawful, the obligatory and the recommended, error and guidance; or "explained, in which the distinction between truth and falsehood is made clear, and the testimony for me as to truthfulness and against you as to fabrication." These are five opinions. With this verse the Khawarij argued against 'Ali regarding his declaring them disbelievers for accepting arbitration (tahkim). This clause is circumstantial (hali).

﴿And those to whom We gave the Book know that it is sent down from your Lord in truth.﴾ That is: those to whom We gave the knowledge of the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms and the scrolls. What is meant is the scholars of the People of the Book, so it is general in meaning but particular in application. This clause is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), and it contains an appeal to the believers among the People of the Book and a criticism of their polytheists and envious ones. The support in the indication that the Qur'an is true is that the People of the Book know that it is true, because it confirms their books and agrees with them.

﴿So do not be among the doubters.﴾ It has been said: the address is to the Messenger, but it is an address to his community. It has been said: it is to every hearer, meaning that when the proof has become manifest, there is no reason to doubt it. It has been said: it is from the kind of stirring up and encouragement, like His saying: ﴿and do not be among the polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 14]. It has been said: ﴿So do not be among the doubters﴾ concerning the fact that the People of the Book know that it is sent down from your Lord in truth, and let not the denial of most of them and their disbelief disturb you. Ibn 'Abbas and Hafs read (munazzal) with doubled letter (tashdid), and the rest read it with single letter (takhfif).

﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice.﴾ Since from the beginning of the surah up to here there are proofs of monotheism, prophethood, resurrection, and criticism of those who oppose these, and from here to the end of the surah there are rulings and narratives, it was fitting to mention these verses here. That is: His decrees and His measures have been completed; this is what Ibn 'Abbas said. Qatada said: "His words" is the Qur'an. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Everything He has informed of, commanded, forbidden, promised and threatened." Al-Hasan said: "Truthful in promise and just in threat." It has been said: "in what it includes of information and ruling," or "in what has been and what will be," or "in what He commanded and what He forbade," or "in encouragement and warning," or "in His saying: these to Paradise and these to the Fire," or "in reward and punishment," or "in the support of His friends and the abandonment of His enemies," or "in the support of the Messenger at Badr and the destruction of his enemies," or "in guidance and misguidance," or "in forgiveness and punishment," or "in bounty and withholding," or "in the expansion and restriction of provision," or "in His giving and His trial." These sayings: the first part of the phrase was interpreted as "truthfulness," and the conjoined part was interpreted as "justice." Al-Hawfi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu al-Baqa' parsed ﴿truthfulness and justice﴾ as two verbal nouns in the place of a circumstantial accusative (hal), while al-Tabari parsed them as specification (tamyiz); Abu al-Baqa' also permitted this. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is not correct." Abu al-Baqa' added that they could be an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi). The meaning of (tammat) is not that it had a deficiency which was then completed; rather the meaning is that it continued and was sound, as in the hadith: "And Hamzah remained (tamma) upon his Islam," and as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the word of your Lord was fulfilled: "I will surely fill Hell"﴾ [Hud: 119], that is: it continued, and it is an expression for the execution of His decrees. So "the Book" is the Qur'an, and ﴿fully explained﴾ means clarified, removing ambiguity; or "favored" with promise and threat; or "divided" into parts according to what suits the interests, i.e., He did not send it down all together; or "in which the rulings are detailed," from prohibition and command, the lawful and the unlawful, the obligatory and the recommended, error and guidance; or "explained, in which the distinction between truth and falsehood is made clear, and the testimony for me as to truthfulness and against you as to fabrication." These are five opinions. With this verse the Khawarij argued against 'Ali regarding his declaring them disbelievers for accepting arbitration (tahkim). This clause is circumstantial (hali).

﴿And those to whom We gave the Book know that it is sent down from your Lord in truth.﴾ That is: those to whom We gave the knowledge of the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms and the scrolls. What is meant is the scholars of the People of the Book, so it is general in meaning but particular in application. This clause is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), and it contains an appeal to the believers among the People of the Book and a criticism of their polytheists and envious ones. The support in the indication that the Qur'an is true is that the People of the Book know that it is true, because it confirms their books and agrees with them.

﴿So do not be among the doubters.﴾ It has been said: the address is to the Messenger, but it is an address to his community. It has been said: it is to every hearer, meaning that when the proof has become manifest, there is no reason to doubt it. It has been said: it is from the kind of stirring up and encouragement, like His saying: ﴿and do not be among the polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 14]. It has been said: ﴿So do not be among the doubters﴾ concerning the fact that the People of the Book know that it is sent down from your Lord in truth, and let not the denial of most of them and their disbelief disturb you. Ibn 'Abbas and Hafs read (munazzal) with doubled letter (tashdid), and the rest read it with single letter (takhfif).

﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice.﴾ Since from the beginning of the surah up to here there are proofs of monotheism, prophethood, resurrection, and criticism of those who oppose these, and from here to the end of the surah there are rulings and narratives, it was fitting to mention these verses here. That is: His decrees and His measures have been completed; this is what Ibn 'Abbas said. Qatada said: "His words" is the Qur'an. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Everything He has informed of, commanded, forbidden, promised and threatened." Al-Hasan said: "Truthful in promise and just in threat." It has been said: "in what it includes of information and ruling," or "in what has been and what will be," or "in what He commanded and what He forbade," or "in encouragement and warning," or "in His saying: these to Paradise and these to the Fire," or "in reward and punishment," or "in the support of His friends and the abandonment of His enemies," or "in the support of the Messenger at Badr and the destruction of his enemies," or "in guidance and misguidance," or "in forgiveness and punishment," or "in bounty and withholding," or "in the expansion and restriction of provision," or "in His giving and His trial." These sayings: the first part of the phrase was interpreted as "truthfulness," and the conjoined part was interpreted as "justice." Al-Hawfi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu al-Baqa' parsed ﴿truthfulness and justice﴾ as two verbal nouns in the place of a circumstantial accusative (hal), while al-Tabari parsed them as specification (tamyiz); Abu al-Baqa' also permitted this. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is not correct." Abu al-Baqa' added that they could be an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi). The meaning of (tammat) is not that it had a deficiency which was then completed; rather the meaning is that it continued and was sound, as in the hadith: "And Hamzah remained (tamma) upon his Islam," and as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the word of your Lord was fulfilled: "I will surely fill Hell"﴾ [Hud: 119], that is: it continued, and it is an expression for the execution of His decrees. The Kufans read (kalimah) here in the singular, while Nafi' read all of these as (kalimat) in the plural; Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir followed him here.

﴿None can alter His words.﴾ That is: none can change His decrees, and none can alter the words of the Qur'an, so that no change reaches them either in meaning or in wording. In the reading of Ubayy: "None can alter the words of God."

﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ That is: All-Hearing of your sayings, All-Knowing of the hidden thoughts.

﴿And if you obey most of those on earth, they will lead you astray from the way of God.﴾ That is: and if you agree with them in what they are upon, from worshipping other than God and legislating what they have legislated without God's permission, most of them, because most of them at that time were disbelievers. "The earth" here means the world; this is what Ibn 'Abbas said. It has been said: "most of those on earth" are the leaders of Makkah, and "the earth" is specific to the land of Makkah. He often condemned "most" in His Book, and generally "most" is not used except for those who follow their desires.

﴿They follow nothing but conjecture.﴾ That is: they do not refer, in their beliefs, to knowledge, nor in what they have legislated, to the judgment of God.

﴿And they do nothing but guess.﴾ That is: they estimate and conjecture. This is an emphasis of what precedes it. Some commentators restricted this obedience and their following of conjecture and guessing to the matter of slaughtered animals, and it is related that the occasion of revelation was the polytheists' dispute with the Messenger about slaughtered animals, and their saying: "We eat what we kill, and we do not eat what God kills." So it was revealed, informing that they estimate by their conjectures and by their guessing.

﴿Indeed your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of those who are guided.﴾ When He, exalted is He, mentioned ﴿they will lead you astray from the way of God﴾, He informed that He is the most knowing of the knowers about the one who goes astray and the one who is guided, and the meaning is that He knows them and you: they are the ones who go astray, and you are the one who is guided. As for (man), it has been said that it is in the place of a genitive, through dropping the preposition and retaining its governing effect, but this is not good, because such a thing is not permitted except in poetry, as in: "Zayd is the best striker of the sword," meaning "with the sword." Abu al-Fath said it is in the place of an accusative governed by (a'lamu) after the preposition is dropped, but this is not good, because the comparative form (af'al al-tafdil) does not govern an object in the accusative. Abu 'Ali said it is in the place of an accusative governed by a verb omitted, meaning "he knows who goes astray," and the omission of it is indicated by (a'lamu). Similar to this is what Abu Zayd recited: 

"And the most striking of us with swords were the helmets"

meaning: "they strike the helmets," and in that case it is a relative (mawsulah), and its relative clause is (yadillu). Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be descriptive (mawsufah) with the verb. Al-Kisa'i, al-Mubarrad, al-Zajjaj and Makki said it is in the place of a nominative, and it is interrogative, a subject, with the predicate being (yadillu), and the clause is in the place of an accusative governed by (a'lamu), meaning: "I know which of the people goes astray," like His saying: ﴿that We may know which of the two parties﴾ [al-Kahf: 12]. This is weak, because suspension (ta'liq) is a branch of the permissibility of governing, and the comparative form does not govern a direct object, so it is not suspended from it. The Kufans permit the comparative form to govern a direct object, and the refutation of them is in the books of grammar. Al-Hasan and Ahmad ibn Abi Shurayh read (yudillu) with a dammah on the yaa', and the subject of (yudillu) is the pronoun of (man), and its object is omitted, meaning: "who misleads the people"; or the pronoun refers to God, in the sense of finding him astray or creating misguidance in him. This sentence is informative, and it contains a threat and a promise, because His being knowing of the one who goes astray and the one who is guided is a metaphor for recompense for each of them.

(p-211)

﴿So eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned, if you are believers in His signs.﴾ It is mentioned that the occasion of its revelation was that they said to the Messenger: "Who killed the sheep that died?" He said: "God." They said: "Then you claim that what you and your companions kill is lawful, and what the falcon and the dog kill is lawful, but what God kills is unlawful?"

And ʿIkrima said: When the prohibition of carrion (al-maytah) was revealed, the Magians of Persia wrote to the polytheists of Quraysh, who had been their allies in the pre-Islamic age (al-jahiliyya), and there was correspondence between them: "Muhammad and his companions claim that they follow the command of God. Then they claim that what they slaughter is lawful, and what God slaughters is unlawful." This troubled some of the Muslims, so God revealed: ﴿And do not eat of that…﴾ [al-Anʿam: 121].

Since the preceding verse contained a denunciation of following misguiders who make the unlawful lawful and the lawful unlawful, and since they used to mention the names of their gods over much of what they slaughtered, He commanded the believers to eat what has had the name of God alone, not of their gods, mentioned over its slaughter (dhakah). This is a command of permission (amr ibaha). What has had the name of God mentioned over it is the slaughtered animal (al-mudhakka), not what has died of its own accord.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "So eat" is a consequence of the denunciation of following the misguiders. Eating what has had God's name mentioned over its slaughter is made conditional upon faith, as you say: "Obey me if you are my son," meaning: "You are believers, so do not oppose the command of God." This is an exhortation to eat what He has made lawful and to abandon what He has forbidden.

﴿And what is it with you that you do not eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned, when He has already detailed for you what He has forbidden to you, except what you are compelled to?﴾ That is: what purpose do you have in refraining from eating what has had the name of God mentioned over it? This is an interrogative that implies denunciation of those who refrain from it; that is, nothing prevents it. ﴿And He has already detailed﴾ [this] in this surah, because it is, according to what has been transmitted, a Meccan surah, revealed all at once. So it is not fitting that ﴿and He has already detailed﴾ refer to the detailing found in al-Baqara and al-Maʾida, since those two were revealed later than this surah.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿and He has already detailed for you what He has forbidden to you﴾ refers to what He did not forbid to you, namely His saying: ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ [al-Maʾida: 3]. End of quotation. We have noted that the detailing of prohibition by what is in al-Baqara and al-Maʾida is not fitting, and the claim that "lā" is extra here is unnecessary; the meaning is sound and clear if it is negating. The construction ﴿alla taʾkulu﴾ originally was fī an lā taʾkulū (in that you not eat), so the preposition fī, which is connected to what is connected to lakum (for you), the predicate of the interrogative mā, was deleted. Whether the phrase ﴿alla taʾkulu﴾ is in the accusative or genitive place is a matter of disagreement (al-khilaf). As for those who held that ﴿alla taʾkulū﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning "abstaining from eating," their view is weak, because an-anna (that) with its operand does not occur as a circumstantial clause. This is explicitly stated by Sibawayh, and we know of no one among those whose opinion is considered who disagrees with him; it has a reason mentioned in grammar. The clause ﴿and He has already detailed﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause.

The two Basrans (al-ʿArabiyyān, i.e., Abu ʿAmr and Ibn ʿAmir? — as stated: al-ʿArabiyyān) and Ibn Kathir read fuṣṣila and ḥurrima in the passive voice. Nafiʿ and Ḥafs read faṣṣala and ḥarrama in the active voice. Al-Akhawan (the two brothers, i.e., Hamza and al-Kisa'i) and Abu Bakr read faṣṣala in the active voice and ḥurrima in the passive voice. ʿAṭiyya is the same, except that he lightened the ṣād. The meaning: ﴿except what you are compelled to﴾ [eat] of ﴿what He has forbidden to you﴾, in the state of choice, for it is lawful for you in the state of necessity. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "mā" here does not intend all that is forbidden, like carrion and others. He and al-Ḥawfi said: it is in the accusative position by way of exception, or the exception is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿ). Abu al-Baqaʾ said: "mā" is in the accusative position as an exception from the genus in terms of meaning, as if He rebuked them for leaving off eating what had the name of God mentioned over it, and that implies permission to eat absolutely.

﴿And indeed many do mislead by their desires without knowledge.﴾ That is: indeed many of the disbelievers who dispute about foods and other things mislead [others] by declaring things lawful and unlawful, and by their desires and appetites, without knowledge, that is, without any law from God, but merely by their own desires, like ʿAmr ibn Luhayy and those beneath him among the polytheists, such as Abu al-Aḥwaṣ ibn Malik al-Jushami, Budayl ibn Warqa al-Khuzaʿi, and Ḥulays ibn Yazid al-Qurashi, who adopted the baḥā'ir (slit-eared she-camels) and the sawā'ib (freed camels).

Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read liyaḍillūna with a fatḥa on the yāʾ here, and in Yunus ﴿Our Lord, so that they may mislead﴾ [Yunus: 88], and in Ibrahim ﴿rivals, so that they may mislead﴾ [Ibrahim: 30], and in al-Hajj ﴿turning aside his side, to mislead﴾ [al-Hajj: 9], and in Luqman ﴿to mislead from the way of God﴾ [Luqman: 6], and in al-Zumar ﴿rivals, to mislead﴾ [al-Zumar: 8]. The Kufans read them with a ḍamma in the six instances, and the two companions agreed with them, except in Yunus and here, where they used a fatḥa.

﴿Indeed your Lord is most knowing of the transgressors.﴾ That is: of those who exceed the limit in transgression, who make lawful and unlawful without permission from God. This is a report that implies a severe warning for whoever transgresses, that is, He will recompense them for their transgression.

﴿And leave alone the outward and the inward of sin.﴾ (al-ithm) is general, encompassing all disobediences. Since He rebuked them for leaving off eating what God's name was mentioned over, they were commanded to leave off sin (al-ithm), whether done openly or done in secret. It is as if He said: abandon acts of disobedience, outward and inward. This was said by Abu al-ʿAliya, Mujahid, Qatada, ʿAṭa', Ibn al-Anbari, and al-Zajjaj.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: its outward is adultery. al-Suddi said: the outward is the notorious adultery that the Arabs used to commit, and its inward is taking secret lovers (akhdan). Ibn Jubayr said: its outward is what God has explicitly forbidden by His saying: ﴿Forbidden to you﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 23], and the verse ﴿and do not marry what your fathers married of women﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 22], and the inward is adultery. Ibn Zayd said: its outward is removing their garments when they circumambulated the House naked, and its inward is adultery. It was also said: its outward is the deeds of the limbs, and its inward is the deeds of the heart, such as arrogance, envy, self-admiration, bad belief, and other sins of the heart. It was also said: its outward is wine and its inward is nabidh (a fermented drink). Mujahid also said: its outward is adultery and its inward is what one intends. al-Maturidi said: the most fitting is that ﴿the outward of sin and its inward﴾ be understood as eating carrion and what has not had God's name mentioned over it. Muqatil said: al-ithm here is shirk. Others said: all sins apart from shirk. All these statements are specifications for which there is no proof, and the apparent meaning is the generality of all acts of disobedience, including shirk and other things, outward and hidden; and every one of those things they mentioned falls within this generality.

﴿Indeed those who earn sin will be recompensed for what they used to commit.﴾ That is: those who earn sin in this world will be recompensed in the Hereafter. This is a threat and warning to the disobedient.

Whether the phrase ﴿alla taʾkulu﴾ is in the accusative or genitive place is a matter of disagreement (al-khilaf). As for those who held that ﴿alla taʾkulū﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning "abstaining from eating," their view is weak, because an-anna (that) with its operand does not occur as a circumstantial clause. This is explicitly stated by Sibawayh, and we know of no one among those whose opinion is considered who disagrees with him; it has a reason mentioned in grammar. The clause ﴿and He has already detailed﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause.

The two Basrans (al-ʿArabiyyān, i.e., Abu ʿAmr and Ibn ʿAmir? — as stated: al-ʿArabiyyān) and Ibn Kathir read fuṣṣila and ḥurrima in the passive voice. Nafiʿ and Ḥafs read faṣṣala and ḥarrama in the active voice. Al-Akhawan (the two brothers, i.e., Hamza and al-Kisa'i) and Abu Bakr read faṣṣala in the active voice and ḥurrima in the passive voice. ʿAṭiyya is the same, except that he lightened the ṣād. The meaning: ﴿except what you are compelled to﴾ [eat] of ﴿what He has forbidden to you﴾, in the state of choice, for it is lawful for you in the state of necessity. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "mā" here does not intend all that is forbidden, like carrion and others. He and al-Ḥawfi said: it is in the accusative position by way of exception, or the exception is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿ). Abu al-Baqaʾ said: "mā" is in the accusative position as an exception from the genus in terms of meaning, as if He rebuked them for leaving off eating what had the name of God mentioned over it, and that implies permission to eat absolutely.

﴿And indeed many do mislead by their desires without knowledge.﴾ That is: indeed many of the disbelievers who dispute about foods and other things mislead [others] by declaring things lawful and unlawful, and by their desires and appetites, without knowledge, that is, without any law from God, but merely by their own desires, like ʿAmr ibn Luhayy and those beneath him among the polytheists, such as Abu al-Aḥwaṣ ibn Malik al-Jushami, Budayl ibn Warqa al-Khuzaʿi, and Ḥulays ibn Yazid al-Qurashi, who adopted the baḥā'ir (slit-eared she-camels) and the sawā'ib (freed camels).

Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read liyaḍillūna with a fatḥa on the yāʾ here, and in Yunus ﴿Our Lord, so that they may mislead﴾ [Yunus: 88], and in Ibrahim ﴿rivals, so that they may mislead﴾ [Ibrahim: 30], and in al-Hajj ﴿turning aside his side, to mislead﴾ [al-Hajj: 9], and in Luqman ﴿to mislead from the way of God﴾ [Luqman: 6], and in al-Zumar ﴿rivals, to mislead﴾ [al-Zumar: 8]. The Kufans read them with a ḍamma in the six instances, and the two companions agreed with them, except in Yunus and here, where they used a fatḥa.

﴿Indeed your Lord is most knowing of the transgressors.﴾ That is: of those who exceed the limit in transgression, who make lawful and unlawful without permission from God. This is a report that implies a severe warning for whoever transgresses, that is, He will recompense them for their transgression.

﴿And leave alone the outward and the inward of sin.﴾ (al-ithm) is general, encompassing all disobediences. Since He rebuked them for leaving off eating what God's name was mentioned over, they were commanded to leave off sin (al-ithm), whether done openly or done in secret. It is as if He said: abandon acts of disobedience, outward and inward. This was said by Abu al-ʿAliya, Mujahid, Qatada, ʿAṭa', Ibn al-Anbari, and al-Zajjaj.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: its outward is adultery. al-Suddi said: the outward is the notorious adultery that the Arabs used to commit, and its inward is taking secret lovers (akhdan). Ibn Jubayr said: its outward is what God has explicitly forbidden by His saying: ﴿Forbidden to you﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 23], and the verse ﴿and do not marry what your fathers married of women﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 22], and the inward is adultery. Ibn Zayd said: its outward is removing their garments when they circumambulated the House naked, and its inward is adultery. It was also said: its outward is the deeds of the limbs, and its inward is the deeds of the heart, such as arrogance, envy, self-admiration, bad belief, and other sins of the heart. It was also said: its outward is wine and its inward is nabidh (a fermented drink). Mujahid also said: its outward is adultery and its inward is what one intends. al-Maturidi said: the most fitting is that ﴿the outward of sin and its inward﴾ be understood as eating carrion and what has not had God's name mentioned over it. Muqatil said: al-ithm here is shirk. Others said: all sins apart from shirk. All these statements are specifications for which there is no proof, and the apparent meaning is the generality of all acts of disobedience, including shirk and other things, outward and hidden; and every one of those things they mentioned falls within this generality.

﴿Indeed those who earn sin will be recompensed for what they used to commit.﴾ That is: those who earn sin in this world will be recompensed in the Hereafter. This is a threat and warning to the disobedient.

﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned, for indeed it is a transgression﴾. Al-Sakhawi said: Makhul said: "The same has been related from Abu al-Darda' and 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit," and he permitted the slaughtered animals of the People of the Book even if the name of Allah was not mentioned over them. A group of scholars held that the verse is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated), and that it is not permissible for us to eat from their slaughtered animals except that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned. This is related from 'Ali, 'A'ishah and Ibn 'Umar. End of quote. This is not called naskh (abrogation) but takhsis (specification). When He commanded the eating of what had the name of Allah mentioned over it, its implication (mafhum) was that one should not eat what did not have the name of Allah mentioned over it, and He confirmed this implication by explicit statement. The apparent ruling is the prohibition of eating what the name of Allah has not been mentioned over, whether deliberately, such as by leaving out the tasmiyah (invocation of the name), or forgetfully. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, 'Abdullah ibn 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah, 'Abdullah ibn Yazid al-Khatimi, Ibn Sirin, al-Sha'bi, Nafi', Abu Thawr and Dawud in one narration said this. Abu Hurayrah, Ibn 'Abbas also in one narration, Abu 'Iyad, Abu Rafi', 'Ata', Ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan, Jabir, 'Ikrimah, Tawus, al-Nakha'i, Qatadah, Ibn Zayd, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, Rabi'ah, and Malik in one narration, and al-Shafi'i and al-Asamm said: it is permissible to eat what was not invoked upon, whether the omission was deliberate or forgetful. Mujahid, Tawus also, Ibn Shihab, Ibn Jubayr, 'Ata' in one narration, Abu Hanifah and his companions, al-Thawri, al-Hasan ibn Hayy, al-Hasan ibn Salih, Ishaq, Malik in one narration, Ahmad in one narration, Ibn Abi al-Qasim, 'Isa and Asbagh said: it may be eaten if the omission was forgetful, and if it was deliberate it may not be eaten. Al-Nahhas chose this view and said: One is not called a transgressor (fasiq) if one is forgetful. It is related from 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas that it is permissible to eat the slaughter of one who forgot the tasmiyah. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is the view of the majority. Abu Bakr al-Ayidhi said: It is disliked to eat the slaughter of one who deliberately omits the tasmiyah. These specifications require evidence. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned﴾ is its general application to what the tasmiyah was left out on. Ibn 'Abbas said in one narration: it refers to carrion (maytah). He also related that it means carrion and the strangled (al-munkhaniqah), up to: and what is slaughtered on the altars (nusub). 'Ata' said: it refers to slaughter for idols, which the Arabs used to do. Ibn Bahr said: it refers to the game of polytheists, because they do not invoke the name when releasing the arrow, and they are not among the people of the tasmiyah. (p. 213) Al-Hasan said: "transgression" (fisq) means disbelief (kufr). Al-Kirmani said: he means together with considering it lawful (istihlal). Others said: fisq means disobedience (ma'siyah). The pronoun in ﴿and indeed it﴾ refers to the verbal noun implied by ﴿eat﴾, i.e., "indeed the eating," as al-Zamakhshari said, and he limited himself to this. Al-Hawfi also permitted that it refers to "ma" (what) in His words ﴿of that over which...﴾, and Ibn 'Atiyyah permitted that it refers to the mention implied by His words ﴿has not been mentioned﴾. End of quote. The meaning of its referring to the negated verbal noun is as if it were said: "indeed leaving out the mention is a transgression." This clause has no place in grammatical analysis (i'rab), and it carries the sense of causation, as if it were said: "because of its transgression."

﴿And indeed the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you﴾. That is, indeed the devils of the jinn, as Ibn 'Abbas and 'Abdullah ibn Kathir said. 'Ikrimah said: the rebellious humans among the Magians of Persia, and their writing to Quraysh was mentioned earlier. That is: they whisper to the disbelievers of Quraysh, by inspiring them with that argument concerning the slaughtered animals mentioned earlier, or through the tongues of the soothsayers (kuhhan) of their time, to dispute with you. Al-Zamakhshari said: with their saying: "Do you not eat what Allah has killed?" And with this, the interpretation of one who interpreted it as referring to carrion is preferred. End of quote. The better view is to take the verse as not being specified by what they mentioned, but rather as a report that what came from the disbelievers' disputing and contending with the believers is from the devils who whisper this to them. For this reason it is concluded with His words ﴿And if you obey them, indeed you are polytheists﴾. That is: if you obey the allies of the devils, indeed you are polytheists, because obeying them is obeying the devils, and that is associating partners (shirk). One does not become a polytheist in reality until one obeys in belief. As for when one obeys in action while one's belief is sound, one is a transgressor (fasiq). This clause is a report which contains a threat. What is most difficult for a believer is to resemble a polytheist, let alone to be judged as a polytheist. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that those who disputed with that argument were a group of Jews, but this is weak, because the Jews do not eat carrion. Except that they may have said that as a sophistry and an answer to the Arabs, in which case it is possible. As for the response to the conditional, al-Hawfi claimed that it is ﴿indeed you are polytheists﴾, with the fa' (then) omitted, meaning "then indeed you." This omission is one of the poetic licenses (darurat), so it does not occur in the Qur'an. Rather, the response is omitted, and ﴿indeed you are polytheists﴾ is the response of an omitted oath. The estimated meaning is: "By Allah, if you obey them," in accordance with His words: "If they do not desist from what they say, they will surely be touched..." and His words ﴿And if You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will surely be among the losers﴾ [al-A'raf: 23]. This construction is most often used with the lam that signals the omitted oath before the conditional "in," as in His words ﴿If they are expelled, they will not go out with them﴾ [al-Hashr: 12], and the response of the conditional is omitted because the response of the oath indicates it.

﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life and made for him a light by which he walks among the people like one whose state is in darkness, from which he cannot emerge?﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: It was revealed concerning Hamzah and Abu Jahl. Abu Jahl threw dung at the Messenger, and when Hamzah returned from his hunting with his bow in his hand, he was informed of that. He had not yet embraced Islam, so he became angry and struck Abu Jahl with it while Abu Jahl was pleading with him and saying: "He has made foolish our minds, reviled our gods and opposed our fathers." Hamzah said: "And who is more foolish than you, who worship stones instead of Allah?" And he embraced Islam. And it is also related from Ibn 'Abbas that it was revealed concerning 'Ammar and Abu Jahl. Zayd ibn Aslam said: it was revealed concerning 'Umar and Abu Jahl. When the mention of the believers and the disbelievers preceded, the Exalted gave an example by likening the believer, who after having been a disbeliever, is like a living person to whom a light has been given, by which he moves as he wishes, and the disbeliever is like one immersed in darknesses, constantly remaining in them, in order to show the difference between the two groups. Life, death, light and darkness are metaphorical: darkness is a metaphor for disbelief, light is a metaphor for faith, and death is a metaphor for disbelief. Al-Maturidi said: death is a metaphor for being in the darkness of the womb, not seeing and not understanding anything, then one is brought out and sees and understands. We say: one who is brought out of the darknesses is not equal to one who is left in them, and likewise the believer who sees the truth and acts upon it is not equal to the disbeliever who does not see. Something similar is the statement of Ibn Bahr, who said: ﴿Is one who was a drop, or a clinging clot, or a lump of flesh, then We formed him and breathed into him the spirit?﴾ End of quote. As for light, it is the light of wisdom, or the light of religion, or the Qur'an, according to different opinions. Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi said: life is the readiness to receive knowledge, so that one acquires universal, primary sciences, which are called reason ('aql). Light is what the composition of those self-evident principles leads to, of unknown theoretical matters. His walking among the people means that he has become one who is present to the sacred knowledge and the spiritual manifestations, looking at them. It may be said that life is the readiness subsisting in the essence of the soul, and light is the connection of the light of revelation and the descent to it. Insight requires two things: soundness of the faculty of reason and the rising of the light of revelation, just as sight requires two things: soundness of the faculty and the rising of the sun. End of summary. This is far from the usages and meanings of Arabic speech. When He mentioned the bestowal of favour upon the believing servant, He attributed it to Himself, saying ﴿We gave him life and made for him a light﴾, and in describing the disbeliever He did not attribute it to Himself but said ﴿like one whose state is in darkness﴾. Since the types of disbelief are many, He said ﴿in darknesses﴾. When He mentioned the making of light for the one who was dead, He said ﴿by which he walks among the people﴾, that is, he accompanies it wherever he turns. He said ﴿among the people﴾ to indicate that its illumination extends to himself and to others among the people, so He mentioned that the benefit of the believer is not limited to himself. He set his activity against the light, and the constant presence of the light with him against the disbeliever's remaining ﴿in the darknesses﴾ and never leaving them. He emphasized this by the entry of the particle ba' into the predicate of "laysa" (is not). The view of those who said that the light and darkness refer to the Day of Resurrection, pointing to His words ﴿Their light runs before them and on their right hands﴾ [al-Hadid: 12], and to the darkness of Hell, is far-fetched. The discussion of the example was preceded in His words ﴿like the example of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17]. Talhah read ﴿afaman﴾ with fa' in place of waw.

﴿Thus has been made attractive to the disbelievers what they used to do﴾. The demonstrative "thus" refers either to the giving of life to the believer, or to the state of the disbeliever in darknesses. That is: just as We gave life to the believer, so it has been made attractive to the disbeliever; or, like the state of the disbeliever in darknesses, it has been made attractive to the disbelievers. The agent is omitted. Al-Hasan said: it is the devil. Others said: it is Allah, the Exalted. Al-Zamakhshari permitted both views. The discussion of adornment (tazyin) has already been given. It was also said: the one who adorns is the great ones among the small ones.

It was also said: the one who adorns is the great ones among the small ones.

And so We have appointed in every town its greatest sinners, that they may plot therein (Qur'an 6:123). That is: just as We appointed in Mecca its chieftains, that they might plot therein, We appointed in every town [such people]. This implies the corruption of the state of the disbelievers contemporary with the Messenger, since their condition is that of those disbelievers, their counterparts, who preceded them. 'Ikrimah said: it was revealed concerning the mockers, meaning that the illustration applies to them. It has also been said that it is coordinated with "Thus He made attractive" (6:122), so the demonstrative in it refers to what was indicated by His saying "Thus He made attractive". End of quote. **Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 6, verses 125–126:**

﴿So whomever Allah wills to guide, He expands his chest to Islam; and whomever He wills to send astray, He makes his chest tight and constricted, as if he were climbing up into the sky.﴾ Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning the Messenger ﷺ and Abu Jahl. Guidance (al-hidaya) here stands in opposition to misguidance (al-dalala). Expanding the chest (al-sharh) is a kinaya (metonymy) for making him receptive to Islam, expanded to accept its obligations. Attributing this to his chest is a majaz (figurative usage) for the person himself, which is why they say "so-and-so has a wide chest" when the person can bear what hardships and obligations come upon him. Attributing the willing of guidance and misguidance to Allah is an isnad haqiqi (literal attribution), because He, exalted is He, is the Creator of that, its Originator, and its Willer. Expanding the chest means facilitating the acceptance of faith upon him, beautifying it for him, and preparing him to accept it. The pronoun of the subject of "guidance" refers to Allah, meaning: Allah expands his chest. It was also said that it refers to the guidance formed from ﴿an yahdiyahu﴾ (that He guide him), meaning: the guidance expands his chest. Ibn Atiyya said: "On this the doctrine of the Qadariyya (the school denying divine predestination of human acts) is built regarding the creation of actions." End of quote. In the hadith there is a question about the manner of this expansion, and that when light enters the heart the chest expands; its sign is turning toward the abode of eternity and withdrawing from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death before it overtakes one. The words "tightness" (al-dayq) and "constriction" (al-haraj) are a kinaya for the opposite of expansion and an isti'ara (metaphor) for the non-acceptance of faith. Al-haraj means extremely tight. The pronoun in (yajal) refers to (Allah). The meaning of "yaj'al" is "yusayyir" (makes), because a human is first created upon the fitra (natural disposition), which is his being prepared for what is cast into him and what is placed within him. So when Allah wills to send him astray, He sends him astray and makes him unable to accept faith. It is also possible that (yaj'al) means "yakhluq" (creates), and ﴿dayyiqan harajan﴾ is in the accusative of circumstance (hal), meaning: He creates him in this state, so he neither hears faith nor accepts it. Following Abu Ali al-Farisi, who held Mu'tazili views (the Mu'tazila being the rationalist school), he held that (yaj'al) here means "yusammi" (names), saying: like His saying: ﴿And they have made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 19]. He said: that is, they named them. Or it means that a ruling of tightness is passed on him, as you say: "this one makes Basra a city (miṣr)," meaning: he rules for it by its ruling, fleeing from attributing the creation of that to Allah, exalted is He. Or it means "making it" obligatory according to his Mu'tazili doctrine. A similar departure from the apparent meaning of the wording is Zamakhshari's statement: ﴿an yahdiyahu﴾ means "an yalṭufa bihi" (that He show him kindness), and He wills to show kindness only to one who is worthy of kindness. ﴿yashrah ṣadrahu lil-islam﴾: He shows him kindness until he desires Islam, his soul is at rest with it, and he loves to enter it. ﴿wa man yurid an yuḍillahu﴾: that He forsake him and leave him to himself, and he is the one who receives no kindness. ﴿yaj'al ṣadrahu ḍayyiqan harajan﴾: He withholds His favors from him until his heart hardens, turns away from accepting the truth, and is closed so that faith cannot enter it. End of quote. All of this is departing from the apparent meaning of the wording and an interpretation according to the doctrine of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school that affirmed human free will and divine justice in a particular way). The comparative clause means that just as he attempts something impossible, since climbing into the sky is a parable for what is far off and beyond ability, and what is constricting for him when he is capable of it, so said Zamakhshari. This is close to the interpretation of Ibn Jurayj, Ata al-Khurasani, and al-Suddi. They said: that is, this person with a constricted, tight chest was attempting to climb into the sky, until he attempted faith or contemplated it, and found its difficulty upon him like the difficulty of climbing into the sky. End of quote. Because this was considered impossible by them, Allah related of them that they proposed their statement: ﴿or you ascend into the sky﴾. Ibn Jubayr said: the meaning is that he finds no path except an ascent, from the intensity of constriction, meaning the earth became narrow for him so he kept ascending toward the sky. It was also said: the meaning is that he is distracted in opinion, his heart flies in the air as a light thing flies when winds blow. Ibn Kathir read (ḍayqan) here and in al-Furqan. It may be a lightened form of ḍayyiq, as they say layyin (soft, from layyin). Al-Kisa'i said: ḍayyiq with shadda (doubled yod) is for physical bodies, and with the lightened form for abstract meanings. It may also be a masdar (verbal noun); they said that as a masdar, "ḍāqa ḍayq" with fatha and kasra on the ḍad have the same meaning. So either it is attributed to the chest for emphasis, or in the sense of an iḍafa (construct): "possessor of tightness," or as a majaz in place of the active participle (ism al-fa'il). These three options are those said regarding describing physical objects with verbal nouns. Nafi' and Abu Bakr read (ḥarajan) with fatha on the ra', and it is a verbal noun: "possessor of ḥaraj," or it is made the very ḥaraj, or it means ḥarija with kasra on the ra' (a verb, "he became tight"). It is narrated from Umar, and some of the Companions recited it for him there with kasra. He said: "Find me a man from Kinana as a shepherd, but from the Banu Mudlij." When he came to him, he said: "O youth, what is the ḥarija among you?" He said: "A tree that grows among other trees, which neither a grazing animal nor a wild animal can reach." Umar said: "Thus is the heart of the hypocrite, nothing of good reaches it." End of quote. This is an indication, Allah knows best, of the way the verb is derived from the same root consonants, as in their saying: istaḥjara (became hard like stone) and istanwaqa (became like a she-camel). Ibn Kathir read (yaṣʿad), the present tense of ṣaʿida. Abu Bakr read (yaṣṣāʿad), its origin being yataṣāʿad, and it was assimilated. The rest of the seven read (yaṣṣaʿʿad) with shadda on the ṣad and the ʿayn, its origin being yataṣaʿʿad. This was also how ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud), Ibn Musarrif, and al-A'mash read. Abu Ali said: ﴿ka-annama yaṣṣaʿʿadu﴾ means from below to above, and he did not mean the shading sky itself, just as Sibawayh said: "al-qaydud (a tall one) in a place other than the sky," meaning in a place other than an elevation. Ibn Atiyya said: It may be that the comparison is to one who climbs a steep ascent, as if he were climbing with it into the air. (Ṣaʿida) means to rise, and (taṣaʿʿada) means to undertake of that what is burdensome upon him. From it is Umar ibn al-Khattab's saying: "Nothing has burdened me as the proposal of marriage has burdened me." It is also narrated: "No proposal has burdened me."

﴿Thus Allah places the filth upon those who do not believe﴾: that is, like that placing, His making his chest tight and constricted. Al-Zajjaj's statement is far-fetched: that is, like what We have related to you (yaj'al). The meaning of "Allah places the rijs" is: Allah casts or Allah makes the punishment (al-'adhab). Al-rijs in the sense of punishment is what the lexicographers said. The construction of (yaj'al) with ʿala may be understood as "nulqi" (We cast), as you say: "I placed your goods some upon others," or it may mean "yuṣayyir" (makes), with ʿalā in the position of the second object. Zamakhshari said: "Allah places" means abandonment and withholding of success; He described it with the opposite of what success is described with, of goodness; or He meant the act leading to rijs, which is punishment, from irtijas, which is agitation. End of quote. This is in line with his Mu'tazili method. The opposite of the good (al-ṭayyib) is the foul-smelling, disgusting odor. Al-rijs and al-najas (impurity) mean the same, said some of the Kufan scholars. Mujahid said: al-rijs is everything in which there is no good. Ata, Ibn Zayd, and Abu Ubayda said: al-rijs is punishment in this world and the next. Al-Zajjaj said: the curse in this world and the punishment in the next. It was also said: al-rijs is wrath. Isma'il al-Darir said: al-rijs is torment, and its origin is the stinking impure, and it is the filth of disbelief.

(p-219) ﴿And this is the path of your Lord, straight﴾: the reference in His saying "this" is to the Qur'an and the law the Messenger brought, so said Ibn Abbas; or to the Qur'an, so said Ibn Mas'ud; or to tawhid (affirmation of Allah's oneness), so said some; or to what He established in the preceding verses concerning this matter and other paths of guidance and paths of misguidance. Zamakhshari said: "This is the path of your Lord": its way, which wisdom requires, and His custom in granting success and abandonment. A similar statement is that of Isma'il al-Darir, meaning this is the handiwork of your Lord. "This" refers to guidance and misguidance. The path is attributed to the Lord in the sense that it is from Him and by His command. ﴿straight﴾: with no crookedness in it. The word ﴿mustaqiman﴾ is in the accusative as an emphatic circumstantial (hal mu'akkida).

﴿We have indeed detailed the verses﴾: that is, We have made them clear, and We did not leave in them any ambiguity or confusion.

﴿for a people who remember﴾: who reflect with their minds. It is as if the verses were something hidden from them which they had not recalled; then when they were detailed, they remembered them.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 6, verses 125–126:**

﴿So whomever Allah wills to guide, He expands his chest to Islam; and whomever He wills to send astray, He makes his chest tight and constricted, as if he were climbing up into the sky.﴾ Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning the Messenger ﷺ and Abu Jahl. Guidance (al-hidaya) here stands in opposition to misguidance (al-dalala). Expanding the chest (al-sharh) is a kinaya (metonymy) for making him receptive to Islam, expanded to accept its obligations. Attributing this to his chest is a majaz (figurative usage) for the person himself, which is why they say "so-and-so has a wide chest" when the person can bear what hardships and obligations come upon him. Attributing the willing of guidance and misguidance to Allah is an isnad haqiqi (literal attribution), because He, exalted is He, is the Creator of that, its Originator, and its Willer. Expanding the chest means facilitating the acceptance of faith upon him, beautifying it for him, and preparing him to accept it. The pronoun of the subject of "guidance" refers to Allah, meaning: Allah expands his chest. It was also said that it refers to the guidance formed from ﴿an yahdiyahu﴾ (that He guide him), meaning: the guidance expands his chest. Ibn Atiyya said: "On this the doctrine of the Qadariyya (the school denying divine predestination of human acts) is built regarding the creation of actions." End of quote. In the hadith there is a question about the manner of this expansion, and that when light enters the heart the chest expands; its sign is turning toward the abode of eternity and withdrawing from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death before it overtakes one. The words "tightness" (al-dayq) and "constriction" (al-haraj) are a kinaya for the opposite of expansion and an isti'ara (metaphor) for the non-acceptance of faith. Al-haraj means extremely tight. The pronoun in (yajal) refers to (Allah). The meaning of "yaj'al" is "yusayyir" (makes), because a human is first created upon the fitra (natural disposition), which is his being prepared for what is cast into him and what is placed within him. So when Allah wills to send him astray, He sends him astray and makes him unable to accept faith. It is also possible that (yaj'al) means "yakhluq" (creates), and ﴿dayyiqan harajan﴾ is in the accusative of circumstance (hal), meaning: He creates him in this state, so he neither hears faith nor accepts it. Following Abu Ali al-Farisi, who held Mu'tazili views (the Mu'tazila being the rationalist school), he held that (yaj'al) here means "yusammi" (names), saying: like His saying: ﴿And they have made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 19]. He said: that is, they named them. Or it means that a ruling of tightness is passed on him, as you say: "this one makes Basra a city (miṣr)," meaning: he rules for it by its ruling, fleeing from attributing the creation of that to Allah, exalted is He. Or it means "making it" obligatory according to his Mu'tazili doctrine. A similar departure from the apparent meaning of the wording is Zamakhshari's statement: ﴿an yahdiyahu﴾ means "an yalṭufa bihi" (that He show him kindness), and He wills to show kindness only to one who is worthy of kindness. ﴿yashrah ṣadrahu lil-islam﴾: He shows him kindness until he desires Islam, his soul is at rest with it, and he loves to enter it. ﴿wa man yurid an yuḍillahu﴾: that He forsake him and leave him to himself, and he is the one who receives no kindness. ﴿yaj'al ṣadrahu ḍayyiqan harajan﴾: He withholds His favors from him until his heart hardens, turns away from accepting the truth, and is closed so that faith cannot enter it. End of quote. All of this is departing from the apparent meaning of the wording and an interpretation according to the doctrine of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school that affirmed human free will and divine justice in a particular way). The comparative clause means that just as he attempts something impossible, since climbing into the sky is a parable for what is far off and beyond ability, and what is constricting for him when he is capable of it, so said Zamakhshari. This is close to the interpretation of Ibn Jurayj, Ata al-Khurasani, and al-Suddi. They said: that is, this person with a constricted, tight chest was attempting to climb into the sky, until he attempted faith or contemplated it, and found its difficulty upon him like the difficulty of climbing into the sky. End of quote. Because this was considered impossible by them, Allah related of them that they proposed their statement: ﴿or you ascend into the sky﴾. Ibn Jubayr said: the meaning is that he finds no path except an ascent, from the intensity of constriction, meaning the earth became narrow for him so he kept ascending toward the sky. It was also said: the meaning is that he is distracted in opinion, his heart flies in the air as a light thing flies when winds blow. Ibn Kathir read (ḍayqan) here and in al-Furqan. It may be a lightened form of ḍayyiq, as they say layyin (soft, from layyin). Al-Kisa'i said: ḍayyiq with shadda (doubled yod) is for physical bodies, and with the lightened form for abstract meanings. It may also be a masdar (verbal noun); they said that as a masdar, "ḍāqa ḍayq" with fatha and kasra on the ḍad have the same meaning. So either it is attributed to the chest for emphasis, or in the sense of an iḍafa (construct): "possessor of tightness," or as a majaz in place of the active participle (ism al-fa'il). These three options are those said regarding describing physical objects with verbal nouns. Nafi' and Abu Bakr read (ḥarajan) with fatha on the ra', and it is a verbal noun: "possessor of ḥaraj," or it is made the very ḥaraj, or it means ḥarija with kasra on the ra' (a verb, "he became tight"). It is narrated from Umar, and some of the Companions recited it for him there with kasra. He said: "Find me a man from Kinana as a shepherd, but from the Banu Mudlij." When he came to him, he said: "O youth, what is the ḥarija among you?" He said: "A tree that grows among other trees, which neither a grazing animal nor a wild animal can reach." Umar said: "Thus is the heart of the hypocrite, nothing of good reaches it." End of quote. This is an indication, Allah knows best, of the way the verb is derived from the same root consonants, as in their saying: istaḥjara (became hard like stone) and istanwaqa (became like a she-camel). (p-219) ﴿And this is the path of your Lord, straight﴾: the reference in His saying "this" is to the Qur'an and the law the Messenger brought, so said Ibn Abbas; or to the Qur'an, so said Ibn Mas'ud; or to tawhid (affirmation of Allah's oneness), so said some; or to what He established in the preceding verses concerning this matter and other paths of guidance and paths of misguidance. ﴿for a people who remember﴾: who reflect with their minds. It is as if the verses were something hidden from them which they had not recalled; then when they were detailed, they remembered them.

﴿For them is the Abode of Peace with their Lord, and He is their Protector because of what they used to do.﴾ That is, for them is Paradise. *Al-Salam* (Peace) is one of the names of Allah, the Exalted, just as the Ka'ba is called "the House of Allah." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada, and the house is ascribed to Him as an honour. Or it means "the Abode of Safety (*al-Salamah*) from every calamity." *Al-salam* and *al-salamah* have the same meaning, like *al-ladhadh* and *al-ladhadhah*, and *al-dalal* and *al-dalalah*. This was said by al-Zajjaj. Or "the Abode of Peace" means the greeting, because the greeting of its people within it is "peace." This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. The meaning of "with their Lord" is: in His hospitality and His reception, as you say, "Today we are with so-and-so," meaning in his honour and hospitality. This was said by a group of scholars. Or it means in the Hereafter after the Gathering, as said by Ibn 'Atiyya. Or it means under His guarantee, as you say, "I have a right over so-and-so that will not be forgotten." Or it is a store kept for them whose reality they do not know, based on His saying: ﴿So no soul knows what has been hidden for them of the delight of the eyes﴾ [al-Sajdah: 17].
