This was said by a group including al-Zamakhshari. Or it is by omitting a noun (an elided genitive, *hadhf mudaf*), meaning "in the presence of the meeting with their Lord," as said by a group. Or it means in His vicinity, as came in "the vicinity of the Most Merciful in the Garden of Eden," using the figurative locative (*al-zarfiyyah al-majaziyyah*, the metaphorical use of a place adverb) which indicates the nobility of rank and station, as He said about the angels: ﴿And those who are with Him do not disdain His worship﴾ [al-Anbiya': 19], and as He said: ﴿In a seat of truth, in the presence of a Sovereign, Omnipotent﴾ [al-Qamar: 55], and as He said: ﴿Build for me, with You, a house in the Garden﴾ [al-Tahrim: 11]. "And He is their Protector" means: their ally and the one who loves them, or their helper against their enemies, or the one who takes charge of rewarding them for their deeds.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 128:

﴿On the Day He gathers them all together: "O company of jinn, you have led astray many of mankind."﴾ The apparent meaning is that the address is general to both the two groups (the jinn and mankind), since the devils were mentioned earlier, and they are the jinn and the disbelievers who are their allies. The believers are also included, those for whom ﴿is the Abode of Peace﴾ [al-An'am: 127]. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya said this meaning, and Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The general emphasis in His words ﴿all together﴾ indicates it." Al-Tibrizi said: "This address indicates that the pronoun in ﴿He gathers them﴾ included the jinn when He gathered them and then addressed them. As for the two groups (thaqalan, mankind and jinn), that is all, or they and other creatures." End of quote. Whoever makes ﴿and the Day﴾ coordinated with ﴿for what they used to do﴾ [al-An'am: 127], so that ﴿and the Day He gathers them﴾ is the Day of their allies, makes the pronoun specific to the believers, and that is far-fetched. The better view is that the time expression (zarf) is governed by the verb of saying that the address is quoted by, meaning: "and on the Day We gather them, We will say: O company of jinn." This is better than what some permitted, namely making it an object of the imperative "remember" (udhkur), because that takes it out of the adverbial function. It is also better than what al-Zamakhshari permitted, namely governing it by an implied verb other than the verb of saying or "remember." His estimate was: ((p-220) ﴿and the Day We gather them﴾ [al-An'am: 22]) and We say ﴿O company of jinn﴾. This is what is not described because of its severity, since it requires omitting two clauses from the speech: the clause "and We say" and the clause of the governing verb. Al-Zajjaj estimated the omitted verb of saying as passive, the estimate being: "Then it is said to them," because it is far-fetched that God would speak to them directly, as shown by His words ﴿and Allah will not speak to them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 174]. Their address is a call of fame and rebuke before the heads of witnesses. Al-Ma'shar means the group, and it is pluralized as al-ma'ashir, as in the saying: "We, the company (ma'ashir) of prophets, do not leave inheritance." Al-Afwah said:

*Among us is a company that did not build for their people, and even if their people built, they corrupted and returned.*

The meaning of "leading astray" (istikthar) here is their misleading many of them and making them their followers, as you say: "So-and-so gathered many soldiers (istakthara min al-junud)" and "So-and-so gathered many partisans (istakthara min al-ashya')." Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada said: "You went to excess in misleading them and seducing them." Hafs recited (yahshuruhum) with the ya', and the rest of the seven readers with the nun.

﴿And their allies from mankind will say: "Our Lord, some of us benefited from others, and we have reached our term which You appointed for us."﴾ The allies of the jinn, that is the disbelievers from mankind, will say: ﴿Our Lord, [some of us] benefited (istamta'a)﴾, meaning gained advantage, ﴿from others﴾. The benefit of mankind from the devils is that they guided them to desires and to the means of reaching them. The benefit of the jinn from mankind is that they obeyed them and helped them to their goals in leading them astray. This meaning was related from Ibn 'Abbas, and Muhammad ibn Ka'b and al-Zajjaj also said it. Ibn 'Abbas also said, as did Muqatil: the benefit of mankind from the jinn is the saying of one of them: "I seek refuge in the greatness of this valley from the evil of its people," when he spent the night in the valley on his journey. The benefit of the jinn from mankind is their boasting over their people and their saying: "We have become masters of mankind, until they are seeking refuge with us." Al-Kirmani said: They used to believe that the earth was filled with jinn, and that whoever was not brought into the protection of a jinn would be struck with madness by the others. Likewise, when they killed game, they sought refuge with them, because they believed these animals belonged to the jinn and that some of them were their mounts. It is also said: the benefit is in their bones being food for the jinn and their animal dung being fodder, and the benefit of mankind from the jinn is their seeking help from them for their aims when they subjugate them by spells, or cast affection to them. End of quote. The aspects of benefit are many, and all these sayings fall under them. So it should be held that these sayings are examples of benefit, not a restriction to any one of them. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿some of us benefited from others﴾ is: some of mankind from the jinn, and some of the jinn from mankind. It was also said: the meaning is that some of mankind benefited from some of their own kind, and some of the jinn from some of their own kind, the benefit being attributed to part of one category with respect to part of it. The earlier saying is that some of each of the two categories benefited from some of each. The term they reached is death. This was said by the majority, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi and others. It was also said: it is resurrection and gathering, but al-Zamakhshari mentioned nothing else. It was also said: it is the ultimate point all of them reached of benefit. This statement from them is an excuse on behalf of the jinn for their having gathered many of them, and an indication that this came by Your decree and Your judgment, since "for every term there is a Book." It is also an acknowledgment of what they had done of obeying the devils, following desire, and denying the resurrection, and a submission and lament over their condition. It was recited (ajalana), in the plural, as well as in the singular masculine form (ajalana, and alladhi). Abu 'Ali said: "alladhi" is a generic that stands in the place of "allati." End of quote. In my view its grammatical analysis (i'rab) is apposition (badal), as if it were said: "the time which," and then it is a generic and cannot be an adjective, due to lack of agreement. In His words ﴿and reached our term which You appointed for us﴾ is evidence for the Mu'tazila in their statement about the "two terms" (al-ajalayn), because they acknowledged this, and among them is the rational faculty and others.

﴿He will say: "The Fire is your dwelling place, wherein you abide forever, except what Allah wills."﴾ That is, the place of your staying, meaning your sojourn. Al-Zajjaj said: Abu 'Ali said: "In my view it is a verbal noun (masdar), not a place, because it governs the state in which they are ‘abiding forever’ (khalidin), and a place has no sense of a verb so as to be a governing word. The estimate is: 'The Fire is the possessor of your sojourn.'" End of quote. Al-Zajjaj's statement is valid with an implied element indicated by "your dwelling place," meaning: "they will sojourn, ‘abiding forever therein.'" The apparent view is that this exception belongs to the sentence that the exception follows. Abu Muslim said: it is from His words ﴿and reached our term which You appointed for us﴾, meaning: except whom You destroyed and cut off. It was said: the term You named for their disbelief and error. This is not good, because if it were as he claimed, the construction would be "except what You will." Also, the statement that there are two terms, the term of destruction and the term named by God, is false. The separation between the excepted and the exception by His words ﴿He will say: The Fire is your dwelling place, wherein you abide forever﴾ creates a discordant construction. The apparent view is that this exception is meant literally, not metaphorically. Al-Zamakhshari said: Or it may be from the speech of one who has been avenged, who gained victory over his enemy and kept gnawing at him with his fangs, while the other asked him to ease his grip, and he said: "May Allah destroy me if I ease your grip, except if I will," knowing that he would not will anything but to be satisfied with him by the utmost of what he could do in terms of reproach and severity. So his saying "except if I will" is among the most severe threats, with mockery of the promise, because it comes in the form of an exception that holds out hope. End of quote. If it is literally an exception, they differed over what was excepted. Some people said: it is the exception of certain individuals among those addressed, namely those who believed in this world from among these disbelievers, through a punishment that befell them. Because these are a category, it was permissible to use "what" (ma) to refer to them, as in His words ﴿marry what women seem good to you﴾ [al-Nisa: 3], where "what" is used for the kind of those who have understanding. This view is far-fetched, because this is an address to the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, so how can an exception of those who believed in this world be valid? And the condition for the excepted item is that its time and the time of what it is excepted from be the same? When you say: "The people stood, except Zayd," it means: except Zayd, for he did not stand. It is not valid to mean: except Zayd, for he does not stand in the future. Likewise, "I will strike the people except Zayd" means: except Zayd, for I will not strike him in the future. It is not valid to mean: except Zayd, for I struck him yesterday. However, if the exception is disconnected (munqati'), it is permissible, as in His words ﴿they will not taste death therein, except the first death﴾ [al-Dukhan: 56], meaning: but the first death, in this world, which they have tasted. Others said: the excepted are the sinners among the people of monotheism who enter the Fire, meaning: except the category of sinners who entered it, for they will not be made to abide forever in the Fire. Others said: the exception is of times, meaning: ‘abiding forever therein’ eternally, except the time in which Allah willed that they should not abide. These differed over determining the time. Al-Tabari said: it is the period between their being gathered and their entering the Fire, and this was permissible from the standpoint of the wording "The Fire is your dwelling place," since the form of the expression does not restrict future time to the exclusion of other times. Al-Zamakhshari said: "except what Allah wills," meaning: they will abide in the punishment of the whole eternity, except what Allah wills, meaning the times in which they are transferred from the punishment of the Fire to the punishment of the freezing cold (zamharir). It is related that they enter a valley of intense cold that separates some of their limbs from others, so they howl and ask to be returned to the blaze. Al-Hasan said: "except what Allah wills" refers to their being in the world without punishment, and this refers to time, meaning: except the time in which they were in the world without punishment. This view faces the same objection as the view that makes it an exception of the individuals who believed in this world. Al-Farra' said: "except" here means "apart from" (siwa), and the meaning is: apart from what He wills of increase in the punishment. Al-Zajjaj also agreed with this. Others said: "except what Allah wills" means the retribution and increase over the punishment, and this refers to an exception from the verbal noun implied by the meaning of the speech, since the meaning is: you are punished by the Fire, ‘abiding forever therein,’ except what He wills of punishment beyond the Fire, for He will punish you with it. In that case it is a disconnected exception, since punishment beyond the punishment of the Fire is not included within the punishment of the Fire. The apparent view is that this exception is part of God's speech to those addressed, and the interpretations of the exception have come on this basis. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "In my view, what is more fitting for this exception is that it is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his community, and it is not something said on the Day of Resurrection. The excepted is one of the disbelievers who on that day would believe in the knowledge of God. As if, when He informed them that it would be said to the disbelievers ‘your dwelling place,’ He excepted for them whoever could believe among those who are seen on that day as disbelievers. The word 'what' refers to the attribute of one who has understanding. This interpretation is supported by the connection to His words ﴿Indeed your Lord is All-Wise, All-Knowing﴾, meaning: those among them who could believe." End of quote, and this is a good interpretation. It was related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "This verse requires halting (waqf) on all the disbelievers." It was said: the meaning of this is that it requires halting on those who have not died, since they may yet become Muslim. (p-222) It was also related from him that he said: "Their matter was put in the measure of their punishment, and its duration is subject to His will, so that God does not judge His creation." Also from him, he said regarding this verse: "It is not fitting for anyone to pass judgment on God regarding His creation, that He does not cause them to enter Paradise or Hellfire." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "There is consensus (ijma') on the eternal everlastingness of the disbelievers, and this is not valid from Ibn 'Abbas." End of quote. Some people clung to the apparent meaning of this exception and claimed that God brings out of the Fire every righteous and wicked person, Muslim and disbeliever, and that the Fire will become empty and ruined. This has been mentioned from some of the Companions, but it is not valid, and the dissent of these people is not considered and is not heeded.

﴿Indeed your Lord is All-Wise, All-Knowing﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: He does nothing except in accordance with the requirement of wisdom, namely that the disbelievers deserve the punishment of eternity. End of quote. This is according to his Mu'tazili doctrine. Ibn 'Atiyya said: They are two attributes appropriate to this verse, because the everlasting abiding of these disbelievers in the Fire proceeds from wisdom. Al-Tibrizi said: (All-Wise) in the governance of the beginning and the return, (All-Knowing) of what the affair of the servants will come to. Isma'il al-Darir said: (All-Wise) decreed eternal abiding for them, (All-Knowing) of them and their punishment. Al-Baghawi said: (All-Knowing) of the one He excepted and of what is in their hearts of righteousness and piety. Al-Qurtubi said: (All-Wise) in their punishment, (All-Knowing) of the measure of their recompense.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 129:

﴿And thus We make some of the wrongdoers allies of others, because of what they used to earn.﴾ When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned that He is the Protector of the believers, in the sense that He preserves and supports them, [He indicated] that the disbelievers are allies of one another in wrongdoing and disgrace. Qatadah said: He makes some of them allies of others in disbelief and wrongdoing, meaning what was mentioned earlier about the jinn and mankind and how some of them enjoy one another. Qatadah also said: Some of them follow others into the Fire, i.e., He makes some of them come after others into entering it. Ibn Zayd said: Its meaning is that We set ﴿some of the wrongdoers﴾ over others and make them agents of retribution against them. This interpretation is far-fetched. When ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwan killed ʿAmr ibn Saʿid al-Ashdaq, ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr said, as he ascended the pulpit: "The mouth of wolves has killed the lateem (darling) of Satan," and he recited ﴿And thus We make some of the wrongdoers allies of others﴾, to the end of the verse. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Its explanation is that when Allah intends evil for a people, He appoints over them their worst, and when He intends good for them, He appoints over them their best. In some of the revealed books it is written: "I destroy My enemies by means of My enemies, then I destroy them by means of My friends." Ismaʿil al-Darir said: We leave the polytheists to one another for support, aid and need. Al-Zamakhshari said: We leave them alone until some of them take others as allies, as the devils and the misguided among mankind did, or He makes some of them allies of others on the Day of Resurrection and companions to them, as they were in the world ﴿because of what they used to earn﴾ of disbelief and sins. End of quotation. His saying "We leave them" is according to his Muʿtazili (the rationalist school of the Muʿtazilah) line of thought.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 130:

﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind, did there not come to you messengers from among you, relating to you My signs and warning you of the meeting of this your Day?﴾ This call is also on the Day of Resurrection, and the interrogative is for rebuke and reproach, since God established the proof against them by sending the messengers, but they did not accept from them. The apparent meaning is that there were messengers from among the jinn to them, just as there were messengers from among humankind to them. It is said that God sent one messenger from among the jinn to them, whose name was Yusuf. It is also said that the messengers of the jinn are the messengers of humankind, so they are God's messengers indirectly, since they are the messengers of His messengers. This is supported by His saying: ﴿They turned back to their people as warners﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 29]. This was said by Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak. It is also narrated that a group of jinn listened to the prophets, then returned to their people and informed them of what had happened with the Messenger, so they are called "messengers of God," though they were not truly His messengers. According to these two opinions, the pronoun refers to ﴿the jinn and humankind﴾. Some people have held to this apparent meaning and claimed that God sent messengers from among the jinn to the jinn. They did not distinguish between those who are accountable and those who are accountable, in that a messenger of their own kind may be sent to them, because they are more at ease and familiar with him. Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Ibn Juraij and the majority said: the messengers were only from among humankind, not the jinn. But since the call and the rebuke were addressed to both together, the address was applied to both in the figurative manner familiar in Arabic speech, through *taghlib* (the convention of giving precedence to one of two groups in a combined reference, here humankind, for their nobility). al-Farra' interpreted it as an elision of a noun, meaning "from among one of you," like His saying: ﴿From them come out the pearl and the coral﴾ [Al-Rahman: 22], meaning from one of them, which is the salt water. And like His saying: ﴿and made the moon therein a light﴾ [Nuh: 16], meaning in one of them (p-223), which is the lowest heaven. And like: ﴿that they may mention the name of God on known days﴾ [Al-Hajj: 28], where by mention is meant the takbir (saying "Allahu akbar"), and by the known days the ten days, meaning on one of those days, which is the Day of Sacrifice. al-Kalbi said: the messengers used to be sent to humankind, and Muhammad ﷺ was sent to both the jinn and humankind. This is also narrated from Ibn Abbas. The meaning of relating the signs is informing them of what was revealed to them: alerting them to the places of pilgrimage, making known the proofs of God's oneness, and complying with His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. Warning (*indhar*) is informing of what is feared. ﴿The meeting of this your Day﴾ means the Day of Resurrection, and the warning of what will occur in it of terrors and dangers, and of the disbelieving deniers' destination to everlasting punishment. al-A'raj read: ﴿Did there not come to you﴾, with the feminine form of the verb in accordance with the word "messengers," using the *ta'*.

﴿They will say: We bear witness against ourselves﴾ The apparent meaning is that this is a report of their affirmation and their acknowledgement of His saying: ﴿Did there not come to you﴾, because the interrogative particle entering upon the negation of the coming of the messengers is for denial, so it amounted to confirmation for them. The meaning is: they said, "We bear witness against ourselves that the messengers came to us and warned us of this Day." This sentence serves here in place of "Yes" (*bala*), and it is expressed clearly in His saying: ﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you, reciting to you the signs of your Lord and warning you of the meeting of this your Day? They will say: Yes﴾ [Al-Zumar: 71]. They acknowledged that God's proof is binding upon them and that they are overcome by it. Ibn Atiyya said: His saying "We bear witness" is an admission from them of disbelief and a confession, meaning: ﴿We bear witness against ourselves﴾ of falling short. End. The apparent meaning of ﴿We bear witness﴾ is the testimony of each one against himself. It is also said: some of us bore witness against others regarding the warning of the messengers.

﴿And the life of this world deceived them﴾ This is a report about them from God, Exalted, and an indication of the cause that led to their disbelief, and a plain statement to them of the most blameworthy aspect, which is deception. It is said: it may be from *gharra al-ta'ir farkhahu*, meaning the bird fed its chicks and satisfied them. The expansion of provision and abundance is a cause of rebellion: "If God had expanded provision for His servants, they would have rebelled in the earth."

﴿And they bear witness against themselves that they were disbelievers﴾ Its apparent meaning is the testimony of each one against himself regarding disbelief. It is also said: some of them bore witness against others. It is also said: their limbs bore witness against them after their denial and the sealing of their mouths. This is far from the context of the verse, and there is a conflict between His saying ﴿and they bear witness against themselves﴾ and the verses that indicate denial, since it is possible that this occurred from groups, one group bearing witness and another denying, or from one group owing to the differing states and stations of the Resurrection across that lengthy day, so that they confess in one station and deny in another. al-Tibrizi said: ﴿and they bore witness﴾ means they confessed against themselves under compulsion, not by choice, and had they wished to say anything else, their own selves would not have obeyed them. al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): why did He repeat the mention of their testimony against themselves? (I answer): The first is a report of what they said, how they speak and acknowledge. The second is a condemnation of them, a rebuke of their opinion, and a description of the shortness of their view of themselves, and that they are a people deceived by the life of this world and its present pleasures. The outcome of their affair was that they were compelled to testify against themselves to their disbelief, to surrender to their Lord, and to seek the hastening of His punishment. He only said this as a warning to listeners in the likeness of their condition. End. We say: the testimony was not repeated, because the one reporting and the object of the report differ. The first is their reporting about themselves, (p-224) and the second is God's report about them that they bore witness against themselves to disbelief. So this testimony is other than the first.

This refers to what was mentioned most recently and what the discourse implies: the coming of the Messengers, reciting the verses and warning of the Gathering, the Reckoning and the Recompense. The reason is that the Lord would not destroy the towns through injustice while their people were unaware. That is, they were not warned by the sending of Messengers to them, nor was an excuse made to them, nor were they informed in advance of what would befall them if they did not follow the Messengers. There is a hadith: "None is more fond of excuse than Allah," and for this reason He sent down the Book and sent the Messengers. Al-Zajjaj (a grammarian and Qur'an commentator) said something close to this. He said: that is, what We have related to you of the matter of the Messengers and the punishment of those who denied, because it was not the case that He would destroy them until He sent a Messenger to them.

It has been said that the reference of "dhalika" (that) is to the question, which is ﴿Did there not come to you...﴾ [al-An'am: 130]. "An lam yakun" would mean: to clarify that it was not the case. This was related by al-Tibrizi. Al-Maturidi said: the reference is to the denial and disobedience that existed among them. It may also refer to the destruction that befell the earlier nations. End of quotation. These two views do not hold together with the words ﴿an lam yakun﴾, because disobedience or destruction is not caused by "it was not the case." 

They permitted the nominative (raf') for "dhalika," taking it as a subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject) whose predicate (khabar) is omitted, meaning: that matter is so. Or as a predicate whose subject is omitted, meaning: the matter is that. They permitted the accusative (nasb) as in "We did that." Then "an lam yakun" is a causal clause (ta'lil, giving the reason). It is also possible that "an" is the one that governs the present tense (an al-nasibah) and is the lightened form of the heavy one (al-mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah), meaning: because the matter was not that your Lord... 

Al-Zamakhshari permitted that "an lam yakun" is not a causal clause but a substitution (badal) for "dhalika," as in His saying: ﴿And We decreed that matter to him, that the last remnant of these would be cut off﴾ [al-Hijr: 66]. If it is a causal clause, then it is in the position of accusative or genitive, on the disputed view of omitting the causal particle. If it is a substitution, then it is in the nominative position. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned only that it is nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: the matter is that.

The word "bizulmin" (with injustice) may be taken as a genitive construction with Allah, meaning: unjust toward them, as in His saying: ﴿Your Lord would not destroy the towns unjustly while their people were righteous﴾ [Hud: 117]. The meaning of ﴿while their people were unaware﴾ is: without having been warned in advance. ﴿And your Lord is not unjust to the servants﴾ [Fussilat: 46]. It may also be taken as a genitive construction with "the towns," meaning: they are unjust, without having warned them. This is the meaning of al-Qushayri's statement: that is, He does not destroy them for their sins before He sends Messengers to them. This second view is more fitting, because the first implies that if He had seized them before the sending of the Messengers, He would have been unjust. According to us, this is not the case, because He judges as He wills and does as He desires. But according to the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school), if He destroyed them while they were unaware, having received no Book or Messenger, He would be unjust, and He is exalted above injustice and above every ugliness.

It has been said: "bizulmin" means with the wrongdoing of those among them who committed shirk (associating partners with God). This is like His saying: ﴿and no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164]. Al-Maturidi said: that is, He would not destroy them through their own wrongdoing with total destruction and punishment unless after a prior warning or their asking for punishment. He does not destroy them while they are heedless of the wrongdoing and sin, because it is permissible for Him to do that. Rather, this is His custom, lest they say: "Why did You not send a messenger to us?" All of this is grace from Him and mercy.

Mujahid said: He does not destroy them for the wrongdoing of some of them against others. It has been said: for the wrongdoing of one of them. It has been said: for the kind of wrongdoing, so that they commit with the wrongdoing other things that God does not approve of among the rest of the ugly deeds. Al-Tibrizi mentioned this.

The meaning of ﴿while their people were unaware﴾ is: He does not explain to them the state of affairs, nor does He remove their ignorance. The meaning is not that they were unaware of what they were being admonished with.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 132:

﴿For each there are degrees according to what they have done﴾. That is: for each of the accountable, believer and disbeliever alike, there are varying degrees of recompense for their deeds, and their variation is according to the relation of some of them to others, or according to the deed of each doer, so that he is at one degree and then advances to another, complete degree, and then to one more complete still. The apparent meaning is that the jinn are included in the generality of the recompense, just as they are included in the obligation (taklif) and in the sending of messengers to them. Al-Dahhak said: "The believing jinn are in the Garden just as the believing humans are." It was also said: "They enter neither the Garden nor the Fire; it is said to them, 'Be dust,' and they become dust like the beasts." Ibn 'Abbas said: "The reward of the believing jinn is their being protected from the Fire." Abu Hanifa said: "The jinn have no reward, because reward (thawab) is a bounty from God, so it is not attributed to them except by a clarification from God; and God mentioned concerning them only the punishment of their disobedient ones, not the reward of their obedient ones." His two companions, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, disagreed with him, saying: "They have reward for acts of obedience and punishment for acts of disobedience," and their evidence is the generality of the Book and the Sunnah. It was also said: "for each of the believers in particular." Al-Maturidi said: "for each of the disbelievers in particular, ﴿degrees﴾ meaning levels (darakat) and grades of punishment, ﴿according to what they have done﴾ of disbelief and sins; because it came after the address to the disbelievers, so it returns upon them."

﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what they do﴾. That is: He is not heedless nor concealed from Him are the measures of the deeds and what follows from them of rewards; and in this is a warning and a threat. Ibn 'Amir read ﴿ta'malun﴾ with the letter ta' (taʾmalūna), in the address form.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 133:

﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient, the Possessor of mercy.﴾ When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned those who obey and those who disobey, and the reward and the punishment, He mentioned that He is the Self-Sufficient (al-Ghani) in every respect; obedience does not benefit Him and disobedience does not harm Him. And despite being Self-Sufficient, He is the Possessor of mercy (dhu al-rahmah), i.e., of complete bounty (al-tafaddul al-tamm). Ibn Abbas said: "﴿Possessor of mercy﴾ toward His allies and the people of His obedience." It was also said: toward all His creation, and among His mercy is the delay of retribution against the disobedient. It was also said: "﴿Possessor of mercy﴾" means the one who makes the benefit of creatures come through one another. Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿Possessor of mercy﴾" means He shows mercy to them by imposing obligations, so as to expose them to lasting benefits.

﴿If He wills, He can remove you and bring after you whomever He wills, just as He produced you from the descendants of another people.﴾ This shows complete power and absolute independence. The address is general to all creation, as in His saying: ﴿If He wills, He can remove you, O people, and bring others [in your place]﴾ [al-Nisa: 133]. The meaning is: if He wills the annihilation of this world and the replacement of you by others of His creation, He will do it. Removal (al-idhhab) here means destruction, the destruction of uprooting, not mere death, generation after generation, because that is something that occurs, so the occurrence is not made conditional upon "if He wills." It was also said: the address is to the people of Mecca. Ata said: it means the Ansar and the Successors (al-Tabi'un). It was also said: "﴿He can remove you﴾, O disobedient ones, ﴿and bring after you whomever He wills﴾ of the obedient kind," and "﴿just as He produced you﴾" is in the position of a verbal noun (masdar) not from the same root as its verb, because the sense of "﴿and bring after﴾" is "and produce (yunshi')." The meaning is: if He wills the removal and the replacement, He will remove you and bring [others] after you; thus each of the removal and the replacement is suspended upon His will. The particle "min" (from) indicates the starting point (li-ibtida' al-ghayah). Ibn Atiyyah said: it is for partitive meaning (li-al-tab'id). Al-Tabari, followed by Makki, said: it has the sense of "I took a dinar from my garment," meaning "in place of it" and "as its substitute." End quote. He means that it is substitutive (badaliyyah), and the meaning is: from the offspring of earlier people whose origin is Adam, peace be upon him. Al-Zamakhshari said: "from the offspring of other people" who were not of your description, and they are the people of Noah's Ark. End quote. He means that you are "from the offspring of a people" who were righteous; so if He willed, He could remove you, O disobedient ones, and bring after you obedient ones, just as you, being disobedient, were produced from obedient people. As for "﴿whomever He wills﴾," it was said that "ma" here means "man" (who). The better view: if the thing being replaced is non-rational, then "ma" is used in its proper place; if it is rational, then the category (al-nawʿ) is intended. Zayd ibn Thabit read "dhurriyyatan" with a fatha on the dhal, and likewise in Al Imran; and Aban ibn Uthman read "dhuriyyatan" with a fatha on the dhal and a lightened raa with kasra, and "dhurya" on the pattern of "darbah." This verse contains a warning against the seizure of Allah, in that He may hasten that [punishment].

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 134:

﴿Indeed, what you are promised is coming.﴾ The apparent meaning of "mā" (what) is generality, covering everything that is promised. Al-Hasan said: it refers to the coming of the Hour, because they used to deny it. It was also said: it refers to the promise and the threat. It was also said: it refers to the victory of the Messenger, which is certainly going to happen. It was also said: it refers to the punishment, ﴿coming﴾ on the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: it refers to the promise of the Day of Resurrection, due to the indication of ﴿and you will not escape Us﴾, and the reference is especially to this previously mentioned threat. Or it may be general without restriction, in which case it implies the enforcement of the threat, and the creed rejects that. End quote. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: the promise is specifically the report of reward, so it is definitely coming, and the specification of the promise with this certainty indicates that the side of the threat is not like that. This view is strengthened by his saying: ﴿and you cannot escape,﴾ that is, you will not get out of Our power and wisdom. So when he mentioned the promise he affirmed it firmly, and when he mentioned the threat he did not go beyond ﴿and you cannot escape,﴾ which indicates that the side of mercy prevails. Thus, in His saying ﴿what you are promised,﴾ there is generality, and what is excluded by evidence is removed from it; or it may be intended to be specific, of the gathering, the victory, the threat, or the promise, that is, with their necessary consequences of reward or punishment, or both together: six opinions.

The phrase "anna" (that) is written separately from "mā," and "mā" is in the sense of "alladhī" (that which). This sentence carries an indication of the shortness of hope, the nearness of the term, and the requital for deeds.

﴿And you cannot escape﴾: that is, you will not be able to get away. One says "a'jazanī al-shay'" meaning "it eluded me," i.e., nothing will escape us regarding what We intend for you. Ibn 'Atiyya said: its meaning is "escaping" (bi-nājīn), and here is an explanation by way of necessary implication.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 135:

﴿Say: "O my people, act according to your station, and I too am acting. You will soon know to whom the ultimate abode belongs. Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed."﴾

Abu Bakr recited ʿalā makānātikum, in the plural wherever it occurs. Whoever reads it in the plural matches the plural of the addressees with the plural, and whoever reads it in the singular means the category (al-jins). Al-makāna is a verbal noun of makkana, so the mīm is original (aṣliyyah), and it has the meaning of "place" (al-makān). It is said that al-makān and al-makāna are mufʿal and mufʿala from al-kawn, so the mīm is augmentative (zāʾidah). Accordingly, the meaning may be "according to your being empowered (tamakkun) in your affair and to the utmost of your capacity and ability," as al-Zajjaj said. The meaning may also be "according to your direction and the condition you are in," as one says, "ʿalā makānatika, yā fulān," when one orders someone to remain steadfast in his state, i.e., "Remain upon what you are upon and do not deviate from it." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "ʿalā nāḥiyatikum," and the meaning of "mā tanḥūn" is "what you intend of good or evil." Ibn Zayd said: "ʿalā ḥālikum." Yaman said: "ʿalā madhāhibikum." Ismaʿil al-Darir said: "ʿalā dīnikum fī manāzilikum li-halākī," addressing the disbelievers of Makkah, "innī ʿāmil" meaning "for your destruction." End of quotation. These expressions are close in meaning.

This command is one of threat and warning, like His saying: ﴿Do whatever you wish﴾ (Fussilat: 40). It is a leaving-alone (al-takhliyah) and a recording (al-tasjil) against the one commanded, that nothing will come from him but evil. It is as if he is commanded to it, and it is obligatory upon him absolutely; he has no escape from it and cannot act contrary to it. The meaning of ﴿innī ʿāmil﴾ is: "upon my station in which I am." Al-Zamakhshari said: "Remain upon your disbelief and your enmity toward me, for I remain upon Islam and upon my patience with you." End of quotation.

The apparent reading is that "man" is the object of ﴿taʿlamūn﴾. They also permitted that it be a subject, an interrogative noun, with ﴿takūnu﴾ as its predicate, the verb being suspended (muʿallaq); the clause then occupies the place of the object if (yaʿlamūn) is transitive to one object, or the place of the two objects if it is transitive to two. ﴿ʿāqibatu al-dār﴾ means its outcome and that to which it ends, and "al-dār" apparently means the abode of the Hereafter. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "It may also be intended as the outcome of the worldly life through victory and dominance, so the verse contains an announcement of the unseen." Al-Zamakhshari said: "The good outcome is that for which God created this abode." This is a subtle path of warning, containing fairness in speech, good manners, and, together with the severity of the threat, confidence that the warner is right and the warned is in falsehood. It was also said: the meaning of ﴿man takūnu lahu ʿāqibatu al-dār﴾ is: who has victory in the abode of Islam, and who has the Hereafter abode, that is, Paradise. In His saying ﴿fa-sawfa taʿlamūn﴾ there is a threat and warning that is not hidden, like His saying: ﴿We will soon attend to you, O two worlds﴾ (al-Rahman: 31), and ﴿Whoever of you turns back from his religion, then God will bring a people﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 54). The poet said:

*When we meet, and the messengers meet between us, you will soon see, O ʿAmr, what God will do.*

Another said:

*Layla will know what debt she has incurred, and what creditor will demand its repayment.*

﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed﴾: that is, they will not prosper. Al-Dahhak said this. ʿIkrimah said: "They will not remain." ʿAta' said: "Whoever disbelieves My blessing will not be happy." It was said: "They will not be safe nor will they be saved from the punishment." In it is an indication that they are the wrongdoers who do not succeed. In His saying ﴿fa-sawfa taʿlamūn man takūnu lahu ʿāqibatu al-dār﴾ there is an alternation (tardīd) between him, peace be upon him, and them. It is known that this threat and warning is specific to them, and that the good outcome of the abode belongs to him, peace be upon him, but it was given the form of the one in the manner of His saying: "Then the worse of the two of you is for the better of you, the ransom," and the poet's saying:

*So whichever of me and you was the worse, let him be led to the leash in humiliation.*

What is worse and what is better is known, but it was presented in the form of alternation to display the form of fairness and to cast the speech in a manner of shared address, relying on the listener's understanding of the meaning.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited ﴿man yakūnu﴾ with the yā' in the masculine, and likewise in al-Qasas.

﴿And they assign to God a share of the produce and cattle that He has created, and they say, "This is for God," according to their claim, "and this is for our partners." But what is for their partners does not reach God, while what is for God reaches their partners. Evil is what they judge.﴾

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Suddi that the Arabs used to set aside, from their crops, their grains, their fruits and their livestock, one portion that they called for God and another portion that they called for their idols. Their custom was to exert great effort to give the idols' share more than God's share, because they believed that the idols were in need, and God is not in need. So when they gathered the crops and the wind blew and carried some of what was for God over to what was for their partners, they left it and did not return it to God's share. They did the opposite as well. If what they had set aside for God's share was irrigated and flowed into the share of their partners, they left it. And in reverse, they blocked it. If anything from their gods' share did not thrive, they gave God's share to them instead. The same applied to livestock. If they suffered drought, they ate God's share and left their gods' share untouched.

When God, exalted is He, mentioned the ugliness of the way of the polytheists of Arabia in denying resurrection (al-ba'th), He mentioned several kinds of their ignorance, as a warning about the weakness of their intellects. In His words ﴿from what He has created﴾ there is an indication that God, exalted is He, was more deserving that the best and finest be set aside for Him, and that His side be the more preferred, since He is the one who brought into existence what they set aside for Him from it, and the one able to make it grow, unlike their idols, which are incapable of what happens to them, let alone of creating anything or making it grow. In His words (from what), with the partitive min (mina al-tab'idiyya), there is an indication of a third division, namely what remained for them apart from the two shares. There is an omission in the speech that the division indicates, that is: and a share ﴿for their partners﴾. Do you not see their words: ﴿This is for God, according to their claim, and this is for our partners﴾? As for ﴿al-harth﴾ (the tilth), it has been said here to mean the crops. It has also been said to mean crops, trees and whatever comes from the earth.

﴿Al-an'am﴾ (the livestock) are camels, cattle and sheep, which they used to draw near to God by slaughtering. It has also been said that it refers to the baḥīra, the sā'iba, the waṣīla and the ḥām. It has also been said that the share from the livestock is the expense of keeping them. In His words (fa-qalu) there is an emphasis on the act, which is the setting aside, by means of speech, so that the act and the speech correspond and reinforce one another. Then they broke this arrangement. In the midst of the speech came His words ﴿according to their claim﴾ as an interjection. It came immediately after their words ﴿This is for God﴾ because it is a false report, since they broke what they had set aside and confirmed by speech. It did not come after their words ﴿and this is for our partners﴾, to affirm that what belongs to their partners is theirs. In most of the speech of the Arabs, al-za'm (claim) implies something short of certainty. The Truth has indicated that they did this without God commanding them to do so, and without Him legislating it for them. This is in line with their custom of enacting rulings for which God gave no permission and which He did not legislate.

Al-Kisa'i read ﴿bi-za'mihim﴾ in both places with a ḍamma on the zay, which is the dialect of Banu Asad. The fatḥa is the dialect of the Hijaz, and the remaining seven readers recited it so. Both are verbal nouns. It has been said that the fatḥa is for the verbal noun and the ḍamma is for the noun. Ibn Abi 'Abla read it with fatḥa on both the zay and the 'ayn. The kasra is a dialect of some of Qays and Tamim, and it was not recited with it. ﴿Bi-za'mihim﴾ is connected to qalu (they said). It has also been said that it is connected to what the word ﴿lillahi﴾ is connected to, namely the sense of settledness. ﴿Shuraka'uhum﴾ [al-An'am: 137] means their gods. Al-shuraka' (partners) derives from al-shirk (association), and the construction is one of specification (idafat takhsis), meaning: the partners whom they associated between themselves and God in the act of drawing near to Him. It does not mean an annexation to an agent or to an object. It has also been said that they were called partners because they treated them as partners in their wealth. The construction then is either annexation to the agent, so the meaning is: this is for our idols that share with us in our wealth, or annexation to the object, so the meaning is: those that we made partners in our wealth. Ibn 'Atiyya said: they named them partners according to their belief about them, that they share with them in good and in evil. The meaning of ﴿fa-la yasilu ila Allah﴾ is: it does not fall in the place of what is spent in the paths of righteousness, such as charity to the poor, visitors to the House of God, and the like. Even if they did this, it would not benefit them, because they associated partners with God. Or, it does not reach those paths at all, which are intended to draw near to God. Al-Hasan said: whenever what was set aside for their idols was lost, they took its replacement from what was for God, and they did not do the same for God. It has also been said: they used to divert from what they had set aside for God to the guardians (sadana) of the idols, and they did not give charity from what they had set aside for the idols. The meaning of ﴿fa-huwa yasilu ila shuraka'ihim﴾ is: by spending on them, by slaughtering their offerings there, and the other, for the expense on their guardians.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: the majority of the interpreters hold that what is meant by His words ﴿fa-la yasilu﴾ and His words ﴿yasilu﴾ is what we have already mentioned of their protection of their gods' share during the blowing of the wind and other things. Ibn Zayd said: it is only that when they slaughtered for God, they mentioned their gods over that slaughter, and when they slaughtered for their gods, they did not mention God. He said: ﴿fa-la yasilu﴾ to any mention, and ﴿fa-huwa yasilu﴾ to the mention of God. End of quote.

The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that what they set aside as a share for their partners is not spent on any of the paths of righteousness that its character requires, and what they set aside as a share for God is spent on the channels of their gods.

﴿Evil is what they judge﴾: this is a comprehensive and severe censure of their rulings, so their present ruling and others are included in it. Al-Zamakhshari said: in their preferring their gods over God, and their doing what was not legislated for them. Al-Maturidi said: that is, how wretched is the judgment of their judgment, in that they put My right alongside the right of the idols and cheated Me. It has also been said that ﴿Evil is what they judge﴾ refers to themselves. The apparent view is that ﴿sa'a﴾ (evil) here is treated like ﴿bi'sa﴾ (how wretched) in expressing blame, as in His words: ﴿Say: how wretched is what your faith commands you﴾ [al-Baqara: 93]. The disagreement that applies to ﴿bi'sama﴾ [al-Baqara: 90] and the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of what follows here, which has been fully discussed in His words: ﴿How wretched is what they have sold themselves for﴾ [al-Baqara: 90] in al-Baqara, also applies, and its ruling is the ruling of ﴿bi'sama﴾ [al-Baqara: 90]. Al-Maturidi explained it by saying: how wretched is the judgment of their judgment. Al-Hawfi analysed it and made the ma a relative pronoun in the sense of alladhi (which). He said: the implied meaning is: evil is that which they judge, their judgment, so their judgment is in the nominative as the subject, and what comes before it is the predicate, and it is omitted because yahkumun (they judge) indicates it. It is also permissible for ma to be a tamyiz (specification) according to the view of those who permit that in ﴿bi'sama﴾ [al-Baqara: 90], so it occupies the accusative position. The implied meaning is: ﴿sa'a﴾ judgment, their judgment, and yahkumun cannot be an adjective of ma, because the purpose is vagueness, but there is an omission in the speech that the ma indicates, and the implied meaning is: evil is the ma of what they judge. Ibn 'Atiyya said: and ma is in the nominative position, as if he said: evil is that which they judge. It does not seem right to me to treat sa'a here as bi'sa and ni'ma (the verbs of praise and blame), because the explicit pronoun here is implied and must be made explicit by agreement of the grammarians. It only seems right to treat it like bi'sa in His words ﴿evil is the example of the people﴾ [al-A'raf: 177], because the explicit pronoun is manifest in the speech. End of quote. This is the view of someone who has picked up a little Arabic and has not firmly established his foot in it. Rather, when sa'a is treated like ni'ma and bi'sa, its ruling is the same as theirs, with no difference at all, whether the agent is implicit or explicit, or the tamyiz. There is no disagreement about the permissibility of omitting the thing praised or blamed, and the tamyiz in them is for the indication of the speech on it. So his saying: because the explicit pronoun here is implied and must be made explicit by agreement of the grammarians, and so on to the end, is a fallen statement, and his claim of agreement, when the agreement is contrary to what he mentioned, is an astonishing marvel.

(p-228)

(p. 229) That is, it is like the adorning of the division of offerings between God and their gods, and their making their gods partners with God in that. Al-Zamakhshari said: Or it is like that eloquent adornment known from the devils. Ibn al-Anbari said: It is permissible that (wa-kadhalika, "and thus") be a new sentence not referring back to what precedes it, so the meaning would be "and thus He adorned." End of quotation. The word "many" (kathir) is meant to refer to those among the polytheists of the Arabs. Mujahid said: "their partners" are their devils, who commanded them to bury their daughters alive for fear of poverty. Al-Kalbi said: "their partners" are their custodians and keepers of their idols, who used to adorn for them the burying of daughters alive. It was also said: their chiefs used to kill the females out of arrogance and the males out of fear of poverty. Al-Zamakhshari said: "the killing of their children" is by burying them alive or by slaughtering them for the gods. In the Jahiliyya, a man would swear: "If a boy is born to me like this, I will surely slaughter one of them," just as ʿAbd al-Muttalib swore.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿zayyana﴾ in the active voice, with ﴿qatla﴾ in the accusative as an object of the verbal noun governed by ﴿awladihim﴾, and ﴿shurakauhum﴾ in the nominative as the subject of ﴿zayyana﴾. The grammar of this reading is clear. A group of readers, including al-Sulami, al-Hasan, and Abu ʿAbd al-Malik, the judge of the army and companion of Ibn ʿAmir, read ﴿zuyyina﴾ in the passive voice, with ﴿qatlu﴾ in the nominative, as a verbal noun governed by ﴿awladihim﴾, and ﴿shurakauhum﴾ in the nominative either by implying a verb, meaning "their partners adorned it," as Sibawayh rendered it, or as the agent of the verbal noun, meaning "the killing of their children was adorned by their partners," as one says: "The riding of the horse was made beloved to me by Zayd," as Qutrub rendered it. According to Sibawayh's reading, the partners are those who adorn, not those who kill, as in the first reading. According to Qutrub's reading, the partners are the killers. Its meaning is that, since they adorned the killing, they were made the killers even though they did not directly perform the killing.

A group read in the same manner, except that they put ﴿shurakaihim﴾ in the genitive. On this reading, the partners are those who were buried alive, because they are partners in lineage and inheritance, or because they are halves of themselves and parts of them. Ibn ʿAmir read ﴿kadhalika﴾ with ﴿awladihim﴾ in the accusative and ﴿shurakauhum﴾ in the genitive, separating the verbal noun, which is annexed to its agent, with the object. This is a matter on which scholars differ regarding its permissibility. The majority of the Basrans prohibit it, both earlier and later scholars, and allow it only in poetic necessity. Some grammarians permitted it, and this is the correct view, because it occurs in this widely transmitted reading attributed to the pure Arab Ibn ʿAmir, who received the Qur'an from ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan before the solecism appeared in the speech of the Arabs. It also occurs in the speech of the Arabs in several verses, which we have mentioned in our book "Manhaj al-Salik" (The Method of the Traveller). No attention should be paid to the statement of Ibn ʿAtiyya: "This is a weak reading in Arab usage, because he attached the verb to its agent, which is ﴿shurakauhum﴾, then separated the annexed noun from the annexed-to with the object, and the leading grammarians do not permit separation with adverbial expressions in this manner except in poetry, as in his saying:

*As the book is inscribed by the hand of a Jewish man, who sometimes approaches or sometimes removes.*

How then could one do it with the object in the most eloquent speech?" However, its justification despite its weakness is that it occurred as an anomaly in a verse recited by Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash:

*So I struck him with a thrust like the stride of the she-camel of Abu Mazada.*

And in the verse of al-Tirimmah, his saying:

*They circle the pastures of Huzi, which were not grazed in its valley because of the clashing of the curved bows and quivers.*

End of Ibn ʿAtiyya's statement. Nor should one pay attention to al-Zamakhshari's statement: "The separation between them, meaning between the annexed and the annexed-to, is widespread; if it were in a place of necessity, which is poetry, it would be vulgar and rejected, so how is it in the Qur'an, which is inimitable for the beauty of its arrangement and its eloquence?" What led him to that was that he saw in some copies of the Qur'an ﴿shurakaihim﴾ written with a yā'. If he had read the children and the partners in the genitive, because the children were ﴿their partners﴾ in their wealth, he would have found an alternative to this forced reading. End of what he said. I am amazed that a non-Arab weak in grammar would reject a pure Arab's widely transmitted reading, whose parallel exists in the speech of the Arabs in more than one verse. I am also amazed at this man's poor opinion of the imam readers whom this community chose to transmit the Book of God east and west, and on whose transmission Muslims relied for their precision, knowledge, and piety. Nor should one pay attention to the statement of Abu ʿAli al-Farisi: "This is ugly and rare in usage. If he had turned away from it, meaning Ibn ʿAmir, it would have been better, because they did not permit separation between the annexed and the annexed-to with an adverb in ordinary speech, despite their breadth in the use of adverbs; they permitted it only in poetry." End of quotation. Since they separated between the annexed and the annexed-to with a clause in the saying of some Arabs: "He is the boy of, if God wills, your brother," then separation with a single noun is easier. Separation has also come in the active participle by preference. Some of the early readers read: "Breaker of His promise, His messengers," with ﴿wa'dahu﴾ in the accusative and ﴿rusulihi﴾ in the genitive. Abu al-Tayyib (al-Mutanabbi) used separation between the verbal noun, annexed to its agent, and the object, following what was reported from the Arabs, when he said:

*I sent to him from my tongue a garden, watered by wisdom as clouds water gardens.*

Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) said: When any such thing occurs, one examines the situation of the Arab speaker and what he brought. If he was eloquent, and what he produced is acceptable to analogy, then it is better to think well of him, because it is possible that it reached him from an ancient dialect whose age has long passed and whose traces have faded. Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla said: What has reached you of what the Arabs said is only a little of it. Had it come to you complete, knowledge and much poetry would have come to you. Similar to this is what Ibn Sirin narrated from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, that only a little of it was preserved and much of it was lost to them, referring to poetry, in a lengthy account. Abu al-Fath said: If that is so, we do not judge an eloquent speaker to be in error when we hear from him something that contradicts the majority.

End of the summary, abbreviated, limited to some of what he said.

Some people of Syria, and what is related from Ibn ʿAmir, read ﴿zayyana﴾ with a kasra on the zāy and a sukūn on the yā', according to the previous reading with separation by the object. The meaning of ﴿liyurdūhum﴾ is "so that they destroy them," from *al-radā*, which is destruction. ﴿Wa-liyalbisū﴾ means "so that they confuse," and ﴿dīnahum﴾ means what they were upon of the religion of Ismaʿil, until they slipped away from it into polytheism. It was also said that ﴿dīnahum﴾ is the religion they were obliged to follow. It was also said: its meaning is "so that they cast them into a confused religion." Al-Nakhaʿi read ﴿wa-liyalbisū﴾ with a fatḥa on the yā'. Abu al-Fath said: It is a metaphor from clothing, an expression for intense mixing. The lām is connected to ﴿zayyana﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: If the adornment is from the devils, then it is in the true sense of causation; if it is from the custodians, then it is in the sense of becoming.

﴿And had God willed, they would not have done it﴾. The apparent reference of the pronoun is to the killing, because it is what is explicitly mentioned and spoken of. The wāw in ﴿fa'aluhu﴾ refers to the many. It was said: the hā' refers to the adornment and the wāw to the partners. It was said: the hā' refers to the confusion, but this is far-fetched. It was said: it refers to all of that if you treat the pronoun as functioning like a demonstrative. This sentence is a rebuttal of those who claim that He creates their actions. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿And had God willed﴾ is a will of compulsion. End of quotation. This is according to his Mu'tazili school.

﴿So leave them and what they fabricate﴾, that is, what they invent of falsehood against God, (p. 231) and the rulings they legislate. This is a command of threat and warning.

Abu Hayyan's commentary on Surah al-An'am (6), verse 138:

﴿And they say, "These are livestock and tilth set apart; none may eat of them except whom we will," by their claim.﴾ He, exalted is He, informed of matters that they legislated for themselves and divisions that they invented and bound themselves to, as slander and lies against God. They set aside from their livestock, crops and fruits a portion and said, "This is ḥijr," meaning forbidden and prohibited. Aban ibn 'Uthman read *naʿam* (singular). The rest of the Seven Readers (al-sabʿa, the seven canonical readers) read *ḥijr* with a kasra on the ḥāʾ and a sukūn on the jīm. *Ḥijr* here means *maḥjūr* (that which is set apart), like *dhibḥ* (slaughtered) and *ṭiḥn* (ground), and the same form applies to the singular, plural, masculine and feminine, because its ruling is that of nouns rather than adjectives, as al-Zamakhshari said. Al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Aʿraj read *ḥijr* with a ḍammah on the ḥāʾ and a sukūn on the jīm. Al-Qurtubi said: Al-Hasan and Qatadah read it with a fatḥah on the ḥāʾ and a sukūn on the jīm, and it is also reported from al-Hasan that he read *ḥijr* with a ḍammah on the ḥāʾ. Aban ibn 'Uthman and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read it with a ḍammah on both the ḥāʾ and the jīm. Harun said: al-Hasan used to put a ḍammah on the ḥāʾ of *ḥijr* wherever it occurred, except in ﴿ḥijran maḥjūran﴾ (Q. 25:22), where he used a kasra. Ubayy, 'Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud), Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, 'Ikrimah, 'Amr ibn Dinar and al-A'mash read *ḥirj* with a kasra on the ḥāʾ, the rāʾ placed before the jīm, and a sukūn on the jīm. This is by metathesis (*qalb*, the transposition of letters), so its meaning is the same as *ḥijr*; or it is derived from *ḥaraj*, which means constriction. *Lā yaṭʿamuhā* means: none may eat of them, *illā man nashāʾ* (except whom we will), and they are the men to the exclusion of the women, or the attendants of the idols. ﴿bi-zaʿmihim﴾ means: by their assertion, which is closer to falsehood than to truth.

﴿And livestock whose backs have been forbidden﴾: they are the *baḥāʾir* (she-camels whose ears were slit), the *sawāʾib* (animals released freely), and the *ḥawāmī* (stallions protected from labour), and their explanation has already passed in Surat al-Ma'idah.

﴿And livestock over which they do not mention the name of God﴾: that is, at the time of slaughter. Abu Wa'il and a group said: they do not perform the Hajj upon them, nor do they say the talbiyah (the pilgrim's call) over them. They were ridden in every manner except during the Hajj.

﴿Fabricating against Him﴾: inventing and lying against God, in that they divided these livestock in this division and attributed it to God. ﴿Iftiraʾan﴾ is in the accusative either as a *mafʿūl li-ajlihi* (object of purpose, an accusative noun giving the reason for the action) or as a *maṣdar* (verbal noun) with an implied verb, meaning *yaftarūna* (they fabricate); or as a *maṣdar* in the sense of *wa-qālū* (and they said), since it carries the meaning of *iftarawā* (they fabricated); or as a *maṣdar* in the position of a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative).

﴿He will repay them for what they used to fabricate﴾: a severe threat and warning.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 139:

﴿And they say: "What is in the wombs of these cattle is exclusively for our males, and forbidden to our wives."﴾ "That which is in their wombs" is the fetuses (al-ajinna), so said al-Suddi. Al-Zamakhshari said: They used to say, concerning the fetuses of the baḥāʾir and the sawāʾib: whatever is born of them alive is exclusively for our males, and the females may not eat of it; and whatever is born dead, males and females share in it. Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah and al-Shaʿbi said: "That which is in their wombs" is the milk. Al-Tabari said: the wording encompasses both the fetuses and the milk. End of quotation. The apparent meaning is the fetuses, because they are what is in the belly in the literal sense; as for the milk, it is in the udder, not in the belly, except by a distant metaphor.

ʿAbd Allah, Ibn Jubayr, Abu al-ʿAliyah, al-Dahhak and Ibn Abi ʿAblah read khālisun with a nominative ending and without a tā' (ta' marbutah), and it is the predicate of mā, with (lidhukūrinā) dependent on it. Ibn Jubayr, as reported by Ibn Jinni, read khāliṣan with an accusative ending and without a tā', and it is in the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial qualifier) from the pronoun contained in the relative clause (ṣilah), or as a ḥāl from mā according to the view of Abu al-Hasan in his permission of placing the ḥāl before its governing element. End of abridged quotation. By his words "as a ḥāl from (mā)" he means: from the pronoun of (mā) contained in the predicate of (mā), which is (lidhukūrinā). By his words "in his permission…on its governing element" he means where the governing element is an adverbial phrase or a prepositional phrase, such as: Zayd is standing in the house. On this reading the predicate of (mā) is (lidhukūrinā).

Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Aʿraj, Qatadah and Ibn Jubayr also read (khāliṣatan) with the accusative, and its grammatical analysis is like that of (khāliṣan) in the accusative. Al-Zamakhshari explained it as an emphatic verbal noun, like al-ʿāfiyah.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Razin, ʿIkrimah, Ibn Yaʿmur, Abu Haywah and al-Zuhri also read (khāliṣatun) in the genitive construction (idafah), and it is either a substitute for (mā), or a subject whose predicate is (lidhukūrinā), and the sentence is the predicate of mā. The majority read (khāliṣatun) with the nominative and with the tā'. Is the tā' for intensification, like rāwiyah, or is it due to agreement with the meaning of mā because they are fetuses, or is it a verbal noun patterned on fāʿilah like al-ʿāfiyah and al-ʿāqibah, meaning "possessing exclusivity"? These are opinions.

Our shaykh ʿAlam al-Din al-ʿIraqi, may God have mercy on him, had mentioned that there is found in the Qur'an no instance of agreement with meaning first and then agreement with wording after it, except in this verse, and he promised us to clarify this in a place. What he mentioned was said by Makki, who said: The verse in the reading of the community came contrary to its counterparts in the Qur'an, because every case of agreement with wording at one time and with meaning at another begins first with agreement with wording, followed by agreement with meaning, such as (man āmana billāh), then He said: (fa-lahum ajruhum). This is how it comes in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech. In this verse agreement with meaning came first, so He said (khāliṣatun), then agreement with wording came, so He said ﴿wa-muḥarramun﴾. Similar to it is "kullu dhalika kana sayyi'atan" in the reading of Nafi' and those who follow him, where it is feminine according to the meaning of (kull), because it is a noun for all that was previously mentioned of sins forbidden; then He said ﴿ʿinda rabbika makruhan﴾ [al-Isra: 38], masculine according to the wording of (kull). Likewise (mā tarkabūna li-tastawū ʿalā ẓuhūrihi), agreement with mā, and the pronoun is singular in agreement with the wording of mā. It is related from the Arabs: "This locust has gone, and has relieved us of its own selves" (anfusihi), where they used the plural (anfus) and singular and masculine pronoun. End of quotation, with some abridgment. Whoever holds that the tā' is for intensification, or that it is in the verbal noun like al-ʿāfiyah, then there is no agreement with the meaning of mā; and even granting that it was agreement with meaning, it is not necessary that it began with agreement with meaning and then with wording, because the relative clause of mā is attached to a deleted verb, and that verb is predicated of the pronoun of mā. It is not necessary that the sense be "and they said: what has settled in the wombs of the cattle," rather the apparent estimate is: "what has settled," so it would have agreed first with the masculine and then with the feminine. When this possibility is admitted, which is the preferred one, it is not evidence that it began with agreement with the feminine and then with the wording. Makki's words "this is how it comes in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech": as for the Qur'an, it is indeed so; as for Arabic speech, agreement with wording first and then with meaning came in it, and this is the more common; and agreement with meaning first and then with wording also came. As for his saying "similar to it is 'kullu dhalika kana sayyi'atan'", it is not similar, rather it agreed first with wording in His saying (kāna), do you not see that He returned the pronoun masculine, then with meaning, so He said sayyi'atan. As for his saying "likewise 'mā tarkabūna'", it is not similar, because it is possible that the estimate is (mā tarkabūnahu), so it agreed first with wording, then with meaning in His saying (ẓuhūrihi), then with wording in the singular pronoun. As for "this locust has gone", it agreed first with the singular pronoun in agreement with wording, then it was pluralized in agreement with meaning, then with wording in the singular pronoun.

And the meaning of (li-azwājinā) is: for our women, i.e., prepared to be spouses; so said Mujahid. Ibn Zayd said: for our daughters.

﴿And if it is dead, they share in it﴾: when the fetus came out dead, men and women shared in eating it, and likewise what died of the cattle that were themselves designated. Abu Bakr read wa-in takun with the feminine ta' (mayytatan) with the accusative, meaning: and if the fetuses that come out are a dead thing. Ibn Kathir read wa-in yakun (maytatun) with the masculine and nominative, as the complete verb kāna. Al-Akhfash permitted that it be the incomplete kāna and made the predicate deleted, the estimate being: and if there is in their wombs a dead thing, and this is remote. Al-Zamakhshari said: The people of Makkah read wa-in takun (maytatan) with the feminine and nominative. If he means Ibn Kathir, it is an error; if he means other Makkans, it may be a sound transmission, and this reading he attributed to the people of Makkah is the reading of Ibn ʿAmir. The rest of the seven read (wa-in yakun) with the masculine and (maytatan) with the accusative, on the estimate: and if what is in their wombs is a dead thing. Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla said: This reading is strengthened by His saying ﴿fa-hum fihi shuraka'﴾, and He did not say fīhā. End of quotation. This is not good, because maytah applies to every dead thing, male or female, so it is as if it were said: "and if it is a dead thing, ﴿they share in it﴾." Yazid read (maytatan) with the shadda (intensive form). ʿAbd Allah read ﴿fa-hum fihi sawā'﴾ [al-Nahl: 71].

﴿He will requite them for their description﴾: that is, the recompense of their describing falsely about God in lawful and unlawful, from His saying: ﴿And do not say, concerning what your tongues describe falsely: "This is lawful and this is unlawful"﴾ [al-Nahl: 116].

﴿Indeed He is Wise, Knowing﴾: that is, ﴿Wise﴾ in their punishment, ﴿Knowing﴾ of their conditions.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 140:**

﴿Those who have killed their children in foolishness, without knowledge, and have forbidden what Allah provided for them, fabricating against Allah, have certainly lost. They have indeed gone astray, and they were not guided.﴾

Most of the Arabs did not bury their daughters alive. But some of Rabi'ah and Mudar used to bury them (wa'd), which means burying them alive. Some of them buried them out of fear of poverty and destitution, and some out of fear of their being taken captive. This verse was revealed concerning that, informing us of the loss of the one who does it. The enormity of killing children and of forbidding what they had forbidden had already been mentioned in their saying: "These are cattle and tilled land, forbidden (ḥijr)." Here the killing of children is mentioned first, followed by the forbidding. In His saying, ﴿in foolishness, without knowledge﴾, there is an indication of the lightness of their minds and their ignorance that Allah is the Provider and the One who decrees captivity and other things. ﴿What Allah provided for them﴾ is for showing its permissibility to them, so they countered Allah's permission with their own prohibition. ﴿What Allah provided for them﴾ includes the sawā'ib (free-roaming animals), the baḥā'ir (slit-eared she-camels), and the crops.

The loss is made to follow from their killing of their children, with the cause given as foolishness and ignorance. It follows from their forbidding of what Allah provided that they have lost, with the cause given as fabrication. Then comes the statement of going astray and the negation of guidance. Each of these seven is a complete cause for blame.

As for the loss: a child is a great blessing from Allah, so whoever strives to nullify that blessing and gift has lost and deserves blame in this world, for their saying: "He killed his child for fear that it would eat with him." And in the Hereafter he deserves punishment, because the fruit of a child is love. Despite the existence of that love, he inflicted upon the child the greatest harm, which is killing, so it is among the greatest sins, and thus deserves the greatest punishment.

As for foolishness, which is the blameworthy lightness, killing a child out of fear of poverty is so, even if poverty is a harm, killing is greater than it. Also, killing is immediate while poverty is merely imagined.

As for ignorance, foolishness arises from it, and ignorance is among the worst of ugly traits.

As for forbidding what Allah has made lawful, it is among the greatest of crimes.

As for fabrication, it is audacity against Allah, and it is among the greatest sins.

As for going astray, it means that they are not rightly guided in the interests of this world or the Hereafter.

As for the negation of guidance, it is a warning that they were never, in what they pursued of that, people of guidance.

Al-Hasan, al-Sulami, the people of Makkah and Syria, and among them (p. 234) Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir, read (qattalū) with the doubled letter (intensive form). Al-Yamani read (sufahā'), in the plural.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 141 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿It is He who produces gardens, trellised and untrellised, and palm trees and crops of varying produce, and olives and pomegranates, similar and dissimilar. Eat of their fruit when they bear fruit, and give its due on the day of its harvest, and do not waste. Indeed, He does not like the wasteful.﴾ ﴿And of the livestock are those for burden and for slaughter. Eat of what Allah has provided you and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾ [al-An'am: 142]

﴿Eight mates: two of the sheep and two of the goats. Say: "Has He forbidden the two males or the two females, or what the wombs of the two females contain? Inform me with knowledge, if you are truthful."﴾ [al-An'am: 143]

﴿And of the camels two and of the cattle two. Say: "Has He forbidden the two males or the two females, or what the wombs of the two females contain? Or were you witnesses when Allah instructed you with this? So who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah to mislead people without knowledge? Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people."﴾ [al-An'am: 144]

﴿Say: "I do not find in what has been revealed to me [anything] forbidden to one who eats it, unless it is carrion, or blood poured out, or the flesh of swine, for indeed it is impure, or [an offense] of wickedness, [over which] other than Allah has been invoked. But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, then indeed your Lord is Forgiving and Merciful."﴾ [al-An'am: 145]

﴿And to those who were Jews We prohibited every animal with claws, and of the cattle and sheep We prohibited to them their fats, except that which their backs or their intestines carry, or what is mixed with bone. That was their recompense for their rebellion. And indeed, We are truthful.﴾ [al-An'am: 146]

﴿So if they deny you, say: "Your Lord is of vast mercy, but His punishment will not be averted from the criminal people."﴾ [al-An'am: 147]

﴿Those who associated will say: "If Allah had willed, we would not have associated, nor would our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything." Likewise did those before them deny, until they tasted Our punishment. Say: "Do you have any knowledge that you can produce for us? You follow not except assumption, and you are not but conjecturing."﴾ [al-An'am: 148]

﴿Say: "To Allah belongs the conclusive proof. So had He willed, He would have guided you all."﴾ [al-An'am: 149]

﴿Say: "Bring forward your witnesses who testify that Allah has forbidden this." And if they testify, do not testify with them, and do not follow the desires of those who denied Our signs and those who do not believe in the Hereafter and who make equals to their Lord.﴾ [al-An'am: 150]

﴿Say: "Come, I will recite what your Lord has prohibited to you: that you not associate anything with Him, and to parents, good treatment; and do not kill your children out of poverty — We provide for you and for them — and do not approach immoralities, what is apparent of them and what is concealed; and do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right. This He has instructed you, that you may use reason."﴾ [al-An'am: 151]

﴿And do not approach the property of an orphan, except in the best manner, until he reaches maturity. And give full measure and weight in justice. We do not charge a soul except [with that within] its capacity. And when you speak, be just, even if it concerns a relative. And fulfill the covenant of Allah. This He has instructed you, that you may remember.﴾ [al-An'am: 152]

**al-Zar'** is the grain that is eaten as food. **al-Hasad** (harvest) is pronounced with a fatha or a kasra on the ha', like al-jidhadh (cutting off), with either fatha or kasra. It is a masdar (verbal noun) of hasada, and its masdar is also hasd, which is the analogical form. Sibawayh said: "They used the masadir (verbal nouns) when they intended the time of an action, on the pattern fi'al, and sometimes they said fa'al for it." Al-Farra' said: "The kasra is the dialect of the Hijaz, and the fatha is the dialect of Najd and Tamim."

**al-Hamulah** refers to camels that carry loads on their backs. This is what Abu al-Haytham said. Mules and donkeys are not included in it, but some included cattle, since it is the custom of some people to load them.

**al-Farsh** refers to sheep. Al-Zajjaj said: "The lexicographers agree that al-farsh are young camels." A poet recited:

> "He left me a hamulah and a farsh, which I milk every day, a milking."

Another said:

> "We were given the farsh of your livestock, and the hamulat, and the young ones of the hajal."
