Thus al-farsh is a term shared by young camels. Abu Zayd said: "It is possible that they were named by the masdar, and it is what is spread out (mafrush) from the household goods, and crops when they are spread out, and the wide open space, and the slight breadth of a camel's sole, and smooth land, according to Abu 'Amr, and the spread of a sandal, and the nest of a bird, and a plant that clings to the earth." A poet said:

> "Like the lip of the fanged one, chewing the farsh."

The discussion of the difference of opinion concerning hamulah and farsh will come, God willing.

**al-Ibil** means camels, singular and plural, and its plural is also ābāl. Ta'abbala al-rajul means he acquired camels. The saying "ma ābala al-rajul" in exclamation is anomalous.

[p. 235] **al-Ḍa'n** (sheep) is well known, pronounced with a sukun or fatha on the hamza, and it is said to be ḍa'in. Both are collective nouns for ḍā'inah and ḍā'in. **al-Ma'z** (goats) is well known, pronounced with a sukun or fatha on the 'ayn, and it is said to be ma'īz, ma'zā, and um'ūz, which are collective nouns for mā'izah and mā'iz. **al-Safḥ** is pouring out; it is the masdar of safaha yasfahu, and al-safḥ is also a place name. **al-Ẓufr** (claw) is well known, pronounced with a ḍamma on the ẓā' and fā', with a sukun on the fā', with a kasra on both, and again with a sukun on the fā'; also ẓufūr. The plural of the triliteral is aẓfār, and the plural of ẓufūr is aẓāfīr and aẓāfir. A man who is aẓfar has long nails. **al-Shaḥm** (fat) is well known.

**al-Hawāyā**: if its form is measured as fawāʿil, it is the plural of ḥāwiyah, like rāwiyah and rawāyā, or the plural of ḥāwiyā', like qāṣiʿā' and qawāṣiʿ. If its form is measured as faʿāʾil, it is the plural of ḥawiyyah, like maṭiyyah and maṭāyā. The explanation of how it becomes ḥawāyā is mentioned in the science of morphology (taṣrīf). It is the twisted intestines found in the bellies of sheep. The disagreement of the exegetes concerning it will come, God willing, the Exalted.

**Halumma** (come on, here): the dialect of the Hijaz is that pronouns do not attach to it, rather it remains the same for singular, dual, and plural, masculine and feminine. Therefore, according to the grammarians, it is an ism fi'l (verb-noun, a word functioning as a verb without its inflections). The dialect of Bani Tamim is that pronouns attach to it in the same manner as they attach to a verb. Therefore, according to most grammarians, it is a verb that does not inflect. The Arabs were bound to use the fatha on the mim in the Hijazi dialect. When it is an imperative addressed to a masculine singular in the Tamimi dialect, what was permissible with ruddu is not permissible with it. The view of the Basrans is that it is composed of ha', which is for alerting, and mim. The view of al-Farra' is that it is composed of hal and umm. You say to feminine plurals: halummun. Al-Farra' also reported halumminna. It is transitive with the meaning of "bring forward," and intransitive with the meaning of "come forward."

**al-Imlāq** is poverty. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and others. It is said: amlaqa al-rajul when he became poor. It is similar to armala (to be destitute), meaning nothing remained for him except al-malaq, which are black stones, and it is the single word malaqah. Nothing remained for him except sand and dust. Mu'arraj said: it is hunger in the dialect of Lakhm. Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: it is spending, and amlaqa malahu means he spent it. Muhammad ibn Nu'aym al-Tirmidhi said: it is extravagance in spending.

**al-Kayl** is the masdar of kala; kala is well known. Then it is applied to the instrument by which measuring is done, like al-mikyal (measure). **al-Mīzān** is a mif'āl derived from al-wazn (weighing), and it is the instrument of weighing, like al-minqāsh, al-midrāb, and al-misbāḥ. Its shapes vary according to regions, like al-mikyal.

* *

﴿It is He who produces gardens, trellised and untrellised, and palm trees and crops of varying produce, and olives and pomegranates, similar and dissimilar.﴾ The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when He, the Exalted, informed them that they had been deprived of things from what Allah had provided them, He began to mention what He had bestowed upon them of provision, which they disposed of without His permission, fabricating and inventing against Him. So He mentioned the two kinds of provision, the plant and the animal. He began with the plant, as He did in the verse similar to this one, and digressed from it to the animal, since they had been deprived of things from both kinds.

**Ma'rūshāt** is an ism maf'ūl (passive participle). It is said: 'arashtu al-karm when you make supports and a trellis for it upon which the vine shoots lean. Are the trellised things those which people planted and trellised, while the others are what grew in the plains and deserts? This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. Or every tree with a trunk, like the palm and the vine, and everything that sprouts without a trunk, like grain. Or what bears fruit and what does not. Or the vine is divided into what is raised on trellises and what lies spread on the ground. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Or what has a wall around it and what has no wall around it, and what spreads over the face of the earth and extends, like the vine, the gourd, and the watermelon, and what stands on a trunk, like the palm, grain, and trees. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Or the vine whose grapes are trellised, and the rest of the trees that are not trellised. Or what some of its branches rise above others and what does not need that. Or what its custom is to be trellised, like the vine and what is similar to it, and what is not trellised, like the palm and what resembles it. These are nine opinions. The apparent meaning is that the trellised is what is given a trellis, whether it is a vine or other, and the untrellised is what is not given that.

Since this verse is concerned with mentioning favor and kindness, what the Arabs need most and what is most abundant in it was placed first, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿in a valley without cultivation﴾ [Ibrahim: 37]. It is the chief of their food. So He said: ﴿and palm trees and crops﴾. Since that verse came after the disbelievers denied monotheism and made others with Him as gods, it digressed from that to the Hereafter, and gave evidence for it with His saying: ﴿It is He who sends down water from the sky, and We bring forth thereby the growth of all things﴾ [al-An'am: 99], so that (palm trees and crops) was included in it. The beginning of the division with the mention of crops was because their grain is small, and it is more indicative of monotheism and complete power, more instructive for reflection, and quicker for benefit than what is larger in size.

The apparent meaning is that (palm trees and what follows) is included in His saying: ﴿gardens, trellised and untrellised﴾, so it is included in ﴿gardens﴾. It was singled out for mention and separated out to magnify its benefit and to express favor through it. Whoever specified the gardens by their division as vines said: the mention of the palm and what follows it is the mention of kinds which He, the Exalted, informed us that He created.

**Ikhtilāf ukulih**, which means its food, that is, what is eaten, is that each kind of palm and crop differs from the other kind in taste, color, size, and smell. The meaning is: "varying in the food of its fruit." **Mukhtalifan** is in the accusative as a hal muqaddarah (anticipated circumstantial accusative, a term describing a state that begins after the action), because at the time of creation it was not yet varying. It was said: it is a hal muqarinah (simultaneous circumstantial accusative), and that is by deleting a noun before it, its estimate being: the fruit of the palm and the grain of the crops. The pronoun in ﴿ukulahu﴾ refers to (palm trees and crops), and it is singular because it falls under the ruling of the coordination. This is what al-Zamakhshari said, but it is not good, because coordination with "wa" does not allow the pronoun of the two conjoined items to be singular. Al-Hawfi said: "The hā' in ﴿ukulahu﴾ refers to what was previously mentioned of these created things." End of quote. According to this, the one who is in the state is not (palm trees and crops) alone, but all that He created, since they all share in the variation of what is eaten. If it were as he claimed, the construction would have been mukhtalifan ukuluha (plural pronoun), unless it is taken with an omitted noun, meaning: the fruit of gardens. This omitted noun was observed, so it was said: ﴿ukulahu﴾ in the singular with regard to it. This is like His saying: ﴿or like darkness in a deep sea, covered by a wave﴾ [al-Nur: 40], or like "dhī zulumāt" (one of darknesses). For this reason He returned the pronoun in ﴿yaghshāhu﴾ [al-Nur: 40] to it. The apparent meaning is that it returns to the nearest preceding mention, which is ﴿al-zar'a﴾ [al-Nahl: 11] (the crops). The hal of (palm trees) is omitted because this hal indicates it. The estimate is: and the palm trees, varying in its food, and the crops, varying in its food. This is like what some interpreted in the saying: Zayd and 'Amr are standing, meaning Zayd is standing and 'Amr is standing. It is possible that the hal is specific to the crops, because their kinds differ greatly in form, like wheat, barley, millet, qatina, salt, lentils, lupine, rice, and other things. Unlike palm trees, where the fruit does not differ in form except by size, small and large.

The discussion of His saying: ﴿and olives and pomegranates, similar and dissimilar﴾ has already preceded, so it suffices and there is no need to repeat it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 141 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Eat of its fruit when it bears fruit.﴾ Since the mention of this verse came in the context of using it as evidence for the Creator and His power, for the Gathering (al-hashr) and the return of the souls to the bodies after non-existence, and for the bringing forth of the body and its formation from crumbling bones, which is the "tailbone" (ʿajb al-dhanab), He said: "Look at its fruit when it bears fruit and at its ripening" [6:99], indicating its origination first and its end. Here, since the context concerns the end result, namely bestowing favour and showing kindness through what He created for us, He said: ﴿Eat of its fruit.﴾ Thus through the two together there is achieved eternal everlasting life and the swiftly passing worldly life. Looking (al-nazar), which is reflection (al-fikr), is placed before eating for this reason. This is a command to permit eating, and it is used as evidence that the basic principle regarding benefits is permissibility and freedom. He restricted it with His words ﴿when it bears fruit﴾, although it is known that if it does not bear fruit there is no eating, as an alert that one should not wait for it to reach the stage of ripeness and maturity, but rather whenever it becomes possible to eat from it, one should do so.

﴿And give its due on the day of its harvest.﴾ What appears is that the pronoun refers to what the phrase "its fruit" refers to, namely all that was mentioned earlier that can be eaten when it bears fruit. It was said that it refers to the palm tree (al-nakhl), since in the verse there is nothing that must have its due given at its cutting except the palm. It was also said that it refers to "the olive and the pomegranate", since they are the nearest mentioned. The pronoun is singular because of the aspects mentioned in His words ﴿varied in its produce﴾. ﴿And give﴾ is a command of obligation. The command to eat was placed before the command to give charity, because giving priority to a person's benefit from what he owns for himself is preferable to the benefit of others, as the Exalted said: ﴿And do not forget your share of this world, and do good as Allah has done good to you﴾ [28:77]. And: "Begin with yourself, then with those you support," and: "Charity is only from surplus wealth" (ʿan ẓahr ghinā).

The due (al-ḥaqq) here is general (mujmal), and it has been disputed whether it is zakat or something else. Ibn ʿAbbas, Anas ibn Malik, al-Ḥasan, Ṭawus, Jabir ibn Zayd, Ibn al-Musayyib, Qatadah, Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, Ibn Ṭawus, al-Ḍaḥḥak, Zayd ibn Aslam and his son, and Malik ibn Anas said: it is zakat. This view is objected to on the basis that the surah is Meccan, and this verse, according to the majority view, is not excepted. Al-Zajjaj related that it was said regarding this verse that it was revealed in Medina. Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn al-Husayn, who is al-Baqir, ʿAṭāʾ, Ḥammad, Mujahid, Ibrahim, Ibn Jubayr, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb, al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas, Yazid ibn al-Asamm, and al-Ḥakam said: it is a right other than zakat. Mujahid said: "If the needy are present, throw to them at the cutting, at the stacking, at the threshing, and at the winnowing." And from him also: "They used to hang the cluster at the time of harvesting, and whoever touched it would eat from it." From Ibrahim: it is the handful which one throws to the needy, and the wording "whatever falls from you of the ears of grain" does not prevent them from it. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn al-Hanafiyyah, Ibrahim, al-Ḥasan, ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfi, and al-Suddi that it is abrogated (mansukhah), meaning its ruling has been superseded (naskh) by the tithe and half-tithe (al-ʿushr wa-nisf al-ʿushr). Sufyan said: I said to al-Suddi: "From whom did it abrogate it, from those who spoke about the scholars?" Abu Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥas said, in summary: Was the zakat intended by it, or was it abrogated by the obligatory zakat, or by the tithe and half-tithe, or is it muhkam (not abrogated) with something other than zakat intended by it, or is it recommended? Five opinions.

If zakat is intended, the apparent meaning is that it is to be given from everything mentioned earlier, so it covers all that the earth produces. This is the view of Abu Hanifa and Zufar, except for firewood, reeds, and grass. Abu Yusuf and Muhammad said: nothing is due on what the earth produces except what has lasting fruit. Malik said: zakat is due on fruits and grains. From fruits: grapes and olives; from grains: wheat, barley, spelt (al-salt), maize, millet, chickpeas, lentils, lupine (al-lubiyā), vetch (al-julbān), rice, and what resembles these, when it reaches five wasqs. Al-Shafiʿi and Abu Thawr said: it is due on dry, staple, storable foodstuffs, not on olives, because it is a condiment. Al-Thawri, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Ḥasan ibn Ṣāliḥ, Ibn al-Mubarak, and Yaḥya ibn Adam said: it is due only on wheat, barley, dates, and raisins. From Ahmad there are several views, the most apparent of which, like the school of Abu Hanifa, is that if it is measurable it is due; so he made it due on almonds because it is measured by volume, and did not make it due on walnuts because they are counted. It is narrated from a group of the early generations, among them ʿAmr ibn Dinar, that there is no charity on vegetables. From Ibn ʿAbbas: he used to take a tenth from the bundles of leeks in Basra. From Ibrahim: on everything the earth produces, even one bundle of greens out of every ten. Al-Zuhri and al-Ḥasan said: the vegetables and fruits are to be given zakat when they ripen and their price reaches two hundred dirhams; al-Awzaʿi said the same regarding the price of fruits. As for the quantity on which zakat is due, Abu Hanifa said: on little and much of what the earth produces. Malik, al-Layth, Ibn Abi Layla, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, and al-Shafiʿi said: one does not give until it reaches five wasqs if it is measurable; if it is not measurable, there is disagreement among Abu Yusuf and Muhammad regarding what is taken into account. They mentioned here subsidiary cases. They said: according to the companions of Malik there is no zakat on walnuts, almonds, hazelnuts, and what resembles them, even if they are stored; just as there is no zakat according to them on plums, apples, pears, apricots, and the like, which dry out and are not stored. Malik counted figs among the fruits. Ibn Habib said: zakat is due on them, and this was the view of a group of Malik's followers: Ismaʿil ibn Ishaq, Abu Bakr al-Abhari, and others. Malik said: there is no zakat on olives. He and al-Shafiʿi said: nor on pomegranates. Al-Zuhri, al-Awzaʿi, al-Thawri, and al-Layth said: zakat is due on olives. From Malik: olives are not estimated (la yukhraṣ), but a tenth is taken from their oil when their measure reaches five wasqs. Abu Hanifa, in all these matters, is according to his principle. Whatever they specified from the general wording of the verse requires evidence, and the evidences are mentioned in the books of jurisprudence.

The apparent meaning is that ﴿on the day of its harvest﴾ is governed by His words ﴿and give﴾, and the meaning is: intend the giving, be concerned with it at the time of harvest, so that it is not delayed beyond the time when giving is possible. It is also permissible that it be governed by His words ﴿its due﴾, meaning: ﴿and give﴾ what is owed ﴿on the day of its harvest﴾, so the entitlement occurs by giving on the day of harvest, and the payment after cleaning (al-taṣfiyah). For this reason some said: there is an omitted element in the speech, its estimated meaning being: "and give its due on the day of its harvest until its cleaning." He said: then the harvest is a cause for the broad (muwassaʿ) obligation, and the cleaning is a cause for the payment. The apparent meaning is that the due must be given from all of it, whether what its owner and his family ate from it or what they left. This is the view of Abu Hanifa and Malik. A group said: what he and his family ate from it does not enter into the due. The apparent meaning is that it is a command that its due be given on the day of its harvest, so it is not estimated (la yakhruṣ) against him. Al-Nakhaʿi said: estimating (al-kharṣ) today is an innovation. Al-Thawri said: estimating is not practised and is not permissible in any case; rather, the owner of the orchard is only to give a tenth of what reaches his hand to the needy, if it reaches five wasqs.

The two ʿArabiyyān and ʿĀṣim read ﴿ḥiṣādihi﴾ with a fatḥah on the ḥāʾ. The rest of the seven read it with a kasrah on it.

﴿And do not be extravagant. Indeed, He does not love the extravagant.﴾ Since the Exalted commanded eating from its fruits and giving its due, He forbade exceeding the limit, saying: "Do not be extravagant." This prohibition includes extravagance in general, so it enters into it extravagance in eating the fruit until nothing of it remains for zakat, and extravagance in giving charity from it until he leaves nothing for himself or his dependants. Abu al-ʿĀliyah and Ibn Jurayj restricted it to giving charity of all the wealth, so that he and his dependants remain a burden upon the people. Ibn Jurayj also said: it is a prohibition regarding eating, so that one eats until nothing remains on which zakat is due. al-Zuhri said: it is a prohibition regarding spending in disobedience. It was said: it refers to diverting charity to a channel other than that for which it was prescribed, as the polytheists diverted it to the channels of their idols. Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 145–146 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who would eat it, unless it be carrion, or flowing blood, or the flesh of swine, for indeed it is an abomination, or a transgression, over which the name of other than Allah has been invoked.﴾ When He mentioned that they had forbidden what they forbade as a fabrication against Allah, He commanded him to inform them that the source of prohibition is only revelation from Allah, the Exalted, and His law, not what the souls desire or what they invent and attribute to Allah, the Exalted. The arrangement here is like the arrangement in al-Baqarah and al-Ma'idah. Here these prohibited things come indefinite: the blood is described by His saying ﴿flowing﴾, and the transgression is described by His saying ﴿over which the name of other than Allah has been invoked﴾. In those two surahs they come definite, because this surah is Meccan, so it was attached to indefiniteness, while those two surahs are Medinan, so those names came as definites by prior reference, referring back to what was previously revealed in this surah. It is related from Ibn 'Amir: ﴿fi ma uhiya﴾ with an opening of the hamzah and the ha', making it a past-tense active verb, and ﴿muharraman﴾ an attribute of an elided noun, its estimate being "matamman" (something eaten), indicated by His saying ﴿to an eater who would eat it﴾, and ﴿yatamuhu﴾ being an attribute of ﴿ta'im﴾. Al-Baqir recited ﴿yatta''imuhu﴾ with a shaddah on the ta' and a kasrah on the 'ayn, the original being yatati'imuhu; its ta' was changed to a ta' (emphatic) and the first radical of the word was assimilated into it. ʿĀʾishah, the companions of ʿAbdullah, and Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah recited ﴿tata''amahu﴾ as a past-tense verb. The phrase ﴿unless it be﴾ is a disconnected exception, since being (the carrion, etc.) is an entity and what precedes it is an entity. It is permissible that its accusative be a substitute according to the dialect of Tamim, and an accusative of exception according to the dialect of the Hijaz. Ibn Kathir and Hamzah recited ﴿takun﴾ with a ta', and Ibn Kathir and Hamzah recited ﴿maytatan﴾ in the accusative, the subject of ﴿yakun﴾ being a pronoun referring to ﴿muharraman﴾, and it was made feminine because the predicate is feminine. Ibn 'Amir recited ﴿maytatun﴾ in the nominative, making kana complete. The rest recited with a ya' and the accusative ﴿maytatan﴾, the subject of kana being a masculine pronoun referring to ﴿muharraman﴾, meaning: "unless the prohibited thing be carrion." According to the recitation of Ibn 'Amir, which is the recitation of Abu Ja'far as Makki mentioned, His saying ﴿or flowing blood﴾ is coordinated with the position of ﴿an yakuna﴾; according to the reading of the others it is coordinated with His saying ﴿carrion﴾. The meaning of ﴿flowing﴾ is poured out, running, like blood in the veins, not like the spleen and the liver, and blood in the veins was permitted after slaughter. It was said to Abu Majlaz: "A pot whose surface is reddened by blood." He said: "Allah, the Exalted, prohibited only the flowing." ʿĀʾishah said something similar, and the consensus of the scholars is upon it. It was said: blood is prohibited because when it separates it has been poured out. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿fa-innahu﴾ refers to ﴿flesh of swine﴾. Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm claimed that it refers to "swine," since it is the nearest mentioned item, and when a pronoun may refer to two things, its reference to the nearer is more preponderant. This was countered by saying that the thing spoken of is the flesh, and the mention of swine came by way of annexation to it, not that it is itself the spoken-of, coordinated item. It is possible to say: the flesh was mentioned as an alert that it is the greatest benefit derived from swine, even though the rest of it shares in the prohibition; or by specifying the cause, namely that it is an abomination; or because the majority is applied to the whole; or the principal is applied to the subordinate, since fat and other parts follow the flesh. The scholars differed concerning this verse: is it muhkam (definitive)? This is the view of al-Sha'bi and Ibn Jubayr, and according to this, nothing among animals is forbidden except in it; this is not the view of the majority. It was said: it is abrogated by the verse of al-Ma'idah, and this abrogation should be understood as abrogation only of the restriction. It was said: everything that has been prohibited is included in the exception, whether by the text of the Qur'an or a hadith from the Messenger ﷺ, by sharing in the cause, which is abomination. What we say is: the verse is Meccan and came after His saying ﴿eight pairs﴾ [al-An'am: 143], and the people of the Jahiliyyah used to forbid what they forbade of the bahirah, the sa'ibah, the wasilah and the hami, from these eight, so the verse is muhkam, and in it He informed that He did not find in what was revealed to him at that time from the Qur'an anything other than what He mentioned; for this reason the relative clause of ﴿ma﴾ came as a sentence headed by a past-tense verb. So everything that was prohibited in Medina had not, at that time, been preceded by revelation in Mecca, so there is no contradiction between what was prohibited in Medina and what was reported as having been revealed to him in Mecca as prohibited. The mention of swine, although it is not among the eight pairs, is because some people were eating it at that time, and because it is most similar to the eight pairs in not being a predatory beast that eats flesh and feeds on it; rather it is of the type of the eight, in that it lives on plants and grazes as the eight graze. The commentators mentioned here several matters on which the people of knowledge differed, and we summarize some of them. As for domestic donkeys, al-Sha'bi and Ibn Jubayr held that eating them is permitted, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ's prohibition of them was for a reason. As for horse meat, the early scholars differed concerning it, and al-Shafi'i, Ibn Hanbal, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan permitted it, while from Abu Hanifah there is disapproval. It was said: disapproval of tanzih (preference). It was said: disapproval of tahrim (prohibition), and this is the view of Malik, al-Awza'i, al-Hakam ibn 'Uyaynah, Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Bakr al-Asamm. Mujahid among the Successors held it, and Ibn 'Abbas among the Companions, though a contrary view is related from him. Qadi al-Qudat Shams al-Din Ahmad ibn Ibrahim ibn 'Abd al-Ghani al-Surujji al-Hanafi, may Allah have mercy on him, wrote a treatise on the ruling on horse meat, which we read to him. They agreed on the prohibition of mules. As for the wild donkey when it has become domesticated, Abu Hanifah and his companions, al-Hasan ibn Salih and al-Shafi'i held that eating it is permitted; Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik that when it has become tame and is used for work as the domestic donkey is, it is not eaten. Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf, Zufar and Muhammad said: it is not lawful to eat any animal with fangs among beasts of prey, or any bird with talons. Malik said: beasts of prey of the wild, or of the land, whether wild or domestic, are not eaten, nor the fox, nor the hyena; there is no harm in eating birds of prey such as the rakham, the eagle, the vulture and others, which eat carrion and that which does not eat. Al-Awza'i said: all birds are lawful, except that they dislike the rakham. Al-Shafi'i said: whatever attacks people with fangs, such as the lion, the wolf and the panther, and among birds whatever attacks with talons, such as the vulture and the falcon, is not eaten, while the fox and the hyena are eaten. Abu Hanifah disliked the spotted crow but not the field crow, and the disagreement concerning the kite is like the disagreement concerning the eagle and the vulture. Abu Hanifah disliked the lizard; Malik and al-Shafi'i said there is no harm in it. The majority hold that the domestic cat is not eaten, while from Malik there is permission to eat it, whether domestic or wild, and from some of the early scholars permission to eat the domestic. Ibn Abi Layla said: there is no harm in eating a snake if it is slaughtered. Al-Layth said: there is no harm in eating the hedgehog, bee larvae, cheese worms, date worms and the like; likewise Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik concerning the hedgehog. Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i said: the mouse is not eaten. Abu Hanifah said: the jerboa is not eaten; al-Shafi'i said it is eaten. From Malik there is prohibition, disapproval and permission concerning the mouse. Abu Hanifah, al-Shafi'i and their companions held that eating the jallalah (an animal that feeds on filth) is disapproved. Malik and al-Layth said: there is no harm in eating it. The author of al-Tahrir wa al-Tahbir said: as for intoxicating drugs such as henbane, the sikran, the lufah and cannabis leaves called hashish, the people of knowledge did not explicitly state their prohibition, and in my view prohibition is closer, because if they are intoxicating they are prohibited by his ﷺ saying: "Whatever in large quantity intoxicates, a small quantity of it is forbidden," and by his saying: "Every intoxicant is forbidden"; and if they are not intoxicating, then bringing harm upon the body is forbidden. Ibn Bakhtishu' related in his book that cannabis leaves cause seventy diseases in the body, and he mentioned among them that it yellows the skin, blackens the teeth and creates pits in them, pierces the liver and heats it, corrupts the intellect, weakens the sight, causes sorrow and removes courage; henbane and the sikran are like cannabis leaves in harm. As for sedatives such as saffron and mandrake, the harmful quantity of them is forbidden; most physicians said: when a great quantity of saffron is used it kills by exhilaration. End, with some abridgment. Abu Bakr al-Razi said concerning His saying ﴿an eater who would eat it﴾ that it indicates that what is forbidden from carrion is that which can be eaten, and it does not include hide that has been tanned, nor horn, nor bone, nor hoof, nor feathers and the like; and concerning His saying ﴿or flowing blood﴾ that it indicates that the blood of gnats, fleas and flies is not impure. End.

﴿Or a transgression﴾: the apparent reading is that it is coordinated with the accusative before it. That which was invoked over with other than Allah's name is called a transgression because it goes deep into the category of transgression; from this is His saying ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned, for indeed it is transgression﴾ [al-An'am: 121]. ﴿Invoked over﴾ is an attribute of it in the accusative position. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that ﴿transgression﴾ be in the accusative as an object of purpose, placed before its governing verb, which is ﴿invoked over﴾, citing the line: "I was moved, and not from longing for fair women is my being moved." He separated between ﴿aw﴾ and ﴿invoked over﴾ with the object of purpose, and ﴿aw invoked over﴾ would be coordinated with ﴿yakun﴾, and the pronoun in ﴿bihi﴾ refers to what it refers to in ﴿yakun﴾. This is a very forced parsing, and a construction on this parsing is outside eloquence, and it is not permissible on the recitation of one who recited ﴿an yakuna maytatun﴾ with the nominative, for then the pronoun in ﴿bihi﴾ would have nothing to refer to, and it is not permissible to posit an elided noun so that the pronoun refers to it, the estimate being: "or a thing ﴿invoked over with other than Allah's name﴾," for such a thing is permitted only in poetic necessity.

﴿But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor exceeding, then indeed your Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ The explanation of the like of this has preceded. Since the beginning of the verse opened with His address to him, saying ﴿Say: I do not find﴾, He concluded the verse with address, saying ﴿then indeed your Lord﴾, indicating His care for him by honouring His address at its opening and its closing.

And to those who became Jews We forbade every animal with claws. The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that, when Allah showed that prohibition derives from divine revelation, He informed that He had forbidden certain things to some of the earlier nations, just as He had forbidden things to the people of this religion, which He mentioned in the previous verse. So prohibition is attributed to Allah, the Exalted, among all nations. In His words ﴿We forbade﴾ there is a refutation of the Jews' claim that Allah had not forbidden anything to them, and that they had forbidden only what Israel (Ya'qub) had forbidden upon himself. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, Qatada and al-Suddi said: "It refers to animals with cloven hooves, such as camels and ostriches, and those without separated fingers, such as ducks, geese and the like." Al-Zajjaj chose this view. Ibn Zayd said: "It refers only to camels," but this specification has been deemed weak. al-Dahhak said: "It refers to the ostrich and the wild ass," and this is weak because it restricts the meaning. al-Kalbi said: "Every animal with a talon among birds, every solid-hoofed animal among quadrupeds, and every animal with a fang among predators." al-Qutabi said: "Here the word 'claw' (zufr) is in the position of 'hoof'; it includes every solid-hoofed quadruped, and the hoof was called a claw figuratively." Tha'lab said: "Everything that does not hunt is clawed, and what hunts is talon-bearing." al-Naqqash said: "This is not consistent, for the lion is clawed." al-Zamakhshari said: "Anything that has a digit (uṣbu') among quadrupeds or birds. Some of the clawed animals had been lawful to them, but when they committed wrongdoing, these were forbidden to them, so the prohibition covered every clawed animal, as proven by His words: ﴿Because of the wrongdoing of those who became Jews, We forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them﴾ [al-Nisa: 160]." Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: "Taking 'claw' to mean 'hoof' is weak, because a hoof is hardly called a claw, and because if it were so, it would have said: 'He forbade them every animal that has a hoof,' and that is false, since the verse indicates the permissibility of cattle and sheep, although they have hooves. Therefore 'claw' must be taken to mean talons and claws, since talons are the instruments by which hunting beasts catch prey. This includes types of predators, dogs, cats and hunting birds. This is specific to the Jews, because ﴿to those who became Jews﴾ indicates restriction, so the prohibition is specific to the Jews and is not forbidden to Muslims. What is narrated about the prohibition of fanged predators and talon-bearing birds is weak, because it is a single report (khabar wahid) contrary to the Book of Allah, so it is not accepted. This supports the madhhab (school) of Malik." Summarized, the end. In this there are several points: First, we do not accept the restriction of 'clawed' to what he said. Second, we do not accept the restriction he claimed. Third, we do not accept the exclusivity. Fourth, we do not accept that the single report about forbidding fanged animals and talon-bearing birds is contrary to the Book of Allah. Everyone who interpreted "claw" as those earlier opinions did holds that the meat, fat and everything else from what he interpreted is forbidden. Some exegetes held that this is by omission of a word (elision of a modifier), and that what is forbidden is not the clawed animal itself but what the clawed animal catches, i.e., the talon-bearing animal that was not trained. This goes against the apparent meaning. Ubayy, al-Hasan and al-'A'raj read (ẓafrun) with a sukun on the fa'. Al-Hasan and Abu al-Sammal Qa'nab also read it with sukun on the fa' and a kasra on the ẓa'.

﴿And of cattle and sheep We forbade them their fat﴾, i.e., the fat of both kinds. The phrase "min" is connected to the later "We forbade" (ḥarramnā), and it is not necessary for it to precede its governing verb. If the construction were: "And We forbade them from cattle and sheep their fat," it would be a strange construction, just as you say: "From Zayd I took his property," and it is permissible to say: "I took from Zayd his property." The idafa (construction) indicates emphasis of specification and connection, for if the statement were: "Of cattle and sheep We forbade them the fats," it would be sufficient to indicate that only the fat of cattle and sheep is meant. It is possible that ﴿And of cattle and sheep﴾ is coordinated with ﴿every clawed animal﴾, so that min is connected to the first "We forbade," and then the second clause came explaining what was vague in the partitive "min" concerning what was forbidden, so He said: ﴿We forbade them their fat﴾. Abu al-Baqa' said: "It is not permissible that (of cattle) be connected to the second 'We forbade'; rather it is coordinated with 'every,' and ('We forbade them') is an explanation of what is forbidden from cattle and sheep." It seems to imply that the return of the pronoun prevents the connection, since the position of a prepositional phrase with min is to be delayed. But delayed from what? As for from the verb, it is granted; as for from the object, it is not granted. Even if we grant that its position is to be delayed from both the verb and the object, it is not impossible; rather it is permissible, just as it is permissible to say: "Struck the boy of the woman her father," and "The boy of the woman struck her father." Even if the position of the object is to be delayed, it is required here to front it because of the return of the pronoun in the subject, whose position is to precede. How then about the object, which together with the prepositional phrase is in one rank, I mean in being an adjunct, so it does not matter which of them you place before the other. The poet said:

"And the stars have stood still in the middle of the sky"

Here he fronted the adverbial phrase obligatorily, because of the return of the pronoun attached to the subject to the prepositional phrase with the adverb. It has been disputed whether this is forbidden to Muslims from the slaughter of Jews. From Malik: prohibition of eating the fat from their slaughter; it is also narrated from him that it is disliked. Some people permitted it from their slaughter, and from what they slaughter that is forbidden to them if a Muslim orders them to do so. Ibn Habib said: "What we know to be forbidden to them from our Book is not lawful to us from their slaughter, and what we know only from their sayings is not forbidden to us from their slaughter." End. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿The food of those given the Scripture is lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 5] is that the fat which is from their slaughter is not lawful to us, that it is not from their food, so it does not enter under the generality of ﴿the food of those﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 5]. Taking His words ﴿the food of those﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 5] to mean slaughtered animals is far-fetched and contrary to the apparent meaning.

﴿Except what their backs carry﴾, i.e., except the fat which the backs of the cattle and sheep carry. Ibn 'Abbas said: "It is what clings to the back of fat, and to the side inside their bellies." It was said: "It is the thick fat of the back, which are the layers of fat on the back, for that was not forbidden to them." al-Suddi and Abu Salih said: "The buttocks are what their backs carry."

﴿Or the entrails (al-hawaya)﴾ is coordinated with ("their backs"), as said al-Kisa'i, and this is the apparent meaning, i.e., and the fat which the entrails carry. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Qatada, Mujahid, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: "They are the intestines (mabari')." 'Ali ibn 'Isa said: "It is whatever the belly contains, gathered and rounded." Ibn Zayd also said: "They are the intestines (bana al-laban)." It was said: "The intestines and the viscera upon which there is fat."

﴿Or what is mixed with bone﴾ is coordinated with ﴿what their backs carry﴾, "with bone" meaning the fat of the buttock, because it is at the coccyx, as said al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj; or the fat of the side; or every fat in the legs, the side, the head, the eyes and the ears, as said Ibn Jurayj also; or the marrow of the bone. The apparent meaning is that these three are excepted from the fat, so they are lawful to them. It was said: "With what is forbidden, the omentum and the kidneys are removed." It was also said: "'Or the entrails or what is mixed with bone' is coordinated with His words ﴿their fat﴾, and thus it is included in the prohibition, i.e., We forbade them their fat ﴿or the entrails or what is mixed with bone﴾ except what their backs carry." Here 'or' is like it in His words ﴿So do not obey from them any sinner or disbeliever﴾ [al-Insan: 24], meaning the negation of what comes after it individually, as you say: "These people deserve to be disobeyed, so disobey this one or that one," meaning: "He forbade them this and this." al-Zamakhshari said: "'Or' has the same function in the saying: 'Sit with al-Hasan or Ibn Sirin.'" End. The grammarians said: "'Or' in this example is for permission, so it is permissible for him to sit with both of them together, or to sit with one of them." The better reading of the verse, if we say that this is coordinated with "their fat," is that 'or' here is for distinction, separating what was forbidden to them from cattle and sheep. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Some people said: ﴿or the entrails﴾ is coordinated with the fats. He said: 'According to this, the entrails enter into the prohibition,' and this is a view which neither the wording nor the meaning supports; rather both reject it." End. He did not explain how the wording and meaning reject this view.

﴿That We repaid them for their rebellion﴾. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "(That) is in the nominative position." al-Hawfi said: "(That) is in the nominative position by presuming an implied subject, its estimate being: 'The matter is that.' It is permissible that it be in the accusative governed by ﴿We repaid them﴾, since it takes two objects, and the estimate is: 'We repaid them that.'" Abu al-Baqa' said: "(That) is in the accusative position governed by ﴿We repaid them﴾," but he did not clarify on what basis it is accusative: is it as a verbal noun, or as an object of 'idh'? It was also said: "It is a subject, and the estimate is: 'We repaid them it.'" End. This is weak, due to the weakness of: "Zayd, I struck him." al-Zamakhshari said: "That is the reward ﴿We repaid them﴾, which is the forbidding of the good things." End. Its apparent meaning is that it is accusative in the manner of a verbal noun. Ibn Malik claimed that a demonstrative pronoun is not accusative when referring to a verbal noun unless it is followed by the verbal noun; you say: "I stood this standing, and I sat that sitting," and it is not permissible to say: "I stood this, nor I sat that." On this basis it is not correct that 'that' is accusative as a reference to a verbal noun. Here "rebellion" (al-baghy) means wrongdoing. al-Hasan said: "It means disbelief." Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: "It is their killing of the prophets without right, their taking of usury, and their eating of people's property falsely." Its parallel is ﴿Because of the wrongdoing of those who became Jews, We forbade﴾ [al-Nisa: 160]. This implies that this prohibition was a punishment for them for their sins and their disobedience to the prophets. The Qadi said: "The prohibition itself cannot be a punishment for a crime committed by them, because obligation is an exposure to reward, and exposure to reward is a benefit." The reply: the prohibition of benefit is possible for one who holds that reward is deserved, and it is possible that it is due to the earlier crime; each of these two is not improbable.

﴿And indeed We are truthful﴾ in reporting what ﴿We forbade them﴾. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is a statement that includes an implicit refutation of their lie in their saying: 'Allah did not forbid us anything, and we only follow Israel in what he forbade upon himself,' and it includes the rejection and refutation of their claim." al-Tibrizi said: "﴿And indeed We are truthful﴾ in completing their recompense in the Hereafter, which was promised as a threat, so the prohibition is an immediate recompense for them in this world, and for them in the Hereafter there is a great punishment." al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿And indeed We are truthful﴾ regarding what We threatened the disobedient with; We do not break it, just as We do not break what We promised to the people of obedience. So when they disobeyed and rebelled, We attached the threat to them and brought punishment upon them." End. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila (al-i'tizal, the rationalist school).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 145–146 (part 1 of 2):

The arrangement here is like the arrangement in al-Baqarah and al-Ma'idah. It was said: everything that has been prohibited is included in the exception, whether by the text of the Qur'an or a hadith from the Messenger ﷺ, by sharing in the cause, which is abomination. What we say is: the verse is Meccan and came after His saying ﴿eight pairs﴾ [al-An'am: 143], and the people of the Jahiliyyah used to forbid what they forbade of the bahirah, the sa'ibah, the wasilah and the hami, from these eight, so the verse is muhkam, and in it He informed that He did not find in what was revealed to him at that time from the Qur'an anything other than what He mentioned; for this reason the relative clause of ﴿ma﴾ came as a sentence headed by a past-tense verb. So everything that was prohibited in Medina had not, at that time, been preceded by revelation in Mecca, so there is no contradiction between what was prohibited in Medina and what was reported as having been revealed to him in Mecca as prohibited. The mention of swine, although it is not among the eight pairs, is because some people were eating it at that time, and because it is most similar to the eight pairs in not being a predatory beast that eats flesh and feeds on it; rather it is of the type of the eight, in that it lives on plants and grazes as the eight graze. The commentators mentioned here several matters on which the people of knowledge differed, and we summarize some of them. As for domestic donkeys, al-Sha'bi and Ibn Jubayr held that eating them is permitted, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ's prohibition of them was for a reason. As for horse meat, the early scholars differed concerning it, and al-Shafi'i, Ibn Hanbal, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan permitted it, while from Abu Hanifah there is disapproval. It was said: disapproval of tanzih (preference). It was said: disapproval of tahrim (prohibition), and this is the view of Malik, al-Awza'i, al-Hakam ibn 'Uyaynah, Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Bakr al-Asamm. Mujahid among the Successors held it, and Ibn 'Abbas among the Companions, though a contrary view is related from him. Qadi al-Qudat Shams al-Din Ahmad ibn Ibrahim ibn 'Abd al-Ghani al-Surujji al-Hanafi, may Allah have mercy on him, wrote a treatise on the ruling on horse meat, which we read to him. They agreed on the prohibition of mules. As for the wild donkey when it has become domesticated, Abu Hanifah and his companions, al-Hasan ibn Salih and al-Shafi'i held that eating it is permitted; Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik that when it has become tame and is used for work as the domestic donkey is, it is not eaten. Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf, Zufar and Muhammad said: it is not lawful to eat any animal with fangs among beasts of prey, or any bird with talons. Malik said: beasts of prey of the wild, or of the land, whether wild or domestic, are not eaten, nor the fox, nor the hyena; there is no harm in eating birds of prey such as the rakham, the eagle, the vulture and others, which eat carrion and that which does not eat. Al-Awza'i said: all birds are lawful, except that they dislike the rakham. Al-Shafi'i said: whatever attacks people with fangs, such as the lion, the wolf and the panther, and among birds whatever attacks with talons, such as the vulture and the falcon, is not eaten, while the fox and the hyena are eaten. Abu Hanifah disliked the spotted crow but not the field crow, and the disagreement concerning the kite is like the disagreement concerning the eagle and the vulture. Abu Hanifah disliked the lizard; Malik and al-Shafi'i said there is no harm in it. The majority hold that the domestic cat is not eaten, while from Malik there is permission to eat it, whether domestic or wild, and from some of the early scholars permission to eat the domestic. Ibn Abi Layla said: there is no harm in eating a snake if it is slaughtered. Al-Layth said: there is no harm in eating the hedgehog, bee larvae, cheese worms, date worms and the like; likewise Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik concerning the hedgehog. Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i said: the mouse is not eaten. Abu Hanifah said: the jerboa is not eaten; al-Shafi'i said it is eaten. From Malik there is prohibition, disapproval and permission concerning the mouse. Abu Hanifah, al-Shafi'i and their companions held that eating the jallalah (an animal that feeds on filth) is disapproved. Malik and al-Layth said: there is no harm in eating it. The author of al-Tahrir wa al-Tahbir said: as for intoxicating drugs such as henbane, the sikran, the lufah and cannabis leaves called hashish, the people of knowledge did not explicitly state their prohibition, and in my view prohibition is closer, because if they are intoxicating they are prohibited by his ﷺ saying: "Whatever in large quantity intoxicates, a small quantity of it is forbidden," and by his saying: "Every intoxicant is forbidden"; and if they are not intoxicating, then bringing harm upon the body is forbidden. Ibn Bakhtishu' related in his book that cannabis leaves cause seventy diseases in the body, and he mentioned among them that it yellows the skin, blackens the teeth and creates pits in them, pierces the liver and heats it, corrupts the intellect, weakens the sight, causes sorrow and removes courage; henbane and the sikran are like cannabis leaves in harm. As for sedatives such as saffron and mandrake, the harmful quantity of them is forbidden; most physicians said: when a great quantity of saffron is used it kills by exhilaration. End, with some abridgment. Abu Bakr al-Razi said concerning His saying ﴿an eater who would eat it﴾ that it indicates that what is forbidden from carrion is that which can be eaten, and it does not include hide that has been tanned, nor horn, nor bone, nor hoof, nor feathers and the like; and concerning His saying ﴿or flowing blood﴾ that it indicates that the blood of gnats, fleas and flies is not impure. End.

﴿Or a transgression﴾: the apparent reading is that it is coordinated with the accusative before it. That which was invoked over with other than Allah's name is called a transgression because it goes deep into the category of transgression; from this is His saying ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned, for indeed it is transgression﴾ [al-An'am: 121]. ﴿Invoked over﴾ is an attribute of it in the accusative position. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that ﴿transgression﴾ be in the accusative as an object of purpose, placed before its governing verb, which is ﴿invoked over﴾, citing the line: "I was moved, and not from longing for fair women is my being moved." He separated between ﴿aw﴾ and ﴿invoked over﴾ with the object of purpose, and ﴿aw invoked over﴾ would be coordinated with ﴿yakun﴾, and the pronoun in ﴿bihi﴾ refers to what it refers to in ﴿yakun﴾. This is a very forced parsing, and a construction on this parsing is outside eloquence, and it is not permissible on the recitation of one who recited ﴿an yakuna maytatun﴾ with the nominative, for then the pronoun in ﴿bihi﴾ would have nothing to refer to, and it is not permissible to posit an elided noun so that the pronoun refers to it, the estimate being: "or a thing ﴿invoked over with other than Allah's name﴾," for such a thing is permitted only in poetic necessity.

﴿But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor exceeding, then indeed your Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ The explanation of the like of this has preceded. Since the beginning of the verse opened with His address to him, saying ﴿Say: I do not find﴾, He concluded the verse with address, saying ﴿then indeed your Lord﴾, indicating His care for him by honouring His address at its opening and its closing.

And to those who became Jews We forbade every animal with claws. The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that, when Allah showed that prohibition derives from divine revelation, He informed that He had forbidden certain things to some of the earlier nations, just as He had forbidden things to the people of this religion, which He mentioned in the previous verse. So prohibition is attributed to Allah, the Exalted, among all nations. In His words ﴿We forbade﴾ there is a refutation of the Jews' claim that Allah had not forbidden anything to them, and that they had forbidden only what Israel (Ya'qub) had forbidden upon himself. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, Qatada and al-Suddi said: "It refers to animals with cloven hooves, such as camels and ostriches, and those without separated fingers, such as ducks, geese and the like." Al-Zajjaj chose this view. Ibn Zayd said: "It refers only to camels," but this specification has been deemed weak. al-Dahhak said: "It refers to the ostrich and the wild ass," and this is weak because it restricts the meaning. al-Kalbi said: "Every animal with a talon among birds, every solid-hoofed animal among quadrupeds, and every animal with a fang among predators." al-Qutabi said: "Here the word 'claw' (zufr) is in the position of 'hoof'; it includes every solid-hoofed quadruped, and the hoof was called a claw figuratively." Tha'lab said: "Everything that does not hunt is clawed, and what hunts is talon-bearing." al-Naqqash said: "This is not consistent, for the lion is clawed." al-Zamakhshari said: "Anything that has a digit (uṣbu') among quadrupeds or birds. Some of the clawed animals had been lawful to them, but when they committed wrongdoing, these were forbidden to them, so the prohibition covered every clawed animal, as proven by His words: ﴿Because of the wrongdoing of those who became Jews, We forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them﴾ [al-Nisa: 160]." Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: "Taking 'claw' to mean 'hoof' is weak, because a hoof is hardly called a claw, and because if it were so, it would have said: 'He forbade them every animal that has a hoof,' and that is false, since the verse indicates the permissibility of cattle and sheep, although they have hooves. Therefore 'claw' must be taken to mean talons and claws, since talons are the instruments by which hunting beasts catch prey. This includes types of predators, dogs, cats and hunting birds. This is specific to the Jews, because ﴿to those who became Jews﴾ indicates restriction, so the prohibition is specific to the Jews and is not forbidden to Muslims. What is narrated about the prohibition of fanged predators and talon-bearing birds is weak, because it is a single report (khabar wahid) contrary to the Book of Allah, so it is not accepted. This supports the madhhab (school) of Malik." Summarized, the end. In this there are several points: First, we do not accept the restriction of 'clawed' to what he said. Second, we do not accept the restriction he claimed. Third, we do not accept the exclusivity. Fourth, we do not accept that the single report about forbidding fanged animals and talon-bearing birds is contrary to the Book of Allah. Everyone who interpreted "claw" as those earlier opinions did holds that the meat, fat and everything else from what he interpreted is forbidden. Some exegetes held that this is by omission of a word (elision of a modifier), and that what is forbidden is not the clawed animal itself but what the clawed animal catches, i.e., the talon-bearing animal that was not trained. This goes against the apparent meaning. Ubayy, al-Hasan and al-'A'raj read (ẓafrun) with a sukun on the fa'. Al-Hasan and Abu al-Sammal Qa'nab also read it with sukun on the fa' and a kasra on the ẓa'.

﴿And of cattle and sheep We forbade them their fat﴾, i.e., the fat of both kinds. The phrase "min" is connected to the later "We forbade" (ḥarramnā), and it is not necessary for it to precede its governing verb. If the construction were: "And We forbade them from cattle and sheep their fat," it would be a strange construction, just as you say: "From Zayd I took his property," and it is permissible to say: "I took from Zayd his property." The idafa (construction) indicates emphasis of specification and connection, for if the statement were: "Of cattle and sheep We forbade them the fats," it would be sufficient to indicate that only the fat of cattle and sheep is meant. It is possible that ﴿And of cattle and sheep﴾ is coordinated with ﴿every clawed animal﴾, so that min is connected to the first "We forbade," and then the second clause came explaining what was vague in the partitive "min" concerning what was forbidden, so He said: ﴿We forbade them their fat﴾. Abu al-Baqa' said: "It is not permissible that (of cattle) be connected to the second 'We forbade'; rather it is coordinated with 'every,' and ('We forbade them') is an explanation of what is forbidden from cattle and sheep." It seems to imply that the return of the pronoun prevents the connection, since the position of a prepositional phrase with min is to be delayed. But delayed from what? As for from the verb, it is granted; as for from the object, it is not granted. Even if we grant that its position is to be delayed from both the verb and the object, it is not impossible; rather it is permissible, just as it is permissible to say: "Struck the boy of the woman her father," and "The boy of the woman struck her father." Even if the position of the object is to be delayed, it is required here to front it because of the return of the pronoun in the subject, whose position is to precede. How then about the object, which together with the prepositional phrase is in one rank, I mean in being an adjunct, so it does not matter which of them you place before the other. The poet said:

"And the stars have stood still in the middle of the sky"

Here he fronted the adverbial phrase obligatorily, because of the return of the pronoun attached to the subject to the prepositional phrase with the adverb. It has been disputed whether this is forbidden to Muslims from the slaughter of Jews. From Malik: prohibition of eating the fat from their slaughter; it is also narrated from him that it is disliked. Some people permitted it from their slaughter, and from what they slaughter that is forbidden to them if a Muslim orders them to do so. Ibn Habib said: "What we know to be forbidden to them from our Book is not lawful to us from their slaughter, and what we know only from their sayings is not forbidden to us from their slaughter." End. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿The food of those given the Scripture is lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 5] is that the fat which is from their slaughter is not lawful to us, that it is not from their food, so it does not enter under the generality of ﴿the food of those﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 5]. Taking His words ﴿the food of those﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 5] to mean slaughtered animals is far-fetched and contrary to the apparent meaning.

﴿Except what their backs carry﴾, i.e., except the fat which the backs of the cattle and sheep carry. Ibn 'Abbas said: "It is what clings to the back of fat, and to the side inside their bellies." It was said: "It is the thick fat of the back, which are the layers of fat on the back, for that was not forbidden to them." al-Suddi and Abu Salih said: "The buttocks are what their backs carry."

﴿Or the entrails (al-hawaya)﴾ is coordinated with ("their backs"), as said al-Kisa'i, and this is the apparent meaning, i.e., and the fat which the entrails carry. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Qatada, Mujahid, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: "They are the intestines (mabari')." 'Ali ibn 'Isa said: "It is whatever the belly contains, gathered and rounded." Ibn Zayd also said: "They are the intestines (bana al-laban)." It was said: "The intestines and the viscera upon which there is fat."

﴿Or what is mixed with bone﴾ is coordinated with ﴿what their backs carry﴾, "with bone" meaning the fat of the buttock, because it is at the coccyx, as said al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj; or the fat of the side; or every fat in the legs, the side, the head, the eyes and the ears, as said Ibn Jurayj also; or the marrow of the bone. The apparent meaning is that these three are excepted from the fat, so they are lawful to them. It was said: "With what is forbidden, the omentum and the kidneys are removed." It was also said: "'Or the entrails or what is mixed with bone' is coordinated with His words ﴿their fat﴾, and thus it is included in the prohibition, i.e., We forbade them their fat ﴿or the entrails or what is mixed with bone﴾ except what their backs carry." Here 'or' is like it in His words ﴿So do not obey from them any sinner or disbeliever﴾ [al-Insan: 24], meaning the negation of what comes after it individually, as you say: "These people deserve to be disobeyed, so disobey this one or that one," meaning: "He forbade them this and this." al-Zamakhshari said: "'Or' has the same function in the saying: 'Sit with al-Hasan or Ibn Sirin.'" End. The grammarians said: "'Or' in this example is for permission, so it is permissible for him to sit with both of them together, or to sit with one of them." The better reading of the verse, if we say that this is coordinated with "their fat," is that 'or' here is for distinction, separating what was forbidden to them from cattle and sheep. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Some people said: ﴿or the entrails﴾ is coordinated with the fats. He said: 'According to this, the entrails enter into the prohibition,' and this is a view which neither the wording nor the meaning supports; rather both reject it." End. He did not explain how the wording and meaning reject this view.

﴿That We repaid them for their rebellion﴾. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "(That) is in the nominative position." al-Hawfi said: "(That) is in the nominative position by presuming an implied subject, its estimate being: 'The matter is that.' It is permissible that it be in the accusative governed by ﴿We repaid them﴾, since it takes two objects, and the estimate is: 'We repaid them that.'" Abu al-Baqa' said: "(That) is in the accusative position governed by ﴿We repaid them﴾," but he did not clarify on what basis it is accusative: is it as a verbal noun, or as an object of 'idh'? It was also said: "It is a subject, and the estimate is: 'We repaid them it.'" End. This is weak, due to the weakness of: "Zayd, I struck him." al-Zamakhshari said: "That is the reward ﴿We repaid them﴾, which is the forbidding of the good things." End. Its apparent meaning is that it is accusative in the manner of a verbal noun. Ibn Malik claimed that a demonstrative pronoun is not accusative when referring to a verbal noun unless it is followed by the verbal noun; you say: "I stood this standing, and I sat that sitting," and it is not permissible to say: "I stood this, nor I sat that." On this basis it is not correct that 'that' is accusative as a reference to a verbal noun. Here "rebellion" (al-baghy) means wrongdoing. al-Hasan said: "It means disbelief." Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: "It is their killing of the prophets without right, their taking of usury, and their eating of people's property falsely." Its parallel is ﴿Because of the wrongdoing of those who became Jews, We forbade﴾ [al-Nisa: 160]. This implies that this prohibition was a punishment for them for their sins and their disobedience to the prophets. The Qadi said: "The prohibition itself cannot be a punishment for a crime committed by them, because obligation is an exposure to reward, and exposure to reward is a benefit." The reply: the prohibition of benefit is possible for one who holds that reward is deserved, and it is possible that it is due to the earlier crime; each of these two is not improbable.

﴿And indeed We are truthful﴾ in reporting what ﴿We forbade them﴾. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is a statement that includes an implicit refutation of their lie in their saying: 'Allah did not forbid us anything, and we only follow Israel in what he forbade upon himself,' and it includes the rejection and refutation of their claim." al-Tibrizi said: "﴿And indeed We are truthful﴾ in completing their recompense in the Hereafter, which was promised as a threat, so the prohibition is an immediate recompense for them in this world, and for them in the Hereafter there is a great punishment." al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿And indeed We are truthful﴾ regarding what We threatened the disobedient with; We do not break it, just as We do not break what We promised to the people of obedience. So when they disobeyed and rebelled, We attached the threat to them and brought punishment upon them." End. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila (al-i'tizal, the rationalist school).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 147–149 (part 1 of 2):

﴿So if they deny you, say: "Your Lord is of boundless mercy, yet His punishment is never averted from the guilty people."﴾ The apparent reading is that the pronoun refers to the nearest previous mention, which is the Jews. This is also the view of Mujahid and al-Suddi. The meaning is: ﴿if they deny you﴾ regarding what you have told them, that God forbade it to them, and they say: "God did not forbid it; Israel (Isra'il) forbade it before." This is said in wonder at their statement and as a magnification of their fabrication, although they know what you have said. ﴿Say: "Your Lord is of boundless mercy"﴾ in that He did not hasten the punishment upon you despite the severity of this crime. This is like when you say, on seeing a great act of disobedience: "How forbearing God is!" while you mean that He grants the disobedient person respite. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the polytheists, with whom the discourse was addressed in His words ﴿Tell me﴾ [al-An'am 6:143] and ﴿Or were you witnesses﴾ [al-An'am 6:144]. The meaning is: ﴿if they deny you﴾ concerning prophethood, messengership, and conveying God's rulings. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿if they deny you﴾ in that, and they claim that God is abundant in forgiveness, that He will not hold us to account for transgression, and that He breaks His threat out of generosity and bounty. So say to them: ﴿your Lord is of boundless mercy﴾ toward the people of His obedience, ﴿yet His punishment is never averted﴾ despite the vastness of His mercy ﴿from the guilty people﴾. So do not be deceived by hope in His mercy, neglecting fear of His retribution. End of quotation. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school). The phrase ﴿the guilty people﴾ is general, encompassing those who deny the messengers and others among the guilty. It is possible that it is an instance of placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun, meaning: ﴿His punishment is never averted﴾ from you. The first complement of "say" (qul) is a nominal sentence, because it is more emphatic in announcement than a verbal sentence. Thus it fits the emphasis on God with "boundless mercy." The second clause is verbal and not nominal; otherwise the structure would be "and possessor of punishment," so that the two descriptions would not be balanced in the announcement. The domain of mercy is broad, so there is no balance. Al-Maturidi said: ﴿if they deny you﴾ in what you call them to of affirmation and monotheism, ﴿say: "Your Lord is of boundless mercy"﴾ if you return from denial. End of quotation. It has also been said: ﴿of mercy﴾ means He does not destroy anyone at the time of disobedience, but He delays, ﴿yet His punishment is never averted﴾ when it descends.

﴿The ones who associated partners with God will say: "Had God willed, we would not have associated, nor would our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything."﴾ This is a report about the future, and it has occurred. It contains a report of the unseen, a miracle for the Messenger, so it happened as God had announced. This statement from them came when their argument had collapsed and the refutation against them was established. They shifted to a true matter, which is that if God had willed that none of this occur, it would not have occurred. They presented this by way of referring the matter to the divine will and the decrees, as deceptive evasion, turning away from the truth, and heresy, not as sound belief. They also said it as sound belief when they committed those acts, clinging to the claim that what God wills is what happens, as one who falls into disobedience says when its reason is explained to him: "This is God's decree; there is no escape from God's decree." Or they said it, and it is true, as an argument for those acts, meaning: had God not willed what we are upon, it would not have occurred, and He would have prevented it between us and it. Al-Zamakhshari said: they mean by their disbelief and rebellion that their polytheism, the polytheism of their fathers, and their forbidding what God permitted, are by God's will and desire; had it not been for His will, none of that would have existed, in the manner of the doctrine of the Mujbira (the determinists) exactly. End of quotation. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila. Al-Maturidi said: the will may be taken to mean approval, or to mean command and summons, since they said: God commanded us to that. It is also possible they said it mockingly and sarcastically. End of quotation. The Mu'tazila have no basis in this verse given these possibilities. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The Mu'tazila have attached themselves to this verse, saying: God has censured this statement of theirs, and He censured it only because their disbelief is not by God's will; rather He created it for them. He said: The matter is not as they said. God censured the polytheists' assumption that what God wills does not incur punishment. As for His censuring their saying "Had it not been for the will, we would not have disbelieved," that is not the case. End of quotation. ﴿Those who associated partners﴾ refers either to the polytheists of Quraysh or to the polytheists of the Arabs; there are two views. ﴿Nor our fathers﴾ is coordinated with the raised pronoun in "associated." The separation by "lā" between the conjunction particle and the conjoined element suffices in place of separation between the two conjoined items by a separate pronoun that follows the attached pronoun, or by something else. According to this, the view of the Basran grammarians is that they do not permit this without separation except in poetry, while the view of the Kufan grammarians is that it is permitted and eloquent in speech. In surah al-Nahl it occurs: ﴿Those who associated said: "Had God willed, we would not have worshipped anything apart from Him, neither we nor our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything apart from Him"﴾ [al-Nahl 16:35]. There He says "apart from Him" twice, and He says "we," thereby emphasizing the pronoun, because the word "worship" can be attributed to the singling out of God in it. This is not objectionable; what is objectionable is worshipping something other than God or something alongside God. So here it is fitting to mention "apart from Him" with worship. As for the wording ﴿we did not associate﴾, association indicates affirming a partner, so the phrase "apart from Him" does not combine with this verb. Had the wording outside the Qur'an been "we did not associate apart from Him," its meaning would not be sound. As for the second "apart from Him," association indicates forbidding some things and permitting some things, so it did not need the phrase "apart from Him." As for the word "worship," it does not indicate the forbidding of anything in the way that the word "associated" does, so it is restricted by His saying "apart from Him." Since "apart from Him" was omitted here, it was fitting that "we" be omitted too, so that the structure is consistent in brevity.

﴿Thus did those before them deny, until they tasted Our punishment.﴾ That is: like this denial referred to in His words ﴿if they deny you﴾, the earlier nations also denied. So the object of the denial is other than their saying ﴿Had God willed, we would not have associated﴾, etc. That is, with a similar doubt, their supposition that God's leaving them is evidence of His approval of their state. The phrase ﴿until they tasted Our punishment﴾ is the limit for the extension of denial up to the time of punishment, because when punishment arrives no denial remains. The Mu'tazila made the denial refer back to His words ﴿Had God willed﴾ [al-An'am 6:137], the clause that is reported by the saying, and they said: God denied them in their statement. The reading of some irregular readings supports this: "kadhaba" (he lied). Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, they brought absolute denial, because God, mighty and majestic, placed in the intellects and sent down in the books what indicates His self-sufficiency and His freedom from willing abominations and desiring them. The messengers reported this. So whoever attributes all forms of abomination, such as disbelief and sins, to God's will and desire has denied entirely, and that is a denial of God, His books, and His messengers, and has thrown the proofs of reason and revelation behind his back. End of quotation. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila.

﴿Say: "Do you have any knowledge that you can bring forth to us? You follow only conjecture, and you are merely guessing."﴾ This is an interrogation in the sense of mockery toward them, and it is a denial: that is, you do not have any knowledge by which you argue, which you could bring forth to us. In your claims you follow only false, corrupt conjecture, and you are merely lying, or estimating and guessing. An-Nakha'i and Ibn Wathhab read ﴿they follow﴾ with the letter ya'. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is an irregular reading (shadh), which the phrase ﴿you are merely﴾ weakens, because it would be a case of iltifat (a shift in grammatical person).

﴿Say: "Then God possesses the conclusive proof. Had He willed, He would have guided you all."﴾ Between "say" and the particle "fa" there is an omitted element, which al-Zamakhshari estimated as: "If the matter is as you claim, that what you are upon is by God's will, then God possesses the conclusive proof against you and against the refutation of your doctrine. ﴿Had He willed, He would have guided you all﴾ among you and among your opponents, for your attributing your religion to God's will requires that you also attribute the religion of those who oppose you to His will, so that you should be loyal to them rather than hostile, respect them rather than oppose them, because will combines what you are upon and what they are upon." End of quotation. This is an interpretation of the verse according to what was previously established in the preceding verses of the Mu'tazila doctrine. What al-Zamakhshari estimated as a conditional omitted element, with ﴿then God possesses the conclusive proof﴾ as its answer, is far-fetched. ﴿Say: "Bring forth your witnesses who testify that Allah has forbidden this. Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 147–149 (part 1 of 2):

﴿So if they deny you, say: "Your Lord is of boundless mercy, yet His punishment is never averted from the guilty people."﴾ The apparent reading is that the pronoun refers to the nearest previous mention, which is the Jews. This is said in wonder at their statement and as a magnification of their fabrication, although they know what you have said. ﴿Say: "Your Lord is of boundless mercy"﴾ in that He did not hasten the punishment upon you despite the severity of this crime. This is like when you say, on seeing a great act of disobedience: "How forbearing God is!" while you mean that He grants the disobedient person respite. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the polytheists, with whom the discourse was addressed in His words ﴿Tell me﴾ [al-An'am 6:143] and ﴿Or were you witnesses﴾ [al-An'am 6:144]. The meaning is: ﴿if they deny you﴾ concerning prophethood, messengership, and conveying God's rulings. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿if they deny you﴾ in that, and they claim that God is abundant in forgiveness, that He will not hold us to account for transgression, and that He breaks His threat out of generosity and bounty. The phrase ﴿the guilty people﴾ is general, encompassing those who deny the messengers and others among the guilty. The domain of mercy is broad, so there is no balance. Al-Maturidi said: ﴿if they deny you﴾ in what you call them to of affirmation and monotheism, ﴿say: "Your Lord is of boundless mercy"﴾ if you return from denial. End of quotation. It has also been said: ﴿of mercy﴾ means He does not destroy anyone at the time of disobedience, but He delays, ﴿yet His punishment is never averted﴾ when it descends.

Al-Zamakhshari said: they mean by their disbelief and rebellion that their polytheism, the polytheism of their fathers, and their forbidding what God permitted, are by God's will and desire; had it not been for His will, none of that would have existed, in the manner of the doctrine of the Mujbira (the determinists) exactly. End of quotation. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila. Al-Maturidi said: the will may be taken to mean approval, or to mean command and summons, since they said: God commanded us to that. It is also possible they said it mockingly and sarcastically. End of quotation. The Mu'tazila have no basis in this verse given these possibilities. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The Mu'tazila have attached themselves to this verse, saying: God has censured this statement of theirs, and He censured it only because their disbelief is not by God's will; rather He created it for them. He said: The matter is not as they said. God censured the polytheists' assumption that what God wills does not incur punishment. Abu Nasr al-Qushayri said: ﴿the conclusive proof﴾ is the clarification of monotheism and the messengers' display of miracles, so He obligated every responsible person to His command. As for His knowledge and will, they are unseen, which no servant can perceive. It is sufficient for the obligation that the servant, if he wished to do what he was commanded, would be enabled to do it; and what is contrary to what is known is possible, so it is not joined to what is impossible in itself. End of quotation. There is something to examine at the end of his statement. Al-Kirmani said: ﴿Had He willed, He would have guided you﴾ with the guidance of compulsion and constraint. End of quotation. This is a Mu'tazili tendency. Abu Nasr ibn al-Qushayri said: This is an explicit statement that disbelief occurs by God's will, exalted is He. Al-Baghawi said: This indicates that He did not will the faith of the disbeliever.
