End of quotation. This is a Mu'tazili tendency. Abu Nasr ibn al-Qushayri said: This is an explicit statement that disbelief occurs by God's will, exalted is He. Al-Baghawi said: This indicates that He did not will the faith of the disbeliever.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah al-An'am 6:147-149 (part 2 of 2)

﴿Say: "Bring forth your witnesses who testify that Allah has forbidden this. And if they testify, do not testify with them."﴾ [al-An'am: 150] He (Allah, exalted is He) exposed their lying against Allah and their fabrication in the prohibition of what they had forbidden while attributing it to Allah, exalted is He. So He said: ﴿Inform me with knowledge﴾ [al-An'am: 143], and He said: ﴿Or were you witnesses﴾ [al-An'am: 144]. When these two possibilities were ruled out, He moved to a possibility other than these two, namely that they summon from among themselves someone who would testify for them that Allah had forbidden what they forbade. Here, (hallumma) is in the dialect of the Hijaz (hulumma, "bring"), and it is transitive, which is why the object after it is in the accusative. That is: bring your witnesses and bring them near. The attribution of "witnesses" to them indicates that these are other than themselves. This is a command in the manner of ta'jiz (challenge to incapacitate), meaning: there is no one who would testify to this as a true testimony, because it is a false claim. For this reason He said: ﴿And if they testify, do not testify with them﴾ [al-An'am: 150], that is: if it is supposed that they testify, then do not testify with them, meaning do not agree with them, because they are liars in their testimony, just as the witnesses for them are liars in their claim. He attributed the witnesses to them, that is, those whom you have prepared as witnesses for you according to what your souls desire. For this reason He described them as ﴿who testify﴾ [al-An'am: 150], meaning: they are believers in testifying for them and in supporting their false claims. Had it been said (hallumma) shuhadaa' (witnesses) in the indefinite form, the meaning that the attribution and the description require would have been lost, since the meaning would become "bring people who testify to the prohibition of that," and the apparent sense would be a request for witnesses of truth, which contradicts the meaning of the verse. Al-Hasan said: "Bring your witnesses from among yourselves." He said: "And you will not find any." Even if they were present, their testimony would not be accepted, because it is false. Ibn 'Atiyya said: If someone fabricates and forges a testimony or reports about prophethood, then you avoid that and do not testify with them. In His saying ﴿so do not testify with them﴾ [al-An'am: 150] there is an emphasis on describing their testimony as utterly false. Abu Nasr al-Qushayri said: If some of them testify for others, it is not accepted, since testimony must be from a Book or upon the tongue of a Prophet, and they have nothing of that. Al-Zamakhshari said: He commanded them to bring their witnesses, though they are witnesses of falsehood, in order to put the proof upon them, to silence them, and to show to those for whom they testify, through the cutting off of the witnesses, that they are not upon anything, since the feet of the witnesses and of those for whom they testify are equal, in that they both return to what can validly be relied upon. His saying ﴿so do not testify with them﴾ [al-An'am: 150] means: do not accept for them what they testified to, and do not confirm them; for if you accept it for them, it is as if you testified with them with a testimony like theirs, and so you would be one of them. End of quote. And this is an exaggeration.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 150:

﴿And do not follow the desires of those who denied Our signs and those who do not believe in the Hereafter, while they ascribe equals to their Lord.﴾ The apparent reading of the conjunction (al-'atf) is that it indicates a difference in the essences (al-dhawat), and ﴿those who denied Our signs﴾ encompasses all who denied the Messenger, even if they affirm the Hereafter, such as the People of the Book.

﴿And those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ is a category of those who denied the signs, and they are the worshippers of idols and those who set up equals (al-'adilun) to their Lord, where 'adil means an equal, that is, they set the idols alongside Him in worship and divinity. It is possible that the conjunction is of differing attributes while the described entity is one, and this is the view of most people; and it appears to be the choice of al-Zamakhshari, for he said: ﴿Do not follow the desires of those who denied Our signs﴾ is a placing of the apparent in the place of the pronoun, to indicate that whoever denies the signs of Allah and sets up others as equal to Him is a follower of desire and nothing else, because if he had followed the proof, he would not have been anything but one who affirms the signs and professes the oneness of Allah. Al-Naqqash said: it was revealed concerning the Dahriyya (materialist naturalists) among the zanadiqa (heretics).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 151–152 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Say, "Come, I will recite to you what your Lord has forbidden you."﴾ When Allah the Exalted mentioned what they had forbidden, fabricating against Him, and then mentioned what He, the Exalted, had permitted them from among the grains, fruits and livestock, He mentioned what He, the Exalted, had forbidden them of things He prohibited them from, and what He had made obligatory upon them of things He commanded them to do. The explanation of ﴿come﴾ has already passed in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿to a common word﴾ [Al 'Imran: 64]. The address in "Say" is to the Messenger, and in "come" it is said to be addressed to the polytheists; it is also said to be addressed to those present with the Messenger, from among believers, People of the Book and polytheists. The context of the verses indicates that it is addressed to the polytheists, although the ruling for others in this regard is the same as theirs. Allah the Exalted commanded him to call all creation to hear what Allah has forbidden, by the law of Islam with which he was sent to the black and the red alike. "Recite" (atlu) means: I narrate and relate, from recitation, which is the following of some letters by others. Ka'b al-Ahbar said: these verses are the opening of the Torah, "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Say: Come, I will recite to you what your Lord has forbidden you: that you associate nothing with Him, and be good to parents﴾" up to the end of the verse. Ibn 'Abbas said: these verses are the muhkamat (clear verses) which Allah mentioned in Surat Al 'Imran; the laws of all creation have agreed upon them, and they have never been abrogated in any religion. It has also been said that they are the Ten Words revealed to Musa, peace be upon him. "Ma" is in the sense of "alladhi" (that which) and is the object of "atlu," i.e., I recite that which your Lord has forbidden you. It has been said that it is verbal (masdariyya), i.e., the prohibition of your Lord. It has been said that it is interrogative, governed by "harrama," i.e., what thing your Lord has forbidden; and this would make "atlu" suspended, but this is weak because "atlu" is not one of the verbs of the heart, so there is no suspension. ﴿Upon you﴾ is connected to "harrama," not to "atlu," so it is from the application of the second (of two verbs). Ibn al-Shajari said: if you connect it to "atlu," it is good, because it is closer, and this is the view of the Kufans. So the estimate is: I recite upon you that which your Lord has forbidden.
* *
﴿That you associate nothing with Him, and [show] kindness to parents﴾. The apparent reading is that "an" is explanatory and "la" is prohibitive, because "atlu" is a verb meaning "to say," and what follows "an" is a clause. Thus "an" combines the two conditions of the explanatory particle: that a verb of saying precede it, and that a clause follow it. This differs from "ay," which is an explanatory particle that may be preceded by a single word or a clause containing a sense of saying or otherwise, and followed by a single word or a clause. Taking it as explanatory is the view of al-Zamakhshari. (If you say): if you make "an" explanatory of the verb of reciting, which is connected to ﴿what your Lord has forbidden﴾, then everything after it must be forbidden, like shirk, and what follows it that has the particle of prohibition, so what is to be done with the commands? (I say): since these commands came together with the prohibitions, and all were preceded by the verb of prohibition, and they share in falling under its ruling, it is known that the prohibition refers to their opposites, which are: pointing to parents, cheating in measure and weight, abandoning justice in speech, and breaking the covenant of Allah. End. That these things share in falling under the ruling of prohibition, and that the prohibition refers to the opposites of the commands, is very remote and a riddle of meanings, and there is no necessity to call for this. As for the conjunction of these commands, it admits two possibilities. One is that they are conjoined to the prohibitions before them, so the prohibition must extend over them, since they are within the scope of the explanatory "an." Rather, they are conjoined to His saying: ﴿Come, I will recite what He has forbidden﴾: He first commanded them with a command whose content is then recounted, and then commanded them again with commands. This is a clear meaning. The second is that the commands are conjoined to the prohibitions and fall under the explanatory "an," and this is valid on the assumption of an omitted element, of which "an" is the explanation, both for it and for the stated matter before it, which its omission indicates. The estimate is: "and what He commanded you with," so "and what He commanded you with" was omitted, indicated by "what He forbade," because the meaning of ﴿what your Lord has forbidden you﴾ is what your Lord has forbidden you from. So the meaning is: "Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has prohibited you from." When the estimate is thus, it is valid for "an" to be explanatory of the verb of prohibition indicated by the prohibition and the omitted verb of command. Do you not see that you may say: "I commanded you not to honour an ignorant man, and to honour a learned man," since it is permissible to conjoin a command to a prohibition and a prohibition to a command, as Imru' al-Qays said:
"They say: Do not perish of grief, and be patient."
We know of no disagreement on this, unlike the mutually divergent clauses of statement, interrogation and imperative, where there is disagreement on conjunction. They have allowed "an" to be masdariyya rather than explanatory, in a position of nominative and in a position of accusative. As for the nominative, it is by presupposing a subject indicated by the meaning, the estimate being: "the recited is (that you do not associate)." As for the accusative, it is in several ways. One: that it is governed by "ʿalaykum," and it is an incitement (idghra'), and the speech is complete at "I recite what your Lord has forbidden you," i.e., hold fast to the absence of association; this is remote because it disconnects speech from its apparent sense. Two: that it is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), i.e., "I recite what your Lord has forbidden you" (that you do not associate). This is remote because what follows it is a command conjoined with a waw, and its prohibition is conjoined with a waw, so it does not fit that it should be an explanation of what was forbidden; as for the commands, it is in terms of meaning, and as for the prohibitions, it is in terms of conjunction. Three: that it is an object of an omitted verb, its estimate: "I enjoin upon you that you do not associate," because His saying ﴿and [show] kindness to parents﴾ is carried upon "I enjoin upon you," ﴿and [show] kindness to parents﴾; this is remote because omission is contrary to the original. These three aspects keep "la" in its original negative sense, and it is intended. Four: that it is in a position of accusative as a substitute for ﴿what He forbade﴾ or for the omitted pronoun in ﴿what He forbade﴾, its estimate being "what He forbade it." These two aspects have "la" as superfluous, as it is in His saying: "What prevented you from not prostrating when I commanded you?" This is weak, because the generality of the forbidden is confined to shirk, since what follows of commands is not included in the forbidden, and after a command there cannot be claimed a superfluous "la" in it, since "an la" in it is evident as prohibitive. Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you say): why did you not say that it is the one that governs the verb in the subjunctive, and make "that you do not associate" a substitute for ﴿what He forbade﴾? (I say): it is necessary that "do not associate," "do not approach," "do not kill," and "do not follow the ways" be prohibitions, because the commands are conjoined to them, namely His saying: ﴿and [show] kindness to parents﴾; for the estimate is: "and be good," ﴿and [show] kindness to parents﴾, "and fulfil," "and when you speak, be just," "and fulfil the covenant of Allah." End. It is not required that all commands be conjoined to all that "la" governs, for we have shown the permissibility of conjoining ﴿and [show] kindness to parents﴾ to "come," and what follows it is conjoined to it, and ﴿and [show] kindness to parents﴾ need not be conjoined to "that you associate." "That you do not associate" includes whoever associates with Allah idols, like the people of Ibrahim, and whoever associates with Allah jinn, and whoever associates with Allah sons and daughters. Ibn al-Jawzi said: it has been said: claiming a partner for Allah. It has been said: obeying other than Allah in disobedience to Allah. The explanation of ﴿and [show] kindness to parents﴾ has passed in Surat al-Baqara.
* *
﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty; We provide for you and for them﴾: "min" here is causal, i.e., "for fear of poverty," in accordance with His saying: ﴿for fear of poverty﴾ [al-Isra: 31]. Killing a child is forbidden except by right. This cause was mentioned because it was the reason for killing children among them. Allah the Exalted explained that He is the Provider for them and for their children, and if He is the Provider, then just as you do not kill yourself, so do not kill your child. When He commanded kindness to parents, He forbade harm to children, and He drew attention to the greatest harm to children, which is ending their lives by killing, out of fear of poverty, as He said in the hadith when he was asked about the greatest of the major sins, and he mentioned shirk with Allah, which is His saying: "That you set up a rival to Allah while He created you." Then he said: "And that you kill your child for fear that he will eat with you." And he said: "And that you commit adultery with your neighbour's wife." This hadith is drawn from this verse. The construction here is ﴿We provide for you and for them﴾, while in al-Isra it is ﴿We provide for them and for you﴾ [al-Isra: 31]. This may be variation in speech. It may also be said that in this verse ﴿for fear of poverty﴾ came, whose apparent sense is that poverty has already befallen the parent, not its expectation and fear, even if he has wealth. So it began with His saying ﴿We provide for you﴾, addressing the fathers and giving them good news of the removal of poverty and referring provision to the Creator, the Provider, and then conjoined the children upon them. As for al-Isra, the apparent construction is that they are well-off, and their killing of them is only for expecting poverty and fear of it. So it began with ﴿We provide for them﴾ [al-Isra: 31], informing that He undertakes their provision, so it is not you who provide for them, and conjoined the fathers to them. The two verses thus convey two meanings. One is that fathers are forbidden to kill children even when they are in poverty. The other is that they are forbidden to kill them even if they are well-off, because of the expectation and fear of poverty. Carrying the two verses upon what conveys two meanings is better than emphasis.
﴿And do not approach the indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is hidden﴾: what is related concerning ﴿of them, what is apparent and what is hidden﴾ is like what is related concerning ﴿Leave the outward and inward of sin﴾ [al-An'am: 120], and it has passed, so there is no need to repeat it.
﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right﴾: this falls under the generality of the indecencies, since it is best not to restrict the indecencies to any one kind. He singled out the killing of the soul from them to magnify this indecency and to make its occurrence grave, and because the exception with His saying ﴿except by right﴾ cannot apply except to killing, not to the generality of indecencies. His saying ﴿which Allah has forbidden﴾ refers to a previously established covenant concerning its prohibition, which is why it is described as "which." The forbidden soul is the believer, the protected non-Muslim (dhimmi), and the covenant-holder. "By right" means by the cause that makes killing obligatory, such as apostasy, retaliation, adultery after marriage, and waging war.
﴿That is what He has enjoined upon you, that you may understand﴾: He pointed to all that has preceded. In the wording "enjoined" there is a kindness and tenderness, and making them trustees for Him, of a kindness that is not hidden. Since reason is the basis of obligation, Allah the Exalted said ﴿that you may understand﴾, i.e., the benefits and advantages of these obligations in religion and the world. "Wasah" is a command that is emphatic and established. Al-A'sha said:
"Indeed, did you not hear the injunction of Muhammad, the Prophet of God, when he enjoined and testified?"
﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan﴾: this is a prohibition against approaching, which encompasses all modes of disposal, and in it is blocking the means. ﴿Except in the way that is best﴾: i.e., by the manner that is best regarding the orphan's right. It did not say merely "in the way that is good," but used the superlative to safeguard the orphan's property, and that a good state is not sufficient in it, but the best manner. The prohibition of approaching people's property is absolute. He specified "orphan" because greed for him is greater, due to his weakness and the scant attention paid to him. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd said: ﴿the way that is best﴾ [al-Isra: 53] is to work for him a righteous work and eat from it in a reasonable manner at a time of need. Al-Zajjaj said: preserving it and increasing it. Al-Dahhak said: preserving its profit through trade, and not taking anything from it. Mujahid said: the way that is best is trade. Whoever is among the guardians who has wealth on which he lives, then it is best, when the orphan's property yields profit, that he not take from it any maintenance, wage or anything else. Whoever is among the guardians who has no wealth and cannot manage it without spending on himself, let him spend from the profit of his management. It has been said: benefiting from his animals and using his slaves, lest guardians withdraw because of the mixing. This was mentioned by al-Marwazi. It has been said: he should eat from it only as a loan, but this is remote, for what excellence is there in this?

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 151–152 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Until he reaches his maturity (ashuddahu)﴾. This is a limit in terms of meaning, not in terms of this verbal construction. Its meaning is: guard the orphan's property for him until he reaches his ashudd, then hand it over to him. The attaining of ashudd here, for the orphan, is the attaining of puberty (al-hulm). This was said by al-Sha'bi, Zayd ibn Aslam, Yahya ibn Ya'mur, Rabi'ah and Malik. Ibn 'Atiyyah related from al-Sha'bi, Rabi'ah, Malik and Abu Hanifah that it is puberty, together with the condition that his wickedness (fisq) is not established. Various sayings have been reported on the interpretation of ashudd that cannot be applicable here, and it seems they were reported in connection with His words ﴿And when he reached his ashudd﴾ [Yusuf: 22]. From Ibn 'Abbas: between eighteen and thirty; and from him: thirty-three; from Ibn Jubayr and Muqatil: eighteen; from al-Suddi: thirty; from al-Thawri: thirty-four; from 'Ikrimah: twenty-five; from 'A'ishah: forty; from Abu al-'Aliyah: his intellect and the gathering of his strength; and from some of them: from fifteen to thirty; and from some of them: sixty years (p-253), as mentioned by al-Baghawi. "Ashudd" is the plural of shiddah, or of shadd, or of shudd, or a plural having no singular from its own form, or a singular having no plural; there are five views. Ibn al-Anbari, along with others, chose the last view, but it is not the preferred one, because the form af'al is absent from singular nouns in lexical usage. Ashudd is derived from al-shiddah, which means strength and endurance. It has also been said that its root meaning is elevation, from "shadda al-nahar" (the day rose high) when it rose. 'Antarah said:

"I knew him when the day had risen high, as if his breast and head had been dyed with al-'izlim."

﴿And give full measure and weight with justice﴾, that is, with equity and evenness. It has been said that al-qist here means a slight addition, so that one is free of obligation with certainty, on the basis of what was narrated: "When you weigh, tip the scale." ﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾, that is, except what it can bear and is not unable to do. Since observing the exact measure of justice, which has neither excess nor deficiency, involves hardship, He mentioned reaching one's capacity and that whatever lies beyond it is pardoned. So the obligation in giving full measure and weight is the possible extent, while exact perfection is not obligatory; al-Tabari said this meaning. It has also been said that the meaning is: We do not burden anyone with what would destroy them, even if it is permissible, like His words ﴿Kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 66]. On this view, it does not refer back to giving full measure and weight. For this reason Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it implies that these commands concern only what falls within human capacity of guarding and caution, not that one is required to achieve absolute justice in the very thing one disposes of.

﴿And when you speak, be just, even if it concerns a near relative﴾, that is, even if the one addressed or spoken against is a relative of the speaker; so one should neither add nor subtract. The speaker's own self, his parents and his close kin are included in "near relative", and he looks to His words ﴿Even against yourselves, or your parents and near relatives﴾ [al-Nisa': 135]. By "speech" here is meant whatever can only be made known through speech: a command, a judgment, testimony, rebuke, mediation between people, and other such matters, since they are bound to speech. Restricting it to judgment, or to command, or to testimony are views for which there is no evidence of restriction.

﴿And fulfil the covenant of God﴾. It may be that it is an idafah to the agent, meaning: fulfil what God has covenanted upon you; and it may be an idafah to the object, meaning: fulfil what you have covenanted with God. It has also been said that it may refer to the covenant between people, and its ascription to God Most High is because He commanded its preservation and fulfilment. al-Maturidi said: His command and prohibition regarding what is lawful and unlawful. al-Tibrizi said: His covenant on the Day of the Covenant. Ibn al-Jawzi said: it includes what He has enjoined upon creation and charged them with, and what a person has obligated upon himself, such as a vow and other things.

﴿That is what He has enjoined upon you, so that you may remember﴾. Since the five mentioned before this are clear and evident matters that must be connected to and understood, they were concluded with His words ﴿so that you may understand (ta'qilun)﴾. These last four are hidden and obscure, requiring ijtihad and much reflection until one arrives at the point of moderation; so they were concluded with His words ﴿so that you may remember (tadhakkarun)﴾. Hafs and al-Akhawan (Hamzah and al-Kisa'i) read "tadhakkarun" wherever it occurs with the dhal lightened, the taa' being deleted, since the original is "tatadhakkarun"; and there is disagreement about the deleted letter: is it the taa' of the present tense or the taa' of the tafa'ala form. The remaining seven read "tadhdhakkarun" with the dhal doubled, the taa' of tafa''ala being assimilated into the dhal.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 151–152 (part 1 of 2):
