"They say: Do not perish of grief, and be patient."
We know of no disagreement on this, unlike the mutually divergent clauses of statement, interrogation and imperative, where there is disagreement on conjunction. They have allowed "an" to be masdariyya rather than explanatory, in a position of nominative and in a position of accusative. As for the nominative, it is by presupposing a subject indicated by the meaning, the estimate being: "the recited is (that you do not associate)." As for the accusative, it is in several ways. One: that it is governed by "ʿalaykum," and it is an incitement (idghra'), and the speech is complete at "I recite what your Lord has forbidden you," i.e., hold fast to the absence of association; this is remote because it disconnects speech from its apparent sense. Two: that it is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), i.e., "I recite what your Lord has forbidden you" (that you do not associate). This is remote because what follows it is a command conjoined with a waw, and its prohibition is conjoined with a waw, so it does not fit that it should be an explanation of what was forbidden; as for the commands, it is in terms of meaning, and as for the prohibitions, it is in terms of conjunction. Three: that it is an object of an omitted verb, its estimate: "I enjoin upon you that you do not associate," because His saying ﴿and [show] kindness to parents﴾ is carried upon "I enjoin upon you," ﴿and [show] kindness to parents﴾; this is remote because omission is contrary to the original. These three aspects keep "la" in its original negative sense, and it is intended. Four: that it is in a position of accusative as a substitute for ﴿what He forbade﴾ or for the omitted pronoun in ﴿what He forbade﴾, its estimate being "what He forbade it." These two aspects have "la" as superfluous, as it is in His saying: "What prevented you from not prostrating when I commanded you?" This is weak, because the generality of the forbidden is confined to shirk, since what follows of commands is not included in the forbidden, and after a command there cannot be claimed a superfluous "la" in it, since "an la" in it is evident as prohibitive. Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you say): why did you not say that it is the one that governs the verb in the subjunctive, and make "that you do not associate" a substitute for ﴿what He forbade﴾? (I say): it is necessary that "do not associate," "do not approach," "do not kill," and "do not follow the ways" be prohibitions, because the commands are conjoined to them, namely His saying: ﴿and [show] kindness to parents﴾; for the estimate is: "and be good," ﴿and [show] kindness to parents﴾, "and fulfil," "and when you speak, be just," "and fulfil the covenant of Allah." End. It is not required that all commands be conjoined to all that "la" governs, for we have shown the permissibility of conjoining ﴿and [show] kindness to parents﴾ to "come," and what follows it is conjoined to it, and ﴿and [show] kindness to parents﴾ need not be conjoined to "that you associate." "That you do not associate" includes whoever associates with Allah idols, like the people of Ibrahim, and whoever associates with Allah jinn, and whoever associates with Allah sons and daughters. Ibn al-Jawzi said: it has been said: claiming a partner for Allah. It has been said: obeying other than Allah in disobedience to Allah. The explanation of ﴿and [show] kindness to parents﴾ has passed in Surat al-Baqara.
* *
﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty; We provide for you and for them﴾: "min" here is causal, i.e., "for fear of poverty," in accordance with His saying: ﴿for fear of poverty﴾ [al-Isra: 31]. Killing a child is forbidden except by right. This cause was mentioned because it was the reason for killing children among them. Allah the Exalted explained that He is the Provider for them and for their children, and if He is the Provider, then just as you do not kill yourself, so do not kill your child. When He commanded kindness to parents, He forbade harm to children, and He drew attention to the greatest harm to children, which is ending their lives by killing, out of fear of poverty, as He said in the hadith when he was asked about the greatest of the major sins, and he mentioned shirk with Allah, which is His saying: "That you set up a rival to Allah while He created you." Then he said: "And that you kill your child for fear that he will eat with you." And he said: "And that you commit adultery with your neighbour's wife." This hadith is drawn from this verse. The construction here is ﴿We provide for you and for them﴾, while in al-Isra it is ﴿We provide for them and for you﴾ [al-Isra: 31]. This may be variation in speech. It may also be said that in this verse ﴿for fear of poverty﴾ came, whose apparent sense is that poverty has already befallen the parent, not its expectation and fear, even if he has wealth. So it began with His saying ﴿We provide for you﴾, addressing the fathers and giving them good news of the removal of poverty and referring provision to the Creator, the Provider, and then conjoined the children upon them. As for al-Isra, the apparent construction is that they are well-off, and their killing of them is only for expecting poverty and fear of it. So it began with ﴿We provide for them﴾ [al-Isra: 31], informing that He undertakes their provision, so it is not you who provide for them, and conjoined the fathers to them. The two verses thus convey two meanings. One is that fathers are forbidden to kill children even when they are in poverty. The other is that they are forbidden to kill them even if they are well-off, because of the expectation and fear of poverty. Carrying the two verses upon what conveys two meanings is better than emphasis.
﴿And do not approach the indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is hidden﴾: what is related concerning ﴿of them, what is apparent and what is hidden﴾ is like what is related concerning ﴿Leave the outward and inward of sin﴾ [al-An'am: 120], and it has passed, so there is no need to repeat it.
﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right﴾: this falls under the generality of the indecencies, since it is best not to restrict the indecencies to any one kind. He singled out the killing of the soul from them to magnify this indecency and to make its occurrence grave, and because the exception with His saying ﴿except by right﴾ cannot apply except to killing, not to the generality of indecencies. His saying ﴿which Allah has forbidden﴾ refers to a previously established covenant concerning its prohibition, which is why it is described as "which." The forbidden soul is the believer, the protected non-Muslim (dhimmi), and the covenant-holder. "By right" means by the cause that makes killing obligatory, such as apostasy, retaliation, adultery after marriage, and waging war.
﴿That is what He has enjoined upon you, that you may understand﴾: He pointed to all that has preceded. In the wording "enjoined" there is a kindness and tenderness, and making them trustees for Him, of a kindness that is not hidden. Since reason is the basis of obligation, Allah the Exalted said ﴿that you may understand﴾, i.e., the benefits and advantages of these obligations in religion and the world. "Wasah" is a command that is emphatic and established. Al-A'sha said:
"Indeed, did you not hear the injunction of Muhammad, the Prophet of God, when he enjoined and testified?"
﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan﴾: this is a prohibition against approaching, which encompasses all modes of disposal, and in it is blocking the means. ﴿Except in the way that is best﴾: i.e., by the manner that is best regarding the orphan's right. It did not say merely "in the way that is good," but used the superlative to safeguard the orphan's property, and that a good state is not sufficient in it, but the best manner. The prohibition of approaching people's property is absolute. He specified "orphan" because greed for him is greater, due to his weakness and the scant attention paid to him. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd said: ﴿the way that is best﴾ [al-Isra: 53] is to work for him a righteous work and eat from it in a reasonable manner at a time of need. Al-Zajjaj said: preserving it and increasing it. Al-Dahhak said: preserving its profit through trade, and not taking anything from it. Mujahid said: the way that is best is trade. Whoever is among the guardians who has wealth on which he lives, then it is best, when the orphan's property yields profit, that he not take from it any maintenance, wage or anything else. Whoever is among the guardians who has no wealth and cannot manage it without spending on himself, let him spend from the profit of his management. It has been said: benefiting from his animals and using his slaves, lest guardians withdraw because of the mixing. This was mentioned by al-Marwazi. It has been said: he should eat from it only as a loan, but this is remote, for what excellence is there in this?

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verses 151–152 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Until he reaches his maturity (ashuddahu)﴾. This is a limit in terms of meaning, not in terms of this verbal construction. Its meaning is: guard the orphan's property for him until he reaches his ashudd, then hand it over to him. The attaining of ashudd here, for the orphan, is the attaining of puberty (al-hulm). This was said by al-Sha'bi, Zayd ibn Aslam, Yahya ibn Ya'mur, Rabi'ah and Malik. Ibn 'Atiyyah related from al-Sha'bi, Rabi'ah, Malik and Abu Hanifah that it is puberty, together with the condition that his wickedness (fisq) is not established. Various sayings have been reported on the interpretation of ashudd that cannot be applicable here, and it seems they were reported in connection with His words ﴿And when he reached his ashudd﴾ [Yusuf: 22]. From Ibn 'Abbas: between eighteen and thirty; and from him: thirty-three; from Ibn Jubayr and Muqatil: eighteen; from al-Suddi: thirty; from al-Thawri: thirty-four; from 'Ikrimah: twenty-five; from 'A'ishah: forty; from Abu al-'Aliyah: his intellect and the gathering of his strength; and from some of them: from fifteen to thirty; and from some of them: sixty years (p-253), as mentioned by al-Baghawi. "Ashudd" is the plural of shiddah, or of shadd, or of shudd, or a plural having no singular from its own form, or a singular having no plural; there are five views. Ibn al-Anbari, along with others, chose the last view, but it is not the preferred one, because the form af'al is absent from singular nouns in lexical usage. Ashudd is derived from al-shiddah, which means strength and endurance. It has also been said that its root meaning is elevation, from "shadda al-nahar" (the day rose high) when it rose. 'Antarah said:

"I knew him when the day had risen high, as if his breast and head had been dyed with al-'izlim."

﴿And give full measure and weight with justice﴾, that is, with equity and evenness. It has been said that al-qist here means a slight addition, so that one is free of obligation with certainty, on the basis of what was narrated: "When you weigh, tip the scale." ﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾, that is, except what it can bear and is not unable to do. Since observing the exact measure of justice, which has neither excess nor deficiency, involves hardship, He mentioned reaching one's capacity and that whatever lies beyond it is pardoned. So the obligation in giving full measure and weight is the possible extent, while exact perfection is not obligatory; al-Tabari said this meaning. It has also been said that the meaning is: We do not burden anyone with what would destroy them, even if it is permissible, like His words ﴿Kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 66]. On this view, it does not refer back to giving full measure and weight. For this reason Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it implies that these commands concern only what falls within human capacity of guarding and caution, not that one is required to achieve absolute justice in the very thing one disposes of.

﴿And when you speak, be just, even if it concerns a near relative﴾, that is, even if the one addressed or spoken against is a relative of the speaker; so one should neither add nor subtract. The speaker's own self, his parents and his close kin are included in "near relative", and he looks to His words ﴿Even against yourselves, or your parents and near relatives﴾ [al-Nisa': 135]. By "speech" here is meant whatever can only be made known through speech: a command, a judgment, testimony, rebuke, mediation between people, and other such matters, since they are bound to speech. Restricting it to judgment, or to command, or to testimony are views for which there is no evidence of restriction.

﴿And fulfil the covenant of God﴾. It may be that it is an idafah to the agent, meaning: fulfil what God has covenanted upon you; and it may be an idafah to the object, meaning: fulfil what you have covenanted with God. It has also been said that it may refer to the covenant between people, and its ascription to God Most High is because He commanded its preservation and fulfilment. al-Maturidi said: His command and prohibition regarding what is lawful and unlawful. al-Tibrizi said: His covenant on the Day of the Covenant. Ibn al-Jawzi said: it includes what He has enjoined upon creation and charged them with, and what a person has obligated upon himself, such as a vow and other things.

﴿That is what He has enjoined upon you, so that you may remember﴾. Since the five mentioned before this are clear and evident matters that must be connected to and understood, they were concluded with His words ﴿so that you may understand (ta'qilun)﴾. These last four are hidden and obscure, requiring ijtihad and much reflection until one arrives at the point of moderation; so they were concluded with His words ﴿so that you may remember (tadhakkarun)﴾. Hafs and al-Akhawan (Hamzah and al-Kisa'i) read "tadhakkarun" wherever it occurs with the dhal lightened, the taa' being deleted, since the original is "tatadhakkarun"; and there is disagreement about the deleted letter: is it the taa' of the present tense or the taa' of the tafa'ala form. The remaining seven read "tadhdhakkarun" with the dhal doubled, the taa' of tafa''ala being assimilated into the dhal.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 153:**

﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it﴾. The Akhawan (Hamza and al-Kisa'i) read *wa-inna hadha* with a kasra on the hamza and a shadda on the nun, as a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*, a new sentence not grammatically dependent on what precedes). ﴿So follow it﴾ is a clause conjoined (*ma'tuf*) to the resumptive clause. The rest read it with a fatha on the hamza. Ibn 'Amir read the nun with a light pronunciation (*takhfif*), while the rest read it with a shadda. 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ishaq read *wa-inna* (with a kasra) like the reading of Ibn 'Amir. As for lightening the nun, it is on the basis that the subject of *inna* has been omitted, and it is the pronoun of the matter (*damir al-sha'n*). The reading with a fatha on the hamza has several explanations:

The first: it is a causal clause (*ta'lil*) from which the lam has been omitted, its implied meaning being: "and because this is My path, straight, so follow it," like His saying: ﴿And that the mosques are for God, so do not invoke anyone alongside God﴾ [al-Jinn: 18]. The lam is explicitly stated in His saying: ﴿For the covenant of the Quraysh﴾ [Quraysh: 1], ﴿their covenant﴾ [Quraysh: 2], ﴿so let them worship﴾ [Quraysh: 3]. Al-Farisi said: "The analogy of Sibawayh's view on the fatha of the hamza is that the fa' is superfluous, in the position of its use in *zaydun fa-qama* (Zayd, so he stood)."

The second explanation: it is conjoined (*ma'tuf*) to *an la tushrikū* (that you do not associate partners), meaning: "I recite to you the prohibition of associating partners and the affirmation of monotheism, and I recite to you that this is My path." This is on the basis that *an* in *an la tushrikū* is a verbal-masdar particle (*masdariyya*), as stated by al-Hawfi. They established this explanation in this way, making it conjoined to the substitute (*badal*) of what was forbidden, which is *an la tushrikū*. Abu al-Baqa' said that it is conjoined to the substituted element (*mubdal minhu*): "recite what He has forbidden, and recite that this is My path, straight," and this is a permissible explanation in speech. On this basis, *al-sirat* is in construct (*mudaf*) to the speaker, who is the Messenger (ﷺ), and his path is the path of God.

The third explanation: it is in the position of the genitive (*jarr*) as a conjunction to the pronoun in *bihi* (with it), as stated by al-Farra': "He commanded you with it," and *bi-anna* has the *ba'* omitted because of the length of *anna* with its complement. Al-Hawfi said: "It is intended (*muradda*), and in this there is no conjoining of a noun to a pronoun for the sake of its intention." Abu al-Baqa' said: "This is corrupt for two reasons: one, the conjoining of a noun to a pronoun without repeating the preposition; and two, that the meaning becomes: 'He commanded you with the straightness of the path.'"

Al-A'mash read: *wa-hadha sirati* (and this is My path), and likewise it is in the codex of 'Abd Allah. Since in the two previous verses He gave detail, in this one He gave a general statement (*ijmal*) that includes everything previously mentioned and all of His law. The demonstrative *hadha* (this) refers to Islam, or the Qur'an, or what occurs in this surah, since all of it concerns monotheism, the proofs of prophethood, and the establishment of the religion; or it refers to these verses that follow this verse, because they are the decisive verses (*muhkamat*) that were not abrogated (*nuskh*) in any religious community among the religious communities. These are four opinions. ﴿So follow it﴾ is a command to follow all of it, and the meaning is: act according to its requirements, of prohibition and permission, of command and prohibition, and of allowance.

﴿And do not follow the paths, lest they scatter you from His way﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the misguidances. Mujahid said: innovations (*bid'a*), desires (*ahwa'*), and dubious matters (*shubuhat*). Muqatil said: what they forbade for themselves of livestock and tillage. It has been said: they are the paths of disbelief, such as Judaism, Christianity, Zoroastrianism, and whatever is similar to them in disbelief and polytheism. In the Musnad of al-Darimi, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) drew for us a line one day, then said: 'This is the path of God.' Then he drew lines to its right and its left, then said: 'These are paths, over each path is a devil calling to it.' Then he recited this verse." And from Jabir, something similar is in the Sunan of Ibn Majah. ﴿Then they scatter﴾ (*fa-tafarraqa*) is in the accusative because it is an answer to the prohibition, meaning: "so they scatter," and the *ta'* was omitted. It was also read as *fa-tfarraqa* with a shadda on the *ta'*.

﴿That He has enjoined on you, that you may be mindful of God﴾. He repeated the injunction for emphasis. Since the straight path is what gathers all obligations, and God commanded following it and forbade the byways, He concluded this with *taqwa* (God-consciousness/piety), which is guarding against the Fire, for whoever follows His path, He saves him with eternal salvation and attains everlasting felicity. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Since the first prohibitions are not committed by an intelligent person who has considered with his intellect, worship came with ﴿so that you may understand﴾ [al-An'am: 151], while the other prohibitions are desires, and among the intelligent there may be one who commits them without remembering. Taking the complete highway includes performing the virtues, and that is the rank of *taqwa*."

(p-٢٥٥) (ثُمَّ / *thumma*) originally indicates a delay in time, and it is also used to indicate a delay in the report. Al-Zajjaj said: it is conjoined to *atlu* (recite), its implied sense being: "Recite what He has forbidden, then recite *﴿We gave*...﴾." It was also said: it is conjoined to *qul* (say), with *qul* understood, meaning: "Then say, *﴿We gave*...﴾." It was also said: the implied sense is, "Then, I inform you that We gave..." Al-Hawfi said: *thumma* orders the recitation, meaning: "We have recited to you the story of Muhammad, then We recite to you the story of Moses." Ibn 'Atiyya said: it indicates a delay in the order of the command that Muhammad (ﷺ) was given, as if he said: "Then, of what We have enjoined, that *﴿We gave Moses the Book﴾*," and what supports this is that Moses (peace be upon him) is earlier in time than Muhammad (ﷺ). Ibn al-Qushayri said: there is an omitted element in the speech, its implied sense being: "Then We had indeed *﴿given Moses the Book﴾* before We sent down the Qur'an upon Muhammad (ﷺ)." Al-Zamakhshari said: it is conjoined to *﴿He has enjoined you with it﴾* [al-An'am: 152]. If you ask: how is it valid to conjoin it to that with *thumma*, when the giving was long before the enjoining? I say: this enjoining is ancient; every nation has been enjoined with it through the tongue of its prophet, as Ibn 'Abbas said: "*muhkamat* (clear verses) which no part of any of the Books has abrogated." So it is as if it were said: *﴿That is what He has enjoined you with﴾* [al-An'am: 153], O children of Adam, in ancient times and in recent times; then, greater than that, that *﴿We gave Moses the Book﴾* and sent down this blessed Book. It was also said: it is conjoined to what came before the middle of the surah, from His saying: *﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob﴾* [al-An'am: 84]. End of quotation. All these opinions are strained. What should be adopted is that it is used for conjunction like *wa* (and), without considering any delay; some grammarians have held this view.

The word *al-Kitab* [al-An'am: 156] here is, without disagreement, the Torah. *Tamaman* (in completeness) is in the accusative either as an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*), or as an infinitive (*masdar*) whose verb is understood as "We completed it completely," the form being a *masdar* with its additional letters omitted, or as a circumstantial state (*hal*), either of the subject or of the object; all of these have been proposed. It was also said: the meaning of *tamaman* is "in a single instalment," that We did not send it down in parts as We sent down the Qur'an; this was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. *Alladhi ahsan* (to him who did good) is a generic reference, meaning: to whoever among the people of his religion was a doer of good; this was said by Mujahid, meaning: a completion of the blessing towards them. It was also said: *alladhi ahsan* refers to a specific person. Al-Mawardi said: it is Abraham, since the prophethood of Moses was a blessing upon Abraham, because he is from his offspring, and doing good to the sons is doing good to the fathers. It was also said: Moses (peace be upon him) is a completion of honour upon the servant who excelled in obedience in conveying and in everything he was commanded. In these interpretations, *alladhi* refers to one who has intellect. Ibn al-Anbari said: *tamaman 'ala alladhi ahsan* means: Moses, [in respect of] knowledge and the ancient Books of God. A similar view is that of Ibn Qutayba, who said: the meaning of the verse is *tamaman* upon what was better in knowledge and wisdom, *al-'ilm* (knowledge) and *al-hikma* (wisdom) coming from the expression "so-and-so *yuhsinu* such-and-such," meaning he knows it. Al-Zamakhshari said regarding this interpretation: *tamaman 'ala alladhi ahsan* refers to Moses in [respect of] knowledge and laws; from *ahsana al-shay'* when one perfects its knowledge, meaning: an increase upon his knowledge in the manner of completion. End of quotation. Ibn 'Atiyya said: *'ala ma ahsan* is [in respect of] his worship of his Lord and his undertaking of the affairs of his prophethood, intending Moses (peace be upon him); this is the interpretation of al-Rabi' and Qatada. End of quotation. In this interpretation, *alladhi* refers to a non-rational being. It was also said: *alladhi* is a verbal-noun (*masdariyya*) particle; this is a Kufan view, and in *ahsan* the pronoun refers to Moses, meaning: completely upon Moses' excellence in obeying Us and in carrying out Our command and Our prohibition; and the *'ala* ("upon") here indicates causation, as you say: "I have done good to you for your good to me." It was also said: the pronoun in *ahsan* refers to God, Exalted is He; this is the view of Ibn Zayd, and whether the object of the goodness is His prophets or Moses, there are two views. The best of all these views is that *ahsan* is a verb. Some Kufan grammarians said: it is permissible that *ahsan* be a noun, the comparative form (*af'al al-tafdil*), and it is in the genitive as an adjective of *alladhi*, even though it is indefinite insofar as it approaches definiteness, since *al* does not enter it, as the Arabs say: "I passed by the one who is better than you" (*marartu bi-alladhi khayrun minka*), and it is not permissible to say "I passed by the one who is knowledgeable" (*marartu bi-alladhi 'alimun*). End of quotation. This is valid according to the Kufan school of speech, but it is an error according to the Basran grammarians. Yahya ibn Ma'mar and Ibn Abi Ishaq read *(ahsanu)* with a *damma* on the *nun*, and this was analysed as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "He is *ahsanu*," and *ahsanu* is the predicate and the relative clause, like the reading of those who read *"mathalan ma baʿwadatan"* (a parable, whatever a gnat is), meaning: completely upon that which (p-٢٥٦) *is the best religion and the most pleasing*, or complete and perfect upon the best form in which Books are, meaning: upon the manner and way that is the best of what Books are; and this is the meaning of al-Kalbi's statement: "He completed the Book upon its best." Al-Tibrizi said: *alladhi* here has the sense of the plural, and *ahsana* is the relative clause of a past verb from which the pronoun, which is the *waw*, has been removed, so *ahsan* remained, meaning: upon those who did good (*'ala alladhina ahsanu*). The omission of this pronoun and the reliance on the *damma* is something the Arabs do. A poet said:

*"If only the physicians were around me..."*

Another said:

*"When they wish, they harm whom they will, and no one can restrain their harm."*

Another said:

*"They grew up in glory, grew grey, and reached full maturity."*

He means *wa-ktahalu* (and they reached maturity), so he removed the *waw*, then removed the pronoun for pause. End of quotation. Our companions restricted this to necessity (*darura*), so the Book of God is not to be interpreted by it.

*﴿And a detailed explanation of all things, and guidance and mercy, that perhaps they may believe in the meeting with their Lord﴾*. That is: perhaps they will believe in the Resurrection. Belief in it is the furthest point of assent, since it is not obligatory by reason, but it is permissible by reason, and revelation made it obligatory. The accusative of *tafsilan* [al-Isra': 12] and what follows it is like the accusative of *tamaman*.

This is a Book that We have sent down, blessed, so follow it and be mindful of God, that you may receive mercy. "This" refers to the Qur'an. "Sent down" (*anzalnahu*) and "blessed" (*mubarak*) are two attributes of "Book," or two predicates of "this," according to the view of those who permit listing several predicates even when they do not form a single predicate. The attribute of being sent down is more emphatic than the attribute of blessing, so it is placed first, because the discourse is addressed to one who denies the prophethood of the Messenger (ﷺ) and denies that divine Books were sent down. Its being blessed for them is a quality that they receive from it, and it comes after the sending down. For this reason the attribute of blessing is delayed and the attribute of sending down is advanced. Describing it with a verb attributed to the "We" of majesty is preferable to describing it with a noun, because attributing it to God, exalted is He, conveys glorification and honour, which would not be present if the construction were *munazzal* ("sent down"), or *munazzal minna* ("sent down from Us"). The blessing of the Qur'an lies in the benefit and increase that follow from it: the uniting of the word of the Arabs through it, its admonitions and wisdoms, its informing about the histories of past nations and the rewards that follow, healing from diseases, intercession for its reader, counting him among the people of God, his being in the company of the noble angels, and other blessings that cannot be counted. Then God, exalted is He, commanded following it, which means acting on what is in it, adhering to what it contains, and returning to it when difficulties arise. The apparent meaning of His words "and be mindful of God" is a command to general mindfulness in all matters. It has been said: be mindful of opposing it, in hope of mercy. Al-Tibrizi said: "Be mindful of other than it, for it is abrogated (*mansukh*)." Al-Tibrizi also said: "In the statement there is an allusion, namely God's description of the Torah as complete, and completeness signals termination." The poet said:

When a matter is complete, its deficiency appears;
Expect its decline once it is said, "It is complete."

So God abrogated (*nasakha*) it by the Qur'an and superseded it with Islam. He described the Qur'an as blessed in many places. The blessed is that which is firm and lasting while continually increasing, and this indicates its permanence and continuance.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 156:

﴿Lest you should say: "The Book was only sent down to two groups before us, and we were indeed unaware of their study."﴾ ﴿Lest you should say﴾ is a maf'ul li-ajlihi (object of purpose). The Kufans estimated it as: "li'alla (lest) you say," and "li-ajli an la taqulu (for the sake of not saying)." The Basrans estimated it as: "karahata an taqulu (out of dislike that you say)." In both schools the governing verb is ﴿We sent it down﴾ [al-An'am: 155], which is omitted, and is indicated by his earlier saying ﴿We sent it down﴾ [al-An'am: 155]. It is not permissible for the governing word to be the ﴿We sent it down﴾ [al-An'am: 155] that is pronounced here, because it is separated from them by ﴿blessed﴾, which is the attribute of ﴿Book﴾ [al-An'am: 155], or the predicate of this; so it is foreign to the governor and the governed. The apparent sense of Ibn 'Atiyya's words is that the governing word is the ﴿We sent it down﴾ [al-An'am: 155] that is pronounced. It was also said: ﴿Lest you should say﴾ is the object, and the governing word for it is ﴿and fear God﴾ [al-An'am: 155], meaning: "fear God lest you say," because there is no proof for you in it. Here "the Book" is a genus noun, and "the two groups" are the People of the Torah and the Gospel, the Jews and the Christians, without disagreement. The address is directed at the disbelieving Quraysh, establishing the proof against them by the sending down of this Book, so that they would not argue, they and the disbelieving Arabs, that they had no Book. It is as if it were said: "And this Qur'an, O assembly of the Arabs, was sent down as a proof against you, lest you say: 'The Torah and the Gospel were only sent down in a language other than ours, to others than us, and we did not know of that; so here is a Book in your tongue with a man from among you.'" Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿lest they say﴾ with the third-person yā' (yaqūlū), meaning the disbelieving Quraysh. Al-Maturidi said: the meaning is that the descent of the Book became manifest to the creation as being upon two groups before us, and they were not, at the time the Torah and the Gospel were sent down, Jews or Christians; rather these two names came to be applied to them because of what occurred from them. ﴿Their study﴾ means their recitation and their studying, and the meaning is "about the like of their study." He used the pronoun in the plural because each group among them is a plurality, as he used it in His saying: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight﴾ [al-Hujurat: 9]. Here ﴿in-na﴾ (wa-in) is the lightened form of the heavy one. The Kufans said: ﴿in﴾ is negative, the lām means "illa" (except), and the estimate is: "wa-ma kunna 'an dirasatihim illa ghafilin (we were not, concerning their study, except heedless)." Qutrub said: in such a construction ﴿in﴾ means ﴿qad﴾ (indeed), and the lām is superfluous. This disagreement is not confined to this verse; it applies to the instances of this construction, and its exposition belongs to the science of grammar. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿wa-in kunna﴾ is the lightened form of the heavy one, the lām is the one distinguishing it from the negative, and the original is "wa-in kunna 'an dirasatihim ghafilin (indeed we were heedless of their study)," with the hā' being a pronoun. End. What he held, that its origin is ﴿wa-in kunna﴾ with the hā' being the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), necessarily entails that the lightened in, from the heavy, governs a deleted hidden pronoun during the lightening, as the grammarians said regarding the lightened form of the heavy. What people have explicitly stated is that the lightened in, from the heavy, when the lām is attached to one of the two components after it, or to one of the two objects of the sister verb that follows it, is inert: it does not govern a visible or a hidden pronoun, neither affirmed nor deleted. So this view he held contradicts the texts, and when the sister verb follows it, it is never, in any way, in the original, upon a pronoun of the matter. ﴿Concerning their study﴾ is connected to ﴿heedless﴾, and this indicates the invalidity of the Kufans' doctrine that the lām means "illa," since what follows "illa" cannot govern what precedes it, and neither can the lām that carries its meaning. They may make ﴿concerning it﴾ connected to a deleted word. It also indicates that the lām is the lām of the beginning (lam al-ibtida'), attached for distinction, so its complement may precede it, since it occurs in a place that is not its original place, just as that is permitted in "in Zaydan la-ta'āmaka la-ākilun," where it occurs in a place that is not its original place; and that is not permitted when it occurs in its original place, which is its entry upon the subject of the nominal sentence.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 157:

﴿Or [lest] you should say: "Had the Book been sent down to us, we would surely have been better guided than them."﴾ This is a shift from the report, to restricting the sending down of the Book to others besides them, and that it was not sent down to them, to a statement of a ruling on a supposition. The "Book" may be intended to mean the Book previously mentioned, and it may be intended to mean the Book which they wished would be sent down to them. The meaning of ﴿better guided than them﴾ is more rightly guided and quicker to guidance, because it was sent down to us in our tongue, so we understand it, reflect upon it, and grasp (p-258) what it contains without straining the mind or learning a language, unlike the Book which was sent down to the two groups (Jews and Christians), for it is in other than our tongue, so we do not know it and cannot be heedless of studying it. Or ﴿better guided than them﴾ is because the Jews and Christians have split into divergent sects, so we do not know the truth from falsehood.

﴿Now there has certainly come to you a clear proof from your Lord, and guidance and mercy﴾. This is a cutting off of their excuse, by restricting the sending down of the Book to the two groups and by their not having had a Book sent down to them; had one been sent down, they would have been better guided than the two groups. The apparent meaning is that the clear proof is the Qur'an, which is the evident, manifest, illuminating argument, since it was sent down to them in their own tongue and it obligated the whole world to its rulings and its law; and guidance and light are among the attributes of the Qur'an. It was said: the clear proof is the Messenger, as said by Ibn 'Abbas.

﴿A clear proof from your Lord﴾ means: a proof. It is the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Qur'an. It was said: the signs of Allah which He manifested in His Book and upon the tongue of His Messenger. It was said: the religion of Allah. Guidance and light, according to these sayings, are among the attributes of that by which the proof was explained. The "fa" in His saying ﴿Now there has certainly come to you﴾, according to what al-Zamakhshari and others estimated, is the answer to an omitted condition. Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is, "If you are truthful in what you used to claim about yourselves, then there has certainly come to you a clear proof from your Lord," so the condition was omitted, and this is among the finest omissions. End. Others estimated it as: "If you are, as you claim, that when a Book is sent down to you, you would be more guided than the Jews and Christians, then there has certainly come to you..." The exegetes unanimously agreed that the purpose of this sentence is to establish the proof against the polytheists of the Arabs and to cut off their argumentation.

* *

﴿Who, then, is more unjust than one who denies the signs of Allah and turns away from them?﴾ That is: after the coming of the clear proof, guidance and light, there is no one more unjust than the one who denies a matter that is manifest and illuminating, about which there is no doubt, and who turns away from it after its soundness and truthfulness have become apparent to him and he has known it, or has been able to know it. The turning away is delayed because it arises from denial, and turning away from a thing comes after seeing it and its appearance. It was said: before the "fa" there is an omitted condition, its estimate being: "If you deny, then none is more unjust than you." The signs of Allah may be intended to mean the Qur'an and the Messenger, and it is preferable that it be understood in its generality.

﴿And turns away﴾ is intransitive, meaning "turned away," and we have explained it on this meaning; and it is also transitive, meaning he turned others away from them, in the sense of "barred him," and in this there is an intensification of the blame, since he denied the signs of Allah and made others turn away from them and deny them. Ibn Wathhab and Ibn Abi 'Abla read ﴿who denied﴾ with the dhal lightened.

﴿We will surely recompense those who turn away from Our signs with a dreadful punishment because of what they used to turn away﴾. He linked the recompense to turning away because it arises from denial. ﴿A dreadful punishment﴾ means its severe kind, like His saying ﴿Those who disbelieved and barred from the way of Allah — We will increase them in punishment upon punishment﴾ [an-Nahl: 88]. A group read (yaṣdufūna) with a damma on the dal.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 158:

﴿Are they waiting for anything but that the angels should come to them, or your Lord should come, or some of the signs of your Lord should come?﴾ The pronoun in ﴿they are waiting﴾ refers to those to whom it was said: ﴿There has certainly come to you clear evidence﴾ [al-An'am: 157], namely the idolaters among the Arabs who deny their Lord, and whose disputes occupy most of the surah. That is: they are only waiting for ﴿the angels to come to them﴾ to seize their souls and punish them, and that is a time when their repentance will not benefit them. This is the view of Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Juraij. It has also been said: ﴿that the angels should come to them﴾ refers to the day of resurrection, when they will see the angels: ﴿On the day they see the angels, there will be no glad tidings that day for the criminals.﴾ It has also been said: this refers to their saying: ﴿or you bring God and the angels as a tribe (qabilan)﴾, that is, messengers from God to them, as they wished. Or ﴿your Lord's command should come upon them, by killing or otherwise﴾, as Ibn Abbas said. Mujahid said: ﴿or your Lord should come﴾ with His knowledge and power, without where or how, to decide between His creatures at the place of standing on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Zajjaj said: or the destruction of your Lord should come upon them. Ibn Atiyyah said: In every interpretation it is by omitting a noun (mudaf): its estimate is "the command of your Lord, or the seizing and reckoning of your Lord." Otherwise, the coming understood from the language is impossible with respect to God, the Exalted. Do you not see that God, the Exalted, says: ﴿So God came to them from where they did not expect﴾ [al-Hashr: 2]? This is a coming that has occurred, and it is figurative, with the noun omitted. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿or there come﴾ all the signs of your Lord, as shown by His saying: ﴿or some of the signs of your Lord should come﴾, meaning the signs of the Hour and total destruction, and ﴿some of the signs of your Lord﴾ are the portents of the Hour, such as the rising of the sun from its west (p-259) and others. End of quote. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Umar, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: it is the rising of the sun from its west. Abu Sa'id narrated it from the Prophet (ﷺ), and in the two Sahihs from him, peace be upon him: "The Hour will not be established until the sun rises from its west. When it rises and people see it, whoever is on the earth will believe, but that is the time when faith will not benefit a soul that did not believe before or did not earn good through its faith." Ibn Mas'ud said, in what Masruq narrated from him: the rising of the sun and the moon from their west. It has also been said: one of the three signs is the rising of the sun from its west, the beast, and the opening of Yajuj and Majuj; this was narrated by al-Qasim from Ibn Mas'ud. Abu Hurayrah said: its rising, the Dajjal, the beast, and the opening of Yajuj and Majuj. It has also been said: the ten signs mentioned in the hadith of al-Bara': the rising of the sun from its west, the Dajjal, the beast, a sinking in the East, a sinking in the West, a sinking in the Arabian Peninsula, the descent of Isa, the opening of Yajuj and Majuj, and a fire that comes out from the bottom of Aden driving people to the place of gathering. The apparent meaning is that they were threatened with a great matter from the signs of the Hour, so that thought would go in every direction. But after that comes the report about this part, that repentance will not be accepted at it when it comes, and the Messenger's explicit statement that the rising of the sun from its west is a time when repentance will not benefit makes it evident that this is the part. It is also possible that this part is the death rattle (gharghara) of a person at death, for that occurs at a time when repentance does not benefit. God, the Exalted, says: ﴿And repentance is not for those who do evil deeds until, when death comes to one of them, he says, "Indeed I have repented now"﴾ [al-Nisa': 18]. In the hadith, the repentance of a servant is accepted as long as he has not reached the death rattle. It is also possible that His saying ﴿on the day some of the signs of your Lord come﴾ is different from His saying ﴿or some of the signs of your Lord should come﴾, so that this refers to what is certain to occur among the signs of the Hour, and His saying ﴿on the day some of the signs of your Lord come﴾ contains an omitted description indicated by the meaning, its estimate being: ﴿on the day some of the signs of your Lord come﴾ by which repentance is withdrawn. It is established by the sound hadith that the rising of the sun from its west is a time when repentance is not accepted, and the repetition of "the signs of your Lord" indicates the difference, for if these were the same as those, the construction would have been "on the day some of them come," that is, some of the signs of your Lord.

﴿On the day some of the signs of your Lord come, faith will not benefit a soul that did not believe before or did not earn good through its faith﴾. The explicit meaning of the verse is that when this part comes, faith will not benefit a disbelieving soul in the faith it produces at that time, nor will it benefit a soul whose faith preceded but which earned no good through that faith. He made the negation of faith dependent on one of two attributes: either the negation of prior faith alone, or prior faith together with the negation of earning good. Its implication is that prior faith alone benefits, or prior faith together with good. The implication of the attribute is strong, so the verse is cited as evidence for the view of the People of the Sunnah that faith does not require works for its validity. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿did not believe before﴾ is a description of ﴿soul﴾, and ﴿or did not earn good through its faith﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon ﴿believed﴾. The meaning is: when the signs of the Hour come, which are compelling and forcing signs, the time of obligation has passed; so faith then benefits no soul that did not put forward its faith before the signs appeared, or that put forward its faith without earning good through it. Thus, as you see, he does not distinguish between a disbelieving soul that believes outside the time of faith and a soul that believed in its time but did not earn good, so that it may be known that His saying ﴿those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 25] combines two companions that should never be separated, until its owner succeeds and is happy; otherwise there is wretchedness and ruin. End of quote. This is in line with his Mu'tazili school. Al-Akhawan read ﴿Unless they come to them﴾ with the ya' (yaʾtiyahum). Ibn 'Amr, Ibn Sirin and Abu al-'Aliyah read ﴿on the day some of it comes﴾ with the ta' (taʾti baʿḍu), like ﴿some of the travelers will pick it up (taltaqituhu baʿḍu al-sayyarah)﴾. Ibn Sirin read ﴿does not benefit a soul﴾ with the ta'. Abu Hatim said: they mention that it is an error on his part. Al-Nahhas said: in this there is a subtle point mentioned by Sibawayh, namely that faith and the soul each include the other, so the feminine is used for faith since it is from the soul and by it. Sibawayh recited, may God have mercy on him:

"They moved as spear-shafts sway, their tips swayed by the passing of the gusty winds."

End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Ibn Sirin also read ﴿does not benefit﴾ with the ta', because faith is attached to a feminine pronoun which is part of it, as in ﴿some of its fingers were lost﴾. End of quote. This is an error, because faith is not a part of the soul. It is possible that it was made feminine according to the meaning of faith, which is knowledge or belief, so it is like ﴿his book came to him and he despised it,﴾ according to the sense of "the scroll." ﴿On the day it comes﴾ is governed by ﴿does not benefit﴾. In this is evidence for the preceding of a معمول (complement) of a negated verb by "lā" over "lā," contrary to those who forbid it. Zuhayr al-Qarawi read ﴿the day it comes﴾ with the nominative, the predicate being ﴿does not benefit,﴾ with an omitted returning pronoun, meaning: does not benefit in it. Even if it is not a description, separation between the noun and its description by the subject is permitted, since it is not foreign, for the modified item, which is the object, and the subject share the governing verb. On this basis one may say: "He struck Hind her male servant, the Tamimi woman." Whoever makes the sentence a circumstantial clause (hal) considers it far-fetched, and whoever makes it a new sentence is even further.

﴿Say: Wait, we too are waiting﴾. That is: wait for what you are waiting for; ﴿we too are waiting﴾ for what will befall you. This is a command of threat and warning. Whoever says it is a command to refrain from fighting holds that it is abrogated, in his view, by the verse of the sword.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 159:

﴿Indeed, those who divided their religion and became sects, you have nothing to do with them in anything. Their affair is only with God; then He will inform them of what they used to do.﴾

When God, exalted is He, mentioned that His path is straight, forbade following other ways, mentioned Musa, peace be upon him, and what was revealed to him, mentioned the Qur'an and commanded that it be followed, and mentioned what the disbelievers await from what is destined for them, He moved on to mention those who followed other ways and were thereby separated from the way of God. This was to alert the believers to unity upon the upright religion, and so that they would not differ as the nations before them differed after they had been agreed upon the laws with which their prophets were sent. As for "those who divided their religion," there are six opinions: they are the Harurriyya (Kharijites) or the people of misguidance from this community, or the people of innovations or desires among them, and this is the view of al-Ahwas and Umm Salama; or they are the Jews, or they and the Christians, and this is the view of Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and Qatada; that is, they divided the religion of Ibrahim, the upright (ḥanīf); or they are the polytheists of the Arabs, or the disbelievers and the people of innovations. As for the Christians, they split into Melkites, Jacobites and Nestorians, and they branched into seventy-two sects. The Jews split into Mosaics, Aaronites, Davidians and Samaritans, and they branched into seventy-two sects. This community split into seventy-three sects, all of them in the Fire except the one that follows what the Messenger and his companions were upon. It has also been said that the meaning of "they divided their religion" is that they believed in some parts and disbelieved in others. He attributed the religion to them because it was incumbent upon them to adhere to it, since it is the religion of God which He imposed upon His servants, and so in this sense it is the religion of all people. Ali and the two brothers (al-Akhawan) recited "fāraqū" here and in Surat al-Rum with an alif, and its meaning is close to the reading of the rest of the seven with the shadda, as one says "ḍā'afa" and "ḍa''afa" (both meaning "to multiply"). It has also been said: they abandoned it and cut themselves off from it, and whoever divides his religion, believing in some parts and disbelieving in others, has indeed separated from the religion that was required of him. Ibrahim, al-A'mash and Abu Salih recited "faraqū" with a light (unshadded) rā'.

﴿And they became sects﴾: that is, factions, each one of them following a single person and not going beyond him.

﴿You have nothing to do with them in anything﴾: that is, you are not part of dividing their religion, nor of their punishment, nor of fighting them. Or it is a report about complete separation and total distance, like the saying of al-Nabigha:

"When you try to commit wickedness against the lion, then I am not from you and you are not from me."

There are four possibilities. Ibn Atiyya said: that is, you will not intercede for them, and they have no connection to you. This applies absolutely to the disbelievers, and by way of emphasis to the sinners and to those who are extreme in the law, since they have a share in dividing the religion. When He negated that he had anything to do with them, He confined the return of their affair, whether to destruction or to being set straight, to Him, exalted is He, and informed that He will requite them for their deeds, and that is a severe warning to them. Al-Suddi said: this is a verse in which no command to fight was given, and it is abrogated (naskh) by the command to fight. Ibn Atiyya said: this statement is not well-founded, for the verse is a report, and a report is not subject to abrogation; rather it implicitly contains a command to make peace, so it is likely that one may say that abrogation occurred in that meaning which has been established in other verses. (p-261)

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 6, verse 160:**

﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, for him is ten times its like; and whoever comes with an evil deed, he will not be recompensed except with its like, and they will not be wronged.﴾: Al-Khudri and Ibn Umar narrated that it was revealed concerning the Bedouins (al-a'rab) who believed after the Hijra (the migration to Medina). For them a good deed was multiplied tenfold, and for the Emigrants (al-muhajirin) it was multiplied nine hundredfold. Ibn Atiyya mentioned this and said: "It needs a chain of transmission that removes all excuse." End of quote.

When Allah said that He would inform them of what they had done, He then mentioned the manner of the recompense. Since His words ﴿Indeed, those who divided their religion﴾ [al-An'am: 159] implied both of its groups among those who remained upon their religion, He divided those who receive recompense into "one who comes with a good deed" and "one who comes with an evil deed." The good deed was interpreted as faith, and "ten times its like" as the multiplying of his rewards, meaning the reward of ten like deeds in Paradise. The evil deed was interpreted as disbelief, and "its like" as the Fire. This is narrated from al-Khudri and Ibn Umar.

Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid, al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazza and others said: here "the good deed" is "there is no god but Allah," and "the evil deed" is disbelief. The apparent meaning is that the number is intended.

Al-Maturidi said: the number is not a strict limit, so that it may not be exceeded or reduced. Rather it is for magnifying that reward, since this number carries weight among people; or it is an illustration, like His words ﴿like the breadth of the heaven and the earth﴾ [al-Hadid: 21]. He also said: "Whoever comes [with]" and did not say "whoever does," to show that the consideration is with what a person ends with and dies upon, not with what he did in the way of deeds. It is as if He said: whoever is concluded with a good deed; and likewise the evil deed. End of quote.

The feminine form of ʿashr (عشرُ, "ten") was used, even though it is attached to the plural of mithl (مِثْلٌ, "like"), which is masculine. This is in consideration of the omitted noun it describes, since the singular of that noun is feminine. The estimated sense is: "for him are ten good deeds like them." A parallel in the masculine is "I passed by three nassabat (نَسّاباتٍ, a plural form of a word meaning 'genealogists')," which takes account of the omitted noun, i.e., "three men who are genealogists."

It was also said: ʿashr was made feminine even though it is attached to something whose singular is masculine, because mithl (أمثالٌ, the plural) is attached to a feminine word, namely the pronoun referring to "good deed" (ḥasana). This is like His words ﴿some of the travellers (al-sayyara) will pick him up﴾ [Yusuf: 10]. This was said by Abu Ali [al-Farisi] and others.

It was also said: the good deed and the evil deed are general terms, and this is the apparent meaning. They are not restricted to disbelief and faith. And ﴿and whoever comes with an evil deed﴾ is restricted to the one whom Allah wills and has decreed to be recompensed for it, and for whom He has not decreed forgiveness. That he has ten like deeds does not indicate that more is added, if the understanding of number is strong in its indication, since the ten is the recompense for the good deed, and whatever exceeds it is a bounty from Allah, as He said: ﴿And Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqara: 261].

Al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, Isa ibn Umar, al-A'mash, Ya'qub, and al-Qazzaz from Abd al-Warith read ʿashrun (عشرٌ) with tanwin, and amthaluha (أمثالُها) in the nominative, as a description of ʿashr. Being "like" does not necessarily require that it be of the same kind; it suffices that it be in a shared measure. Eternal bliss and perpetual punishment are not of the same kind as what is given as their likeness, but bliss shares with the good deed the quality of both being good, and punishment shares with the evil deed the quality of both being evil. The apparent meaning of "whoever comes" is generality. It was also said: it is restricted to the Bedouins who embraced Islam, as mentioned in the occasion of revelation. It was said: it is restricted to those who believed among those who divided their religion. It was said: it refers to this community, and this is the least of the multiplication. It was said: the tenfold applies to some deeds and the seventyfold to others.

﴿And they will not be wronged﴾: their reward is not diminished, and their punishment is not increased.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 161:

﴿Say: Indeed, my Lord has guided me to a straight path.﴾ He, exalted is He, commanded him to proclaim the Sharia (the sacred law) and to reject whatever lies outside it. He described it as a straight path with no crookedness in it, and this points to His saying: ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it﴾ [al-An'am: 153]. Since the sects had been mentioned, He commanded him to inform them that he is not among those sects, but is upon the straight path. He attributed the guidance to his Lord to show that He alone is worshipped by him, as if it were said: "My Object of worship has guided me, not your idols." The meaning of ﴿guided me﴾ is that He created guidance in me. Some of the Mu'tazilah (a theological school that emphasized human reason and divine justice) said: "He showed me the way." Al-Maturidi (the eponym of the Maturidi school of theology) said: "This is false, for there is no benefit in singling him out, since all people are like that."

﴿a upright religion﴾, grounded in truth and proof.

﴿the creed of Abraham, a hanif, and he was not of the polytheists﴾. He reminded them that this religion upon which he is, is the creed of Abraham, (p-262) who is the Prophet whom the people of the revealed religions and faiths venerate, and whom the disbelievers of Quraysh claimed they followed. So God, exalted is He, refuted them by His saying: ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾.

The word ﴿dinan﴾ is in the accusative by an implied verb, "He informed me" (ʿarrafanī), because "hadani" indicates it, or by an implied "hadani" itself, or by an implied "follow" and "adhere to" (ittabiʿū wa-ilzamū), or as a verbal noun (maṣdar) of "hadani" in meaning, as if he had said "guidance" (ihtidaʾan), or as a substitute (badal) for "to a path" according to its position, because it is said: "I guided the people to the road." God, exalted is He, said: ﴿and guide you to a straight path﴾ [al-Fath: 2].

The Kufans and Ibn ʿAmir read ﴿qiyaman﴾, and its explanation was discussed at the beginning of Surat al-Nisa'. The rest of the Seven Readers read ﴿qayyiman﴾, on the pattern of ﴿sayyid﴾. The word ﴿millata﴾ is a substitute (badal) for His saying ﴿dinan﴾. The word ﴿hanifan﴾ has been discussed in its grammatical analysis (iʿrab) in His saying ﴿but the creed of Abraham, a hanif﴾ [al-Baqarah: 135] in Surat al-Baqarah. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: ﴿hanifan﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of Abraham.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 162:

﴿Say: Indeed my prayer, my sacrifice (nusuk), my living and my dying are for God, Lord of the worlds.﴾ The apparent meaning is that the prayer is the one that was prescribed for him. It has also been said: the night prayer. It has also been said: the Eid prayer, given its pairing with the sacrifice. It has also been said: nusuk is applied to supplication, humility, and worship in general, and also to the sacrificial animal. As for the verse itself, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, and Ibn Qutayba said: it refers to the sacrificial animals that are slaughtered for God. They combined the two, as in His saying: ﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice﴾ [al-Kawthar: 2]. This is supported by the fact that the verse was revealed in a context already mentioned, and the dispute about it occurs in the surah. Al-Hasan said: it means the religion and the way. It has also been said: pure worship. The meaning of ﴿my living and my dying are for God﴾ is that no one possesses them except God; or, my life is for His obedience and my death is my return to His recompense; or, what I do in my life of righteous deeds and what I die upon of faith is for God. These are three opinions. Abu Abd Allah al-Razi said: the meaning of their being for God is that they are created by God's creation, and this indicates that the servant's obedience is created by God. End of quote. Ibn Atiyya said: God commanded him to declare that his intention in his prayer and his acts of obedience, including sacrifice and other things, and his conduct throughout his life, and his state at his death, of sincerity and faith, is solely for God, the Mighty and Majestic, seeking His face and seeking His pleasure. In the Prophet's (ﷺ) proclamation of this statement there is something that obliges the believers to follow his example, so that they are bound in all their deeds to intend the face of God, the Mighty and Majestic, and His conduct in all of that is as He wills.

Al-Hasan and Abu Haywa read (nusuki) with the sin sukun (unvowelled), and what is narrated from Nafi' regarding the sukun of the first-person ya' in (mahyaya) is a joining of two consonants with sukun, where the pause (waqf) form has been applied to continuous speech (wasl). The better form in Arabic is the fatha. Abu Ali said: it is anomalous in analogy (qiyas), because it combines two sukun-marked letters, and anomalous in usage. Its justification is that it has been heard from the Arabs: "haqqatā al-biṭān" (the two rings of the belly-band met), and "li-fulānin baytā al-māl" (so-and-so has the two houses of wealth). Abu Khalid narrated from Nafi' (mahyaya) with a kasra on the ya'. Ibn Abi Ishaq, Isa, and al-Jahdari read (mahyayya) according to the dialect of Hudhayl, like the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"They outran my desire (hawayya)."

Isa ibn Umar read (salati wa nusuki wa mahyaya wa mamati) with a fatha on the ya', and it is narrated from Asim the sukun of the first-person ya'.

The apparent meaning is the negation of every partner, so it is general over every partner. Restricting it to what is said, that He has no partner in the world, or no partner in the acts of worship by which I draw near to Him, or no partner in creation and governance, or no partner in whatever acts He wills, is less appropriate. It is better taken as an illustrative example and not as a literal restriction. The reference of "that" (*dhalika*) is to what comes after the two commands, ﴿Say: Indeed, my Lord has guided me﴾ [al-An'am: 161] and ﴿Say: Indeed, my prayer﴾ [al-An'am: 162] and what follows them, or to His saying ﴿He has no partner﴾ alone. There are three opinions, the first of which is the most apparent. The definite article in "al-Muslimin" (the Muslims) is the *al-'ahd* (the article of specific reference), and it refers to this community (*umma*). This is because the Islam of every prophet precedes the Islam of his community, since they take his law from him. This was said by Qatadah. It was also said: "From among the Arabs." It was said: "From among the people of Makkah." Al-Kalbi said: "The first of them in this time." It was said: "The first of them in excellence, rank and precedence on the Day of Resurrection." It was said: "Since I was a prophet, I was a Muslim. I was a prophet while Adam was between water and clay." Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: "Its meaning is 'among the Muslims' in submission to God's decree and destiny, since it is known that he is not the first of every Muslim." End of quotation. In this there is a nullification of the word "first" (*awwal*), and words should not be nullified (p. 263). The best of these opinions is the first opinion.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 164:

﴿Say: "Shall I seek a lord other than Allah, when He is the Lord of all things?"﴾ Al-Naqqash (d. 351 AH) related that it was narrated: the disbelievers said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Return, O Muhammad, to our religion, worship our gods and leave what you are upon, and we will guarantee for you everything you want in your worldly life and your Hereafter." So this verse was revealed. The hamza here is interrogative, and its meaning is denial and reproach. It is a response to them when they invited him to their gods. The meaning is: how could it be that I call upon other than Allah as lord, when other than Him is a thing that is lorded over (marbub)?

﴿And every soul earns only against itself﴾ That is: every soul does not earn anything whose consequence falls upon anyone other than itself.

﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ That is: no sinful soul bears the sin of another soul. The meaning is that it is not held to account for other than its own burden. This is an emphasis of the sentence before it, and it is a reply to their saying, "Follow our way, and we will bear your sins" (Q. 29:12).

﴿Then to your Lord is your return, and He will inform you of that about which you used to differ﴾ That is: your return to Him is on the Day of Resurrection. "Tanbi'ah" (informing) is an expression for recompense. What they differed about concerns the religions and creeds, and He will recompense you for what they entailed of reward and punishment. The context of these sentences is that of a report, but the meaning is one of warning and threat. It has also been said: "about which you used to differ" refers to the matter of me, from the statements of some of you that he is a poet and a sorcerer, the statements of some of you that he forged it, and some of you that he had it written down, and the like.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 6, verse 165:

﴿It is He who made you successors on the earth, and raised some of you above others in rank, that He may try you through what He has given you.﴾

He, exalted is He, reminds them of His blessing upon them, since the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent, and he, Muhammad (ﷺ), is the Seal of the Prophets. So his community (ummah) succeeded all the other nations, and no nation will come after them to succeed them, since the Hour will be established upon them. Al-Hasan said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "You will complete seventy nations, you are the best of them and the most honoured of them before Allah." It is also narrated: "You are the last of them and the most honoured of them before Allah." The raising of ranks means elevation in worldly positions, knowledge and abundance of provision. The phrase "that He may try you" is connected to His saying "and raised." In what He has given you of that, (He tries you with) status, wealth and knowledge, and how you will conduct yourselves in that. It was said: the address is to the children of Adam, who were made successors on the earth after the jinn or after the angels. It was also said: some of them succeed others. And it was said: "successors of the earth" means that you possess it and dispose of it.

﴿Indeed your Lord is swift in punishment, and indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ Since trial reveals the evildoer and the good-doer, the obedient and the disobedient, He mentioned these two attributes and concluded with them. Since the prevailing character of the verse-endings before it is warning, he began with His saying "swift in punishment," meaning for whoever disbelieves in what Allah the Exalted has given him. The swiftness of His punishment, if it is in this world, the swiftness is evident; and if it is in the Hereafter, He is described as swift because its occurrence is certain, since everything that is coming is coming. Since the aspect of mercy is more hoped-for, he emphasized that by the entry of the lam into the predicate, and the two attributes are formed in the intensive pattern. And in the aspect of punishment he did not use its attribute; thus he did not say "Indeed your Lord is punishing," and "swift in punishment" is not of the category of the attribute-like adjective (al-sifah al-mushabbahah).
